papers.abstract: Language models typically increase per-token computation through deeper or looped layers and latent reasoning steps, while richer residual connections improve information flow across layers. We instead increase computational capacity: the number of active computational states a model maintains. We introduce the Lattice of Latents, a set of per-layer horizontal latent streams that run recurrently along time, alongside the vertical residual stream that flows through depth. Like hyper-connections, mHC, and attention or value residuals, the Lattice enhances the residual stream, but rather than adding or rerouting residual pathways through depth, it provides companion computational states that persist across tokens. Unlike hybrid Transformer-SSM architectures, whose recurrent states primarily serve as internal memory for sequence mixing, these latents directly condition the vertical stream's attention, KV-cache writes, MLP computation, and decoding. On Transformers trained on 20B FineWeb-Edu tokens, a 406M-parameter Lattice model lowers validation perplexity from 15.41 to 14.40 over a parameter-matched Transformer. These gains extend across architectural variants. The Lattice composes with prior residual-stream enhancements: with hyper-connections and input residuals, it lowers validation perplexity from 15.41 (base Transformer) and 14.22 (Transformer with the same enhancements) to 13.61. On Gated DeltaNet, Mamba-2, Triadic GDN, and GDN-Mamba-2 hybrids, it improves perplexity at every tested native state size, with Lattice-GDN and Lattice-Triadic-GDN variants outperforming pure baselines with 4x larger native states. These results identify persistent per-layer state as a complementary axis for scaling language-model computation.
authors: Shivam Duggal, Zongze Wu, William T. Freeman, Antonio Torralba, Richard Zhang, Eli Shechtman
bullets: Introduces horizontal latent streams that persist across tokens while complementing the vertical depth-wise residual stream.
The latent states condition attention, KV-cache writes, MLP computation, and decoding—not merely sequence mixing.
A 406M-parameter Lattice model reduces validation perplexity from 15.41 to 14.40 versus a parameter-matched Transformer.
Combining the Lattice with other residual enhancements further lowers perplexity to 13.61.
Improvements also hold across several recurrent and hybrid architectures, including variants outperforming baselines with 4× larger native states.

Figure 9: Ablating top-to-bottom residual-stream flow. Feeding each token’s top-layer state back into the bottom of the network at the next token adds a nonlinear path through the residual stream. Jacobi on vertical applies this feedback to the vertical residual stream, analogous to the concurrent Full-Bandwidth Transformer (Wang et al., 2026); Jacobi on Lattice applies it to the horizontal latents; the last bar applies both. We call it “Jacobi” because the feedback is trained and evaluated with three parallel, teacher-forced Jacobi sweeps (J3; App. A.2.3), at the cost of extra forward passes. Both forms of feedback help, and they compound: 16.94 (Transformer) and 15.52 (single-pass Lattice) fall to 14.92 with feedback on both. FineWeb-Edu val perplexity, trained on 10B tokens.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes a novel LLM architecture axis (per-layer persistent latent streams) with broad architectural relevance.
papers.title: Latent Lattice Language Models
papers.tldr: Lattice of Latents improves language-model perplexity by adding persistent per-layer recurrent latent states that directly support computation alongside the standard residual stream.

papers.abstract: We study how to learn an autoregressive next-token generator $f\colon\Sigma^\star\to\Sigma$ from a class $\mathcal{F}$, given chain-of-thought (CoT) demonstrations of length $T$ generated by $f$. We present a simple algorithm based on bagging, which outputs a majority vote of generators that are trained to be CoT-consistent on bootstrap samples of the training data. For binary token sets, it achieves the optimal sample complexity of $O((d_{\mathrm{VC}}+\log(1/\delta))/\epsilon)$, independent of the CoT length $T$, where $d_{\mathrm{VC}}$ is the VC dimension of $\mathcal{F}$. For finite token sets $\Sigma$, the VC dimension is replaced by a multiclass analogue, the Graph dimension $d_{\mathrm{G}}$, and the sample complexity is optimal up to a $\log|\Sigma|$ factor. The number of generators in the majority-vote ensemble is $O(\log(T/\delta))$, and we show that the ensemble can be distilled into a single generator in $\mathcal{F}$ at the expense of $n\log(nT)$ unlabeled prompts.
authors: Awni Altabaa, John Lafferty, Omar Montasser
bullets: Learns next-token generators from chain-of-thought demonstrations using bootstrap sampling and majority voting.
For binary tokens, achieves optimal sample complexity O((d_VC + log(1/δ))/ε), independent of demonstration length T.
For finite token sets, obtains a near-optimal bound using the Graph dimension, with only a log|Σ| factor gap.
Uses O(log(T/δ)) generators in the ensemble.
The ensemble can be distilled into a single generator using n log(nT) unlabeled prompts.

figures.caption: Table 1: Sample complexity of realizable learning with chain-of-thought supervision. Here d, dG, dL, and dDS are the VC, Graph, Littlestone, and DS dimensions of F , and d⋆ is its dual VC dimension. papers.selection_reason: Theoretical analysis of learning autoregressive next-token generators from CoT demonstrations; relevant to LLM reasoning.
papers.title: Optimal Autoregressive Chain-of-Thought Learning via Bagging
papers.tldr: Bagging enables optimal, CoT-length-independent learning of autoregressive generators, with compact ensembles that can also be distilled into one generator.

papers.abstract: A useful memory need not resemble the question it helps answer. Jetriever ranks each stored memory by Jev's decision score for its usefulness to the current question, replacing similarity search with full-pool utility scoring. On InMind's 125 indirect-query tasks, it places the gold exchange first in 84.8% of cases; matched BM25 and MiniLM controls reach 1.6% and 0.0% when indexing user turns. A 20-question comparison separates finding evidence from ranking it: Jev and Qwen3.5 9B each find 90% of gold exchanges by rank 50, while Laya finds 30%; at rank one, Jev reaches 85% and Qwen3.5 9B 40%. On a dimension-proportional random sample of 60 MemoryAgentBench questions, Jetriever's four-dimension score is 55.4%, against 44.3% for ReFind on the same questions. Jev retrieval costs USD 0.00834 per InMind question and USD 0.03103 per MAB question on average. These results show the value of world knowledge, scores that rank decisive memories first, and affordable full-pool scoring.
authors: Ruizhe Li, Licheng Zhang, Mingxuan Du, Zhendong Mao
bullets: Addresses cases where the most useful memory does not resemble the query.
Uses Jev’s decision score to rank every stored memory by usefulness to the current question.
On InMind, it ranks the gold exchange first in 84.8% of cases, versus 1.6% for BM25 and 0.0% for MiniLM controls.
Jev finds 90% of gold exchanges within the top 50 and ranks 85% first in a 20-question comparison.

papers.abstract: Constrained Markov decision processes (CMDPs) typically bound expected cumulative cost from an initial state. Such a guarantee can be insufficient when a policy must remain feasible after every history it may encounter. We introduce \emph{subprocess-constrained MDPs} (S-CMDPs), which require the expected discounted cost of each continuation, conditional on any reachable history, to satisfy a bound determined by the current state. This stronger requirement changes the structure and complexity of the problem: we show that stationary policies can be strictly suboptimal, and finding even an approximately optimal stationary policy is NP-hard. We adapt a recently introduced value-set iteration framework to show that history-dependent policies surprisingly overcome both obstacles. Our polynomial-time algorithm represents such a policy implicitly: its expected reward is within $\epsilon$ of the optimal feasible value, it violates each subprocess cost bound by at most $\delta$, and its action distribution can be computed in polynomial time for any given history.
bullets: Standard CMDP guarantees from the initial state may not ensure feasibility throughout execution.
S-CMDPs constrain the expected discounted cost of every continuation based on the current state.
Stationary policies can be strictly suboptimal, and finding an approximately optimal stationary policy is NP-hard.
A value-set iteration framework constructs an implicitly represented history-dependent policy.
The algorithm achieves ε-near-optimal reward with at most δ violation of each subprocess constraint, while computing actions in polynomial time per history.

papers.abstract: Grading student responses is costly and time-consuming. Moreover, human annotators are prone to bias, fatigue, and rater drift, which further limits grading reliability. Various methods have been employed to develop automated essay scoring (AES) systems to reduce these costs and address bias-related issues. These methods range from early text-feature-based systems to current machine-learning and transformer-based models. Specifically, large language models (LLMs) offer the potential to streamline the development of AES systems. However, they are subject to well-known limitations, such as hallucinations and prompt sensitivity. This creates a need to explore the potential of a mixed-methods approach that leverages the synergies among individual LLMs through ensemble formation. We evaluate the potential of ensembles of LLMs to match human-rater agreement when grading student responses in economics and medical education across 103 criteria. We use 631 German-language responses and corresponding human ratings by 2 to 5 annotators from a previously conducted assessment. We experiment with 523 rubric-based prompt configurations across 15 open-weight LLMs and assess their consistency with human raters using Krippendorff's alpha for inter-annotator agreement (IAA) and the Alternative Annotator Test (alt-test). Our results show that replacing one human rater with the best-performing LLM--prompt configuration maintains or improves IAA for 91 of the 103 criteria and that LLMs pass the alt-test for 90 criteria. Our findings suggest that current state-of-the-art LLMs can support AES of German responses in economics and medical education, reducing human workload and enabling faster processing, while validation against human ratings remains necessary.
authors: Daniel Baumartz, Alexander Mehler, Patrick Schrottenbacher, Leon Hammerla, Sebastian Gombert
bullets: Addresses the cost, bias, fatigue, and rater-drift challenges of human grading.

papers.abstract: A harness turns a model into a system that completes tasks: it builds the prompt, exposes tools and decides when work is done. Harness comparisons hold the model fixed. Model comparisons hold the harness fixed. We vary both: five shipped harnesses, 18 artifact-producing tasks, four locally deployable open-weight models from 0.75B to 4.7B and a 35.5B anchor, with one deterministic checker scoring all 360 ladder cells. The completion-controlling harness, Mingbird, has the highest mean at every size. Of four pre-registered paired contrasts, two survive Holm correction, at 0.75B and 4.7B. Thirteen of sixteen paired intervals exclude zero under the deployment reading, with leads from 0.075 over the strongest rival to 0.819 over the weakest. The completion gate is not the carrier: disabling all six executable checks moves the mean by +0.080, +0.117, +0.003 and -0.004, every interval including zero, and only at 1.9B does disabling it create empty runs. Removing one repeat-blocking rule alone costs 0.411 at 0.75B and leaves eight of eighteen tasks with no artifact. The harness effect is a progress effect: it decides whether a run leaves anything on disk. Of 357 usable cells, 127 leave none of their declared artifacts and 85 of those exit normally, so a scorer that reads exit status credits work that was never written. Whether the effect grows or shrinks with size, four rungs cannot settle: a floor arm produces a rise, a ceiling a decline, and a cross-family rung a peak.
bullets: The study compares five shipped harnesses across 18 tasks, four 0.75B–4.7B local models, and a 35.5B anchor using one deterministic checker.
Mingbird achieves the highest mean score at every tested model size, though only two of four pre-registered contrasts remain significant after Holm correction.
Harness effects mainly reflect whether runs leave artifacts on disk: 127 of 357 usable cells produced none, including 85 that exited normally.
Disabling executable completion checks has little consistent effect, while removing one repeat-blocking rule sharply reduces performance at 0.75B and causes artifact-free tasks.
Four model-size rungs are insufficient to determine whether harness effects systematically grow or shrink with scale.

An open marker means it includes zero, and a marker is drawn in red when its interval crosses zero and in the arm’s color otherwise. Under the deployment reading every point estimate lies to the right of the dashed line at zero, and under the rescored reading all but one do. The intervals are tightest at 4.7B, where the two arms separate on nearly every task, and the verdicts that change between readings sit at 3.7B, where 36 of the 58 rescored cells are.

Removing the arm whose floor is a reply contract (b) leaves a spread that shows no trend at all. The pre-specified gap to goose (c) is non-monotone, and the gap to the best baseline (d) falls from 0.461 to 0.071 because the strongest competitor changes from goose to pi. The two readings differ mainly at 3.7B, where most of the rescored cells sit.

Figure 4: Where each arm’s cells end, as a share of the usable cells it has. The orange segment is the quiet stop: a run that exits normally and leaves none of its declared artifacts. It is 4 of 70 cells for Mingbird and 34 of 72 for mini-swe-agent, with pi at 10 of 72, goose at 15 of 71 and OpenCode at 22 of 72. The figure reads the same counts as Table 8.

Figure 5: The precision ladder under its two readings. Markers are level means of the paired gap and bars are 95% task-bootstrap intervals. The filled series uses all eighteen tasks. The lighter dashed series drops the tasks both arms solve at that level, which is the contrast the slope is fitted to, so the second series is the one the test reads. Under the deployment reading (a) the gap is largest at 4.85 bits and collapses as precision falls, because compression costs both arms the ability to finish. Under the rescored reading (b) the two high-precision levels move toward zero, because the cells pi lost there had produced work that the rescoring credits.

Table 1: The model ladder. Parameter counts, quantization, and file sizes are read from the served artifacts (ollama show, ollama list) rather than from model names. File sizes are the served artifacts’ byte counts in decimal gigabytes, which is the basis the server’s own listing uses. A binary unit tool reports the same files about 7 percent smaller. Architecture is the served GGUF architecture, and the two architectures differ: qwen35 and granite are dense decoders, and the 35.5B model is a mixture of experts that routes each token to eight of its 256 experts (the served artifact’s expert_used_count), which is where its active-parameter figure comes from. All models run on one Ollama 0.40.6 server at a 32K context. The Qwen3.5 rows form a within-family ladder and the 3.7B Granite row is a cross-family anchor. The 35.5B anchor is analyzed separately. papers.title: Harness Leverage Across Model Size: A Ladder of Five Local Agent Harnesses from 0.75B to 4.7B

papers.abstract: Large language models often produce hallucinated answers, motivating selective prediction policies that abstain on uncertain queries. However, heuristic uncertainty thresholds alone do not provide statistical control of errors among accepted predictions. Linear Expectation Constraints (LEC) reduce selection-conditioned error rate (SCER) calibration to a nonpositive expected linear-loss constraint, but the associated loss is non-monotonic in the acceptance threshold. We construct an exact counterexample under i.i.d. sampling demonstrating that LEC's empirical threshold-selection rule can violate the population SCER target. To address this risk-transfer gap, we introduce Stability-Compensated Linear Expectation Control (SC-LEC), which uses the negative linear risk of a theoretical full-data reference to compensate for threshold-selection instability. For local expansion beyond a safe anchor, we derive two finite-sample certificates: a stability-based certificate exploiting rank crossings and a direct certificate using the structure of threshold expansion to reduce conservatism. With a valid population anchor margin, our certificate conditions ensure finite-sample marginal SCER control, and independent margin certification further provides a $1-\delta$ high-probability guarantee for this calibration-averaged control. Experiments on CommonsenseQA, ARC-Challenge, and TriviaQA show useful retention gains beyond the same certified anchor, while revealing conservative behavior in small-margin regimes.
authors: Zhiyuan Wang, Yuanchang Ye, Jiahao Yuan, Jinhao Duan, Xiaoshuang Shi, Weijun Xie, Ye Wei, Kaidi Xu
bullets: LEC can fail to control population selection-conditioned error because its threshold-dependent loss is non-monotonic and threshold selection is unstable.
SC-LEC compensates for this risk-transfer gap using the negative linear risk of a theoretical full-data reference.
Two finite-sample certificates support threshold expansion: one based on rank crossings and another exploiting threshold-expansion structure.
Given a valid population anchor margin, the certificates ensure marginal SCER control; independent margin certification yields a $1-\delta$ high-probability guarantee.
Experiments on CommonsenseQA, ARC-Challenge, and TriviaQA show retention gains beyond the certified anchor, but conservative behavior when margins are small.

papers.title: Stability-Compensated Threshold Calibration for Selection-Conditioned Risk Control in Large Language Models

papers.abstract: Benchmark contamination is not new, but recent model releases show it in a sharper form. We use the term benchleaking for the case in which a benchmark's own test examples enter training data, so that a score reflects recall rather than capability. This differs from benchmaxxing, which optimizes toward a benchmark without seeing its test set. We document two escalations over the past month. First, in post-training, the traces have become explicit: recent audits show an agent stating hidden test requirements it was never given in 23% of its attempts, where its predecessor did so in none, and continuing to follow them after the task is changed to contradict them (Schaeffer and R\"auker, 2026; Lo and Lo, 2026). Second, the problem has reached pre-training. Using few-shot continuation on 20 benchmarks across four public base models, we find that some base models write out other test examples---complete questions, options, and answers---that appear nowhere in their input. For the recently released ERNIE-5.5-Flash-Base, 96% of HumanEval problems leak with their reference implementations and 85% of OpenBookQA questions leak with their answers, against 9% and none for DeepSeek-V4-Flash-Base. To quantify what a reported score owes to such examples, we define an Anti-Hack score: the benchmark score recomputed with every leaked example marked wrong and the number of examples unchanged. Averaged over the suite, it costs DeepSeek-V4-Flash-Base 1.5 points and Hy3-preview-Base 1.3, against 5.0 for MiMo-V2.5-Base and 16.6 for ERNIE-5.5-Flash-Base. Open base models are the foundation of much downstream research, so benchleaking now affects more than leaderboard rankings. We call for decontamination reports and contamination-adjusted scores to become standard practice.
authors: Yiwei Qin, Muhang Xie, Xuefeng Li, Mohan Jiang, Dayuan Fu, Tiantian Mi, Qipeng Guo, Pengfei Liu
bullets: Benchleaking means benchmark test examples enter training data, causing scores to reflect recall rather than capability; it differs from benchmark-directed optimization without test-set access (“benchmaxxing”).
Recent audits found explicit hidden-test traces in 23% of attempts by one agent, compared with none for its predecessor, including persistence when task requirements changed.
Few-shot continuation tests across 20 benchmarks and four public base models found some models generating complete unseen test questions, options, and answers.
Leakage varied sharply: ERNIE-5.5-Flash-Base leaked 96% of HumanEval problems and 85% of OpenBookQA questions, while DeepSeek-V4-Flash-Base leaked 9% and none, respectively.
The proposed Anti-Hack score removes leaked examples from evaluation; average score penalties ranged from 1.3–1.5 points for some models to 16.6 for ERNIE-5.5-Flash-Base.

papers.selection_reason: This paper discusses 'benchleaking' (benchmark contamination) in LLMs, specifically analyzing how base models (e.g., DeepSeek, ERNIE) have learned test data during pre-training. It fits the 'Language Foundation Models' topic by addressing evaluation and training data integrity for LLMs.
papers.title: Benchleaking Is Accelerating: Benchmark contamination has worsened sharply in the past month -- from post-training down to pre-training base models
papers.tldr: Benchmark contamination (“benchleaking”) has recently intensified from post-training systems to base models, inflating benchmark scores through memorized test examples.

papers.abstract: Text-based model collaboration requires a large model to generate intermediate responses before a smaller model can use its guidance, adding large-model decoding cost to inference. We introduce POND (Prefill-Only, No-Decode), a method that uses a frozen large sender for prefill and a small receiver for all autoregressive decoding. A trainable bridge maps the sender's hidden states to additional attention keys and values, allowing the receiver to use these representations throughout generation. POND also supports periodic review, in which the sender processes the receiver's partial response and updates its guidance through additional prefill passes while preserving the receiver's existing KV cache. Across reasoning and coding benchmarks, POND improves receiver performance with senders from different model families. In particular, GLM-5.3 provides gains comparable to those of Qwen3.8-Max when paired with a Qwen receiver, supporting the effectiveness of representation transfer between independently trained model families. POND further demonstrates its ability to generalize across domains. When trained on math and coding tasks, it transfers directly to general knowledge tasks without additional domain-specific training. These results demonstrate that large frontier model prefill representations can improve small-model generation without requiring large-model autoregressive decoding.
authors: Qichao Wang, Tingyu Qu, Pengcheng Wu, Yiran Zhong, Feida Zhu, Zhiqi Shen, Peilin Zhao, Steven Hoi
bullets: Addresses the inference overhead of generating textual guidance with a large model before small-model generation.
Uses a trainable bridge to convert frozen sender hidden states into attention keys and values for the receiver.
Supports periodic review, where the sender updates guidance from the receiver’s partial output while preserving the receiver’s KV cache.
Improves reasoning and coding performance across independently trained model families, with gains comparable to a stronger sender pairing.
Transfers from math and coding training to general-knowledge tasks without domain-specific retraining.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of POND. A frozen sender prefills the input, and a trainable bridge compresses its last layer hidden states into a shared latent message, which layer-specific adapters project into KV entries for the receiver. The receiver, fine-tuned jointly with the bridge, generates the full response. At review boundaries, the sender prefills the newly generated segment and the resulting entries are appended to the latent memory, leaving the receiver’s KV cache untouched.

Figure 2: Accuracy gains and sender compute savings. Left: Math and code scores for the receiver (Qwen3.5-4B), the receiver with POND, and the sender (GLM-5.3); labels give the gain in points. Center: Estimated sender FLOPs for GLM-5.3 (40B active) with 1k input and 10k output tokens. Prefill-only guidance reduces sender compute from 880 to 80 TFLOPs. Right: Fraction of sender compute saved, T/(L + T ), as a function of output length T with L = 1k. Estimates use 2Pactive FLOPs per token and exclude attention, routing, communication, and bridge or receiver inference. The panels are not a matched end-to-end comparison of accuracy and cost.

Table 1: Math and code results. Senders are frozen and prefill-only. POND uses one latent transfer; +Review adds periodic prefill updates. Acc.: accuracy/pass@1 (%, higher is better); Token: total decoded receiver tokens, including both thinking and final-response tokens (thousands per 100 runs, lower is better); Speed: end-to-end latency (s/run, lower is better). Bold marks the better of POND and +Review for each metric, including ties. Improve compares the bold value with the receiver alone: accuracy gain in percentage points, or relative reduction in tokens/latency; an upward latency arrow indicates an increase. Avg averages the five tasks.

Table 2: Knowledge benchmark results. Configurations, metrics, and metric-wise bolding follow Table 1. Improve reports accuracy gains (percentage points) or relative token/latency reductions (%) against the receiver; upward latency arrows denote increases. Avg averages all four tasks. Differences and reductions are computed before rounding.
Table 3: Training and review controls. Suite-average accuracy. Receiver-only training uses math/code data; POND uses Qwen3.8-Max as the sender.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes POND, a 'prefill-only, no-decode' method using a latent bridge to transfer representations from large to small models, improving efficiency and model collaboration.
papers.title: Latent Bridge: Asking for Help Without Words
papers.tldr: POND lets a small model benefit from a large model’s hidden representations without paying the cost of large-model autoregressive decoding.

papers.abstract: Large language models read Thai through subword tokens, without a word segmenter. Yet Thai treebanks, speech metrics and morphological resources are built on words, often at several granularities, and word boundaries resolve ambiguities that subword tokens leave open. LATTE (Lattice ATTentive Encoding) reads a text at several granularities at once, through a lattice of dictionary words, but it is a large GPU model. We distil it into LATTE-WordSeg-Lite, a CPU segmenter of 1.17M parameters that keeps the lattice as features. It outputs compounds, words and morphemes in one pass, and learns only from annotated data and text whose licences allow commercial use. To compare it with other tools, published Thai scores do not suffice, as they come from different files, splits and scorers. We therefore rebuild seven test sets from pinned sources and score twelve systems under one protocol. With the unit that fits each test set, LATTE-WordSeg-Lite scores above DeepCut on five sets, four of them from corpora that its teachers learnt from. Called line by line on one CPU thread, it runs 23 times as fast as DeepCut. We release the model, the benchmark scripts and all predictions.
authors: Thodsaporn Chay-intr, Kobkrit Viriyayudhakorn, Thanaruk Theeramunkong
bullets: Addresses Thai’s need for word- and morpheme-level boundaries beyond subword tokenization.
Distils the lattice-based LATTE approach into a 1.17M-parameter CPU model.
Produces compound, word, and morpheme segmentations in one pass.
Rebuilds seven test sets and evaluates 12 systems under a common scoring protocol.
Outscores DeepCut on five test sets and releases the model, scripts, and predictions.

papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are rapidly advancing mathematical discovery, moving beyond benchmark-level problem solving to tackle frontier research problems. This progress is ushering mathematics into an era of proof abundance, raising a fundamental challenge: how can we ensure the correctness of the ever-growing volume of AI-generated proofs and transform them into trustworthy, machine-verified mathematical knowledge? We introduce Turing Agent, an agent harness designed to orchestrate end-to-end formal verification of research-level mathematics. Its wo-scale architecture integrates theorem formalization and proof formalization agents, empowered by structured proof decomposition, parallel verification, accumulated proof experience, and selective semantic review. Leveraging our collaborations with theoretical computer science (TCS) researchers, we focus our evaluation on TCS, a particularly demanding domain characterized by intricate quantification, complex dependencies, and stringent semantic requirements. Against direct generation and general-purpose coding harnesses, including Codex CLI and Claude Code, Turing Agent achieves approximately 57-62% faithful formalization success on Formal TCS Bench and 83% overall pass@1 on a TCS-focused subset of RLMEval, using GLM-5.3 and DeepSeek-V4-Pro. Notably, Turing Agent, built on DeepSeek, successfully completes the formal verification of three previously unresolved TCS tasks from OpenAI's October 2026 collection. One particularly challenging TCS problem required about a hundred formally verified auxiliary claims. Moreover, by actively exploring and refining the formalization process, Turing Agent can uncover simpler alternative proofs, expose unnecessary dependencies in original proofs, and generate reusable mathematical knowledge as a byproduct of verification.
authors: Yang Chen, Qianyi Wang, Ronghui Yang, Zhanhao Li, Yu Cong, Chen Zhang, Hangfan Zhang, Shao Zhang, Shuai Li, Toru Takisaka, Chao Xu, Yi Zhou, Zhihao Tang, Xiao Wang, Bo Zhang, Shuyue Hu
bullets: Addresses the challenge of ensuring correctness as AI-generated mathematical proofs become more abundant.
Uses separate theorem- and proof-formalization agents, accumulated proof experience, parallel verification, and selective semantic review.
Evaluated on demanding theoretical computer science tasks involving complex quantification and dependencies.
Reports approximately 57–62% faithful formalization success on Formal TCS Bench and 83% pass@1 on a TCS-focused RLMEval subset.
Completed formal verification of three previously unresolved TCS tasks and produced simpler proofs, reduced dependencies, and reusable formal knowledge.

RLMEval results are shown separately for PFR and TLB and combined as Total. PFR covers additive combinatorics and entropy methods from the Polynomial Freiman–Ruzsa project, with applications to linearity testing in TCS. TLB (Testing Lower Bounds) covers information-theoretic lower bounds for statistical hypothesis testing.

Figure 2 | Turing Agent coordinates theorem formalization (TF) and proof formalization (PF) agents. TF agents provide checked Lean statements and definitions, while PF agents construct proofs and request semantic review when needed. The resulting proof undergoes final verification. In its runtime, Turing Agent coordinates recursive DAG construction, parallel proof formalization, and selective semantic review. Experience from successful and failed attempts is extracted and reused, while checked branch proofs are assembled for final verification.

Figure 3 | Research-level TCS verification beyond standard benchmarks. Of the 121 TCS problems in OpenAI’s mathematical research collection, 22 had not been fully verified in Lean. Among these, we highlight three examples formally verified by Turing Agent using DeepSeek-V4-Pro and DeepSeekV4.1-Flash.

Figure 1 | Three challenges in automated formal verification. The formal statement must preserve the original claim (faithfulness), the code must pass Lean’s syntax and type checks (validity), and the proof must discharge all obligations without gaps (completeness). Our Turing Agent is designed to satisfy these requirements throughout the formalization process.

papers.abstract: Automated essay scorers (AES) based on large language models (LLMs) promise human-level accuracy. However, training, fine-tuning, and evaluating LLMs for specific assessment tasks is costly. In particular, the question arises whether these AES should be trained for specific domains or whether models based on generic LLMs might be sufficient. Human annotations, by contrast, are often more valid but far more expensive. This study evaluates whether ensembles of AES systems based on general-purpose LLMs can approximate human ratings of medical-education writing tasks by leveraging encoded linguistic and conceptual knowledge. The goal is to assess whether general-purpose models are applicable for assisting or potentially replacing human annotation in this domain. We experiment with 11 AES systems and 8 different LLMs and evaluate 668 student responses to 12 tasks, using \numprint{2076} evaluations by 7 human annotators. These ratings are aggregated to create consistent performance levels that can be used as target classes for classifiers trained on AES outputs. Our results show that learner classes based on human ratings can be accurately reconstructed using a linear SVM trained on a small set of AES features. A single classifier generalized well across tasks and domains, with reasoning and content features being most predictive. This suggests that out-of-the-box LLMs, even without domain-specific fine-tuning, can support automatic essay grading in medical education. While individual AES systems are insufficient alone, their combination approximates human evaluators, pointing to a reduced need for manual scoring or its supplementation with automated methods.
authors: Daniel Baumartz, Alexander Mehler, Mevl\"ut Bagci, Maxim Konca

papers.abstract: Training coding agents for long-horizon tasks requires environments with verifiable feedback. Existing pipelines often follow a linear process that ends with validation, establishing usability but providing little guidance on improving training value. Recursive self-improvement (RSI) often requires model rollouts or model training followed by downstream evaluation, with costs and feedback delays amplified on long-horizon tasks. How can we use timely, reliable proxy signals to improve training value and synthesize environments at scale? We present RepoFactory, an automated pipeline that converts real repositories into verifiable environments where agents build complete projects from scratch given a language specification. Its Environment Evolution Loop optimizes a multiplicative objective combining validity, structural coupling, and implementation scope through proxy feedback. RepoFactory produces 10,159 environments across 17 software domains. Training Qwen3.5-35B-A3B on these environments yields RepoHorizen-35B-A3B, which achieves gains of 22.6 percentage points on NL2Repo-Bench and 8.5 points on average across five benchmarks covering long-horizon coding and agentic tasks in real-world production settings, compared with 17.5 and 6.4 points without environment evolution. These results highlight the training value of RepoFactory environments and the additional gains from the Environment Evolution Loop.
authors: Yang Tian, Tianyu Zheng, Xiyuan Yang, Yaxin Du, Chengran Yang, Bo Zhao, Jian Yang, Bryan Dai

papers.abstract: Expressive Neural Architecture Search (NAS) search spaces are desirable as they do not restrict the space of potential architectures to what is already established. However, few search spaces are expressive enough to represent a broad range of architecture families, and those that are have focused primarily on image classification problems. The task of autoregressive sequence modelling has become ubiquitous in modern machine learning, but no existing search space supports the construction of and search over sequence models from fundamental operations, instead imposing strong inductive biases on the structure of potential architectures. This work describes how the expressive einspace search space can be extended to yield a search space capable of representing autoregressive models using fundamental operations. We perform a series of experiments showing that the novel einspaceAR search space can find capable autoregressive sequence models from scratch--i.e., without imposing strong inductive biases. We believe that our einspaceAR search space will be a useful part of the NAS toolbox and that the techniques described in this work can serve as a blueprint for the integration of autoregressive modelling in other expressive search spaces.
authors: Thomas Woehrle, Linus Ericsson, Henry Gouk, Elliot J. Crowley
bullets: Existing expressive NAS spaces rarely support autoregressive sequence modeling and typically impose strong structural biases.
The proposed einspaceAR search space represents and constructs autoregressive models from fundamental operations.
Experiments show that einspaceAR can discover capable autoregressive sequence models from scratch.
The approach is presented as a reusable blueprint for adding autoregressive modeling to other expressive search spaces.

papers.abstract: Recent self-improving coding agents have achieved strong benchmark performance by iteratively modifying their own executable implementations. A common pattern uses downstream task-derived evidence to decide which candidates or lineages continue evolving, which we term evaluate-and-select. Obtaining this signal requires repeatedly executing evolved agents on downstream tasks, so broader exploration incurs increasing evaluation cost, while repeated optimization against a fixed evaluation distribution may encourage benchmark-specific adaptation. We ask: can coding agents self-improve without downstream task evaluation inside the evolution loop? We introduce Explore-then-Integrate (ELITE), which integrates implementation mechanisms rather than selecting a single exploratory child to continue the lineage. At each generation, ELITE proposes diverse focused improvements, implements them independently from the same parent, and inspects the resulting programs to identify complementary, redundant, and conflicting mechanisms before reimplementing a compatible subset as one coherent descendant. No downstream task outcomes or task-solving trajectories of evolved candidates are used to guide evolution; only deterministic checks of structural and operational validity are used inside the loop. On SWE-bench Pro, ELITE improves the initial agent from 60.0% to 85.6%, compared with 86.7% for the Darwin Godel Machine (DGM) and 88.3% for the Huxley-Godel Machine (HGM), while using zero candidate task evaluations and reducing observed wall-clock evolution time by 8.8x and 3.2x, respectively, under the evaluated configurations. In cross-benchmark transfer without further adaptation, ELITE averages 73.3% on SWE-bench Verified and 69.3% on Polyglot. Together, these results demonstrate the feasibility of coding-agent self-improvement without downstream candidate task evaluation in our setting.
authors: Zhe Ren, Guowei Rong, Yimeng Chen, Nanbo Li, Piotr Pi\k{e}kos, Mateusz Ostaszewski, Dandan Guo, J\"urgen Schmidhuber

papers.abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) now assist users across sessions of images and text, carried by an external memory of what was said and shown. When such an assistant answers wrongly, the failure usually began earlier, in how a record was written, updated or retrieved, and the answer alone does not say where. We formalize multimodal memory as four stages, Write, Update, Retrieve and Answer, and define nine error types across them. A stage-resolved analysis on Mem-Gallery traces most failures to a source stage, and most of those lie before the answer. Injecting known errors against fact-preserving control edits, we then follow each tainted record downstream. Early errors survive to the answer as apparent evidence, and hurt most when no other record holds the fact. A diagnosis that trusts the quoted evidence therefore blames the stage where the error surfaces, not the one where it began. We propose MemDoctor, in which the MLLM that built the memory diagnoses its own failures. It traces each needed fact backward through the four stages, accepts a diagnosis only when the cited evidence is found in memory, and repairs that stage before answering again. On a 4B backbone, MemDoctor improves accuracy on both Mem-Gallery and MemLens, outperforming all evaluated 8B baselines, and the same loop also improves MuRAG and A-Mem.
authors: Ruiyang Jiang, Xinyang Liao, Weikai Huang, Yuqi Niu, Junjie Zhou, Yubin Zheng
bullets: Frames multimodal memory failures as nine error types across four stages: Write, Update, Retrieve, and Answer.
Finds that most failures originate before the final answer, with early errors propagating as misleading evidence.
Shows that evidence-based diagnosis alone can misattribute an error to the stage where it becomes visible.
Uses backward fact tracing and memory-grounded diagnosis to repair the responsible stage before re-answering.
Improves accuracy on Mem-Gallery and MemLens, and also benefits MuRAG and A-Mem, using a 4B backbone.

papers.title: MemDoctor: Stage-wise Error Attribution and Repair for MLLM Agent Memory
papers.tldr: MemDoctor traces MLLM memory failures back through Write, Update, Retrieve, and Answer stages, repairs the originating error, and improves accuracy across several memory benchmarks.

papers.abstract: We present K2-Horizon, a fleet of six fully open language models, from a 0.9B dense model to a 375B-A23B MoE, built for general-purpose reasoning and agentic work across math and science, software engineering, deep research, office automation, and beyond. The models lead or are competitive with strong open models of their size on agentic and coding benchmarks. On the modeling side, to strengthen reasoning, we introduce Mixture-of-Value Attention (MoVA), applying MoE to attention value projections, and softplus attention gating, a more flexible, theoretically motivated gate. Our 36B-A4B model uses both and nearly matches a 32B dense model trained on the same data, with one-seventh the active parameters. We also introduce Uno, lossless diffusion adapters that speed up decoding by up to 2.2x without a separate draft model. Our release follows the LLM360 definition of open source for transparency and reproducibility: the full development history, including intermediate checkpoints from every training stage, pre-training data, training logs, and all training, evaluation, and infrastructure code, notably our production-scale xLLM framework for dense and MoE training and the RL360 reinforcement-learning stack. Beyond the data itself, we release and document in detail every pipeline that built it, the part of model development that open releases most rarely disclose. These pipelines produced roughly 10T synthetic pre-training tokens, showing that synthetic data can be a major ingredient of pre-training at scale. Four of the models share one 22T-token pre-training corpus and recipe, revealing consistent scaling behavior and enabling controlled studies of scale and sparsity. All artifacts are available at https://ifm.ai/k2/
authors: K2 Team, Zhengzhong Liu, Haonan Li, Xuezhe Ma, Alexander Moreno, Subham Sekhar Sahoo, Rupesh Kumar Srivastava, Mikhail Yurochkin, Hadi Abdine, Yash Akhauri, Adharsh Babu, David Bellamy, Jalaj Bhandari, Dani Bouch, Wail Bouhedja, Weili Cao, Ahmad Chamma, Po-Chun Chang, Junlin Chen, Lingjie Chen, Zhoujun Cheng, Kyle Chickering, Ryandito Diandaru, Evan Dufraisse, Chaitanya Dwivedi, Bilal El Bouardi, Desai Fan, Richard Fan, Chengqian Gao, Rifo Ahmad Genadi, Jonathan Geuter, Charles Guille-Escuret, Willis Guo, Dhawal Gupta, Seungwook Han, Tingxu Han, Shibo Hao, Besher Hassan, Guowei He, Ming Shan Hee, Joel Hestness, Yu Huang, Yuan Huang, Haolong Jia, Linghao Jin, Junu Kim, Lingjing Kong, Nurkhan Laiyk, Andrej Leban, Liqun Ma, John Maggs, Amr Mohamed, Mukhesh Narra, Omkar Pangarkar, Aldo Pareja, Khiem Pham, Varad Pimpalkhute, Nikhil Ranjan, Elizaveta Rebrova, Hector Ren, Shaurya Rohatgi, Guokan Shang, Jianshu She, Chufan Shi, Aaryamonvikram Singh, Daria Soboleva, Kartik Sreenivasan, Suqi Sun, Yuekai Sun, Bowen Tan, Liping Tang, Shengkun Tang, Muzi Tao, Mallikarjuna Tupakula, Micah Villmow, Hongyi Wang, Huijuan Wang, Renxi Wang, Yongxin Wang, Yuqi Wang, Zhenting Wang, Shicheng Wen, Yingquan Wu, Anze Xie, Andrew Xing, Matthew Yang, Shuanghai Yu, Kerem Zaman, Zenan Zhai, Hongli Zhan, Xuezhou Zhang, Anshun Asher Zheng, Zhe Zhou, Richard Zhuang, Eric P. Xing
bullets: The fleet targets math and science, software engineering, deep research, office automation, and other general-purpose workloads.
Mixture-of-Value Attention and softplus attention gating improve reasoning efficiency; a 36B-A4B model nearly matches a same-data 32B dense model with one-seventh the active parameters.
Uno provides lossless diffusion adapters that accelerate decoding by up to 2.2× without requiring a separate draft model.
The models are reported to lead or remain competitive with strong open models of similar size on agentic and coding benchmarks.
The release includes checkpoints, data, logs, training/evaluation/infrastructure code, development pipelines, and a 22T-token shared corpus for reproducibility and scaling studies.

figures.caption: Figure 46: (Top) Training overview for diffusion-augmented LLMs. Gray cells indicate AR-weight training, while the blue cell indicates diffusion-weight training. (Bottom Left) System throughput of Uno and the base AR model, normalized to the base AR model at batch size 64; the annotation reports the per-request speedup at batch size 1. We use the 1K/8K throughput test on one H200 GPU with Nano-vLLM and benchmark-derived acceptance rates, using the Linear sampler with B = 4 at batch size 64 and the Tree sampler with (B,K, V ) = (16, 32, 32) at batch size 1. (Bottom Right) Performance across agentic and long-context reasoning benchmarks. The benchmark values are reproduced from Uno’s opening figure. Our sampler preserves the AR model’s output distribution (Section 9.3), enabling lossless acceleration without sacrificing response quality.

Figure 50: Agent evaluation harness: the trusted control box holds all secrets and routes each task by capability: browser, tool, and lighter filesystem tasks run in a fresh-per-task Docker sandbox, while computer-use tasks run in a disposable golden-image VM. Each lane has a fail-closed egress lock that allows only the model API and blocks all other Internet access.

Figure 20: File manipulation pipeline from public documents. Source files are found by web searches over sectors and occupations, then crawled and filtered. Each task combines an input package, a task family and a sampled plan, from which an LLM writes the request. Teacher models solve the tasks in two harnesses, with a randomized environment and, in some rollouts, a simulated user.

Figure 2: Mixture-of-Value Attention in the 36B model. A router selects 4 of 64 nonlinear value experts and combines their weighted outputs into the values used by attention. Each expert produces values for all eight KV heads jointly. Since only the combined values are cached, the KV-cache size is unchanged. Solid arrows carry representations, and dashed arrows carry routing decisions or weights. Query/key positional embeddings, attention-output gating, the output projection, and the residual connection are omitted for clarity.

Figure 1: Training time of all six K2-Horizon models, measured from W&B run logs and drawn on a shared axis of training days. The 32B and 36B-A4B rows show pre-training, mid-training and SFT only; each includes four mid-training stages plus an SFT with final decay. Gaps between stages (data preparation, ablations, queueing) are excluded. Pre-training, mid-training and SFT durations are wall-clock run times, with mid-training stages separated by white lines; RL durations sum the logged rollout-step times. Thin bars below a row are RL experts trained in parallel, so each RL block spans its longest serial path. The 375B post-training takes 13.3 days (RL 4.7, SFT 8.6 in two phases: a constant-learning-rate phase, run in two segments, then a linear decay); the 7B and 3.7B take 14.1 and 13.2 days, and the 0.9B 3.6 days. Ticks mark events of negligible duration (checkpoint averaging, weight merging) or without a logged duration (FTPO; the first 0.9B math RL stage, delivered as a checkpoint).

Figure 38: RL360 architecture. The rollout, sandbox, inference, and training layers communicate through explicit service boundaries and can be scaled independently. Miles collects trajectories and rewards, Harbor executes agents in task environments, SMG routes inference requests to SGLang, and Megatron-LM updates the policy.

Figure 17: Overview of PRism data processing. Curation combines archived events with repository code, and annotation adds semantic labels. The resulting corpus provides inputs for five synthesis branches. The prism is schematic; band widths are not to scale.

Figure 22: O*NET-grounded tool-use data synthesis, adapted from Somerstep et al. (2026). The tool ecosystem keeps only Smithery MCP servers that an agent can reach and whose tools return real data. Each O*NET task is matched to servers by embedding similarity, and an occupation with several matched (task, server) pairs is expanded by an LLM into a self-contained workplace request, a cross-tool workflow and an answer key; information-withheld variants (dashed) omit key parameters so the agent must ask for them. Rollouts run against LLM-simulated tools and, for multi-turn data, a role-inverted simulated user that sees only the agent’s final replies.
Figure 32: Factoid & Source-Specific Question Generation Pipeline. Well-posed factoid questions drive factual recall capability, while ambiguous source-specific questions drive abstention capability.

Figure 31: ML-Theory Task Generation Pipeline. (1) A subtree around a central result is selected from the paper’s proof graph; boundary results become assumptions and internal results become subtasks. (2) Proposer–reviewer pairs write the subtasks and harden the central question. (3) An executed reference solution and a checker per subtask decide the answers; three quality checks (cold solve, shortcut probe, consistency check) send the task back for revision or reject it. (4) In Harbor, a solver is rewarded only if every checker passes. Violet: agent roles; teal: executed code.

Figure 14: WZIP compression ratio versus the number of documents compressed together (log scale); a higher ratio means less diverse text. Dashed lines are natural code and web data. v0 is an earlier version of our pipeline without search and diversity knobs.
Figure 21: File manipulation pipeline from GitHub repositories: from a file to a task.
Figure 26: Source-grounded question synthesis pipeline.
Figure 27: Feedback-driven question synthesis pipeline.
Figure 29: Kaggle trajectory synthesis pipeline. From Kaggle datasets to MLE-bench-style tasks and data-science agent trajectories.

Figure 4: Normalized pre-training loss of the four models trained on the same 22T-token corpus, on the accepted trajectory. Each model’s loss is divided by its median over the final 1% of steps, and progress is counted after the 3,000-step warmup. Every 100th step is shown, without smoothing.

Figure 10: Evaluation performance of the 375B-A23B model during Phase 2 pre-training and four mid-training stages. Shaded regions indicate the training stages. Phase 2 and mid-training results use distinct markers because their evaluation protocols differ, so discontinuities between the two curves should not be interpreted as direct performance gains.

Figure 39: Knowledge Work expert model evolution during RL. Thin lines are raw per-step values, heavy lines a 5-step sample-weighted rolling mean; each curve ends at the exported checkpoint. Trajectory length counts every token after the initial prompt, with the generated part shown dashed.
Figure 41: Search expert model evolution during RL.
Figure 40: Tool Use expert model evolution during RL.

Figure 19: Building RL coding environments from GitHub pull requests. Filtering reduces the annotated PR corpus with deterministic rules, then scores survivors with an LLM judge and draws a domain-balanced sample stratified by difficulty. Rewriting derives the reference patches from the diff without a model and uses the model only for the task specification, the predicted environment, and the test commands. Environment synthesis is an agent loop that produces a container image. The two checks below it are distinct: acceptance is mechanical, whereas the trajectory judge runs a solver against an already-accepted environment and decides whether it is worth training on. Solid arrows carry artifacts and dashed arrows carry feedback: acceptance failures return to the responsible sub-agent, and judged misalignment returns to the rewrite stage. Filter thresholds, the eight scoring dimensions of the filtering judge, the checklist items, and the selection rule are given in the text.

Figure 33: How one PR chain becomes a single long episode. Each PR is attempted in its own fresh agent session against the same working tree, so state reaches the next turn two ways: through the filesystem, which accumulates, and through a compacted handoff, which does not. Per-turn context therefore stays roughly constant however long the episode runs, while cumulative token usage climbs until it crosses the budget, at which point the run stops and the partial episode is kept. The whole episode runs inside a sandbox in which the network tools are gated: dependency installs resolve against a local package mirror and git operations against a local repository mirror, so a build can still fetch what it needs while the obvious routes to the upstream change are closed. The gating is at the tool layer rather than the network layer, so the public internet remains reachable by an agent that writes its own client; we did not observe this in the trajectories we inspected. The number of turns an episode reaches is set by the budget rather than by the number of PRs the chain offers.

Figure 7: Spike episodes. (a) Flagship loss at the peak of each episode, on the final trajectory (blue dots) and on branches later erased when the run resumed from a checkpoint (red crosses; a replay of the same steps counts again), with rollbacks of more than 250 steps (triangles). The grey line is the median loss of the final trajectory; phase 2 is shifted by 210,000 steps. (b) Position of each episode within its run, pooled over the two flagship phases and the main runs of the five smaller models (977 episodes on final trajectories). Half of the episodes (49.7%) fall in the first 40% of a run (dashed line).

Figure 47: Single-stream decode rate against cached context, normalized to each model’s short-context rate. The horizontal axis divides context length by the model’s hidden width so that all models share one scale. Markers show where reading the KV cache costs as much as reading the weights. Full benchmark results are in our repository.

Figure 3: Training loss across the phase boundary. Left: the last 10,000 steps of phase 1. Right: the first 10,000 steps of phase 2, which restarts the step counter, discards the optimizer state and re-warms the learning rate over 1,000 steps (shaded). Grey: loss at every step; colored: running median over 201 steps. The two phases use different data, so their loss levels are not directly comparable.

Figure 51: Agentic safety by adversarial setting across the four models. Every model degrades sharply from direct requests to indirect injection. The shaded multi-round column is annotation-derived and shown for completeness rather than as a model comparison.
Figure 45: Gold issues grouped by how many of the 11 models found them, stacked by gold severity. Of the 72 issues that no model found, 57 are minor, 14 moderate and 1 serious.

Figure 11: Evaluation performance and training loss of the 3.7B model across pre-training and four mid-training stages. The left panel reports MMLU-Pro, GSM8K, and MBPP at their available checkpoints; distinct markers denote the different evaluation protocols used during pre-training and mid-training. The right panel shows train loss, sampled at the same checkpoints.

Figure 25: Socratic dialogue data generation. A student model attempts each question and a teacher model with the reference answer guides it with hints until the answer is correct. Student turns become assistant outputs for SFT.

Figure 5: Spike shapes in the flagship. (a) A single-step transient in phase 1, peaking at about 15 times the usual fluctuation above the baseline (loss 1.07 against 0.89); training continues unaffected. (b) A wide excursion in phase 1 that begins at step 84,114 on a branch later erased by rollback: the loss rises from about 0.9 to 5.4, stays above 2 for 151 steps and is still above baseline when the branch ends at step 84,547. The run then resumes from step 82,001, and the final trajectory over the same steps (blue) shows no excursion. (c, d) Distributions of episode duration and of peak z-score (Equation 12) on the accepted trajectory, for the two phases; triangles mark the examples in (a) and (b), and the wide excursion lies on an erased branch and is not counted.

Figure 24: Condensed mining prompt. Queue construction is deterministic for a fixed dataset and exclusion set; scientific and runtime feasibility are assessed from the paper and executable repository.

Figure 43: 375B-A23B’s agentic behavior on Terminal-Bench 2.1 across training checkpoints (using the Terminus-2 harness). Dashed and dotted lines show Fable-5 (high effort) and GPT-5.5 (xhigh) as reference baselines, evaluated on the same tasks and harness.

Figure 49: Per-task scores for K2-Horizon and K2-V2 across all 87 shared tasks. K2-V2’s advantages cluster in the jailbreak and secret-protection tasks; K2-Horizon’s largest gains are the benign over-refusal sets.

Figure 48: Mean score by safety domain (further out is better; both panels share the same radial scale). Left: K2-Horizon (solid, filled) against K2-V2 (solid, unfilled) and Kimi K3 and DeepSeek-V4-Flash (dashed) under the same harness and judge (K2-V2 runs 87 of the 88 tasks). Frontier-level on direct-harm refusal and multi-turn safety; behind Kimi K3 on over-refusal, bias, and cyber/privacy but ahead of DeepSeek-V4-Flash overall. Compared to K2-V2, the profiles cross: K2-V2 is wider on adversarial surfaces, whereas K2-Horizon is wider on over-refusal and truthfulness. Right: the K2-Horizon family. The refusal core degrades only gradually with size (general refusal 0.976 at 375B to 0.873 at 0.9B); the smallest sizes fall furthest on the judgment domains (physical safety, truthfulness, ethics/sycophancy).

Figure 44: Excerpts from a flagged db-wal-recovery attempt by the released 375B-A23B on Terminal-Bench 2.1. After opening, the database deletes the encrypted log it must recover, and the agent finds the task’s solution on GitHub. Quotes are verbatim from the agent’s per-turn analysis; [. . . ] marks omissions.

Figure 52: K2-Horizon family on the agentic surface: severity <2 rate on direct malicious requests by task source (further out is safer). Language-mediated sources hold up down the size ladder; code execution and filesystem access stay weak at every size.

Figure 6: Gradient norm before clipping for the 375B flagship, in bins of 2,000 steps over all executed steps of each phase: median (line) and 5th to 95th percentile (band), on a log scale. The dashed line is the clipping threshold of 1.0, which engaged on 1.5% of steps in phase 1 and 0.5% in phase 2.

Figure 8: Resumes near step 199,500 in phase 1. (a) One resume from the checkpoint at step 199,500: the loss rises from about 0.9 to above 9 at step 199,540, and the run is stopped at step 199,543. (b) The original run (top row) and every later resume, one row each in order, from its starting step to the furthest step reached; red marks steps with loss above 2. The replay after the rollback to step 196,000 starts left of the axis, and the last resumes, from step 200,000, run past its right edge (arrowheads).

Figure 9: Training loss across the four mid-training stages (context lengths 32k, 128k, 512k and 512k). Dotted lines mark stage boundaries. Light: loss at every step; solid: running median. The stages differ in data mixture and context length, so loss levels are not comparable across them.

Figure 13: Socratic teacher–student dialogue generation. Hard, prime-free problems are posed to a student agent that sees only the problem. A teacher agent that also sees the reference answer checks each attempt and either probes the student’s reasoning or, once the attempt is correct, ends the dialogue. The teacher prompt (plain Socratic or a sampled persona) and both agents’ reasoning effort serve as diversity knobs. Completed dialogues are rendered as pre-training documents from the student’s perspective.
Figure 35: Fraction of tasks solved without and with the advisor, by category. Advised reruns are applied only to tasks the solver failed on its own.

Figure 23: Task factory. A coding agent runs this loop without supervision: it finds a problem with a checkable answer, grounds it as a Harbor task, passes it through three gates that are never skipped, measures its difficulty against a real agent, and logs every attempt, pass or fail, to a ledger that it reads before building the next task.

Figure 36: How a new dataset is processed: load the source, test it with the general converter and process_entry, decide whether a fix is needed, find the cause, write and test a dataset-specific fix, and save the output for each dataset.

Figure 30: From technical documents to interactive simulator tasks. A design agent defines the task, and an implementation agent writes the simulator. Candidates are checked for correct execution, repeatability, and direct leaks of hidden values. A policy using only information available to the solver must then beat both inaction and random actions by a preset margin in average score across the same test seeds. Eligible failures receive bounded repair and are checked again. Accepted tasks support trajectory generation and automatic scoring.

Figure 42: Knowledge Work expert pass@k during RL, in non-overlapping bins of 250 prompt groups. pass@k is the unbiased estimator 1− ( n−c k ) / ( n k ) over the n = 32 samples each prompt receives, counting a sample as correct when its base reward exceeds 0.5.

Figure 28: The research lab. Ten researcher agents with distinct personas and skills act on one shared, real-time world through a command-line tool, and a Concordia game master enforces the rules and checks four win conditions. Competition comes from non-exclusive pulls on open problems, where the first accepted paper scoops the rest, and from the leaderboards and the race for public engagement. Collaboration comes from the larger credit pot for co-authored papers, payments and escrowed deals, shared git repositories, and the collaborative variant in which the whole team pursues one goal. Each researcher’s trajectory and a selection of the simulated public’s decisions are filtered and used as mid-training data. Shaded boxes hold task or result state; dashed arrows are public announcements.

Figure 37: Token cost of the three tool presentation formats. (a) Average size of the rendered tool block per sample. On our data (771K samples with tools, 249K unique toolsets), Markdown uses 18.5% fewer tokens than JSON and XML 15.2% fewer. The savings are similar or larger on BFCL and τ2-bench toolsets. (b) Per-tool savings over the 747K unique tools in our data, grouped by the tool’s size in JSON. Markdown is shorter than JSON for 99.5% of tool uses. Small tools save the most (up to ∼48%), because JSON syntax makes up a larger share of them. Tools over 1K tokens save only about 7%. All averages are weighted by how often each tool or toolset occurs.

Figure 15: Predicting benchmark scores of large models from small-scale runs. Stage 1 fits a scaling law to each validation set’s loss over a grid of small models and evaluates it at the target model size P and token budget N . Stage 2 maps losses to each benchmark’s score with a sparse regression fitted on separate ablation runs, and is applied to the extrapolated losses. Shaded boxes are data; unshaded boxes are fitted models or inputs to them.

Figure 16: Production pre-training mixes by category (% of training tokens), using the categories of Table 16. Slices run clockwise from the top in legend order. Left: the mix used for the dense 3.7B, 7B, and 32B models and the 36B-A4B model. Right: the second-phase mix of the 375B-A23B model. Shares sum to 100 up to rounding.

Table 1: Architecture configurations of the K2-Horizon family. All models use SwiGLU feed-forward networks. Backbone counts exclude the input embedding and output projection matrices; total counts include both. Active backbone counts include shared components and selected experts, accounting for both feed-forward and value-expert routing in MoVA. For sparse models, the dense FFN dimension applies to the initial dense layers; subsequent layers use the listed expert configuration. FFN denotes a feed-forward network. Active routed-expert counts exclude the shared expert. Parameter counts are rounded to three decimal places; model names denote nominal size classes.

Figure 18: Abbreviated annotated PR record. Selected fields are shown in a compact notation; ellipses mark omitted paths and diff context. Full records also contain base files, commit patches, events, annotation scores, and rationales.

Figure 12: A document is a dataset of tokens: each token is a label for the context before it. An error such as 2 + 2 = 5 is one mislabeled token, and the tokens around it remain correct labels. This is why we do not discard synthetic trajectories that contain mistakes.

Table 3: Mid-training recipe. All models use AdamW with β1 = 0.9, β2 = 0.95, and gradient-norm clipping at 1.0. For each stage, the table lists the context length, the global batch size in tokens, the number of optimizer steps, the resulting token count in trillions, the peak learning rate, the number of warmup steps, and the weight decay. Weight decay is set once per model and shared across its stages, except the 0.9B model. Mid-training starts from the average of the final pre-training checkpoints: four spaced 1,500 steps apart for the 375B model (phase-2 steps 235,500 to 240,000), four spaced 4,000 steps apart for the 3.7B and 7B models (steps 1,088,000 to 1,100,000), and six spaced 5,000 steps apart for the 32B and 36B models (steps 1,075,000 to 1,100,000); the 0.9B model uses no averaging. Sequence lengths use k = 1,024 tokens. †Before stage 1, the 0.9B model runs a brief context-extension phase of about 2,000 steps on separate data, which is not listed in the table.

Table 40: Accuracy and TPF of Uno, Mercury 2, Diffusion-Gemma, and Nemotron-Labs-Diffusion on agentic and non-agentic benchmarks. Subscripts report TPF. Mercury 2 results are from Artificial Analysis, and its TPF is not available. For Uno, subscripts report “TPF1 / TPF2,” where TPF1 uses the system-throughput-optimal Linear sampler with B = 4, and TPF2 uses (B,K, V ) = (16, 32, 32), optimized for per-request throughput. We highlight the best result per row in bold. ∗Reported by Artificial Analysis’s live tracker on August 30, 2026.

Table 39: Tokens per forward pass (TPF) and throughput of K2-Horizonwith autoregressive (AR) decoding and with its parallel samplers via Uno-adapters. papers.abstract: Takehi et al. (2026) report that GPT-6 Astra, given the weights of small neural networks as text, can say what they were trained to do, repair them, and write new ones without training. I re-ran the core of that study with Claude Opus 5.5 in ten pre-registered experiments, with untrained-network and permutation controls and hand audits of every sandboxed code cell. Reading was mixed: Claude named 3 of 4 Atari games from policy weights and found the measured copying heads in 15/15 character-LM runs, but its answers about training data often followed priors. Unlike the original, it identified a sycophantic Gemma 3 270M finetune from weights alone in 6/6 runs. One-shot weight edits took a failing MountainCar policy from 0% to 100% success and a hovering LunarLander policy from 0% to 85.6%; zero-shot networks beat PPO at 100k steps on 4 of 5 environments, each implementing a textbook controller. With no training or forward passes, Claude wrote a 1.48M-parameter 9x9 Go network that won 85-94% of games against three PPO opponents. Given Qwen3.5-0.8B's weights and 10, 25 or 50 forward passes of 64 practice problems, Claude raised MATH-500 from 6.7% to 51.4%, 55.2% and 58.1% (+51.4 points at 50 passes, 95% CI [47.9, 55.0]; original 48.1%), GSM8K from 11.6% to 68.2% and IFEval from 22.2% to 54.2%. Unlike the original, which removed an internal loop direction, every edit acted at the output: it scaled the final norm, raising the effective sampling temperature, and lowered the logit of "Wait" while raising that of . The norm scaling alone reaches only 20.9-22.1% on MATH-500. On Gemma 3 270M, which rarely loops, no edit helped (-0.8 points), as in the original.
bullets: Claude identified 3/4 Atari policies, detected copying heads in 15/15 character-LM runs, and recognized a sycophantic Gemma finetune in all 6 runs.
One-shot edits repaired MountainCar from 0% to 100% success and LunarLander from 0% to 85.6%; zero-shot networks beat PPO at 100k steps in 4/5 environments.
Without training or forward passes, Claude wrote a 1.48M-parameter 9×9 Go network winning 85–94% against three PPO opponents.
Editing Qwen3.5-0.8B with 10–50 practice-problem forward passes raised MATH-500 from 6.7% to 58.1%, GSM8K to 68.2%, and IFEval to 54.2%.
Unlike the original study, edits targeted output behavior—mainly final-norm scaling and changing the “Wait” logit—and did not help Gemma, which rarely loops.

papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) judges are increasingly used to monitor the outputs of LLM-based AI agents, yet formal guarantees on the reliability of these judges remain largely absent, limiting confidence in their use for safety-critical oversight. We consider certifying such a judge and define its risk over safety classifications of prompt--response pairs drawn from a deployed generator. We apply a PAC-Bayes framework to this setting, refining existing compression-based methodology with the use of tighter bounds and more efficient coding. We show that standard parameter-efficient fine-tuning can yield non-vacuous and even tight certificates for safety judges, for both classification and Brier risk, without holding out data for validation. We introduce LoRA-GT, which shares a single quantisation scale across layers and achieves the tightest certificates with minimal degradation in predictive performance. Across five guardrail models and four benchmarks, we find that certificate tightness is governed more by adaptation complexity than by base model scale. Finally, we show how far quantisation can be pushed before the resulting increase in risk outweighs the bound tightening gained from shorter descriptions. Together, these results provide a practical route toward certifiable scalable oversight and offer insight into how the complexity of safety adaptations shapes generalisation.
authors: Tom A. Lamb, Philip H. S. Torr, Tim G. J. Rudner
bullets: Targets the lack of formal reliability guarantees for LLM judges used in safety-critical oversight.
Defines judge risk on safety classifications of prompt–response pairs from a deployed generator.
Combines tighter PAC-Bayes bounds with efficient parameter coding and standard parameter-efficient fine-tuning, without a validation holdout.
Introduces LoRA-GT, a shared-scale quantisation method that achieves the tightest certificates with minimal predictive degradation.
Across five guardrail models and four benchmarks, certificate tightness depends more on adaptation complexity than base-model scale; excessive quantisation eventually harms risk.

papers.abstract: Agentic memory systems give LLMs persistent memory by extracting experience into text and retrieving it at query time, but the model itself does not evolve: however many interactions it has had, it starts each query the same. Extraction errors compound, implicit cross-session patterns that no single fragment states cannot be surfaced, and the construction cost grows with every conversation. Fine-tuning on past interactions does change the weights, but requires backpropagation at serving time and degrades on long histories. We introduce CLAM (Carried Latent Adapter Memory), which combines the strengths of both: a recurrent hypernetwork performs parametric consolidation, compiling a stream of session activations into a low-rank adapter in a single forward pass with no gradient steps and no language-model generation calls, while a complementary episodic buffer supplies verbatim detail at inference. A gated latent state carries knowledge across sessions in fixed size, so the parametric memory accumulates without growing. On LoCoMo and LongMemEval-S across three open models (2-7B parameters), CLAM leads all agentic baselines by 1-45 points and all gradient-based parametric methods by 10-45 points, while requiring zero generative LLM calls, zero gradient steps, and 3-151x less wall-clock time than extraction systems to build its memory. The two channels are complementary: the consolidated adapter adds 12-15 accuracy points when the episodic buffer misses the gold evidence, and still adds 4-5 points even with an oracle buffer.
bullets: Addresses growing costs, extraction errors, and missed cross-session patterns in text-based memory systems.
Uses a recurrent hypernetwork and gated latent state to consolidate session knowledge into a fixed-size adapter.

Outperforms reported agentic and gradient-based baselines on LoCoMo and LongMemEval-S across three 2–7B open models.
Builds memory 3–151× faster than extraction systems and improves accuracy by 12–15 points when episodic retrieval misses evidence, and 4–5 points with an oracle buffer.

papers.selection_reason: Recurrent hypernetwork consolidates session activations into a low-rank adapter for persistent LLM memory; directly fits LLM memory.
papers.title: Instant Weight-Space Consolidation for Long-Term Memory in LLMs
papers.tldr: CLAM gives LLMs fixed-size, persistent parametric memory by consolidating session activations into a low-rank adapter in one forward pass, complementing an episodic buffer without generation or gradient updates.

papers.abstract: Diffusion language models (DLMs) can write several tokens per forward pass. Open-weight DLMs commit, in any order, every masked position whose confidence passes a threshold. If none does, a fallback commits the most confident one, and the commits are never revised. Wide windows let the decoder commit far ahead of the text, which should speed up decoding but often costs accuracy. It is unclear where the model is confident and which commits cause errors. We trace every commit of four off-the-shelf DLMs on math, code, translation and summarization, and rerun failing answers with one step changed. Most tokens become confident only near the frontier, the leftmost masked position, so committing only there, still several tokens per step, is about as fast as committing anywhere. The accuracy loss comes from committing tokens before the text to their left, and committing one token per step does not reduce it. The worst case is an early end-of-sequence token that cuts the answer short. Fallback commits are 11-35% of commits but start 61-72% of the failures that left-to-right decoding avoids. Changing only the step where such a failure starts repairs it more often than changing a similar earlier step. Committing only at the frontier recovers most of the lost accuracy on all four models. Our code is available at https://github.com/rmakarovv/fast-at-the-frontier.
authors: Roman Makarov, Zhe Xu, Jian Kang
bullets: The study traces every token commit from four off-the-shelf DLMs across math, code, translation, and summarization tasks.
Most tokens become confident near the leftmost masked position, so frontier-only committing retains similar speed while reducing premature commitments.
Committing one token per step does not fix errors caused by committing ahead of the frontier.
Fallback commits make up 11–35% of commits and initiate 61–72% of failures avoided by left-to-right decoding.
Early end-of-sequence commits can truncate answers; changing the failure-starting step repairs errors more often than changing an earlier step.

papers.selection_reason: Analyzes threshold decoding behavior in diffusion language models, relevant to LLM decoding and efficiency.
papers.title: Fast at the Frontier, Wrong at the Fallback: A Commit-Level Analysis of Threshold Decoding in Diffusion Language Models
papers.tldr: Threshold decoding in diffusion language models is fast but loses accuracy mainly when it commits tokens ahead of the left-to-right frontier, especially through fallback decisions.

papers.abstract: Multiplicative gating improves Transformer feed-forward networks (FFNs), but it reduces intermediate representation width under a fixed parameter budget. This trade-off is particularly relevant to Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models, where individual experts have limited capacity. We introduce ParGLU, a partially gated FFN that combines SwiGLU and ReLU$^2$ in two parallel branches. ParGLU matches the parameter count and principal matrix computation budget of conventional SwiGLU. We evaluate ParGLU in 30M, 75M, and 152M MoE language models using three random seeds per scale. ParGLU outperforms SwiGLU across all three seeds at 75M and 152M, reducing mean validation NLL by 0.0200 and 0.0249, respectively. Results at 30M are mixed. Controlled ablations show that increasing backbone width or expert width strengthens ParGLU's relative performance. Ablation studies further show that combining SwiGLU and ReLU$^2$ improves performance over either architecture alone. Token-frequency analysis reveals larger improvements on low-frequency tokens. These findings show that fully gated FFNs are not always the most effective use of an MoE expert's parameter budget. Partial gating can improve language modeling in MoE Transformers.
bullets: Addresses the trade-off between multiplicative gating and FFN representation width in capacity-limited MoE experts.
Uses a partially gated FFN with parallel SwiGLU and ReLU² branches.
Outperforms SwiGLU at 75M and 152M model scales across three seeds, while results at 30M are mixed.
Wider backbones or experts strengthen ParGLU’s relative gains, with larger improvements on low-frequency tokens.
Combining the two branches performs better than either SwiGLU or ReLU² alone.
