papers.abstract: Post-training improves language-model reasoning, but how it changes the use of internal information and verbalized chain of thought (CoT) remains unclear. We study successive SFT, DPO, and RLVR checkpoints of Olmo-3-7B-Instruct on multi-digit addition, using carry values as known intermediate state. Probes recover carry information from internal activations with similar accuracy in SFT and RLVR, although manipulating this information does not reliably control model outputs. In contrast, the usefulness of verbalized reasoning differs: CoTs produced by RLVR yield higher accuracy across receiving checkpoints than those produced by SFT or DPO. We also show that carry-related statements receive higher importance scores after RLVR than matched random controls. DPO shows similar sensitivity to carry-related statements but without comparable accuracy gains. These results suggest that post-training changes the usefulness of written reasoning and sensitivity to its content in meaningful ways, although greater sensitivity does not necessarily coincide with better problem performance.
bullets: Studies successive SFT, DPO, and RLVR checkpoints of Olmo-3-7B-Instruct on multi-digit addition.
Internal probes recover carry values similarly after SFT and RLVR, but manipulating carries does not reliably control outputs.
RLVR-generated chain-of-thought produces higher accuracy across receiving checkpoints than SFT- or DPO-generated reasoning.
After RLVR, carry-related statements receive greater importance than matched random controls.
DPO increases sensitivity to carry-related statements without comparable accuracy gains, showing sensitivity and performance can diverge.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Analysis of important spans in the CoT. (a) For each span in the CoT, we cluster based on semantic similarity and show the mean importance score derived from the Thought Anchors method (Bogdan et al., 2025). For a given span, we suppress all attention to that span and calculate its importance as described in Section 7. (b) Each receiver continues from the same Full-generated prefix. We measure disruption as the percentage of correct cases where the digit in the column corresponding to the reasoning span changes. A carry unit is a reasoning span where a carry gets used directly; a carry episode is two spans, one where a carry is computed and another, the follow-up span, where that carry gets used. We include random spans and random pairs (episodes) as controls. Error bars are 95% problem-level bootstrap confidence intervals for (a) and (b).

Figure 3: We measure probe test accuracy at three token locations: the final token of the prompt; 2/3rd of the way through the CoT; and at the answer digit token. We train probes separately for three variables: the incoming carry at a digit; the outgoing carry at a digit; and an output digit. No probes are shown for finding the output digits at the answer digit token, as the answer would often be already available (up to tokenization effects). Probes are trained separately for each variable, layer, digit, and location. The results shown are averaged across digits. Overall, the probe test accuracy remains stable across layers and very similar across models, while showing only minor differences at different token locations. Shaded regions show 95% confidence intervals from problem-level bootstrap resampling. Dash-dot lines show uniform random-chance accuracy.

Figure 2: Analysis of chain-of-thought behavior across models. (a) Final-answer accuracy for problems where both Answer Only and Free CoT terminate within 2048 tokens, paired separately for each checkpoint. Full gains 6.2 percentage points over its Answer Only baseline (adjusted p = .034); see Section C for sample counts and statistical testing details. (b) For each of {2, 4, 6} digits, we show the percentage of correct and completed samples with respect to the number of output tokens used, up to a maximum of 2048. Notably, the Full model saturates less with additional CoT tokens than the other two models (c) For each model, we produce an on-policy CoT and feed it to each of the other models using teacher forcing before asking for a final answer. All three models perform similarly when receiving a given CoT, but CoTs sourced from Full provide an advantage across all three models. Error bars are 95% problem-level bootstrap confidence intervals for (a) and (c); the shaded region for (b) is the 95% Wilson binomial confidence interval.

Figure 4: Importance scores for semantic clustering of reasoning spans on subtraction problems. The top cluster by importance, subtraction step headings, take the form of "Step <num>: Subtract the <units/tens/hundreds/...> place". Specified clusters involving the use of borrows are highlighted; some other mentions of borrow fall into the lexical borrow mention cluster. More details on clustering are provided in Section H.2. Error bars are 95% problem-level bootstrap confidence intervals.

Figure 5: Exact symbolic overlap between the evaluation equations and the public post-training data. Each row contains 98 unique ordered equations after duplicate equations from different carry categories are collapsed. Coloured segments show the earliest post-training stage in which an exact relation occurs; grey denotes no detected occurrence. The search finds 76 two-digit equations, one four-digit equation, and no six-digit equations.

Figure 18: Secondary outcomes during on-policy generation. Conditions suppress either the incoming-carry application, a matched non-carry span, the two-unit carry episode, or a matched pair of non-carry spans. Exactanswer accuracy includes a short answer continuation used when the primary continuation contains no parseable final answer. Natural termination and fallback use are measured on the primary continuation. Off-target changes count incorrect answer digits outside the selected carry column and are computed only when an answer is parseable. Points are means and error bars are 95% confidence intervals from resampling problems.

Figure 20: Comparison of checkpoint-native and common-Base J-Lens ranks at layer 23. Each point is one of the 30 selected carry applications. Rows show the known next token at the carry-value and result-value locations; columns show the checkpoint whose residual state is read. Both axes use a logarithmic scale. Points below the dashed diagonal receive a better (smaller) rank from the common-Base decoder. The annotation in each panel counts such cases; ties are not counted as improvements.

Figure 13: Immediate final-answer accuracy over normalized CoT progress. Rows show operand length, columns show the checkpoint that produced the reasoning, and line colour shows the receiver checkpoint. Each source cohort contains completed traces whose original final answer is correct; the panel title gives its size. At each tenth of progress, the nearest observed reasoning boundary is supplied to the receiver before requesting a direct answer. Non-direct intermediate continuations are excluded and completed endpoint decodes are retained. Shaded regions are 95% problem-bootstrap confidence intervals.

Figure 6: SFT final-answer accuracy by operand length and maximum carry-chain length. Each interior cell pools standard-format examples with the indicated properties across Answer Only and Free CoT. Blank cells are combinations absent from the evaluation set. The marginal row and column are unweighted means of the displayed interior cells.

Figure 14: Cumulative observed commitment over normalized CoT progress. A source–receiver trajectory is committed once its directly elicited answer is correct at the current boundary and every later retained boundary. Rows show operand length, columns show the source checkpoint, and line colour shows the receiver checkpoint. The analysis includes all 45 four-digit and 32 six-digit shared-source problems for each source; shaded regions are 95% problem-bootstrap confidence intervals.

Figure 9: Final-answer accuracy with the standard output convention and with the result digits written from least to most significant (LSD). Operands are conventionally formatted in both conditions. The standard and LSD conditions use separate samples of 384 and 192 problems, respectively, with both prompt conditions for every problem. Error bars are 95% bootstrap confidence intervals.

Figure 7: DPO final-answer accuracy by operand length and maximum carry-chain length. Each interior cell pools standard-format examples with the indicated properties across Answer Only and Free CoT. Blank cells are combinations absent from the evaluation set. The marginal row and column are unweighted means of the displayed interior cells.

Figure 8: Full final-answer accuracy by operand length and maximum carry-chain length. Each interior cell pools standard-format examples with the indicated properties across Answer Only and Free CoT. Blank cells are combinations absent from the evaluation set. The marginal row and column are unweighted means of the displayed interior cells.

Figure 11: Final-answer accuracy across controlled carry structures. No Carry has no carry-producing column; Isolated Carry has one non-propagating carry; Long Carry Chain propagates a carry across every operand digit; Carry Distractor has locally carrysuggestive patterns but no long chain; and Random provides carry-balanced coverage. All examples use standard operand and answer formats. Bars pool both prompt conditions; error bars are 95% bootstrap confidence intervals.

Figure 10: Final-answer accuracy with conventionally written operands and with | between adjacent operand digits. The answer remains conventionally formatted, and the delimited prompt explains the notation. The standard and delimited conditions use separate samples of 384 and 192 problems, respectively, with both prompt conditions for every problem. Error bars are 95% bootstrap confidence intervals.

Figure 15: Effect of suppressing a reasoning unit on the final answer, grouped by the unit’s normalized position in the CoT. The left panel shows the mean KL divergence over factual-answer tokens. The right panel shows clean minus suppressed summed log probability for those tokens; negative values therefore indicate that suppression increased their probability. Points give equal-problem-weighted means across SFT and Full source traces, and error bars are 95% confidence intervals from resampling problems.

Figure 16: Dependence on an earlier reasoning unit as a function of unit distance. The left panel shows mean per-token KL on a logarithmic scale; the right panel shows the fraction of source–target pairs with mean KL of at least 0.01 nats. Values are averaged within each problem before being averaged across problems. Error bars are 95% problem-bootstrap confidence intervals.

Figure 17: Map of directed dependencies between reasoning units. Source and later affected units are placed into ten equal-width bins of normalized CoT progress. Each cell gives the mean per-token KL for the observed source–target airs in that bin; the narrow strips marked “Mean” summarize the populated cells along each axis.

Figure 19: Analysis of the residual stream content, at early (7), middle (15), and late (23) layers, across a carry span ((e.g. "9 + 1 (carry-over) = 10")), and at the token endpoints of the previous, current, and next reasoning spans. The change is measured between the two models shown at the top of each column. Top: we measure the raw % change in residual stream value. The changes concentrate just before the carry value is mentioned. Bottom: using readouts from the J-Lens (Gurnee et al., 2026), we measure the Jensen-Shannon (JS) divergence between each models distribution. These results mirror those of the change in raw residual stream.

Figure 12: Final-answer accuracy by operand length for standard-format inputs and answers. Bars pool Answer Only and Free CoT prompt instances; error bars are 95% Wilson confidence intervals for the pooled binomial proportions.

Figure 21: Illustrative layer-23 token distributions under the common-Base decoder. Panels A and B show the five highest-probability tokens from Full residual states immediately before the carry value and result value in the same reasoning unit; <sp> marks a leading space. Orange highlights carry-related tokens in Panel A and the correct numeric result in Panel B. Panel C compares the probabilities of the unadjusted subtotal 14 and the correct carry adjusted result 15 at the result location of “6 + 8 + 1 = 15,” using Base, SFT, DPO, and Full residual states with the same Base decoder. These cases are qualitative examples and are not averages over the 30-unit sample.

Table 4: Direct comparison of the Free CoT-minusAnswer Only effect between Full and SFT. All quantities use the same problems, each with a completed response in all four checkpoint-by prompt conditions.

Table 5: Free CoT problems retained for probe training and evaluation after excluding responses that do not terminate within 2,048 tokens. The original training and test sets each contain 64 problems at every digit length for each checkpoint.

Table 6: Probe test accuracy on the test problems available for both SFT and Full, in percent. Each checkpoint entry first pools target columns in proportion to their number of test predictions and then averages equally over the 32 layers; brackets give the minimum and maximum layer accuracy. The majority baseline is computed under the same target-column weighting. Result-digit prediction at answer-digit locations is omitted because the target digit has already been emitted.

Table 10: Exploratory activation-patching effects on 15 eligible natural problem pairs. Effects are changes in counterfactual-versus-factual log probability, in nats, relative to the same-input cross-checkpoint control. Each cell contains 30 directed cases. Confidence intervals are 95% percentile intervals from resampling whole matched problem pairs.

Table 9: Performance of the selected distributed carry interventions. Interchange is the rate at which the generated answer changes to the exact counterfactual answer. Other digits preserved is the rate at which all non-target answer digits remain unchanged. The held-out evaluation contains 64 pairs per checkpoint.

Table 3: Paired comparison of Answer Only and Free CoT prompting among completed responses. Accuracies are percentages; ∆ is Free CoT minus Answer Only in percentage points, with an unadjusted 95% problem-paired bootstrap confidence interval. Gains and losses count problems that Free CoT changed from incorrect to correct and from correct to incorrect, respectively. Holm p gives the exact McNemar p-value after correction across checkpoints.

Table 7: Problem-weighted effect of steering along the incoming-carry probe direction relative to three norm-matched orthogonal directions. The outcome is the change in counterfactual-versus-factual completeanswer log probability, measured in nats. Confidence intervals are 95% percentile intervals from resampling whole arithmetic problems.

Table 8: Cross-checkpoint replay results on 100 arithmetic problems. Log probabilities are sums over the correct answer tokens, averaged over problems. Accuracies are from deterministic continuations. Without supplied reasoning, SFT and Full obtain 99% and 98% accuracy, respectively; their mean correct-answer log probabilities are −0.154 and −0.392.

Table 11: Summary of the text-only clustering. Addition pools 202 SFT and Full reasoning traces across four- and six-digit problems. Subtraction pools 94 SFT and Full traces from four-digit problems. ARI is the median pairwise adjusted Rand index across ten single-initialization fits.

papers.selection_reason: Analyzes post-training effects on verbalized reasoning in LLMs; relevant to language foundation model behavior.
papers.title: How Post-Training Influences Verbalized Algorithmic Computation in Language Models
papers.tldr: Post-training chiefly improves how language models use verbalized reasoning, not their internal encoding of intermediate computation.

papers.abstract: Program evolution provides a promising approach to discover agent memory designs and study the choices underlying their effectiveness. We introduce MAPE, a framework that evolves whole memory programs from minimal seeds through a standardized lifecycle interface and an iterative diagnosis-proposal loop. Experiments on LoCoMo and LongMemEval yield an absolute accuracy gain of up to 12% over manually designed baselines at 35% of the serving cost, with further evaluations supporting transfer across serving backbones and benchmarks. Empirical analyses and ablations identify and validate two recurring design patterns: retaining raw conversations as retrievable evidence preserves details omitted from extracted memories, while composing retrieved evidence according to query intent helps the answering model use it effectively. Transplanting the composition module into five existing memory systems improves accuracy across all five. Beyond these patterns, the search objective shapes where computation goes: optimizing serving cost alongside accuracy shifts computation from LLM-based memory construction to selective processing at query time while retaining competitive accuracy. Together, these findings offer empirical lessons for agent memory design. Code is available at https://github.com/ash-ding/MAPE.
bullets: Evolves complete memory programs from minimal seeds using a standardized lifecycle and iterative diagnosis–proposal loop.
Evaluated on LoCoMo and LongMemEval, achieving up to 12% absolute accuracy gain at 35% of the serving cost of manually designed baselines.
Finds that retaining raw conversations preserves details lost in extracted memories, while query-intent-based evidence composition improves answer use.
The composition module transfers across five existing memory systems and improves accuracy in each.
Jointly optimizing accuracy and serving cost shifts computation toward selective query-time processing; scope is supported by evaluations across backbones and benchmarks.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of MAPE’s program evolution framework. Candidate programs are proposed using archived designs and diagnostic feedback, checked for execution errors, and evaluated on the search set. Their implementations, results, and diagnoses are retained to guide subsequent proposals. Evolution follows either an accuracy-only objective (MAPE-A) or joint accuracy–cost objectives (MAPE-P). Shortlisted programs undergo held-out evaluation for final selection.

Figure 2: Pipeline of MAPE-ALME, evolved under the accuracy-only objective on LongMemEval. Build retains both extracted atomic notes and raw conversations. Retrieve combines dense and sparse rankings through reciprocal rank fusion (RRF) and returns relevant notes and raw conversational evidence. Compose implements Query-Routed Scaffolding (RQS), which routes queries to type-specific scaffolds according to query intent, preparing context for the answering model.

Figure 3: RQS transplanted from MAPE-ALME into five human-designed memory systems, evaluated on the LongMemEval evaluation set with Qwen3-30B-A3BInstruct-2507 as the serving backbone. Bold values indicate absolute accuracy gains in %.

Figure 4: A LoCoMo temporal example comparing MAPE-ALCM and MAPE-PLCM across serving backbones. The programs differ in the date representation and answer context passed to the QA model. Qwen answers are taken from held-out traces; GPT-4.1 mini answers are illustrative. Evidence and context excerpts are abbreviated.

Figure 5: LongMemEval search trajectories using Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct-2507 on the 100-question search set. Panels a and b show accuracy-only and accuracy–cost search, respectively. Blue lines show candidate accuracy, dashed lines show the best accuracy so far, and bars show lifecycle serving cost per 1,000 queries. Stars mark selected programs; orange circles mark the final Pareto frontier. Callouts identify representative design changes.

Figure 6: LoCoMo search lineages using GPT-4.1 mini on the 233-question search set. Panels a and b show accuracy-only and accuracy–cost search, respectively. Nodes represent candidates; colour encodes serving cost on a logarithmic scale. Grey edges indicate primary parents, and orange paths trace the lineages of the highest-accuracy candidates. Dashed lines mark maximum search accuracy; dark rings mark the final Pareto frontier. The no-memory seed is displayed off-scale at the bottom.

Table 1: Accuracy and lifecycle serving cost on the LoCoMo evaluation set with two serving backbones. For each system, without uses the default evidence rendering, while with applies RQS to the same retrieved evidence. Avg is computed over all questions, and column abbreviations follow Table 2.

Transfer details are provided in Appendix D.1.

Values are accuracies in %, with Avg computed over all questions. Column abbreviations follow Table 2.

Results provide the question-type breakdown of Table 3. The bold row denotes the full system; ablation definitions follow Table 8. Values are accuracies in %, with Avg computed over all questions. papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have emerged as primary interfaces for factual retrieval, yet current evaluation paradigms rely almost exclusively on explicit entity names. In this work, we demonstrate that LLM knowledge is fundamentally lexically anchored: models possess extensive factual information but find it significantly difficult to retrieve without explicit name tokens. To quantify this limitation, we introduce ShadowBench, a rigorously hardened, shortcut-resistant benchmark designed to evaluate Latent Entity Association via a novel Dual-Trait Association (DTA) task. Our evaluation reveals a pervasive "Shadow Gap" across all model scales$\unicode{x2013}$up to the frontier models GPT-5.4 and Claude-Sonnet-4.6$\unicode{x2013}$where removing lexical anchors causes performance drops of over 20%. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this lexical dependency exposes a critical vulnerability in AI safety. Applying ShadowBench to Machine Unlearning, we find that state-of-the-art algorithms (e.g., Gradient Difference, NPO) achieve only superficial lexical erasure. While unlearned models fail on direct queries, our novel Latent Entity Leakage Rate (LELR) metric reveals that for popular entities, models explicitly reconstruct the "forgotten" entity in their internal reasoning traces in over 74% of cases, utilizing residual shadow knowledge to solve associative tasks. Conversely, for niche entities, models retain high shadow accuracy (60-90%) via implicit attribute correlation despite 0% LELR. Ultimately, ShadowBench indicates that current unlearning paradigms create an "Illusion of Forgetting," demonstrating that existing methods act as superficial output filters and are not yet reliable for achieving true parametric erasure.
bullets: LLMs struggle to retrieve facts when explicit lexical anchors are removed, revealing a broad “Shadow Gap” across model scales.
ShadowBench introduces a shortcut-resistant Dual-Trait Association task for measuring latent entity associations.
On direct unlearning queries, models may appear to forget entities while retaining recoverable associative knowledge.
The Latent Entity Leakage Rate (LELR) exposes internal reconstruction for popular entities, while niche entities can remain implicitly recoverable without explicit reconstruction.
The findings suggest current unlearning methods provide superficial output filtering rather than reliable parametric erasure.

figures.caption: Figure 1: The ShadowBench Construction Pipeline. A three-stage architecture designed to isolate latent entity association. Stage 1 involves discovery and stratification of entities by popularity. Stage 2 implements an iterative hardening process to neutralize lexical, syntactic, and temporal heuristics. Stage 3 utilizes combinatorial permutations and domain-matched hard negatives to synthesize final probes. This systematic sanitization ensures that success on ShadowBench is strictly contingent upon latent semantic reasoning rather than superficial pattern matching.

Figure 4: Latent Entity Leakage in an “Unlearned” Reasoning Model. This trace from the unlearned Qwen model shows that while the model has a high loss on direct lexical queries for “Elon Musk,” it maintains a fully intact semantic graph. The model explicitly names the forbidden entity to bridge the relationship between the Hyperloop concept (Question) and Neuralink (Option D), while successfully identifying and eliminating distractor entities.

Figure 5: The Shadow Gap Scaling Trajectory. Accuracy comparison between Direct QA (grey) and ShadowBench (blue) across Qwen3-8B, GPT-5.4-mini, and GPT-5.4. This confirms that the performance penalty for removing lexical anchors remains a rigid structural bottleneck even as models transition from open-weights to frontier-scale architectures.

Figure 3: The Illusion of Forgetting across Training Epochs (Elon Musk target). We track the divergence between lexical recall (ROUGE, grey) and latent association (Accuracy and LELR, green/blue). ROUGE collapses almost immediately, while the LELR remains near 1.0, proving the model still explicitly identifies the target in its latent reasoning trace. True erasure of the “Shadow” only occurs at the point of catastrophic model collapse (e.g., GD+KL Epoch 3).

Figure 8: Forget Set Generation Prompt. This template was utilized to synthesize the Dforget training set, given the entire Wikipedia content. By enforcing the inclusion of the entity’s explicit name in the output, we ensure the dataset targets the model’s lexical retrieval pathways, providing a clean contrast to the anonymized associations in ShadowBench.

Figure 7: ShadowBench One-Shot Prompt Template. This template is designed to induce the Dual-Trait Association logic by providing a clear example of entity identification followed by attribute matching. This standardization ensures that the model is evaluated on its associative capability.

Figure 6: The Persistence of the Shadow Gap across Model Scales. Accuracy comparison between direct name-based recall (Direct QA, grey) and anonymized attribute association (ShadowBench, blue) for Llama-3-8B-Instruct, Qwen3-8B, and GPT-5.4. While absolute performance improves monotonically with model capacity and reasoning depth, a significant “Shadow Gap” remains universal. Even the frontier-scale GPT-5.4 suffers a substantial accuracy drop when lexical anchors are removed, proving that current LLM knowledge retrieval is fundamentally dependent on explicit entity names regardless of scale.

Figure 2: The Persistence of the Shadow Gap. Accuracy comparison between Direct QA (grey) and ShadowBench (blue). Entity name acts as mandatory retrieval trigger; removing it caused accuracy drops across all scales. Notably, Claude-Sonnet-4.6 established the highest baseline (>98% direct recall) yet still exhibited a ∼16% performance drop for niche entities, confirming that lexical anchoring is an inherent property of Transformer-based retrieval. Additional results are provided in Appendix B.1.

Figure 10: Unlearning Failure: Latent Entity Leakage (Qwen3-8B). Despite achieving a high forget-loss on direct queries for “Elon Musk,” the unlearned model explicitly reconstructs the forbidden identity in its scratchpad to solve the ShadowBench task. This qualitatively confirms the persistence of the latent conceptual node.

Figure 9: Baseline Success Case (Qwen3-8B). The base model demonstrates robust latent association. It correctly identifies “Jeff Bezos” as the bridge between the founding of Blue Origin and the leadership of Amazon, explicitly naming the latent entity in its reasoning trace.

Figure 11: Unlearning Failure: Catastrophic Model Collapse. In this failure mode, aggressive unlearning has destroyed the model’s structural linguistic weights. The model fails to associate facts about neighboring entities (e.g., Mark Zuckerberg) and produces repetitive, non-semantic tokens.

Table 2: Unlearning Performance Matrix. While SOTA methods successfully induce direct lexical forgetting (Direct Forget ROUGE drops), latent associations remain largely intact in reasoning models (Qwen). In non-reasoning models (Llama), unlearning is achieved only via catastrophic weight degradation.

Table 1: Baseline Performance across Model Scales. ShadowBench accuracy (%) comparing Standard (Std) decoding and Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning. Accuracy rises steadily with model capability (Llama < Qwen < GPT < Claude), and reasoning provides a consistent dividend for reasoning-optimized models. However, a pervasive gap between lexical recall and latent association remains across all model scales.

Table 7: ShadowBench v1 Results (Lexical Anonymization Only). Scores are artificially inflated due to models exploiting un-neutralized gendered pronouns or chronological era-mismatches as deductive shortcuts.

Table 8: ShadowBench v2 Results (Pronoun Neutralization and GPF). Accuracy scores after replacing gendered pronouns and enforcing a strict ±25-year generational window for distractors. While overall accuracy drops relative to v1, performance remains partially inflated as models pivot to exploiting domain-specific gender cues (e.g., “WTA” or “Best Actress”) to eliminate distractors, necessitating the strict demographic homogeneity introduced in v3.

Table 3: ShadowBench v3 Dataset Composition. We balanced the total number of QA pairs to ensure statistical parity between tiers. Lower Tier entities require a significantly larger entity pool to achieve comparable scale to the fact-dense Upper Tier.

Table 6: Controlled Sensitivity Analysis. Accuracy (%) on a matched 1:1 entity subset. Controlling for distractor pool size resolves baseline anomalies (e.g., Sports), revealing a universal Popularity Bias and CoT dominance across all model scales.

Table 9: Multi-Domain Unlearning Generalization. Evaluation of NPO+KL unlearning across domains and tiers. While direct lexical recall is suppressed, latent associations persist through two distinct leakage modes.

Table 11: Hyperparameter Search and Checkpoint Selection. Evaluation metrics across different configurations. Checkpoints that exceeded the Utility Perplexity threshold (> 100) were disqualified. Bolded rows represent the Pareto-optimal checkpoints selected for final evaluation in Table 2.

Table 4: Controlled Sensitivity Subset Statistics. This subset matches entity counts and QA pairs 1:1 across tiers to verify that distractor saturation does not confound the observation of Popularity Bias.

Table 5: Direct QA vs. ShadowBench Accuracy. Detailed numerical breakdown of the scores visualized in Figures 2, 5, and 6. Direct QA (Direct) established the factual recall ceiling, while ShadowBench (SB) measured associative retrieval.
Table 10: Full-Dataset Empirical Variance. Accuracy (µ±σ) across 5 trials on the full corpus. The negligible variance confirms that ShadowBench results are robust to sampling and decoding noise.

papers.title: ShadowBench: Exposing Lexical Anchoring and the Illusion of Forgetting in Large Language Models

papers.abstract: Reasoning models achieve strong performance through long chains of thought (CoT), but often spend more tokens than needed to solve a problem. Existing ways to shorten the CoT require additional training for each model, add a fixed steering vector to the model's hidden states, or use decoding heuristics such as stopping early or banning words like "wait", which can reduce accuracy. We propose DoubtLess, a training-free decoding method in which a much smaller reasoning model steers the large one towards brevity. The small model reads the large model's CoT so far twice, once prompted to be brief (the brief thinker) and once prompted to be verbose (the verbose thinker), and the difference between its two logit vectors, scaled by a strength, is added to the large model's logits at every step of the CoT. On seven benchmarks of competition mathematics, graduate-level science and competitive programming, DoubtLess shortens the CoT of Qwen3-32B by 31% with unchanged accuracy, outperforming five inference-time baselines. We also show that DoubtLess reduces thinking tokens per turn by 20% in a self-debugging coding agent with unchanged task performance. It also generalizes to two other model families with unchanged accuracy. When combined with training-based compression, it further shortens the CoT of a model already trained for brevity. Ablations and behavioral analysis show that DoubtLess reduces repeated checking, with most token savings coming after the correct answer first appears in the CoT. Our code is available at https://github.com/leoluolol/DoubtLess.
bullets: Addresses overly long chains of thought and limitations of training-based or heuristic shortening methods.
At each reasoning step, a small model reads the current CoT in brief and verbose modes; their logit difference steers the large model toward brevity.
Shortens Qwen3-32B CoT by 31% with unchanged accuracy across seven mathematics, science, and programming benchmarks.
Reduces thinking tokens per turn by 20% in a self-debugging coding agent while preserving task performance, and generalizes across two other model families.
Analysis attributes savings mainly to reducing repeated checking after the correct answer first appears; further compression is possible when combined with brevity training.

papers.abstract: LLM-based multi-agent systems (MAS) have attracted growing attention for improving reasoning through interaction among multiple agents. In this work, we focus on parallel multi-agent reasoning systems, where several agents solve the same problem over multiple rounds and aggregate their outputs into a final answer. Despite their strong reasoning performance, uncertainty estimation for such systems remains underexplored: the reliability of a MAS depends not only on individual generations, but also on how agents interact and evolve across rounds. We propose SAUCE (Sequential Agent Uncertainty through Consensus Evolution), a lightweight, training-free uncertainty estimator that formulates MAS uncertainty as sequential inference over a latent system-level belief. SAUCE aggregates round-level agreement and generation-uncertainty signals through a filtering-style update. Across five backbones, five benchmarks, and two MAS protocols, SAUCE improves misclassification detection, selective prediction, and calibration over a broad set of uncertainty estimation baselines, including standard log-likelihood-based methods and MAS-specific estimators.
bullets: Targets uncertainty estimation for multi-agent systems whose reliability evolves through agent interactions and repeated rounds.
Models system uncertainty as sequential inference over a latent, system-level belief.
Combines round-level agreement with generation-uncertainty signals using a filtering-style update.
Evaluated across five backbones, five benchmarks, and two multi-agent protocols.
Improves misclassification detection, selective prediction, and calibration over established baselines.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview. (A) Two MAS trajectories can reach the same final answer but differ greatly in reliability: a stable run whose outputs converge across rounds (top) is more trustworthy than an unstable run whose outputs oscillate (bottom). A static view that only considers the final output cannot distinguish them, motivating uncertainty estimation from interaction dynamics. (B) SAUCE models multi-round interaction as a sequence of round-level observations (Mt, Rt), where agreement is weighted by generation uncertainty, and performs a filtering-style update over a latent system-level belief. The resulting trajectory summary defines the SAUCE uncertainty score u(x, τ) (Eqn. 11).

Figure 4: Probabilistic view of SAUCE. A latent system belief st evolves across rounds and emits a noisy observation ot formed from the agents’ outputs. SAUCE’s per-round estimate is the posterior expectation E[st | o1:t]=µt.

Figure 3: Distribution of (a) the baseline agreement signal M̄t and (b) SAUCE’s posterior-mean estimate µt (each averaged over rounds) for correct vs. incorrect MAS outputs (MMLU-Pro, Gemini-2.5FL, DyLAN). SAUCE sharpens the separation between classes (AUROC 0.579→0.805). Densities are normalized independently in each panel.

papers.abstract: Compositional generalization remains challenging when language models must combine familiar reasoning operations in unfamiliar ways. The Scenario-Based Commonsense Reasoning Evaluation (SCoRE) 2026 tests this ability on three mixed domains absent from training and requires models to identify the complete set of correct options for each question. We introduce Route-Verify-Vote (RVV), a framework for procedure-conditioned self-consistency that uses language models without parameter updates. Route uses the provided domain label to select a reasoning procedure that guides the model in representing and applying the relevant constraints. Verify prompts the model to assess each option against those constraints. Vote aggregates complete answer sets and allocates additional samples to questions with a small vote-count margin between the two most frequent sets. Samples for each question follow the same domain-specific procedure. On the official test set, voting over 16 sampled answer sets per question achieves an exact-set accuracy of 74.6%. Adaptive RVV reaches 77.3%, and combining models on selected domain routes raises accuracy to 79.4%. The final system ranked second among participating systems. These results support domain-specific reasoning procedures and answer-set disagreement as useful tools for allocating inference-time computation in mixed-domain reasoning.
bullets: Targets compositional generalization across unseen mixed domains requiring complete correct answer sets.
Uses a three-stage, parameter-free framework: Route selects a domain procedure, Verify checks each option against its constraints, and Vote aggregates sampled answer sets.
Adaptive sampling focuses additional computation on questions with close vote margins.
Achieves 74.6% exact-set accuracy with 16 samples, 77.3% adaptively, and 79.4% when combining models across selected routes.
The final system ranked second in the SCoRE 2026 evaluation.

papers.abstract: Model architecture shapes the scaling behavior, training efficiency, and inference cost of LLMs, making it a central focus of both industry and academia. In industry, teams such as those behind DeepSeek, Qwen, and Kimi routinely introduce architectural innovations, yet public reports rarely document which ideas succeeded, which were abandoned, and why. In academia, limited compute and inconsistent baselines often restrict evaluations to small-scale, single-point comparisons, making it difficult to establish whether improvements hold at larger scales or translate into broader impact. ArchSpace addresses both gaps as a public platform for Recording, Reviewing, and Referencing Architecture Researc}: each proposal is recorded with its experiments and reasoning, reviewed by the community, and referenced by later work. To evaluate ideas before costly large-scale training, ArchSpace leverages scaling laws to predict model loss at larger scales from smaller experiments, a practice widely adopted in industry. We provide initial references that make the platform usable: Qwen3.5 and OLMo3 baselines, fitted scaling laws, and a reusable training recipe. Ideas validated through this review can in turn become new baselines, and ArchSpace thereby aims to broaden the range of ideas that shape the next generation of models.
authors: Jie Wang, Tong Zhu, JiaHao Kuang, Zhe Xu, Yunkai Chai, Dehong Zheng, Yu Cheng, Tao Ji, ZhouHan Lin, Qi Zhang, Bowen Zhou
bullets: Addresses poor documentation of successful, abandoned, and unexplained architecture choices in industry.
Helps academia overcome limited compute and inconsistent baselines that hinder large-scale evaluation.
Records proposals with experiments and reasoning, enables community review, and links validated ideas to later work.
Uses small-scale experiments and fitted scaling laws to predict loss at larger model scales.
Provides initial Qwen3.5 and OLMo3 baselines plus a reusable training recipe; its scope is an initial platform and reference set.

papers.abstract: Remasking allows diffusion language models to revisit generated text, but effective correction requires knowing when and what to revise. Our diagnosis on Sudoku reveals two gaps. Hidden states contain error information that token confidence does not reliably expose, and remasking an isolated error usually reproduces it when the surrounding context remains fixed. These findings motivate DiVR , a verifier that predicts whether a partially generated sequence will reach a correct answer. Trained on the final correctness of the model's own trajectories, DiVR decides when to regenerate a block and which alternative to retain, while the generator itself stays unchanged. On five reasoning benchmarks with LLaDA-8B-Base, DiVR raises the average accuracy of the fine-tuned generator from 35.3\% to 43.4\% at $1.9$-$3.5\times$ the cost of greedy decoding, above search baselines that use $3.8$-$7.4\times$. It also complements post-training such as supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning, and generalizes to other generators, including Dream.
authors: Minhae Oh, Jeonghye Kim, Jinwoo Koo, Yeongoon Kim, Jimin Seo, Minsik Seol, Jungwoo Lee
bullets: Token confidence can miss errors, and remasking isolated errors often reproduces them because context remains unchanged.
DiVR verifies whether a partially generated sequence is likely to become correct using the model’s own completed trajectories.
It decides when to regenerate a block and which candidate to retain without changing the generator.
On five reasoning benchmarks, accuracy increased from 35.3% to 43.4% with 1.9–3.5× greedy-decoding cost, versus 3.8–7.4× for search baselines.
The verifier complements supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning and transfers to other generators, including Dream.

figures.caption: Figure 2: DiVR-guided block re-decoding. DiVR scores the canvas, masked suffix included, after each block (B = 4 here, 32 in the experiments). A score below θ triggers four alternatives of the block from the same prefix, and the best-scoring state (s1, 0.91) replaces the original. Text and scores are illustrative.

Figure 1: Diagnosis on uniquely solvable 4× 4 Sudoku. (a) Wrongness AUROC of hidden-state probes and confidence on matched observations. (b) After re-masking a wrong cell, the original digit stays highly probable and the gold digit rarely outranks it. (c) Gold-guided repair on 77 failures: reopening the wrong cells alone fixes few, and the per-puzzle best setting is an oracle upper bound.

Solid lines give success (%) and dashed lines the verification-inclusive cost relative to greedy (square). The vertical line is θ = 0.5, chosen on the GSM8K development set beforehand, and ∗ marks a paired McNemar difference from it at p < 0.05.

Figure 4: Verifier reliability on greedy GSM8K states. Mean score versus empirical success at the first non-final block and the final state (300 observations each), and markers are bins with at least ten observations. Platt parameters are fitted on development states.

Each panel is one model and each block one generator (untuned or SFT for LLaDA-8B-Base, released or diffu-GRPO for LLaDA-8B-Instruct); every method in a block runs on that generator, with one verifier for the math columns and one for the code columns. Each panel shows the block that fell below θ (Original), the four alternatives decoded from the same state, and their scores. The highest-scoring candidate (bold) is kept. ←↩ marks a line break.

Fixed counts the greedy errors that guided decoding corrects, out of 413 on GSM8K, 377 on MATH-500 and 322 on Countdown, and the repair block is the first block at which an alternative replaced the original. TPR and FPR treat a wrong greedy answer as positive and a first-block score below θ as a flag. Most repairs begin in the first block.

Table 10: Decision calibration for regenerate-or-continue. 436 paired greedy states from 150 GSM8K test problems. A rule regenerates when the raw score is below θ, and predictions apply the development-fitted Platt map to the state each action leads to. papers.selection_reason: Verifier-guided regeneration for diffusion language models is relevant to language foundation model inference and reasoning.
papers.title: Learning When Diffusion Language Models Should Regenerate
papers.tldr: DiVR improves diffusion language model reasoning by learning when to regenerate whole blocks and which alternatives to keep, raising accuracy while using less computation than search baselines.

papers.abstract: Coding agents tackle successive tasks on an evolving repository, carrying forward edits and writing memory before the next task is known. Selecting memory for unknown next tasks requires balancing future usefulness against the costs of writing and reading it. The actor must also decide when acting on available memory saves effort as the task unfolds. We introduce Coding-Repository Memory (CoReMem), a cost-internalizing framework that guides memory design and actor adaptation through measured memory value on the next task. Prospective segment valuation compares runs of the next task with and without individual trajectory segments from the same inherited repository state, guiding a compact memory built around anchors: repository locations and executable checks. Actor adaptation estimates on-policy memory value within rollout groups with and without memory, using a reward that prioritizes resolution and penalizes step count in successful runs. Provenance-gated value credit assigns the additional value term to steps identified as using memory-supplied anchors, while every step retains outcome credit. On ChainSWE, CoReMem raises the 27B actor's resolve rate from 21.0% to 25.7%, with 17% fewer steps and 11% fewer total cache-aware tokens, including memory-module calls, relative to the untrained actor model without memory.
authors: Peiwen Li (Yale University), Harshit Verma (Yale University), Sophia Zhou (Yale University), Haiwen Wang (Yale University), Ngoc Bui (Yale University), Heng Chang (Tsinghua University), Fei Fei (Goodvision AI), David van Dijk (Yale University), Rex Ying (Yale University)
bullets: Targets memory selection when future tasks are unknown and repositories evolve.
Builds compact memory from repository-location and executable-check anchors using segment-level prospective valuation.
Adapts the actor with rollout-based memory valuation, provenance-gated credit, and rewards favoring resolution with fewer steps.
On ChainSWE, raises resolve rate from 21.0% to 25.7%, while reducing steps by 17% and cache-aware tokens by 11% versus an untrained actor without memory.

figures.caption: Figure 4: Overview of CoReMem. (a) Prospective segment valuation of memory. A memory m written from the trajectory τk is valued by the change ∆y(m | bk) it causes on task k+1, run from the inherited tree Sk with and without m. Removing each of the seven segments of τk gives its value νc, and the segments that pay are kept as anchors A(m). (b) Cost-internalizing on-policy valuation. A group of G sessions mixes sessions with their own memory (m), no memory (∅) and a misplaced memory (m̃) under the reward Ri, and V̂b = R̄m − R̄∅ is the memory’s value on-policy. (c) Step-level provenance-gated value credit. Only the steps that the gate ωt marks as acting on an anchor from the memory receive the value credit.

Figure 7: Evidence for M2 and M3. Top, steps per task and resolve rate of the with-memory arms in training order, where up and to the left is better and the larger marker is the full method. Bottom, paired differences in the memory benefit to resolve rate and in the step cost of a misplaced memory, blue for 27B and green for 9B as above, with 95% intervals.

Figure 2: What crosses coding-task boundaries and where memory is valued and optimized. Existing settings keep memory within one task, transfer general experience across independent tasks, or carry memory while resetting the repository. Our setting carries both repository state and memory to unseen future tasks. The ⟲ and ↓ symbols indicate whether memory is valued and optimized on its source task or on future tasks.

Figure 6: Steps, resolve per token and resolve per dollar against no memory for the API-served models. Top, each point is one memory layer on one model, and the shaded quadrant is where a memory lowers steps and raises resolve per thousand total tokens, which CoReMem w/o training reaches on all three models. Bottom, the change in resolve per dollar at list prices, with full numbers in Table 3 of App. D.

Figure 1: Memory on the next task. A memory written at the end of one flake8-simplify task hands two anchors, a location (WHERE) and a check (VERIFY), to the next task on the same repository; the post-trained actor model acts on them at steps 1 and 6 and skips the exploration it would otherwise start with (step counts illustrative).

Figure 5: From segment values to the memory design. The median change in steps (νc) and in thousand actor tokens (κc) when one segment is removed from the current task’s trajectory (Eq. (3); 27B actor model). Blue bars mark segments whose removal adds steps. The right columns give the field each segment becomes in the memory design, kept as a main field (blue), in reduced form (light blue) or dropped (gray), and what the next task gets from each of them.
Figure 10: A real memory and its anchors. The memory has 889 characters and 18 anchors.

Figure 8: Training dynamics of the 27B actor on the test sessions with the memory. Lines are means over three replays and bands their standard deviation. Update 0 is the untrained actor, also drawn as the dashed line. The number beside each panel is the paired difference at update 20.

Figure 9: A real trajectory split into segments (flake8-simplify, training split, frozen 27B actor). Verbatim except [...] cuts and the omitted command fences; segment labels and step numbers are ours.

Figure 11: The instruction under which the actor writes its memory, verbatim from the deployed file. It states what the next session can see, fixes the memory’s two blocks and five line types, sets the rules and shows the finished shape. Bold, shading and gray placeholders are ours.
Table 3: Cost and outcome of each memory layer for the API-served models on the test set. Overall columns as in Table 1, with the list-price cost per session and resolve per dollar.

Table 2: Anchors the next task can act on, per memory layer. 27B frozen actor model, test set; an anchor is used when it occurs only in the memory and appears in a message of the next task’s session; brackets give 95% intervals over the test chains.
Table 7: The seven segments of a trajectory. The first five partition the transcript, and the last two come from the boundary.
Table 8: From segments to lines. Results of the segment study (App. I). Counts are boundaries where the segment helped and hurt the next task. BH marks the multiplicity correction across segments.

Table 4: The post-trained actor on SWE-bench Verified. All 500 instances, one task each, no memory, 3 replays per row. The untrained row serves the zero-update adapter on the same path, and tags give the change against it (∗∗ for a paired 99% interval that excludes zero). Raw counts tokens with no credit for caching, and Limit hit is the share of instances that end at the step limit.

Table 5: The memory layer off the training distribution: successive tasks of one repository on an external dataset. SWEContextBench (SCB) pairs are two-task chains of one repository in one image, the next task opening at an independent checkout from the first, so only memory crosses the border. CoReMem w/o training writes its memory under the instruction of Figure 11; we updated the writer instructions by adding that the next session starts from a new checkout without the earlier changes, that the memory should not include a summary of or reason for the changes, and that the memory should only include one clause per DID line. The adapted instructions were written after observing the first runs on the set, whose memories were getting cut off because of note length.

papers.selection_reason: Cost-aware persistent memory for coding agents, fitting LLM agent memory and retrieval beyond context.
papers.title: CoReMem: Cost-Internalizing Memory for Successive Coding Tasks with Prospective Valuation
papers.tldr: CoReMem improves coding-agent performance on successive repository tasks by valuing memory prospectively and internalizing its writing, reading, and action costs.

papers.abstract: We investigate whether and how LLMs encode goals: internal neural representations that precede and guide action, and that are flexible enough to be realized through many different execution paths. We construct a coding setting with multiple sub-tasks that allows us to evaluate goal-seeking behavior and the selection of sub-goals. In this setting, we localize an encoding of the next sub-goal in the outputs of a sparse set of attention heads. The same heads can be used to decode the LM's future actions in natural language (e.g., "I'm checking if a word is a palindrome"). We verify that this encoding is causal for next action and is plastic: transplanting it into a different environment, e.g., another programming language, triggers the same operation realized with a different sequence of tokens. The LM also sustains the encoding throughout the action's execution, which is puzzling because a transformer LM without recurrence cannot carry a state forward for more tokens than it has layers left. We propose that it does not need to. Under a non-recurrent goal-seeking (NRGS) account, the LM frequently re-reads the goal from the task specification, compares it with the progress visible in the growing context, and pursues what remains. We test the predictions of this account with targeted causal interventions.
authors: Arnab Sen Sharma, Eric Todd, Sheridan Feucht, Andy Arditi, Rohit Gandikota, Natalie Shapira, Gabriele Sarti, Constanza Fierro, Lisa Schut, David Bau
bullets: A coding setting evaluates goal seeking and sub-goal selection across multiple tasks.
A sparse set of attention heads encodes the next sub-goal and can predict future natural-language actions.
Causal interventions show this encoding guides the next action and can transfer across environments, such as programming languages.
The encoding persists during execution, despite transformers’ limited ability to carry state across layers.
Targeted interventions support a non-recurrent account in which the model repeatedly compares the specified goal with visible progress.

figures.caption: Figure 6: The progress encoding carried in goal head query dictates the selection of next operation. In the destination run with prompt (pdst : abd → b), where the first sub-task a is prefilled, the LM picks up the next sub-task in the sequence b. When the query states of the goal heads at the pivot token are replaced with corresponding states from a source run (psrc : acb → c), it transfers the source progress. This transfer causes the LM to select d, the first task in destination task-list ({a,b,d}) which hasn’t been completed in source {a,b}.

Figure 1: Goal pursuit and its non-recurrent implementation in a transformer LM. A goal such as implementing merge sort (G) decomposes into sub-goals g1, g2, g3, each realized as a sequence of tokens (left). (i) An idealized agent commits to a sub-goal gk, keeps it active while pursuing it, and moves on once it is done. (ii) A transformer LM cannot persist a state across long sequence of tokens without running out of layers. (a) The intent to pursue gk = “divide into two halves” is nonetheless pre-committed: it is already readable at the indent token, multiple tokens before its implementation. (b) Because this commitment cannot be carried forward, the LM compensates with frequent re-computation: the LM frequently re-encodes the current sub-goal gk by reading the task span, and the progress-so-far eprog from the growing context tape, and compares the two to produce the next token (the sub-sub-goal). Different levels of goal hierarchy are maintained in the same way. (c) Once the sub-goal gk is complete, the LM moves on to the next sub-goal gk+1.

Figure 5: Goal heads frequently re-read the goal from the task span. The source prompt (i) and the destination prompts (ii) have different tasks, but they share a common initial sub-tasks which can be prefilled in

Figure 3: Temporal persistence of the sub-goal encoding. Cosine similarity between a sub-goal’s goal-head encoding at the equals sign token with the encoding sampled x% through an implementation, averaged over data types and languages. As the model progresses through an implementation of a sub-goal, its encoding remain more similar to implementations of the same sub-goal across different languages (dashed teal line) than for different sub-goals in the same language (solid orange line). This shows that sub-goal encodings persist in the LM computations until it’s implementation is finished.
Figure 15: Qwen2.5-Coder-Instruct: 14B vs. 32B. Each point contains scores for 253 readouts. The larger 32B model gives better readouts at all four pivots in both measurements.
Figure 36: GOALSCOPE generations for Qwen2.5-32B-Instruct compared to the same model fine-tuned on risky financial advice Turner et al. (2025); Soligo et al. (2025), across four prompts.

Figure 7: Applying GOALSCOPE beyond code generation. (a) We apply GOALSCOPE to few-shot ICL prompts and measure whether it can verbalize implicit relations of input-output pairs from few-shot examples. GOALSCOPE correctly identifies the implicit rule 80%+ of the time for certain relations such as antonym, country-capital, and person-occupation. (b) We also apply GOALSCOPE to chat settings. While readouts do not always reflect sampled generations, we find that readouts for an emergently misaligned model (Turner et al., 2025) qualitatively diverge from those of an innocent model (Figure 36b) at early token positions.

Figure 4: Goal heads mediate implementation. “Sufficiency” ablation preserves the selected heads’ access to the description of the next subgoal and blinds all the other attention heads in layers 20–63. “Necessity” ablation blinds only the selected heads by sinking their attention to the first token, while other heads operate as usual. Bars show LM’s success rate of implementing the next sub-goal with the ablation. Only 122 goal heads can sustain LM performance, but it drops sharply when 250 goal heads are blinded.

Figure 8: Illustrative example of the prompt. N subgoals are specified in natural language. For the target sub-goal gk, the LM’s generated code is prefilled up to a pivot point. On the same figure, we identify the pivot points where we probe for the upcoming operation with background highlights

Figure 9: Locating the goal heads. Left: source and destination prompts request different predicates in different programming languages. A separate target prompt requests the source predicate in the destination language. The two destination-language implementations share a common prefix and differ in the next token. We patch source head contributions into the destination using the maskweighted intervention in Equation (2), and jointly train the masks to promote the target continuation. Right: the selected 122 heads in Qwen2.5-Coder-32B-Instruct selected with a threshold τ = 0.9 over the trained masks.
Figure 32: GoalScope readouts while Qwen2.5-Coder-32B-Instruct implements the Gale-Shapley stable marriage algorithm.

Figure 10: The full prompts used to measure faithfulness and causality throughout this paper. We inject the goal head encoding at the last token position (highlighted) and keep performing the same injection at every generation steps.
Figure 11: Prompt for the LLM judge to evaluate faithfulness. Note that we ask the judge to make a subjective decision of whether the readout is a non-trivial part of the LLM’s upcoming operation gk.

Figure 12: Comparison of readout sources. We compare the readout quality of the encoding captured with the goal-heads vs full attention outputs and residual states. Across different encoding sources, we use the same hparams: additive_norm steering with α = 0.1, at layers 35–45. Each bar shows the average readout score over the four pre-implementation pivots, across the same 253 specifications (out of total 1012 points). Goal heads consistently give better readout performance compared to the larger representations.

Figure 25: Query transfer setup for multi-token generation. (i) From the source run (here with prompt psrc : acb→ c), we cache the query states of the goal heads at the pivot. papers.selection_reason: Mechanistic study of goal encoding and goal-seeking in LLMs contributes to understanding reasoning in large language models.
papers.title: Goal Encoding in LLMs
papers.tldr: LLMs encode and causally use flexible next-sub-goals, re-reading task specifications to sustain goal-directed behavior without recurrent state.

papers.abstract: Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) often underperforms full fine-tuning, especially in heterogeneous and continual-learning settings in which substantial forgetting occurs. In general, it suffers from an undesirable learning-forgetting trade-off across diverse fine-tuning settings. We identify a potential contributor: LoRA adapters, especially high-rank ones, frequently fail to realize the available capacity afforded by the configured rank. Specifically, we find that standard LoRA updates have effective rank far below their configured rank, limiting how broadly the update energy is distributed. Therefore, we propose training mechanisms that optimize the original objective while maximizing adapter effective rank. Our main method adds a simple, stable, differentiable, and SVD-free R\'enyi-2 effective-rank regularizer to the language-modeling loss. We also connect capacity maximization to norm-bounded updates. In mixed-domain rank sweeps on three models evaluated with multiple random seeds, a penalty weight of $\lambda=0.01$ lowers mean Wiki perplexity at every tested rank of at least $16$ relative to unpenalized LoRA. Mean training perplexity improves or increases by at most $0.02$ in all but one model-rank comparison. Single-task and scheduling experiments further show that the balance between learning and retention depends on the configuration. We also observe that several LoRA variants in the literature also suffer from the identified capacity issue, and our approach provides a complementary axis of improvement to LoRA-based parameter-efficient fine-tuning. These results suggest that effective rank is not only a post-hoc diagnostic of adapter quality, but a trainable objective for improving the learning-forgetting frontier. Our code is available at https://github.com/tomohiro-sawada/lora-capacity-utilization
bullets: Standard LoRA updates often have effective rank well below the configured rank, especially at higher ranks.
The proposed method adds a stable, differentiable, SVD-free Rényi-2 effective-rank regularizer to the language-modeling objective.
Across mixed-domain rank sweeps on three models, a penalty of λ=0.01 reduced mean Wiki perplexity at every tested rank of at least 16 versus unpenalized LoRA.
Training perplexity generally improved or changed by at most 0.02, with one model–rank exception.
The balance between learning and retention remains configuration-dependent; effective rank is proposed as a trainable objective, not only a diagnostic.

papers.abstract: State space models (SSMs) are an emerging alternative to Transformers. SSMs offer linear-time inference and parallel training, but most implementations make the parallel scan efficient by making the recurrence diagonal: each channel of the hidden state is multiplied by an input-dependent real or complex number. These numbers commute, so the state records which inputs occurred but not their order. We formalize this with representation theory, which explains and fixes the state-tracking failures previously reported for SSMs. The state update defines a linear representation of the monoid of input sequences, and we show that an SSM tracks a group at every sequence length exactly when that group is a quotient of the group generated by its transition matrices. Two consequences follow. Diagonal real- and complex-valued SSMs can track only commutative groups, while the transition matrices of any SSM that can track a group must split into independent blocks over the real, complex, and quaternion numbers. We then introduce HyperSSM, which adds quaternion channels while keeping linear-time inference and parallel training. Trained only on final answers, HyperSSM solves the group tasks of recent state-tracking benchmarks exactly with at most five state numbers. This includes $S_5$ with 32 generators, where previous SSMs are at chance, and HyperSSM generalizes to sequences 25 times longer than those seen in training. Because the theory says what the transitions must encode, the learned weights of the linear recurrence can be interpreted directly. We demonstrate this by recovering the calibration of a real gyroscope, the rotations of imperfect qubit gates and the geometry of protein backbones.
authors: Anif N. Shikder, Ramit Dey, Jan Minac, Lyle E. Muller
bullets: Diagonal real- or complex-valued SSM transitions commute, so they cannot represent noncommutative group structure or reliably track input order.
The paper characterizes exactly when an SSM tracks a group: the group must be a quotient of the group generated by its transition matrices.
Any SSM capable of tracking a group must decompose into real, complex, and quaternionic blocks; this motivates HyperSSM.

HyperSSM solves group-tracking benchmark tasks exactly using at most five state numbers, including an $S_5$ task where prior SSMs perform at chance, and extrapolates to sequences 25× longer than training.
The learned recurrence weights are directly interpretable and recover structure from gyroscope calibration, imperfect qubit-gate rotations, and protein-backbone geometry.

(a) Orientation of a moving body measured by a real gyroscope (BROAD; held-out recordings); physical model: integration of the sensor readings. (b) Bloch vector of a qubit following a gate sequence, with imperfect gates (2% under-rotation and 2◦ axis tilt); physical model: simulation using ideal gates; HyperSSM achieves errors below the lower axis limit (10−3 degrees) at all sequence lengths; complex diagonal SSM uses three layers. Details on Clifford gates and ideal Clifford+T gates are provided in SM S11. (c) Orientation of residue j relative to the frame of residue i, computed from the torsion angles, on held-out PDB proteins; physical model: reconstruction using standard bond geometry. In all three cases, HyperSSM uses a single quaternion channel (four state variables); the complex diagonal SSM uses 128 state variables.

FIG. 1. Order in a linear memory. (a) One step of a selective SSM; shaded, the tracking regime (no decay, x0 = 1, one transition per symbol). (b) After a word w, a channel holds the ordered product Q(w); it tracks the group if a continuous readout recovers π(w) from Q(w) at every length. (c) A complex channel stores a phase; turns add, and order is lost. (d) A quaternion channel stores a 3D orientation; 90◦ turns about x and z in either order give different states. (e) q and −q are the same rotation; a sign-invariant readout tracks A5, a sign-aware one tracks Q8. (f) H tracks A5 but not S5; M2(H) tracks S5.

FIG. 3. A HyperSSM layer. Each channel follows the linear recurrence of a diagonal SSM, with input uk, hidden state x (j) k , transition a(j)(uk) and input term B̄(j)(uk)uk, with multiplication in its own algebra A(j). Channels evolve independently, mix only in the readout C, and are computed by the same parallel scan.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces a quaternion state-space model with representation-theoretic analysis of recurrent memory, directly relevant to LLM architectures and recurrent memory mechanisms.
papers.title: Symmetry in Time: A Representation Theory of Linear Recurrent Memory
papers.tldr: A representation-theoretic analysis shows why diagonal SSMs lose sequence order, and HyperSSM fixes this with quaternion-valued state channels while preserving efficient inference and training.

papers.abstract: Merging independently fine-tuned checkpoints into a single multi-task model requires no data, no labels, and no gradient steps. In practice the task vectors of different tasks interfere, and the standard remedies--averaging, magnitude pruning, sign election--operate entry by entry, ignoring that each delta induces a low-dimensional update on the hidden features it acts upon. We recast merging as a subspace interference problem. For every two-dimensional weight tensor we take the top-r right-singular subspace of each task's delta--the input directions along which that task moves the representation most--and remove from each task vector the component lying in the union of the other tasks' subspaces. The resulting Joint Null-Space Projection (JNSP) is closed-form and order-independent, needs no forward pass, and is defined entirely by the checkpoint set. On eight CLIP image-classification tasks JNSP merges ViT-B/16 experts to 89.45% average accuracy without using a single image, 11.88 points above the strongest parameter-wise training-free baseline (TIES-Merging, 77.57%), 14.22 above Task Arithmetic, and 0.98 above WUDI's data-free consensus merge (88.47%). The gain holds across three backbones on the independently trained TALL release (+10.8, +12.6, +9.1 over TIES for ViT-B/16, ViT-B/32, ViT-L/14) and replicates there at 89.20%; controls confirm the source--a single shared subspace instead of per-task ones loses 2.9 points, and a sequential variant collapses to 69.6%. On RoBERTa-large the same projection underperforms plain task arithmetic, which we report rather than hide. Code is available at https://github.com.
bullets: Addresses interference between task vectors during data-free, training-free checkpoint merging.
Uses top-r right-singular subspaces of each weight-delta tensor and projects each task update into the joint null space of the others.
The closed-form, order-independent method requires neither forward passes nor data, labels, or gradient steps.
Achieves 89.45% average accuracy on eight CLIP image-classification tasks, outperforming reported training-free baselines; results also replicate across multiple ViT backbones.
Performance is not universal: JNSP underperforms plain task arithmetic on RoBERTa-large.

Figure 4. Qualitative comparison on held-out test images. Figure 3. How JNSP merges one tensor. (1) The top-r right singular vectors Si of ∆i are the input directions task i moves most. (2) The other tasks’ bases are stacked and orthonormalized to U∪; the orange wedges are directions task i must give up; Si itself is not added to U∪, but any part of it inside the peer union is removed. (3) ∆i is projected onto Ni, keeping ∆̃i and removing the rest; the kept parts are summed into θmerge. The construction never depends on task order.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes Joint Null-Space Projection (JNSP) for data-free merging of foundation model checkpoints (CLIP, RoBERTa), addressing subspace interference in model merging.
papers.title: Joint Null-Space Projection for Data-Free Model Merging
papers.tldr: JNSP merges independently fine-tuned models without data by removing task-update components that lie in other tasks’ important input subspaces, substantially improving multi-task accuracy on CLIP benchmarks.

papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can supply autonomous systems with plans, predictions, and judgments, but these contributions are sometimes wrong. This review asks how a system can maximize an LLM's utility while managing its fallibility. Our answer is to adapt the system's reliance on the LLM as evidence about the LLM's performance accumulates. Systems built from imperfect components, such as noisy sensors and faulty software, have long worked in this way, and the classical methods they use can be applied to LLM-based systems as well. A system can change its reliance on an LLM in several ways, depending on the LLM's role and on the other components in the system. Each change needs an estimate of the LLM's reliability, and the LLM's role and the kind of contribution it makes determine what to estimate. Classical methods from decision theory, estimation, and online learning then turn these estimates into reliance decisions. These decisions can reduce how often LLM errors affect the system. However, some errors matter even when they are rare. An independently verified mechanism can prevent such errors from being executed. Without one, adapting reliance using reliability estimates can still keep their risk within a bound. Studies on adapting reliance on LLMs are emerging but limited, and the reviewed comparisons suggest that adapting reliance can improve system performance.
authors: Ekta U. Samani, Christopher G. Atkeson
bullets: Reviews how autonomous systems can use LLM plans, predictions, and judgments despite their fallibility.
Advocates adapting LLM reliance based on observed performance and the LLM’s role in the system.
Applies classical decision-theoretic, estimation, and online-learning methods to convert reliability estimates into reliance decisions.
Independent verification is needed to prevent rare but consequential errors; otherwise, adaptive reliance can help bound their risk.
Emerging studies suggest adaptive reliance can improve system performance, though evidence remains limited.

figures.caption: Fig. 1. Blocksworld example used throughout this review, adapted from [12]. For one Blocksworld problem, the LLM generates a plan and a validator checks it. The robot executes an accepted plan as shown in (a). Feedback generated from this can be used in three different ways: (b) adding invalid-plan feedback to the prompt, (c) fine-tuning the model on outcomes from many such problems, and (d) using validator results and execution outcomes as evidence to change how the surrounding system relies on the LLM.

papers.selection_reason: Reviews methods for managing LLM fallibility in autonomous systems, focusing on adapting reliance based on reliability estimates rather than a specific technical implementation.
papers.title: Maximizing LLM Utility While Managing LLM Fallibility
papers.tldr: Systems can improve LLM-based performance by adapting how much they rely on an LLM as evidence of its reliability accumulates, while independently preventing or bounding high-impact errors.

papers.abstract: Post-training of large language models typically combines supervised fine-tuning (SFT) with preference-based fine-tuning such as Direct Preference Optimization (DPO). Human-annotated and synthetically generated preference data differ substantially in per-sample cost, but prior work typically holds sample count fixed when comparing the two. In this work, we explicitly study the interplay between cost and performance by comparing the effect of post-training with human and synthetic preference data under a fixed, dollar-matched annotation budget. We train and evaluate multiple base model families across helpfulness and summarization tasks. We find that synthetic data is far more cost-efficient at low-to-moderate budgets, achieving high win rates with as little as \$200--\$400. On helpfulness, human data closes the gap only at budgets roughly two orders of magnitude larger; on summarization, it does not close the gap at any tested budget. We also find that human-annotated data varies in reliability: one widely used human preference source substantially underperforms another, and the gap persists even after standard remedies such as domain restriction and deduplication.
authors: Shourik Banerjee, Ethan Mendes, Mohit Raghavendra, Wei Xu, Alan Ritter
bullets: Compares human-annotated and synthetic preference data using dollar-matched, rather than sample-matched, budgets.
Evaluates multiple base model families on helpfulness and summarization after SFT and preference fine-tuning.
Synthetic data achieves strong win rates at low-to-moderate budgets, including roughly $200–$400.
On helpfulness, human data catches up only at budgets about two orders of magnitude larger; on summarization, it does not catch up within tested budgets.
Human preference sources differ substantially in reliability, and the gap remains after domain restriction and deduplication.
