papers.selection_reason: Directly compares human and synthetic preference data for LLM post-training under fixed dollar budgets.
papers.title: Human or Synthetic? What a Fixed Budget Buys for Post-Training
papers.tldr: Under equal annotation budgets, synthetic preference data is generally much more cost-effective than human data for post-training LLMs, especially on summarization.

papers.abstract: How does data shape language model (LM) behavior throughout pretraining? We investigate this question through a case study on entity comparison, e.g., Between France and Brazil, which country is larger?, across nine comparison tasks spanning five entity types. We begin with controlled experiments in which we train small LMs (163M parameters) on mixtures of natural text from pretraining corpora and synthetic task data. Our analysis identifies three distinct phases of learning: (1) an early phase where the LM selects entities by frequency, (2) a middle phase where the LM selects entities by position in the prompt (first vs. last mentioned entity), and (3) a late phase where the LM selects the entity that is the correct answer. We show that the emergence of these three phases is causally determined by statistical properties of the training data. With small amounts of task-specific synthetic data, we observe only the first two phases and the model fails to learn the task; with large amounts, the model jumps directly from the frequency-based heuristic to solving the task correctly. Moreover, changing the entity frequency distribution from a naturally occurring Zipfian distribution (a small number of entities are very common and the vast majority are rare) to a uniform one weakens the frequency phase and speeds up learning of the task. Lastly, we show that the three phases of training dynamics from our controlled experiments appear in the open source model OLMo-2 32B. Together, our findings demonstrate that properties of pretraining data are causal drivers of heuristic learning and show that small-scale synthetic experiments can predict training dynamics at larger scales.
authors: Yik Siu Chan, Jing Huang, Yanai Elazar, Atticus Geiger
bullets: Across nine comparison tasks and five entity types, models exhibit three learning phases: frequency-based selection, prompt-position selection, then correct answers.
Small amounts of synthetic task data produce only the first two phases and fail to yield task learning; larger amounts skip the positional phase and enable correct solving.
Replacing naturally Zipfian entity frequencies with a uniform distribution weakens frequency-based behavior and accelerates learning.
The same three-phase dynamics appear in the open-source OLMo-2 32B model, suggesting controlled small-scale experiments can predict larger-scale behavior.

figures.caption: Figure 1: (a) An example of the entity comparison task we use to disentangle the three candidate strategies. The task requires comparing the areas of two countries; the correct answer is Brazil in the given example. However, if the model relies on positional or frequency bias, it would predict France. (b) The importance of each strategy across training checkpoints, measured by the decrease in accuracy when the feature for that strategy is removed. The frequency heuristic (orange) is most predictive of LM behavior in the earliest checkpoints, but is quickly taken over by the positional heuristic (blue), and the correct algorithm (green) appears in late training. The three-phase structure appears in both the small controlled setting and the large-scale natural text pretraining setting of OLMo-2 models, up to 32B parameters.

Figure 6: Feature importance across training checkpoints for OLMo-2 1B, 7B, 13B, and 32B. Solid lines and shaded regions show mean and standard deviation across 3 prompt variations per checkpoint. Figure 3: Learning trajectories across four ratios of synthetic task data to Zipfian natural text (0%, 0.01%, 0.1%, 1%). Solid lines and dark shaded regions show mean and standard deviation across 3 training seeds. The frequency phase is invariant to task supervision, but the correct algorithm phase only emerges above a critical density. Below this density (0%, 0.01%), the model never reaches the correct algorithm and instead defaults to positional shortcuts.

Figure 2: (a) Occurrences of 215 countries (and territories) in the OLMo-2-13B pretraining corpus, which follow a Zipfian distribution with a long tail. (b) Country frequency correlates with the area attribute (log-log Pearson’s r = 0.62), meaning that predicting the more frequently mentioned country as the larger one is a viable heuristic the model can adopt.

Each cell is colored by the feature with the largest drop-one accuracy at that checkpoint, and the number is that feature’s drop-one accuracy (%). Throughout training, accuracy is consistently higher when the correct entity is more frequent than when it is less frequent.
Figure 11: Prediction accuracy of feature subsets for the small LM trained on uniform natural text mixed with 0.1% uniform synthetic data.

Each line is one checkpoint, from early (dark purple) to late (yellow) training; lines move to the right as mentions accumulate. A line that falls gradually means countries differ widely in how often they are mentioned (a few are very frequent, many are rare). A line that drops almost vertically means nearly all countries have about the same number of mentions. papers.selection_reason: Demonstrates how pretraining data statistics causally produce heuristic-then-correct phases in LM entity comparison, informing LLM training dynamics.
papers.title: Pretraining Data Statistics Shape the Phases of Learning Entity Comparison in Language Models
papers.tldr: Pretraining data statistics causally shape how language models progress from frequency and positional heuristics to correctly solving entity-comparison tasks.

papers.abstract: To keep long interaction contexts tractable, stepwise group-relative training for multi-turn LLM agents materializes each source trajectory into multiple response rows and valid tokens. This expansion creates an outer-accounting problem distinct from within-trajectory credit assignment: row-based outcome statistics can count one episode outcome multiple times, while token-level reduction can assign unequal aggregate objective mass across trajectories. We term these effects outcome-statistics multiplicity and objective-mass imbalance. We introduce Outcome-Mass Alignment (OMA), a two-component method that makes both accounting choices explicit. Outcome Alignment computes outcome statistics over unique source trajectories, while Mass Alignment controls aggregate objective mass after within-trajectory aggregation of optimizer-native token objectives. Neither redesigns the base optimizer's credit assignment, importance ratios, or clipping. Across matched ALFWorld GRPO comparisons at two model scales, where failed trajectories typically expand much more than successful ones, OMA improves matched-horizon endpoint success by 7.0-9.4 percentage points. Ordinary WebShop exhibits weak or reversed expansion-outcome coupling and correspondingly mixed effects, whereas in a success-oriented WebShop setting, WebShop-SOL, OMA improves success nAUC from 0.399 to 0.511. Component ablations and GiGPO and GSPO comparisons further support component separability and cross-optimizer compatibility. These results show that trajectory expansion always defines an implicit weighting rule, but its practical effect depends on how expansion couples to outcomes and optimizer-native updates.
authors: Dawei Zhang, Yubin Huangfu, Jessica Fan, Boyu Wei, Likang Wu, Hongke Zhao, Ming He, Zhu Teng
bullets: Problem: Expanding each trajectory into response rows and tokens can multiply episode outcomes and assign disproportionate training mass across trajectories.
Method: Outcome Alignment computes statistics over unique source trajectories; Mass Alignment balances aggregate mass after within-trajectory token-objective aggregation.
Scope: OMA leaves the base optimizer’s credit assignment, importance ratios, and clipping unchanged and is compatible with multiple optimizers.
Results: In matched-horizon ALFWorld GRPO experiments, OMA improves endpoint success by 7.0–9.4 percentage points; effects are mixed on ordinary WebShop but positive in WebShop-SOL.
Key limitation: Benefits depend on how trajectory expansion correlates with outcomes, so OMA is not uniformly effective across environments.

papers.selection_reason: Addresses trajectory expansion bias in multi-turn LLM agent RL, with experiments on ALFWorld and transferable relevance to embodied agent training.
papers.title: Outcome-Mass Alignment: Controlling Length-Dependent Trajectory Influence in Multi-Turn LLM Agent Reinforcement Learning
papers.tldr: Outcome-Mass Alignment (OMA) corrects trajectory-level outcome overcounting and unequal objective weighting in multi-turn LLM agent RL, improving success when failed trajectories expand more than successful ones.

papers.abstract: During the supervised learning phase, autoregressive language models are typically trained by minimizing the negative log-likelihood of the training data, which decomposes as a sum of token-level cross-entropies via teacher forcing. This objective is simple and efficient but potentially suffers from so-called exposure bias: a mismatch between the way the model is trained and the way it is used at inference time. Can we instead design sequence-level loss functions that incorporate inference-time decoding procedures, such as greedy decoding or autoregressive sampling? We show that two natural attempts lead to loss functions that are fundamentally flawed: unbounded below. We further show that these two flawed loss functions are intimately connected: using autoregressive Gumbel tricks, the sampling based loss is the expected greedy loss under Gumbel perturbations. Since the pathology stems from the dependence of the decoded sequence on the model parameters, we analyze the update direction obtained by applying a stop gradient on the sampling procedure, leading to a moment matching direction. While it is not the gradient of any loss function, we prove that it defines a valid descent direction in function space for the autoregressive negative log-likelihood. Despite these theoretical insights, the moment matching direction suffers from high variance. We conclude that teacher forcing may well be ``all you need'' for supervised learning of autoregressive models.
authors: Mathieu Blondel, Micha\"el E. Sander, Germain Vivier-Ardisson, Tianlin Liu, Vincent Roulet
bullets: Teacher forcing trains autoregressive models with token-level negative log-likelihood but may introduce exposure bias.
Two natural sequence-level losses based on greedy decoding and autoregressive sampling are unbounded below.
Using autoregressive Gumbel perturbations, the sampling loss is shown to equal the expected greedy loss.
Stop-gradient analysis yields a moment-matching update that is a valid function-space descent direction for autoregressive likelihood, but has high variance.
The results suggest that teacher forcing may remain preferable for supervised training.
papers.selection_reason: Analyzes sequence-level training objectives for autoregressive LLMs and shows teacher forcing may be optimal; relevant to LLM training research.
papers.title: On the Difficulty of Sequence-Level Supervised Learning for Autoregressive Language Models
papers.tldr: Sequence-level objectives that account for inference-time decoding can be mathematically ill-behaved or high-variance, supporting teacher forcing as a robust supervised-learning approach.

papers.abstract: Long-horizon language agents accumulate tool results and replies until the history no longer fits the context window. Current agents shrink this history by having a model summarize it, so each compaction rereads and rewrites the history it replaces, and cache-aware triggers decide when to compact while taking the size of the result as given. We present Folio, a context manager that records, folds, and recovers history through one set of handles. While the agent runs, Folio records three linked levels: a short turn note the model writes as part of its ordinary reply (L1), an event manifest of every call written by the runtime (L2), and the captured source records (L3). Because these views already exist, the runtime folds the context programmatically, selecting coarser views for older turns. The fold prints the handles that index L2 and L3, so recovery tools that read bounded pages, compute over full text in files, and keep findings in a persistent dossier reach the evidence the agent needs with little added input. The fold trigger prices an explicit landing point that includes the retained budget. On 75 LOCA-bench tasks with DeepSeek-V4-Pro behind every system, Folio solves 66 tasks against 54 for the same runtime with model-written compaction and 49-59 for Claude Code, Codex, and SoL-Pi, in about half their working time, at 2.4 times lower cost than that runtime; each fold takes a median of 0.6 seconds.
authors: Yubo Ruan, Tao Peng, Jiao Zhang, Chuanguo Ma, Lei Xu, Han Zhou, Wenwu Wang, Xiafei Lv, Xingjie Zhou, Guiju Fan, Hao Wang, Fenghui Zhang, Mao Miao, Shuo Li
bullets: Addresses context-window overflow from accumulating tool results and replies in long-running agents.
Records linked history views: model-written turn notes (L1), runtime event manifests (L2), and source records (L3).
Programmatically folds older turns into coarser views while preserving handles for bounded, evidence-focused recovery.
Uses a fold trigger that accounts for an explicit retained-context budget and landing point.
On 75 LOCA-bench tasks, solved 66 versus 54 for model-written compaction, with roughly half the working time and 2.4× lower cost; folds took a median of 0.6 seconds.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of FOLIO. Record: the runtime turns tool events into a three-level indexed history. Fold: the cost-aware trigger selects views of this history to build the active context. Recover: the handle in the outline (t3.12) is passed to scan for a bounded read or to ctx to compute over the full text, and the result is kept in the dossier.

Figure 2: Folding and recovery on one example. (a) Turn t3 exists as a turn note (L1), the manifest row of call t3.12 (L2), and the 900-row table it returned (L3). Within the layout budget L, the fold shows t1 briefly, t2 with its full note, and t3 with the row of t3.12; the open turn t4 keeps a raw head and tail. (b) Through the same handle, scan checks one value and ctx counts every row; the finding and its source go to the dossier, which the next fold carries.

papers.selection_reason: Context folding and recovery for long-horizon language agents directly targets LLM memory and long-context management.
papers.title: Folio: Recoverable Multi-Resolution Context Folding for Long-Horizon Language Agents
papers.tldr: Folio manages long-horizon agent context by programmatically folding multi-resolution history and enabling targeted recovery, improving task completion while reducing time and cost in the reported evaluation.

papers.abstract: We argue that a binding constraint for personal agents is not model capacity but the form in which context is represented: the agent does not know which entity a phrase denotes, when a fact held, or which source record licenses a claim. We call the missing representation spatio-temporal context (STC) and define it on two axes. The temporal axis carries event time, validity intervals and ingestion time. The spatial axis is a relational space in which entities are points, typed relations are edges, and distance is semantic rather than geographic; physical places are one entity type among many. Every relation is anchored to immutable source records, and every answer must be closed over those records. We formalise the substrate and six invariants, a context operator that composes temporal intersection with relational expansion, an ambiguity-preserving resolution state machine, a conflict detector that converts mutually exclusive facts into user adjudication rather than silent overwrite, and a four-regime consumption taxonomy spanning query, insight, triage and proactive reminder. We describe a local-first prototype of the retrieval layer built on SQLite with on-device embeddings and hybrid lexical-dense recall, report measurements from a deployed store of 341 documents, 340,079 chunks and 190,271 embedded vectors, and specify, but do not yet implement, the analytic layer on which the framework depends. We close with an evaluation protocol with per-invariant metrics for evidence coverage, temporal correctness, conflict precision and interruption cost. The proposal targets the representation of context rather than the volume of it.
authors: Haitao Cheng, Jerry Hu, Longdong Mao, Dong Huang, Dongming Li, Lijuan Zhang, Mengting Zhang
bullets: Motivates STC as a solution to unresolved entity references, temporal validity, and unsupported claims—not insufficient model capacity.
Represents context across temporal dimensions and a semantic relational space, with every relation anchored to immutable source records.
Defines six invariants, temporal-relational context composition, ambiguity-preserving resolution, and conflict handling through user adjudication.
Introduces four consumption modes: query, insight, triage, and proactive reminder.

Describes a local-first SQLite retrieval prototype and an evaluation protocol covering evidence coverage, temporal correctness, conflict precision, and interruption cost; the analytic layer remains unimplemented.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes an evidence-grounded spatio-temporal context substrate with retrieval and conflict resolution for personal agents, directly relevant to agent and LLM memory.
papers.title: Time and Space: A Dual-Axis, Evidence-Grounded Context Substrate for Personal Agents
papers.tldr: The paper proposes spatio-temporal context (STC), an evidence-grounded representation for personal agents that links entities, time, relations, and source records to support reliable answers and actions.

papers.abstract: Laya is a small model that answers a multiple-choice question about a text in one pass: the question, the options (each with a name and a description) and the text form one sequence of at most 512 tokens, the window, in the English release. A longer text is silently cut at the end, and we measure what that costs. Test documents place a held-out row's text, the evidence, at a chosen token offset among distractor text; 177 items, five tasks, three checkpoints (released, short-row fine-tune, long-document fine-tune), four window sizes and 93,275 scored requests. When the evidence lies beyond the window, accuracy falls to 26.4% for the released checkpoint (27.2% for both fine-tunes), near the 27.0% of guessing and below the 35.6% of always giving the commonest label. Confidence gives no warning (AUROC 0.50 to 0.55 for telling cut from read requests; 0.5 = chance), and the runtime's truncation flag also fires on requests whose evidence was visible. The released checkpoint reads visible evidence badly once text precedes it: 38.5% pooled against 60% when the evidence comes first, so a larger window alone gains +6.2 points. Fine-tuning on long documents adds +27.6 points on visible evidence over the short-row fine-tune (95% interval +22.3 to +33.1) and nothing on cut evidence. That is an in-family result: training rows and test documents share generator and question types, and the main filler is of the training kind. With encyclopedic filler never seen in training the gain is +13.2 (+9.9 to +16.6), with rows of other tasks as filler -2.0. Among training-free rearrangements a 312-token window scan helps most (+11.9 points over the default for the released checkpoint) at six to eleven forward passes. Documents are synthetic, labels are LLM-made and one backbone is studied, so these diagnose this model, not long documents in general.
authors: Mohammed Nayeem Khan, Allan Kevin T
bullets: Evidence beyond the input window reduces accuracy to near-guessing levels, while truncation flags can also fire when evidence remains visible.
The released model reads visible evidence much better when it appears first; increasing the window alone yields only a modest gain.
Fine-tuning on long documents substantially improves performance on visible evidence but does not help when evidence is cut off.
A training-free window scan provides the strongest tested improvement, at the cost of multiple forward passes.
Results are limited to synthetic documents, LLM-generated labels, and one model backbone.

papers.abstract: Advances in large language models (LLMs) are rapidly transforming formal theorem proving. Yet further progress remains constrained by the lack of a transparent and effective data recipe for systematically improving theorem-proving models. In this work, we argue that effective agentic provers require strong mathematical skill priors to ground theorem proving and agentic trajectories to enable long-horizon, interactive proof construction. To this end, we synthesize an agent-native 33.7B-token mid-training corpus covering decomposition, search, self-verification, and revision, together with verifier-grounded agentic trajectories. We further introduce the daVinci-Prover harness, which enables models to construct proofs and interact with a Lean verifier in an isolated workspace, and use it to collect approximately 36K high-quality agent trajectories for supervised fine-tuning. Our mid-training recipe yields an average improvement of 13.7 points over the matched Qwen3-8B SFT-only baseline across MiniF2F, FATE-M, and ProofNet. When applied to the Qwen3.5 series, our approach also yields strong performance across theorem-proving benchmarks and achieves near-saturating MiniF2F performance with memory compaction. The results highlight agent-native mid-training as an effective foundation for developing stronger interactive theorem-proving agents.

papers.abstract: It is common to train Large Language Models (LLMs) for agentic tasks with Reinforcement Learning (RL) from scalar rewards. However, this throws away the fine-grained information about the environment that the agent experienced during the trial (e.g., error logs). To utilize this rich information, recent works wrap the agent in a harness that refines its own inputs through reflection or compaction and hands past experience to future rollouts, but the construction of the handed-off artifacts (e.g., a playbook) is itself not learned. We want the best of both worlds: gradient updates from a scalar reward, while also utilizing environment information to hand off experience. As a concrete testbed, we fix the Agentic Context Engineering (\ace{}) harness and train one model to act, reflect, and curate task-local playbooks. Our method, \acerl{}, evaluates candidate experience-handoff artifacts by their downstream effect on future actor rollouts, and co-optimizes the role-specific behaviors (action generator, insight reflector, and playbook curator) under a fixed scaffold. Across agentic benchmarks, \acerl{} achieves higher held-out performance than baseline methods. The results suggest that agent training should optimize not only the actions in the current rollout, but also the model-written experience that future rollouts inherit.
authors: Doyoung Kim, Byeongguk Jeon, Kailin Zhang, Sherry Yang
bullets: Scalar-reward RL overlooks useful trial information such as error logs.

papers.abstract: As large language models (LLMs) advance toward increasingly long inputs, soft context compression offers a promising approach to efficient inference by converting long inputs into compact memory slots. Under limited memory budgets, effective context compression remains challenging because task-relevant evidence varies substantially across queries, ranging from localized evidence to multiple distant spans or information dispersed throughout the full document. Instead of compressing everything indiscriminately, we propose CoMem, a query-guided selective context compression framework that learns memory representations conditioned on both the document and the query. CoMem develops Contrastive Compressor Learning to achieve query-sensitive yet context-preserving memory representations. To inject a strong prior over query-dependent evidence distributions, we devise a same-context hard negative mining strategy by pairing a single document with multiple queries, requiring the compressor to selectively retain information according to each query's distinct evidence needs. To address the restricted information flow imposed by causal masking, we further enable bidirectional attention among memory slots. Experiments demonstrate that CoMem consistently outperforms existing context compression methods across compression ratios on question answering and RULER-NIAH benchmarks. Our code is available at https://github.com/scar-on/CoMem.
authors: Sikui Zhang, Haowei Liu, Ziyun Gan, Chunfeng Yuan, Guangze Gao, Nian Liu, Boyu Cai, Bo Li, Xiaolei Lv, Jun Gao, Bing Li, Weiming Hu

Applies contrastive compressor learning with same-document, multi-query hard negatives to distinguish differing evidence needs.
Enables bidirectional attention among memory slots to improve information flow despite causal masking.
Outperforms existing compression methods across compression ratios on question answering and RULER-NIAH benchmarks.

papers.abstract: Language models rely on finite token contexts, limiting access to earlier interactions. We introduce Recursive State-Augmented Language Models (Recursive SALM), a framework in which a persistent latent state evolves with each observation and generates adaptations of a pretrained language model. A modular read-transition-write architecture separates observation encoding, latent dynamics, and predictor adaptation. We develop deterministic and stochastic formulations. The experiments evaluate only deterministic SALM with frozen GPT-2 small and exclude earlier evidence from its decoder context. On a four-turn hypothesis-inference task, latent-gated LoRA reaches 89.1% accuracy, comparable to 88.0% for a trained full-context LoRA baseline, with earlier evidence available solely through a 64-dimensional state. Zeroing or shuffling the state substantially reduces accuracy. In a two-turn task with codewords unseen in training, several interfaces improve candidate ranking over chance, but rarely generate the exact codeword under the evaluated training schedule. These experiments show that persistent latent-conditioned adaptation can support sequential inference when earlier evidence is absent from the decoder context.
bullets: Addresses the limited memory of finite-token contexts by maintaining a state that evolves with each observation.
Uses a modular read–transition–write architecture to encode observations, update latent dynamics, and adapt the predictor.
In deterministic experiments with frozen GPT-2 small, latent-gated LoRA achieved 89.1% accuracy on a four-turn hypothesis-inference task, close to the 88.0% full-context baseline.
Removing or shuffling the 64-dimensional state substantially reduced accuracy, supporting its role in retaining earlier evidence.
On unseen-codeword tasks, interfaces improved candidate ranking over chance but rarely generated the exact codeword under the tested training schedule.

papers.abstract: Transferring LLMs into System One decision models typically replaces the language modeling head with a decision head while retaining the full backbone, making every decision pay for all layers. Yet it remains unclear how much depth such decisions require. We find that decision information is concentrated in intermediate layers, with early layers building essential features and the final six layers removable without loss, while independently trained smaller models largely mimic the full model rather than developing specialized decision capabilities. These findings suggest that efficiency requires not simply smaller backbones, but shared computation across different depths. Building on this, we propose \method{}, which jointly trains a full model with prefix sub-models that share its final layers and decision head through self-distillation. A lightweight gate reads the hidden state at each exit to determine whether additional computation is needed, allowing one model to operate at multiple layers. Across seven decision benchmarks, our approach matches or outperforms independently trained models at every depth, while achieving better accuracy-efficiency trade-offs through adaptive computation.
bullets: Decision information is concentrated in intermediate layers; the final six layers can be removed without accuracy loss.
Independently trained smaller models mostly mimic the full model instead of learning specialized decision representations.
The proposed method jointly trains a full model and prefix sub-models that share later layers and a decision head via self-distillation.
A lightweight gate chooses whether each input needs additional layers, enabling multi-depth inference in one model.
Across seven decision benchmarks, the method matches or outperforms independent models at every depth with improved accuracy-efficiency trade-offs.

The model runs layer by layer, with a lightweight gate evaluating the hidden state at each intermediate exit. If ge ≥ τ , it runs the final block and returns a decision; otherwise, it continues from the saved states without recomputation.

papers.abstract: Natural Language Inference models can be sensitive to localized lexical changes. We introduce Shared Multiscale Input-Reference Conditioning (SMIC), which constructs a single input-dependent multiscale reference and reuses it across Transformer layers. Each layer applies its own multiscale transformation to the shared reference and injects the resulting conditioning feature before the attention update. We instantiate SMIC in a token--context Transformer (TCT) and conduct from-scratch comparisons against decoder-based and Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) baselines across all three ANLI rounds. TCT-SMIC attains the highest observed ten-seed mean accuracy on all three ANLI rounds. The ablations further support the contribution of SMIC. We evaluate a real-valued Llama-style plug-in and extend deletion/insertion diagnostics to pretrained ModernBERT encoder and Llama decoder models with and without SMIC. Across the evaluated perturbation protocols, TCT-SMIC exhibits comparatively low pooled-attention redistribution and smaller signed accuracy changes. We further establish a finite-sample bound on average subset-mass redistribution in terms of the mean Jensen--Shannon divergence between the restricted and renormalized attention distributions.
bullets: Addresses sensitivity of Natural Language Inference models to localized lexical perturbations.
Builds one input-dependent multiscale reference, transforms it per layer, and injects the result before attention updates.
Implemented in a token–context Transformer (TCT) and compared with decoder-based and MLP baselines on all three ANLI rounds.
TCT-SMIC achieved the highest observed ten-seed mean accuracy across all ANLI rounds; ablations support SMIC’s contribution.
Perturbation diagnostics found comparatively low pooled-attention redistribution and smaller signed accuracy changes; a finite-sample redistribution bound is also derived.

papers.title: SMIC: Shared Multiscale Input-Reference Conditioning across Transformer Layers for Natural Language Inference
papers.tldr: SMIC improves NLI robustness to localized lexical changes by sharing an input-dependent multiscale reference across Transformer layers.

papers.abstract: Looped Transformers increase effective depth by repeatedly applying a shared block, offering a parameter-efficient approach to language modeling. However, most existing works directly reuse each loop's output as the next's input, which can lead to hidden-state scale growth and perturbation amplification as recurrence deepens. We propose Rectified Looped Transformer (RLT), which redesigns feedback between loops using an interpolation schedule inspired by flow-based modeling. At each loop, RLT forms the next input by linearly interpolating between the current state and its prediction. Such interpolation distributes state changes across loops, encouraging a smoother trajectory from the initial input to the final output. Theoretical analysis proves that, under appropriate assumptions, RLT keeps state magnitudes uniformly bounded across loops and reduces the worst-case perturbation amplification. We evaluate RLT on language modeling corpora and downstream benchmarks. At matched training and inference depths, RLT consistently achieves lower perplexity than a standard looped Transformer, while exhibiting greater robustness to input perturbations and variance in inference depth. Consistent with the theoretical results, latent trajectory analysis shows that RLT maintains more stable hidden-state norms across loops, which also facilitates extrapolation-based decoding strategies. Notably, RLT achieves these gains without requiring additional trainable parameters or extra recurrent block evaluations, thus providing a simple yet more stable feedback mechanism for looped Transformers.
authors: Musheng Li, Jiawei Zhang, Ziyuan Liu, Yuantao Gu
bullets: Looped Transformers reuse a shared block to increase effective depth, but repeated direct feedback can amplify hidden-state scales and perturbations.
RLT interpolates between the current state and its prediction at each loop, producing smoother state transitions.
Theory shows bounded state magnitudes and reduced worst-case perturbation amplification under suitable assumptions.
Experiments report lower perplexity than standard looped Transformers at matched depths, plus greater robustness to input perturbations and inference-depth variation.
Stable hidden-state trajectories support extrapolation-based decoding; the approach adds no trainable parameters or recurrent block evaluations.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces a novel architectural modification (Rectified Looped Transformer) to improve stability and parameter efficiency in language modeling.
papers.title: Rectified Looped Transformer
papers.tldr: Rectified Looped Transformer stabilizes repeated Transformer computation through interpolated feedback, improving language modeling performance and robustness without added parameters or computation.

papers.abstract: Shared history in human dialogue is not merely a repository of facts, but the foundation of evolving relationships and mutual understanding. However, mainstream conversational memory systems rely on passive semantic similarity over external fact stores, frequently retrieving topically similar records while missing relationally pivotal experiences. Inspired by cognitive psychology's Self-Memory System (SMS), we propose MindMem, a mental-state-driven memory framework that asynchronously consolidates shared experiences into source-linked mental states of the character, the user, and their relationship. At each turn, a specialized mental-state reasoner (Mind) contextualizes these persistent states to anticipate latent user needs, form proactive intentions, and recover supporting episodic evidence that surface-level matching overlooks. To evaluate history-sensitive adaptation beyond factual recall, we introduce MemReal-Bench, a longitudinal benchmark grounded in month-long real-user interactions across dyadic and group scenes. By pairing Direct Question Answering (DQA) with Situated Memory Realization (SMR), it tests whether agents bridge the gap between knowing past facts and naturally using shared history, world rules, and relational trajectories. On MemReal-Bench, MindMem reaches 59.03% SMR and 82.58% DQA, exceeding the strongest memory baseline by 24.19 and 9.19 percentage points, respectively, and outperforming oracle target-memory injection on SMR. Code and dataset are available at https://github.com/jiazhicheng7-ctrl/MindMem.
authors: Zhicheng Jia, Shuchen Wu, Zhuoshi Tong, Haisen Liao, Sicheng Zhou
bullets: Targets the limits of similarity-based memory, which often retrieves topical facts but misses relationship-critical experiences.
Asynchronously consolidates interactions into source-linked mental states for the character, user, and their relationship.
Uses a mental-state reasoner to anticipate user needs, form proactive intentions, and retrieve relevant episodic evidence.
Introduces MemReal-Bench, a longitudinal benchmark evaluating factual recall and situated use of shared history in dyadic and group conversations.
Achieves 59.03% SMR and 82.58% DQA, outperforming the strongest baseline by 24.19 and 9.19 percentage points, respectively.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes a persistent, mental-state-driven memory mechanism for LLM-based dialogue agents.
papers.title: We Are What We Remember: Mental-State-Driven Memory for Long-Term Character Dialogue
papers.tldr: MindMem uses psychologically inspired mental-state memory to help dialogue agents understand and naturally apply long-term shared history.

papers.abstract: On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) trains a student on next-token targets from a teacher, a frozen copy of the student that additionally receives privileged information, such as a worked solution, hidden from the student. Whether student gains reflect that information remains unclear. Taking the worked solution as privileged information, we audit four stages across three Qwen3 scales on mathematics: Source, whether the teacher can use the solution; Encoding, whether the resulting token targets are useful; Transmission, whether the student learns from the targets; and Expression, whether the student applies the learned behavior without the solution. With the solution, the teacher solves hard problems and recovers from student errors, yet the teacher does not reliably recognize errors, and its token targets do not favor correct trajectories. Repeated training makes successes within the student's reach more frequent rather than unlocking new ones, and corrections the student learns to predict are not reliably expressed in free generation. To isolate the solution's contribution, we vary its availability separately from teacher and student thinking modes. The largest gains occur when a teacher in thinking mode supervises a student trained and evaluated without an explicit thinking trace, and problem-only teachers often match or exceed privileged-solution teachers: the gain tracks the teacher's thinking mode rather than the solution, a pattern we call reasoning arbitrage. Accuracy gains alone therefore do not establish transfer of reasoning from privileged solutions: bottlenecks lie after Source, across Encoding, Transmission, and Expression. Future evaluations must measure what the solution adds to otherwise identical training.
bullets: The audit examines four stages: whether teachers use solutions, encode them into useful targets, transmit them to students, and whether students express the behavior independently.

Across three Qwen3 scales on mathematics, teachers can solve hard problems and recover from errors with solutions but do not reliably identify errors or favor correct trajectories in their token targets.
Repeated training mainly increases successes already within the student’s reach rather than unlocking new capabilities.
Learned corrections are not reliably used during free generation, revealing failures in transmission and expression.
The largest gains come from thinking-mode teachers supervising students without explicit thinking traces; problem-only teachers often match or exceed solution-privileged teachers.

papers.selection_reason: Audits self-distillation of reasoning LLMs and proposes a training-diagnostic view transferable to LLM reasoning research.
papers.title: Privileged Information Does Not Guarantee Privileged Guidance: Auditing On-Policy Self-Distillation for Reasoning Models
papers.tldr: Auditing on-policy self-distillation shows that privileged worked solutions do not reliably transfer their reasoning to students, with gains driven more by teacher thinking mode than by the solution itself.

papers.abstract: Applications built on large language models assign the model a role through its system prompt, intending to shape how it responds for their use case. We introduce a validation framework for extracting and injecting occupational role vectors, activation-level directions that capture how someone in a given occupational role would distinctively respond to a task or question. We validate these vectors through two complementary lenses, on Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct. The interpretability lens asks whether each vector is a stable, separable, domain-consistent representation of its role: extracted vectors are highly reproducible across repeated runs and sampling temperatures, remain separable even for very similar roles, and agree more with themselves across in-domain and out-of-domain questions than with other roles' signal. The control lens asks whether injecting a role vector during generation makes the model express the role, and sustain it over a conversation, as well as a role prompt does. On Qwen, injecting the vector alone makes the model express the intended role substantially more often than unsteered, but at best matches a role prompt; on both models, adding the vector to the prompt strengthens the role in single answers but did not slow the role's decline over 30 turns. Together, the two lenses show why both are needed: out of domain the role is expressed only subtly, yet the activations still encode it; and a vector that is stable and separable can still barely steer the model's behavior.
authors: Jose L. Sampedro Mazon, Ilmi Yoon, Nadim Saad
bullets: Introduces a framework to extract, validate, and inject activation-level vectors representing occupational roles.
Evaluates vectors in Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct using interpretability and behavioral-control tests.
Vectors are reproducible, separable—even for similar roles—and more consistent with themselves across domains than with other roles.
Vector injection increases role expression, but generally does not outperform role prompts and does not prevent role weakening over 30 conversational turns.
Shows that representational stability does not necessarily imply strong behavioral steerability, motivating both validation lenses.

Table 24: French positive control: a language vector (system prompt “Always answer in French.” against the native default side) injected at the role-vector sites, 30 calibration questions, T = 1.0, strengths 0.1 to 0.8 (rows show the strengths at which the original share condition is met). Original rule (committed before any run): the vector steers if, at some strength, the share of answers detected as French is at least 50 pp above the unsteered share and the mean answer length is within 50% of the unsteered mean answer length. The original rule did not name a length unit; the script measured tokens, and French text takes more tokens than English text for the same content, which inflates the token ratio (verdict i); verdict (ii) measures length in characters. Amended rule (verdict iii; amendment dated 2026-10-04 20:28, committed after the original-definition Llama result had been seen at 14:21 and the garbled Llama output had been inspected): an answer is clean French if at least 98% of its letters are Latin script, its share of French function words is above 0.12 and above its share of English function words, and the median of three coherence judge trials is at least 75; the vector steers if the clean-French-and-coherent share is at least 50 pp above the unsteered share at some strength. The amended rule is the primary reading; all three readings are shown. Verdicts are per model and site over all strengths. Printed as two panels.

papers.abstract: System One models promise fast, general-purpose decision-making without lengthy token generation. However, understanding their capability spectrum and decision reliability requires more than aggregate performance on current benchmarks. Existing evaluations often provide limited insight into the breadth of model capabilities and the reliability of their decisions. We introduce SO-Arena, a benchmark characterizing the capability spectrum and decision reliability of System One models across 11 domains and five capability families. For the capability spectrum, SO-Arena offers evidence-grounded evaluation through reliable sources and manual verification of reference labels against model-visible inputs; fine-grained capability assessment through domain-specific difficulty criteria; and realistic interactive evaluation, where models iteratively execute actions in sandboxes. Reasoning-intensive tasks further enable system one-two comparison. Beyond accuracy, SO-Arena assesses decision reliability through two complementary measures: decision stability under controlled option-set changes and missing-answer recognition when no valid option is available. Evaluations across 21 models reveal that the benefits of scaling and additional reasoning vary substantially across domains. More importantly, strong overall performance does not necessarily imply reliable decision-making: the best-performing System One model ranks only seventh in reliability. Together, these findings highlight the need to characterize capability spectrum and decision reliability as complementary dimensions, providing a systematic view of the strengths and limitations of System One models.
authors: Lichen Li, Ziping Dong, Sicheng Feng, Qi Li, Xinchao Wang
bullets: Benchmarks 21 models across 11 domains and five capability families.
Uses evidence-grounded labels, domain-specific difficulty criteria, and interactive sandbox tasks.
Measures reliability through decision stability under option changes and recognition of unavailable valid answers.
Finds that scaling and added reasoning help unevenly across domains.
The top-performing model ranks only seventh in reliability, separating capability from decision dependability.

papers.abstract: Knowing when a large language model's (LLM's) response can be trusted is critical for its safe use. Uncertainty quantification (UQ) can help LLMs recognize if their responses may be unreliable. Existing taxonomies organize UQ methods by uncertainty source or estimation mechanism. They leave unresolved the question of where uncertainty is observed in the model's computation. The answer matters because the observation point determines whether an estimator has access to enough information to recover a given target, and how well it can recover it. Drawing on mechanistic interpretability, we define four mechanistic observation lenses: the structural lens observes component updates, the representational lens observes hidden states, the distributional lens observes token probabilities, and the semantical lens observes distributions over meanings. We relate these lenses through the residual stream and order them by the information they carry, which gives a principle for selecting UQ methods for different targets. We survey existing methods through the four lenses. Furthermore, we distinguish evaluation targets, criteria, and metrics to clarify different UQ evaluation protocols. Finally, we identify open problems and research directions to connect uncertainty estimation to the internal computation and downstream use of LLMs.
authors: Xiaoyu Liang, Virginia Ceccatelli, Aliai Eusebi, Tobias Braun, Nils Loose, Carlo Malagnino, Lorenzo Cavallaro

Relates the lenses through the residual stream and orders them by the information they carry.
Surveys existing UQ methods and distinguishes evaluation targets, criteria, and metrics.
Highlights open problems linking uncertainty estimates to internal computation and downstream use.

papers.abstract: Enterprise agents accumulate memory across dozens of sessions in which facts contradict, get superseded, and blur as similarly named entities collide in embedding space. The field treats this as a retrieval problem; we show it is not. On ENT-310, a synthetic enterprise sales-agent memory benchmark of 310 queries (210 answerable, 100 unanswerable), a vanilla Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) reader over a memory store already matches strong memory systems on the recall pillars. Retention and currency are near-saturated, roughly 0.93 to 0.98 for every competent system, so recall is essentially solved. What remains unsolved is resolution: which entity a query refers to, which time-state is current, and whether to commit an answer at all or decline when evidence is insufficient. We propose DISCERN (DISambiguation and Cross-session Episodic memoRy Navigation), an agent-memory framework built on a single rule: preserve at write, resolve at read. At write time DISCERN builds a strictly additive bi-temporal provenance graph that never merges confusable entities and never drops superseded values. At read time a zero-LLM tool surface drives an agentic loop that navigates this graph and commits exactly one of four gated terminal actions. A four-judge LLM-as-a-Judge council scores two axes: answer correctness on answerable questions, and the answer-versus-abstain decision as a classification problem. On ENT-310, DISCERN is the best-calibrated system on abstention (F1 0.924 versus at most 0.802 across eight baselines) and leads macro answer correctness under equal pillar weighting (0.861 versus 0.806 for the strongest baseline), a lead driven by entity resolution (0.800, where no baseline exceeds 0.40). Applied with zero tuning to the full LoCoMo corpus, the same pipeline again leads macro answer correctness (0.663 versus 0.638) and stays among the best-calibrated on false-premise abstention.
authors: Chirag Ahuja, Vladislav Tanov, Ramcharan Kakarla, Jonathan Taws
bullets: Frames persistent memory as a resolution problem—not primarily retrieval—because retention and currency are already near-saturated.
Builds an additive bi-temporal provenance graph that keeps confusable entities separate and preserves superseded values.
Uses a zero-LLM tool surface and agentic read loop with four gated terminal actions, including abstention when evidence is insufficient.
On ENT-310, achieves abstention F1 of 0.924 and macro answer correctness of 0.861, driven by substantially better entity resolution than baselines.
Also leads macro answer correctness on LoCoMo without tuning, while remaining well calibrated for false-premise abstention.

Figure 3: DISCERN read-time routing. The agent orients (Phase 1, read_profile_summary), runs a mandatory ambiguity check for underspecified queries (Phase 2, find_similar_entities), gathers targeted or raw evidence (Phases 3–4), and commits one of four terminal actions. The EarnedAbstainGate abstains only on demonstrated absence, a DeclineRouter sends a surviving decline to CLARIFY when confusable candidates remain and to ABSTAIN when none do, and a citation-or-abstain renderer requires every committed answer to cite its evidence. This procedure realizes the predicates of Eq. 1.

Right (read time resolves): an adaptive policy navigates the views with a small read-only tool surface and commits one of four governed actions (answer, update, clarify, abstain) under the EarnedAnswerGate and EarnedAbstainGate, the DeclineRouter, and the near-miss guard.

papers.abstract: Post-training can improve rewarded behavior while weakening capabilities users still need. We study two GRPO branches from a shared supervised checkpoint in a multilingual mixture-of-experts model. The released branch gains 36.07 points on MATH but loses 19.32 F1 points on XQuAD-Indic, while XQuAD-English improves under the same scoring rule. An independently trained sibling adds Indic instruction following and language-aware shaping. It recovers the regressing Indic task scores and preserves MATH, but does not restore script compliance and trades off competition mathematics and code. In a later round, judge training is followed by a sharp extraction decline from the Indic branch; reward-free distillation from its earlier checkpoint restores most of the lost F1. A MATH score decomposition associates most of the measured gain with increased boxed-answer emission; accuracy among boxed answers changes little. These results show why benchmark scores should be read alongside the response forms they reward.

MATH gains were largely associated with more boxed-answer emission, while accuracy among boxed answers changed little.
Benchmark scores should be evaluated alongside the response forms they incentivize.

papers.abstract: As memory-augmented agents increasingly support long-term and personalized interactions, reliable recall of emotional experiences while preserving their associated affect becomes necessary. However, existing evaluations usually assess emotion accuracy and factual memory grounding separately, overlooking event-affect correspondence. In this work, we formulate Affective-Episodic Retrospection (AER) as a task that explicitly evaluates the recovery of past events, associated affects, and their correspondence, and define Event-Affect Decoupling as a failure mode where the correct emotion is recalled but associated with the wrong episode. To diagnose Event-Affect Decoupling, we propose EM-TRACE, a stage-wise framework that decomposes AER into retrieval, affect recovery, and realization. On a controlled GoEmotions-based benchmark, Emotion-only retrieval achieves 28.65% affect recovery but retrieves the target episode for only 4.44% of queries, yielding a UAR of 24.21%. Further analysis reveals that event retrieval and affect assignment introduce distinct binding failures. These findings show that reliable AER requires grounded recall of emotional experiences, where episode retrieval, affect recovery, event-affect binding, and generation quality should be evaluated jointly. Our code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/A412/.
authors: Tingna Xie, Ming Wang, Shi Feng, Yongkang Liu
bullets: Defines Affective-Episodic Retrospection (AER) as jointly recovering past events, their affects, and event–affect correspondence.
Identifies Event-Affect Decoupling as a distinct failure mode missed by separate emotion and factual-memory evaluations.
Proposes EM-TRACE, a stage-wise diagnostic covering retrieval, affect recovery, and realization.

papers.abstract: Language-model agents can share conversational history across sessions, but persistence does not guarantee retrieval of current decisions and their provenance. This engineering study presents Memory-TCG, a Conversation ESAA extension inspired by ringing, resonance and renormalization (RRR), and an exploratory synthetic evaluation comparing chronological retrieval, two simplified baselines (B, recency-aware, and B', authority-aware), full RRR, and variants under three output budgets. With 480 facts and 1,024 tokens, full RRR recalled 0.44 of current decisions, versus 0.06 for chronological retrieval and 0.58 for the oracle ceiling; with 4,096 tokens it recalled all of them. B' and the no-resonance variant matched full RRR in decision recall across all nine scale-budget combinations, as expected when the active decision set and the adapter ordering are the same. The isolated contribution of ringing to decisions was not measured: comparator D1 cuts facts before the graph is built, and the product retains active decisions by rule. Before the output limit, full-RRR conflict F1 was 0.615 at all three scales; after it, at 480 facts and 1,024 tokens, it was 0.000. Reserving 20% of the budget for conflicts raised that F1 to 0.431 in that scenario, at the cost of lowering decision recall from 0.44 to 0.34, and to 0.930 at 4,096 tokens without decision loss. Fixtures are repetitive, comparators are simplified, and the evaluation was not independently replicated; the results support an engineering analysis, not a claim of selectionist superiority.
bullets: Persistent conversation history does not ensure retrieval of current decisions and their provenance.
The study compares chronological retrieval, recency- and authority-aware baselines, full RRR, and variants across three output budgets using synthetic conversations.
At 1,024 tokens and 480 facts, full RRR recalled 0.44 of current decisions, compared with 0.06 for chronological retrieval; at 4,096 tokens, it recalled all decisions.
Simplified baselines and the no-resonance variant matched full RRR in decision recall, so the isolated contribution of ringing was not established.
Conflict F1 fell to 0.000 after the output limit in the 480-fact, 1,024-token setting; reserving 20% of the budget improved it to 0.431 but reduced decision recall to 0.34.

papers.abstract: Backpack language models predict with a strictly linear combination of non-contextual per-word sense vectors, weighted by non-negative contextualization scores. We show that non-negativity conflates two properties: the linear readout, which carries the interpretability, and the conic combination, which merely restricts it. We relax the latter by computing the sense weights with differential attention, a difference of two softmax maps with a learned per-sense gain, so context can actively inhibit a sense; we call the result a differential Backpack. At equal parameters on WikiText-103 this cuts the Backpack's perplexity gap to a Transformer by 31%, improves over the softmax Backpack at every sense count, persists with a shrinking margin up to 350M parameters on OpenWebText, and is localized at the sense layer by ablations and controls. The learned inhibition is directly interpretable (a financial context drives the river sense of bank to -0.50), and the preserved per-sense attribution predicts counterfactual removals exactly. We tested a number of combination rules, showing the linear interface is nearly free. Making the readout nonlinear gains only 0.43 perplexity points while invalidating two thirds of the decomposition. The differential Backpack's senses are also better representations, improving zero-shot sentence similarity by up to 33%.
authors: Konstantinos Skianis, Giannis Nikolentzos, Polykarpos Meladianos, Michalis Vazirgiannis
bullets: Backpack models use interpretable linear combinations of non-contextual sense vectors, but standard non-negative weights cannot suppress irrelevant senses.
Differential attention computes signed sense weights as the difference between two softmax maps with learned per-sense gains.
On WikiText-103, the method reduces the perplexity gap to a Transformer by 31% and outperforms the softmax Backpack across sense counts.
Improvements persist up to 350M parameters on OpenWebText and are localized to the sense layer through ablations and controls.
Signed weights remain interpretable: for example, financial context inhibits the river sense of “bank,” while the model improves zero-shot sentence similarity by up to 33%.

papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents increasingly operate over long Web interaction histories, making memory management critical for reliable and efficient decision making. Existing methods primarily optimize storage, retrieval, or compression, but the memories most semantically relevant to the current state are not necessarily those that most improve the agent's action. We introduce MemCredit, a decision-centric memory framework that shifts memory selection from semantic relevance to decision utility. MemCredit estimates the state-, reference-context-, and policy-conditional marginal contribution of individual memories through controlled counterfactual interventions, and distills these intervention-derived credits into a lightweight utility estimator. At inference time, semantic relevance is used only for high-recall candidate generation, while predicted utility arbitrates which memories are retained under a fixed token budget, without modifying the underlying agent policy or requiring additional environment interaction. We evaluate MemCredit on ALFWorld and WebShop against representative memory baselines. On ALFWorld, MemCredit achieves 86.57 SR@50 under a 500-token historical-memory budget, compared with 65.67% for BM25 retrieval. Counterfactual analysis further shows that memory utility is sparse, strongly state dependent, and poorly captured by semantic relevance. These results suggest that decision utility provides a more effective principle than relevance alone for long-horizon agent memory management.
authors: Quanjiang Guo, Sijie Wang, Qianyang Zhu, Ben Zhang, Jinchuan Zhang, Ke Yan, Zhao Kang
bullets: Targets the mismatch between semantically relevant memories and memories that actually improve actions.
Uses controlled counterfactual interventions to estimate each memory’s state-, context-, and policy-conditional utility.
Distills intervention-derived credits into a lightweight utility estimator; relevance only generates high-recall candidates.
Retains memories by predicted utility without changing the agent policy or requiring extra environment interaction.
On ALFWorld, reaches 86.57 SR@50 with a 500-token memory budget versus 65.67% for BM25; utility is sparse and state dependent.

papers.abstract: LLM-based recommendation agents can search catalogs, inspect products, ask users, and revise rejected recommendations. However, these behaviors are often governed by hand-designed workflows, while existing training methods optimize isolated components such as query rewriting or list ranking rather than the interaction policy as a whole. We present SimRec, a reinforcement learning framework that trains the full interaction policy of a tool-integrated recommendation agent. SimRec introduces two components. A task-anchored user simulator provides feedback on every recommendation: conditioned on the current task need rather than on user profile, and it can be an external LLM or the recommender itself under self-play. A task-aligned reward optimizes the whole trajectory with GRPO, crediting natural retrieval quality and valid tool use alongside the final hit, with training-only target injection to handle sparse hits over large catalogs. On ESCI and Amazon C4, SimRec improves the NDCG@100 of a Qwen3-4B agent from 32.23% to 35.42% and from 22.94% to 24.72%}, outperforming training-free agents on far larger backbones and task-aligned baselines on NDCG. Analysis shows that the trained agent verifies candidates, uses preferences, and recovers from rejected recommendations far more often than its untrained counterpart. Our code is available at https://github.com/ZJU-REAL/SimRec .

Uses a task-anchored user simulator, via an external LLM or self-play, to provide feedback after each recommendation.
Optimizes complete interaction trajectories with task-aligned GRPO rewards for retrieval quality, valid tool use, and final recommendation hits.
Adds training-only target injection to mitigate sparse successful hits in large catalogs.
Improves NDCG@100 for a Qwen3-4B agent from 32.23% to 35.42% on ESCI and from 22.94% to 24.72% on Amazon C4.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) has become central to post-training large language models (LLMs). However, popular RL methods like GRPO incur non-negligible overhead by computing both old-policy and current-policy likelihoods to form importance sampling ratios. In this work, we propose Likelihood-Gated Policy Optimization (LGPO), which enforces a soft trust region constraint via likelihood-based gating, eliminating the need to compute old-policy likelihoods. Empirically, we show that removing the importance sampling correction term does not harm training stability, whereas removing the trust region mechanism can lead to collapse. Moreover, ratio-based clipping can fail in fully on-policy training: the importance ratio stays at 1, so the ratio-based trust region constraint never activates. Under standard training settings where GRPO is stable, LGPO achieves comparable training stability and peak performance while reducing training time by ~18% on average relative to a standard implementation that recomputes old-policy likelihoods. In fully on-policy training, where GRPO fails, LGPO remains stable, enabling more efficient and robust LLM RL post-training across training regimes.
authors: Shuibai Zhang, Junhyuck Kim, Gyeongman Kim, Jaewoong Cho
bullets: Importance-ratio computation adds overhead by requiring old- and current-policy likelihoods.
LGPO removes old-policy likelihoods and enforces a soft trust region through likelihood-based gating.
Removing importance-sampling correction does not harm stability, but removing trust-region control can cause collapse.
LGPO matches GRPO’s stability and peak performance under standard settings while reducing training time by about 18% on average.
LGPO remains stable in fully on-policy training, where ratio-based clipping cannot activate and GRPO fails.

papers.abstract: Language models evolve, but the observations, revisions, and context accumulated through user interactions should remain usable. Each new model must be able to retrieve past evidence, track revisions, and add new observations. We present MIGRO, a decoupled long-term memory system that treats experience as a persistent state shared across successive language models. MIGRO follows a simple principle: preserve historical evidence exactly, organize it approximately, and decide what to retrieve only when the question is known. We call this asymmetric fidelity with deferred selectivity. A shared semantic index supports retrieval, while exact records retain observations and their historical relationships. Because models differ in vocabulary and tokenization, host-specific interfaces convert selected evidence into inputs the receiving model can use. Reversible encoding reduces archival storage while enabling exact recovery. The shared state and its access interfaces let successive hosts read and extend the accumulated experience. On matched LoCoMo states, MIGRO scores 7.3% higher and uses 99.3% less private memory than the strongest quality baseline. After handoff, continued writing retains 99.9% of full-history rebuilding quality by extending the inherited state. On million-token BEAM histories, MIGRO uses 57.5% less private storage on average than the most compact baseline. MIGRO combines high answer quality, continued memory growth across hosts, and low storage cost. Code is available at https://github.com/zOUMINGXI/MIGRO.
authors: Mingxi Zou, Yinghui Xu, Jiaxiang Chen, Langzhang Liang, Wei Zhu, Peng Ye, Runkai Zhao, Ruoxi Jiang, Sijin Chen, Song Wang, Zhuo Wang, Lizhen Qu, Zenglin Xu
bullets: Addresses the challenge of retaining observations, revisions, and context as language models are replaced.
Uses asymmetric fidelity: exact historical records, approximate semantic organization, and query-time retrieval selection.
Combines a shared semantic index, reversible archival encoding, and host-specific interfaces for differing vocabularies and tokenization.
On reported benchmarks, improves quality and reduces private memory/storage versus baselines, while preserving continued memory growth after handoff.

papers.abstract: Small open models suit private customer-service deployments but trail frontier models in two ways: they miss what the written policy requires in a given situation, and they act inconsistently on what they know. We study whether such a model can close both gaps from its own deployment logs and their reference outcomes, without a stronger teacher model. Our starting point is a Gemma 4 12B agent that reads its domain policy from on-demand skills rather than from its system prompt. In each round, the deployed system serves a fresh batch of tasks; the base model diagnoses failed conversations and writes rules into the skills, and a rule survives only if it passes code checks, counterexample self-review, a paired retest, and a noise-calibrated validation gate. Reinforcement learning (GRPO) then trains a LoRA adapter on complete multi-turn, tool-using conversations. On the retail and airline domains of $\tau^2$-bench, without training or selecting on official tasks, the agent after two rounds improves on this starting point by 12.5 pass$^1$ points in retail and 19.5 in airline, and by 18.4 and 22.0 pass$^4$ points. It also exceeds the benchmark's reference agent, which runs the same model with the whole policy in its system prompt, by 11.8 and 8.0 pass$^1$ points and by 22.8 and 16.0 pass$^4$ points, closing most of the gap to three frontier models under the same protocol. A $2\times2$ ablation shows that the rules rescue tasks the agent never solved and carry policy knowledge that RL with the rules in context does not internalize, whereas the trained weights make solved tasks reliable.
authors: Yujia Zhang, Xinqi Ren, Shixiong Zhou, Jia Meng
bullets: Targets two gaps in small open models: missing situation-specific policy knowledge and inconsistent actions.
The agent extracts rules from deployment failures, filters them through checks and retests, then trains on complete tool-using conversations with GRPO.
After two rounds on retail and airline τ²-bench domains, it substantially improves over its starting point and surpasses the policy-in-prompt reference agent.
A 2×2 ablation suggests external rules provide new knowledge, while trained weights make already-solved tasks more reliable.
The study closes most of the gap to three frontier models under the same evaluation protocol.

papers.title: Knowledge in the Harness, Reliability in the Weights: Teacher-Free Co-Evolution of an LLM Agent
papers.tldr: A small LLM agent improves both policy knowledge and behavioral reliability through teacher-free co-evolution of its external skills and LoRA-trained weights.

papers.abstract: We introduce the multi-head quantum neural network (QNN), a quantum module compatible with noisy intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ) devices that can replace transformer blocks inside pre-trained large language models (LLMs) with little loss in accuracy and with far fewer parameters than the blocks it replaces. Encoding a model's $D$ hidden neurons into a qubit register is the obstacle: amplitude encoding scales poorly in circuit depth and angle encoding in qubit count, so neither is practical at production-scale width. We instead partition the hidden space into $k$ disjoint heads, angle-encode each into an $n_q$-qubit register, process the heads in parallel, and couple them through constrained classical linear layers, the mixers. Performing surgery on Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct-2507, we show that a single multi-head QNN with $145\,281$ trainable parameters ($D=2048$, $k=32$, $n_q=8$, $L=4$) can replace a contiguous span of eight transformer blocks, displacing $16.33\%$ of the model's parameters. Ablations show that, for a single replaced block, the quantum heads (circuits followed by a learned readout), and not the classical mixers alone, recover the displaced function, whereas for fused spans the mixers alone come within $1$-$3\%$ of the full module in perplexity. Whether this benefit is specific to trained, entangling quantum circuits is not established: controls that switch the entangler off (two seeds), or freeze the circuit at its initial or at uniformly random angles (one seed), beat the full module on held-out perplexity, and a parameter-matched classical multilayer perceptron remains a few percent ahead of the full module. We train classically with exact statevector simulation, then execute the quantum heads of our fusion checkpoints on a $156$-qubit IBM Heron processor, showing that NISQ-scale quantum modules can be installed in a production-scale LLM and run on hardware.
authors: Maforikan Amoussou, Borja Aizpurua, Sukhbinder Singh, Rom\'an Or\'us, Hans-Arno Jacobsen
bullets: Partitions the hidden dimension into parallel angle-encoded quantum heads coupled by constrained classical mixer layers.
A 145,281-parameter module replaced eight transformer blocks in Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct-2507, covering 16.33% of model parameters.
For one replaced block, quantum heads were important for recovering the displaced function; for fused spans, mixers alone came within 1–3% of the full module in perplexity.
Controls with disabled, frozen, or random circuits, plus a parameter-matched MLP, sometimes performed better than the full quantum module.
The quantum heads were simulated classically during training and executed on a 156-qubit IBM Heron processor.

papers.selection_reason: Investigates replacing transformer blocks in a 30B LLM with quantum modules, directly relevant to LLM architecture research.
papers.title: Multi-head Quantum Neural Networks: Replacing Transformer Blocks with NISQ Modules inside a 30-Billion-Parameter LLM
papers.tldr: A multi-head NISQ-compatible quantum module can replace transformer blocks in a 30B-parameter LLM with far fewer parameters, but its added benefit over classical alternatives remains unproven.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning sharpens LLM reasoning, but parameter updates are expensive, forgetful, and opaque; training-free libraries swap gradients for a textual store but still use trajectory-level, correlation-based admission and flat structure. To address both, we propose HyperSkill, a Training-Free Omnimodal GRPO framework that keeps the backbone frozen and replaces gradient updates with auditable edits to a Hypergraph-Indexed Skill-Library, where skills are advantage-bearing nodes and compositions are hyperedges. It has three components: training-time distillation admits counterfactually checked skills and learns a protocol skill from failures; gated hypergraph retrieval injects advantage-ranked skills where a per-dataset gate admits them; and an execution protocol makes the frozen backbone commit to an answer. On 11 text, vision-language, and omnimodal benchmarks, HyperSkill is best or tied on every dataset and beats the best baseline by 13.0 average F1 points while keeping the backbone frozen. Our software and data are publicly available at https://github.com/LHRLAB/HyperSkill.
authors: Haoran Luo, Shangkai Lin, Jinyang Wu, Xinliang Zhou, Luu Anh Tuan
bullets: Targets costly, forgetful, and opaque gradient-based RL updates, plus flat trajectory-level skill libraries.
Distills counterfactually checked skills and learns a protocol skill from failures.
Uses advantage-ranked hypergraph retrieval with dataset-specific gating, followed by an execution protocol for answer commitment.
Evaluated across 11 text, vision-language, and omnimodal benchmarks; it is best or tied on all and exceeds the best baseline by 13.0 average F1 points.
Scope: relies on dataset-specific gating and is evaluated on the reported 11 benchmarks.

papers.abstract: Long-context multimodal intelligence requires revisiting earlier images as conversations and documents accumulate, yet retaining an image does not guarantee reliable access to its details. By varying context length, redistributing a fixed text passage around the image, and changing positions without adding text, we identify the positional relation between images and questions as a direct influence on visual access. To address this gap, we propose Visual Position Re-Anchoring (VPR), a training-free method that shifts cached visual-key rotary phases toward a short-context reference before question processing. It operates directly on the existing KV cache, preserving standard attention computation without extracting attention maps or adding model forward passes. We develop static and continuous compensation schedules, using the static schedule by default. Across ten checkpoints and ten benchmarks, static VPR improves 97 of 100 model--task scores. Further analysis shows greater attention to regions containing answer evidence across six checkpoints, with minimal runtime overhead under fixed rotary frequencies. These findings demonstrate an efficient way to sustain visual access through positional adjustment within the cache.
authors: Juntao Xu, Qichai Zhao, Rui Sun, Zhouyang Jiang, Shiwei Wu, Zhi Li, Kaisheng Ma, Yu Liu
bullets: Image–question positional relationships can impair visual access even when the image remains in context.

papers.abstract: Deep neural networks typically realize dense computation by propagating information through all intermediate channels, while many approximation methods rank and retain individual computational components. We ask whether dense neural computation can instead be represented exactly as an expectation over a combinatorial state space, and approximated by evaluating only its most probable configurations. We introduce a novel probabilistic state-space framework for Transformer MLPs. The framework partitions the intermediate dimension into channel groups, defines an input-dependent distribution over binary inclusion states, and uses importance-corrected masked outputs such that the full expectation exactly recovers the dense MLP output. The key algorithmic novelty is NORDER-II, which enumerates complete joint states in decreasing probability without constructing or sorting the exponentially large state space. Truncating this ordering yields an anytime approximation governed by cumulative probability mass and a state budget. On Llama-3.2-1B and Gemma-2-2B, NORDER-II at a state budget of B=2048 achieves 92.4% and 93.8% MLP-output approximation accuracy, compared with 76.9% and 79.8% for Channel Top-k. When the first, middle, and last MLP layers are approximated jointly, WikiText-2 perplexity remains within 0.06% and 0.54% of dense inference. Relative to expected-count Grouped Top-k, NORDER-II yields 82.6% to 126.4% relative accuracy gains with only 0.18% to 0.19% additional local analytic FLOPs. These results establish the significance of joint-state structure beyond atomic salience and point to a new paradigm for neural computation: dense layers can be viewed as structured probabilistic inference over combinatorial computational states. This framework opens a path toward adaptive, probability-mass-controlled computation in pretrained neural networks.
authors: Victor O. K. Li, Yang Han, Jacqueline C. K. Lam
bullets: Partitions MLP channels into groups and defines input-dependent binary inclusion states with importance-corrected outputs.
NORDER-II enumerates complete joint states in decreasing probability without materializing the exponential state space.
At budget B=2048, it achieves 92.4% and 93.8% MLP-output accuracy on Llama-3.2-1B and Gemma-2-2B, outperforming Channel Top-k.
Joint approximation of selected MLP layers keeps WikiText-2 perplexity within 0.06% and 0.54% of dense inference.
Results support probability-mass-controlled, adaptive computation based on joint-state structure rather than individual channel salience.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces NORDER-II to approximate dense MLP computation via probabilistic state enumeration, offering a new efficiency mechanism for LLMs.
papers.title: Probabilistic State Space Enumeration in Neural Network Computation
