papers.abstract: AI coding agents can now construct scientific workflows, but operating them on shared cyberinfrastructure (CI) raises problems that code generation does not solve. Agents need current knowledge of the workflow system and its execution sites and access to the runtime state of distributed executions, while facilities need to attribute every agent action to a user and bound it by that user's privileges. We present PegasusAI Studio, an AI-assisted science gateway built on the Pegasus and HTCondor stack. Studio makes CI legible to agents by projecting one facility-curated knowledge base into the native configuration of several coding agents, by introspecting workflow interfaces and execution sites, and by grounding diagnosis in workflow and scheduler telemetry. Agent actions operate within a trust envelope that combines federated authentication, per-user execution environments and scheduler credentials, provider-neutral model access, observability, and approval controls for state-changing actions. The same application runs as a JupyterHub-based gateway on a research cloud and as an Open OnDemand application on HPC systems. We evaluate Studio through case studies of legacy CASA weather workflow modernization, a gravitational-wave reanalysis, an EEG analysis built with an open-weight model, and an Event Horizon Telescope (EHT) M87 image reconstruction that recovered from two failed runs to a zero-failure execution. The evaluation establishes that these mechanisms operate as designed.
authors: Komal Thareja, Mats Rynge, Berent Aldikacti, Angelina Ju, Ian Lumsden, Anirban Mandal, Rajiv Mayani, Kin Wai Ng, Hamza Safri, Michael Stealey, Sai Swaminathan, Michela Taufer, Karan Vahi, Michael Zink, Ewa Deelman
bullets: Addresses the gap between AI-generated workflow code and safe, observable execution on shared scientific infrastructure.
Projects a curated knowledge base into multiple coding agents and introspects workflow interfaces and execution sites.
Grounds agent diagnosis in workflow and scheduler telemetry for distributed-run awareness.
Constrains actions through federated identity, per-user environments and credentials, observability, and approval controls.
Case studies across scientific workflows, including EHT M87 reconstruction, show the mechanisms operating as designed, including recovery from two failed runs to a zero-failure execution.

figures.caption: Figure 7: The results stage for the EHT reconstruction’s successful run inside Studio. The run lists its 40 result files (per-day panel images, closure statistics, the ring-measurement table, and the summary report), each with a preview and a download, and a link that opens the run directory in JupyterLab. The preview shows the April 6, 2017 reconstruction by all three pipelines, one day’s reconstructions produced on the gateway pool.

Figure 1: The two tiers and the two platform deployments. One container image holds a complete single-user workflow environment. The platform tier that spawns and authenticates it is either the JupyterHub gateway on a research cloud or an OOD app on a campus cluster. Every process in the container, agents included, runs as the user’s own identity with the user’s scheduler token, over a Pegasus and HTCondor stack. Model access goes through a provider-neutral gateway with a prompt guard, and usage telemetry flows to a collector inside the platform.

Figure 5: The workflow lifecycle as the unit of integration. Each transition makes structured information from the workflow and execution systems available to Studio, including planner output, scheduler state, the JSONL event stream, and analyzer reports, together with the introspected argparse schema derived from the workflow generator. Proposed fixes return to the workflow as patches, closing the diagnose, fix, and resubmit lifecycle through replanning and resubmission rather than relying on terminal scraping.

Figure 9: The EHT reconstruction inside Studio. Left: the graph of the successful third gateway run, with the per-day fan-out of the three imaging pipelines collapsed into one node per pipeline. Right: the workflow-debugger agent’s summary after rebuilding and verifying the four container images. The same workflow and scheduler records that drive the graph supplied the diagnostic context to the agent.

Figure 3: The public gateway’s sign-in page. A user signs in through CILogon with their home institution’s credentials, and the workspace is created on first sign-in. The page summarizes the three-step lifecycle (describe, run, watch) and the parts of the workspace.

Figure 2: The Studio home page. The navigation rail on the left lists the views in the order a scientist works (home, analyses, data, examples, resources, notebooks), followed by the chat, terminal, website, feedback, and settings entries. The home page offers four starting actions and four example requests that each hand a prompt to the assistant, and a link that starts the guided tour.

Figure 4: The run panel of a workflow project in Studio, here for a streamflow workflow the assistant built from one chat prompt. The settings (gauge list, lookback window, retry policy, minimum number of gauges, and an optional site catalog) are derived from the generator’s argparse interface by abstract-syntax-tree introspection, without executing user code. Every field, default, and help string comes from the interface the agent wrote. Below the settings the user chooses where the workflow runs (Studio’s shared pool, or only nodes the user connects from their own cluster or allocation). One button prepares, plans, and submits the workflow.

Figure 6: Studio’s live graph view of a completed run, driven by the same event stream the agent reads, beside the chat in its workflow-debugger mode. The workflow (five stream gauges fetched, analyzed, and combined) was built from one chat prompt, and the chat transcript on the right is the agent explaining the fix that made this run succeed after an earlier failure. Node colors track live scheduler state (succeeded, running, pending, failed, held).

Figure 8: The help card. After a failed workflow has been re-run and the rerun has finished, Studio asks one question at the point where the answer is meaningful: did the assistant’s suggestion fix it? The four answers are one click each, and the card is rate-limited so that it does not become a survey users learn to dismiss. Here the EEG workflow of Section 8.5 succeeded on its fourth run after the assistant diagnosed the earlier failure. The chat is in its default mode, which routes each message to a specialist agent role.

papers.abstract: AI agents can write code, use scientific software, and revise computational workflows, opening new possibilities for MRI research. Effective assistance requires connecting acquisition physics, data conventions, specialized tools, and scientific validation. We present MRFoundry, an open-source, extensible package that connects MRI knowledge to agent actions and output checks. Project-local memory preserves decisions and evidence, while reviewed contributions allow researchers to improve shared guidance. Researcher-supervised examples demonstrate skill-guided sequence auditing and acquired-data reconstruction, connecting tool use, output checks, and documented decisions. Alongside MRFoundry, we introduce MRI Agent Bench to compare agents with and without the package across models and MRI task domains. Across 240 paired Core evaluations spanning 24 task types and ten models, all-checks-passed completion increased from 67.5% without MRFoundry to 78.3% with it. Across 134 Hard pairs, completion increased from 36.6% to 44.8%. MRFoundry makes MRI workflow expertise available as reusable guidance that researchers can inspect, adapt, and extend within existing agent and scientific software environments. MRFoundry is openly available at https://github.com/KeWang0622/MRFoundry.

papers.abstract: Recent work has identified a set of emergent symbolic mechanisms that support abstract reasoning in large language models, but it remains unclear what factors drive the emergence of these mechanisms. To address this question, we trained neural networks from scratch on abstract sequence tasks, varying both architectural and data distributional factors, and investigated the effects of these factors on the emergence of symbolic mechanisms. Using representational, attentional, and causal mediation analyses, we first confirmed that transformer-based language models trained from scratch on our task developed symbolic mechanisms. We then found that, across multiple axes of data diversity, greater diversity produced stronger symbolic signatures. Surprisingly, the same signatures emerged in modified transformer architectures and even multilayer perceptrons, indicating that architectural inductive biases are not necessary for the development of symbolic mechanisms. We also observed consistent patterns in an entity-attribute binding task. Together, these findings identify data diversity, not architecture, as the primary driver of emergent symbolic computation in neural networks.
bullets: The study examines what causes symbolic mechanisms supporting abstract reasoning to emerge.
Networks were trained from scratch on abstract sequence tasks while varying architecture and data distribution.
Representational, attentional, and causal mediation analyses confirmed the emergence of symbolic mechanisms in transformers.
Greater diversity across multiple data dimensions produced stronger symbolic signatures.
Similar mechanisms emerged in modified transformers, multilayer perceptrons, and an entity–attribute binding task.

papers.abstract: Attention, the core of language models, is a digital calculation over tokens: an exponential selects them, a division normalizes and a positional code sets the order. We show that attention can instead emerge from the synchronization of a receiver with its context tokens. Each past token is an oscillator whose state carries its content and whose frequency drifts with its age. The present token selects them by content, aligning an antenna with its query, and by position, setting the frequency of a receiver with its dial. Solving Kuramoto's problem for this receiver yields an attention layer in closed form with two phases: above a critical coupling set by the context, the receiver locks and its weights normalize; below it, it stays silent and its weights sum to less than one. Trained networks use both phases to select, abstain and count, fail where the theory predicts and keep reading far beyond the training length. Each part of attention finds its place in one device, a radio head: it tunes in to what to hear and when, and stays silent when nothing relevant is on air.
authors: Llu\'is Arola-Fern\'andez, Aissam Khadraoui, Alex Arenas
bullets: Models past tokens as oscillators whose content and age determine their state and frequency.
Uses Kuramoto synchronization to derive a closed-form attention layer with normalized weights above a critical coupling threshold.
Below the threshold, the receiver abstains, producing weights that sum to less than one.
Trained networks exploit both phases to select, abstain, and count, and continue reading beyond their training length.
The theory predicts observed failure cases, though the abstract does not specify quantitative results or evaluation settings.

papers.selection_reason: Derives an attention layer from oscillator synchronization, a novel architectural mechanism for LLMs.
papers.title: Everything in its right place: attention is a radio head
papers.tldr: The paper reinterprets attention as a radio-like synchronization process in which a receiver locks onto relevant context tokens and can remain silent when none are relevant.

papers.abstract: Retrieval-augmented language model systems generally select context by query-conditioned relevance. We argue that long-lived AI systems require a second operator: activation-conditioned memory availability. We specify an architecture in which request and goal cues seed an authorized memory graph, activation and fan attenuation allocate a bounded traversal frontier, retrieved entities recursively emit cues, and a typed evidence graph is reconstructed before generation. The specification yields five architectural consequences about candidate selection, traversal control, graph regularization, evidence reconstruction, and reinforcement. We derive implementation-level cost estimates and define ablations, failure conditions, and a reproducible evaluation protocol. The central claim is narrowed or falsified if a simpler graph reranker matches full traversal on causal and temporal recovery under equal budgets. This architecture-and-analysis preprint reports no benchmark measurements. If the claim holds, retrieval returns the evidence path that makes a memory available, not only a ranked list.
bullets: Motivation: Query relevance alone may be insufficient for long-lived AI systems that must recover causally and temporally linked memories.
Method: Request and goal cues seed a memory graph; activation and fan attenuation bound traversal, while retrieved entities recursively emit cues.
Output: A typed evidence graph is reconstructed before language-model generation.
Analysis: The work specifies architectural consequences, cost estimates, ablations, failure conditions, and a reproducible evaluation protocol.
Scope: This is a preprint with no benchmark measurements; the claim is testable against a simpler graph reranker under equal budgets.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Activation-guided graph retrieval control loop. The self-loop at recursive cues and path expansion is Section 3.3’s recursive cue generation: a retrieved entity’s new cues re-enter frontier allocation before the stop criteria release the result to evidence reconstruction. Authorization is evaluated before content-bearing activation or expansion; only qualified downstream outcomes update future availability.
Table 1: Querying estimates request relevance; activation controls memory availability.

papers.selection_reason: Activation-conditioned memory graph retrieval for long-lived language-model systems, fitting persistent LLM memory mechanisms.
papers.title: Activation-Guided Graph Retrieval for Cognitive Memory Reconstruction in Language Model Systems
papers.tldr: An architecture proposes reconstructing memories by activation-guided traversal of an authorized graph, returning evidence paths rather than only relevance-ranked context.

papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly trusted with mathematical, scientific and engineering work, yet their mistakes are often confidently written and hard to spot. A single wrong step tends to propagate, making the model waste inference tokens following a false premise. Existing safeguards either check only the final answer and restart from scratch, or rely on a verifier LLM that competes for GPU capacity and slows down response time. We propose online, deterministic verification: many kinds of reasoning steps can be validated by code, so a step can be verified in real time, as it is written, without any model call or GPU use. Whenever a check fails, we point out the mistake and let the model continue from the same spot. We demonstrate this approach on symbolic mathematics, where derivations already contain explicit expressions that a computer algebra system can check in milliseconds. Tested on the ASyMoB benchmark with three open-weights models, our online validation improves accuracy by 1.4-5.6 percentage points, corresponding to a 1.8-14.9% net reduction in incorrect answers, while increasing token usage by only 6-7%. Because the verifier is independent of the model, the approach complements progress in LLMs rather than competing with it: every new model can benefit immediately, and the benefit grows as deterministic checkers extend to more kinds of reasoning steps.
authors: Rotem Elimelech, Michael Shalyt, Ido Kaminer
bullets: Targets errors that propagate through LLM reasoning and are costly to detect only at the end.
Uses code-based, real-time verification of reasoning steps rather than a separate verifier LLM.
When a check fails, the model is alerted and continues from the error location instead of restarting.
On ASyMoB with three open-weight models, accuracy improved by 1.4–5.6 percentage points with 6–7% more tokens.
Demonstrated for symbolic mathematics; broader gains depend on extending deterministic checkers to other reasoning steps.

Passed checks leave generation uninterrupted. When a check fails, the continuation after the offending step is discarded, corrective feedback is appended, and generation resumes. Verification requires no additional model call or GPU computation.

papers.selection_reason: Real-time error correction during LLM reasoning using code verification is a novel LLM method.
papers.title: Catch It Where It Happens: Real Time Error Correction During LLM Reasoning
papers.tldr: Online deterministic checks catch reasoning errors as they occur, improving mathematical accuracy with minimal extra token use and no verifier-model overhead.

papers.abstract: Berglund and van der Merwe formalized byte-pair encoding and bounded how far an appended string can change a tokenization, leaving the converse open: how far can a string prepended on the left change it, which dictionaries make that ripple infinite, and can it be computed efficiently when finite? We answer all three for every dictionary. The origin radius, how far a prepend can change covering spans, is decided with radius certificates by a product of two runs of the automaton that guesses the final tokens, in time polynomial in the dictionary written out, and it is infinite exactly when one periodic word has two canonical tilings with no common boundary. Under their ordering condition it is infinite exactly when some rule (t, t) finds its two copies adjacent at its own stage, and such a rule makes any dictionary infinite. A finite radius makes every window of a width read off the radii have a cut, and the radius is finite exactly when such cuts are dense. The token machine completes for every dictionary, and the tokenization is subsequential, extending what Berglund, Martens and van der Merwe proved for proper ones under one pass per rule. A streaming tokenizer emits after every symbol exactly the tokens that no continuation changes, in polynomial time, answering a question of Dalirrooyfard and Ye. Boundedness of the label measure, the edit distance of the token sequences, is decided for every dictionary in polynomial time as well, and under the ordering condition the largest distance one edit causes over dictionaries of m rules lies asymptotically between m^2/10 and m^2/2. GPT-2's merge table carries 244 effective self-pairs, so its origin radius is infinite from the forty-second merge on, and that of cl100k, o200k and Llama 3 from their first. Every measured number is its program's output, and what is not executed is named.
bullets: Determines the origin radius for every dictionary in polynomial time using radius certificates based on products of automaton runs.
Shows the radius is infinite exactly when a periodic word has two canonical tilings without a common boundary; under an ordering condition, self-pairs characterize infinitude.
Proves that finite radius yields dense cuts and that the token machine is complete, making tokenization subsequential for every dictionary.
Develops a streaming tokenizer that emits tokens stable under all continuations, and decides boundedness of token-sequence edit distance in polynomial time.
Reports infinite origin radius for GPT-2 from its 42nd effective self-pair and for cl100k, o200k, and Llama 3 from their first; asymptotic edit-distance bounds are given under the ordering condition.

papers.selection_reason: Formal results on BPE tokenization and streaming tokenizers; technically transferable to LLM tokenization.
papers.title: The Left Ripple of Byte-Pair Encoding: Certified Lookbehind for Every Dictionary
papers.tldr: The paper completely characterizes how far left-prepending can alter byte-pair tokenization and provides efficient algorithms for detecting finite or infinite ripple.

papers.abstract: Knowledge editing has emerged as a promising approach for efficiently updating embedded knowledge in large language models (LLMs). It first computes an ideal target hidden state that steers the LLM toward the new output, and then edits the model parameters so that the original hidden state is mapped to this target. While most existing methods focus on the second stage of parameter editing in preserving other knowledge, we find that the upstream construction of the target hidden state also plays an important role in allocating the model's limited capacity space. We first establish a theoretical connection between interference in the parameter space and interference between target hidden states, showing that the two are positively correlated. Building on this insight, we propose a simple yet effective $\ell_1$ regularization method that prunes away unnecessary ``tentacles'' of each knowledge vector, retaining only the essential components. With fewer extraneous tentacles, each edit affects less other knowledge, enabling better coexistence. Extensive experiments across multiple LLMs and benchmark datasets verify the effectiveness of our method. Code: https://github.com/wintersdragon-c/STO.
authors: Dongyao Chen, Jiayun Lei, Zhiyuan Ji, Zhiying Deng, Wei Liu, Xiaobo Sun
bullets: Knowledge-editing methods must allocate limited model capacity when constructing target hidden states, not only when editing parameters.
The paper shows a positive correlation between interference among target hidden states and interference in parameter space.
It applies ℓ1 regularization to prune extraneous “tentacles” from knowledge vectors while preserving essential components.
Experiments across multiple LLMs and benchmark datasets verify improved coexistence of edited and existing knowledge.

papers.selection_reason: Knowledge editing in LLMs via sparse target optimization fits LLM research.
papers.title: Capacity Allocation at the Source: Sparse Target Optimization for LLM Knowledge Editing

papers.abstract: Does a useful self-update remain useful after the model updates again? Third Eye separates immediate performance from the outcome of a further native update. We evaluate five 3-8B backbones on math and code: 64 fresh runs, three candidates per run, and three continuations per candidate. Selection and final scoring use disjoint items. In the balanced Qwen3-4B/Llama-3.2-3B comparison, immediate-selected utility is near zero, but continuation reduces it by 1.78 percentage points (simultaneous 95% interval [0.68, 2.88]). Candidate-averaged immediate utility is already negative: selection partly accounts for the apparently neutral first step. Continuation also lowers utility for SmolLM3-3B and Llama-3.1-8B; Qwen3-8B remains inconclusive. Target and out-of-distribution losses dominate retention changes. Matched recipe and recipient-donor controls identify neither a reliable mitigation nor a single mechanism. The results support evaluating persistent self-updates as adaptation transitions, with independent scoring and a no-update baseline, rather than interpreting immediate performance as their full value.
authors: Sujato Dutta, Padala Indira Sneha, Kypu Mahitha, Shashank Vanga, Neeraj Choudhary
bullets: Third Eye separates immediate utility from the utility of a subsequent native update.
Across five 3–8B backbones on math and code, continuation often reduces update utility; Qwen3-8B is inconclusive.
In the balanced Qwen3-4B/Llama-3.2-3B comparison, immediate-selected utility was near zero, while continuation reduced it by 1.78 percentage points.
Candidate-averaged immediate utility was already negative, suggesting selection can mask first-step harm.
Independent scoring and a no-update baseline are needed to assess persistent self-updates; no reliable mitigation or single mechanism was identified.

papers.selection_reason: Evaluates the persistence of self-improvement in LLMs, directly relevant to test-time adaptation and LLM memory mechanisms.
papers.title: Third Eye: Beyond Immediate Gains in Recursive Self-Improvement
papers.tldr: A self-update that appears harmless or useful immediately can become harmful after the model updates again, so recursive persistence must be evaluated directly.

papers.abstract: Time-series forecasting has recently seen a paradigm shift with the introduction of foundation-style models that adapt large pretrained language architectures to sequential data. However, effectively exposing fundamental temporal structures, such as trend, scale, and temporal dependence, to these models remains an open challenge, particularly when the available observations are limited. In this paper, we conduct an exploratory empirical study across different generations of forecasting architectures and propose StatPrompt-LLM, a lightweight statistical refinement of Time-LLM. StatPrompt-LLM augments the existing Time-LLM prompting mechanism with dataset-level statistical information and introduces a zero-initialised autoregressive bypass as a complementary linear forecasting pathway. We evaluate our framework on electricity and meteorological time-series benchmarks, including ETTh1, ETTh2, and Weather, under full-prefix and reduced-prefix configurations. Under the 10% reduced-prefix configuration, StatPrompt-LLM achieved lower in-sample prediction errors than Time-LLM, with unweighted average relative reductions across datasets of 40.2% in MSE and 21.4% in MAE. Full-prefix results were more dataset-dependent. Ablation analyses revealed relatively modest and dataset-dependent changes when selected additional statistical descriptor groups were masked within the combined architecture. Computational profiling indicated additional model parameters and runtime overhead relative to Time-LLM.
bullets: Addresses the challenge of exposing trend, scale, and temporal dependence to foundation-style forecasting models with limited observations.
Extends Time-LLM prompting using dataset-level statistical information and a zero-initialised autoregressive bypass.
Evaluated on ETTh1, ETTh2, and Weather benchmarks under full-prefix and 10% reduced-prefix settings.
With 10% prefixes, it reduced in-sample MSE by 40.2% and MAE by 21.4% on average relative to Time-LLM; full-prefix results varied by dataset.
Ablations showed modest, dataset-dependent effects from masking descriptor groups, while profiling found increased parameters and runtime.

papers.abstract: DeepSeek Sparse Attention (DSA) reduces the computational cost of attention through token-level selection. However, its indexer still scores the entire causal prefix for each query, making indexing a dominant source of latency in long-context inference. Notably, the indexer alone can account for more than 50% of total prefill GPU time at long context lengths. To address this bottleneck, we propose ADIndex, an Adaptive and Distillation-driven Indexing method for token-level sparse attention. ADIndex integrates three key components: (i) a layer-wise calibration strategy that adaptively accommodates cross-query retrieval overlap, motivated by our observation of pronounced inter-layer heterogeneity; (ii) a group-level distillation scheme that leverages this heterogeneity to efficiently train adaptive layer-wise group indexers, capturing salient retrieval signals from individual queries; and (iii) a low-latency inference strategy that reduces repeated full-prefix scans through token bank sharing within query groups while retaining query-specific refinement. Experiments on DeepSeek-V3.2 and GLM-5.1 demonstrate that ADIndex preserves near-lossless task performance on LongBench, LongBench v2, and RULER while delivering substantial efficiency gains over standard DSA, including prefill and decoding kernel speedups of up to 6.22x and 3.40x, respectively, at a context length of 256K across the layer-wise reuse configurations, as well as an end-to-end serving speedup of 1.54x at a context length of 128K.
authors: Jin-Fei Qi, Yiduo Li, Jiang-Xin Shi, Kan Liu, Tao Lan, Hanlin Tang, Yu-Feng Li
bullets: Targets the indexer bottleneck, which can exceed half of prefill GPU time at long context lengths.
Uses layer-wise calibration to handle heterogeneous cross-query retrieval overlap across layers.
Trains adaptive layer-wise group indexers through group-level distillation while retaining query-specific refinement.
Reduces repeated full-prefix scans via token-bank sharing within query groups.
On DeepSeek-V3.2 and GLM-5.1, reports up to 6.22× prefill, 3.40× decoding-kernel, and 1.54× end-to-end serving speedups while maintaining near-lossless LongBench, LongBench v2, and RULER performance.

figures.caption: Figure 2 Overview of ADIndex. During training, a lightweight group indexer learns the group-level retrieval requirements of neighboring queries through distillation from the frozen DSA indexer. During inference, the trained group indexer constructs a shared token bank through a single full-prefix scan per group. The original DSA indexer then performs query-specific Top-K refinement over the shared bank augmented with newly visible post-anchor tokens.

Figure 1 Motivating observations for ADIndex. (a) Indexer overhead. The plot shows indexer time proportion during prefill and decoding at different context lengths. The indexer can alone account for 54.2% of total prefill GPU time at 128k context length. (b) Layer-wise overlap heterogeneity. The plot shows per-layer maximum union sizes of the original indexer’s Top-K selections (K = 2048) for query group sizes G ∈ {4, 8, 16}, computed over all complete prefill query groups from 100 sequences of approximately 128K tokens each. Colored vertical dashed lines indicate the corresponding no-overlap upper bounds GK. (c) Distillation-driven coverage gains. The plot shows absolute gains in Top-2048 coverage of the distilled group indexer over the frozen mean-pooling baseline. Coverage measures the fraction of the original DSA indexer’s per-query Top-2048 selections included in the shared bank. The group size G = 16 and bank budget P = 8K are fixed, while the number of indexing heads in the group indexer varies. Gains are positive in almost all layers and remain robust across head counts. Selected layers from shallow (7, 12), mid (34, 38), and deep (50, 59) parts of the model are highlighted in warm colors, while the remaining layers are shown in gray. Pale warm and cool backgrounds indicate positive and negative gains, respectively; the horizontal dashed line marks zero gain.

papers.abstract: Preference labels align model training, but the judgments behind them are difficult to inspect or verify. In this paper, we examine how preference construction can be checked when intermediate decisions are recorded, and which of them remain uncertain. We present Symbolic Preference Labeling, a method in which a pretrained language model classifies predefined attributes of prompts and responses. Explicit rules assign response verdicts, and a fixed verdict ranking determines the preference label. Each preference label has a recorded derivation: the response verdicts and preference label can be recomputed from the stored attribute assignments, rules, and verdict ranking without rerunning the language model. On 200 prompts annotated by human raters, the language model produces valid structured outputs for 192 prompts. All eight parsing failures occur in the subset of self-harm prompts marked as harmful. Using 465 preference pairs, we train one policy model with direct preference optimization across five training seeds. Mean measured benign refusal is 40.82 percent on 1,319 benign prompts that resemble unsafe ones, and mean measured toxic refusal is 84.98 percent on 655 toxic prompts. This study distinguishes the reproducibility of preference labels from attribute correctness. The recorded derivations make preference construction open to inspection, while attribute correctness and semantic safety require separate validation.
bullets: Preference construction is audited through stored derivations that allow labels to be recomputed without rerunning the language model.
A pretrained language model classifies predefined prompt and response attributes, after which explicit rules determine verdicts and preferences.
On 200 human-annotated prompts, 192 produced valid structured outputs; all parsing failures occurred among harmful self-harm prompts.
A policy trained on 465 preference pairs showed measured benign refusal of 40.82% and toxic refusal of 84.98% across the evaluated prompt sets.
Reproducible label derivations do not establish attribute correctness or semantic safety, which require separate validation.

papers.abstract: The demand for personalized LLMs is shifting from style imitation toward content quality. We investigate whether self-distillation can bridge this gap in existing fine-tuning paradigm. To address this limitation, we introduce MIRROR(Meta- personalization by Internalizing Reference-Revealed On-policy Reflections), a novel self-distillation framework that shifts LLM personalization from imitation toward preference internalization. First, we replace reference-token imitation with reference-revealed on-policy self-distillation, aligning the model's next-token distributions along its own generation trajectories with those of its reference-conditioned self, thereby internalizing user preferences rather than reproducing reference wording.Second, we introduce MIRROR-F, a focal plug-in that augments on-policy distributional alignment with selective supervision over informative reference tokens, thereby strengthening content generation while preserving user-specific expression. Across three personalized generation benchmarks, two model scales, and complementary reference-based and LLM-based evaluations, MIRROR and MIRROR-F achieve leading overall personalization performance and superior text quality, while exhibiting less catastrophic forgetting than SFT-based baselines on three unseen personalized generation tasks. The gains are consistent across model scales and application scenarios, translating to improved performance in LLM personalization tasks.
bullets: Targets the shift from stylistic imitation toward higher-quality, preference-aware content generation.
Aligns on-policy token distributions from the model’s own generations with those of its reference-conditioned counterpart.
MIRROR-F adds selective supervision on informative reference tokens to strengthen content generation while preserving personal expression.
Across three benchmarks, two model scales, and multiple evaluations, both methods show strong personalization and text-quality performance.
The framework also reduces catastrophic forgetting relative to SFT baselines on three unseen personalization tasks.

papers.abstract: Activation steering manipulates large language model behavior by intervening on internal activations, but the mechanistic basis of these interventions remains poorly understood. We decompose refusal steering into component-level interventions across four open-weight models, identifying the sparse subsets of attention and MLP components whose steering suffices to reproduce the full behavioral effect. We find that refusal directions concentrate in sparse component mechanisms comprising 28--48\% of upstream components, retaining 88--101\% of steering effectiveness. Within these mechanisms, effective steering further concentrates in approximately 50\% of residual stream dimensions, retaining 85--98\% of the component-mechanism baseline, consistent with a privileged basis structure. Sparsity thus operates at two levels: which components are steered, and which dimensions within those components carry the signal. Together these findings show that refusal is not diffusely encoded across a transformer but assembled by a structured, identifiable mechanism, providing a foundation for mechanistic understanding of how refusal behaviors are represented and steered. To facilitate reproducibility, we release all code and raw experimental results in https://github.com/wang-research-lab/Refusal_Mechanisms.
bullets: Across four open-weight models, sparse attention and MLP component subsets reproduced most of the full refusal-steering effect.
These subsets comprised 28–48% of upstream components while retaining 88–101% effectiveness.
Within selected components, about half of residual-stream dimensions retained 85–98% of the component-level effect.
The results suggest a privileged basis structure and an identifiable mechanism for refusal behavior.
Code and raw experimental results are publicly released for reproducibility.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Two-level sparsity in transformer refusal mechanisms. The residual stream passes through a sequence of attention and MLP components; a sparse subset (28–48% across models) forms a sufficient mechanism to steer refusal behavior, where steering a component via orthogonalization means removing the output’s projection onto the refusal direction. Zooming into each identified component, effective steering also requires intervening on only the same ≈ 50% of residual dimensions across all components, consistent with a privileged basis structure in the residual stream. Prior work steers all dimensions of all upstream components simultaneously by intervening on the residual stream; we instead steer individual component outputs, allowing the residual connection to proceed unaltered.

Figure 2: Residual stream steering effectiveness as a function of dimension percentage. Each marker shows the ASR recovered relative to full-dimensional steering, plotted against the fraction of hidden dimensions used. Marker labels indicate the corresponding norm explanation threshold t – the fraction of ∥r∗∥2 explained by the retained dimensions. Across all four models, retaining ∼50% of dimensions at the 95% norm threshold recovers over 90% of full steering ASR, with some models exceeding the dense baseline. Performance degrades sharply only as the budget falls below the 50% norm threshold, confirming that the refusal direction is concentrated in a sparse set of high-magnitude coordinates.

Figure 7: Distribution of refusal direction coefficients at l∗. Coordinate values of r∗ for each model. Blue bars represent typical dimensions within the central distribution; red bars with black outlines denote statistical outliers (> 2.5× IQR). The y-axis is log-scaled to make the sparse high-magnitude dimensions visible. Summary statistics (µ, σ) and outlier counts are provided for each model.

Figure 5: Component write profiles sorted by refusal importance rank. Top 10% of coordinates by write magnitude shown for each component, sorted by |r∗i | descending so the most refusal-important coordinates appear on the left. Outputs are unit-normalised to control for LayerNorm-induced scale differences. Point size scales with write magnitude; color indicates relative layer depth (early: purple, late: gold). High-magnitude writes are distributed throughout the coordinate space rather than concentrated at high refusal importance ranks, indicating component-specific rather than shared sparse subspaces.

Figure 4: Per-component linear attribution to the refusal direction. For each component in the identified mechanism, bars show the scalar projection of its difference-in-mean vector onto r∗, measuring how much each component contributes to assembling the refusal direction at l∗. Attention components (orange) and MLP components (blue) are shown by layer index. Negative values indicate components that write against the refusal direction. Each reconstruction scores (fraction of ∥r∗∥2 recovered) is provided in the top left.

Figure 10: First-Round Component Ablation: Initial Redundancy. The absolute drop in ASR when individual components are removed from the initial, unpruned candidate circuit. The flat profile across all models indicates that no single component acts as a bottleneck in the presence of the full redundant set.

Figure 6: Exhaustive steering performance of the difference-in-means direction extracted from each layer’s input. Steering is performed in the residual stream at the layer input, replicating prior work. The highest performing steering direction is highlighted in red and is used to find the mechanism in our study. All directions are extracted from the last post-instruction token. The highest ASR value is also used as a reference value that the mechanisms in Table 1 compare against.

Figure 3: Sparse mechanisms versus their complement sets. Each arrow points from the complement (excluded components, hollow diamond) to the identified mechanism (included components, filled circle). Mechanisms comprising 28–48% of upstream components reproduce 88–101% of the full steering effect, while their complements – the remaining 52–72% of components – largely fail to elicit refusal.

Figure 8: Component cosine similarity with r∗ on harmful vs. harmless prompts. Colored bars show the IQR of cosine similarity between each component’s last-token output and r∗ over harmful prompts (blue: MLP, orange: attention). Outlined boxes show the corresponding IQR over harmless prompts. Red lines indicate the selectivity shift – the difference in mean cosine similarity between the two distributions. A large upward red line indicates a component that aligns more strongly with the refusal direction on harmful content than harmless content.

Figure 9: Mechanism Sufficiency: Leave-One-Out ASR Drop. The absolute drop in Attack Success Rate (ASR) when each individual component is removed from the identified sparse mechanism. Higher bars indicate components that act as critical bottlenecks for successful refusal steering. Blue bars represent MLP layers, and orange bars represent Attention mechanisms.

papers.abstract: Since large language model (LLM) agents rely on long-term memory, what they store now shapes what they do later. A memory manager decides how each input changes this memory and which records the agent acts on. It can fail in two ways: keeping a fact that has since changed (outdated memory), or storing a planted passage or injected instruction (memory poisoning). Most prior work studies them separately, yet they call for opposite write decisions, so no fixed write rule handles both. We therefore formalize memory robustness as handling both without doing worse on other inputs. Since accuracy checks only the answer, we measure robustness with evidence-conditioned accuracy (ECA), which also checks that the records the manager selects include all the evidence the answer needs, updated and free of attacks. However, existing memory systems and defenses are not more robust than an untuned manager on our test sets. We improve robustness with a simple one-shot recipe that fine-tunes the manager on episodes synthesized around a single conversation with inserted changes and attacks. On three backbones, it improves every category score on our test sets and more than doubles the untuned manager's overall ECA, though robustness remains incomplete.
bullets: LLM memory managers must handle two conflicting failures: retaining changed facts and storing injected or malicious content.
The paper introduces evidence-conditioned accuracy (ECA), which evaluates both answer correctness and whether selected memory contains complete, updated, attack-free evidence.
Existing memory systems and defenses are no more robust than an untuned manager on the authors’ test sets.
Fine-tuning on synthesized episodes built from a single conversation with inserted changes and attacks improves every tested category across three backbones.

papers.selection_reason: Robust memory management for LLM agents addressing outdated and poisoned memory; fits LLM memory.
papers.title: Accept Changes, Reject Attacks: Robust Memory Management for LLM Agents
papers.tldr: A one-shot, episode-based fine-tuning recipe makes LLM-agent memory managers more robust to both outdated facts and memory-poisoning attacks, substantially improving evidence-conditioned accuracy while leaving room for improvement.

papers.abstract: Long-term memory enables large language model (LLM) agents to maintain personalized and temporally coherent interactions, but repeated LLM inference for memory admission, extraction, and organization introduces substantial cost and latency. We present SLICE-Mem, a lightweight memory framework that combines salience-guided admission and predicate-centered information extraction. A compact classifier identifies user turns worth retaining, and a semantic-dependency-based extractor converts admitted turns into concise memory entries. This online pipeline requires no generative LLM calls, while cross-entry reconciliation is deferred to an offline consolidation stage. We evaluate SLICE-Mem on the weekly subset of Memora and LongMemEval-S using 8B and 30B Qwen backbones for memory construction and consolidation on both benchmarks. Compared with the generative-memory baseline MemOS under the Qwen3-30B configuration, SLICE-Mem's online pipeline achieves 46.60 versus 46.68 FAMA (Forgetting-Aware Memory Accuracy) on Memora Weekly and 56.8% versus 59.3% accuracy on LongMemEval-S, while reducing total LLM token consumption by 92.4% and 99.5%, respectively. These results demonstrate that SLICE-Mem can preserve useful evidence for long-term memory with substantially less reliance on LLM-based memory construction.
bullets: Targets the cost and latency of repeated LLM inference for memory admission, extraction, and organization.
Uses a compact salience classifier to select user turns and a semantic-dependency extractor to create concise memory entries.
Runs online memory construction without generative LLM calls, deferring cross-entry reconciliation to offline consolidation.
On Memora Weekly and LongMemEval-S, it achieved near-baseline quality while reducing total LLM token consumption by 92.4% and 99.5%, respectively.
Quality was slightly below MemOS under Qwen3-30B: 46.60 vs. 46.68 FAMA on Memora Weekly and 56.8% vs. 59.3% accuracy on LongMemEval-S.

papers.abstract: Multilingual large language models are increasingly deployed in settings where visible reasoning traces support verification, education, and safety auditing, yet standard evaluations typically measure only final-answer agreement or holistic response similarity. As a result, they establish outcome consistency without determining whether users across languages receive comparable supporting evidence. We introduce a trace-level divergence framework that compares visible reasoning traces as structured sequences, decomposing agreement into structural similarity, order consistency, and holistic similarity, with pair-specific calibration to enable comparison across languages. Across three reasoning benchmarks, seven languages, and six frontier LLMs, the natural baseline---embedding each whole response and comparing the two by cosine---systematically overstates agreement: $52.1\%$--$67.3\%$ of examples in the top quartile of holistic similarity are not in the top quartile of structural similarity. This dissociation is stable across sentence encoders and step segmentations, and blind bilingual annotation studies in two English-anchored language pairs show that human judgments align with structural similarity rather than with the holistic baseline. A same-language control shows that the level of divergence is language-specific: two English traces for paraphrases of the same question agree more closely than an English trace and its counterparts in other languages. Our results show that answer-level and holistic evaluations can substantially overestimate the consistency of multilingual explanatory artifacts, motivating trace-level evaluation for reliable multilingual deployment.
bullets: Introduces a trace-level divergence framework that compares reasoning traces by structure, step order, and holistic similarity, with language-pair calibration.
Evaluates three reasoning benchmarks, seven languages, and six frontier LLMs.
Whole-response embedding similarity overstates agreement: 52.1%–67.3% of highly similar examples are not highly similar structurally.
Bilingual human judgments align with structural similarity rather than the holistic baseline.
Divergence is language-specific, motivating trace-level evaluation for multilingual deployment.

papers.selection_reason: Trace-level analysis of multilingual LLM reasoning; fits language foundation model reasoning evaluation.
papers.title: Same Answer, Different Reasons: Trace-Level Divergence in Multilingual Large Language Models
papers.tldr: Multilingual LLMs can give the same answer while providing substantially different reasoning traces, so answer-level and whole-response similarity metrics overestimate cross-language consistency.

papers.abstract: Language-model systems can separate contextual computation, persistent storage, and exact execution instead of updating all capabilities through one shared parameter system. We investigate FEM-ASM, a finite-element-method-inspired organization in which independently constructed document states and deterministic executable skills contribute typed proposals to a shared language-model state. An explicit residual operator reconciles proposals attached to common interface nodes. We evaluate this organization through controlled experiments and negative results rather than claiming a physical finite-element formulation of language. An attention-free Multi-Mesh prototype learns causal language modeling but does not establish competitive general capability. A versioned store contains 52,809 reconstructive memory elements near a 1.7-billion-floating-value budget; reconstruction is incomplete, with approximately 75\% token accuracy. Support-aware lexical indices make these elements addressable under provenance-controlled query construction. For executable arithmetic, positional result observations substantially improve neural rendering relative to a repeated global result vector, and output substitutions change the model's preferred answer. A bounded attachment demonstration further measures the effect of making selected evidence available, without establishing the utility of loading an entire multi-billion-value store. The results support a separation of storage, execution, and neural coordination, while identifying unresolved limitations in question-only retrieval, unrestricted answer generation, and end-to-end efficiency.
bullets: Uses independently constructed document states and deterministic executable skills that submit typed proposals to a shared model state.
An explicit residual operator reconciles proposals attached to common interface nodes.
An attention-free Multi-Mesh prototype supports causal language modeling, but does not demonstrate competitive general performance.
Reconstructive memory contains 52,809 elements with about 75% token accuracy; support-aware lexical indices enable provenance-controlled addressing.
Positional arithmetic-result observations improve neural rendering, while unresolved issues include incomplete retrieval, unrestricted generation, and end-to-end efficiency.

papers.title: Beyond the Parameter Monolith: Reconstructive Memories, Executable Skills, and Residual Assembly for Language Models
papers.tldr: FEM-ASM explores separating language-model storage, execution, and coordination through reconstructive memories, executable skills, and residual proposal assembly, with promising component-level findings but no evidence of competitive general capability.

papers.abstract: We show that the causality of language models (LMs) may not be necessary nor optimal. This is the case when system behavior (denoted as $S$) is incorporated as a first-principle Bayesian feature. Here, $S$ refers to extra dominant factors beyond the data space, and they involve coupled effects. Despite being the de facto foundation of modern architecture, recent studies indicate persistent mismatches and contradictions with causality. These issues largely stem from system behavior rather than the data distribution. We therefore propose the SBD framework, which incorporates $S$ as an irreducible component of the evidence lower bound (ELBO). SBD theoretically reveals a counter-intuitive Causality Tax phenomenon, where causality emerges as a suboptimal approximation with an additional structural error, due to the obliviousness to $S$. To address the challenge of latent variable analysis, we validate the SBD-predicted impact of $S$ via implicit measurements, theoretical-bound-guided controls, and Neural Tangent Kernel (NTK) evaluations. In particular, we construct Green Shell (GSH) to show the possibility of reducing Causality Tax. GSH is a non-causal variational family, and it replaces the sequential dependency chain of $S$ components with a divide-and-conquer partition. NTK spectra in the lazy-training regime confirm that GSH always achieves significantly tighter error bounds than causality, with $7dB+$ improvement in signal-to-noise ratio. In the relatively later stage of lazy-training, GSH further leads to superior generalization (up to $20\%$ richer multi-scale fitting capabilities). Taken together, SBD establishes system behavior as a complementary theoretical abstraction besides causality and distribution fitting, opening new research avenues such as designing and optimizing LM base models.
bullets: Motivation: Persistent LM mismatches may arise from system behavior—coupled factors outside the observed data distribution—rather than from data alone.
Method: The SBD framework incorporates system behavior as an irreducible component of the ELBO and analyzes its effect through implicit measurements, theory-guided controls, and NTK evaluations.
Contribution: It identifies Causality Tax, where causal modeling becomes a suboptimal approximation because it overlooks system behavior.
Approach: Green Shell (GSH) uses a non-causal, divide-and-conquer variational structure instead of a sequential dependency chain.
Results: NTK analyses report tighter error bounds with 7 dB+ higher signal-to-noise ratio and up to 20% richer multi-scale fitting capabilities in later lazy-training stages.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes a non-causal LM base model and theoretical analysis of causality in language models.
papers.title: To Explore The Strange New World Beyond Data Distribution: System Behavior, Causality Tax, and Non-causal Base Model
papers.tldr: The paper argues that language-model causality can impose a structural “Causality Tax” when system behavior beyond the data distribution is ignored, and proposes a non-causal alternative that improves theoretical and measured performance.

papers.abstract: Large language models reinvent the wheel all the time. They conflate task-solving with the execution of the solutions, which forces them to solve every problem from scratch. We show that once a task has been reasoned through, the application of its solution to a new problem instance can be done very efficiently and with little involvement from language models. We introduce agentic reasoning caching, a method for constructing robust CPU-executable agentic reasoning caches (ARCs) from LLM reasoning traces. ARCs show on-par performance with frontier LLMs across a range of difficult mathematical and scientific tasks, are fully explainable, continually trainable, robust to input perturbations, and 16-291x cheaper to invoke than the source model.
authors: Peter Belcak, Greg Heinrich, Saurav Muralidharan, Shizhe Diao, Pavlo Molchanov
bullets: Separates task-solving from applying a previously derived solution to new instances.
Constructs agentic reasoning caches (ARCs) from LLM reasoning traces for CPU execution.
Matches frontier LLM performance across difficult mathematical and scientific tasks.
ARCs are explainable, continually trainable, and robust to input perturbations.
Reported invocation cost is 16–291× lower than the source model.

papers.selection_reason: Constructs reusable reasoning caches from LLM traces, a persistent external-memory mechanism for language models.
papers.title: CPU-ARC: Agentic Reasoning Caching for on-CPU Reasoning Reuse
papers.tldr: CPU-ARC reuses LLM-derived reasoning through explainable, CPU-executable caches, achieving frontier-level performance at 16–291× lower invocation cost.

papers.abstract: A conversational agent that remembers has to decide what to keep. Retrieval-augmented generation keeps the transcript and searches it; the alternative is to compact each turn into atomic facts and search those. We compare the two on LoCoMo, with both arms answering all 1,985 questions in one window, against the same stores, with the same generator and judge, and both predictions on one row, which licenses McNemar's exact test on the 512 questions where they disagree. On the four categories comparable work reports, compaction scores 71.4 per cent against 64.6, a lead of 6.8 points (p = 5.5e-08) at 34 per cent fewer prompt tokens. On all five, including the adversarial set comparable work drops, the lead falls to 2.0 and stops being significant, because the baseline leads adversarial by 14.6. That loss has a structure. Our lead falls as the reference answer demands more source wording, 9.6 points ahead at one or two reference words and 3.1 behind past eight, with token overlap moving the same way, so the judge is not the cause. Compaction keeps what a fact asserts and discards how it was said, so it wins where the answer is a value and loses where it is a phrasing. We also report four negative results with their power calculations.
authors: Osamudiamen Edogun, Joshua Obigwe, Irfan Mehmood
bullets: On four comparable LoCoMo categories, compaction scored 71.4% versus 64.6% for retrieval-augmented generation, using 34% fewer prompt tokens.
Across all five categories, the advantage fell to 2.0 points and was not significant because retrieval performed better on the adversarial set.
Compaction’s lead declined as answers required more source wording: from 9.6 points for one or two reference words to 3.1 points behind beyond eight.
The paired evaluation used identical stores, generator, and judge, with McNemar’s exact test on 512 disagreements.
The approach preserves asserted facts but loses the original phrasing, limiting performance on wording-sensitive questions.

papers.abstract: Chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning has emerged as a powerful paradigm for extending the computational capabilities of transformer-based models. A growing body of recent work has begun to uncover the fine-grained computational power of transformers augmented with CoT, as well as their connections to classical complexity theory. In this work, we advance this line of research by establishing the first hierarchy theorem for CoT-based computation. Our main result shows that for any reasonable resource bound $r(n) \geq n$ and any $\varepsilon > 0$, \[ \mathrm{CoT}(r(n)) \subsetneq \mathrm{CoT}(r(n)^{1+\varepsilon}), \] where $\mathrm{CoT}(r(n))$ denotes the class of decision problems solvable by transformers using $O(r(n))$ CoT reasoning steps on inputs of length $n$. Our result shows that increasing the number of CoT reasoning steps provably yields strictly greater computational power, establishing CoT steps as a fundamental resource in transformer-based computation. Unlike classical hierarchy theorems, which are typically proved via diagonalization, our approach leverages known coarse-grained simulations between CoT-augmented transformers and Turing machines in both directions. Building on these connections, we adapt the classical padding technique from complexity theory to this setting to obtain a tight hierarchy. A key technical contribution of our work is the implementation of padding within the transformer-based CoT model.
authors: Thanh Le, A. Pavan, N. V. Vinodchandran
bullets: Proves that, for any reasonable resource bound r(n) ≥ n and ε > 0, CoT(r(n)) is strictly contained in CoT(r(n)^{1+ε}).
Establishes CoT reasoning steps as a fundamental computational resource for transformers.
Transfers classical complexity-theoretic ideas using coarse-grained simulations between CoT transformers and Turing machines.
Adapts padding techniques to the CoT setting, with padding implementation as a key technical contribution.
Scope: the result concerns decision problems and asymptotic CoT-step bounds.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Padding argument for Lemma 3.1. Write m = |X| and N = m+ f(m), with f chosen as in the proof. The transformer T ′ simulates T on a padded input with essentially the same absolute CoT budget. The assumed class equality yields a transformer S with budget O(r(N)). Finally, R generates the padding using CoT and simulates S. Dashed vertical lines separate supplied input from generated tokens; gray blocks denote padding. Bar lengths are schematic.

papers.title: A Tight Hierarchy for Chain of Thought
papers.tldr: More Chain-of-Thought steps strictly increase the computational power of transformer models, yielding a tight resource hierarchy.

papers.abstract: LLM agents benefit from using memory systems to improve performance on long-horizon, multi-session tasks. However, memory introduces a critical attack surface. Malicious instructions encountered in one session may be stored and propagated through memory before being retrieved and acted upon in later sessions. Because memory systems differ in how they process and retrieve information, the downstream effects of poisoning can vary significantly across systems. To quantify the effects of poisoning across different memory architectures, we introduce MemoryDojo, a benchmark for tracing the lifecycle of poisoned information through agent memory and measuring its influence on subsequent agent behavior. MemoryDojo is easily extensible, consists of 155 multi-session long-horizon trajectories covering four domains, and supports five different memory systems. Through our evaluation, we find that all memory systems are susceptible to memory poisoning, with substantial variation in downstream effects. We further propose a memory-aware poison optimization process that increases the poisoning efficacy, highlighting differences between memory architectures. We hope that MemoryDojo will support research on understanding and mitigating agentic memory risks.
authors: David H. Yang, Blake Bullwinkel, Amanda Minnich, Mohammad Mohammadi Amiri, Giorgio Severi
bullets: Targets memory poisoning in long-horizon, multi-session LLM agents.
Provides 155 trajectories across four domains and supports five memory systems.
Traces poisoned information from storage through retrieval to downstream agent behavior.
Finds all evaluated memory systems are susceptible, with substantial variation in impact.
Introduces memory-aware poison optimization that increases poisoning efficacy.￼

papers.abstract: Prompt learning adapts vision-language models such as CLIP by optimizing a short learnable prompt. The cross-entropy objective pulls this prompt toward base-class specialization, whereas generalization to unseen classes benefits from staying close to CLIP's zero-shot feature space. Because both objectives act on the same prompt, their gradients conflict at convergence, and in our experiments no single-prompt loss design clearly improves on the cosine baseline. We propose Decoupled Mode Connectivity (DMC), which gives each objective its own prompt. Starting from a base-trained prompt, DMC trains a specialization prompt and a generalization prompt, and merges their text features with a fixed coefficient at test time, at the inference cost of a single prompt. A linear mode connectivity (LMC) corridor in text-feature space keeps the classification loss low for every classifier interpolated between the two endpoints, and a Visual Anchor KL term preserves CLIP's zero-shot class-similarity distribution of each image during specialization. We further argue that such regularizers should satisfy class-permutation invariance (CPI), and show via Fano's inequality, in an idealized model, that violating CPI lower-bounds the drop in novel accuracy by a term proportional to the mutual information between the prompt and the base-class labels. Across 11 datasets, DMC improves the average harmonic mean of base and novel accuracy over MergeTune for both CoOp and KgCoOp, and its interpolation curves pass beyond the single-prompt operating point, shifting the base-novel frontier rather than trading along it. Code is available at https://github.com/IemProg/DMC.
authors: Imad Eddine Marouf, Khalid Oublal, Enzo Tartaglione, St\'ephane Lathuili\`ere
bullets: Problem: A single prompt must balance base-class specialization with preservation of CLIP’s zero-shot behavior, causing conflicting objectives and limited generalization.

Method: Train separate specialization and generalization prompts from a base-trained prompt, connect them through a low-loss text-feature interpolation corridor, and merge their features using a fixed coefficient.
Regularization: Use a Visual Anchor KL term to preserve CLIP’s image-level class-similarity distribution, while enforcing class-permutation invariance.
Theory: Fano’s inequality links violations of class-permutation invariance to reduced novel-class accuracy through prompt–base-label mutual information.

Results: Across 11 datasets, DMC improves the average harmonic mean of base and novel accuracy over MergeTune for both CoOp and KgCoOp, with interpolation curves extending beyond the single-prompt trade-off point.

After DMC (right): the converged DMC corridor lies inside the low-loss valley, with the operating point at α = 0.20 marked by the star; the inset confirms base and novel accuracies are both high and stable along the corridor.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes Decoupled Mode Connectivity (DMC) for prompt learning in vision-language models to improve generalization to novel classes, addressing a key LLM/MLM challenge.
papers.title: Decoupled Mode Connectivity for Base-to-Novel Generalization in Vision-Language Models
papers.tldr: DMC improves base-to-novel generalization in vision-language prompt learning by separately optimizing specialization and generalization prompts, then merging their text features at inference.

papers.abstract: Long-context language models often neglect information in the middle of the input, a phenomenon known as "lost-in-the-middle". Part of this gap may stem from the long-range decay of rotary position embedding (RoPE), which weakens the positional signal between distant tokens. Existing input compression deletes low-importance tokens, and attention reweighting acts only after RoPE has weakened this signal. RoPE-level methods modify positions directly but apply the same remapping to every query. To address these limitations, we propose QGPM (Query-Guided Positional Modulation), a training-free method that reshapes RoPE positions using query relevance from the model's own attention heads. QGPM builds a broad relevance map for lower layers and a sharp one for upper layers. Low-relevance tokens advance by less than one position on fast-rotating planes, pulling relevant evidence toward the query. Slow-rotating planes keep the original layout, with every token in place. Experiments on NoLiMa and RULER with multiple context lengths show that QGPM improves over base models and strong baselines, with the largest gains on retrieval tasks, and generalizes across multiple backbones. Our code is available at https://github.com/iZHpy/QGPM.
authors: Peiyu Zhang, Heng Ping, Shinibali Bhattacharyya, Anwesan Pal, Nikos Kanakaris, Kevin Cheang, Shixuan Li, Wei Yang, Paul Bogdan
bullets: Targets positional-signal decay that can cause models to overlook information in the middle of long inputs.
Uses attention-derived query relevance to reshape token positions rather than deleting tokens or reweighting attention afterward.
Applies broad relevance maps in lower layers and sharper maps in upper layers; preserves the layout on slow-rotating RoPE planes.
Experiments on NoLiMa and RULER across context lengths show gains over base models and strong baselines, especially for retrieval tasks.
Generalizes across multiple model backbones.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of QGPM. (a) A plain prefill reads the attention from the query to each context sentence in a few selected heads. The fused sentence ranking is shaped into a broad relevance map and a sharp score map. Context before the first relevant sentence is protected and keeps a score of 1. (b) Each map sets a positional stride for every token on every frequency plane. Low-relevance tokens advance by less than one position on fast planes. Slow planes, relevant sentences, and the query keep unit stride. Cumulative sums give the remapped positions. (c) In the answering pass, the lower layers use the broad map and the upper layers use the sharp map. Decoding continues in unit steps from the last position of each map.

papers.abstract: Existing time series language models predominantly follow an offline, one-shot paradigm: they process fixed-length inputs independently and do not retain past states. This static approach fundamentally misaligns with the continuous nature of real-world streaming applications and fails to maintain the historical context necessary for cross-window reasoning. To bridge this gap, we introduce Continuous & Live Time Series Understanding (CL-TSU), a novel paradigm that shifts the focus toward maintaining a persistent, stateful understanding over open-ended data streams. To systematically evaluate this paradigm, we present LiveTS-Suite, the first comprehensive data suite tailored for CL-TSU, supporting data generation, model training, and systematic evaluation across 18 tasks spanning six core capabilities. It comprises over 5K streams totaling 2.2B timesteps, annotated with 15K specific response events. We further design an evaluation protocol that jointly assesses response timeliness, content accuracy, and computational efficiency. Building on this foundation, we propose TimeOmni-Live, the first live time series understanding model. It integrates a hybrid time series encoding for natively temporal input, a stream-persistent hybrid memory mechanism to effectively preserve exact historical evidence and long-term task states, and an elastic stream-inference synchronization strategy to reduce processing lag. Evaluations show that TimeOmni-Live establishes a strong baseline for CL-TSU, outperforming frontier LLMs (90.0 vs. 79.3 for Opus 5) with only 4B parameters and achieving 206$\times$ lower p95 latency than its backbone. Deployment on a Jetson edge device further shows its ability to support real-time continuous temporal understanding locally at the edge.
authors: Tong Guan, Alexander Chemeris, Yiqing Guo, Warren Jin, Zhao Li, Shirui Pan, Ming Jin
bullets: Introduces Continuous & Live Time Series Understanding (CL-TSU), replacing offline one-shot processing with persistent stateful reasoning over open-ended streams.
Presents LiveTS-Suite: 18 tasks across six capabilities, covering over 5K streams, 2.2B timesteps, and 15K response events.
Combines hybrid temporal encoding, persistent memory for historical evidence and task states, and elastic inference synchronization to reduce lag.
Reports a score of 90.0 versus 79.3 for Opus 5, with 206× lower p95 latency than its backbone using a 4B-parameter model.
Demonstrates real-time continuous understanding on a Jetson edge device.

papers.abstract: Language-model agents use experience through external retrieval and parameter learning. Consolidating stored experience into model weights requires deciding both which experience to train on and when its external records can leave retrieval. Admission based solely on student mastery can exclude useful teacher demonstrations, while removal immediately after training can discard guidance that the model still needs. We introduce ENGRAM, a framework that separates training admission from memory release. A demonstration-aware gate admits skills based on student mastery or sufficient successful teacher demonstrations. The student learns from selected action traces with context from an Engram Trace Graph (ETG). A verification gate then compares the updated model without episodic retrieval against the base model with retrieval on reserved probes. Release requires valid training participation and scores meeting both relative and absolute criteria; records for skills that fail verification remain retrievable. Experiments across interactive and reasoning benchmarks show consistent gains over frozen-weight ETG controls, with ablations supporting demonstration-aware admission and selective adapter activation. A controlled held-out comparison shows that verified release substantially reduces the retrievable footprint while remaining close to retain-all performance and outperforming immediate and budget-matched random release. ENGRAM also improves task performance while reducing input-token usage and model calls. Skill-level verification further reduces retrievable experience through selective archival, retaining external guidance for skills that do not meet the release criteria. Code is available in anonymous.4open.science/r/engram-anonymous.
authors: Ruiyi Yang, Zechen Li, Lihuan Li, Du Yin, Hao Xue, Flora D. Salim
bullets: Separates training admission from memory release to avoid discarding useful demonstrations or guidance prematurely.
Uses a demonstration-aware gate, Engram Trace Graph context, and selected action traces for training.
Releases records only after reserved-probe verification meets relative and absolute criteria; failed skills remain retrievable.
Reduces the retrievable-memory footprint while staying close to retain-all performance and outperforming immediate or random release.
Improves task performance while reducing input-token usage and model calls across interactive and reasoning benchmarks.

papers.abstract: Agent skills are short documents that teach a language model how to handle a class of tasks. To save context, these documents are increasingly compiled into low-rank adapters (LoRA), which keep the behaviour but lose the text: an adapter is hard to read, edit, audit or move to another model. We ask whether the skill document can be written back from the adapter and its frozen base model, and we score each recovered document by the share of the original's key instructions it states and by the tasks it solves. Reading the weights alone recovered little with the methods we tried; a learned map from weights to text passed on about one bit of the document. Running the adapter worked much better. The Executing Writer, a small writer trained on top of the adapted model, recovers 39-44% of the key instructions of held-out skills, against 1.3-1.5% with another skill's adapter, and on adapters fitted to 41 external skills its documents restore 85-91% of the original's task gain. These strongest results are on adapters whose training stored the document; adapters trained on behaviour alone are much harder for trained writers (1-2% of instructions). For these adapters we test an agent that runs the base and adapted models and writes a skill from where they differ. On ALFWorld its skills recover 58-71% of a LoRA's gain and carry over to models that cannot load the LoRA, lifting Llama-3.1-8B from 5% to 55%. Whether such a skill comes from the adapter depends on what the adapter learned: when its behaviour cannot be guessed, the adapter is the source; when it can, a reward loop without the adapter does as well.
authors: Saranya Dintakurthy Swadha, Pavan C Shekar, Arpit Jain, Aswanth Krishnan
bullets: LoRAs preserve skill behavior while obscuring the readable, editable, and transferable skill document.
Reading adapter weights directly performs poorly; a learned weight-to-text mapping recovers only about one bit of document information.
An Executing Writer recovers 39–44% of key instructions for skills whose training stored the document, and restores 85–91% of the original task gain across 41 external skills.
For behavior-only adapters, an agent comparing base and adapted models recovers 58–71% of the LoRA’s gain on ALFWorld and transfers the skill to models unable to load the adapter.
The skill appears to originate from the adapter when its behavior is not otherwise predictable; otherwise, a reward loop without the adapter can achieve similar results.

papers.abstract: Data-use auditing in Large Language Models (LLMs) aims to determine whether the given data has been used for training, thereby supporting data ownership safeguards. A dominant solution is data watermarking, which embeds traceable signals into training data and detects them in model outputs. Recent studies have proposed many watermarking-based auditing methods in LLMs. However, systematic investigation from an adversarial perspective remains limited: non-compliant LLM providers would use unauthorized copyrighted datasets for training their own models to enhance model capabilities, while attempting to evade detection by auditors, thereby avoiding legal liability. To fill this research gap, we propose a novel evasion framework, termed Logit Laundering, where the non-compliant LLM provider manipulates model outputs at inference time to undermine detectable watermark signals. Specifically, we design a logit reshaping module to suppress watermark-induced statistical signals by integrating a statistical bias estimator as a plug-and-play component. This design keeps the model parameters unchanged and performs manipulation only in the logit space, thereby enabling auditing evasion while minimizing the impact on model's learned knowledge. To further balance evasion effectiveness and model utility, we introduce a confidence-aware scaling module to adaptively calibrate the suppression strength based on next-token prediction confidence. Extensive evaluations show that Logit Laundering can successfully evade existing various state-of-the-art auditing methods, significantly attenuating detectable signals, while preserving model utility on downstream tasks. Our work highlights the need for exploring more robust auditing methods to guard against evasion behaviors.
authors: Ruihan Hu, Wei Luo, Yu-Ming Shang, Jiakai Wang, Chuxuan Zhang, Mei Li, Xi Zhang, Meikang Qiu
bullets: Targets watermark-based auditing used to detect whether copyrighted or otherwise protected data trained an LLM.
Applies plug-and-play logit reshaping to remove watermark-induced statistical signals without changing model parameters.
Uses confidence-aware scaling to adapt suppression strength according to next-token prediction confidence.
Evaluations show successful evasion across various state-of-the-art auditing methods while preserving downstream-task utility.
Highlights the need for auditing methods that are robust to inference-time evasion.
