papers.abstract: Knowledge Graphs (KGs) and Large Language Models (LLMs) represent two approaches for knowledge representation and reasoning over heterogeneous data. Recent research has explored their integration through Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation (GraphRAG) systems, which use KGs to provide structured context to LLMs. However, existing GraphRAG approaches treat KGs as homogeneous graphs and rely on textual similarity between the input prompt and the context, rather than using it as a source of deterministic knowledge. This work proposes an agent-based GraphRAG system that introduces a symbolic layer to integrate deterministic reasoning alongside text similarities. This approach is based on the definition of typed centralities for KGs, where centrality measures are computed separately for each specific KG's class. This information is used to construct a symbolic representation that is provided to the LLM as a deterministic source. The proposed system was mathematically validated and evaluated on a real-world POLE (Person, Object, Location, Event) dataset, comparing reasoning and information retrieval with and without the symbolic layer. The results indicate that the our approach leads to responses that are more consistent with the context, improving the generated outputs.
authors: Rosario Napoli, Antonio Celesti, Massimo Villari, Maria Fazio
bullets: Addresses the limitation of treating knowledge graphs as homogeneous and relying mainly on text similarity.
Computes centrality measures separately for each knowledge-graph class, such as Person, Object, Location, and Event.
Provides the resulting symbolic representation to an LLM alongside retrieved context.
Mathematically validates the approach and evaluates it on a real-world POLE dataset.
Reports improved consistency with context for reasoning and information-retrieval outputs when using the symbolic layer.

papers.abstract: We show that the Transformer's recurrent successors --- such as selective state-space models (SSMs), Receptance Weighted Key Value (RWKV), and Retentive Network (RetNet) --- can be characterized as infinite-impulse-response (IIR) systems. The zero--pole geometries of these IIR systems characterize the temporal modes they can represent. However, to trade parallelism, the algebraic structures of the parameterizations of these recurrent systems often give rise to poles constrained to the real axis, thereby inducing an architectural bias in their recurrent dynamics. To unify these recurrent architectures and eliminate their pole geometry bias, inspired by the lattice--ladder realization of general IIR systems, we present \textsc{Mira} (\textbf{M}odal \textbf{I}IR \textbf{R}ecurrent \textbf{A}rchitecture), a unified family of linear-time recurrent architectures for building large language models (LLMs) with a highly parallel algebraic structure. Each \textsc{Mira} block realizes a higher-order IIR system that represents temporal modes from token streams through a lattice--ladder structure, followed by a feed-forward network (FFN). This realization enables the model to represent the temporal modes associated with both real and complex-conjugate poles. We pretrain \textsc{Mira-S}, a 12-layer small-scale LLM with 0.14B parameters composed entirely of \textsc{Mira} blocks. Throughout the pretraining, \textsc{Mira-S} achieves lower perplexity than strong recurrent baselines, exhibits stronger context-window generalization beyond the training length, and attains higher throughput with a dedicated CUDA kernel.
authors: R\'ois\'in Luo, Ihsan Ullah, Christian Gagn\'e, Dong Li, Karyn Morrissey
bullets: Recurrent successors to Transformers can be viewed as infinite-impulse-response systems whose pole geometry determines representable temporal modes.
Common parameterizations bias poles toward the real axis, limiting recurrent dynamics.
MIRA uses a lattice–ladder realization to support both real and complex-conjugate poles in a unified recurrent architecture.
A 0.14B-parameter, 12-layer MIRA-S model achieves lower perplexity than strong recurrent baselines and generalizes better beyond its training context length.
A dedicated CUDA kernel provides higher throughput; the abstract does not specify detailed experimental settings or numerical gains.

papers.selection_reason: Presents a unified recurrent architecture for LLMs inspired by IIR lattice-ladder realizations, directly relevant to LLM architecture research.
papers.title: MIRA: Mitigating Pole Geometry Bias in Recurrent Language Models
papers.tldr: MIRA removes real-pole constraints in recurrent language models, enabling richer temporal dynamics while maintaining linear-time, highly parallel computation.

papers.abstract: Persistent-memory systems choose not only which records are retrieved but which prior information can alter current inference. We propose Jacobian-causal memory control (JCMC), which represents each authorized memory intervention by a predicted influence signature in a shared behavioral measurement space, selects interventions against a target effect and side-effect budget, and compares predicted with observed effects before retaining or rolling back the intervention. Under explicit smoothness and bounded-estimation assumptions, we prove a quadratic local-approximation bound, characterize the target effects reachable by a set of signatures, bound selection regret under signature error, and bound non-additive interactions between simultaneous memories. The paper reports no benchmark measurements; it defines a paired counterfactual estimator and an evaluation protocol comparing JCMC with relevance, graph, and policy-filtered retrieval baselines. The central claim is narrowed or falsified if those simpler baselines match effect targeting, side-effect control, and rollback utility under equal model, memory, policy, and cost budgets.
bullets: Addresses the problem of deciding which authorized memories should alter current language-model inference, beyond simple retrieval.
Predicts each memory’s influence signature in a shared behavioral measurement space and selects interventions under target-effect and side-effect constraints.
Uses paired counterfactual estimates to compare predicted and observed effects, retaining or rolling back interventions accordingly.
Provides theoretical bounds for local approximation error, reachable target effects, selection regret, and interactions among simultaneous memories.
No benchmark results are reported; the proposed evaluation compares JCMC with relevance-, graph-, and policy-filtered retrieval under matched budgets.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Jacobian-causal memory control loop for persistent memory. The diagram omits product-specific coefficients, thresholds, and storage schemas; the research object is the observable control loop.
Table 1: Relevance is a candidate signal. Jacobian-causal memory control treats recall as an intervention with expected and observed effects.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes Jacobian-causal memory control for persistent memory interventions in language model systems, directly relevant to LLM memory and retrieval.
papers.title: Jacobian-Causal Memory Control for Persistent Memory in Language Model Systems
papers.tldr: JCMC controls persistent-memory interventions by targeting desired behavioral effects while limiting side effects and rolling back inaccurate interventions.

papers.abstract: Conversational recommender systems often treat user sessions in isolation, limiting their ability to capture how user intent evolves over time. While large language models (LLMs) have improved semantic understanding, they are typically used as isolated components, without addressing how memory, retrieval, and decision-making should be integrated at the system level. In this work, we propose a memory-aware multi-agent architecture for conversational recommendation, in which LLMs act as orchestration layers that coordinate intent refinement, query construction, and interaction flow. A key design principle is the integration of long-term memory as a first-class component, influencing both routing decisions and semantic query formation. We evaluate the system through cross-session memory experiments, multi-turn conversational simulations, and supervisor-driven interaction studies on the Amazon Reviews dataset. Results show that memory-enabled interactions recover up to 63\% of the gap toward explicit-query scenarios and prevent semantic degradation in extended dialogues. In addition, supervisory orchestration increases user acceptance by +28.9 percentage points, highlighting the importance of structured orchestration in guiding interaction and output quality. We also observe an exposure bottleneck between retrieved candidates and displayed recommendations. While LLM-reranking does not improve Hit@K, it consistently enhances semantic consistency and diversity. To capture these effects, we introduce the Semantic Consistency Score (SCS), a complementary evaluation measure. Overall, the results emphasize the importance of system-level design choices, suggesting that effective conversational recommendation benefits from explicit memory integration, orchestration, and evaluation beyond traditional ranking metrics.
authors: Emilly Pitman de Castro, Vanessa Silva, Gustavo Kanno, Marcus Santos, Bruno Ferraz do Amaral, Marcelo Nogueira, Lucas Francisco Pellicer, Lucas Lanaro, Pedro Augusto Luiz, Jo\~ao Renato Ribeiro Manesco, Giovanni Carbinatti, Isabela de Lima Santos, Lucas Oliveira Jeronymo, Jeison Fappi, Raul Rotilli Aguirre, Fabio Andr\'e Frantz, Renata De Paris, Fabiana Marucci, Lohan Silva, Vinicius Diniz Reolon, Wandemberg Gibaut
bullets: Targets session-isolated recommenders that fail to track evolving user intent and lack system-level integration of memory, retrieval, and decision-making.
Uses LLMs to orchestrate intent refinement, query construction, routing, and interaction flow, with long-term memory informing these processes.
Evaluated on Amazon Reviews through cross-session memory experiments, multi-turn simulations, and supervisor-driven interactions.
Memory recovers up to 63% of the gap toward explicit-query scenarios, while supervisory orchestration raises user acceptance by 28.9 percentage points.
LLM reranking does not improve Hit@K but improves semantic consistency and diversity; the proposed Semantic Consistency Score captures these effects and exposes an exposure bottleneck.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes LLM-orchestrated multi-agent conversational recommendation with long-term memory as a first-class component, directly relevant to LLM memory and retrieval integration.
papers.title: Memory-Aware Multi-Agent Architecture with LLM-based Orchestration for Conversational Recommendation
papers.tldr: A memory-aware, LLM-orchestrated multi-agent system improves conversational recommendation across sessions by integrating long-term memory, structured coordination, and semantic evaluation.

papers.abstract: LLM agents do not learn from corrections across sessions. A user fixes the same mistake at the start of every conversation. Existing agent memory systems primarily handle facts, such as preferences, entities, and conversational history, rather than procedural knowledge. We present Forge Decision Context (forge_dc), a system that captures behavioral signals from human corrections and self-assessed tool-call failures, compiles them into imperative RULE directives, and injects them at the decision points where they apply. We evaluate forge_dc alongside four predecessor approaches on DC-Bench, a new benchmark of 71 scenarios across nine behavioral dimensions, built from real executed agent traces in a deterministic mocked-tool environment. forge_dc reaches 95% compliance, up from 55% with naive retrieval, while injecting approximately 10 times fewer tokens per query. Across the five-stage progression, the strongest systems represent behavioral memory as explicit directives and deliver it at the decision points where it applies. The results identify representation, activation, and placement as central design choices for persistent behavioral learning.
bullets: Targets persistent procedural learning, addressing repeated user corrections that existing fact-focused memory systems fail to retain.
Captures human corrections and self-identified tool-call failures, then compiles them into imperative RULE directives.
Evaluated on DC-Bench: 71 scenarios spanning nine behavioral dimensions in a deterministic mocked-tool environment.
Achieves 95% compliance versus 55% for naive retrieval while using roughly 10× fewer tokens per query.
Finds that behavioral-memory representation, activation, and placement are key design choices.

papers.selection_reason: Persistent behavioral memory for LLM agents via rule compilation and decision-point injection.
papers.title: Decision Context: Persistent Behavioral Learning for AI Agents
papers.tldr: Forge Decision Context enables AI agents to retain and apply behavioral corrections across sessions by injecting concise rules at relevant decision points.

papers.abstract: Financial institutions construct knowledge graphs (KGs) from shared SEC 10-Ks to serve risk analysis, portfolio management, and investment research, whose analytical needs differ. Extraction must adapt without fragmenting shared grounding, typing, and temporal rules. Hand-authored persona prompts and fine-tuning add cost. Weight-free prompt optimization offers an alternative, but unconstrained evolution of a monolithic prompt can rewrite shared rules alongside persona guidance, obscuring changes and complicating review. We introduce FinEvolveKG, a KG-construction harness separating reusable general and persona-policy blocks and mechanically confining GEPA, a reflective prompt optimizer, to the designated block. During persona adaptation, the approved general block remains byte-stable and every optimizer edit is localized to a separately versioned persona policy. A dual objective balances generic temporal-KG quality with persona-relevant facts, motifs, and multi-hop connectivity. We evaluate five mutation scopes on ticker-disjoint 10-K splits, with three seeds for the persona-conditioned arms (v3-v5) across three personas. On the three-seed mean, the complete two-stage block-constrained workflow (v4) improves over the frozen prompt baseline (v1) by 19.4-30.9% and over the tested unconstrained full-prompt workflow (v5) by 2.2-6.4%, leading v5 on both objective components and winning all nine paired-seed comparisons with the lowest seed variance in every persona. Without further optimization, v4 also exceeds v5 across all evaluated out-of-distribution (OOD) shifts. An SME audit supports using the generated triplets as ground truth; a blinded two-SME audit favors v4 over v5 in 70.1% of contrast-enriched judgments. These results show that mechanically attributable evolution can coexist with strong empirical performance, without attributing the gains causally to the boundary.
authors: Abhinav Arun, Jayita Bhattacharyya, Fabrizio Dimino, Bhaskarjit Sarmah, Stefano Pasquali
bullets: Addresses the need to adapt KG extraction to different financial personas without changing shared grounding, typing, and temporal rules.
Separates general and persona-policy prompt blocks, mechanically confines GEPA edits to the persona block, and versions each change.
Optimizes a dual objective covering generic temporal-KG quality and persona-specific facts, motifs, and multi-hop connectivity.
Across three personas and ticker-disjoint 10-K splits, the complete workflow improves over the frozen baseline by 19.4–30.9% and over the unconstrained workflow by 2.2–6.4%.
It also shows lower seed variance, wins all nine paired-seed comparisons, and remains stronger under evaluated OOD shifts; the authors do not claim the boundary itself caused the gains.

Released blocks carry their version and persona diff and are composed with their decomposed scores for production KG construction and downstream analyst workflows.

Table 2: Persona ownership: what each persona prioritizes over the same underlying schema.
Table 1: Mutation scopes and optimization conditions.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces a constrained prompt evolution framework for financial knowledge graph construction, separating general and persona-specific blocks to maintain stability and quality.
papers.title: FinEvolveKG: Controlled and Attributable Prompt Evolution for Financial Knowledge Graph Construction
papers.tldr: FinEvolveKG makes financial KG prompt evolution reviewable by optimizing only versioned persona policies while preserving shared rules, achieving stronger and more stable results than frozen or unconstrained prompts.

papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are attractive rerankers for recommendation. Running an expensive model on every request is costly, and for users with sparse interaction histories it often lowers quality. We present CascadeRec, a two-tier LLM reranking cascade deployed in production at a large financial planning and analysis (FP&A) SaaS provider. It serves content recommendations to enterprise tenants on AWS EKS and GKE. A lightweight Tier-1 model reranks every request. A router escalates only the requests where extra inference-time compute is likely to help, and sends them to a more expensive Tier-2 procedure (self-consistency sampling, multi-path reasoning, or a larger model). The system has run in a production A/B experiment for over a month. Compared with uniform use of the expensive tier, CascadeRec has reduced inference cost by about 10%, with minimal latency impact and no quality regression observed to date. Tenant data cannot be released, so we also evaluate the pipeline on public benchmarks (MovieLens-1M and Amazon-Electronics). Segment-level analysis with paired-bootstrap confidence intervals shows that uniform LLM reranking lowers NDCG@10 for sparse-history users by up to 30%, and its only statistically significant gain appears on the segment with the longest histories. Escalating cold users can make the loss larger instead of repairing it. Which segments benefit from escalation depends on the domain, and this motivates the segment-gated rollout we use in production. We describe the deployment architecture, the measured benefits, and lessons learned, including inter-tenant load imbalance as a driver for cascading and the handling of LLM output-parsing failures at the serving layer.
authors: Kai Zhao, Guilin Zhang, Xiang Cheng, Xiquan Cui, Henry Heng, Xu Chu, Alet Blanken
bullets: Uniform expensive LLM reranking can hurt sparse-history users, lowering NDCG@10 by up to 30% on public benchmarks.
A lightweight Tier-1 reranks every request, while a router sends potentially beneficial cases to a more expensive Tier-2 procedure.
The production system runs across multi-tenant AWS EKS and GKE deployments with minimal latency impact reported.
Escalation benefits vary by user segment and domain; cold-user escalation can worsen performance, motivating segment-gated rollout.
The deployment addresses practical serving issues including inter-tenant load imbalance and LLM output-parsing failures.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces a cascade architecture for LLM reranking that reduces inference cost by routing requests based on user history, demonstrating a practical efficiency strategy.
papers.title: CascadeRec: Deployed Adaptive LLM Compute Allocation for Multi-Tenant Content Recommendation
papers.tldr: CascadeRec reduces costly LLM reranking by selectively escalating requests to a stronger tier, cutting production inference cost by about 10% without observed quality loss.

papers.abstract: Circuit design for analog integrated circuits (ICs) is challenging because circuit topology, device sizing, and circuit performance are tightly coupled. Existing large language model (LLM)-based methods either rely on inference-time correction around frozen models or train on limited circuit types without directly using simulation outcomes as training signals. A key bottleneck is that existing datasets do not provide sufficient task information for training LLMs on end-to-end specification-conditioned design. To fill this gap, we first construct a large-scale simulation-grounded dataset with 8,626 design tasks across 10 different types of analog circuits, where each task includes a textual description, labeled I/O ports, loading condition, target specifications, a testbench, and a reference netlist. Using this dataset, we present SAFTAC, a simulation-augmented fine-tuning framework that trains LLMs to generate and revise analog circuit design. SAFTAC combines three-stage supervised fine-tuning, which progressively builds the capabilities required for analog circuit design and feedback-guided correction, with simulation feedback-augmented reinforcement fine-tuning, which further optimizes models using simulation-grounded rewards. We evaluate SAFTAC under single-pass generation and two-pass generation with simulation feedback, showing improvements over the strongest closed-source LLM by 15.9% and 7.8%, respectively.
authors: Junsheng Huang, Yifan Sun, Zhuoer Zhang, Ning Wei, Yening Liu, Michael Molter, Pavan Kumar Hanumolu, Elyse Rosenbaum, Bin Hu, Huan Zhang
bullets: Addresses the difficulty of end-to-end, specification-conditioned analog IC design, where topology, sizing, and performance are tightly coupled.
Introduces a dataset of 8,626 simulation-grounded design tasks spanning 10 analog circuit types, with specifications, testbenches, and reference netlists.
Uses three-stage supervised fine-tuning followed by simulation feedback-augmented reinforcement fine-tuning.
Supports both single-pass generation and two-pass generation with simulation feedback.
Reports improvements over the strongest closed-source LLM of 15.9% for single-pass and 7.8% for two-pass generation.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of the automated data generation pipeline for analog circuit design tasks. Each step is guided and checked by human experts. (b) A data sample is provided for reference, with the Python testbench code omitted for brevity.

Figure 2: Overview of the simulation feedback-augmented RFT pipeline. It combines standard circuit design tasks and simulation feedback-guided correction tasks. In both tasks, the generated netlist is evaluated through circuit topology check, BO sizing, and simulation. The resulting outcome is converted into a reward signal and used to update the policy with GRPO.

papers.selection_reason: Applies large language models to a specific engineering domain (analog circuit design) using a simulation-augmented fine-tuning framework.
papers.title: SAFTAC: Simulation-Augmented Fine-Tuning of Open-Source LLMs for Analog Circuit Design
papers.tldr: SAFTAC fine-tunes open-source LLMs with simulation-grounded data and rewards to generate and iteratively correct analog circuit designs.

papers.abstract: Longitudinal relational agents rely on memory for continuity, but remembering can lead to intrusion, clinical overconfidence, emotional manipulation, and opacity. We present Relic, a governance architecture for diegetic relational agents, and Gumi, a subject-specific companion agent initialized and governed through Relic. The architecture separates what the system can observe, what researchers can review, what Gumi can remember, and what Gumi can say. We describe three mechanisms. Relic represents sensitive safety signals as researcher-facing governance objects rather than user-facing explanations or agent memories. Shared Continuity Memory organizes relational markers around subject-confirmed wording, corrections, explicit follow-up permissions, and recall limits. We specify a runtime mediation layer for delivery, proactivity, session identity, output transformation, and platform allowlists; adoption across live paths remains partial. These mechanisms aim to preserve relational continuity without turning Gumi into a clinical assistant, mood tracker, general-purpose assistant, or opaque profiling system. We contribute the architecture, object model, researcher workbench design, and a proposed evaluation framework for governed relational memory. An exploratory pilot involved the author as P1 and one external participant as P2. Weekly self-reports from P1 and researcher-led interviews with P2 provide descriptive observations of early use and perceived naturalness. The pilot does not support claims about clinical efficacy, diagnosis, therapeutic outcomes, general usability, or deployment safety. Relic provides research infrastructure intended to make relational memory, safety constraints, and agent behavior inspectable and testable.
bullets: Addresses risks of longitudinal memory, including intrusion, emotional manipulation, clinical overconfidence, and opacity.
Introduces Gumi, a subject-specific companion governed by Relic, with separate layers for observation, researcher review, agent memory, and user-facing speech.
Uses researcher-facing safety objects, consent- and correction-centered continuity memory, and runtime mediation for delivery, proactivity, identity, output, and platform access.
Provides an architecture, object model, researcher workbench, and proposed evaluation framework; adoption across live paths remains partial.
An exploratory pilot with two participants offers descriptive observations only and does not establish clinical efficacy, general usability, or deployment safety.

papers.abstract: The vast amount of information available in lengthy, distributed documents makes finding relevant answers difficult, especially when the answer requires connecting evidence from multiple sources. Standard Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems often struggle with this type of "multi-hop" reasoning and frequently face issues with context fragmentation. In this paper, we propose a hybrid RAG framework that integrates the structured reasoning of knowledge graphs with the broad semantic coverage of dense vector retrieval. Our approach employs a multi-stage pipeline using transformer-based summarization and semantic chunking to improve context retention. We construct a dynamic knowledge graph to capture explicit relationships between entities while simultaneously maintaining a dense vector index. During inference, the system uses a hierarchical mechanism that prioritizes graph traversal for precision and falls back to vector retrieval when necessary. We evaluated our framework on the MultiHop-RAG dataset. The results show that this hybrid approach outperforms standalone vector and graph-based baselines, achieving higher Exact Match scores and improved retrieval accuracy for complex queries. This confirms that merging structured reasoning with standard vector retrieval creates a more robust system for handling complex knowledge-intensive questions.
bullets: Addresses context fragmentation and difficulty linking evidence across distributed, lengthy documents.
Uses transformer-based summarization and semantic chunking to retain relevant context.
Builds a dynamic knowledge graph alongside a dense vector index.
Prioritizes graph traversal for precise retrieval, with vector search as a fallback.
Outperforms standalone graph- and vector-based baselines on MultiHop-RAG in Exact Match and retrieval accuracy.

papers.abstract: Instruction tuning of large language models and large vision language models relies on massive training data, which incurs substantial computational and storage costs. Meanwhile, training data often contains redundancy, noise, and low quality samples. Existing data selection methods mostly rely on diversity, importance, or a combination of both, without explicitly constraining the distributional consistency between the selected subset and the full data in the embedding space. We propose QMAC, a quality aware multiband characteristic function matching method that formulates data selection as a joint optimization problem of distribution matching and quality filtering. QMAC matches the empirical characteristic functions of the selected subset and the full data across multiple frequency scales, capturing both global semantic coverage and local perturbations, while using task related quality scores to filter noisy and low quality samples. We systematically evaluate QMAC on 4 data types, 8 target models, and 44 benchmarks. Experimental results show that QMAC outperforms existing data selection baselines on standard image-text instruction data, substantially surpasses random selection on standard text instruction, image-text reasoning, and text reasoning data, and exceeds full data training in multiple model and budget combinations. The code will be made publicly available upon acceptance of the paper.
authors: Peng Sun, Yi Yang, Mingshuo Chen, Chunxiao Li, Yao Zhu, Huawen Shen, Tianfan Fu
bullets: Addresses the computational and storage costs of massive instruction-tuning datasets containing redundant, noisy, and low-quality samples.
Formulates data selection as joint distribution matching and quality filtering in embedding space.
Matches empirical characteristic functions across frequency bands to preserve global semantic coverage and local variation.
Uses task-related quality scores to remove noisy or low-quality examples.
Outperforms existing baselines across evaluated data types, models, and benchmarks, and exceeds full-data training in some model–budget settings.

papers.abstract: Increasing the batch size during training is a common practice in large language model (LLM) pretraining, yet the theoretical justification behind its success is not well understood. Analyses of stochastic optimization often assume uniformly bounded stochastic gradient variance, yet recent evidence suggests that this assumption fails in many practical nonconvex problems. The Blum--Gladyshev (BG-$0$) noise model relaxes this assumption by allowing the variance to grow quadratically with the distance from initialization, suggesting that batch size schedulers can help by controlling the variance growth during training. However, this growth can be overly conservative in practice. We empirically investigate variance growth in LLM pretraining and observe that a generalized BG model with a tunable growth exponent provides a tighter description of practical noise behavior. Motivated by this observation, we introduce the generalized BG-$a$ noise model, which interpolates between bounded variance ($a=0$) and BG-$0$ noise ($a=2$). Under $L$-smoothness, we derive an information-theoretic lower bound with growth-dependent oracle complexity $Ω(ε^{-(4+a)})$ and establish a matching upper bound in $ε$-dependence by increasing the batch size as the iterates move away from initialization. Finally, we propose an adaptive batch scheduler that controls variance growth through dynamic batch size adjustments during training. In pretraining OLMo2 models of up to 1B parameters on C4, our scheduler achieves a lower validation loss than both small and large batch training under matched token budgets, while using less than 10\% of the iterations of small batch training.
bullets: Motivation: Standard bounded-variance assumptions may not describe stochastic gradients in practical nonconvex LLM pretraining.
Method: Introduces the generalized BG-$a$ noise model, interpolating between bounded variance and quadratically growing variance.
Theory: Derives a growth-dependent oracle lower bound of $Ω(ε^{-(4+a)})$ and a matching-in-$ε$ upper bound using increasing batch sizes.
Algorithm: Proposes an adaptive scheduler that adjusts batch size to control variance as training progresses.

Result and scope: On OLMo2 models up to 1B parameters trained on C4, the scheduler achieves lower validation loss than fixed small or large batches under matched token budgets, with fewer than 10% as many iterations as small-batch training.

papers.abstract: Large language models provide a variety of responses at inference (generation) that conventionally depend on a temperature parameter. Using a conditional mutual information approach, a quantitative, entropy based analysis of response variety is given. Three limiting behaviors are defined: arbiter, independent (conditionally) and neutral (deterministic) that span no to maximal mutual information. We give examples of each behavior and suggest their application to: temperature analysis, language analysis, prompt compression, and knowledge graphs.
bullets: Defines an entropy-based measure of response variety using conditional mutual information.
Introduces three limiting behaviors: arbiter, conditionally independent, and neutral (deterministic).
These behaviors span a range from no to maximal mutual information.
Provides examples and discusses applications to temperature analysis, language analysis, prompt compression, and knowledge graphs.

papers.abstract: Alignment does not eliminate behavioral errors in language models. Models may still refuse benign requests, call unnecessary tools, or yield to false user claims. Current methods mitigate such errors as a computation problem, and rarely explore if the desired behavior is already encoded in the model's representation. Motivated by the observation that behavior-relevant information remains linearly decodable from the final hidden state even when the resulting logits produce the undesired behavior, we introduce HeadEdit, a gradient-free method that calibrates model behavior through the unembedding matrix. HeadEdit extracts a low-rank behavioral subspace from paired completions and uses each prompt's coordinates within it to generate a vocabulary-wide correction, thereby implementing implicitly adaptive steering without manually specified target tokens or parameter updates. HeadEdit improves all nine experimental settings across three tasks and three model families, with negligible inference overhead and no systematic loss of general capabilities. It also reveals a connection to gradient-based alignment. HeadEdit's low-dimensional representation partly predicts how preference tuning changes output logits on unseen prompts. The subspace learned from the model can also be reused after tuning, improving performance without re-extracting or retuning. These results show that HeadEdit provides a practical, lightweight, and interpretable way to calibrate model behavior through the unembedding matrix.
bullets: Addresses residual behavioral errors such as unnecessary refusals, tool calls, and susceptibility to false user claims.
Uses paired completions to learn behavior-relevant directions, then steers outputs without gradients, parameter updates, or manually chosen target tokens.
Improves performance across nine settings spanning three tasks and three model families, with negligible inference overhead and no systematic loss of general capabilities.
The learned subspace partly predicts preference-tuning logit changes on unseen prompts and can be reused after tuning without re-extraction.
Provides a lightweight, interpretable link between representation-based steering and gradient-based alignment.

papers.abstract: Token-level certainty is widely used as a proxy for correctness in LLM training and inference. However, the performance of certainty-based methods depends both on the information in certainty scores and on how those scores are used. We therefore directly assess certainty's predictive ability through controlled empirical evaluations across models and tasks. We distinguish two prediction targets: identifying questions a model is more likely to answer correctly and distinguishing correct from incorrect responses to the same question. In our experiments, certainty is generally better at identifying questions a model is likely to answer correctly than at distinguishing correct from incorrect responses to the same question. Certainty also varies systematically across token types and positions within words, reflecting local properties of words and text form. Information about question difficulty appears early in generation, while the weaker information about answer correctness is more concentrated near the end. These findings show that the information certainty provides for decisions depends on the prediction target, the model, the certainty metric, and which token positions in the response are included in aggregation. We further demonstrate the practical value of these findings for test-time compute. We allocate the number of responses using certainty early in generation and weight answer votes using certainty near the end of each response. Compared with a fixed-sampling majority-voting baseline, this approach increases overall accuracy from 78.71\% to 79.54\% while reducing generated-token cost by 82.4\%.
bullets: Certainty better predicts which questions a model will answer correctly than which response to a given question is correct.
Certainty varies by token type and word position, so aggregation choices affect its usefulness.
Difficulty information appears early in generation, whereas weaker correctness signals concentrate near the response’s end.
Using early certainty to allocate samples and late certainty to weight votes raises accuracy from 78.71% to 79.54% while cutting generated-token cost by 82.4%.
The findings depend on the prediction target, model, certainty metric, and selected token positions.

papers.selection_reason: Analyzes token-level certainty in LLMs and proposes a test-time compute strategy using certainty for sampling and voting, directly relevant to LLM reasoning and test-time adaptation.
papers.title: Certainty Is Not Just Correctness: Rethinking Token-Level Certainty in LLM Reasoning
papers.tldr: Token-level certainty is more useful for judging question difficulty than answer correctness, but strategically using it at different generation stages improves accuracy while greatly reducing test-time compute.

papers.abstract: Selective intent routing allows an assistant to act on reliable predictions while deferring uncertain requests. Standard confidence scores primarily reflect the base model's representation, leaving an opportunity to incorporate complementary evidence without changing its decisions. We introduce a signed lexical gate that combines a sentence classifier's logit margin with a sparse lexical model's support for the classifier's predicted intent. By assigning positive evidence to lexical agreement and negative evidence to a lexically favored competing intent, the gate retains more information than either unsigned lexical confidence or a hard agreement rule. An independent binomial calibration stage selects an operating threshold for a specified risk target. Across ten runs on BANKING77, CLINC150, and HWU64, the proposed score reduces area under the risk-coverage curve by 15.8%, 15.1%, and 11.8% relative to a learned semantic-only gate. At a nominal 5% error target, it increases accepted coverage by 1.83 and 5.14 percentage points on BANKING77 and HWU64, while CLINC150 is already near full coverage. At a stricter 2% target, the simultaneous binomial procedure yields a nonempty policy in all 30 dataset-run combinations at the available calibration budgets. Matched controls show that the proposed feature improves average error ranking over the tested unsigned lexical-confidence feature, with dataset-dependent gains over binary agreement. The resulting two-feature gate provides a compact, interpretable confidence enhancement for risk-calibrated intent routing while preserving the base classifier's predictions.
bullets: Combines the classifier’s logit margin with positive lexical support for its predicted intent and negative support for a competing intent.
Uses an independent binomial calibration stage to choose thresholds for specified error-risk targets.
Reduces area under the risk-coverage curve by 15.8%, 15.1%, and 11.8% on BANKING77, CLINC150, and HWU64, respectively, relative to a semantic-only gate.
At a 5% error target, accepted coverage rises by 1.83 and 5.14 percentage points on BANKING77 and HWU64; CLINC150 is already near full coverage.
Matched controls show improvements over unsigned lexical confidence, with dataset-dependent gains over binary agreement.

papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents increasingly act as service consumers. They select operations and report whether a task is complete. In an asynchronous distributed service, an accepted call or immediate state read does not establish that the required state became observable by its deadline. We introduce execution-grounded completion contracts, which treat completion as a service-level outcome. An independent control plane observes a deadline-bound service-state predicate, admits completion, and directs recovery while the agent performs the task. We evaluate placement and deletion in a live multi-provider data service with heterogeneous models and an injected transfer delay. Across policies, some tasks that missed the deadline were accepted and some that met it were rejected. Under enforcement, accepted completions remained consistent with later observations; all included healthy tasks completed, and unresolved faulted tasks terminated as unverified. The results show that completion of these tasks can be governed by independent observation of service state rather than by the agent's self-assessment.
bullets: Addresses the gap between accepted operations or immediate reads and deadline-bound observable outcomes in asynchronous services.
Uses an independent control plane to monitor service-state predicates, admit or reject completion, and direct recovery.
Evaluated placement and deletion in a live multi-provider data service with heterogeneous models and injected transfer delay.
Some accepted tasks missed deadlines, while some rejected tasks met them, showing agent reports were unreliable.
Enforcement kept accepted completions consistent with later observations and terminated unresolved faulted tasks as unverified.

papers.abstract: Parallel decoding speeds up masked diffusion language models by writing several tokens per forward pass. Published commit rules choose these tokens by testing the predicted distributions. Under sampling the written tokens are drawn, and these tests do not see them. We find that answer quality follows the reliability of the tokens actually written. An answer's log probability splits into this reliability and the dependence within each step. We propose PACT, a training-free commit rule that draws the tokens first, certifies the set it will write and spaces the positions of each step apart. This certificate holds at every temperature, and we show that no rule with the same guarantee commits more positions. Experiments use four models of the LLaDA and Dream families and HumanEval, MBPP, GSM8K, MATH500 and IFEval benchmarks. PACT reaches the quality of published commit rules with fewer forward passes. Spacing removes positions from each step, yet it usually lowers the total cost because later steps then write more tokens. At the same speed, published decoders also write a word twice in a row far more often than PACT. These results suggest that commit rules should certify the tokens they write. Code is available at https://github.com/LiZaiyuan0619/PACT.
bullets: Existing commit rules assess predicted distributions rather than the tokens actually sampled during decoding.
PACT samples tokens first, certifies the set to write, and spaces selected positions apart; its guarantee holds at every temperature.
The paper decomposes answer log probability into written-token reliability and within-step dependence, motivating certification of actual writes.
Across LLaDA and Dream models on HumanEval, MBPP, GSM8K, MATH500, and IFEval, PACT matches published quality with fewer forward passes.
Spacing generally lowers total decoding cost and reduces repeated word writes compared with published decoders.

papers.abstract: As Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) large language models are increasingly deployed in distributed environments, from federated learning to edge-cloud systems, their architecture harbors an underexplored landscape of security vulnerabilities. Moving beyond textual analysis, we uncover structural memorization: a novel vulnerability where a fine-tuned model memorizes not only its training data but also the internal pathway used to process it, creating a characteristic routing fingerprint unique to the training process. We provide comprehensive empirical evidence that structural memorization emerges consistently even from a few samples, and that its intensity is directly influenced by the choice of trainable modules. We show that these memorized expert pathways can be stealthily recovered through the model's unconditional generation, using only routing and output logits, with no knowledge of the fine-tuning data or procedure. In distributed deployments, this vulnerability is amplified as routing information is exposed at multiple trust boundaries, including federated aggregation points, edge-cloud interfaces, and multi-tenant monitoring systems. Recovery exposes a critical blind spot: traditional membership inference metrics, viewed through the lens of expert routing, fail to identify memorized data corresponding to these structural pathways. To close this gap, we devise composite metrics combining reference model tail likelihood with complexity-aware normalization, significantly improving detection of memorized routing structures. This enables adversaries to pinpoint critical experts shaped by fine-tuning, whether dominant or dormant, and execute targeted attacks such as router manipulation or backdoor injection in realistic distributed settings where attackers lack training data but can observe routing patterns across system components.
bullets: Structural memorization records internal expert pathways alongside training data, even when fine-tuning uses few samples.
The strength of these routing fingerprints depends on which model modules are trainable.
Attackers can recover pathways from unconditional generation using only routing information and output logits, without training data or procedure knowledge.
Distributed systems amplify exposure across federated aggregation, edge-cloud, and multi-tenant monitoring boundaries.
Composite metrics using reference-model tail likelihood and complexity-aware normalization improve detection beyond standard membership-inference measures.

papers.abstract: On-policy distillation (OPD) trains a student on its own responses using token-level feedback from a teacher. As responses grow longer, the student's prefix can depart from the teacher's own reasoning, weakening its feedback on later tokens. Updates based on this feedback can reinforce the same deviations in later responses and destabilize training. Prior approaches such as length control and loss reweighting limit learning from problematic responses but leave their prefixes unchanged. Fixed cutoffs can also discard later reasoning. We propose \textbf{Adaptive Teacher Intervention for On-Policy Distillation (ATI-OPD)} to improve subsequent teacher guidance by revising the student's reasoning prefix. ATI-OPD replaces the earliest high-disagreement segment with a short teacher segment, then lets the student resume its own reasoning from the revised text. To handle renewed disagreement, it excludes persistently divergent suffixes from the distillation loss while retaining useful student continuation. Training diagnostics show less teacher-student disagreement, fewer gradient spikes, and fewer extremely long responses. Across five mathematical reasoning benchmarks and two teacher-student pairs, ATI-OPD improves average student-only accuracy over standard OPD.
bullets: Long responses can cause student prefixes to drift from the teacher, weakening later feedback and destabilizing training.
The method replaces the earliest high-disagreement segment with a short teacher-generated segment, then resumes student reasoning.
Persistently divergent suffixes are excluded from the distillation loss while preserving useful student continuation.
Diagnostics show reduced disagreement, fewer gradient spikes, and fewer extremely long responses.
Across five mathematical reasoning benchmarks and two teacher–student pairs, ATI-OPD improves average student-only accuracy over standard OPD.

papers.abstract: Foundation models can generate scientific code, but authoring a scientific simulator (an executable program encoding hypotheses about how mechanisms generate observable signals) requires iterative refinement. Scientific adequacy rarely admits a unique implementation or exact test, so simulators must instead be judged against limited real observations. We study this setting as scientific simulator authoring under weak empirical feedback, where distributional comparisons between simulated and real signals guide revision, and the target is the simulator itself rather than only its generated samples. We introduce SimAuthor, a persistent authoring harness that retains and revises executable simulators, separates scalar search scores from structured discrepancy feedback, and accumulates reusable implementation mechanisms. We evaluate SimAuthor on six biomedical tasks spanning cardiac and respiratory audio, photoplethysmography (PPG), and electrocardiography (ECG). Under a fixed 100-attempt budget, SimAuthor outperforms PUCT score search on all six tasks, generally outperforms textual-strategy optimization, and achieves the highest endpoint score on five of six. The authored simulators also improve on unseen recordings, transfer to independent pretrained representations, and yield substantial out-of-distribution gains in downstream ECG classification. Finally, 111 of 138 audited revisions alter program structure and account for 86.1% of the signed score improvement. These results suggest that persistent revision can progressively convert foundation-model knowledge into better executable scientific simulators from limited empirical evidence.
bullets: Addresses simulator authoring when scientific adequacy lacks a unique implementation or exact test.
Maintains and revises executable simulators, separating scalar search scores from structured discrepancy feedback and reusing implementation mechanisms.
Evaluated on cardiac and respiratory audio, PPG, and ECG tasks under a fixed 100-attempt budget.
Outperformed PUCT score search on all six tasks and achieved the best endpoint score on five; it also generalized to unseen recordings and downstream ECG classification.
Most audited revisions changed program structure, accounting for 86.1% of signed score improvement.

papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have reached expert-level performance on competition mathematics largely through the volume of search placed around them: candidate solutions are sampled in quantity and retained only when an external criterion accepts them. Such a procedure improves the outcome that survives it while leaving untouched what the model represents. We examine that question where no external criterion exists: translating statements between the dialects of neighbouring subfields, where fidelity turns on the level of generality at which content is asserted. The source leaves that level implicit in its vocabulary, so a faithful translation must recover it from the relation between the theories. We introduce an instrument that codes truth, content and scope in separate blind queues, with a judge-free measure of whether a rewrite states the hypothesis implicit in its source, and establish its sensitivity with a planted-positive control. Across seven models from four families, translating towards the general framing widens the domain of quantification in 60.6% of rewrites and narrows it in none; translating towards the concrete framing narrows it in 28.3% and widens it in 0.3%. The hypothesis that would prevent it is stated in 21.6% of model rewrites and 4.2% of human statements. Capability does not govern the asymmetry: it appears in every model tested, and the most capable widens least. It replicates on the half of the benchmark held out by a pre-registered rule, and on statements written by mathematicians. Instructing a model to state every hypothesis it requires raises that rate but not its sensitivity to direction. We argue that these systems have acquired an object-level correspondence between subfield vocabularies without the constraint under which a translation between theories carries hypotheses to hypotheses.
bullets: The study tests translation between neighboring mathematical subfields, where implicit scope and assumptions determine fidelity.
It introduces a judge-free instrument that separately codes truth, content, and scope, validated with planted-positive controls.
Across seven models, translations toward general frameworks widened quantification in 60.6% of cases and never narrowed it; concrete-directed translations narrowed it in 28.3% and widened it in 0.3%.
Models stated the hypotheses required by their rewrites in 21.6% of cases, versus 4.2% for human statements; the asymmetry appeared across all models.
Explicitly prompting models to state every required hypothesis increased disclosure but did not improve directional sensitivity.

Above, the pin is not promoted and the result is false, since Z/2Z is a Z-module without a basis (the repair is shown in red). papers.abstract: Critic-free reinforcement fine-tuning (RFT) for agentic large language models is often done through GRPO-style methods, which compute a group baseline over repeated rollouts to reduce target variance. However, this setup is ill-suited to agents acting in stateful environments such as live services or security sandboxes, where repeated rollouts are impractical to obtain and aggressive updates entrench the noise of long, sparsely verified trajectories. We propose \textit{Follow the Winners} (FTW), a critic-free policy-learning algorithm that adapts the cross-entropy method to RFT, replacing group rollouts with an ordinal filter on replay-buffer samples that yields polynomial concentration in the order statistic of returns. We derive FTW through a control-as-inference lens, which also recovers GRPO and DPO as specific modelling choices, identifying GRPO as risk-neutral while DPO and FTW share a bounded risk-seeking offset that FTW controls. We identify this offset as an inherent trade-off of variance reduction through ordinal filters on samples, whereas a critic model induces a different trade-off between bias and variance. Scaled to agentic LLM post-training, FTW matches GRPO and PPO on Sokoban and Search-R1 baselines, showing a viable trade-off from a value model or group rollouts to CPU memory.
bullets: Targets stateful environments where repeated rollouts are impractical and long trajectories are sparsely verified.
Applies an ordinal filter from the cross-entropy method to replay-buffer samples.
Uses a control-as-inference formulation that connects FTW with GRPO and DPO.
Controls the bounded risk-seeking effect introduced by ordinal filtering.
Matches GRPO and PPO baselines on Sokoban and Search-R1 while trading value models or group rollouts for CPU memory.

papers.abstract: Large language models are increasingly used where small syntactic errors matter, yet character-level reasoning is still evaluated mostly through isolated probes and aggregate accuracy. We introduce SyntaxBench, a diagnostic benchmark and statistical evaluation framework for character-level reasoning. It contains five core tasks, character counting, letter containment, palindrome detection, edit distance, and longest-string selection, plus index_to_span, a harder substring-extraction stress test. The five core tasks use paired English and character-length-matched random-string inputs. index_to_span documents share a 200-500 word band and are not character-length matched. All six tasks use zero-, one-, and four-shot prompts. We evaluate eight open-weight models from 2B to 32B parameters across 11 reasoning-mode configurations. The framework reports exact-match and relaxed accuracy, Cohen's kappa, paired McNemar tests with odds ratios, bootstrap confidence intervals, Kendall's tau, class-conditional metrics, tokenization analysis, and multiple-comparison-corrected tests. Three findings stand out. First, tokenization shapes accuracy: random strings are more character-visible than English strings (1.892 vs. 3.169 characters per token), and character-counting accuracy falls as English words occupy more tokens. Second, reasoning mode is not uniformly helpful: Gemma4-31B is nearly unchanged across modes on the near-saturated tasks, while Qwen3.6-27B is worse with thinking on palindrome detection (0.952 non-thinking vs. 0.886 thinking at four-shot). Third, index_to_span remains largely unsolved; the best four-shot exact-match accuracy is 6.75%. Character-level evaluation needs controlled inputs, paired tests, and analyses of tokenization and reasoning mode rather than aggregate accuracy alone.
bullets: Introduces six diagnostic tasks covering counting, containment, palindromes, edit distance, string selection, and substring extraction.
Pairs English and character-length-matched random-string inputs to isolate tokenization effects, with zero-, one-, and four-shot settings.
Evaluates eight open-weight models using exact and relaxed accuracy, paired statistical tests, confidence intervals, tokenization analysis, and multiple-comparison correction.
Random strings are more character-visible than English, and English counting accuracy declines as words use more tokens.
Reasoning mode is task- and model-dependent; index_to_span achieves only 6.75% best four-shot exact-match accuracy.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces SyntaxBench, a diagnostic framework for character-level reasoning in LLMs, analyzing tokenization effects and reasoning modes to evaluate model capabilities.
papers.title: SyntaxBench: A Statistical Diagnostic Framework for Character-Level Reasoning in Large Language Models
papers.tldr: SyntaxBench shows that character-level reasoning in LLMs depends strongly on tokenization and reasoning mode, while substring extraction remains largely unsolved.

papers.abstract: Mainstream large language models rely on a tokenizer to encode text into a token sequence. Different tokenizers may yield token sequences of substantially different lengths for the same text. With a fixed model architecture, shorter token sequences correspond to lower inference time. We propose a tokenizer training approach named Counting and Filtering (CNF) and a text encoding algorithm called Min-Cost Encoding (MCE). MCE defines a cost function over a text segment, and determines the best segmentation by globally minimizing the overall segmentation cost. CNF builds a raw vocabulary by directly counting valid substrings, and then constructs the final vocabulary through a filtering step based on actual token usage when segmenting the training corpus with MCE. The CNF-MCE conbination offers several advantages over BPE, including higher token efficiency, greater scalability, and lower dependency. Across six text categories and two vocabulary-size groups, CNF-MCE consistently achieves better compression than the evaluated BPE tokenizers. With a 250K vocabulary, CNF-MCE increases compression rate by 26% and 30% on English web text over the o200k_base and qwen250k tokenizers. Experiments scaling the vocabulary to 1M entries on English web text demonstrate sustained improvements over BPE, with a token efficiency improvement of over 60% and vocabulary utilization rising from 52.9% to 96.9%. The MCE algorithm does not depend on a merge list (as in BPE) or token probability (as in UnigramLM), making it applicable to a wide range of vocabularies, including those built from BPE, UnigramLM, CNF, and others. Language models trained from scratch at the 1.8B and 8B scales achieve comparable average performance to models using the BPE tokenizers across 11 benchmarks. These results demonstrate that CNF-MCE can improve token efficiency significantly while maintaining competitive downstream performance.
bullets: Targets inefficient tokenization, where longer sequences increase inference cost.
Uses Min-Cost Encoding (MCE) to find globally optimal text segmentations under a defined cost function.
Trains vocabularies with Counting and Filtering (CNF), combining substring counting with usage-based vocabulary filtering.
Outperforms evaluated BPE tokenizers across six text categories and two vocabulary-size groups; gains persist at 1M vocabulary size.
Models trained with CNF-MCE achieve comparable average performance to BPE-based models across 11 benchmarks.

papers.abstract: Researchers use large language models as agents in social simulations, where agents are prompted with observations and background information intended to shape their actions. Yet LLM agents have been shown to substantially change their behavior under meaning-preserving prompt variations, creating a validation problem for social simulation. One plausible hypothesis is that this brittleness reflects a lack of grounding and can be reduced by enriching the context provided to the agents. Whether richer context improves robustness remains unclear, in part because context richness and robustness are rarely defined in ways that support controlled comparisons. We address the first need with controlled context enrichment, a set of prompt substitution rules that systematically enriches distinct types of context: neutral padding, generic social background, descriptive decision grounding, and normative decision grounding. We address the second by introducing selective robustness as a validation criterion: insensitivity to meaning-preserving prompt variation combined with a directional response to decision-relevant changes in the social world. We demonstrate the framework in a Prisoner's Dilemma-like game, showing how it can be used to identify which forms of context enrichment produce more desirable and robust agent behavior. We find that these forms of enrichment produce distinct behavioral patterns that vary between the two models tested.
authors: Mattia Greiche, Reihaneh Rabbany, Maximilian Puelma Touzel
bullets: Motivated by LLM agents’ behavioral brittleness under meaning-preserving prompt variations, which challenges social-simulation validation.
Defines controlled context enrichment through four prompt types: neutral padding, generic social background, descriptive decision grounding, and normative decision grounding.
Introduces selective robustness: invariance to meaning-preserving prompt changes alongside directional responses to decision-relevant changes in the social environment.
Demonstrates the framework in a Prisoner’s Dilemma-like game, identifying distinct behavioral effects of different enrichment strategies.
Finds that enrichment effects and behavioral patterns vary across the two tested models.

papers.abstract: LLM agents use context compaction to manage growing interaction histories, but summarizing long histories with large models can introduce substantial delays. Compaction therefore requires balancing information retention against latency. We observe that structured summary slots can retain information when generated independently. Based on this observation, we present SpecCompact, a framework that accelerates compaction through slot-parallel semantic speculation. SpecCompact fine-tunes a small drafter and generates slots in parallel. The target model verifies each proposed line and repairs rejected content, while subsequent drafting uses the updated slot prefix. System optimizations further reduce repeated context processing and model calls. Across AppWorld and $\tau^3$ benchmarks with two target models, SpecCompact achieves $2.04$--$5.63\times$ compaction speedups over Hermes-style summarization. Separate downstream evaluations reveal model- and task-dependent performance trade-offs. A user study within Hermes further shows an $8.68\times$ median compaction speedup.
authors: Yulu An, Yifei Feng, Xiangyang Yin
bullets: Addresses the latency of summarizing growing agent histories while preserving important information.
Uses a small fine-tuned drafter to propose structured summary slots in parallel.
A target model verifies each proposed line, repairs rejected content, and guides subsequent drafting.
Reports 2.04–5.63× speedups on AppWorld and τ³ with two target models, plus an 8.68× median speedup in a Hermes user study.
Downstream quality shows model- and task-dependent trade-offs.

papers.selection_reason: Accelerates LLM agent context compaction via speculative verification, directly relevant to long-context and memory efficiency.
papers.title: SpecCompact: Accelerating LLM Agent Context Compaction with Slot-Parallel Semantic Speculative Verification
papers.tldr: SpecCompact speeds up LLM-agent context compaction by speculatively generating summary slots in parallel and having a target model verify and repair them.

papers.abstract: Under stochastic decoding, a single context can elicit many different answers from a language model. Characterizing this variation typically requires many expensive autoregressive rollouts, each revealing only one realization. We ask whether the activations produced while reading the context can directly forecast the model's rollout activations. We train context--answer metamodels that map a context activation sequence to point or distribution forecasts of mean-pooled answer activations. We find that (i) the four metamodel families we study forecast mean-pooled answer activations with high fidelity, and the distribution metamodels also capture rollout variability; (ii) performance improves as the training set grows to 500,000 prompts, and the metamodels generalize zero-shot to out-of-domain datasets; (iii) their forecasts retain behavior-predictive signal; and (iv) context activations from Qwen2.5 predict mean-pooled answer activations from Qwen3.5 and Gemma 4, suggesting that activation forecasts can transfer across models. Together, these results suggest that context activation traces can support scalable forecasts of behaviors in LLM answers before the first answer token is generated.
bullets: The work addresses the cost of characterizing stochastic answer variation, which normally requires many autoregressive rollouts.
Context–answer metamodels map context activation sequences to point or distribution forecasts of mean-pooled answer activations.
Four metamodel families achieve high-fidelity forecasts, with distribution models also capturing rollout variability.
Performance scales with training data, generalizes zero-shot across datasets, and preserves behavior-predictive information.
Forecasts can transfer across models: Qwen2.5 context activations predict answer activations from Qwen3.5 and Gemma 4.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes metamodels to forecast LLM answer activations from context, suggesting a mechanism for predicting future behavior and retaining predictive signal.
papers.title: Context--Answer Metamodels: Forecasting LLM Activations Before the First Answer Token
papers.tldr: Context activations can forecast the content-related activation patterns and variability of an LLM’s future answers before generation begins.

papers.abstract: Looped Transformers increase effective depth by re-executing shared layers, but three limitations hinder their adoption: memory grows with the loop count, compute can only be adjusted in whole-block steps, and the loop count is hard to change after training. We propose LooM (Loop-invariant Memory), which addresses each in turn. In a causal encoder-decoder (CED), LooM loops only the decoder layers after the first, which read a global memory written once per token, and each of them publishes the key-value (KV) entry for a token only on its first visit, so the cache does not grow with the loop count. These layers loop independently, providing every budget from 3 to 21 layer executions per token, and one model trained on randomly sampled budgets covers all of them without a router. With enough loops, LooM outperforms a single-pass baseline trained on the same data on language modeling, zero-shot accuracy and long-context perplexity, while using the same cache size. Our analysis further shows that the training budget distribution decides what extra depth buys. These results suggest that a CED is a natural place to loop: memory is written once, and depth becomes a budget chosen at deployment.
authors: Lele Yang, Muxi Diao, Zhonghao Yan, Jiankang Chen, Bin Wen, Tingting Gao, Wentao Zhang, Kongming Liang, Zhanyu Ma, Weiran Xu
bullets: Targets looped Transformer limitations: loop-dependent memory growth, coarse compute control, and fixed post-training loop counts.
Loops decoder layers after the first, using global memory written once per token and publishing each token’s KV entry only on its first visit.
Independent layer loops provide budgets from 3 to 21 layer executions per token; one model supports all budgets without a router.
With sufficient looping, LooM improves language modeling, zero-shot accuracy, and long-context perplexity over a same-data single-pass baseline while keeping cache size unchanged.
Training-budget distributions determine what additional depth provides; the approach supports deployment-time depth selection.

papers.selection_reason: Novel looped transformer architecture that keeps cache size constant, improving long-context perplexity and efficiency.
papers.title: LooM: Loop-Invariant Memory for Causal Encoder-Decoder Language Models
papers.tldr: LooM enables flexible, memory-efficient looping in causal encoder-decoder language models, allowing deployment-time depth adjustment without increasing cache size.

papers.abstract: Small language models offer a compact basis for shell simulation without executing submitted commands, but full-output decoding requires them to predict recurring utility structure alongside content that varies across executions. We introduce template gap reconstruction (TGR), which supplies reusable output literals interspersed with sentinels to be interleaved with autoregressively generated gaps. A template selector chooses which template to be reconstructed, with the empty template retaining full-output decoding. We construct a template bank from 18.7 million outputs collected across heterogeneous execution environments and train a template selector and five reconstruction models initialized from various small language model checkpoints on a target environment excluded from bank construction. Evaluation demonstrates that TGR improves output edit similarity (O-ES) over full-output decoding (FOD) when the optimal template covers more than 25\% of the template, while performing similarly for lower-coverage outputs. Additionally, TGR outperforms FOD for shorter gap sequences, with O-ES values of 0.964 and 0.812, respectively, while maintaining similar performance for longer sequences. TGR reduces the number of tokens generated by 26.3--38.3\% across used tokenizer families. These results support using a reusable output structure as a practical design choice for small shell simulators, improving response fidelity and shortening generation targets while keeping template selection and residual prediction central to response quality.
bullets: Addresses the difficulty of predicting recurring shell-output structure alongside execution-specific content without running commands.
Provides reusable output templates with sentinels; the model autoregressively generates only the missing gaps.
A template selector chooses a reconstruction template, while an empty template preserves full-output decoding.
Improves output edit similarity when templates cover more than 25% of the output and performs similarly at lower coverage.
Outperforms full-output decoding on shorter gap sequences, with O-ES of 0.964 versus 0.812, while maintaining similar performance on longer sequences.

papers.abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) assumes that language models can reason over relations stated in their context rather than fall back on associations memorized during pretraining. We study this evidence-conditioned relational reasoning in isolation, with the facts supplied directly in the prompt rather than retrieved. \textsc{Rel-Bloom} is a controlled multilingual diagnostic of 450 multiple-choice questions built from 30 Wikidata relations; the same source relations are instantiated at five Bloom-inspired levels (Remember, Understand, Apply, Analyze, Evaluate) and under three veracity conditions (Factual, Counterfactual, Neutralized). Across 43 models, six languages, and two multilingual settings (226,800 predictions), three findings stand out. First, accuracy drops sharply from Apply to Analyze in every evaluated open-weight model series, reaching 47.2 percentage points for the Large Granite bucket, but not for either Gemini model. Second, Evaluate items remain a bottleneck even for models near ceiling on the other task types: Gemini~3.1 Pro averages 99.5\% on the other four levels but 60.7\% on Evaluate. Third, item- and relation-level difficulty rankings are consistently preserved across languages, indicating a difficulty structure partly shared across languages within this benchmark. Across knowledge conditions, Counterfactual contexts are generally harder than Factual ones, while removing entity identities can improve higher-level performance in some model regimes. Greater model capability therefore does not by itself ensure reliable reasoning over supplied relational evidence. Relevant resources are available at: https://huggingface.co/spaces/QCRI/non-parametric-memory-relational-reasoning.
authors: Zohreh Abbasi Liasi, Batoul Hammoud, Anas Madkoor, Ehsaneddin Asgari
bullets: Evaluates 43 models across six languages using 450 controlled multiple-choice questions covering 30 Wikidata relations.
Tests five Bloom-inspired reasoning levels and three knowledge conditions: factual, counterfactual, and neutralized.
Accuracy drops sharply from Apply to Analyze in open-weight models, while Evaluate remains difficult even for highly capable models.
Difficulty rankings are largely consistent across languages, suggesting shared cross-lingual structure in relational reasoning difficulty.
Counterfactual contexts are generally harder; removing entity identities can sometimes improve higher-level reasoning.

Items are then evaluated in six languages under two multilingual settings. The 43 models comprise 41 open-weight models from seven model families, analyzed as eight model series because Qwen2.5 Base and Qwen2.5 Instruct are treated separately, plus two Gemini models.

papers.selection_reason: Studies LLM reasoning over non-parametric (externally supplied) relational evidence, directly relevant to LLM memory and LLM capability research.
papers.title: Reasoning over Non-Parametric Memory in Multilingual LLMs: A Cognitive-Based Analysis of Relational Knowledge

papers.abstract: Public bodies increasingly rely on AI-produced evidence, including classifications, summaries and assessments. These outputs can inform policy decisions and service delivery, making their reliability a matter of public accountability. Establishing whether this evidence can be relied upon requires testing its outputs and examining how organisations decide whether those tests are sufficient. We combine technical evaluation with analysis of AI governance requirements, informed by measurement theory and management-based regulation. We compare eight GPT-4o configurations classifying 1,200 UK Prime Minister's Questions into 21 policy topics, against human-coded labels and across unchanged repeats. Accuracy ranges from 68.2% to 70.3%, yet 24.3% of questions receive different labels, with changes in topic shares and rankings. Configurations agree more with one another than with human coding: agreement does not guarantee correctness. Under the implemented score-extraction procedure, the proportion flagged for human review ranges from 0.9% to 41.0%. We analyse 37 UK and EU policy documents. Both sets expect testing and oversight, but reporting expectations do not consistently cover changing answers, shared errors, selective evaluation, substantive conclusions or review routing. Some UK guidance explicitly addresses stability. The UK sample emphasises public bodies checking their own use; the EU places substantial testing duties on providers while leaving them important choices about measures and acceptance thresholds. Without appropriate checks, evidence could misrepresent policy issues, redirect attention or resources, and leave errors undetected. Public policy should require organisations to justify reliance through checks beyond aggregate accuracy, clear responsibility, access to expertise and scrutiny of results.

Accuracy was similar across configurations (68.2%–70.3%), but 24.3% of questions changed labels across unchanged repeats, altering topic shares and rankings.
Configurations agreed more with one another than with human coding, showing that agreement does not ensure correctness.
The implemented score-extraction procedure flagged between 0.9% and 41.0% of cases for human review.
Analysis of 37 UK and EU policy documents found gaps in requirements for reporting instability, shared errors, selective evaluation, substantive conclusions, and review routing.

papers.abstract: Long-running LLM agents compact their context, replacing most history with a summary. We ask whether handoff summaries state permissions or requirements the record does not support, whether such sentences change what the next instance (the successor) does, and where they come from. Synthetic tool-use tasks carry a ground-truth permission ledger; same-snapshot replay reruns the successor with those whole sentences replaced by neutral filler. Two AI readers, reading only rule-flagged held-out summaries, confirmed unsupported restrictions in 1.2% and 2.4% of all readable summaries from two open-weight models, and unsupported authorizations in 0.1% and 1.3%. For restrictions, a pre-specified replay test was not significant (p = 0.58); a follow-up, planned after it, found a fragile effect (p = 0.027). Neutralizing false approvals cut unauthorized actions from 24 to 7 of 120 held-out runs (post hoc; later set: 17 to 11 of 48). Most development restrictions followed the agent's earlier reasoning that an action needs approval (post hoc). In pre-specified tests, replacing the system prompt's "Some actions need approval." with one saying where requirements come from cut unsupported restrictions from 5.0% to 1.8% of development summaries and, on held-out templates, from 1.8% to 0.3% (both p < 10^-9), while requests for approvals the ledger requires barely changed. Code and data: https://github.com/Chuw1/handoff-audit
bullets: Studies whether self-written summaries make unsupported claims about what successor agents may or must do.
Uses synthetic tool-use tasks with a ground-truth permission ledger and same-snapshot replay with flagged sentences neutralized.
Unsupported restrictions appeared in 1.2% and 2.4% of readable summaries; unsupported authorizations in 0.1% and 1.3% across two models.
Neutralizing false approvals reduced unauthorized actions in held-out runs, though some follow-up findings were post hoc or fragile.
Explicitly stating where requirements come from reduced unsupported restrictions in development and held-out templates, while preserving needed approval requests.
