papers.selection_reason: Studies handoff summaries as compressed agent context and their behavioral effects, relevant to agent memory and context management in LLM agents.
papers.title: When Do Summaries Become Instructions? Unsupported Policy in LLM Agents' Self-Written Handoff Summaries
papers.tldr: LLM handoff summaries sometimes invent action restrictions or permissions, and clarifying the source of requirements sharply reduces unsupported restrictions.

papers.abstract: While multi-turn agentic reinforcement learning (RL) excels on long-horizon tasks, its performance gains remain highly sensitive to interaction constraints. Evaluating across sampling breadth $K$ and interaction depth $T$ via $Pass@(K,T)$, we show that trajectory-level RL advantages depend on sufficient turn budgets, diminishing significantly when budgets tighten. Besides, agentic RL does not uniformly elevate single-step decision quality; rather, its strength concentrates in error recovery and long-horizon resilience. To mitigate the deployment risks caused by this budget dependence, we provide a preliminary discussion on the benefits and limitations of process supervision signals and introduce BudgetMix RL as an alternative that varies interaction budgets during training. Experiments demonstrate that BudgetMix RL achieves robust performance across diverse execution settings. Project Page: https://rethinking-agentic-rl.github.io/
authors: Kejian Zhu, Zhuoran Jin, Shangqing Tu, Tianyi Men, Yupu Hao, Jiachun Li, Kang Liu, Jun Zhao
bullets: Performance is evaluated across sampling breadth and interaction depth using Pass@(K,T).
Trajectory-level RL benefits diminish substantially when turn or interaction budgets are tight.
Agentic RL does not consistently improve single-step decision quality.
The study discusses process supervision and proposes BudgetMix RL, which varies training budgets to improve robustness across execution settings.

papers.abstract: Long-horizon language-model agents accumulate increasingly large interaction histories, making context compaction essential for efficient execution. Existing learned compaction methods often rely on downstream task outcomes or solver behavior, coupling training to specific tasks or agents. We introduce SumOne, a standalone summarizer trained to preserve information in agent histories through masked reconstruction. Given a summary of the expired history, a frozen reconstructor recovers randomly masked portions of the original trajectory; reconstruction quality, combined with a length penalty, provides a task-agnostic reward for optimizing the summarizer with GRPO. This yields self-supervision directly from raw trajectories, without reference summaries or downstream task execution. At inference time, only the lightweight summarizer is retained, enabling plug-and-play context compression for otherwise unchanged agents. We conduct a systematic evaluation of SumOne in long-horizon search and software-engineering tasks. SumOne reduces estimated inference cost by approximately 78\% on DeepSearchQA and 75\% on SWE-bench Verified relative to operating with full context, with absolute decreases of 0.04. The same checkpoint also transfers across downstream models and agent harnesses without additional fine-tuning.
authors: Jizhe Zhang, Ang Li, Chenheng Zhang, Yisen Wang

Reduces estimated inference cost by about 78% on DeepSearchQA and 75% on SWE-bench Verified, with reported absolute decreases of 0.04.
A single checkpoint transfers across downstream models and agent harnesses without additional fine-tuning.

papers.abstract: Long-term problem-solving processes, such as scientific research and software development, proceed along an evolving trial-and-error trajectory toward a central goal. We term these \textit{exploration tasks}, which require models to remember not only facts but also how solutions are tested against intermediate outcomes and early attempts are continually revised or revived. However, existing long-term memory research focuses on factual recall and updates, overlooking the interconnected nature of exploration. We observe that exploration processes naturally form graphs, with branching approaches linked by revisions and reconsiderations. Motivated by this, we propose \textsc{LExMem}, a graph-guided benchmark designed to evaluate \underline{\textsc{Mem}}ory in \underline{\textsc{L}}ong-term \underline{\textsc{Ex}}ploration tasks. We model exploration processes as graphs and introduce an evolutionary mechanism to increase their structural complexity, yielding 224 dialogues and 2,018 question-answer instances derived from graph structures. Building on the same insight, we propose \textsc{LExGraph}, a graph-based memory framework that incrementally organizes dialogues into interconnected memory nodes and retrieves evidence through hybrid retrieval and neighbor expansion. Extensive experiments demonstrate that \textsc{LExMem} poses a significant challenge to existing retrieval- and memory-based systems, whereas \textsc{LExGraph} achieves superior performance and generalizes effectively to external benchmarks. Codes and datasets are available at https://github.com/mbzuai-nlp/LExMem.
authors: Chongyuan Dai, Yaling Shen, Zirui Song, Junfeng Liao, Jinpeng Hu, Xiuying Chen
bullets: Targets exploration processes where solutions branch, are tested, revised, and revisited—not just factual recall.
Introduces LExMem, a graph-structured benchmark with 224 dialogues and 2,018 question-answer instances.

Experiments show LExMem challenges existing memory and retrieval systems, while LExGraph performs strongly and generalizes to external benchmarks.

papers.abstract: The performance of large language model (LLM) agents depends on both the underlying model and the harness that governs interaction with tools and the environment. Yet harness design remains largely manual, and automating it requires navigating an open-ended search space through costly end-to-end evaluations. We introduce HarnessFlow, a framework for optimizing complete executable harnesses under a limited candidate-evaluation budget, with the model and task environment held fixed. HarnessFlow organizes candidates and their evaluation histories in a refinement tree, using a Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS)-based policy to balance exploitation and exploration. A coding agent refines selected harnesses using archived code, execution feedback, and a library of reusable harness mechanisms. With 15 refinement attempts per benchmark, HarnessFlow achieves the highest mean test scores among the compared methods on six benchmarks spanning agentic tasks, coding, and web interaction. The optimized harnesses achieve an average score of 69.48%, outperforming the initial harnesses and Meta-Harness by 10.89 and 3.95 percentage points, respectively, while incurring lower average per-task execution costs than hand-engineered baselines. These results suggest that structured harness search offers a promising route toward automating the design of capable and efficient LLM agents.
authors: Zhi Hong, Qianlong Wang, Hongchen Wei, Aidan Wu, Daohong Ying, Mingze Kong, Bei Liu, Chong Luo

papers.abstract: Decision models read a document and return a probability for each of a fixed set of options instead of generating text. Several appeared in 2026, but none has published results outside English. We describe Zuse, three decision models (4B, 9B and 27B) that train a low-rank adapter and a pointer head on frozen open-weight bases, targeting 27 European languages, and use them to study how this design behaves across languages and tasks. On a broad European suite of 11 sources excluded from training, covering 9 task groups and 27 languages, a development set that also guided model selection, the 27B model reaches 87.5% accuracy with a pooled expected calibration error of 0.016, and 0.035 when weighted per source. Post-hoc analyses of these single-seed results give three findings. First, miscalibration is structured by task rather than language: on parallel reading and topic items in 26 languages the confidence gap varies about as much as sampling noise, while across sources it spans -0.07 to +0.09, with knowledge tasks overconfident and acceptability judgements underconfident at all three sizes, so one fitted temperature cannot correct both. Second, the share of decisions that can be automated at a 5% error budget follows chance-corrected skill (Spearman 0.97 over 33 source and model pairs) more closely than raw accuracy (0.91). Third, reach beyond the training languages is set by the base model: across 210 languages, changing the training run moved scores by at most about 2 points within a size, while languages outside the base's documented list trail by 23 to 28 points at every size. On English public suites Zuse is behind Jev and Kev, including Kev models on the same bases. We also report two pitfalls in building multi-source training data: label-word collision between topic schemes, and an injection augmentation that taught a shortcut. Zuse can be tried at https://bineric.com/zuse.

Cross-language reach largely follows the base model: languages outside its documented coverage score substantially lower, and Zuse trails Jev and Kev on English public suites.

papers.abstract: Multimodal models have often scored below text-only baselines in the BabyLM Challenge (Klerings et al., 2024; Takmaz et al., 2025). We test whether additional recurrent computation helps close this gap. Recurrence increases computation by reusing layers without adding parameters or training data. Using a single implementation, we compare standard and looped Transformers under a 100M-word budget, with three seeds per main condition. Each image is represented by one feature vector from a frozen DINOv2 encoder, used as a prefix token. Caption words count toward the budget, so multimodal training also changes the language data. In a pre-registered text-only comparison, a 12-layer stack repeated four times exceeds a standard 48-layer Transformer by 5.4 BLiMP percentage points at matched inference compute. However, multimodal training lowers BLiMP accuracy by about 3.8 points in both architectures, with no clear mitigation from recurrence. An exploratory loop-side no-image control, trained with the multimodal language data and batching schedule, scores 5.7 points below the text-only baseline. Adding the visual prefix raises accuracy by 1.85 points on average, but this contrast is uncertain with three seeds. These results suggest that changes in language data and its presentation are a major source of the drop. Diagnostic tests show that the models use visual information; its contribution to grammatical generalization remains uncertain under this single-vector interface.

A matched no-image control suggests that altered language data and batching, rather than visual input alone, drive much of the multimodal drop.
Visual prefixes improve accuracy by 1.85 points on average in the exploratory comparison, but this result is uncertain with three seeds.
Diagnostic tests confirm visual information is used, while its role in grammatical generalization remains unclear with the single-vector interface.

papers.abstract: Knowledge editing has become a key technique for updating knowledge in large language models. However, existing methods neglect the geometric structure of the knowledge representation space, leading to two key limitations: they cannot distinguish which pre-trained knowledge should be preferentially preserved (core vs. non-core) nor which new edits are inherently difficult (hard vs. easy). To address this, we propose GEdit, a geometry-aware framework built on a Low-Rank Plus Diagonal (LR+D) factor model that captures the intrinsic low-rank structure of Transformer FFN hidden representations. GEdit features two complementary mechanisms. First, the low-rank regularization applies targeted protection on a low-rank core knowledge subspace. Second, the adaptive regularization dynamically adjusts the regularization strength based on each edit request's editability: relaxing constraints for hard edits to ensure success, and tightening them for easy edits to better preserve pretrained knowledge. Extensive experiments on GPT2-XL, GPT-J, and LLaMA-3-8B under large-scale editing scenarios, including both mini-batch and fully sequential editing settings with up to 10,000 continuous updates, show that GEdit consistently and significantly outperforms state-of-the-art baselines in both editing success and knowledge preservation.
authors: Bingqing Liu, Wei Liu, Jun Wang, Xiaobo Sun, Yuhua Li, Ruixuan Li

papers.abstract: While Large Language Models (LLMs) excel in high-resource languages, their performance often degrades in low-resource languages due to tokenization inefficiencies, generative instability, and linguistic interference. This paper presents AssameseLM-E2B and its instruction-tuned variant, AssameseLM-E2B-it, a 2-billion-parameter model adapted specifically for low resource Assamese language. Built upon the Gemma-4 architecture, the model incorporates an expanded byte-level BPE vocabulary to reduce tokenization overhead by nearly 500% compared with multilingual 2B--3B baselines. We employ a parameter-efficient Continual Pre-Training (CPT) pipeline with Hybrid LoRA, followed by Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) on a balanced, multi-domain dataset to enhance instruction-following and Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) capabilities. Evaluation demonstrates a Bits-per-Byte (BPB) score of 0.7488 on FLORES-200, alongside an overall RAG score of 96.7% and 100% refusal accuracy on adversarial unanswerable prompts. Comparative analysis reveals significant limitations in general-purpose baselines, including receptive-productive decoupling, generative degradation on Romanized Assamese, and unintended Bengali script assimilation. These results demonstrate the potential of parameter-efficient adaptation for developing capable, locally deployable language models for low-resource languages under constrained computational resources.
bullets: Targets low-resource Assamese challenges including tokenization inefficiency, unstable generation, and interference from related languages.

Reports a 0.7488 BPB score on FLORES-200, a 96.7% overall RAG score, and 100% refusal accuracy on adversarial unanswerable prompts.
Scope is Assamese-focused and emphasizes deployment under constrained computational resources.

papers.abstract: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) language models send each token through a few of many expert subnetworks. Serving methods make these models faster by running even fewer experts per token, and they are validated on accuracy benchmarks. We show that these methods can weaken the model's refusal of harmful requests, and we introduce SafeStart, which largely restores refusal while keeping most of the speedup. In vLLM on one RTX A6000, keeping about two thirds of the selected experts speeds up offline decoding by 15 to 28% at batch size 8. We find that, at this setting, under a jailbreak that tells the model not to refuse, the share of harmful requests that the model answers rises by 18.4 percentage points on Qwen1.5-MoE, 9.5 on OLMoE, and 6.6 on DeepSeek-V2-Lite, the three of nine models where it rises significantly, while MMLU accuracy drops by less than two points. We discover that most of this increase arises while the model processes the prompt and generates its first few tokens. SafeStart therefore runs all experts for the prompt and the first eight generated tokens, and the reduced set of experts afterwards, through a fused kernel in vLLM. With experts removed, SafeStart keeps at least 85% of the offline decode speedup at batch sizes 8 and 32 and brings the change under this jailbreak to between -2.1 and +1.3 points for three expert-reduction methods on these three models. On 889 held-out requests, in an analysis fixed before generation, truncation raises harmful compliance by 5.8 to 21.4 points, and SafeStart leaves a rise of 0.6 to 2.6 points, non-inferior to the original model on two of the three models. Our results show that faster MoE serving need not cost safety: a serving system can keep most of the gain from running fewer experts by running all of them at the start of each response, and it should test refusal, not only accuracy, before it enables such a method.
authors: Erfan Baghaei Potraghloo, Saeid Shokoufa, Seyedarmin Azizi, Arya Fayyazi, Souvik Kundu, Mehdi Kamal, Massoud Pedram

papers.abstract: The full-attention layers of large language models (LLMs) make every generated token more expensive than the previous one, slowing models down on long-context tasks. Hybrid models reduce this cost by replacing most full-attention layers with linear-attention layers, but the first still dominate decoding at long contexts. We accelerate these remaining layers without any training or weight changes using combined sparse attention: each layer attends to a sliding window of recent tokens, a pinned prefix, and a fixed budget of most relevant tokens in the context. The window size and budget are found on a per-layer basis using a multi-objective search algorithm. Across six hybrid models from three families, from 4B to 397B parameters, the selected configurations preserve their baseline model's accuracy on 21 long-context datasets. Decoding 64k/256k tokens becomes up to 1.26x/2.22x faster on Qwen3.5-4B, 1.20x/2.23x on Qwen3.5-122B-A10B, and 1.16x/2.06x on Ornith-1.0-397B.

papers.abstract: Explicit reasoning can help language models generate code, but it also introduces a practical risk: the model may spend so much of its output budget reasoning that it never produces usable code. We study this behaviour in relatively small open-weight reasoning models, framing it as reasoning-trace overflow. Across seven models and six code benchmark settings, we measure how much of a fixed 32k-token output budget is spent on reasoning, whether that reasoning improves pass@1, and whether lightweight inference-time controls can mitigate overflow. Our results show that the value of reasoning is highly conditional. Overflow is rare on simpler function-level tasks, but becomes common on harder code-generation benchmarks and for particular model families: on several model--benchmark pairs, more than half of generations exhaust the full 32k-token budget while still reasoning. Most complete overflow is associated with repetitive reasoning loops, although substantial long reasoning also occurs without looping. Disabling reasoning can therefore be competitive for overflow-prone models, simply because it ensures that an answer is produced. At the same time, reasoning remains valuable for stronger models on harder algorithmic and code-understanding tasks. Finally, prompt steering can substantially reduce overflow for some models but is inconsistent, while budgeted transitions provide more direct control and can improve both performance and token efficiency for overflow-prone models. These findings suggest that explicit reasoning should be treated as a controllable resource for code generation, rather than an always-on capability.
authors: Lukas Twist, Helen Yannakoudakis, Jie M. Zhang
bullets: The study evaluates seven small open-weight reasoning models across six code-generation benchmark settings using a fixed 32k-token output budget.
Reasoning-trace overflow is uncommon on simpler function-level tasks but frequent for some models on harder benchmarks, often involving repetitive loops.
Reasoning provides conditional benefits: disabling it can be competitive for overflow-prone models, while stronger models still benefit on difficult algorithmic and code-understanding tasks.
Prompt steering sometimes reduces overflow, whereas budgeted transitions offer more direct control and can improve performance and token efficiency.
The findings support treating explicit reasoning as a controllable resource rather than an always-on capability.

The dashed red line marks the full output budget, and the percentage above each violin reports the reasoning-trace overflow rate.

papers.abstract: Small LoRA adapters trained on Tajik news and books lowered Qwen3's Tajik text loss at every size we tried, from 0.6B to 8B, by 0.60 to 1.45 nats per token, but none of them improved Tajik reading comprehension where it can be measured. On Belebele the 1.7B and 8B adapters left accuracy unchanged and the 4B adapter lowered it by 3.7 points; at 0.6B the score rose by 4.2 points but sits near chance and coincides with a change in which answer letter the model prefers, so we do not read it as understanding. At 8B, continued pretraining on about 375 million tokens of raw Tajik text was followed by a Belebele gain of 9.9 points. After a further supervised fine-tuning stage, our main model, e3, is 11.4 points above Qwen3-8B on Belebele; its English MMLU changed by -1.2 points, and a loss larger than 3.3 points is excluded. The same heavy recipe applied to Qwen3-0.6B-Base brought its text loss close to that of the 8B model after books-only pretraining, while its multiple-choice answers stayed near chance and its English MMLU fell by 7.6 points. We report 15 trained models and their 5 starting models from June to October 2025, scored in 2026 on one harness with paired intervals, and we report what went wrong: lost training records, a thinking-mode dataset with almost no reasoning in it, later branches whose training data was never documented, and a 4-bit release that contains no transformer layers.
authors: Tohir Saidzoda, Madina Abdusalomzoda, Nasimjon Rajabov, Akhrorkhon Ikromov, Komron Giyosiev, Abubakr Abdullozoda, Amin Jalilov, Jonibek Kishvarov, Rahmonali Sharipov, Mariyamkhon Shodyeva
bullets: LoRA adaptation reduced Tajik text loss across 0.6B–8B models, but comprehension gains were absent or unreliable.
On Belebele, 1.7B and 8B adapters were unchanged, the 4B model fell 3.7 points, and the 0.6B increase likely reflected answer-letter bias.
At 8B, continued pretraining on roughly 375M raw Tajik tokens improved Belebele by 9.9 points.
The final e3 model improved Tajik Belebele by 11.4 points over Qwen3-8B, while English MMLU declined by 1.2 points.
The study documents scope and reproducibility issues, including undocumented data branches and an invalid 4-bit release.

papers.abstract: Personal agents draw on past conversations to tailor their responses to each user. Their memory systems store and update what each user says, and coding agents now also rewrite the harness that turns this memory into the model's context. Such patches risk overfitting, because one tested only on the failures it targets can fix those cases and help nowhere else. We present Reglos, a training-free personal memory agent that tests whether harness changes help beyond the failures they were written to fix. Its self-evolving memory adds to each user's append-only record with every conversation, as new preferences supersede old ones and facts can be forgotten. Its harness improves through recursive self-improvement, in which a coding agent proposes patches from failure traces and a critic from a second model family screens each one for benchmark gaming. After the harness is frozen, a fixed evaluator decides which further patches to accept. With the same backbone behind every system, Reglos outperforms state-of-the-art memory systems such as Mem0, MemOS and EverOS, reaching 61.3% and 84.0% on PersonaMem-v2 and LongMemEval-S with Qwen3.8-27B, and 57.5% and 87.2% with GPT-5.6 Luna.
authors: Sen Yang, Jiaduo Lin, Zehong Huang, Wen Liu
bullets: Maintains an append-only per-user memory that updates preferences and forgets outdated facts.
Uses a coding agent to propose harness patches from failure traces and a second-model critic to screen them for gaming.
Freezes the harness before a fixed evaluator determines which additional patches to accept.
Outperforms reported memory systems on PersonaMem-v2 and LongMemEval-S across two backbones, according to the abstract.

papers.abstract: When a language model chooses a number between 1 and 30, every integer in the range is valid, yet the model can favor particular answers. We use numerical choice to study how preference is processed across layers and tokens. Perturbation probing and gradient attribution nominate neurons for activation interventions. In a selected Qwen3-4B case, a pre-answer edit changes 17 to 15 while both runs first emit 1. After the edit ends, selective cache and attention-output replacements trace part of its continuing influence on the second digit. Replacing one attention head's output or the other heads' outputs jointly produces similar immediate readout contributions; both interventions restore 17 but have different final log-odds effects on 7 versus 5. Holding later multilayer perceptron (MLP) outputs at their values from the edited run without either replacement reduces this effect gap from 0.119 to 0.0025 nat. Later computation therefore changes how similar local contributions affect the continuation. Retrospective estimates across eighteen contexts capture much of the probability movement but miss the selected answer switch. Prompt tests also separate influence from answer changes: one held-out prompt retains influence without switching, and only one of twelve fresh wordings qualifies for the reader/MLP test; there, joint MLP clamping again reduces the gap between the two reader effects while the answer remains 17. These results use numerical choice as a controlled case for studying persistent state and conditional downstream processing; they do not establish the origin or a complete circuit of natural numerical preference.
bullets: Uses choices between 1 and 30 as a controlled setting where every answer is valid.
Combines perturbation probing, gradient attribution, activation edits, and selective cache/attention-output replacements.
In a Qwen3-4B case, an intervention changes the final answer from 17 to 15 even though both runs initially emit 1.
Similar local attention contributions can lead to different final effects because later MLP computation alters their influence.
Results across additional contexts show persistent influence does not always cause an answer switch; the study does not establish the origin or full circuit of numerical preference.

papers.title: When Every Choice Is Correct: A Causal Study of Numerical Preference in Language Models
papers.tldr: A causal study of numerical choices shows that answer preferences can persist across tokens and be reshaped by later computation, without identifying a complete underlying circuit.

papers.abstract: Generative models trained on the output of earlier models lose knowledge across generations, rare knowledge first. The remedies that work all bring in information from outside the loop, and the theory of model collapse treats that supply as given: a fixed archive, drawn from a fixed distribution. We argue that the supply is the problem, and that cultural evolution has the theory of it. We read model collapse as Rogers' paradox: a population that comes to rely on copying ends up no better off than one that never copied, because copies go stale unless someone keeps learning for themselves. We test the identification in three steps. First, Rogers' model, fitted only to fully synthetic training, predicts to within a few percentage points how much rare knowledge language models, from word trigrams to a pretrained transformer, retain under other mixtures of fresh data. Second, when the world itself changes, a lineage that copies its own past needs more fresh data to keep up the faster the world changes, as Rogers' model says it must and as analyses that assume a fixed target cannot; a lineage that restarts every generation from fixed pretrained weights is largely insulated, because those weights are knowledge that is never copied. Third, we close the loop: when the people who write a model's training data can ask the model instead of finding things out, the supply of fresh data becomes endogenous. At equilibrium, the model is exactly as reliable as it is costly for people to find out for themselves, the population is no better off than without the model, and every increase in the share of model-written text must be paid for by more people learning for themselves. Users who check what they are told and relearn when it is wrong break the paradox. Filters that select plausible text are conformist and accelerate collapse; only checks that carry new information act as critical learning.
bullets: Synthetic training causes knowledge loss across generations, with rare knowledge disappearing first.
A cultural-evolution model predicts retention under mixtures of synthetic and fresh data, from simple language models to pretrained transformers.
As the world changes faster, self-copying lineages require more fresh data; fixed pretrained knowledge is comparatively insulated.
When models influence what people write, fresh-data supply becomes endogenous: greater reliance on model text requires more independent learning.
Plausibility filters worsen collapse, whereas fact-checking and relearning can preserve new information.

papers.selection_reason: Applies cultural evolution theory (Rogers' paradox) to explain and predict model collapse in LLMs, analyzing the endogeneity of training data supply.
papers.title: Who Pays for the Knowledge Models Copy? Model Collapse as Rogers' Paradox
papers.tldr: Model collapse is a version of Rogers’ paradox: copying model outputs saves effort but erodes rare and current knowledge unless people keep generating and checking fresh information.

papers.abstract: Hyper-Connections (HC) architectures are increasingly adopted in frontier language models, yet their components remain insufficiently understood and introduce non-negligible training overhead. In this work, we systematically study the HC architecture to understand its components and identify simpler, more efficient designs. We find that learned read/write gating without mixing and unconstrained mixing with fixed gates form two effective interaction groups: either alone achieves performance comparable to mHC. We also identify repeated access to the expanded residual state as a major source of training overhead, even without mixing. These findings lead to SimpleHC, which simplifies the architecture by removing residual mixing and simplifies execution through shared memory access, using the resulting additive structure and shared gate inputs. Layer-specific gates share a group-entry state, enabling batched reads and deferred writes; scalar corrections exactly preserve preceding sublayer output contributions. Our analyses support both the retained residual structure and the design of shared memory access. SimpleHC incurs only 2.4% extra end-to-end training time over a vanilla residual baseline at the largest tested scale. It maintains performance comparable to mHC when scaling from 15B to 30B MoE models, exhibits smoother gradient dynamics during standard training, and remains stable under stress. We hope SimpleHC will encourage a broader pursuit of simplicity in foundation model design, making performance gains more accessible and practical at scale.
authors: Xiangdong Zhang, Xiaohan Qin, Sunan Zou, Tuo Dai, Bizhao Shi, Zhuo Xia, Yebin Yang, Yizhou Chen, Yuliang Liu, Yu Cheng, Junchi Yan
bullets: Hyper-Connections improve language-model architectures but contain poorly understood components and costly repeated access to expanded residual states.
Learned read/write gating without mixing and unconstrained mixing with fixed gates are separately effective interaction designs.
SimpleHC removes residual mixing and uses shared memory access, shared gate inputs, and deferred writes for more efficient execution.
It adds only 2.4% end-to-end training time over a vanilla residual baseline at the largest tested scale.
SimpleHC matches mHC performance from 15B to 30B MoE models, with smoother gradients and stability under stress.

papers.selection_reason: Architectural simplification and scaling of Hyper-Connections for large language models.
papers.title: On the Design of Hyper-Connections: Simplification, Stability, and Scalability

papers.abstract: Graphs play an increasingly important role in large language model (LLM) systems, supporting structural reasoning, knowledge grounding, retrieval, and memory. As these systems evolve toward the agentic era, graphs also organize execution dependencies and multi-agent communication, linking intermediate observations and retained information to subsequent decisions. However, understanding their contribution requires distinguishing the function of each graph operation, the component responsible for its computation, and the subsequent use of its output. This survey introduces an operation-level role--locus taxonomy for reasoning, knowledge and evidence, retrieval and memory, execution, and coordination. We compare how graph observations and external computations guide decisions, how memory representations and updates support later tasks, and how dependencies constrain execution and information delivery. These comparisons distinguish improvements in local metrics from downstream task performance while retaining the conditions under which results were reported. We then organize benchmarks, comparison designs, process diagnostics, and system costs into an evaluation framework. Finally, we identify open challenges in adaptive computation and stopping, memory maintenance, and dependency-aware recovery. The survey provides a basis for assessing when graph mechanisms are useful and for evaluating their effects across components and stages.
authors: Haihui Liu, Yang Chen, Zice Qiu, Yun Zhang, Jialun Zhong, Wenhua Wang, Yanzeng Li, Tian Wang
bullets: Graphs increasingly connect observations, retained information, execution dependencies, and agent communications in LLM systems.
The operation-level role–locus taxonomy distinguishes what each graph operation does, which component computes it, and how its output is used.
The survey compares graph observations and external computations, memory updates, and dependency-based execution and information delivery.
Its evaluation framework covers benchmarks, comparison designs, process diagnostics, and system costs while separating local metric gains from downstream task performance.
Open challenges include adaptive computation and stopping, memory maintenance, and dependency-aware recovery.

papers.selection_reason: A survey on graph-mediated LLM systems, providing a taxonomy for reasoning, memory, and execution, which is relevant to understanding memory and retrieval mechanisms in LLM agents.
papers.title: Graph-Mediated Large Language Model Systems in the Agentic Era: Reasoning, Knowledge, Retrieval, Execution, and Coordination
papers.tldr: This survey presents a taxonomy and evaluation framework for understanding how graph operations support LLM reasoning, knowledge, retrieval, memory, execution, and multi-agent coordination.

papers.abstract: Reasoning models allocate test-time compute across distinct behaviors such as planning, deriving, and verifying. However, models frequently "overthink," continuing to verify and re-derive long after finding a correct answer. This wastes expensive compute and can even degrade performance. Existing interventions, such as token budgets or steering, primarily regulate reasoning duration rather than targeting specific behaviors. In this work, we demonstrate that Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) routers provide a natural, training-free interface for behavioral control. We first split reasoning traces into sentence-level segments and label each with one of six reasoning behaviors (planning, execution, restatement, fact, reflection, and conclusion), so that every token carries the behavior of its segment. Linear probes on router logits predict this label nearly as well as probes on the residual stream, the model's full hidden state and the standard target for probing, while using about half as many features. These signals generalize: experts associated with a reasoning behavior on one dataset predict the same behavior on the others, across six datasets spanning five domains (math, code, science, knowledge, and commonsense). Building on this, we selectively edit expert router scores during inference to curb overthinking. Across four models and four benchmarks, this intervention reduces the number of generated tokens by a median of 30.4% (and up to 63.3%). Crucially, it encourages the model to stop once the problem is solved, rather than skipping essential reasoning steps. Accuracy never drops by more than 0.5 percentage points, and frequently improves. Ultimately, MoE routing offers both an interpretable lens into reasoning states and a lightweight mechanism for optimizing test-time compute.
authors: Shengjie Wang, Mohsen Fayyaz, Nanyun Peng
bullets: Problem: Reasoning models may continue planning, deriving, or verifying after reaching a correct answer, wasting compute and sometimes degrading performance.
Method: Label sentence-level reasoning segments with six behaviors, probe MoE router logits for these behaviors, and selectively edit expert scores during inference.
Routers predict reasoning behavior nearly as well as full residual representations while using about half as many features.
Behavior-associated experts generalize across six datasets and five domains, suggesting routing captures reusable reasoning states.
Across four models and four benchmarks, router editing cuts generated tokens by a median of 30.4%—up to 63.3%—with accuracy decreases no larger than 0.5 percentage points and occasional improvements.

papers.selection_reason: Demonstrates a novel, training-free interface using MoE routers to control reasoning behaviors and optimize test-time compute, effectively curbing overthinking in reasoning models.

papers.abstract: Expert deactivation at inference time changes both token routing and expert weights, and its effect on performance depends on how these changes are implemented. We compare removal, freezing, remaining-expert renormalization, and unnormalized re-routing on identical disabled sets across five instruction-tuned checkpoints from four model families, with a base OLMoE checkpoint as an additional comparison. We develop a weight-sum model that relates the loss of expert contributions and changes in branch scale to the weight rule used during training. With half of the experts deactivated according to activation-based rankings, remaining-expert renormalization yields the highest perplexity in models trained with raw router probabilities, whereas unnormalized re-routing yields the highest perplexity in models trained with normalized weights. Perplexity ranges from 1.4 to 73 times the intact baseline when the training rule is retained, and from 14 to 28,740 times the baseline under a rule mismatch. Task outcomes vary across evaluation types: on OLMoE, GSM8K strict-match accuracy falls to zero under all four implementations. Extending the model to changes in the number of active experts yields a further prediction, supported by the OLMoE experiments: the perplexity penalty from additional renormalization increases as fewer experts are activated.
authors: Hao Cheng (Zhejiang Gongshang University), Zhiyu Yang (Chang'an University), Bo Ma (Zhejiang Gongshang University), Hanzhang Jia (University of Sussex)
bullets: The study compares removal, freezing, renormalized re-routing, and unnormalized re-routing on identical disabled experts across multiple checkpoints.

With half the experts disabled, renormalization performs worst for models trained with raw router probabilities, while unnormalized re-routing performs worst for models trained with normalized weights.
Perplexity penalties are much larger under rule mismatch, ranging from 14–28,740× the intact baseline versus 1.4–73× when the rule is retained.
On OLMoE, GSM8K strict-match accuracy drops to zero for all tested implementations; additional renormalization is increasingly harmful with fewer active experts.

papers.selection_reason: Analysis of inference-time expert deactivation and weight rules in mixture-of-experts LLMs.
papers.title: Matching the Training-Time Weight Rule in Inference-Time Expert Deactivation
papers.tldr: Inference-time expert deactivation is most reliable when its routing-weight rule matches the rule used during training.

papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents increasingly rely on external memory stores to retain information across conversations, typically via dense vector embeddings searched with approximate nearest-neighbor methods. The fruit fly's olfactory circuit computes a locality-sensitive hash of sensory input using a strikingly different mechanism - sparse random projection followed by winner-take-all competition - and prior work (Dasgupta et al., 2017) showed this scheme, dubbed FlyHash, preserves neighbor structure better per bit than conventional random-hyperplane hashing (SimHash) on several benchmarks. We apply FlyHash, to our knowledge for the first time, to LLM agent memory retrieval, and ask three questions a practitioner actually needs answered: does the quality advantage hold under a correctly matched-bit protocol (it does, robustly, across 10 seeds and four datasets spanning two modalities, with one specific, previously undocumented comparison pitfall identified and corrected along the way); does that advantage translate into real memory and latency savings, including against the dense-vector indexing (HNSW) practitioners default to today (no: at equal bits FlyHash's codes are larger and slower to compare than SimHash's, and HNSW dominates both hash methods at ordinary scale; a sparse-set comparison we introduce recovers most but not all of a naive latency gap, leaving hashing's practical case narrower and more specific than the quality result alone implies); and does the advantage survive genuine, non-circular agent-memory relevance labels rather than the nearest-neighbor-by-embedding proxy this literature otherwise relies on (it does). We report all three answers precisely, including the two that narrow rather than flatter the headline result, and release our implementation, a working agent-memory demo, and a full account of the methodological pitfalls we found and corrected.
bullets: Applies FlyHash—sparse random projection with winner-take-all hashing—to LLM agent memory retrieval.
Confirms a robust quality advantage over SimHash across 10 seeds and four datasets spanning two modalities, using matched-bit comparisons.
Identifies and corrects a previously undocumented comparison pitfall in evaluating FlyHash against SimHash.
Finds no general memory or latency advantage: FlyHash codes are larger and slower to compare at equal bits, while HNSW dominates at ordinary scale.
Introduces a sparse-set comparison that narrows, but does not eliminate, the latency gap; the quality benefit also holds with non-circular relevance labels.

papers.selection_reason: Applies FlyHash to LLM agent memory retrieval with careful evaluation and a new application; directly relevant to LLM memory.
papers.title: FlyHash for LLM Agent Memory: An Empirical Validation and a New Application
papers.tldr: FlyHash improves hash-based retrieval quality for LLM agent memory, including with genuine relevance labels, but its practical speed and memory advantages are limited compared with SimHash and HNSW.

papers.abstract: Most memory systems for LLM agents are retrospective, preserving and retrieving past information to inform current decisions. Proactive agents, however, also require prospective memory: retaining future-directed intentions and realizing them when appropriate opportunities arise, even without explicit requests. Crucially, remembering the right intention does not guarantee acting at the right time: a related observation may call for waiting, while a later cue may make the same intention actionable. Inspired by cognitive theories of human prospective memory, we introduce Pro-Memory, a memory framework that separates maintaining future intentions from deciding when and how to realize them. Pro-Memory preserves pending objectives linked to their supporting evidence, assesses new observations against their original goals and activation conditions, and coordinates appropriate contributions with the agent's ongoing actions. It further updates intention states based on actions actually issued or evidence of resolution, while an experience memory distills feedback from completed episodes into guidance for future decisions. Experiments on two benchmarks spanning delayed-intention tasks and open-ended proactive assistance demonstrate consistent improvements in proactive task performance over representative memory approaches across multiple LLM backbones, while limiting unnecessary interventions.
authors: Yuanchen Bei, Zhining Liu, Tianxin Wei, Weizhi Zhang, Zhichen Zeng, Philip S. Yu, Hendrik Hamann, Jingrui He, Hanghang Tong
bullets: Addresses the gap between remembering future goals and deciding when they should become actionable.
Separates intention maintenance from realization, linking pending objectives to supporting evidence and activation conditions.
Updates intention states based on issued actions or resolution evidence, while learning from completed episodes.
Improves proactive performance across delayed-intention and open-ended assistance benchmarks with multiple LLM backbones.
Limits unnecessary interventions by distinguishing cues that require waiting from those that warrant action.

papers.selection_reason: Presents a prospective memory framework for LLM agents to retain and realize future intentions, directly matching agent memory and persistent memory mechanisms.
papers.title: Prospective Memory for Proactive LLM Agents
papers.tldr: Pro-Memory equips LLM agents with prospective memory to retain future intentions and act on them only when the right cues and timing arise.

papers.abstract: The memory of production agents is increasingly becoming a bottleneck and is built almost exclusively from text: key points are extracted from out-of-limit context and retrieved into context at query time. Therefore, every new query incurs an additional cost that grows with the accumulated history. Weight memory is a complementary alternative that internalizes knowledge into model parameters and answers with no context at all, and has recently proven effective in self-evolving agents for internalizing skills and behaviors. However, its application in episodic and semantic memory, such as user-specific facts, remains comparatively unexplored, and a gap remains between earlier attempts at weight memory and text-based systems regarding recall performance. We study how to make weight memory competitive as a long-term factual store by applying on-policy self-distillation (OPSD). It trains a context-free student from a teacher, which is the same model conditioned on the user's memory, together with a verify-then-regenerate router that lets weight and text memory each cover the queries they handle best. On the HaluMem benchmark, OPSD matches or surpasses strong text-memory baselines, including full-context prompting and retrieval systems, while reading fewer tokens per query. We further conduct an extensive study that characterizes the behavior of weight memory and analyzes how different training recipes affect its performance. As agent harnesses move toward persistent, multi-session deployments, these results position weight memory as a practical, low-cost component of agent memory and provide insights into feasible training and evaluation protocols for combining it with retrieval.
authors: Zeyu Fang, Jun Yin, Yongsheng Mei, Xu Han, Chaitali Joshi, Zhongkai Sun, Jie Hao, Bin Guo, Chengyuan Ma, Benjamin Z. Yao, Chenlei Guo
bullets: Addresses the cost and scaling limits of text-only memory, where each query requires retrieving accumulated history.
Trains a context-free student from a memory-conditioned teacher using on-policy self-distillation (OPSD).
Uses a verify-then-regenerate router to assign queries to weight memory or text memory based on which handles them best.
On HaluMem, OPSD matches or surpasses strong text-memory baselines while reading fewer tokens per query.
Studies weight-memory behavior and training recipes for combining persistent parameter memory with retrieval.

papers.selection_reason: Directly studies persistent memory mechanisms for LLM agents, comparing weight memory with text-based retrieval memory.
papers.title: Route to Remember: Adaptive Memory Selection for LLM Agents
papers.tldr: On-policy self-distillation and adaptive routing make weight-based memory a competitive, lower-context-cost complement to text-based memory for long-term LLM-agent facts.

papers.abstract: Small Language Models (SLMs) are increasingly deployed on consumer-grade hardware, yet their ability to preserve information across progressively longer contexts remains insufficiently understood. Existing benchmarks primarily evaluate retrieval-oriented tasks, providing limited insight into whether successful retrieval reflects comprehensive long-context memory preservation. To address this limitation, this paper introduces Simple Retrieval-Reconstruction Memory (SRRM), a lightweight and fully reproducible benchmark that jointly evaluates Targeted Retrieval and Global Information Reconstruction. This study also proposes the Memory Preservation Ratio (MPR), a benchmark-level metric that quantifies the relationship between retrieval and reconstruction performance. SRRM was evaluated using a synthetic dataset on three Qwen2.5 models (0.5B, 1.5B, and 3B parameters) across context loads ranging from 10 to 100 factual statements. Experimental results show that reconstruction performance deteriorated substantially faster than retrieval accuracy as contextual information increased, indicating that retrieval alone is insufficient to characterize long-context memory preservation. Among the evaluated models, Qwen2.5-1.5B achieved the highest retrieval accuracy (86.7%), reconstruction performance (45.7%), and MPR (0.53), outperforming the larger Qwen2.5-3B model (72.2%, 18.5%, and 0.26, respectively). These findings demonstrate that increasing parameter count does not necessarily improve long-context memory preservation. Overall, SRRM provides a reproducible and extensible benchmark for systematically evaluating long-context memory while revealing complementary memory behaviors that remain hidden under retrieval-only evaluation frameworks.
bullets: Introduces SRRM, a lightweight benchmark combining targeted retrieval with global information reconstruction.
Defines Memory Preservation Ratio (MPR) to relate retrieval and reconstruction performance.
Evaluates three Qwen2.5 models from 0.5B to 3B parameters on synthetic contexts containing 10–100 factual statements.
Qwen2.5-1.5B performed best, while the larger 3B model performed worse, showing that more parameters do not guarantee better memory preservation.
Scope: results are based on a synthetic dataset and the evaluated Qwen2.5 models.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overall architecture of the proposed SRRM benchmark. Synthetic information is generated and organized into conversational context before being evaluated through Sequential Retrieval and Summary Reconstruction tasks. Performance is measured using retrieval accuracy, Critical Information Recall (CIR), token consumption, inference time, and hardware memory usage.

Figure 2: Overall organization of the proposed SRRM benchmark. The benchmark begins with four independently generated synthetic information categories, which are subsequently organized into a balanced benchmark sequence using a deterministic Round-Robin strategy. Each information item is assigned a sequence identifier and category identifier before being grouped into predefined context sizes. The constructed benchmark is then evaluated through two complementary tasks, namely Sequential Retrieval and Summary Reconstruction, while multiple performance metrics are collected to provide a comprehensive analysis of the short-term memory capability of the evaluated language models.

Figure 4: This figure illustrates the evaluation workflow of the Sequential Retrieval Test. After the complete conversation history has been constructed, benchmark questions are automatically generated from the corresponding ground-truth annotations. Each model response is subsequently compared with the expected answer to determine whether the retrieved fact is correct or incorrect. The final retrieval performance is then calculated using the proportion of correctly answered questions.

Figure 7: As shown in Figure 7, retrieval performance varies across the evaluated models as the context size increases. The figure presents the overall accuracy trend for Qwen2.5-0.5B, Qwen2.5-1.5B, and Qwen2.5-3B under identical benchmark conditions. The numerical retrieval accuracy corresponding to each evaluation level is summarized in Table 13.

Figure 10 visualizes the mean retrieval accuracy for each evaluated language model across the four benchmark information categories. Color intensity represents retrieval performance averaged over all evaluated context sizes, while the numerical values indicate the corresponding percentage accuracy for each model–category combination.

Figure 13: Demonstrates that all evaluated models achieved substantially higher retrieval performance than reconstruction performance. Although the magnitude of this difference varies across the Qwen2.5 model family, the same overall pattern is consistently observed, indicating that successful retrieval of previously presented information does not necessarily translate into equivalent preservation of that information during summary generation. This observation suggests that retrieval and reconstruction represent related but distinct memory capabilities, supporting the motivation for evaluating both tasks independently within the proposed SRRM benchmark.
Figure 9: Overall comparison between mean retrieval accuracy and mean CIR score.

Figure 5: Figure 5 illustrates the evaluation workflow of the Summary Reconstruction Test. After the complete conversation history has been constructed, the language model is instructed to reconstruct every previously presented factual statement as a structured summary. The generated summary is subsequently compared against the benchmark ground-truth facts through automatic line-by-line matching, producing the Critical Information Recall (CIR) score that represents the proportion of correctly reconstructed information.
Figure 11: Category-specific reconstruction performance heatmap matrix

Table 12: The SRRM benchmark records multiple computational metrics alongside memory performance to provide a more comprehensive evaluation of language models. These metrics quantify computational efficiency by measuring context size, response length, inference latency, and hardware resource utilization throughout the benchmark. Together, they complement the retrieval- and reconstruction-based evaluations by revealing the computational trade-offs associated with increasing model parameters and context sizes.

Table 5: As shown in Table 5, the benchmark evaluates three parameter scales within the Qwen2.5 family while maintaining the same inference framework and context length. This controlled selection enables the study to isolate the effect of parameter scaling on information retention performance.
Table 1 : Comparison of Existing Long-Context Benchmarks

Table 11: The SRRM benchmark evaluates language models under five progressively increasing context sizes to analyze the effect of information load on short-term memory performance. Instead of modifying the dataset itself, the benchmark gradually increases the number of information items presented to the model while preserving the same information order and distribution. This controlled context scaling enables consistent comparisons across different parameter sizes under identical experimental conditions.

Table 15 : Reports the exact CIR scores obtained by each evaluated model at every benchmark level. The tabulated values complement the graphical representation shown in Figure 8 by providing precise reconstruction scores for each context size, facilitating direct comparison across different parameter scales.

Table 4: Comparison between existing benchmark objectives and the proposed SRRM benchmark. SRRM extends previous evaluations by jointly measuring targeted retrieval, global information reconstruction, and computational efficiency under progressively increasing factual contexts.

Table 13: reports the exact retrieval accuracy obtained by each model at every evaluated context size. Presenting the numerical results in tabular form complements the graphical representation in Figure 7 by providing precise values for each experimental condition, enabling direct comparison across both models and context levels.

Table 14: summarizes the overall retrieval characteristics of each evaluated model. Mean Accuracy represents the average retrieval accuracy across all five context sizes, Max Accuracy and Min Accuracy denote the highest and lowest recorded retrieval performance, respectively, while Accuracy Drop measures the absolute decrease in retrieval accuracy between the evaluations conducted with 10 and 100 information items.

Table 16 : Summarizes the overall reconstruction characteristics of each evaluated model. Mean CIR represents the average reconstruction score across all five context sizes, Max CIR and Min CIR indicate the highest and lowest reconstruction scores observed during the benchmark, respectively, while CIR Drop denotes the absolute decrease in reconstruction performance between the evaluations conducted using 10 and 100 information items.

Table 18 summarizes the benchmark-level ranking derived from the retrieval and reconstruction evaluations presented in the preceding sections. The ranking provides a consolidated comparison of overall memory performance across the evaluated models while preserving the detailed retrieval, reconstruction, and category-level analyses reported previously. As such, it serves as a concise reference for comparing the relative benchmark performance of the evaluated Qwen2.5 model family.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes a benchmark for evaluating long-context memory preservation in small language models, directly relevant to long-context processing and memory evaluation.
papers.title: SRRM: A Retrieval-Reconstruction Benchmark for Evaluating Long-Context Memory in Small Language Models
papers.tldr: SRRM shows that retrieval accuracy alone overestimates long-context memory in small language models, as reconstruction degrades much faster with increasing context.

papers.abstract: Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT) demands more than empathic validation, requiring instead a structured formulation of the interplay among situations, automatic thoughts, emotions, and behaviors. Therapists formalize this interplay through a Cognitive Conceptualization Diagram, where maintaining longitudinal coherence necessitates continuous evidential adjudication to separate tentative hypotheses from established findings. Current dialogue systems track conversational history via retrieval or static profiles but lack the representational capacity to encode epistemic status. Consequently, provisional interpretations are often prematurely reified as established facts, inadvertently biasing downstream interventions. Addressing this limitation, CCDWiki is introduced as a plug-and-play advisor conceptualizing longitudinal therapy as evidence-grounded hypothesis adjudication. The approach encodes each clinical hypothesis as a mutable entry bound to corroborating and contradicting evidence. Across sessions, accumulating data strengthens supported entries, preserves provisional ones, and retracts contradicted assumptions. The resulting formulation distills into concise guidance for unmodified therapeutic language models. Experiments demonstrate substantial improvements in both conceptualization and intervention quality without requiring backbone retraining.
authors: Mingwen Zhang, Ruiyang Song, Qinying Wang, Yuchen Wang, Changsheng Ma, Minqiang Yang
bullets: Addresses the problem of therapy systems prematurely treating tentative interpretations as established facts.
Represents each CBT hypothesis as a mutable entry linked to supporting and contradicting evidence.
Updates formulations across sessions by strengthening supported hypotheses, preserving provisional ones, and retracting contradicted assumptions.
Distills the evolving formulation into concise guidance for an unchanged therapeutic language model.
Experiments show substantial gains in conceptualization and intervention quality without backbone retraining.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of CCDWiki. At response, client-attributable evidence from the longitudinal dialogue updates a dynamic Cognitive Conceptualization Diagram through Evidence-Adjudicated Longitudinal Formulation (EALF). FormulationConditioned Intervention Planning (FCIP) then jointly selects a formulation target, therapeutic intent, compatible CBT technique, and case-specific guidance.

Radial positions support comparisons on the same spoke but are not raw UED values, and greater radial distance does not imply better response quality because the descriptors have no common favorable direction. Panels show (a) DeepSeek V4 Pro, (b) GLM4-9B, (c) InternLM3-8B, and (d) Qwen3-8B.

Figure 1: Comparison between session-isolated responseoriented approaches and CCDWiki. Existing approaches can lose state changes, leave evidence untraceable, and yield intervention plans that drift across sessions. CCDWiki maintains a case-specific, evidence-grounded state with confidence and provenance, supporting longitudinal, actionable guidance.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces a plug-and-play memory advisor that maintains evidence-grounded clinical hypotheses across sessions for language models, fitting persistent external memory for LLMs.
papers.title: CCDWIKI: Decoupling Case Formulation from Response Generation in Longitudinal CBT Dialogue
papers.tldr: CCDWIKI improves longitudinal CBT dialogue by maintaining evidence-grounded, revisable clinical hypotheses and using them to guide interventions without retraining the language model.

papers.abstract: Under expert parallelism, mixture-of-experts (MoE) layers pay all-to-all token dispatch, grouped GEMMs, and a combine step in every layer. In decode each rank holds only 1-256 tokens: dispatch latency and weight traffic dominate while tensor-core utilization is inherently low. In fused operators such as DeepGEMM's Mega MoE, dispatch and computation overlap only by sharing every SM: dispatch warps compete with TMA/MMA and epilogue warps for registers, shared memory, and issue slots; every phase shares one CTA resource budget, synchronization spans the whole SM array, and every replay ends with a workspace-clean pass and a cross-rank barrier. We present GC-MoE, an open-source FP8/FP4 MoE inference operator for NVIDIA Hopper and Blackwell GPUs that uses CUDA Green Contexts to split the device into a small communication partition and a large compute partition. Each role gets its own kernel, resource budget, and synchronization domain, so dispatch and GEMM tune independently. A three-node CUDA Graph (four on Hopper with fused shared experts) launches the dispatch and grouped-GEMM kernels as concurrent roots; a token-ring handshake starts computation on the first filled ring blocks, and double-buffered receive counters remove the trailing cross-rank barrier between replays. The compute partition runs operand-swapped tcgen05 block-scaled MMA on Blackwell and register-A WGMMA with in-register FP4 decoding on Hopper, with fused SwiGLU, requantization, and optional shared experts. On 8 H20 GPUs GC-MoE accelerates DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash decode by 1.188x on average on both the routed and shared-expert suites (peaks 1.296x and 1.353x); on 8 B300 GPUs it accelerates GLM-5.2 and DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash by 1.106x (1.123x with fused shared experts, peak 1.209x), beating Mega MoE at all 54 measured points at matched accuracy. GC-MoE reserves only 20 of 148 SMs on B300 for dispatch.
authors: Yong Li, Kan Liu, Tao Lan
bullets: Targets decode-time MoE bottlenecks where all-to-all dispatch and weight traffic dominate and tensor-core utilization is low.
Uses CUDA Green Contexts to assign dispatch and grouped GEMM separate SM partitions, resource budgets, kernels, and synchronization domains.
Overlaps work through CUDA Graph roots, token-ring handshaking, and double-buffered receive counters that eliminate trailing cross-rank barriers.
Supports FP8/FP4 inference on Hopper and Blackwell, with fused SwiGLU, requantization, and optional shared experts.
Reports 1.188× average speedup on 8 H20s and 1.106× on 8 B300s, outperforming Mega MoE at all 54 matched-accuracy test points.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Architecture of one GC-MoE layer replay. The child CUDA Graph holds three nodes: role1 (dispatch) and role2 (grouped GEMM) have no dependency edge and are concurrent roots, whereas role3 (finalize/combine) depends on both (solid arrows). Dashed arrows map each role to the green context that launches it—role1 to the 20-SM communication context, role2 and role3 to the 128-SM compute context—each with its own balanced workqueue so that the driver co-schedules them on disjoint SM sets. All cross-rank state lives in one symmetric-memory workspace whose boxes name the buffers exchanged over NVLink (double arrows): activations and scales, routing metadata, the role1→role2 token ring, the role2→role3 combine buffer, and the counters and parity signals. Every synchronization object is device-persistent and replay-aware, so a replay needs no host-side reset.

Figure 1: Execution timelines. (a) On B300 the baseline is DeepGEMM’s Mega MoE, one persistent fused kernel on all 148 SMs: after routing counts and a tag-1 cross-rank barrier, the dispatch warps stream tokens, scales, and routing metadata into a per-block token ring while the GEMM consumes each ring block as soon as it is full. The phases overlap, but on the same SMs, with the dispatch warps and their staging buffers carved out of every SM’s register file and shared memory; the tail is max(Tcombine, tclean + ttag2)—the workspace clean overlaps the combine, but the tag-2 barrier is still a cross-rank round trip on every replay. (b) GC-MoE runs role1 (dispatch) on the 20-SM communication context and role2 (grouped GEMM) plus role3 (combine) on the 128-SM compute context. Role2 starts when the first ring block is filled (dashed trigger), and parity-double-buffered receive counters remove the tag-2 barrier, so the next replay can start as soon as role3 completes (green band). Each role is an ordinary kernel with its own register, shared-memory, and synchronization budget, so the dispatch and GEMM paths can be optimized independently. Bars are illustrative; measured end-to-end speedups span 1.03–1.30× across the routed-expert sweeps and 1.01–1.35× including shared experts (Section 6.2). Partitions are the B300 values.

papers.selection_reason: CUDA-level MoE inference optimization that reduces latency and improves tensor-core utilization; transferable to efficient LLM serving.
papers.title: GC-MoE: Overlapping Expert-Parallel Token Dispatch with FP8/FP4 Grouped GEMM via CUDA Green Contexts
papers.tldr: GC-MoE speeds up low-token MoE decoding by isolating communication and computation on separate GPU partitions and overlapping them efficiently.

papers.abstract: Why do language models fail on long inputs? The common answer is length. We show that, for retrieval, length is cheap and competition is not. On five open models (0.5B to 3B parameters, four families), neutral filler costs nothing: accuracy stays at 0.97 to 1.00, up to 32K tokens on Qwen2.5-1.5B. Statements in the format of the evidence, placed at the same positions, drop it to 0.16 to 0.33. A single statement that gives the queried key a rival value multiplies the loss by 9 to 110, and every additional rival adds to it. Inside the model, one quantity tracks the failure: the attention mass left on the evidence. Across 126,473 trials it explains up to 58% of the variance in loss; log length explains at most 8%. The masked-filler protocol behind the claim that length alone hurts reproduces on MMLU (11 to 18 points lost at 30K tokens), but fails a visible control in retrieval: masking costs 45 accuracy points at 32K tokens, while the same filler left visible costs none. In retrieval, context rot is a competition for attention. We release the probe and all 126K trial-level measurements.
bullets: Neutral filler preserves retrieval accuracy—even up to 32K tokens—while same-format statements sharply reduce it.
A single rival value for the queried key increases loss 9–110×, with additional rivals worsening performance.
Attention remaining on the evidence explains up to 58% of loss variance; log context length explains at most 8%.
A masked-filler protocol can make length appear harmful, but visible filler has no effect in the retrieval control.
The study evaluates five open models across 126,473 trials and releases the probe and measurements.

papers.selection_reason: Analyzes why retrieval fails on long inputs, attributing context rot to attention competition rather than length; relevant to long-context understanding.
papers.title: Length Is Cheap, Competition Is Not: Attention Predicts Context Rot in Retrieval
papers.tldr: Retrieval failures in long contexts are driven mainly by competing evidence that steals attention, not by context length alone.

papers.abstract: We introduce Dory1.0-4B, a 4-billion-parameter looped (latent-recurrent) language model with elastic depth: a single checkpoint serves different inference compute budgets. Dory1.0-4B is built on a normalized Transformer (nGPT) backbone with interleaved sliding-window and full-attention layers, organized into an input block, a shared recurrent block, and an output block. At inference, the recurrent block can be applied a variable number of times. We pre-trained Dory1.0-4B on 6 trillion tokens. The first 4.5 trillion tokens were trained in NVFP4, and additional pre-training then extended the context length to 256K tokens. Next, we post-trained the model using Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) and Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR), with a difficulty-aware loop curriculum that routes harder prompts to deeper loops. Increasing the loop count improves accuracy, with the largest gains on coding, agentic, and long-context benchmarks. With two or more loops, Dory1.0-4B outperforms larger models such as Qwen3.5-9B, Gemma 4 12B, and Gemma 4 26B-A4B on average across 12 benchmarks. Looping also makes Dory1.0-4B more token-efficient on agentic benchmarks: with four loops, it generates 1.3-2.5x fewer tokens than with one loop, as the extra computation is spent in latent space rather than on longer outputs. To reduce memory during looping, Dory1.0-4B caches keys and values only from the last loop, keeping its KV-cache footprint equal to that of a non-looped model at any loop count while retaining most of the accuracy gains. We open-source the BF16, MXFP8, NVFP4, and GGUF quantized checkpoints.
bullets: Uses a normalized Transformer with interleaved sliding-window and full-attention layers, divided into input, recurrent, and output blocks.
Variable loop counts provide elastic inference compute, with harder prompts routed to deeper loops during post-training.
More loops yield the largest accuracy gains on coding, agentic, and long-context benchmarks.
With at least two loops, it outperforms several larger models across 12 benchmarks, according to the abstract.
Caching only the final loop’s keys and values keeps KV-cache memory comparable to a non-looped model; quantized checkpoints are released.

figures.caption: Figure 3 | Overview of the post-training pipeline for Dory1.0-4B. The base context window is 262,144 tokens (256K). SFT trains on packed sequences of 262,144 tokens, and samples loop counts for each microbatch randomly, while RLVR routes harder prompts to deeper loops with higher probability.

Figure 2 | Dory1.0-4B’s looped nGPT architecture. A 16-layer input block produces a fixed representation 𝑢. A 40-layer recurrent block refines the state over 𝑘 passes (up to four), sharing all of its weights and learned scales across each loop. Each loop adds 𝑢 to the current state, initialized as 𝑠0 = 𝑢, and applies L2 normalization before and after the recurrent block. A 16-layer output block processes the final state before the LM head. Within each block, an eight-layer pattern contains three SWA–SwiGLU pairs followed by one full-attention–SwiGLU pair, giving a 3:1 ratio of sliding-window attention (SWA) to full attention. SWA uses a window of 𝑊 =1024 tokens with RoPE base 𝜃S = 104; full attention uses 𝜃F = 107. RoPE acts on all Q/K dimensions. Each sublayer updates the residual stream by blending its normalized output with the normalized residual using learned per-channel weights, then normalizing the result.
Figure 5 | Loop-curriculum ablation with an early SFT checkpoint.

Figure 1 | Accuracy and token efficiency of Dory1.0-4B across inference loop counts 𝑘. (a) An equal-weight average of 12 benchmarks: SciCode, SWE-Bench Verified, Terminal-Bench v2.1, 𝜏3- Banking, GDPval-AA v2, GPQA Diamond, Humanity’s Last Exam (HLE), IFBench, AA-LCR, GDP.pdf, and AA-Omniscience accuracy and non-hallucination, with GDPval-AA v2 Elo normalized as (Elo − 500)/20. (b) Reduction in the number of output tokens needed to solve agentic tasks as the number of loops increases.

Figure 4 | Illustration of difficulty-aware loop routing at 𝛼 = 0.3. A generic distribution of loop-1 pass rates supplies the within-batch midpoint quantiles 𝑞𝑖, which are combined with uniform sampling 𝑢𝑖. After sorting the resulting scores, lower scores fill deeper loop slots first. The output histogram preserves the input prompt counts and shows the assigned loop counts within each difficulty bin: darker segments denote more loop counts.

Figure 6 | Self-speculative decode throughput relative to autoregressive 𝑘 = 4, using 𝑘 = 1 drafting, 𝑘 = 4 verification, and four draft tokens. Curves compare KV reuse with and without activation reuse. Throughput is measured over output positions 128–896 of 1,024-token generations. Points show geometric means across three repeat blocks and error bars show block ranges.

Table 2 | Evaluation results for Dory1.0-4B across inference loop counts. All scores are percentages except GDPval-AA v2, which is reported in Elo. GDPval-AA v2 is normalized as (Elo − 500)/20 for unweighted average score over 12 benchmarks. papers.selection_reason: Looped latent-recurrent LLM architecture with elastic depth and KV-cache reduction fits LLM architectures and memory-efficient inference.
papers.title: Dory1.0-4B: A Looped Normalized-GPT
papers.tldr: Dory1.0-4B is a 4B-parameter recurrent language model that improves accuracy and token efficiency by flexibly repeating shared latent layers at inference.

papers.abstract: With the rise of Group Agent such as Claude Tag, agents increasingly serve as digital workers for long-term team collaboration. These agents operate over shared contexts that continuously accumulate through multi-user interactions. However, existing agent memory systems are mainly designed for individual users and struggle to capture group-level knowledge in shared contexts, including group relationships and collaboratively formed knowledge. Manual memory strategies further limit adaptation to diverse and evolving shared contexts. To this end, we propose \textbf{EvoGroup (EvoG)}, a self-evolving harness for group agents that starts from a minimal six-tool cold start and adapts through interaction with shared context. EvoG uses confidence and task outcomes to select informative trajectories, while also eliciting self-reflections on uncertainty in low-confidence cases. The analysis agent then examines selected trajectories through adaptive progressive disclosure, followed by bucketed analysis to synthesize high-level findings that guide the evolve agent in revising the Harness. Empirically, pass@1 on held-out split of EverMemBench improves from 71.07\% to 89.58\%, surpassing both self-evolving memory and human-designed harnesses, including Claude Code (85.83\%). To evaluate generalization, we freeze the evolved harness and evaluate it on the unseen GroupMemBench, where, with GPT-5.5, it demonstrates effective generalization and outperforms both memory baselines and human-designed harnesses.
bullets: Targets the gap between individual-user memory systems and the relationship- and collaboration-aware knowledge needed by group agents.
Starts with six tools and evolves through interaction, using confidence and task outcomes to select informative trajectories.
Uses self-reflection for uncertain cases, adaptive progressive disclosure, and bucketed analysis to guide harness revisions.
Improves EverMemBench held-out pass@1 from 71.07% to 89.58%, exceeding reported self-evolving and human-designed baselines.
A frozen evolved harness also generalizes effectively to the unseen GroupMemBench, outperforming memory and human-designed baselines.
