papers.abstract: Why do some of the world's most powerful Artificial Intelligence (AI) systems still struggle to reason about cause and effect? Causal discovery, the ability to discern the underlying drivers of a system, is fundamental to scientific inquiry and has traditionally relied on structured data and statistical methods. Recently, Large Language Models (LLMs) have been explored as an alternative paradigm for causal inference, leveraging their broad knowledge and reasoning capabilities. Yet, despite their linguistic fluency, LLMs often rely on surface-level pattern recognition rather than genuine causal logic. While it is known that LLMs stumble in this domain, we lack a precise map of where, why, and how significantly these failures occur. In this paper, we propose a systematic stress-test framework across six critical dimensions: model scale, causal graph complexity, prompting strategy, metadata quality, data quality, and sensitivity to uncertainty. Our findings reveal a significant "optimism bias" in LLMs; models consistently overestimate causal links, leading to low precision across the board. Furthermore, we demonstrate that traditional evaluation metrics can be deceptive: while reasoning-heavy models lead in performance, the highest scores often occur when uncertainty in inference is overlooked. Once uncertainty is integrated into the evaluation, performance drops, providing a more honest reflection of causal reliability. We also find that, while scaling model size improves outcomes, these gains are fragile; performance degrades sharply as the quality of metadata decreases. This work serves as a practical guide to the blind spots of LLMs, offering a clear-eyed assessment of when these tools can be integrated into a causal discovery pipeline and when they are likely to lead researchers astray.
authors: Ankitkumar Patel, Jigarkumar Patel, Amit Kumar, Supreetha Sreeram, Venkatesh Kulkarni
bullets: Evaluates LLM causal discovery across model scale, graph complexity, prompting, metadata quality, data quality, and uncertainty.
Finds a consistent optimism bias: LLMs overestimate causal relationships, resulting in low precision.
Shows that conventional metrics can overstate performance when uncertainty is ignored; uncertainty-aware evaluation lowers scores.
Larger models perform better, but their gains degrade sharply with lower-quality metadata.
Provides practical guidance on when LLMs may support causal discovery and when they risk misleading researchers.

papers.selection_reason: Systematically evaluates LLM robustness in causal inference tasks, identifying failure modes like 'optimism bias' and fragility, which is relevant to understanding LLM reasoning capabilities.
papers.title: Stress-Testing the Robustness of LLM-Based Causal Inference
papers.tldr: A systematic stress test shows that LLMs often overpredict causal links, and their apparent causal-reasoning gains are fragile—especially under uncertainty and poor metadata.

papers.abstract: Language models often spread a concept across many internal dimensions, making their features difficult to interpret. Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) recover clearer features after training. We ask whether models can instead learn interpretable output coordinates directly. We introduce Mixture of Wide Experts (MoWE), a sparse feed-forward layer in which selected experts read the full representation but write to fixed, disjoint output coordinates. On a controlled task with known hidden causes, this design preserves predictive performance while localizing causes more clearly than dense and standard mixture-of-experts (MoE) models. At approximately matched compute, we train two 19-layer runs of each architecture for 10 billion tokens. MoWE achieves evaluation cross-entropy 2.417 versus 2.452 for dense, while standard MoE reaches 2.22. We measure native-coordinate readability by asking a language-model judge to describe each coordinate from passages where it is strongly active and test that description on new passages. Correcting for descriptions that also fit other coordinates gives a specificity score of 0.523 for MoWE, 0.375 for dense, and 0.268 for standard MoE. TopK SAEs trained on the same FFN updates score 0.489 for dense and 0.556 for MoWE, making native MoWE comparable to the dense SAE. In the first case study, we identify a four-coordinate causal path supporting the model's prediction of degrees after the prompt A right angle is 90. We then copy seven angle-related coordinate values into the model as it processes A rectangle has four, changing its next-token prediction from sides to degrees. In the second, one fixed coordinate set detects hazardous requests and another steers the next token toward refusal. These examples show that MoWE combines sparse conditional computation with coordinates that can be identified and reused directly.
authors: Tavish Mankash, Vardhaman Kalloli, Keshava Prasad, Deepan Muthirayan
bullets: Addresses the difficulty of interpreting concepts distributed across many model dimensions.
Routes inputs to selected experts that read the full representation but write to disjoint, fixed coordinates.
On a controlled task, MoWE outperforms dense models in predictive performance and improves coordinate specificity over dense and standard MoE models, though standard MoE has lower cross-entropy.
Native MoWE coordinates approach the readability of sparse-autoencoder features and can reveal causal paths and steer predictions.
Demonstrations include detecting hazardous requests, inducing refusals, and changing an angle-related prediction from “sides” to “degrees.”

papers.selection_reason: Introduces Mixture of Wide Experts (MoWE), a novel sparse feed-forward architecture for LLMs that uses fixed, disjoint output coordinates to improve feature interpretability, directly relevant to LLM architecture and interpretability.
papers.title: Mixture of Wide Experts: Sparse Routing for Interpretable Native Coordinates
papers.tldr: MoWE uses sparse experts with fixed output coordinates to make language-model features more interpretable and directly reusable while largely preserving predictive performance.

papers.abstract: Steering vectors (SVs) are residual-stream directions that shift the behavior of LLMs when added to hidden states at inference time. While prior work has mainly used SVs as post-hoc controls, we ask whether the same directions can also guide parameter updates during post-training. We study this question across supervised learning, including SFT and distillation, and reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR). Our framework considers two intervention regimes: a hidden-state hook during teacher-forced supervised training, and an advantage-repair mechanism on wrong rollouts in GRPO. For each regime, we analyze three design axes, which are the steering direction, its placement, and the operation used to combine it with training. In supervised settings, SV injection improves over plain SFT and distillation, with gains scaling with the off-policy gap and reaching up to a $12\%$ improvement when distilling from thinking-mode teachers. These gains hold across three random seeds. In RL settings, applying a correctness-contrast direction as advantage repair on wrong rollouts, including otherwise zero-gradient all-wrong groups, recovers a learning signal that transfers to held-out math benchmarks and acts as a composable auxiliary signal that adds to existing zero-variance remedies such as entropy-aware advantage shaping. We further identify three failure boundaries. In detail, code generation can break the direction, cross-family layer transfer can break the placement, and inference-time application on an SV-trained checkpoint can break the intervention regime. Together, these results establish steering vectors as a conditional but effective training signal for LLM post-training. Our code is available here.
bullets: The study extends steering vectors from inference-time behavior control to parameter updates during SFT, distillation, and RL with verifiable rewards.
It tests hidden-state injection for supervised training and correctness-contrast advantage repair on wrong GRPO rollouts.
Supervised steering improves over plain SFT and distillation, with gains increasing with the off-policy gap and reaching up to 12% when distilling from thinking-mode teachers.
In RL, advantage repair restores learning signals for otherwise zero-gradient all-wrong groups and transfers to held-out math benchmarks.
Effectiveness has boundaries: directions may fail for code generation, layer placement may not transfer across model families, and inference-time steering may fail on SV-trained checkpoints.

papers.selection_reason: The paper introduces a novel method for using steering vectors as a training signal during LLM post-training (SFT, distillation, RLVR). This directly contributes to the architecture and training of Large Language Models.
papers.title: Steering Vectors as a Training Signal in LLM Post-Training
papers.tldr: Steering vectors can improve LLM post-training when injected into supervised learning or used to repair RL advantages, but their effectiveness depends on the direction, placement, and intervention regime.

papers.abstract: Knowledge distillation can transfer reasoning from stronger teachers to frozen students through reusable prompts, but avoiding weight updates does not eliminate supervision. Without ground-truth answers, teacher solutions are unverified, and agreement with the teacher can reward shared mistakes. We introduce Knowledge-to-Prompt (K2P) for label-free knowledge distillation to prompts. K2P synthesizes reusable instructions from teacher solutions, refines them using paired teacher and student responses, and guides search and selection with answer agreement. It retains candidates that adaptive search may undervalue and selects on reserved questions. Deployment uses only the frozen student and selected prompt. Our theory separates generation and selection gaps and gives conditions under which agreement-guided construction yields accuracy guarantees despite imperfect teacher references. Across reasoning tasks and students, K2P outperforms label-free alternatives overall and remains competitive with supervised prompt optimization. Ablations and archive diagnostics assess the contributions of teacher solutions and refinement, while revealing the limits of agreement-guided selection.
bullets: Addresses unverified teacher solutions and shared-error risks in label-free distillation.
Synthesizes instructions from teacher solutions and refines them with paired teacher and student responses.
Uses adaptive search, agreement-guided selection, and reserved questions to retain and evaluate prompt candidates.
Provides theory separating generation and selection gaps, with conditions for accuracy guarantees under imperfect references.
Outperforms label-free alternatives overall and remains competitive with supervised prompt optimization, while exposing limits of agreement-based selection.

papers.selection_reason: Label-free prompt distillation improves reasoning in frozen LLMs, fitting language foundation model reasoning methods.
papers.title: K2P: Label-Free Knowledge to Prompt Distillation
papers.tldr: K2P distills a teacher’s reasoning into reusable prompts for frozen students without ground-truth labels, using teacher–student agreement to search and select prompts.

papers.abstract: We introduce Type-6 logic, a variant of dynamic epistemic logic augmented with two operators (uncertainty and recurrence), designed to model the inferential dynamics of contemporary large language model (LLM) chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning. Type-6 accounts for common LLM reasoning pathologies such as unlicensed revision, enthymemes, loopbacks, and unverifiable/incorrect claims. We propose a verifier based on Type-6 logic that builds a graph out the trace, and checks it against Type-6's axioms and inference rules. We evaluate our framework on LLM-generated CoTs four splits spanning formal and informal reasoning. Our verifier detects structurally unsound reasoning steps that surface-level heuristics miss, and allows for easy visualisation of the model's reasoning process. In our corpus, our verifier shows that derived contradiction is the most common hard-fail category in CoT, and that only about 3\% of the propositions of a trace have impact on the final derivation. Ablation studies show that other verification methods (LLMs-as-judges, other neurosymbolic approaches, etc.) cannot be considered interchangeable: for example, agreement between LLMs-as-judges and LINC is $κ\approx 0.034$, and this persists within a method across underlying models. Type-6, however, is the most agreed-with method amongst the ones we tested. We prove our verifier runs on average-case linear time; and release our logic specification and artefacts.
bullets: Models CoT as dynamic epistemic processes with uncertainty and recurrence operators.
Builds a graph from each reasoning trace and checks it against Type-6 axioms and inference rules.
Evaluated on four formal and informal reasoning splits; derived contradictions were the most common hard-fail category.
Finds that only about 3% of trace propositions affect the final derivation.
Runs in average-case linear time and supports visualisation; the authors release the logic specification and artefacts.

papers.abstract: Linear activation steering is a powerful approach for controlling and specializing large language models by adding linear representations of concepts to their activations at inference. While effective, existing methods often steer with a fixed strength, independent of how much steering any given input requires. In this work, we introduce Contextual Linear Activation Steering (CLAS), which decomposes activation steering into a fixed steering direction and a context-dependent steering coefficient. This decomposition preserves the interpretability of the steering direction while enabling the steering strength to vary with context. It also enables CLAS to perform selective steering: steering multiple behaviors across different portions of a single generation, which cannot be achieved using a fixed steering strength. In addition, across a wide range of steering benchmarks and language models, CLAS consistently outperforms standard linear activation steering and matches or exceeds ReFT and LoRA in settings with limited labeled data. Notably, CLAS achieves this using directions that also serve as reliable concept monitors, a property that directions learned via fine-tuning lack. We therefore propose CLAS as an interpretable and accurate method for controlling and specializing large language models.
authors: Brandon Hsu, Daniel Beaglehole, Adityanarayanan Radhakrishnan, Mikhail Belkin
bullets: Fixed-strength steering applies the same intensity regardless of the input’s needs.
CLAS separates a fixed, interpretable steering direction from a context-dependent steering coefficient.
This supports selective steering of multiple behaviors within different parts of one generation.
Across diverse benchmarks and language models, CLAS outperforms standard linear steering and matches or exceeds ReFT and LoRA with limited labeled data.
Its steering directions also function as reliable concept monitors, unlike directions learned through fine-tuning.

papers.abstract: Human working memory lets people maintain and update information. Large language models (LLMs) face a related demand when tracking updates within a single prompt without writing out intermediate states, yet existing tests differ in their constraints on written steps. We introduce a working-memory-inspired probe of cumulative state tracking with program-computed answers, 3 to 100 updates, and final-state, intermediate-state, or multi-target queries. It compares protocols on identical items. Across 18 LLMs, accuracy is 84.9% on single-step arithmetic but 31.7% on core items requiring one number after three to seven updates. From 50 updates on, no model exceeds 10% accuracy. Core accuracy reaches 88.0% under a larger budget and instructions to write steps and place the answer on the last line, mainly due to the instruction changes rather than the budget. Core accuracy also correlates positively with public Berkeley Function Calling Leaderboard scores. These findings show that strong single-step arithmetic does not ensure reliable cumulative tracking and that output protocols substantially change measured accuracy. We release the generator, items, scoring code, and responses for reproducible comparisons across depths, query types, and protocols.
authors: Dengzhe Hou, Lingyu Jiang, Deng Li, Zirui Li, Fangzhou Lin, Kazunori D Yamada
bullets: Introduces a working-memory-inspired probe with program-computed answers, 3–100 updates, and final-, intermediate-, or multi-target queries.
Across 18 LLMs, accuracy drops from 84.9% on single-step arithmetic to 31.7% on core tasks with 3–7 updates; beyond 50 updates, no model exceeds 10%.
Accuracy reaches 88.0% when models are instructed to write steps and put the answer on the last line, driven mainly by the protocol change rather than a larger budget.
Core accuracy positively correlates with public Berkeley Function Calling Leaderboard scores.
The released generator, items, scoring code, and responses support reproducible comparisons across depths, query types, and protocols.

papers.abstract: Continuous diffusion language models show promising potential in text generation tasks, but are prone to problems such as text repetition, semantic drift, and generation quality degradation when the generation length exceeds the training length. To address these challenges, we propose RangeSWA, a training-free length extrapolation method. The method combines local sliding-window attention, remote block summaries, and dynamic content retrieval to preserve local details and support long-range context access. In addition, generation degradation caused by length extrapolation is mitigated through positional remapping, conditioning attention correction, and denoising-stage-adaptive window scheduling. We conducted experiments on multiple continuous diffusion language models, and the results show that RangeSWA can effectively reduce generative perplexity and text repetition rates in long-text generation.
bullets: Addresses repetition, semantic drift, and quality degradation when generation exceeds the training length.
Uses local sliding-window attention, remote block summaries, and dynamic content retrieval to balance local detail with long-range context.
Applies positional remapping, conditioning-attention correction, and denoising-stage-adaptive window scheduling to mitigate extrapolation degradation.
Experiments across multiple continuous diffusion language models show reduced perplexity and text repetition in long-text generation.

papers.abstract: The order in which tokens are predicted in language modeling has a profound impact on the quality of generated sequences. Autoregressive and masked diffusion models iteratively fill in tokens and can exploit such orderings across generation steps, but how to leverage an ordering for one-step parallel language modeling is unclear. We introduce asynchronous flow map language models (aFMLMs), which incorporate prediction order into one-step modeling by learning the flow maps of asynchronous flows. These flows specify an ordering through a tokenwise time schedule that controls the relative denoising progress of tokens. We formulate a general class of asynchronous flows that admit both prescribed and learned, state-adaptive schedules, show that they define valid flow maps, and develop new methods for their flow map distillation. The resulting models can generate all tokens in a single forward pass by internalizing the ordering encoded in the flow into their hidden computations. On Sudoku solving and code generation for GSM8K math word problems, aFMLM establishes new state-of-the-art one-step performance.
bullets: Addresses how token ordering can improve one-step parallel language modeling.
Uses tokenwise time schedules to control relative denoising progress across tokens.
Supports both prescribed and learned, state-adaptive asynchronous schedules.
Introduces flow-map distillation methods so models internalize ordering in their hidden states.
Achieves state-of-the-art one-step results on Sudoku solving and GSM8K code generation.

papers.abstract: LLM agents performing long-horizon tasks accumulate tool results that later steps may need. Passing the full history to every invocation is costly even when it fits within the context window, while reducing it risks omitting needed information. Existing context management methods can overlook how earlier tool results are used in subsequent execution, leaving needed information out of context. We introduce ContextRender, which manages context through a persistent graph of execution dependencies. We develop Tool-Flow Analysis to track how later operations reuse information from earlier tool results, providing a signal called observed reuse. A renderer combines this signal with recency and semantic relevance to select results within a fixed history budget, retaining omitted results for later use. Across AppWorld and 8-objective QA with three execution models, ContextRender outperforms the evaluated context management baselines using a 6K history budget, well below the models' maximum context windows. Within this budget, it achieves task performance close to or above that of passing the full history while reducing mean inference cost by 10.2%-32.2% relative to Full history. Ablations show that observed reuse improves task performance and retention of results reused later.
bullets: Full-history context is costly, while aggressive reduction can omit information needed by later steps.
It maintains a persistent execution-dependency graph and uses Tool-Flow Analysis to estimate observed reuse of prior tool results.
A renderer combines observed reuse with recency and semantic relevance under a fixed history budget, while retaining omitted results for possible later use.
Across AppWorld and 8-objective QA with three execution models, it outperformed evaluated baselines using a 6K history budget.
Performance was close to or above full-history prompting while reducing mean inference cost by 10.2%–32.2%; ablations confirmed the value of observed reuse.

figures.caption: Figure 3: CONTEXTRENDER architecture. The runtime adapter records messages, tool calls, and complete tool results in a persistent context graph. Tool-Flow Analysis records observed reuse as execution dependencies. Before each model invocation, the renderer includes the accumulated execution history if it fits within the history budget B; otherwise, it selects tool results using observed reuse, recency, and semantic relevance. Omitted results remain stored for later invocations.

papers.abstract: Large reasoning models improve performance on challenging problems by allocating additional computation before answering, but longer reasoning does not always lead to better results and can introduce substantial redundant reasoning on simple problems. Conversely, aggressively shortening reasoning can degrade performance on difficult ones. Effective reasoning therefore requires dynamically deciding when additional computation is useful based on the reasoner's capabilities and evolving solution state. Existing approaches often rely on predefined budgets or intervention rules, retrain the target reasoner, or require additional supervision. We introduce MetaCtrl, a lightweight controller that adaptively regulates a frozen reasoner without predefined token budgets or reasoner retraining. We formulate reasoning regulation as a sequential metacognitive control problem: MetaCtrl observes the evolving reasoning trace and decides whether to continue, simplify, skip redundant steps, or conclude reasoning. It is trained directly with reinforcement learning using a reward that prioritizes correctness while favoring shorter trajectories among correct solutions, requiring neither supervised intervention trajectories nor problem-specific budgets. Across seven benchmarks spanning mathematics, science, and code, MetaCtrl consistently improves the accuracy of LRMs while reducing their reasoning length. On DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B, it improves average accuracy by 4.7 points while reducing generation length by 53.3%. Without further training, the same controller transfers to an unseen reasoner (e.g., Qwen3-14B), improving average accuracy by 2.9 points and reducing generation length by 50.3%. These results establish MetaCtrl as a plug-and-play controller for improving reasoning accuracy while substantially reducing inference-time generation. The code is available at https://github.com/binbin2xs/MetaCtrl.
bullets: Addresses the trade-off between excessive reasoning on simple problems and insufficient reasoning on difficult ones.
A lightweight controller monitors the evolving reasoning trace and chooses whether to continue, simplify, skip redundant steps, or stop.
Requires no predefined token budget, reasoner retraining, supervised intervention traces, or problem-specific budgets.
Across seven mathematics, science, and code benchmarks, it improved accuracy while reducing reasoning length.
On DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B, accuracy rose by 4.7 points and generation length fell by 53.3%; it also transferred to Qwen3-14B without further training.

papers.abstract: Agentic workflows are increasingly shifting towards long-horizon tasks, such as open-ended scientific work, where models benefit from long context windows. However, at ultra-long context (above 1M tokens), full attention is prohibitively expensive. A promising approach is sparse attention, in which a dedicated indexer selects a subset of keys for the attention. Yet current methods of indexing either still have quadratic cost in context size or lose accuracy at ultra-long context scale. We address this with Latent Sparse Attention (LSA), an efficient attention method that maintains accuracy at ultra-long context. In LSA, keys are hierarchically clustered in a learned latent space, and queries score the hierarchy of clusters instead of scoring every key, making prefill, decode and training faster at long context. We propose two variants, Distilled-LSA (D-LSA), which can be applied to pre-trained models via distillation, and Native-LSA (N-LSA), which is trained natively on the next-token loss alone. On GLM-5.3-FLASH (QWEN-3.8-27B) at 10M tokens, D-LSA speeds up one attention layer by 22.7x (72.4x) in prefill and 4.6x (42.5x) in decode over its original sparse attention (full attention), while keeping similar accuracy across a variety of tasks. N-LSA matches the accuracy of full attention with a training speedup of 1.6x per layer at 128k tokens. LSA offers practical and efficient attention for models to benefit from ultra-long context.
authors: Ales Kubicek, Andrea Caciolai, Liangzu Peng, Sukrit Sumant, Benjamin Hoover, Fraser Greenlee, Ruairidh M. Battleday, Radim Urban, Torsten Hoefler, James C. R. Whittington
bullets: Targets the prohibitive cost and accuracy degradation of existing sparse attention beyond 1M tokens.

Introduces Distilled-LSA for adapting pretrained models and Native-LSA for native next-token-loss training.
At 10M tokens, D-LSA substantially accelerates prefill and decode while maintaining similar accuracy across evaluated tasks.
N-LSA matches full-attention accuracy and provides per-layer training speedups at 128k tokens.

papers.selection_reason: Subquadratic sparse attention for ultra-long context via latent hierarchical key selection; directly fits efficient attention and long-context models.
papers.title: Latent Sparse Attention: Towards Subquadratic Ultra-Long Context Attention
papers.tldr: Latent Sparse Attention enables efficient ultra-long-context attention by hierarchically routing queries to learned key clusters instead of examining every key.

papers.abstract: The quadratic scaling of attention is a fundamental bottleneck limiting the long-context capabilities of large language models (LLMs). A variety of approaches have attempted to circumvent this, but they either fail to match attention's expressiveness (e.g., sliding-window or linear attention variants with fixed-size state) or only achieve constant-factor speedups (e.g., sparse attention methods whose indexers themselves scale quadratically). In this paper, we derive an asymptotically subquadratic sparse attention method based on a hierarchical, tree-structured indexer, which we call Zyphra Hierarchical Attention (ZHA). ZHA constructs a tree of recursively compressed key summaries over the KV cache, which future queries traverse from the top down to retrieve a sparse subset of keys. Crucially, by iteratively growing the tree's depth, the total cost including routing and final attention grows sublinearly in sequence length, resulting in overall subquadratic (but superlinear) scaling for attention. We demonstrate that ZHA can be cheaply applied to existing pretrained models with only a short KL distillation training stage over a few billion tokens, and maintains performance on long-context retrieval and challenging reasoning, mathematical, and agentic coding evaluation tasks. Moreover, we show that our method is highly robust to tree geometry including very deep trees of up to 6 levels. Finally, we develop a detailed performance model and show that our approach scales subquadratically, dramatically outperforms competing methods beyond 1 million context, and ultimately has the potential to extend effective context windows to the hundreds of millions or billions of tokens.
authors: Leon Lufkin, Cutter Dawes, Alexander Speicher, Kamesh Krishnamurthy, Tom\'as Figliolia, Beren Millidge
bullets: Addresses quadratic attention cost, which limits long-context scaling.
Builds a hierarchical tree of compressed key summaries that queries traverse to select sparse keys.
Joint routing and attention cost grows subquadratically—sublinear in sequence length for the relevant computation, but still superlinear overall.
Can be added to pretrained models using a short KL-distillation stage and maintains long-context retrieval, reasoning, math, and coding performance.
The authors report strong scaling beyond 1 million tokens and potential context windows of hundreds of millions to billions of tokens; performance depends on the method’s tree-based indexing scope.

figures.caption: Figure 3: Overview of the ZHA architecture: (a) tree construction and (b) sparse routing. During tree construction, for each chunk of contiguous key nodes, we construct a compressed key node at the higher level by an attention-weighted sum of the keys, where the attention is computed with respect to the learned reference queries. In practice, we use multiple reference queries and store the key nodes for each in parallel. This process continues recursively with higher level key nodes being constructed from the summaries of lower levels. During routing, we start at the top of the tree and compute dot-product similarity scores between our query and the key nodes of that level. We select the set of nodes to expand using top-p, and then recursively descend the tree until we reach the leaf nodes corresponding to raw KV cache entries. The union of all the leaves we reach defines the sparse KV cache subset that we dispatch to the main attention.

Figure 8: For a fixed top-p, and hence sparsity level, ZHA (here, R = 1, C = 8, p = 0.75) scales subquadratically according to our decode roofline model, eventually dramatically outperforming both dense attention and the MSA sparse attention variant. Importantly, we have not empirically validated the scaling at these ultra-long context lengths due to the lack of existing LLMs which can operate at these contexts. Because of this, while we can obtain subquadratic latency, it is unclear to what extent reasoning and retrieval performance degrades at the level of depths required for these ultra-long contexts. Latencies are modeled per-token decode times for the attention subsystem of one layer at batch size 1.

papers.abstract: We study whether a language model can help design controllers whose behavior can be formally checked. In proof-carrying evolution (PCE), a search proposes controllers together with their certificates. Their mathematical forms are fixed; a proposer chooses their numerical parameters together. Certificate checks guide selection, and only a certified candidate can be returned. The deployed artifact is a control law and its certificate; the language model is used only during design. We compare four language models with classical search and synthesis on docking under a speed limit, pursuit of a maneuvering target, and attitude control on SO(3), using paired runs and shared proposal allowances. Certificates are checked in exact rational arithmetic during search on the linear problems. On SO(3), the search uses floating-point checks, followed by exact re-verification of every reported champion. The best run of each method also receives Lean 4 proofs of its stated control properties. On the linear problems, the strongest models beat the standard classical baselines on every run, but a classical optimizer that chooses certificates for the same objective closes most of that lead. Among the cited pursuit champions, the ranking does not survive a change from Euler to zero-order-hold dynamics. On SO(3), no model detectably outperforms CMA-ES when mixed with classical mutation. When models write every proposal, one tested model improves on CMA-ES and the other performs worse than its mixed variant. All search medians remain below the hand-tuned law. In a docking control with the objective and mutation operator held fixed, retaining certified candidates yields new certified designs in every run; removing this rule yields none.

papers.abstract: Multi-turn negotiation remains a challenging problem for large language model (LLM) agents. While LLMs can conduct natural-language dialogue, existing benchmarks predominantly assess only agreement rates, overlooking whether negotiated commitments actually create value once executed. To address this gap, we introduce TradeWar, a multi-country simulation benchmark that translates negotiation dialogues into concrete tariff and trade-share policies, enforces capacity and network constraints during settlement, and evaluates outcomes via an Economic Health Index (EHI). To solve this execution-grounded task, we propose TACTIC (Trade-aware Adaptive Consolidation and Theory-of-mind for International Commerce), an agent that iteratively refines its negotiation strategy across episodes-without updating base LLM weights-by leveraging prior experience, opponent behavior, and past settlement outcomes. Despite using zero-shot chain-of-thought (CoT) prompting, PromptLLM attains a 75% agreement rate but only 57.1 final EHI (*100), whereas TACTIC reaches 68.8. Across 20 sequential episodes and three seeds, TACTIC's final EHI improves from 58.2 to 73.2, compared with 65.2 for an ablation without cross-episode updates. Under technology-controls and energy-crisis shocks, TACTIC also exhibits smaller performance degradation than PromptLLM and MemoryLLM. These results indicate that CoT deliberation and interaction memory alone do not fully address delayed execution feedback, whereas settlement-grounded adaptation improves long-horizon negotiation in TradeWar.
authors: Xiangyu Kong, Ruirui Yang, Xia Hou

papers.abstract: Linear attention scales linearly with sequence length, but its finite-state memory can limit long-context retrieval. In gated linear recurrences, memory retention depends on state decay, which is shaped jointly by gate parameters A_log and dt_bias and by input activations. In controlled Gated DeltaNet (GDN) experiments, both parameters remain highly correlated with their initial values after training, highlighting the importance of initialization. Therefore, we introduce Dual-Axis Memory Initialization (DAMI), which jointly configures these parameters before training. DAMI assigns geometric timescales across heads for varied retrieval distances and a low-high-low input-sensitivity profile across layers. A small activation sample calibrates the GDN-family implementation to match both behavioral targets without adding trainable parameters. Across GDN, KDA, GDN2, Mamba-2, and RWKV-7, DAMI improves average RULER-style retrieval accuracy by 5.29 to 16.71 percentage points over the corresponding random-initialization baselines. Performance on language modeling, commonsense reasoning, and 2K real-world retrieval remains broadly comparable to those baselines. Our code is available at https://speedai.com/research/dami.
authors: Zhangchi Feng, Harry Jiang, Yangyifei Luo, Ray Zhang, Richong Zhang

papers.abstract: Large closed-source reasoning models expose only their final answers. The intermediate reasoning that produces those answers is hidden behind API surfaces, tool-call policies, and safety filters. Existing chain-of-thought (CoT) extraction methods assume a side channel: a visible reasoning field, a scratchpad carried through tool calls, or a signed/encrypted reasoning block. We reproduce three representative state-of-the-art extraction methods and find that, on Claude-Sonnet-5.5 accessed through the standard chat-completions interface, all three return zero CoT tokens. The failure is structural rather than a bug: the reasoning field is absent, named tool selection is rejected, free-text scratchpad arguments are filtered, and no replayable reasoning block is exposed. We therefore take a different route. We present RECAST, a reconstruction-based framework that conditions a decoder on the question and the target model's final answer, reconstructs a first-person structured rationale, cleans it, and builds SFT-ready data. To the best of our knowledge, RECAST is the first system to reconstruct CoT from frontier closed models such as Claude-Sonnet-5.5, GPT-6.1, and Gemini 3 without using hidden reasoning channels. We instantiate RECAST on Claude-Sonnet-5.5 and additionally obtain successful qualitative reconstructions on GPT-6.1 and Gemini 3 with the same answer-only protocol. The system is open-source and packaged as an agent skill: one prompt deploys it and runs the complete pipeline to produce SFT-ready CoT data. This preprint describes the system, its threat model, and a controlled artifact validation; it does not claim large-scale benchmark improvements.
authors: Qi Wang, Kang Xu, Chengcheng Wan, Jiangtao Wang
bullets: Existing CoT extraction methods fail on Claude-Sonnet-5.5’s standard chat interface because reasoning fields, tool calls, scratchpads, and replayable blocks are inaccessible or filtered.

papers.abstract: Cultural value alignment requires not only model optimization but also a well-specified target grounded in real-human evidence. Yet how such targets should be grounded in human data remains largely unexplored, raising three fundamental questions: (1) whose values should be represented? (2) where should cultural values be observed? and (3) what signals reveal underlying values? We investigate these questions through Re3Culture, a large-scale dataset linking (i) Representative communities: 700+ human participants across four cultures recruited through cultural-affiliation screening and demographic-aware sampling; (ii) Realistic scenario: culturally sensitive scenarios selected by community members, e.g., family and kinship; and (iii) Revealed value signals: 1,400+ value surveys, 20,000+ topic-grounded behavioral principles and explicit value priorities with responses for 6,000+ situated questions. Our analysis shows why these choices matter for defining the target, with three implications. First, estimating cultural values requires both community affiliation and broad internal coverage. Substituting other cultures or restricting subgroup coverage shifts value estimates. LLM simulations also disproportionately reflect particular subgroups. Second, values must be observed in concrete, community-guided situations. Abstract questionnaire profiles weakly recover situated priorities, and communities differ in which scenarios they identify as culturally value-revealing. Third, value priorities should be elicited explicitly, not learned from response preferences or bottom-line answers alone. Preferences conflate value agreement with other response-level qualities, and similar answers can be derived from different value priorities. By addressing these requirements, Re3Culture provides the first human-grounded resource that explicitly informs target definition for cultural value alignment.

papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are used in many domains, but molecular property prediction with them is still little explored. In this work we evaluate the capability of 7 frontier LLMs to predict molecular properties together with a self-reported uncertainty from in-context examples, and compare them with classical baselines trained on the same molecules. We use 4 datasets and screen each for contamination of the training data of the LLMs: three are clean, and the fourth, ESOL, is memorised by most of the models and serves as a comparison. On the clean datasets every LLM improves with the context, at 30 examples the most accurate one beats every baseline. The requested reasoning effort changes accuracy little. The self-reported uncertainty ranks the prediction errors weakly, with Spearman rank correlations of up to 0.46, about the level reached by the uncertainties of the baselines. Combining uncertainty and prediction, on lipophilicity the most certain half of the best LLM is the most accurate at small context sizes; on BACE and antiviral, and on lipophilicity at large context sizes, the best LLMs are on par with the best baseline. On the contaminated ESOL dataset the LLMs show no improvement with the context size, as expected for a memorised dataset, and their stated uncertainty is smaller on the molecules whose value they recall.
authors: Matthias Busch, Marius Tacke, Tamadur Albaraghtheh, Sviatlana V. Lamaka, Mikhail L. Zheludkevich, Roland C. Aydin, Christian Feiler, Christian J. Cyron
bullets: Seven frontier LLMs were evaluated on four molecular-property datasets against classical baselines trained on the same molecules.

Self-reported uncertainty weakly ranked errors, reaching Spearman correlations of up to 0.46—similar to baseline uncertainty.
On memorized ESOL, context brought no improvement and models reported lower uncertainty for molecules whose values they recalled.

papers.abstract: Task Vectors (TVs) provide a compact way to steer large language models, but they are typically treated as atomized directions merely extracted from hidden states, leaving their internal functional structure poorly understood. Motivated by prior work that decomposes in-context learning into Task Recognition (TR) and Task Learning (TL), we ask whether a single TV can likewise be decomposed into functionally meaningful components. We formulate a TR/TL-based decomposition from candidate-label unembeddings, separating each TV into TR, TL, and residual components, and try to optimize the TR and TL coefficients using Bayesian optimization for more effective intervention. We evaluate this formulation across multiple model families, classification tasks, and both instruction- and demonstration-based TVs. Across these settings, TR/TL-based optimization identifies intervention directions that outperform the original TVs. Although optimization over random directions can also improve performance, TR/TL-based search yields more reliable gains, particularly for instruction-based TVs. Moreover, isolated interventions on the decomposed components produce distinct logit-level effects that are consistent with their intended functional roles. Together, these results suggest that TVs are not monolithic steering directions, but can be decomposed into functionally meaningful components that support both interpretation and control.
authors: Yukiya Horiba, Hakaze Cho, Takahiro Yakoh
bullets: Addresses the limited understanding of task vectors as seemingly atomized steering directions.
Uses candidate-label unembeddings to formulate a TR/TL/residual decomposition and Bayesian optimization of component coefficients.
Evaluates the approach across multiple model families, classification tasks, and instruction- or demonstration-based task vectors.
The optimized TR/TL interventions outperform original task vectors, with especially reliable gains for instruction-based vectors.
Component-specific interventions produce distinct logit effects consistent with their intended functional roles.

papers.abstract: Clinical trial failures are a major barrier to efficient drug development, incurring substantial costs and delaying patient access to effective therapies. Structured approaches such as the Hierarchical Interaction Network (HINT) predict trial outcomes by explicitly modelling interactions between drugs, diseases and protocols, but make limited use of the free text in trial registrations. We evaluate two domain-specific language models, BioBERT (108M parameters) and BioMistral (7B parameters), for phase-level outcome prediction on the TOP benchmark (12,477 trials), representing each trial as text built from ten ClinicalTrials.gov fields. We compare fine-tuning (full fine-tuning for BioBERT, low-rank adaptation for BioMistral) with probing, in which the pretrained model is frozen and only a lightweight classifier is trained on its embeddings. On the held-out test set of each phase, all four language-model variants achieved higher ROC-AUC (0.613--0.772) and PR-AUC (0.649--0.901) than the published HINT results, corresponding to relative PR-AUC gains of 10--20\%. F1 differences were small and mixed, and no model, including HINT, clearly exceeded the F1 of a trivial classifier that predicts success for every trial. Under the configurations tested, probing performed comparably to fine-tuning: fine-tuned models scored highest on ROC-AUC and PR-AUC in Phases I and II, and frozen BioMistral embeddings in Phase III (ROC-AUC 0.772; PR-AUC 0.901), although most differences between variants were below 0.03 and were not tested for significance. These results suggest that pretrained biomedical representations already encode signal relevant to trial outcome, and that probing is a computationally cheaper alternative to fine-tuning for this task.
authors: Burak Bakkar, Hana Moalla, Mohamed Salem Jedidi, Haifa Ben Messaoud, Nicolas Lopez Carranza
bullets: Clinical-trial failure motivates better phase-level outcome prediction using information in registration text.
BioBERT and BioMistral represented trials as text from ten ClinicalTrials.gov fields and were evaluated with fine-tuning or frozen-embedding probing.
All four variants exceeded published HINT results in ROC-AUC and PR-AUC, with reported relative PR-AUC gains of 10–20%.
Fine-tuning was strongest in Phases I–II, while frozen BioMistral embeddings performed best in Phase III; most variant differences were small and untested for significance.
F1 gains were limited: no approach clearly surpassed the trivial always-success classifier on F1.

papers.abstract: Language models face two opposing concerns: monoculture, in which models err in correlated ways, and multiplicity, in which equally accurate models make conflicting decisions. The rise of reasoning models has complicated this debate: On the one hand, reasoning may increase model agreement if models anchor on the same salient features or follow similar reasoning paths. On the other hand, stochastic reasoning traces may introduce additional branch points leading to more diverse predictions. We resolve this tension by distinguishing reasoning as an intervention from reasoning as an observed behavior. We compare agreement under controlled changes in reasoning effort with agreement across observed reasoning lengths, measuring both against the agreement expected from model accuracy. Across nine models from two developers and three classification tasks, enabling reasoning increases agreement between models evaluated on the same individuals. Yet the individuals who elicit longer reasoning traces receive less consistent predictions across models. Both patterns persist after accounting for differences in accuracy. Asking models to reason more thus promotes agreement, while observing them reason longer signals disagreement.
bullets: The study addresses the tension between correlated model errors (monoculture) and conflicting decisions among similarly accurate models (multiplicity).
It separates reasoning as a controlled intervention from reasoning as an observed behavior.
Across nine models, two developers, and three classification tasks, increased reasoning effort raises agreement on the same individuals.
Individuals producing longer reasoning traces receive less consistent predictions across models.
Both effects remain after accounting for model accuracy.

papers.selection_reason: Investigates reasoning behavior in LLMs, a core aspect of modern LLM research and architecture.
papers.title: Does Reasoning Make Language Models Agree?
papers.tldr: Reasoning has opposite effects on language-model agreement depending on how it is studied: prompting more reasoning increases agreement, while longer observed reasoning traces signal less consistent predictions.

papers.abstract: Sparse tuning is widely used to adapt large language models due to its parameter efficiency. However, its effectiveness depends not only on the number of trainable parameters, but also on the feature-interaction topology of the sparse update's structural support. Limited or uneven connectivity in this support may isolate subsets of feature dimensions, forming information islands that restrict direct task-specific interactions through the trainable update. To address this issue, we propose Small-World Induced Fine-Tuning (SWIFT), a sparse tuning framework inspired by small-world connectivity. SWIFT combines block-diagonal sparse updates for local feature mixing with a fixed deterministic scattering permutation that routes the mixed outputs across feature groups without additional trainable parameters. We further show theoretically that certain random sparse-update models and block-diagonal updates can exhibit information islands, whereas a sufficiently scattering permutation guarantees positive block-level expansion when the trainable block-diagonal factor consists of equal-sized, structurally dense square blocks. Extensive experiments on commonsense reasoning, natural language generation, and image classification demonstrate that SWIFT outperforms the evaluated parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) baselines on average and can match or surpass full fine-tuning. Implementation is available at https://github.com/xianchaoguan/SWIFT
authors: Xianchao Guan, Zijun Xiong, Yifeng Wang, Yubo Cui, Yaowei Wang, Guo-Sen Xie, Xin Li, Zheng Zhang
bullets: Sparse tuning can suffer from limited feature connectivity, creating information islands in the update structure.
SWIFT uses block-diagonal updates for local feature mixing and a fixed scattering permutation to route information across feature groups without extra trainable parameters.

Experiments across commonsense reasoning, text generation, and image classification show SWIFT outperforms evaluated PEFT baselines on average and can match or exceed full fine-tuning.

papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) acquire extensive factual knowledge during pre-training, which may include sensitive, private, or copyrighted information, motivating the development of unlearning methods that selectively remove specific knowledge while preserving general capabilities. However, existing approaches typically optimize entire responses without explicitly identifying the knowledge to be forgotten, resulting in coarse and uncontrolled forgetting. To address this, we revisit the forgetting target of LLM unlearning and introduce Knowledge Association (KA), which characterizes the association between a query context and its target knowledge and is instantiated by the corresponding conditional predictive distribution, as the fundamental target of forgetting. Based on KA, we propose Knowledge Association Reinforcement Unlearning (KARU), a unified reinforcement learning framework that suppresses forgotten knowledge associations while preserving retained ones. Specifically, KARU derives complementary mechanisms from the KA-based formulation: token-level reward construction for finer-grained forgetting supervision, distribution-level regularization for precise knowledge suppression, and proximity-aware retain sampling to mitigate collateral degradation. Experiments across diverse LLMs on representative benchmarks demonstrate that KARU consistently improves forgetting effectiveness over existing baselines while maintaining comparable retention performance and general utility.
authors: Wutong Xu, Yun Qu, Haiyan Feng, Qi Wang, Xiangyang Ji
bullets: Existing unlearning methods can forget coarsely because they optimize complete responses without isolating the knowledge to remove.
The paper defines Knowledge Association (KA) as the conditional predictive distribution linking a query context to target knowledge.
KARU uses reinforcement learning with token-level rewards, distribution-level suppression, and proximity-aware sampling of retained knowledge.
Experiments across diverse LLMs and benchmarks show improved forgetting effectiveness with comparable retention and general utility.
The method targets selective knowledge removal, with scope determined by the identified knowledge associations.

papers.title: What Should LLMs Forget: Reinforcement Unlearning of Knowledge Associations
papers.tldr: KARU treats context–knowledge associations—not whole responses—as the target of LLM unlearning, enabling more precise forgetting while preserving retained knowledge and general utility.

papers.abstract: Agent systems built on local large language models are increasingly marketed through the vocabulary of cognitive architecture: modules named global workspace, theory of mind, causal reasoning, or active inference are listed as features, and the presence of the name is taken as the presence of the mechanism. We ask the prior question -- does the named computation actually happen -- and contribute a transferable verification method for the claim-implementation gap: a four-question static audit protocol with line-number evidence and call-chain tracing, demonstrated on two systems. We audit a system claiming 25 cognitive mechanisms, pre-register falsifiable predictions for 11 modules and execute the interventions, replicate the protocol on the IIT-phi core of a second, independent system with its own pre-committed falsification criteria, and run two repair experiments as positive controls. In 18 of 25 modules the computed value never reaches any production output; three idle-wiring shapes new to the dead-code and code-smell literatures emerge (connected-but-never-called, called-but-inert, called-but-content-blind). Of 61 frozen criteria across 12 interventions, 53 were confirmed, two partially adjudicated, five falsified, one adjudication-ambiguous. Repairs raised planner task success from 0.028 to 1.000 and cut state-controller error by 52%. Module names and module computations must be audited as independent claims; the protocol and the five-class failure taxonomy are reusable for the claim-implementation gap at two-system, case-level depth.
authors: Peter Chen, Ni Zhang, Ying Xu, Siyuan Zhang
bullets: Audits 25 claimed cognitive-architecture mechanisms using static code tracing, falsifiable predictions, interventions, replication, and repair controls.
In 18 of 25 modules, computed values never reached production outputs; three previously undescribed idle-wiring patterns were identified.
Across 12 interventions and 61 frozen criteria, 53 were confirmed, five falsified, two partially adjudicated, and one remained ambiguous.
Repair experiments improved planner task success and reduced state-controller error, showing that implementation defects can materially affect behavior.
Findings are case-level across two systems; the authors argue module names and actual computations must be evaluated independently.

papers.selection_reason: Develops a transferable verification protocol to audit whether LLM-based agents actually implement claimed cognitive mechanisms (e.g., Theory of Mind), addressing the claim-implementation gap.
papers.title: Real Computation or Merely Naming? A Pre-Registered Mechanism Audit of 25 Cognitive-Architecture Modules in an LLM-Based Agent System
papers.tldr: A pre-registered audit finds that many named cognitive modules in LLM agents do not perform meaningful computation, and offers a reusable method for verifying implementation claims.

papers.abstract: We release Saidzoda-Tajik-LFM-2.6B, a Tajik adaptation of the 2.6B-parameter hybrid model LFM2.5-2.6B-Base, built for tool calling in Tajik on modest hardware. The recipe has two stages: LoRA continued pretraining (CPT) on 1,485,319 cleaned Tajik web documents for 3 epochs, then one epoch of supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on a mix of machine-translated Tajik tool calls, English tool calls kept as replay, and Tajik instructions. On a 174-item tool-calling test set built from BFCL v3 and machine-translated to Tajik, strict full-call accuracy on Tajik prompts rises from 20.69 for the base model to 64.14 (paired difference +43.45 points, 95% interval +35.2 to +51.7); a lenient parser that also accepts the base model's own call formats puts the base at 31.72. English shows no detectable change (76.55 and 77.24). Every CPT checkpoint scores zero: CPT removes the native tool-call format and, as the lenient re-scoring shows, part of the skill itself. Outside tool calling, accuracy on a Tajik knowledge benchmark rises from 28.0 to 35.0, Belebele Tajik shows no significant change, and English MMLU falls from 60.8 to 52.5. The model is not a general Tajik assistant. It almost never declines when no tool fits (6.9% correct on Tajik, against 31.0% for the base under the lenient parser), it is weak at multi-turn calls, and its calls should be checked before they are executed. We describe the data, the training settings and every evaluation in enough detail to repeat them.
authors: Tohir Saidzoda, Nekruz Maxudov, Bedil Karimov, Abubakr Abdullozoda, Amin Jalilov, Jonibek Kishvarov, Rahmonali Sharipov, Mariyamkhon Shodyeva
bullets: The model is adapted from LFM2.5-2.6B-Base for Tajik tool calling on modest hardware.
LoRA continued pretraining uses 1,485,319 cleaned Tajik web documents, followed by SFT on translated Tajik tool calls, English replay data, and Tajik instructions.
Strict Tajik full-call accuracy increases from 20.69 to 64.14, while English performance remains essentially unchanged.
All continued-pretraining checkpoints score zero on tool calling, indicating loss of the native format and some underlying skill—not just formatting mismatch.
Knowledge accuracy improves, but English MMLU declines; the model is weak at refusals and multi-turn calls, so generated calls require validation.

papers.selection_reason: Details the adaptation of a hybrid model to Tajik for tool calling using LoRA continued pretraining and supervised fine-tuning, analyzing the effects of CPT on model capabilities.
papers.title: Saidzoda-Tajik-LFM-2.6B: Adapting a 2.6B Hybrid Model to Tajik Tool Calling, and What Continued Pretraining Takes Away
papers.tldr: A two-stage LoRA adaptation substantially improves Tajik tool calling, but continued pretraining erases the base model’s native tool-call format and harms several broader capabilities.

papers.abstract: Unlike autoregressive (AR) models, diffusion language models (DLMs) permit parallel token updates, flexible generation, and bidirectional attention, but leading systems rely on costly pretraining or full-model fine-tuning. We present Build Your Own DLM (BYOD), a generalizable LoRA-only recipe for parameter-efficient AR-to-DLM conversion. Without architecture-specific tuning, BYOD induces diffusion generation in Gemma 2 9B, Llama 3.1 8B, Qwen2.5 7B, and Ministral 8B; to our knowledge, this is the first reported AR-to-DLM conversion of a Mistral model. The adapters comprise 4.1-5.8% of final parameters while every base-model parameter remains frozen; each 25,000-iteration conversion needs at most 102.4M tokens, processed in 3.1-4.0 hours on one Google Colab GPU. All four models generate from fully masked sequences, use bidirectional context in a controlled attention test, and retain substantial parent-model knowledge. BYOD-Gemma is the strongest BYOD conversion on our nine-task evaluation, reaching 50.6% average accuracy compared with 51.9% for LLaDA 8B Instruct in the same harness. Open-generation quality at low network function evaluation (NFE) budgets remains the principal limitation: BYOD perplexity is 8.3-11.1 versus 4.1 for LLaDA and 2.2-3.0 for the AR parents when generating 128 tokens in 64 steps. To enable further experimentation and inspection, we provide a standalone training and evaluation implementation and interactive demos for all four conversions. BYOD thus provides a practical route for extending diffusion generation to other existing model families while identifying the gap that efficient conversion must next close.
authors: Ruurd J. A. Kuiper, Robert A. Bagheri
bullets: Addresses the high pretraining and full-fine-tuning costs of building diffusion language models.
Uses an architecture-agnostic, LoRA-only conversion recipe with all base-model parameters frozen.
Demonstrated on Gemma 2, Llama 3.1, Qwen2.5, and Ministral; the latter is reported as the first Mistral AR-to-DLM conversion.
Converted models support fully masked generation, bidirectional context, and retain substantial parent-model knowledge.
Task performance is competitive, but open-generation quality at low sampling budgets remains the main limitation.

papers.selection_reason: Parameter-efficient LoRA-only conversion of autoregressive LLMs to diffusion language models is directly relevant to LLM architecture advances and training-efficiency methods.
papers.title: BYOD: Build Your Own DLM - Efficient Autoregressive-to-Diffusion Language Model Conversion
papers.tldr: BYOD converts pretrained autoregressive language models into diffusion language models using only lightweight LoRA adapters, enabling efficient experimentation without modifying base-model weights.

papers.abstract: Language agents increasingly tackle long-horizon tasks in interactive environments, where actions often depend on latent preconditions. The core difficulty is not trajectory length but recovery: when a prerequisite is missing or an earlier decomposition fails, trying another plausible action rarely helps. ReAct and later reflection or adaptive-planning methods support local correction, but express recovery as free-form text, with no explicit control state linking the terminal goal, the active goal, and the failure source. We introduce the Verify--Backtrack Loop (VBL), a training-free extension of ReAct that turns precondition discovery and failure diagnosis into structured planning-state updates. VBL maintains the task decomposition as a bounded goal stack and, on goal activation, execution failure, or material state change, jointly verifies two horizons---whether the active goal contributes to the terminal goal and whether it is feasible in the current state. These dual-horizon judgments, combined with typed failure attribution, trigger explicit operations---Push, Pop, retry, or BacktrackTo the parent. We evaluate VBL with Qwen3.5-9B, GPT-4o, and DeepSeek-V3.2 on AppWorld, ALFWorld, and ScienceWorld. VBL improves over ReAct and reflection-based control on every backbone--benchmark pair. On the challenging AppWorld setting, it improves task success by up to 22.07 percentage points over ReAct. Ablations show that removing either verification or diagnosis degrades performance, in several settings below ReAct, confirming that the two mechanisms are complementary. These results show that reliable long-horizon interaction benefits from revising the planning state, not merely the next action.
authors: Mingyang Liu, Qingcan Kang, Shixiong Kai, Tao Zhong, Mingxuan Yuan, Xin Li, Linqi Song
bullets: Targets failed prerequisites and flawed decompositions, rather than relying on another plausible action.
Extends ReAct with a bounded goal stack and dual-horizon checks for goal relevance and current feasibility.
Uses typed failure attribution to trigger Push, Pop, retry, or BacktrackTo-parent operations.
Improves over ReAct and reflection-based control across all tested backbone–benchmark pairs; AppWorld gains reach up to 22.07 percentage points over ReAct.
Ablations show verification and diagnosis are complementary, with removing either sometimes reducing performance below ReAct.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Control structures compared. (1) ReAct interleaves thought, action, and observation in a linear loop. (2) ReflAct replaces the thought with reflection on the current state relative to the task goal, but the loop stays linear. (3) VBL maintains an explicit goal stack: VERIFY checks alignment and readiness when due is set (on activation, after failure, or after a material state change), a completed goal is removed with POP, and a failure is routed through DIAGNOSE to one of PUSH (insert a prerequisite), a local retry, or BACKTRACKTO (resume from the parent). The executor receives the root task text together with the active goal—here g2—not the full stack.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces the Verify--Backtrack Loop (VBL) for long-horizon language agents, a training-free method for structured precondition recovery and failure diagnosis in planning states.
papers.title: Verify--Backtrack Loop: Structured Precondition Recovery for Long-Horizon Language Agents
papers.tldr: VBL improves long-horizon language-agent recovery by explicitly verifying goals and diagnosing failures to drive structured backtracking.

papers.abstract: Deploying 6G network slices across administrative domains requires an online decision for each arriving request: which domain hosts each virtual network function, how traffic crosses domain boundaries, and whether the slice is admitted. This joint decision problem is NP-hard under continuous arrivals. Experiments on a parametrized family of multi-domain topologies show that no fixed planning strategy dominates across all regimes: the performance ranking reverses between topology classes, and feasible placements exist for most rejected requests but remain undiscovered. These findings identify the plan layer as the decisive performance lever. We introduce ORION, a hierarchical orchestrator in which two LLM agents translate service intents into structured requests and generate abstract placement plans. A cooperative multi-agent RL coordinator selects the cross-domain partition, treating the plan as a persistent soft prior, while per-domain agents place the functions. ORION main contribution lies at the plan layer: an outcome-driven episodic memory that records, for each completed attempt, the network-condition profile, the proposed plan, and its verified feasibility outcome. The memory feeds verified successes and labelled failures back to the planner, thereby closing the adaptation loop using deployment feasibility rather than a scalar reward assigned to the planner's own proposals. To isolate the effect of the plan quality, we evaluate the planner on held-out topology families while keeping the downstream selection and execution mechanisms fixed. Under this controlled setting, the proposed memory improves admission by $4.6$--$11.5$ percentage points over the same planner without memory, while importance-based retention accounts for most of the improvement over a first-in-first-out store.
authors: Mahmoud S. Mayaleh, Fetia Bannour, Nour-El-Houda Yellas
bullets: Multi-domain slice placement jointly decides function hosting, inter-domain routing, and admission under an NP-hard online setting.
Fixed planning strategies do not generalize across topology regimes, and many rejected requests may have feasible but undiscovered placements.
ORION combines LLM-based intent and plan generation with multi-agent RL for cross-domain selection and per-domain function placement.
Its outcome-driven episodic memory stores network conditions, plans, and verified success or failure outcomes to guide future planning.
On held-out topology families, memory improves admission by 4.6–11.5 percentage points; importance-based retention outperforms FIFO storage.

papers.abstract: Automatic assessment of textual CEFR levels is an important task in educational natural language processing. However, accurate CEFR level prediction remains challenging due to the naturally imbalanced distribution of CEFR levels and the ambiguous boundaries between adjacent levels. To address these challenges, we propose a unified training objective that combines focal loss with supervised contrastive learning. Focal loss mitigates class imbalance by emphasizing underrepresented and difficult examples, while supervised contrastive learning learns more discriminative representations by encouraging intra-class compactness and inter-class separation. We evaluate the proposed method on sentence- and document-level CEFR assessment in both monolingual and multilingual settings. Experimental results demonstrate that our method consistently outperforms strong baselines across all settings, establishing new state-of-the-art performance on multiple CEFR assessment benchmarks.
bullets: Addresses class imbalance and ambiguous boundaries between adjacent CEFR levels.
Combines focal loss to emphasize difficult or underrepresented examples with supervised contrastive learning for more discriminative representations.
Evaluates sentence- and document-level assessment in monolingual and multilingual settings.
Consistently outperforms strong baselines and achieves state-of-the-art results on multiple CEFR benchmarks.

papers.abstract: This study investigates the effectiveness of large pre-trained language models (LLMs) for knowledge entity relation extraction (KERE) from academic papers. Existing studies have examined individual types of LLM-based strategies and evaluated model performance using metrics such as precision and recall. To provide a broader evaluation, this study investigates multiple strategies, including closed-source LLM-based CoT prompting, LoRA-adapted open-source LLMs, LLM-enhanced small pre-trained language models (SLMs), and SLM-enhanced closed-source LLMs. In addition, this study introduces two strategies, namely SLM-enhanced open-source LLMs and closed-source LLM-enhanced open-source LLMs. These strategies are evaluated from multiple perspectives, including metrics, their ability to mitigate errors observed in SLMs, and potential directions for model optimization. This study manually constructs two annotated datasets in the NLP domain, covering Abstract and Full-Text datasets. Experimental results show that the LoRA-adapted T5 model achieves the highest macro F1 scores of 0.7408 and 0.7013 on the Abstract and Full-Text datasets, respectively. SLMs also benefit from LLM-generated entity descriptions under the LLM-enhanced SLM strategy. Error analysis further reveals that the effectiveness of LLM-based strategies in mitigating SLM errors varies across error types. Based on the identified limitations and error patterns of these strategies, several optimization directions are proposed. In addition, combining strategies with different error patterns further improves KERE performance.
bullets: Compares closed-source LLM prompting, LoRA-adapted open-source LLMs, SLM–LLM enhancement, and newly proposed hybrid strategies.
Introduces two manually annotated NLP datasets covering academic abstracts and full-text articles.
LoRA-adapted T5 achieves macro F1 scores of 0.7408 on abstracts and 0.7013 on full text.
LLM-generated entity descriptions improve SLM performance, though error mitigation varies by error type.
Combining strategies with complementary error patterns further improves KERE performance.

papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can generate structured outputs, but existing constrained-decoding methods mainly enforce syntax and cannot directly enforce satisfaction of a formal specification. We introduce a neuro-symbolic, specification-guided decoding framework that combines LLM generation with symbolic reasoning. At each step, the framework refines the decoding grammar by filtering out values that cannot be extended to an output satisfying the specification. We present a forward-only variant that guarantees specification satisfaction by construction, and a backtracking variant that revises earlier feasible choices when their downstream consequences leave only values that the LLM itself judges unsuitable. The framework is model-agnostic, requires no retraining, and builds on existing grammar-constrained decoding mechanisms. Experiments on configuration and constraint-solving benchmarks show that the forward-only variant reliably produces specification-compliant outputs while reducing repeated LLM inference compared with rejection sampling and incurring modest symbolic-reasoning overhead. The backtracking variant further reduces cases in which the model is forced to select values that it has itself judged unsuitable, thereby substantially improving adherence to the LLM's stated interpretation of the prompt.
authors: Alessandro Previti, Konstantinos Vandikas, Mario Alviano, Mats Carlsson, Albin Larsson Forsberg, Alexandros Nikou, Athanasios Karapantelakis, Aneta Vulgarakis
bullets: Refines the decoding grammar at each step by removing values that cannot lead to a specification-satisfying output.
A forward-only variant guarantees compliance by construction and reduces repeated LLM inference versus rejection sampling.
A backtracking variant revises earlier choices when later constraints leave only values the LLM considers unsuitable.
Model-agnostic and compatible with existing grammar-constrained decoding, with modest symbolic-reasoning overhead.
Evaluated on configuration and constraint-solving benchmarks, improving specification adherence and alignment with the model’s prompt interpretation.

papers.abstract: Long-context diffusion repeatedly pays for both token interaction and feed-forward computation. We formulate these costs as two separate budgets: the edges available to an attention graph and the experts activated for each token. This view connects local, dilated, and global attention with conditional expert computation without assuming that sparsity alone preserves document-level information. We specify normalized masked attention, distinguish denoising depth from sampling iterations, and derive graph and compute bounds. A reported sparse-expert configuration, denoted DualBudget, is analyzed across scientific summarization, multi-hop question answering, dialogue, and sentence-pair prediction. All supplied table measurements are retained. The length study shows gains over the listed baselines through 16K, together with measurable degradation as length increases. Ablations reveal mixed changes across the three reported scores, while the cost record indicates a 20% reduction relative to DiffuSeq under an unspecified timing convention. The analysis separates these observations from unmeasured claims about training speed, absorbing states, global coherence, and deployment memory.
authors: Alexandros Christoforos, Chadbourne Davis, Paul Raj
bullets: Models long-context diffusion costs using two budgets: attention-graph edges and activated feed-forward experts.
Unifies local, dilated, and global attention with conditional expert computation without assuming sparsity preserves document-level information.
Defines normalized masked attention, distinguishes denoising depth from sampling iterations, and derives graph and compute bounds.
Evaluates the DualBudget configuration on scientific summarization, multi-hop QA, dialogue, and sentence-pair prediction.
Results show gains over listed baselines through 16K, mixed ablation effects, and measurable degradation as sequence length grows.

papers.abstract: While prior work has highlighted that systematic nation-level bias in large language models (LLMs) can pose operational risks for international relations (IR) applications, many existing evaluations still lack a clearly specified unbiased reference (ground truth), limiting fully quantitative and cross-setting measurement. Using an expanded corpus of 722 official UN Security Council (UNSC) records, we measure nation-level bias with five complementary tests, thereby extending prior approaches to cover a broader set of bias expression channels: opinion ranking (WOW), association sorting (AK+-), vote simulation (PVS), opposition attribution (F-Oppose), and framing (Headliner). To enable grounded bias evaluation, we explicitly define an unbiased status for each test; in particular, for WOW and AK+- where ground truth is difficult to specify, we propose an action-based pseudo unbiased status derived from observable voting behavior to construct a quantifiable baseline. Benchmarking 4 LLMs (GPT-4o-mini, Llama 3.3-70B, Mistral-22B-Small, and Qwen3-30B) across the five permanent members of the UNSC, we find a test-agnostic macro-pattern: relative to the reference baselines defined for each test, model outputs lean toward the opposition (red) side for China and Russia and toward the supportive (blue) side for the U.K., the U.S., and France. These results underscore the need to audit IR-facing LLM deployments with grounded, multi-test benchmarks tied to explicit reference points.
authors: Jonghyeon Choi, Yeonjun Choi, Beakcheol Jang
bullets: Evaluates nation-level bias using 722 official UN Security Council records and five complementary tests: opinion ranking, association sorting, vote simulation, opposition attribution, and framing.
Defines test-specific unbiased reference statuses to support quantitative, cross-setting comparisons.
Introduces action-based pseudo-unbiased baselines for opinion ranking and association sorting, derived from observable voting behavior.
Across four evaluated LLMs, outputs lean opposition-oriented for China and Russia, and supportive-oriented for the U.K., U.S., and France.
Highlights the need for grounded, multi-test audits of LLMs used in international-relations applications.
