papers.abstract: Recursive textual memory can carry earlier errors into later updates, yet task performance alone does not establish memory reliability. We define self-consistency bias as the persistence of incorrect claims already present in the incoming memory. We present KEEPER, a comparative analysis of four auxiliary objectives along information-content and update-sensitivity axes within a shared recursive interface, examining how supervision targets relate to agent performance. Among evaluated conditions, reward-related prediction achieve the highest task performance before and after offline reinforcement learning, outperforming joint supervision. A claim-level analysis of one baseline trajectory documents error persistence despite corrective observations. Together, these analyses motivate evaluating error persistence and valid-information retention alongside task outcomes.
authors: Jinkyeong Choi, Chaebin Jeong, Junsung Jeon, Donghyeon Park
bullets: Introduces self-consistency bias: the persistence of incorrect claims in incoming memory.
Compares four auxiliary objectives by information content and update sensitivity within a shared recursive interface.
Reward-related prediction achieves the highest task performance before and after offline reinforcement learning among evaluated conditions.
A claim-level analysis shows that errors can persist despite corrective observations.
Motivates tracking error persistence and valid-information retention alongside task outcomes.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of auxiliary memory supervision and evaluation. We compare behavioral cloning (BC) alone, BC with each objective, and BC with all four. (b) Recursive inference, shared across conditions with auxiliary objectives inactive. The generated memory keeps a valid fact but also an incorrect claim inherited from pt−1 (self-consistency bias), which misleads the policy; error persistence is therefore evaluated together with valid-fact retention. papers.abstract: Supervised fine-tuning of Model Context Protocol (MCP) agents is typically conducted on a static data distribution, which fails to adapt to the student's evolving capabilities and leaves newly exposed weaknesses insufficiently addressed. To address these challenges, we propose \method, an agent--data mutual evolution framework that enables MCP agents to improve through a closed loop of task evolution, trajectory evolution, and supervised fine-tuning. Specifically, \method\ assesses the student's established capabilities and capability gaps from rollout feedback to identify learning targets. Task evolution then translates these targets into executable tasks by adapting the instructions and observable environment states of compatible verified seed tasks while keeping their verifiers aligned. To provide reliable and efficient demonstrations for these tasks, trajectory evolution uses reusable skills to recover failed teacher rollouts and refine successful ones. The resulting task--trajectory pairs are used to fine-tune the student, while accepted tasks seed subsequent evolution. To close the loop, we re-evaluate the updated student and use its feedback to guide the next round of data evolution. Experiments on Toolathlon, MCPMark, and MCP-Atlas demonstrate consistent improvements over the initial student, yielding absolute gains of 16.5\%, 10.2\%, and 12.6\%, respectively. Project page: https://github.com/xagao/EvoMCP.
authors: Xuanang Gao, Kepeng Lin, Xinyan Shi, Yong Deng, Shuheng Shen, Changhua Meng, Xiaofeng Wu, Jie Yang, Wei Liu
bullets: Addresses the limits of static supervised fine-tuning data for evolving MCP agents.
Uses rollout feedback to identify capability gaps and learning targets.
Evolves verified seed tasks while preserving aligned verifiers, then recovers or refines teacher trajectories with reusable skills.
Fine-tunes the student on evolved task–trajectory pairs and repeats the process using new feedback.
Reports absolute gains of 16.5% on Toolathlon, 10.2% on MCPMark, and 12.6% on MCP-Atlas over the initial student.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes a co-evolution framework for agents and training data, addressing the static data distribution problem in agent fine-tuning. This is a form of test-time adaptation and continual learning for LLM agents.
papers.title: EvoMCP: Co-evolving MCP agents and training data
papers.tldr: EvoMCP co-evolves MCP-agent tasks and training trajectories in a feedback loop, improving agents by continually targeting newly revealed capability gaps.

papers.abstract: Gated Delta Networks (GDNs) offer linear-time sequence modeling, yet long-context prefill remains costly due to dense intra-chunk computation, recurrent-state updates, and intermediate state storage. We introduce SparseGDN, a hardware-aware framework that combines structured intra-chunk approximation with input-dependent recurrent-event selection while producing outputs for every token. A block-adjacent solver reduces local Delta-solve computation, while a dynamic selector allocates recurrent-update budgets across head pairs. The GPU implementation materializes updates only for selected events and reconstructs token outputs using compact state snapshots and group-local interactions, reducing computation and memory traffic. We evaluate SparseGDN on Qwen3.5-4B and Qwen3.5-9B across RULER tasks and context lengths from 4K to 128K. Retaining approximately 29% of recurrent events on average, SparseGDN achieves 1.50-1.94x GDN-core prefill speedups over native FLA kernels, including online selection overhead.
authors: Jiedong Zhuang, Peng Zhao, Jialin Tang, Haoji Hu
bullets: Targets the high cost of dense intra-chunk computation, recurrent-state updates, and intermediate storage in long-context GDN prefill.
Uses a block-adjacent solver for approximate local Delta computation and an input-dependent selector for recurrent-event allocation across head pairs.
Materializes only selected updates and reconstructs token outputs from compact state snapshots and group-local interactions.
On Qwen3.5-4B/9B across RULER and 4K–128K contexts, retaining about 29% of recurrent events yields 1.50–1.94× GDN-core prefill speedups over native FLA kernels, including selection overhead.

figures.caption: Figure 3 End-to-end SparseGDN execution pipeline. The block-adjacent intra-chunk kernel computes transformed values U, compact update coefficients, and selector scores. The dynamic selector converts these scores into a structured event mask. Only selected events trigger deferred W materialization and recurrent-state updates, producing compact event states. During output reconstruction, the mapped output kernel retrieves the appropriate preceding event state from HBM and applies the accumulated gap decay, while computing group-local interactions and producing outputs for every token.

Figure 1 GDN-core prefill latency across context lengths for Qwen3.5-9B and Qwen3.5-4B. Compared with FLA GDN, SparseGDN additionally includes the online selector overhead. Latency is aggregated over all 24 GDN layers. SparseGDN reduces latency at every context length, reaching 1.93× and 1.94× speedup at 128K for the 9B and 4B models, respectively. Lower is better.

Figure 9 Accuracy--efficiency trade-off across retention budgets. Each panel plots the aggregate RULER score difference ∆, defined in Table 3, against the geometric mean GDN-core speedup over 4K–128K. Point labels show measured recurrent-event keep rates. Solid lines connect nondominated configurations among the evaluated sparse operating points. The cross marks the approximately 49%-keep configuration, which is dominated by the approximately 39%-keep configuration for both models under these aggregate metrics. Speedups include online selection. Higher and farther right is better.

Figure 5 Dynamic event selection and packing. Here, ZBi denotes the i-th 16-token block of the pre-activation output-gate tensor Z within a chunk. Chunk scores determine the retention order within each head pair. Recurrent lifetime and output-visibility proxies weight the estimated gains from larger budgets, which determine the low-, medium-, and high-retention tiers. The example assigns 9, 4, and 3 pairs to these tiers. Selected events are packed in temporal order into CSR chains for recurrent execution.

Figure 11 Complete-model prefill peak allocated memory across context lengths. Measurements use BF16, batch size one, use_cache=True. The shaded region shows the absolute memory saved by SparseGDN wherever both paths complete. The dashed line marks the nominal 80 GB device capacity as a reference. Crosses indicate Native OOM at 256K and are placed on this reference line for display; they do not represent measured allocation peaks. SparseGDN completes at that length for both models. Lower is better.

Figure 7 Per-stage GDN-core prefill latency. The top and bottom rows show Qwen3.5-4B and Qwen3.5-9B, respectively. The left column compares native Intra with SparseGDN Intra plus online Selector; the middle and right columns compare H and O. For SparseGDN, H includes deferred W materialization. Each component reports the median of per-iteration CUDA-event times summed over all 24 GDN layers. The stacked Intra-plus-Selector bars sum the two component medians. Boxed values denote the corresponding native-to-sparse latency ratios. Lower latency is better.

Figure 8 GDN-core speedup across batch sizes and context lengths. Speedup is Native/Sparse, includes online selection, and uses batch latencies aggregated over all 24 GDN layers. Crosses mark configurations without a paired speedup because Native runs out of memory. Crosses are placed at a fixed height for display and do not represent measured speedups. The corresponding sparse-only outcomes are detailed in Table 2. Every completed paired configuration favors SparseGDN. Higher is better.

Figure 2 Two empirical structures observed in layer 16 of native-dense Qwen3.5-4B on an 8K RULER input (niah_multikey_3, row 0). (a) Adjacent chunk-boundary states are frequently nearly stationary, while the magnitudes of their changes vary substantially across value heads. (b) The left panel shows |M−1 − I|, averaged over 123 complete 64-token chunks and all 32 value heads. Here M is the native Delta-solve matrix defined in Section 2.3; subtracting I removes the unit diagonal, and absolute values are taken elementwise before averaging. The coefficients concentrate near the causal diagonal and weaken across more distant token blocks. This observed locality motivates the block-adjacent approximation, whose computation support is shown in the right panel.

Figure 6 Tier-aware scheduling of heterogeneous recurrent event chains. High-, medium-, and low-retention head pairs induce event chains with different workloads. Scheduling them in physical-head order can place a long high-tier chain behind shorter tasks, creating an SM straggler and extending kernel completion time (left). SparseGDN orders chains by expected workload and uses event-count-adaptive execution to distribute them across SMs (right), reducing load imbalance and tail latency. The red dashed line denotes kernel completion.

papers.abstract: Growing submission volumes have renewed interest in using large language models (LLMs) to support peer review. It remains unclear how such evaluation should be structured, how much the model matters, and whether LLM scores predict research impact. We evaluate five paradigms across three input representations and three LLMs on 232 stratified ICLR 2025 submissions. Direct absolute rating matches comparative ranking on rank correlation with human scores, yet compresses most predictions above the accept threshold, flagging almost none of the papers reviewers scored below it. A base-rate-matched recalibration control locates the cause: comparative ranking supplies placement, not better ordering, and after recalibration Direct Rating reaches higher agreement than Elo while making 24% as many API calls. Abstract-only input beats full-paper summarization, and model choice matters as much as paradigm choice. Replicating on all 11,513 scored submissions reproduces these patterns, shows absolute agreement depends on the evaluated set's score spread, and finds none beating an always-reject baseline in accuracy. Human scores track citations better than any paradigm, with one exception: Group Rating retains its citation correlation after controlling for human scores, and alone ranks within the accepted pool. Ranking quality alone cannot assess review quality; calibration, thresholds, model, and target outcome all matter.
bullets: Evaluates five LLM review paradigms across three input representations and three models using ICLR 2025 submissions.
Direct absolute rating and comparative ranking have similar rank correlation, but direct ratings are heavily compressed above the acceptance threshold.
After base-rate-matched recalibration, Direct Rating agrees more with human scores than Elo while using 24% as many API calls.
Abstract-only input outperforms full-paper summarization, and model choice matters as much as paradigm choice.
Human scores better predict citations overall; Group Rating uniquely preserves citation correlation after controlling for human scores and ranks within accepted papers.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of the experimental pipeline. Papers pass through three input representations (top), then through (a) absolute rating methods, which score each paper independently, or (b) comparative rating methods, which infer a latent rating from head-to-head outcomes and rescale it to 1–10. Only the comparative family is rescaled, so inflation and other absolute-error metrics are not comparable across families. Inline metrics give the best configuration in each family on the stratified 232-paper sample at the fixed ≥ 6 threshold.

Figure 7: Score distributions for the five paradigms vs. ground truth (abstract-only, GPT-4o-mini). Absolute methods (Direct, Anchor) compress scores into a narrow 6–8 range, while comparative methods (Elo, Swiss) preserve broader distributions closer to ground truth. Annotated below each: µ (mean), σ (standard deviation), ρ (Spearman correlation).

Figure 2: External validity on the 126 test papers carrying a retrievable citation count, a complete set of paradigm scores and a recorded decision. a, Paradigm rank under three evaluation targets; the lines cross, so none is best on all three. The decision target counts the 18 withdrawn submissions as non-accepted, which leaves the ordering unchanged. b, Spearman ρ with citation count, as an open circle (raw) joined to a filled circle (controlling for the mean reviewer score). Only Group Rating retains its correlation after the control (ρ = 0.304, p = 0.0006, surviving Bonferroni correction across the eighteen tests in Table 11). Anchor’s partial value is negative and Swiss’s exceeds its raw value, so the two are given as positions on a common axis rather than as a decomposition.

Figure 3: Population-scale false-positive (strong paper wrongly filtered) and false-negative (low-quality paper wrongly accepted) rates as a function of the accept threshold, swept from 5 to 7. The dashed gray line marks the fixed ≥ 6 threshold used in Table 9; the dotted green line marks the base-rate-matched threshold of Elo and Swiss; Direct Rating’s, at 7.67, lies beyond the plotted range. Direct Rating’s curves are flat across the plotted range because only 1.8% of its predictions fall below 7, which is why a fixed threshold at 6 makes it appear degenerate.

Figure 4: Error localization by ground-truth score bin (population scale, threshold ≥ 6). For each paradigm, blue bars show false-positive counts (strong papers wrongly filtered) and orange bars show false-negative counts (low-quality papers wrongly accepted). Direct’s errors are almost entirely false negatives, since its inflation accepts nearly all low-quality papers, whereas Elo and Swiss distribute the error budget across both classes, with false positives concentrated at borderline ground-truth scores.

Figure 6: Score distributions by input representation (all paradigms pooled, GPT-4o-mini). Violin shapes show density and box plots show quartiles; ground truth (gray) is shown for reference. The three representations differ little in spread (pooled σ 1.56, 1.62 and 1.59 for abstract-only, vanilla and objective), and all are far narrower than ground truth (σ = 2.16). Annotated below each group: µ (mean), σ (standard deviation), ρ̄ (mean Spearman correlation with ground truth across paradigms).

Figure 9: Cross-model performance heatmaps. Left: Cohen’s κ (practical decision utility). Center: Spearman ρ (ranking potential). Right: grade inflation (calibration). GPT-4o-mini Elo achieves the highest κ despite slightly lower ρ than Direct.

Figure 12: Ranking potential versus grade inflation (left) and versus decision utility (right) for all 15 configurations. GPT-4o-mini Direct sits at high ρ but near-zero κ, while Elo converts similar ρ into higher κ through calibration.

Figure 11: Model capability profiles averaged across paradigms, on five axes: the decision utility metrics (κ and macro F1), the threshold-free AUC-ROC, ranking potential (ρ), and a calibration axis plotting 1− inflation/4 so that a larger radius is better on every axis.

Figure 5: Interaction between paradigm and input representation. Left: Spearman ρ (higher is better). Right: Mean Absolute Error (lower is better). Abstract-only consistently outperforms across paradigms, and Elo achieves the lowest MAE regardless of input representation.

Figure 8: Robustness check: Spearman ρ (left) and Cohen’s κ (right) under four ground-truth aggregations, of which the trimmed mean coincides with the mean (Appendix M). Paradigm rankings are identical across variants.

Table 2: Best paradigm per model by ranking potential (ρ) and by decision utility, measured here by κ, abstractonly, 232-paper sample. The best paradigm differs by model and by criterion. Appendix N reports all fifteen configurations.

Table 8: Cross-model comparison, all fifteen configurations: five paradigms × three models (abstract-only, 232- paper sample). The Group rows, including GPT-4o-mini’s, use the original score-ordered grouping (Appendix D); the corrected GPT-4o-mini abstract-only Group run is reported in Table 1. Three cells rest on fewer papers, where a response or a group assignment failed: GPT-4o-mini Group n = 230, GPT-oss-120B Direct n = 230 and GPT-oss-120B Anchor n = 228. Table 2 summarizes the per-model best.

Table 5: All review methods, ranked by Pearson correlation (GPT-4o-mini, 232-paper sample). Input: input representation; Corr.: Pearson r against ground truth; Acc.: exact-match rate on the rounded 1–10 score scale, which is not the binary accept/reject accuracy of Table 6; Infl.: grade inflation. The Group vanilla and objective rows are computed on 230 papers, two having failed group assignment; the Group abstract row is the perpaper mean of the three randomized-grouping runs and covers all 232.

Table 7: Ordering-quality metrics for six representative methods, chosen to span the paradigms and input representations discussed in the text rather than to rank the top six on any single column. The first three numeric columns are NDCG@10, NDCG@20, and NDCG over all papers. Top-k precision is computed with a stable sort, so for paradigms that assign the same score to large blocks of papers it reports one arbitrary tie-break rather than a property of the ordering; see the discussion of Direct + Abstract below.
Table 1: Review paradigm comparison under abstractonly input (GPT-4o-mini). Column headings as in Table 4. The Group row is a three-run mean (Appendix D); all other rows are single runs.

Table 3: Test–retest reliability of the GPT-4o-mini Direct paradigm at temperature 0.3 (three independent runs, n = 11,513 papers, abstract-only). Reliability bands per Koo and Li (2016): < 0.5 poor, 0.5–0.75 moderate, 0.75–0.9 good, > 0.9 excellent.
Table 4: Input representation compared, averaged across all five paradigms (GPT-4o-mini). r: Pearson; ρ: Spearman; τ : Kendall; Infl.: grade inflation.
Table 6: Binary classification performance (reject/accept) on the stratified 232-paper sample. Accuracy in %; AUC is AUC-ROC on the continuous scores.

Table 9: Population-scale results for GPT-4o-mini (abstract-only), at the fixed ≥ 6 accept threshold and at each paradigm’s own base-rate-matched threshold (the cut at which its predicted reject rate equals the true rate). Recalibration is order-preserving, so ρ and inflation are unchanged by it. ρ and inflation are computed on all 11,513 scored ICLR 2025 papers; decision metrics on the 8,655 non-withdrawn papers (true reject rate 59.5%). Direct rows use the mean of three independent runs (ICC(2,1) = 0.417); because those scores are means of three integer ratings, Direct’s closest achievable predicted reject rate is 62.4% rather than 59.5%.

Table 10: Population-scale decision quality against the recorded ICLR 2025 accept/reject decisions rather than the ≥ 6 score rule. The qualitative pattern is unchanged: Direct Rating is reject-blind at a fixed threshold and recovers under recalibration, where it moves ahead of Elo. Under these labels Direct Rating is the one configuration whose accuracy exceeds the always-reject baseline, and only by 0.3 points.

Table 11: Spearman ρ between score and citation count, overall and within ICLR decision strata. ∗ denotes p < 0.05. The human correlation survives stratification. As in Table 1, the Group row is the per-paper mean of three randomized-grouping runs and the other rows are single runs. Group Rating is the only LLM paradigm to reach significance among accepted papers.

Table 12: Operating points at the fixed ≥ 6 accept threshold, using population-scale numbers (Table 9). These are a comparison among the configurations tested, not a deployment recommendation: under base-rate-matched thresholding (Section 4.5) Direct Rating attains the highest κ, and no configuration here reaches the 59.5% accuracy of always rejecting. The cost ratio cFP/cFN is the relative cost of filtering a strong paper (FP) versus admitting a low-quality one (FN).

papers.abstract: Training-free expert pruning makes two decisions: which experts to remove, and what the layer computes when its router still selects a removed expert. Published methods change both at once. Holding the mask fixed, we compare replacement operators from three families on OLMoE, DeepSeek-V2-Lite and Moonlight, with Granite as a fourth router, using paired, multiplicity-corrected tests. The largest effect is a choice usually left implicit: the survivors' gate scale. On routers trained without top-k renormalization, renormalizing the survivors' gates, a common implementation choice, costs 0.8-8.5 points and reverses whether rerouting beats MoNE's mean-output replacement; on two routers trained with renormalization, the trained scale wins at 50% pruning. We introduce the tilted novice, a closed-form low-rank map of the pruned expert's input whose rank-0 case is MoNE's constant. At 50% pruning it adds 1.2-1.8% parameters and gains 3.45 and 1.37 points over the constant on OLMoE and Moonlight, stable across calibration draws and largely unchanged by 4- and 3-bit quantization. No operator dominates: trained-scale rerouting is best on DeepSeek-V2-Lite, and a partial copy of each pruned expert is statistically indistinguishable from the tilted novice on two models. Evaluation can change conclusions: at 25% pruning MoNE's constant keeps 92-97% of dense multiple-choice accuracy but only 5-65% of GSM8K and 0-17% of code scores, and the calibration domain moves the mask 4-9 times more than resampling. We propose a five-item reporting checklist.
authors: Ezza Ali, Sehrish Bibi, Momina Moetesum, Faisal Shafait
bullets: The study isolates replacement operators while keeping the pruning mask fixed across several MoE models and routers.
Survivor gate renormalization can reduce accuracy by 0.8–8.5 points on routers not trained with top-k renormalization and can reverse method rankings.
The proposed tilted novice improves over MoNE’s constant replacement by 3.45 points on OLMoE and 1.37 points on Moonlight at 50% pruning, with small parameter overhead.
Operator performance is model-dependent: trained-scale rerouting leads on DeepSeek-V2-Lite, while partial expert copies match the tilted novice on two models.

Evaluation task and calibration domain matter substantially; multiple-choice retention can overstate performance on math and code tasks, while calibration shifts the pruning mask more than resampling.

papers.selection_reason: Training-free expert pruning for MoE LLMs; directly relevant to efficient inference and large language model architecture.
papers.title: What We Keep of What We Forget: Replacement Operators and Routing Semantics in Training-Free MoE Expert Pruning
papers.tldr: Replacement semantics—especially survivor gate scaling—strongly affect training-free MoE pruning results, and no single replacement operator is best across models or tasks.

papers.abstract: Process reward models (PRMs) score reasoning steps, but best-of-N selection also requires a rule that aggregates those scores. We study that rule as a separate evaluation object. StrictPRMBench fixes mathematical reasoning pools, scorer evidence, and the source trace of a deletion intervention, so that different reducers face the same recorded selection problem. Across seven scoring checkpoints and two benchmarks, the stored N=32 outcomes give higher deletion-induced selection instability for product than geometric mean (GM) in all 14 cells. The equal-cell difference is +0.0965; a shared-problem bootstrap, conditional on these checkpoints and frozen pools, gives a 95% interval of [0.0846,0.1086]. A pre-injection-defined sensitivity excludes replacement slots that are either reducer's clean winner and retains 4,459 of 4,622 cell-problem records. The retained difference is +0.0986 [0.0875,0.1098]. Effects are heterogeneous: the two Qwen cells have positive percentile-bootstrap intervals on retained support but two-sided exact paired p-values of 0.0625 and 0.0703. Clean-pool Qwen accuracy does not detect a product advantage, but this is not an equivalence result. We provide versioned outcome records, CPU reanalysis, and an explicit evidence-availability contract. The contribution is a diagnostic evaluation protocol and a reproducible audit of recorded selector behavior, not a new PRM, a universally optimal reducer, or evidence of deployment-wide harm. Raw-score replay and outcome-record reanalysis are distinguished: missing primary edited-score vectors limit independent evaluation of new reducers under the same stress.
bullets: Isolates PRM score aggregation as a separate evaluation target in best-of-N reasoning selection.
Freezes reasoning pools, scorer evidence, and deletion traces so reducers face identical recorded selection problems.
Across seven checkpoints and two benchmarks, product shows higher deletion-induced instability than GM in all 14 stored N=32 cells.
The effect remains under a pre-injection-defined sensitivity analysis, while effects vary across checkpoints and Qwen results are statistically inconclusive by exact paired tests.
Provides versioned outcome records and CPU reanalysis; missing edited-score vectors limit testing new reducers under the same stress.

The human counts describe a selected 200-card subset, not deployment prevalence. The example at left is illustrative.

papers.abstract: Speech language models have expanded automatic speech recognition (ASR) from transcription to general speech-to-text generation. Yet existing benchmarks still assume a single ground-truth transcript per utterance, an assumption that struggles when models produce readable, formatted, or structured outputs. In this work, we introduce Grounded Generative Speech Recognition (GSR), reformulating speech recognition as generating semantically grounded text instead of a single transcript. We define a grounded reformulation space that characterizes all valid textual realizations supported by the input speech, and establish a four-level hierarchy of reformulation capabilities, including literal transcription, canonical reformulation, semantic reformulation and speech-grounded structuring. Based on this formulation, we present GSR-Bench, the first comprehensive benchmark designed to evaluate generative speech recognition systems beyond exact transcript matching. GSR-Bench covers diverse scenarios including refined meeting transcription, cross-dialect translation, context-aware speech understanding, and robustness under silent or noisy acoustic conditions. To address the limitations of word-level evaluation metrics, we develop a multi-dimensional evaluation framework combining speech grounding assessment and LLM-based semantic judgment, whose reliability is validated through human preference studies. Extensive experiments across representative architectures, ranging from conventional ASR systems to end-to-end Speech-LLMs, reveal fundamental trade-offs between transcription fidelity and generative reformulation ability. Our analysis further identifies critical failure modes, including acoustic hallucination, unsupported generation, and instruction drift, providing insights into the design and evaluation of future grounded generative speech systems.
authors: Qing Wang, Qihan Hu, Hang Lv, Yan Yang, Boqing Liu, Xuechao Zhu, Zehan Li, Hongjie Chen, Jian Kang, Jie Li, Yongxiang Li, Lei Xie
bullets: Existing ASR benchmarks assume one correct transcript, limiting evaluation of readable, formatted, or structured outputs.
The proposed four-level hierarchy spans literal transcription, canonical and semantic reformulation, and speech-grounded structuring.

A multidimensional framework combines speech-grounding assessment with LLM-based semantic judgment validated by human preference studies.
Experiments expose trade-offs between transcription fidelity and reformulation ability, along with acoustic hallucination, unsupported generation, and instruction drift.

papers.abstract: Long-horizon LLM agents play an important role in solving complex and sustained tasks, with ever-growing interaction contexts. However, these accumulated contexts will raise substantial computational cost and obscure key decision-relevant evidence. Existing methods typically train external compressors or context-management agents to rewrite context as shorter hard-token sequences, but such external selection may not align with the LLM's evolving representation and is necessarily lossy. In this paper, we introduce Agentic Soft-Token Compression (ASTC), a training-free compression method using soft tokens within LLM agent for long-horizon tasks. Specifically, ASTC uses the model's native recurrent dynamics to determine the already absorbed information, leveraging the commonly-used hybrid Gated Delta Network (GDN)-attention. It then carries this information forward as agentic soft tokens while retaining exact values as hard tokens. The resulting compact sequence reduces later-layer computation and yields reusable KV caches, extending the savings across the agent's trajectory. Extensive experiments on long-horizon tasks show that ASTC matches or exceeds the uncompressed agent's accuracy with up to 50.68% fewer end-to-end Attention Pairs, while trained compressors require 15.4 to 103.7 times more Attention Pairs per successful task. These findings highlight agentic soft tokens as a model-native way to carry absorbed context forward as the task representation evolves.

papers.abstract: LLM-based simulated interviewees support interviewer training and the evaluation of mental health interviewing systems. Existing studies have primarily focused on improving human-likeness through richer patient profiles and behavioral modeling. However, human-likeness alone does not establish their reliability. Reliable simulation requires preserving profile-grounded clinical facts (informational invariance) while adapting disclosure and interaction behavior to the interview (relational adaptivity). To this end, we introduce PsyInterviewee, which separates a protected truth channel from a dynamic interaction channel and verifies generated clinical claims against the profile. Specifically, asymmetric write permissions allow dialogue context to update disclosure and behavioral states without authorizing new clinical facts; these states guide what profile-supported information is revealed and how it is expressed. In an automated evaluation of interactions between LLM-based interviewers and interviewees, PsyInterviewee achieves higher scores than four representative baselines on most metrics across both axes, as assessed by two LLM judges. Ablations suggest that the two channels contribute to clinical grounding and response modulation, respectively.
authors: Jiawei Zhang, Huachuan Qiu, Ruocheng Guo, Zijun Shi
bullets: Targets a reliability gap: human-like behavior alone does not ensure clinically grounded interviewees.

Ablations indicate that the two channels support clinical grounding and response modulation, respectively.

papers.abstract: Memory has become central to self-evolving LLM agents, which store and retrieve experience from past rollouts to guide future decisions. Existing systems represent this experience as free-form natural language and maintain it by rewriting, which fits tasks whose experience is narratable. However, in scientific discovery and optimization, experience is often a quantity measured by an oracle under a specific context. Rewriting it as text leaves no index for where a record should be, replaces a measurement with a description, and cannot express how interventions interact. To address this, we argue that agent memory for biomolecule optimization should instead be indexable, quantitative, and structured, and we introduce MEMIG. This memory construction framework realizes these three properties. In detail, MEMIG addresses each insight with a domain-grounded identifier and accumulates the quantitative effect measured by a property oracle, so that updates remain local and retrieval becomes an exact lookup. Next, MEMIG connects insights whose interventions are applied together and measures their epistasis by decomposing each evaluated set. Our results show that MEMIG improves performance in most settings across in silico antibody optimization tasks.
authors: Yunhui Jang, Zach Wang, Jai Doshi, Kangway Chuang, Sidney Lisanza, Taylor Joren
bullets: Targets the limitations of free-form, rewritten language memories for scientific optimization, where experience is measured quantitatively under specific contexts.
Uses domain-grounded identifiers to index insights and accumulates property-oracle measurements through local updates.
Links jointly applied interventions and decomposes evaluated sets to estimate their epistatic interactions.
Improves performance in most tested settings across in silico antibody optimization tasks.
Scope: results are reported for in silico antibody optimization; the abstract provides no specific datasets or numerical gains.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of MEMIG. MEMIG constructs an epistasis graph with antibody-grounded identifiers. Directed edges organize property → germline → region → mutation hierarchies, while undirected edges connect co-occurring mutations and store their epistatic effects.

Given a starting antibody, MEMIG identifies the matching identifiers, retrieves the corresponding insights with their neighbors, and curates them into natural language. The curves report the centered rolling mean with a half-width of 30 rollouts, computed within each memory step. Notably, the ordering of rollouts within the same memory is random, so a downward slope does not imply performance decrease. Each dot marks the mean over all rollouts of that memory step.

Each point is the mean improvement over all rollouts sharing a memory step, and error bars indicate the standard error across those rollouts. To remove this smoothing, we report the mean improvement of every rollout sharing a memory step as a single point in Figure 7, with error bars indicating the standard error across those rollouts. papers.abstract: Sparse MoE mechanism significantly improves the trade-off between model capacity and inference efficiency. However, practical deployment still requires storing all experts, resulting in substantial memory overhead. We show that expert outputs in MoE layers exhibit structured redundancy. Across different models and task categories, the stable rank and entropy effective rank of expert outputs are consistently far below the nominal number of experts, while expert output distributions also exhibit fewer effective modes. Motivated by these observations, we reformulate expert pruning as a structure-preserving expert subset selection problem and efficiently optimize it via a greedy strategy, rather than only independently scoring and ranking individual experts or exhaustively searching over expert combinations. We propose two expert pruning methods under the unified structure-preserving framework: Projection Energy Expert Pruning (PEEP), which preserves the functional subspace by maximizing weighted projection energy, and Distributional Coverage Expert Pruning (DCEP), which preserves the distributional geometry by minimizing weighted coverage error. Both methods incorporate router-derived weights as priors, enabling them to jointly preserve the global structural relationships among experts while accounting for the local importance of individual experts. Experiments on DeepSeek-V2-Lite and Qwen3-30B-A3B demonstrate that, at the expert retention ratios of 75% and 50%, our methods outperform the state-of-the-art baselines on the majority of benchmarks and consistently achieve the best average performance across both general tasks and mathematical reasoning tasks.

papers.abstract: Why does length generalization (LG) depend so sharply on the positional encoding (PE)? Relative schemes extrapolate fixed offsets, absolute schemes fix positions, and neither handles growing offsets. We give a realizability theory for a deliberately controlled abstraction, a single positional-only attention head, that derives this well-documented empirical pattern and says precisely where it holds and breaks. The device is a simulation transfer operator $T_L$ that re-evaluates a selected length-$L_0$-realizing positional kernel on the longer grid, with a scalar $\alpha_L \in [0,1]$ read off before any training from $(\Phi, t_n)$ alone. Here $\alpha_L$ serves as the computable witness of that taxonomy's derivation, not as a stronger empirical predictor. Our results are a relative-head deep-row characterization for kernels with a strict unique global maximizer (Theorem 2), an absolute/relative duality that derives the pattern (Proposition 4), a learned-absolute underdetermination result, and a static expressivity bound; a sufficiency theorem (Theorem 1) bridges $\alpha_L$ to LG, and the general deterministic case is a precise open conjecture (correcting a tempting but invalid "outside-colspan" argument). Experiments confirm the structure: in the controlled single-head regime $\alpha_L$ exactly separates the taxonomy's generalizing and non-generalizing (PE, task) cells (2625 trained-model measurements; stable at vocab 64/d=128). Together, these results turn the received PE taxonomy into a positional-kernel transfer theorem, and identify the content and depth mechanisms that escape it. The theory concerns the positional channel alone: tasks whose targets depend on token content, including the standard length-generalization suite such as addition and sorting, fall outside Theorem 2.
authors: Jiasong Han, Yunkai Chai, Jintao Wang
bullets: Defines a transfer operator that reevaluates a length-$L_0$ positional kernel on longer grids and computes a pre-training witness $\alpha_L$.
Characterizes relative-head generalization for kernels with a strict unique global maximizer and establishes an absolute/relative duality.
Shows that learned-absolute schemes are underdetermined and derives a static expressivity bound.
Experiments on 2,625 controlled trained-model measurements show $\alpha_L$ exactly separates the studied generalizing and non-generalizing positional-encoding/task cells.
The theory does not cover content-dependent tasks such as addition or sorting; the general deterministic case remains an open conjecture.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of the method. Select (fit) a single positional head’s kernel at length L0 realizing the task’s target pattern RL0 ; transfer the same kernel to a longer grid via TL (re-evaluate ΦLWΦ⊤ L , no retraining); old rows keep their argmax by the causal-mask identity (Thm 1); score the new rows [L0, L) to read off αL ∈ [0, 1]. The whole pipeline uses only (Φ, tn), with no Transformer training, no data samples, and no learned Transformer parameters (only a deterministic kernel-selection on the PE basis).

Figure 2: The offset taxonomy, derived (Theorem 2, Prop. 4). A relative kernel length-generalizes a fixed relative offset; a clamped learned-absolute encoding does the reverse; and neither handles a growing offset (the shared blind spot, right column). Throughout, the relative statements are for kernels with a strict unique global maximizer, the hypothesis of Theorem 2; the accompanying text explains why it is needed and what the L0-fit contributes. This 2 × 3 verdict is exactly the empirical PE taxonomy, here a consequence of what a single positional head can realize.
Figure 4: Empirical LG (solid) and training-free αL (dashed) vs. test length L (train L0=20), 1L1H. αL tracks both who generalizes and how LG decays with L.

Figure 5: Training-free α60 (left) and empirical LG@60 (right) over (PE, task), 1L1H. Agreement is strong in this single-head regime; the content-driven disagreements (which emerge at depth, not shown here) are characterized in §7.

Figure 3: Training-free αL vs. empirical LG across the three tiers (5 seeds). Left (1L1H, the setting the theory describes): learnable cells (blue) give Spearman ρ=0.90. Center, right (scale, 2L4H, 4L4H): the graded rank correlation weakens (its bootstrap CI includes 0) as the content channel rescues low-αL cells, yet high αL remains a sufficient screen at every depth (precision ≥ 0.92).

Figure 6: H3: learnable-cell Spearman ρ(αL, LG) (circles) drops with depth (its bootstrap CI includes 0 at depths 2, 4), while sufficiency precision (squares) stays ≥ 0.92 with tight CIs. αL remains a sufficient screen at all depths.

Table 1: Positioning against the closest LG frameworks. αL’s niche: pre-training, keyed to the PE’s feature map, continuous, single-head, with matched sufficiency and relative-head necessity (the general necessary condition is conjectural).

Table 3: Training-free αL (at L=60) vs. empirical LG accuracy (mean over 5 seeds), 1-layer 1-head and scale (2L4H) tiers. Top: αL tracks 1L1H LG. Bottom: at scale, the content/recency channel (outside the positional-only abstraction, S3) lets ALiBi/NoPE generalize where αL=0, making the predictor’s onesidedness visible.

Table 10: RoPE frequency sweep on content-neutral skip-3 (1L1H). No discriminating cell: where the model generalizes the taxonomy is right; at scale 0.03 αL under-predicts (false negative); at 0.01 the model cannot learn at all.
Table 2: The evaluation grid. Each axis follows the theory’s categories or standard practice; the reason given for each level is the reason it was included.

Table 6: Interior fixed-absolute positions (1L1H, mean over 5 seeds). Absolute encodings realize and transfer them; relative encodings do not learn them at all. Compare first, where RoPE scores α60 = 0.20 purely because position 0 is the causal boundary.

Table 8: L0-sensitivity (1L1H, predictor αL / empirical LG at L=3L0). The screen AUC is 1.0 at every training length and the per-cell verdicts are stable; the separation is not an artifact of L0=20. Generated by experiments/l0_sensitivity.py.

Table 7: Scale robustness: cell-level Spearman ρ(αL, LG) on learnable cells, at the paper’s default size vs. a larger model. The predictor is identical; only the trained models change. The scale study uses 2 seeds (700 rows), and both columns are computed on the cells the two studies have in common, so the 2L4H entry (0.36) is over 19 cells rather than the 20 of Table 4, where the same quantity over all 20 cells is 0.31.

Table 9: Content-driven induction (target = token after the previous occurrence of xi): positional αL = 0 for all PEs, yet 2-layer models generalize (LG up to 0.84). α+ L flags the realizable through the content channel regime αL misses; residual PE-modulation of content LG is future work.

Table 12: αL for sinusoidal under the same sweep. The absolute verdict is invariant (first≈1 everywhere; growing offsets ≈0). The bounded-offset cells (prev/skip3) are the only entries whose verdict moves with frequency – they degrade as frequencies are added (num:8→32 drives prev 0.47→0.00); the other cells’ raw αL shifts stay sub-threshold (e.g. first 0.93→1.00) and never flip the verdict. This is what the theory predicts: enlarging the realizable space does not help the L0-fit select a transferring kernel (existence ̸= selection, Prop. 3). Verdict movement appears precisely at the selection gap and nowhere else.

Table 11: αL for RoPE under varying frequency count num (feature dimension m=2 num) and θ-base. The verdict is invariant: fixed relative offsets transfer (prev, skip3=1.00 everywhere), growing offsets never transfer (copy/reverse≈0), and the kernel the L0-fit selects does not hit a fixed absolute position (first stays at chance; a monotone kernel in the family could, but the fit does not select it, see the discussion after Prop. 4). For low-frequency scaling see Table 10.

Table 4: Depth trend (H3), learnable cells (train acc > 0.8), 5 seeds. The Spearman column is cell-level with a bootstrap 95% CI over the (PE, task) cells; the precision column is the rate Pr[LG ≥ 0.7 | αL ≥ 0.5] with a bootstrap 95% CI over the high-αL rows. αL stays a high-precision sufficient indicator at every depth (precision CIs well above chance); the graded rank correlation, by contrast, is significant only at depth 1 – at depths 2, 4 its CI includes 0, consistent with αL acting as a binary screen rather than a graded predictor once content rescues low-αL cells.
Table 5: Inductive-bias ablation (75 rows in the 1L1H setting). The cross-entropy fit, not the min-norm interpolant, drives the αL–LG correlation.

papers.selection_reason: Theoretical analysis of length generalization and positional encoding relevant to long-context models.
papers.title: A Positional Realizability Theory of Length Generalization in Single-Head Attention
papers.tldr: A realizability theory explains when positional encodings enable length generalization in a controlled single-head, positional-only attention setting.

papers.abstract: Transformer-based language models have achieved remarkable success in automated short answer grading (ASAG). However, current methods in ASAG struggle to comprehend, reason about and evaluate complex mathematical answers involving symbols and formulas. These score-only methods fail to generalize across diverse responses and skill states associated with identical scores. Moreover, they ignore the potential upward bias introduced by generative Artificial Intelligence (AI) usage in assessing students' performance and knowledge mastery. To address these limitations, we propose AICG (AI-aware Cognitive-supervised Grading), a two-branch multi-task framework. The first branch combines RoBERTa-based regression, ordinal, and classification heads for individual-answer grading. The second branch uses an expert-designed Q-matrix to associate responses with assessed skills and jointly predicts G-DINA-derived skill mastery and learning gain. Through the shared encoder, these skill-level targets provide cognitive supervision for answer grading beyond score labels. AICG further uses a Gen-AI detector, trained through supervised contrastive pretraining followed by linear classification, to estimate assistance probabilities and convert them into reliability weights, attenuating unreliable cognitive evidence during learning assessment. We conduct experiments on 49,402 instructor-graded responses spanning 19 academic semesters. Relative to RoBERTa regression, AICG reduces mean absolute error (MAE) by 50.3% and improves quadratic weighted kappa (QWK) from 0.798 to 0.927. Ablations identify Q-matrix-guided cognitive supervision as the primary source of improvement, while AI-aware weighting further reduces overall MAE by 4.2% over the unweighted cognitive model and consistently improves MAE and QWK across the four most recent post-Gen-AI semesters.
authors: Shengran Guo, Min Chi, Feifei Qiao, Varad Patwardhan
bullets: Addresses the difficulty of evaluating symbolic, formula-based answers and distinguishing different skill states behind identical scores.
Uses a shared RoBERTa encoder with regression, ordinal, and classification grading heads, plus Q-matrix-guided prediction of skill mastery and learning gain.
Detects likely Gen-AI assistance and converts assistance probabilities into weights that reduce the influence of potentially unreliable cognitive evidence.
On 49,402 responses across 19 semesters, AICG reduces MAE by 50.3% versus RoBERTa regression and raises QWK from 0.798 to 0.927.
Cognitive supervision drives most of the gains; AI-aware weighting provides additional improvements, especially in recent post-Gen-AI semesters.

The shared RoBERTa encoder supports parallel cognitive-supervision and individual-response-grading branches. Solid and dashed arrows denote prediction and supervision flows, respectively.

papers.selection_reason: Develops AICG, a framework for automated math grading that uses LLMs for cognitive supervision (Q-matrix) and Gen-AI detection to handle complex symbolic reasoning.
papers.title: Beyond Response Scoring: An AI-aware Cognitive Supervision Framework for Automated Mathematical Short Answer Grading
papers.tldr: AICG improves mathematical short-answer grading by combining score prediction with skill-level cognitive supervision and Gen-AI-aware reliability weighting.

papers.abstract: LLM agents execute tasks through repeated model calls over evolving histories of reasoning, actions, and tool feedback. Aggregate speculative-decoding metrics merge these distinct decisions, providing limited guidance on where draft supervision is needed. We present TraceSpec, a framework connecting trajectory evaluation with adaptive draft training. It combines dynamic execution with fixed-prefix replay and introduces TraceSpec-Traj, a corpus of 10,000 training states and 2,500 test states spanning browsing and software engineering. Analysis of five speculative baselines reveals that aggregate acceptance can rise with context length while declining within matched late browsing actions. Workload and phase further distinguish these trends, motivating supervision guided by trajectory conditions. TraceSpec trains on intermediate assistant turns and allocates a fixed prediction budget using state-conditioned estimates of prefix-aware acceptance gaps. Across three target sizes and two temperatures, it improves replay throughput by 12.5% to 22.6% over its DSpark base. Qwen3-4B ablations show that adaptive allocation increases accepted length by 3.3% to 10.0% over fixed full-turn supervision, with additional comparisons substantiating the roles of state conditioning and consecutive-token agreement. The resulting evaluation resources, trajectory findings, and training strategy connect the analysis of agent execution to practical draft improvement.
authors: Jihao Zhao, Shuaishuai Zu, Pengfei Li, Biao Qin, Guanghuan Fang, Ben Feng, Baochuan Yang
bullets: Aggregate acceptance metrics can obscure differences across reasoning, browsing, and tool-use states, especially in later browsing actions.
TraceSpec combines dynamic execution, fixed-prefix replay, and state-conditioned estimates of prefix-aware acceptance gaps.
TraceSpec-Traj provides 10,000 training states and 2,500 test states from browsing and software-engineering trajectories.
Adaptive intermediate-turn supervision improves replay throughput by 12.5%–22.6% over DSpark across tested target sizes and temperatures.
Scope: results focus on trajectory replay and evaluated agent workloads; findings also indicate workload and phase affect speculative-decoding behavior.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces TraceSpec, a framework for improving speculative decoding in LLM agents by connecting trajectory evaluation with adaptive draft training. This addresses agent execution and LLM architecture.
papers.title: TraceSpec: Understanding and Improving Speculative Decoding for LLM Agents
papers.tldr: TraceSpec improves speculative decoding for LLM agents by using trajectory-aware analysis and adaptive draft training, increasing replay throughput over its baseline.

papers.abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation is becoming agentic. A search harness writes queries, reads results, reformulates, and decides when to stop. This largely solves accuracy: a harness with only BM25/grep and MiniMax M3 answers 85% of BrowseComp-Plus and 91% on multi-hop FRAMES in our runs, without compiled or vector indexes. It exposes a context problem: an undisciplined loop repeats queries, rereads documents, and fills the window with unused passages. The missing layer is knowledge compilation: a configurable ingestion pipeline where LLMs enrich documents with context no chunk contains alone--navigation hierarchies with claim-evidence leaves, entity graphs, timelines, mind maps, ontologies, wikis, and memory. Compilation is not a better retriever: under a competent harness, structural artifacts gave no detectable accuracy gain on FRAMES, and a PageIndex-style outline degraded at scale. It is a supply layer. A navigation tree whose leaves are claim-evidence pairs--the mechanism we measure--cuts query tokens by 91% when evidence suffices and adds 1.9% when it does not, a 38% average reduction; this implies a 2% break-even sufficiency rate and a measured rate near 43%. A decision gate cuts latency from 140 s to 30 s, though substitution's token saving is bought with retrieval rounds and carries its own latency cost. Other artifacts--ontology, graph, wiki, timeline, mind map, memory--pay off in deployment (governance, integration, onboarding, temporal orientation, continuity) where accuracy benchmarks cannot see them. We describe RAGFlow's pipeline and harness (open source at https://github.com/infiniflow/ragflow), which turns the loop into five disciplined stations and keeps the context entering the model the smallest sufficient set; together they form an agent-native database: a store that hands the agent compiled, governed context instead of a ranked list of passages.
authors: Zhichang Yu, Baining Cao, Sbaaoui Idriss, Qi Wang, Gangqiang Xu, Ling Qin, Xiaoling Jin, An Liu, Shaohao Cai, Xiaoyang Bao, Shengle Chen, Changchang Ding, Pengfei Zhu, Jingxiang Xu, Yifeng Mao, Lu Liu, Hai Jin, Yingfeng Zhang
bullets: Agentic search harnesses can achieve strong retrieval-augmented answering with simple BM25/grep retrieval, but uncontrolled loops waste queries, reread documents, and fill context windows.
The proposed supply layer compiles documents into structures such as claim-evidence navigation trees, entity graphs, timelines, ontologies, wikis, and memories.
Claim-evidence navigation trees reduced query tokens by 38% on average, with 91% savings when the compiled evidence sufficed and a 1.9% increase otherwise.
A decision gate reduced reported latency from 140 seconds to 30 seconds, while retrieval-round substitution introduces its own latency cost.

Structural artifacts showed no detectable FRAMES accuracy gain under a competent harness, so their value is primarily efficiency, governance, integration, onboarding, temporal orientation, and continuity.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Context as infrastructure. Knowledge compilation is the supply side: an ingestion pipeline that enriches raw documents into typed context artifacts. The harness is the control side: it decides which artifact, if any, enters the window and when the loop stops. Tools are the contract between them. Arrows show the flow of context, not control. The navigation tree (highlighted), whose leaves are claim–evidence pairs, is the mechanism measured in this paper; the ontology artifact (highlighted) is the one whose value is primarily commercial rather than benchmark-visible.

Figure 2: Measured token and latency effects. Top: conditional change in total query tokens on FRAMES when projected evidence is sufficient (hit), insufficient (miss), and averaged over the benchmark. Bottom: end-to-end latency with and without the decision gate, with claim-leaf trees present. Negative bars are savings.

Table 2: The deployment ledger. Every row is defined for production collections, not FRAMES; the unit is the collection (or the reviewer team), and the comparison is against the same collection before the artifact or against a shadow control. Targets are pre-registered per deployment; a direction is reported only after the target is met, and audit coverage is an invariant rather than an average. The navigation-tree row refers to the claim-leaf variant; a carrier without claim leaves carries no evidence and is judged only on the organizational terms of Table 1. The mind map is a navigation-tree layout and is judged on the navigation terms of the navigation-tree row, the timeline on the temporal terms of its own row.

Table 1: Compilation artifacts, the context they add at ingestion, and the ledger on which each is evaluated. FRAMES results are from the controlled harness in Section 8; deployment value is assessed with the metrics and instrumentation in Table 2, not with benchmark accuracy. The two carrier-only rows remove the claim–evidence leaves, so their deployment value is organizational only—they arrange content, they do not add evidence.

Table 3: Accuracy audit of the structural variants on the full FRAMES benchmark. The two navigation-tree rows share the same carrier; the only change is whether claim–evidence leaves are present. “Neutral” means no improvement large enough to be distinguished from run-to-run variation in a single run, and it does not rule out a small effect below the resolution of this design; “negative” means a loss of that kind. We report the direction and the failure mode the audit supports, not point estimates: each variant was run once. The claim-leaf row is the measured mechanism, not a structural baseline.

Table 4: Main measurements on FRAMES with the Tree template and glm-4-flash extraction. Token changes are relative to the uncompiled BM25/grep harness; negative is a saving, and dashes indicate quantities not measured separately. The first three rows are conditional splits of the same benchmark—hit and miss are defined by the gate’s verdict—and the FRAMES average is over all evaluated questions. The last two rows are arm means, not conditional splits: each is the mean change of that arm against the uncompiled baseline over the queries in that arm (evidence present, evidence absent), so −52% is not comparable with the −91% hit figure or with the −38% average. The arm-mean query counts are smaller still and are not reported separately.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes 'knowledge compilation' as a memory mechanism for LLMs in agentic systems, transforming raw retrieval results into structured, navigable context to reduce token usage and improve efficiency.
papers.title: Context as Infrastructure: Knowledge Compilation for Retrieval in Agentic Systems with Harnesses
papers.tldr: Knowledge compilation can make agentic retrieval more efficient by supplying governed, navigable context, even when it does not improve benchmark accuracy.

papers.abstract: The ability to integrate new information and deduce its consequences is central to learning, understanding, and reasoning in large language models (LLMs). Whether information arrives during training or in-context, models must not only store local facts, but propagate their long-range implications globally. To explore information integration in LLMs, we introduce two complementary natural language benchmarks for large-scale evaluation of deductive reasoning as a function of inference depth. The first is a formal graph benchmark enabling controlled evaluation over a wide range of graph topologies and integration tasks; the second is a knowledge composition benchmark grounded in real-world knowledge graphs. We use these benchmarks to compare knowledge integration from information encoded in context versus information encoded in model weights during pretraining, evaluating a set of open models implicitly, without chain of thought. We find that accuracy decays sharply with increased composition length for both pretrained and in-context knowledge. Information presented in-context, however, substantially outperforms deduction over information encoded in weights. These results quantify a fundamental limitation of current models with direct implications for prompt-based control of agent behavior and for continual learning strategies, and they provide a foundation for developing training, prompting, and integration methods that support deeper reasoning.
authors: Alexander Detkov, Dashiel Karish, Matthew Oleynikov, Matt Thomson
bullets: Introduces two benchmarks for evaluating deductive reasoning across increasing inference depths.
Uses a controllable formal graph benchmark and a real-world knowledge-composition benchmark.
Compares knowledge supplied in context with knowledge encoded in model weights, without chain-of-thought prompting.
In-context knowledge substantially outperforms deduction over pretrained knowledge, though both degrade with longer compositions.
Findings highlight limitations relevant to prompt-based agent control and continual learning.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Models receive graph adjacency in-context but integrate the information poorly, failing at long-range inferences. DeepSeek, Kimi, Nemotron, and 12 other models answer questions about a random graph of 50–60 nodes given in the prompt as a list of edges, with reasoning off. Each question concerns the nodes exactly k hops from a start node, so k = 1 questions require only direct-neighbor information. a) Verify: is a given node exactly k hops away? Accuracy falls from 93–100% at k = 1 to 49–56% at k = 3, close to chance. b) Count: how many nodes are exactly k hops away? Models count correctly 43–69% of the time at k = 1 and ≤ 16% from k = 2. c) Name one: name a node exactly k hops away. Models name a neighbor at 99–100%, but a node two hops away at only 9–40%. d) Enumerate: list every node exactly k hops away. Models list all neighbors at 71–100%, but no model lists more than 12% of sets correctly from k = 2.

Figure 2: Models compose facts from the prompt far better than from memory. DeepSeek, Kimi, and Nemotron answer k-hop Wikidata questions with reasoning off and information given in context, in memory, or both. a) The chain’s facts are given in the prompt under invented names, among 16 decoy chains with the same relations. All models compose at ≥ 94% up to k = 3, but at k = 6, Kimi composes at 29%, while DeepSeek and Nemotron Ultra fall to chance. b) The facts are recalled from memory without supporting facts in the prompt. Composition reaches only 37–64% at k = 2 and ≤ 12% from k = 4, although every fact is known. c) The facts are given in the prompt under their real names, among 16 real decoy chains, so the model can use both the prompt and memory. Accuracy reaches 36–71% at k = 6.

papers.selection_reason: Benchmarks LLM knowledge integration across in-context and parametric memory, with direct implications for memory reasoning and continual learning.
papers.title: ImplicitHop: Evaluating knowledge integration across context and memory
papers.tldr: ImplicitHop shows that LLMs struggle to integrate multi-step knowledge, with performance declining sharply as inference depth increases, especially for pretrained knowledge.

papers.abstract: Natural-language skills enable large language model (LLM) agents to reuse procedures across tasks, yet most systems retrieve individual skills from a flat SkillBank without explicitly modeling the high-level strategy that governs their selection and use. We introduce TalentRL, a strategy-guided reinforcement learning framework for hierarchical routing over procedural memory. Coarse-grained talents represent recurring strategies for skill use, while fine-grained skills provide executable procedures. For each task, the policy model selects a talent that guides execution and softly prioritizes its associated skills during similarity-based retrieval. However, since task outcomes depend jointly on talent selection, retrieved skill context, and downstream execution, terminal rewards alone cannot isolate the contribution of the routing decision. TalentRL therefore trains talent routing with reward contrasts between rollouts of the same task under matched interventions on the talent-conditioned context, and optimizes downstream execution with group-relative advantages. Across seven open-domain and multi-hop question-answering benchmarks, talent-aware supervised fine-tuning improves average success rate by 7.53%, 6.71%, and 9.21% over the corresponding zero-shot baselines for Qwen2.5-7B, Qwen3-8B, and Llama-3.1-8B, respectively. Reinforcement learning further improves these SFT checkpoints by 7.58% to 9.32%, and TalentRL achieves the highest average success rate among all compared methods on all three backbones. On the agentic benchmarks ALFWorld and WebShop, TalentRL achieves the highest ALFWorld success rate (99.3%) and the highest WebShop score (90.7) among all compared methods.
authors: Huancheng Chen, Xiaodi Sun, Zhaoqiong Huang, Michelle Chang, Jingwen Lu
bullets: Addresses the limitation of flat SkillBanks, which retrieve skills without modeling the overarching strategy for using them.
Introduces hierarchical routing: coarse-grained talents guide execution and softly prioritize associated fine-grained skills.
Uses matched rollout reward contrasts to train talent selection and group-relative advantages for downstream execution.
Across seven QA benchmarks and two agentic benchmarks, TalentRL consistently improves performance and achieves the best reported results among compared methods.
Reported peaks include 99.3% success on ALFWorld and a 90.7 score on WebShop.

figures.caption: Figure 1. Overview of TalentRL. (A) The policy model selects a talent that guides downstream execution and provides a soft prior for similarity-based skill retrieval. (B) Reward contrasts across matched intervention rollouts train talent routing, while group-relative advantages optimize downstream execution, both updating the shared policy model. (C) Talent-aware SFT initializes talent routing and downstream execution from outcome-guided demonstrations.

Figure 2. Talent selection of the final TalentRL policies. (a) Search7 test sets, as % of questions per dataset. (b) ALFWorld by task type over the seen (140) and unseen (134) splits. (c) WebShop on 500 goals. Percentages below 10% are omitted from the bars.

Table 2. Search7 success rate (%) after RL. Within each backbone, the highest and second-highest distinct values for each metric are bold and underlined, respectively; ties receive the same formatting. Evaluation details are provided in Appendix A.

Table 1. Comparison of SkillRL-SFT and TalentRL-SFT on Search7, with zero-shot results as a reference. Success rates (%) are reported, with the best result for each metric within each backbone in bold.

Table 3. ALFWorld success rate and WebShop average score/success rate (%). Baseline values are paper-reported, not protocol-matched reproductions. Plain SFT and TalentRL-SFT are Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct students; their ALFWorld columns use the 140 valid-seen games. TalentRL is initialized from the TalentRL-SFT checkpoints. Best and second-best results are bold and underlined, respectively.
Table 4. Primary Qwen2.5-7B Search7 training, routing, and retrieval configuration. Interactive-task protocols are described separately below.

Table 5. Talent-specific generation guidance and preset talent–skill associations for Search7. The selected talent provides natural-language guidance for execution and a soft prior for skill retrieval. Associated skills are not necessarily all included in the execution context. papers.selection_reason: LLM agent skill routing over procedural memory fits LLM memory subtopic.
papers.title: TalentRL: Strategy-Guided Reinforcement Learning for Hierarchical Skill Routing
papers.tldr: TalentRL improves LLM agents’ procedural-memory use by learning high-level strategy selection alongside skill retrieval through contrastive, strategy-guided reinforcement learning.

papers.abstract: Agentic LLM assistants must repeatedly decide whether to answer from memory or to call a tool such as web search. Unnecessary searches cost latency and money; missing ones yield confident but unsupported answers. Prior work mostly measures verbalised confidence or trains new adaptive-retrieval methods, and rarely audits the search decisions that deployed products actually make. We introduce a benchmark of 400 multiple-choice questions that combines widely known inside-knowledge (IK) questions, which should be answered directly, with outside-knowledge (OK) questions about facts from news published after the models' training cut-offs (to our knowledge), which should trigger search or, without tools, abstention. Each item offers an abstain option, and two action-level scores, NAS and KIS, reward searching on OK questions and restraint on IK questions. Across five commercial LLMs with and without their vendors' web search, GPT-5 mini and Grok 4 Fast search on over 90% of OK but only 1% of IK questions, whereas Mistral Small searches on just 20% of OK questions, often abstaining instead of using its tool; one product's search indicator proved unusable. Searching is partly triggered by explicit temporal cues: on uncued OK questions, the NAS of the two selective models falls from about 0.72 to 0.57--0.58. The scores thus measure the search triggering of specific products, not metacognition in a strict sense.
bullets: Introduces 400 multiple-choice questions covering answerable inside knowledge and post-cutoff outside knowledge, with abstention available.
Defines NAS and KIS scores to reward searching for outside knowledge and avoiding unnecessary searches for inside knowledge.
Evaluates five commercial LLMs with and without vendor web search, focusing on deployed search behavior rather than verbalized confidence.
GPT-5 mini and Grok 4 Fast search on over 90% of outside-knowledge items but only 1% of inside-knowledge items; Mistral Small searches about 20% of outside-knowledge items.
Explicit temporal cues strongly influence search: two selective models’ NAS drops from about 0.72 to 0.57–0.58 without cues.

papers.abstract: Estimating whether a problem is too complex for a large language model (LLM) before the model attempts it can guide model routing, how to allocate test-time compute, and suggest the need for new tools to aid the agent. While existing estimators rely on the problem text, LLM-annotated task difficulty labels, or signals obtained after a model attempts to solve the problem, such as its hidden states, none explicitly leverage the constraint structure inherent in the problem: the variables to assign and how the constraints over them interact. We introduce CIRCE, which extracts a problem's structure by using a cheap LLM to construct a Constraint Intermediate Representation that deterministically compiles into the constraint graph. Across seven reasoning benchmarks (including SAT, logic, and math) and four LLMs, even a randomly initialized GNN encoder improves predictions of LLM response correctness, reducing negative log-likelihood from 0.465 to 0.423 and increasing AUROC from 0.691 to 0.727 relative to the strongest baseline for each metric.
authors: Chenhao Hong, Jiakai Xu, Kaushiki Singh, Yusen Zhang, Eugene Wu
bullets: Targets pre-attempt difficulty estimation for model routing, test-time compute allocation, and tool selection.
Uses a cheap LLM to convert problems into a Constraint Intermediate Representation, which deterministically compiles into a constraint graph.
A graph neural network encodes the constraint structure to predict LLM response correctness.
Evaluated across seven SAT, logic, and math reasoning benchmarks and four LLMs.
Improves prediction over the strongest baselines, lowering NLL from 0.465 to 0.423 and raising AUROC from 0.691 to 0.727.

papers.abstract: There exists little mathematical theory explaining why Transformer architectures are empirically successful even for non-Markovian data. To this end, this paper studies next-token prediction via stochastic optimal control theoretically trained Transformers for such sources, where we consider either stationary and ergodic non-Markovian sources or those which are hidden Markov models of some finite order (possibly non-stationary). In either case, we first obtain error bounds via finite models with finite window approximations. For stationary ergodic sources, the resulting error is bounded by an entropy gap; for $N$th order Markovian sources, it decays at an exponential rate $\alpha^{\lfloor M/N\rfloor}$, where $M$ is the window length and $\alpha$ is determined by filter stability (and the Dobrushin coefficients of the transition and measurement kernels). We then construct a Transformer of depth $M+1$, one head per layer, realizing the truncated filter, and we optimally train it with stochastic control developed in earlier work, which rigorously returns a near optimal Transformer. In particular, we show that for a non-Markovian source, either under stationarity and ergodicity for general models or under filter stability for hidden Markov models, an optimally trained Transformer has arbitrarily small performance error with increasing context length, data, and approximation refinement. Numerical studies accompany the theory.
authors: Ka\u{g}an Akman, Jake Feldman Starosta, Naci Saldi, Serdar Y\"uksel
bullets: Develops theoretical error bounds using finite-model and finite-window approximations.

For finite-order hidden Markov sources, the error decays exponentially with context length under filter stability.

Shows near-lossless prediction in the limiting regime for general stationary ergodic sources and stable hidden Markov models; numerical studies support the theory.

papers.abstract: Large language models have been shown to memorise and reproduce verbatim sequences from their training data, raising concerns about privacy leakage, intellectual property exposure, and the limits of generalisation. Recent theoretical work suggests that attention heads may contribute to this behaviour by functioning as associative memory mechanisms, with memorisation capacity scaling with the number of heads. At the same time, empirical work has shown that many attention heads are redundant and can be pruned with limited impact on downstream performance. Despite these parallel findings, the effect of pruning redundant heads on memorised-sequence reproduction remains unexplored. In this work, we demonstrate that zeroing out a substantial fraction of attention heads prior to inference can significantly suppress verbatim memorisation while preserving, or even improving, language modelling performance on the benchmark used to identify redundant heads. Evaluating GPT-2-XL(1.5B) on known memorised sequences, we find that pruning 729 task-redundant heads reduces the memorisation count by 91.5%, while improving WikiText-103 perplexity by 0.92. These findings suggest that attention-head redundancy can be exploited to mitigate memorisation at inference time, without retraining or modifying the training data.
bullets: Addresses privacy and intellectual-property risks from large language models reproducing training sequences.
Zeros out task-redundant attention heads before inference, without retraining or changing training data.
On GPT-2-XL, pruning 729 heads reduced memorisation count by 91.5%.

The result suggests attention-head redundancy can be used for inference-time memorisation mitigation.

papers.abstract: Chain-of-thought (CoT) monitoring is a promising way to oversee increasingly capable agents. It succeeds in part because current models appear limited in their ability to control what they verbalize in their reasoning traces. We investigate the source of this limitation and link it to an entropy collapse in the first few tokens following the opening thinking tag. We exploit this mechanism to recover CoT controllability through two inference-time interventions on initial tokens: prefilling, where even a single token can substantially increase controllability, and banning frequent opening tokens combined with in-context examples, which improves average compliance by 34-41 percentage points across models. These interventions recover mainly addition and style controllability (adding or transforming information), while suppression controllability (avoiding or removing information) exhibits more varied responses, suggesting distinct underlying mechanisms. Consistent with this, the two groups behave as separate capabilities: across models, performance correlates positively within these groups, while cross-group correlations are mostly negative. Importantly, we find that the relationship with monitorability depends on the evaluation: addition and style controllability more consistently positively correlate with monitorability, while suppression often shows negative associations. Our findings motivate the development of controllability evaluations that distinguish difficulty initiating a specific opening from general limitations of the ability to alter reasoning content, alongside separate reporting of control tasks and categories.
authors: Hugh Van Deventer, Dmitrii Troitskii, Laura Ruis
