papers.abstract: On-Policy Self-Distillation (OPSD), which aligns a student model's token-level distribution with that of its self-teacher prompted by privileged context, has emerged as a promising direction to mitigate reward sparsity in sequence-level post-training paradigms. However, OPSD often fails to achieve continuous performance gains during training. In this paper, we find that the model's limited self-teaching capability underlies this phenomenon by generating unreliable guidance on certain samples. To address this problem, we propose Teacher-Evolution Self-Distillation (TESD), which enables the self-teacher to generate rollouts and receive environmental feedback based on task correctness and context independence. First, using these rewards as training objectives, we perform teacher-oriented optimization to continuously enhance the model's self-teaching capability during distillation. Second, by estimating teacher guidance reliability from these rewards, we apply adaptive student-oriented optimization to down-weight samples with unreliable guidance. Extensive experiments across multiple datasets and model scales show that TESD consistently outperforms representative token-level and sequence-level methods, highlighting the necessity of improving supervision quality in OPSD.
authors: Shufan Shen, Zhongni Hou, Chao Bi, Yufei Zhang, Guojun Yin, Shuhui Wang
bullets: OPSD can stagnate because its self-teacher produces unreliable guidance for some samples.
TESD trains the self-teacher with environmental feedback on task correctness and context independence.
It estimates guidance reliability and adaptively down-weights samples with weak supervision.
Experiments across multiple datasets and model scales show consistent gains over representative token- and sequence-level methods.

figures.caption: Figure 3: Overall framework of TESD. Given an input query, the student first generates rollouts, which provide the privileged context for the self-teacher. Then, TESD optimizes the student and the self-teacher, respectively. For the self-teacher, it interacts with the environment and learns from the obtained rewards of correctness and independence. For the student, it is supervised by the logits of the self-teacher. The loss value is adaptively weighted by the teacher’s mean reward of the corresponding input query, which estimates the quality of teacher guidance.
Figure 11: Case studies of different methods on the Physics subset of the SciKnowEval benchmark using Qwen3-8B.

Figure 1: (a) In OPSD, the self-teacher provides guidance indiscriminately across all samples without improving its own capabilities, thereby degrading the quality of supervision delivered to the student. (b) TESD improves the self-teacher using the environmental rewards of its rollouts while delivering adaptive guidance by down-weighting samples with unreliable supervision. (c) TESD achieves more continuous performance improvement than current OPSD methods.

papers.abstract: Linear attention and state space models (SSMs) offer efficient alternatives to softmax attention by maintaining a fixed-size recurrent state, but this design requires careful management to preserve useful historical associations and limit interference. The delta rule helps reduce interference through correction of the value associated with each key, but it does not explicitly account for how related value features are distributed across the state. We observe that a state $\boldsymbol{S}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_k\times d_v}$ can be viewed as a bank of $d_k$ addresses storing $d_v$-dimensional values. While a key-side read $\boldsymbol{S}^\top\boldsymbol{k}$ retrieves the value associated with $\boldsymbol{k}$, a value-side read $\boldsymbol{S}\boldsymbol{e}$ aggregates addresses whose stored value features match the selector $\boldsymbol{e}$. Based on this observation, we propose Dual DeltaNet (DDN), which extends Kimi Delta Attention (KDA) with a two-sided delta rule. The key-side delta rule reads with the current key to correct its associated value, while the complementary value-side delta rule reads with selected features of the current value to reorganize the addresses it occupies. We derive a chunkwise parallel training algorithm and a rank-2 recurrence that increases arithmetic intensity during inference. Compared with KDA, GDN-2, and Mamba-3, DDN achieves the strongest overall performance across language modeling, zero-shot downstream tasks, and retrieval, while incurring modest training and inference overhead relative to KDA. authors: Yixiao Qian, Yaxin Zhang, Song Chen, Jiaxu Liu, Shengze Cai, Chao Xu

papers.abstract: A memory can be outdated for present-day reasoning yet indispensable for reconstructing the past. Relevance-based retrieval overlooks this tension: semantic relevance, evidence-grounded validity, and query-specific eligibility are distinct. We propose CALM, a conflict-aware lifecycle memory governance framework that decouples persistent memory preservation from query-time admission. CALM converts heterogeneous records into evidence-grounded memory cells, updates validity and lifecycle states using support, conflict, and dependency signals, and admits query-appropriate evidence through training-free or learned gating informed by temporal applicability. Across LongMemEval-S and LoCoMo with Qwen and GPT backbones, CALM outperforms state-of-the-art baselines, achieving the best overall accuracy. Compared with simple filtering and reranking, query-conditioned admission further improves evidence selection. Conflict-blocking and robustness analyses show CALM suppresses erroneous retrieved memories while retaining useful evidence. Historical-reconstruction experiments demonstrate that preserving superseded records supports accurate earlier-state reasoning without compromising current-state answers.

papers.abstract: Why do multilingual language models generalize across languages even without shared vocabulary? The Platonic Representation Hypothesis posits that models trained on different data, objectives, and modalities converge toward a shared statistical model of reality. Extending this intuition to representations inside a single multilingual model, we propose the Relational Identifiability Hypothesis: relations in a shared world can promote entity alignment by ruling out alternative cross-lingual correspondences, making corresponding entities more likely to become directly readable without an additional transformation. We test this hypothesis in a controlled bilingual Transformer whose two token-disjoint languages describe the same modular-arithmetic world. We find that the languages can develop a shared answer subspace without aligning corresponding numbers. Cross-lingual alignment emerges selectively when the available relations constrain number correspondences: subtraction makes zero task-level identifiable, inducing selective alignment, while an order-sensitive operation produces broad alignment across numbers. These patterns predict success in zero-shot cross-lingual transfer. Together, our results show that relational structure in a shared world can promote entity alignment and enable transfer.
bullets: A controlled bilingual Transformer models two token-disjoint languages describing the same modular-arithmetic world.
The languages can share an answer subspace without directly aligning corresponding numbers.
Relations constrain possible cross-lingual correspondences: subtraction selectively aligns zero, while an order-sensitive operation broadly aligns numbers.
The resulting alignment patterns predict successful zero-shot cross-lingual transfer.
The study is limited to a controlled synthetic arithmetic setting.

papers.abstract: Complex Temporal Knowledge Graph Question Answering (TKGQA) involves more than retrieving facts: the timestamp or validity interval of one fact can constrain the search for another, while multiple intervals may jointly determine the answer. Existing single-agent TKGQA methods typically investigate these facts within a single reasoning context, where evidence from different event histories can become interleaved and distractors can misdirect subsequent retrieval. Distributing investigations across agents can separate event-specific evidence into distinct contexts, but effective collaboration must still be learned because question decomposition, subtask investigation, and evidence synthesis are interdependent. To address these limitations, we propose \textbf{Co}-Evolving \textbf{S}elf-Play \textbf{T}imeline \textbf{A}gents (CoSTA), which organizes facts into navigable timelines, delegates investigations to workers, and uses a coordinator to synthesize their original timestamped observations. CoSTA initializes a shared policy through role-conditioned distillation and jointly optimizes both roles through co-evolving self-play with final-answer rewards. Across three benchmarks, CoSTA achieves state-of-the-art overall performance, with particularly strong gains on complex multi-fact questions, while its compact variants outperform the evaluated closed-source LLM agents.

papers.abstract: Monitoring a model's chain of thought (CoT) is useful for safety only if the final answer depends on the written steps. Prior measurements use natural tasks where true reasoning is unknown. We measure it against an exact ground truth on a synthetic box-swap task where every intermediate state is known. We replace one step inside a model's own chain with a wrong but valid state and check whether the answer follows the edit. We evaluate 25 open-weight models--Qwen3 (0.6B-14B, base and post-trained), Gemma 3 (1B-12B), Llama 3 (1B-8B), and 8 OLMo 2 checkpoints--on 7,200 items each. We find five results: (1) Reliance rises with size and saturates. In Qwen3, answer reliance rises from 16-18% at 0.6B to 97-100% at 14B; a logistic in log N fits well (R^2 = 0.89), and Gemma 3 and Llama 3 follow this trend. (2) Capability is the main driver. Across all models, reliance and step accuracy correlate at r = 0.99; equally capable models are equally reliant, regardless of family. (3) Size still matters at matched correctness. On problems solved correctly before the edit, reliance increases with size among capable models (rho = 0.80, p = 0.002). (4) Post-training does not change reliance. Base and post-trained Qwen3 differ by at most 0.03 from 4B upward; a large gap at 1.7B matches a large capability gap. (5) No model up to 14B solves the task internally. Without written steps, every capable model is at chance once a problem has four or more swaps. OLMo 2 checkpoints never become capable, making the training-token axis a limitation. On tasks requiring step-by-step computation, scale makes the chain of thought more load-bearing, supporting CoT monitoring in this regime.
bullets: Reliance on edited reasoning steps rises with model size and then saturates, reaching 97–100% for 14B Qwen3 models.
Reliance closely tracks reasoning capability across model families, including Gemma 3 and Llama 3.
Even at matched correctness, larger capable models depend more on their written steps.
Base and post-trained Qwen3 models show nearly identical reliance from 4B parameters upward.

No tested model internally solves sufficiently complex tasks without written steps; the findings are limited to this synthetic step-by-step setting and do not cover models that remain incapable, such as OLMo 2 checkpoints.

papers.abstract: Repeating transformer layers can improve language model performance without adding parameters. However, the added computational depth increases both forward and backward computation costs during training. Training such models requires choosing a backward window that controls how many final layer repetitions retain gradients during backpropagation. Longer windows improve per-token learning efficiency but increase per-update cost, while shorter windows reduce per-update cost but sacrifice per-token efficiency. Understanding which window performs better requires examining different training budgets. Prior work compares backward windows across computational budgets. When training budgets increase, it remains unclear whether the same window continues to perform best. We measure how the relative performance of two windows shifts as training budgets grow. Our method isolates per-token efficiency by training both windows on identical data, and compares complete training recipes at approximately equal training time at each budget. Results show that shorter windows lose much of their advantage as budgets grow. Controlled experiments show that both benefits decrease at larger budgets, with a greater decline in the benefit of extended training. Backward window comparisons depend on the available budget, and the preferred window among the tested candidates can change as the budget grows.
bullets: Repeating transformer layers improves performance without increasing parameter count but raises training computation costs.
The backward window controls how many final layer repetitions receive gradients, trading per-token efficiency against per-update cost.

Both windows’ benefits decline at larger budgets, especially the benefit of extended training.
The preferred window can change as the training budget grows.

papers.abstract: LLM-guided evolutionary search iteratively selects existing programs, uses LLMs as mutation operators to generate a new program, and evaluates it to guide subsequent search. To preserve diversity and reduce the risk of premature convergence, it often adopts the island model, in which groups of programs, called islands, evolve separately. However, this structure alone does not guarantee distinct search directions, as islands may start from similar programs or converge toward similar solutions during evolution. This suggests that diversity must be considered throughout the search process, from initializing islands with distinct programs to developing island trajectories and sharing discoveries across islands. To this end, we propose HoliDivEvolve , a holistic approach to establishing and effectively utilizing island diversity throughout evolutionary search. Specifically, we introduce diverse initialization to establish different initial programs, trajectory adaptive island selection to allocate computation based on current score, recent growth, and the remaining search budget, and growth adaptive migration to share alternative ideas across islands. Experiments across diverse benchmarks show that HoliDivEvolve achieves competitive performance on most evaluated tasks. We further conduct controlled analyses to examine how our design choices affect search behavior and final performance.
authors: Seockbean Song, Youngsik Yoon, Sungjae Lee, Siwei Wang, Wei Chen, Jungseul Ok
bullets: Island models alone may fail to maintain distinct search directions because islands can begin similarly or converge toward similar solutions.
The approach uses diverse initialization to create distinct starting programs.
Trajectory-adaptive island selection allocates computation using current score, recent growth, and remaining search budget.
Growth-adaptive migration shares alternative discoveries across islands.
Experiments across diverse benchmarks show competitive performance on most evaluated tasks, with controlled analyses of design choices.

papers.abstract: On-policy distillation (OPD) trains a student using teacher predictions on student-generated responses. Some methods insert teacher-written segments, or bridges, but disagree on how to train on those tokens. We compare no loss, forward KL and reverse KL on identical trajectories using Qwen3-1.7B as student and Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 as teacher. We separate gradients by which model wrote each token. Under our short training runs and BF16 inference, pre-specified tests detected no added accuracy benefit from teacher text as context or as a training target. A one-paragraph bridge after the student's first paragraph is only 2.7% of the tokens and contributes a small gradient nearly orthogonal to the student-token gradient. In this main comparison, the three loss treatments gave similar gradient directions and were statistically equivalent in accuracy within a +/-5 percentage-point margin. An exploratory pilot placing the bridge where failed responses disagreed most with the teacher suggested a benefit from teacher-token loss. A pre-specified replication did not confirm this, and fourfold weighting showed no significant accuracy benefit. Two limitations bound these findings. Among the tested amounts of training on fixed responses, gains peaked after four updates before the student increasingly failed to stop generating. None of the tested online training variants met the criteria for stable stopping and improved accuracy. Our evaluations used BF16 inference, which rounds away most of the small weight changes. When evaluated in exact FP32, the tested replication models frequently reached the response-length limit. Our accuracy findings therefore concern BF16 inference; they do not establish that teacher-token supervision is generally unnecessary.

An exploratory disagreement-based bridge placement suggested benefit from teacher-token loss, but replication and fourfold weighting found no significant accuracy gain.
None of the tested online variants achieved both stable stopping and improved accuracy; conclusions are specific to BF16 inference and short training runs.

papers.abstract: Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) have spurred growing interest in temporal knowledge graph question answering (TKGQA). Most existing methods rely on semantic retrieval augmented generation (RAG), which suffers from fundamental limitations in complex temporal reasoning. On the one hand, semantic-based RAG methods struggle to capture the multi-hop causal knowledge required for complex temporal reasoning. On the other hand, these methods introduce excessive redundant knowledge, trapping LLMs in spurious reasoning chains that potentially result in erroneous answers. To address these problems, we propose a Temporal Causal Chain-guided RAG (TCC-RAG) to retrieve a concise yet sufficient set of causal knowledge to support complex temporal reasoning. Specifically, we reformulate the temporal knowledge graph into a multi-view causal cue graph, with causal cues inducing connections that explicitly encode temporal evolution and causal dynamics. Based on the causal cue graph, we construct a query-specific temporal causal chain to guide the retrieval process, enabling the model to focus on a concise set of causally relevant knowledge. Finally, we introduce a causal evidence filter to refine the retrieved knowledge, ensuring its causal consistency with the underlying temporal logic of the query. Experiments show that TCC-RAG achieves substantial performance gains of 10.72% and 8.40% on two TKGQA benchmarks, and delivers a remarkable 62.97% improvement for multi-step temporal reasoning.
authors: Xinxun Zhang, Yuxiang Wang, Shanshan Feng, Jun Zhang, Tieyun Qian, Binhang Yuan, Kai Yin, Xiao Yan, Jiawei Jiang
bullets: Targets the limitations of semantic RAG in multi-hop temporal-causal reasoning and its redundant, misleading retrieved knowledge.
Reformulates temporal knowledge graphs as multi-view causal cue graphs encoding temporal evolution and causal dynamics.
Builds query-specific temporal causal chains to guide retrieval toward sufficient, causally relevant knowledge.
Uses a causal evidence filter to enforce consistency with the query’s temporal logic.
Reports performance gains of 10.72% and 8.40% on two TKGQA benchmarks, including a 62.97% improvement in multi-step temporal reasoning.

figures.caption: Fig. 2: The framework of TCC-RAG. (a) Temporal facts are organized into a Temporal Event Graph (TEG) and two temporally sorted indices: the Subject Causal Cue Index (SCCI) and Object Causal Cue Index (OCCI). (b) NER and LLM extraction ground query entities through matching and consistency checking. Relation, cue, and role parsing then guide view routing and temporal chain retrieval. (c) The Causal Evidence Filter removes equivalent duplicates and selects a sufficient subset of query-consistent facts. (d) The LLM reasons over the filtered evidence to generate answers. When structured retrieval yields no facts, semantic retrieval provides fallback candidates that also pass through the filter.

papers.abstract: Historical experience can guide scientific coding at multiple levels, but task-level retrieval may miss implementation lessons that become relevant during execution. We introduce MUSE, a memory management framework combining multi-level memory with selective runtime injection for scientific coding agents. MUSE builds global, approach-level, and implementation-level memory from historical trajectories. At initialization, the agent receives global memory and problem-matched approach-level memory. During execution, current interactions are used to retrieve implementation-level memory. An LLM gate selects relevant experience and generates specific review advice, or skips injection. Across four benchmarks spanning numerical problem solving, kernel optimization, and scientific software repair, MUSE outperforms retrieval and memory baselines on all evaluation metrics. Ablations support the multi-level design and gated injection, while transfer experiments show that memory remains useful across kernel benchmarks. These results show that multi-level memory and selective runtime injection enable effective reuse of experience in scientific coding. Code is available at https://github.com/hr-jin/MUSE.
authors: Haoran Jin, Defu Lian, Xiting Wang, Hong Xie
bullets: Builds global, approach-level, and implementation-level memories from historical trajectories.
Provides global and problem-matched approach memory at initialization, then retrieves implementation lessons during execution.
Uses an LLM gate to inject relevant review advice or skip unnecessary memory injection.
Outperforms retrieval and memory baselines across four benchmarks covering numerical solving, kernel optimization, and software repair.
Ablations support the multi-level and gated designs; transfer experiments indicate usefulness across kernel benchmarks.

papers.abstract: Multi-Token Prediction (MTP) is now a common ingredient in language-model pre-training, as it improves downstream performance and enables faster inference through speculative decoding. We identify a flaw in standard MTP training, in which a residual component of the MTP gradient interferes with both next-token and multi-token learning, increasingly so with scale. Specifically, the MTP cross-entropy gradient can be decomposed exactly into a KL self-distillation term that pulls each MTP head toward the model's own next-token prediction (NTP) distribution and improves speculative decoding, and a residual that has a low signal-to-noise ratio and buries the useful KL signal. We introduce the KL gradient-recovery trick: when two distributions share a linear output head, the gradient of their KL divergence can be recovered exactly by combining their cross-entropy gradients through straight-through gradient routing. Unlike minimizing the KL directly, this trick requires no vocabulary-sized logit matrices and is compatible with standard fused cross-entropy kernels. This enables Soft Multi-Token Prediction (Soft-MTP), a one-line code change to MTP that removes the noisy residual and backpropagates only the KL self-distillation signal by reusing the existing NTP and MTP cross-entropy computations. Soft-MTP supports both DeepSeek- and Meta-style MTP, adds no parameters, and incurs no measurable overhead. From 167M to 1.2B parameters, Soft-MTP improves over standard MTP with lower NTP perplexity, faster speculative decoding and higher zero-shot accuracy at every scale, lower MTP perplexity from 689M onward, and stronger math and code reasoning after fine-tuning at 1.2B. Soft-MTP also matches, if not exceeds, direct KL divergence minimization on most metrics. Soft-MTP is, in effect, a free lunch for MTP optimization. Our code can be found at https://github.com/JaydenTeoh/Soft-MTP.
bullets: Standard MTP gradients contain a noisy residual that increasingly interferes with next-token and multi-token learning as models scale.
The authors decompose the gradient into a useful KL self-distillation component and a low-signal residual.
A gradient-recovery trick extracts the KL signal using existing cross-entropy computations and fused kernels, avoiding vocabulary-sized logit matrices.
Soft-MTP is a one-line modification compatible with DeepSeek- and Meta-style MTP, with no added parameters or measurable overhead.
Across 167M–1.2B parameters, it improves perplexity, speculative decoding speed, zero-shot accuracy, and—at 1.2B—math and code reasoning after fine-tuning.

papers.abstract: Language-model answers are often treated as a visible record of the internal decision that produced them. We test this assumption in conflicting-context question answering, where two supplied documents support incompatible answers. A model can process the disagreement and still return a one-sided answer, even under prompts that ask it to disclose conflict. In Qwen 0.8B, hidden source commitment is captured by a residual source-choice direction whose sign tracks which document the answer uses. Sparse middle-layer MLP writers feed the same coordinate, and steering the coordinate changes the chosen source. A transfer run on Gemma 3 1B preserves the source-choice readout and sparse-write bridge under LLM-audited labels. Conflict disclosure follows a different pattern, appearing weaker, later-layer, and only partially steerable. These results support a practical monitoring strategy for retrieval systems that detects silent source commitment with residual readouts and pairs conflict-surfacing prompts with disclosure steering when the model has selected a side under disagreement.
authors: Samuel Dawit Assefa, Jae Won Cho
bullets: In conflicting-context QA, models may choose one document without explicitly disclosing the disagreement.
A residual source-choice direction tracks which source the answer follows in Qwen 0.8B.
Sparse middle-layer MLPs write to this direction, and steering it changes source selection.
The readout and sparse-write mechanism transfer to Gemma 3 1B under LLM-audited labels.
Conflict disclosure is weaker, later-layer, and only partly steerable, motivating combined monitoring and prompting strategies.

papers.title: Hidden Commitment: When Language Models Silently Pick a Side and How Steering Can Surface It
papers.tldr: Language models can silently commit to one conflicting source, but residual-stream readouts and steering can reveal and influence that hidden choice.

papers.abstract: Test-time training (TTT) layers replace the linear fast-weight memory of modern recurrent architectures with a small neural network trained online by gradient descent. This nonlinear memory is more expressive than the linear memories of Gated DeltaNet and Mamba-2, but is difficult to parallelize: existing implementations such as TTT-MLP rely on sequential, block-wise weight updates that run several times slower than chunkwise-parallel linear recurrences. Moreover, their block-wise execution only approximates the token-by-token online recurrence, whereas linear recurrences admit an exact chunkwise-parallel evaluation. We introduce ParaTTT (PTTT), an algorithm for parallelizing arbitrarily deep nonlinear memories by iteratively refining estimates of the inner-loop gradient trajectory. Starting from a guess of the hidden-layer gradients, each refinement consists of three chunkwise-parallel passes: a forward pass that evaluates the resulting feature trajectory, an exact gated-delta-rule pass that computes the readout trajectory and its feature gradients, and a backward pass that propagates these gradients into a new estimate. The exact online gradient descent recurrence is a fixed point of the iteration, while decoding requires no refinement iterations. We prove geometric convergence for a two-layer variant under sufficient contraction conditions. In practice, two iterations suffice. With two refinement steps at 4K context, PTTT evaluates the inner-loop trajectory $32\times$ faster than TTT-MLP with the block approximation at matched error, while the full 340M model trains $4.9\times$ faster. Models trained at 340M and 1.3B parameters match or exceed Gated DeltaNet and Mamba-2 and remain competitive with same-size Transformers on language-modeling perplexity and zero-shot accuracy, with better recall than the linear recurrences.
authors: Noel Loo, Neehal Tumma, T. Konstantin Rusch, Mathias Lechner, Alexander Amini, Daniela Rus
bullets: TTT layers use more expressive nonlinear memories than linear recurrent alternatives but are difficult and slow to parallelize.
ParaTTT iteratively refines hidden-layer gradient trajectories using three chunkwise-parallel passes: forward, gated-delta readout/gradient computation, and backward propagation.
The exact online gradient-descent recurrence is a fixed point of the refinement process; decoding requires no refinement iterations.
Two refinement steps are typically sufficient; at 4K context, inner-loop evaluation is 32× faster than block-approximated TTT-MLP at matched error, while the full 340M model trains 4.9× faster.
At 340M and 1.3B parameters, models match or exceed Gated DeltaNet and Mamba-2, remain competitive with similarly sized Transformers, and show better recall than linear recurrences.

figures.caption: Figure 2: One iteration of ParaTTT; the recurrences are evaluated in chunkwise-parallel form over all T tokens. (1) A parallel forward pass evaluates the hidden layers from the current estimate of their pre-activation gradients. (2) The readout runs exactly on the resulting features and DELTARULEGRAD returns each token’s feature gradient. (3) A parallel backward pass propagates it through the hidden layers using shifted reads of the transposed recurrences (see Step 3 in Section 3.2 for details) and updates the estimate. (4) After N iterations a final forward pass and readout produce the output.

Figure 1: Parallelism and approximation in nonlinear TTT. Each cell represents a hidden preactivation gradient δzt(W) = ∂ℓt/∂zt|W, with the layer index omitted. Columns index tokens; downward steps mark computational dependencies, not approximation error or elapsed time. (a) Exact gradients δz⋆t use the latest online weights W̄t−1, including decay. (b) Block-wise TTT, as used by TTT-MLP (Sun et al., 2025) and Titans (Behrouz et al., 2025b), evaluates gradients at shared block-entry weights Wblk s for s < t ≤ s + b, omitting earlier within-block updates. (c) ParaTTT refines the full gradient trajectory using three chunkwise-parallel passes per round. The block size b and refinement count N control the respective approximations; the exact trajectory is a fixed point of the ParaTTT iteration.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces ParaTTT, a method to parallelize Test-Time Training (TTT) layers, which is highly relevant to online adaptation and efficient LLM training.
papers.title: ParaTTT: Parallelizing Test-Time Training Layers with Deep Memories
papers.tldr: ParaTTT makes nonlinear test-time training memories efficiently parallelizable, achieving large speedups while preserving accurate online behavior and strong language-modeling performance.

papers.abstract: Existing code reveals past implementation decisions but rarely explains the reasoning behind them. When coding agents implement new features or modify existing functionality, past decisions may conflict with new task instructions. This raises a fundamental question for agentic software evolution: when multiple implementations satisfy the same functional requirements, how do coding agents decide whether to follow existing code or new task instructions? We investigate this question through bidirectional, controlled experiments in purpose-built repositories, followed by validation in real-world open-source repositories. Our approach isolates three competing sources of guidance: (1) agents' default preferences, (2) repository precedents, and (3) explicit task instructions. We conduct 5,625 trials across four coding agents and six implementation pairs, with validation in four open-source repositories spanning three programming languages. We find that agents share the same default implementation choices, yet overwhelmingly follow repository precedent when it conflicts with those defaults (359/360 trials). Crucially, not all precedents carry equal influence: three supporting local files yield 96% adoption, compared with only 4% for sibling-resource files, and changing file placement alone can shift adoption from 0% to 100% at a fixed example count. When new task intent conflicts with existing code, written priority rules achieve substantially higher success than code examples alone (59/60 versus 38/60 joint successes for two agents on two implementation pairs). The effectiveness of explicit rules also extends to open-source repositories, where a harness-loaded rule raises joint success from 0/120 to 117/120. These findings motivate design-decision traceability that preserves not only implementation choices but also the rationale and priorities that should guide future changes.
authors: Haichao Zhu, Geyang Xu, Zhaorui Yang, Jiyuan Wang, Qian Zhang
bullets: The study separates three influences on agent decisions: default preferences, repository precedents, and explicit task instructions.
Across 5,625 controlled trials, agents followed conflicting repository precedents in 359 of 360 cases, though influence depended strongly on precedent location.
Three supporting local files drove 96% adoption, while sibling-resource files drove only 4%; changing file placement alone shifted adoption from 0% to 100%.
Written priority rules outperformed code examples for resolving conflicts and also improved outcomes in four real-world open-source repositories.
The findings support preserving the rationale and priority of design decisions, not just their resulting code.

papers.selection_reason: Investigates how coding agents balance repository precedents with new task instructions when evolving existing code.
papers.title: Precedent or Intent? What Coding Agents Follow When Evolving Existing Code
papers.tldr: Coding agents usually follow existing repository patterns over their default choices, but explicit priority rules can reliably steer them toward new task intent when precedents conflict.

papers.abstract: Large language models are increasingly used for financial guidance, yet little is known about whether their advice changes across social identities in Global South contexts. We introduce the Indian Financial Automated Advice Bias (IFAAB) benchmark, a counterfactual audit dataset of 31,734 GPT-4o-generated financial-advice responses for synthetic Indian personas varying by gender, caste, education, employment, residence, age, and district. Holding the underlying request fixed, we evaluate disparities in LLM-implied wealth, income, savings, projected gains, textual similarity, advice topics, and qualitative bias judgments. In the gender-only audit, male-labelled profiles receive 60.1\% higher initial total resources and 46.8\% higher post-advice total resources than comparable female-labelled profiles; in the caste-augmented audit, the post-advice total-resource gap remains 49.4\%. Adding district information reduces the aggregate post-advice total-resource gender gap to 7.9\%, revealing strong geographic conditioning. Standalone caste comparisons also show systematic stratification: relative to General-category profiles, OBC, SC, and ST profiles receive significantly lower post-advice total resources, respectively. Textual audits show low semantic similarity between paired gendered responses, with an average TF--IDF cosine similarity score of 0.44. Qualitative analysis shows that women are more often steered toward cautious saving, community support, and basic financial literacy, while men receive more growth-oriented advice involving investment, entrepreneurship, and asset accumulation. IFAAB provides a reusable benchmark for evaluating fairness, suitability, and consumer-protection risks in LLM-mediated financial advice, and highlights the need for locally grounded, intersectional evaluation of AI systems in high-stakes economic domains.
bullets: Introduces a benchmark of 31,734 financial-advice responses across personas varying in gender, caste, education, employment, residence, age, and district.
Holding requests fixed, audits implied wealth, income, savings, projected gains, response similarity, advice topics, and qualitative bias.
Male-labelled profiles receive higher implied resources than comparable female-labelled profiles; caste-linked disparities also persist.
District information substantially reduces the aggregate gender resource gap, indicating strong geographic conditioning.
Women are more often directed toward cautious saving and basic literacy, while men receive growth-oriented investment, entrepreneurship, and asset-accumulation advice.

papers.abstract: Coding agents are typically provided end-to-end behavioral specifications that the code they produce should satisfy, such as tests and input--output examples. How many such specifications must a developer provide, and which ones, for the agent to produce the developer's intended program? We argue that this cannot be determined a priori, for it depends on the structure of the implementation, which is left to the agent to decide. An agent first commits to a structure---a decomposition into data types, modules, and functions---which fixes a class of candidate programs; behavioral specifications then select a program within that class. A set of tests that suffices for one structure may leave another badly underdetermined, requiring different edge cases or exponentially more examples. Since the structure is chosen by the agent, developers cannot ensure their specification is complete without reverse-engineering it from thousands of lines of generated code. To resolve this, we introduce Skeleton Coding, in which developers jointly specify the structure---in high-level, code-like format---alongside behavioral specifications. Theoretically, we model AI-assisted coding as a control problem, and show that skeletons can reduce exponentially the number of tests developers must supply to steer an agent toward an acceptable program. Empirically, across four models and three benchmarks, the best-performing skeleton specifications reduce mean test error by 48.4% relative to the best end-to-end behavioral specifications. Even when the agent can query a complete reference implementation, adding a skeleton reduces mean test error relatively by up to 27.0%. Skeletons also narrow the average gap between small and large models by about 52.4% while lowering implementation cost by 15--26x, and reduce code erosion by 24.7% on average.
authors: Aditya Golatkar, Alessandro Achille, Renos Zabounidis, Vlad Sobal, Yangruibo Ding, Baishakhi Ray, Jonathan Buck, Guy Van den Broeck, Maryam Fazel, Pietro Perona, Wei Xia, Stefano Soatto
bullets: Behavioral tests alone may be insufficient because their effectiveness depends on the implementation structure chosen by the agent.
Skeletons specify decompositions into data types, modules, and functions, narrowing the candidate-program space before behavioral tests select details.
A control-theoretic analysis shows skeletons can reduce the number of required tests exponentially in some cases.
Across four models and three benchmarks, skeletons reduced mean test error by 48.4% versus the best end-to-end behavioral specifications.
Skeletons also reduced implementation cost, narrowed the small/large-model performance gap, and mitigated code erosion; scope is limited to the evaluated models and benchmarks.

Adding architecture sections to the markdown file slightly raises mean pass rate, but the resulting pass rate remains below that achieved with skeleton-based specifications. We then measure error rate across the hidden suite. On average, no number of tests provided results in a program that passes all hidden tests. (Middle) Even providing a full behavioral specification is not enough: We measure the pass rate with access to an oracle providing the full and exact input-output behavior. Even so, adding a skeleton with local contracts increases the pass rate averaged across models by 10.9% relative to the same setup without a skeleton on ProgramBench. (Right) A skeleton specifying the local contract for slicing a strided view.

Figure 2: Value of different types of specifications. We generate specifications of different kinds and measure the error rate of a coding agent using them. No matter the format, behavioral specifications that describe only end-to-end behavior underperform specifications that describe the developer’s intended structure. Of the structural specifications, code-like specifications that describe function signatures and invariants outperform design files in natural language. Adding overly detailed specifications decreases the accuracy of smaller models.

Figure 7: Structural specifications produce less eroded code than behavioral specifications: Across all benchmarks and models, structural specifications reduce code erosion by up to 24.7%, compared to the task-only prompt. Meanwhile, behavioral specifications increase it. Verbosity varies little across conditions.

Figure 5: Skeletons bridge the gap between large and small models: Skeleton specifications significantly improve performance of smaller models, leading to accuracy similar to that of larger models at a lower cost. In particular, the entire cost–performance Pareto frontier (dashed) is formed mostly by small models with structural specifications.

Figure 8: Skeletons reduce query effort and cost during iterative repair: For iterative repair tasks, using skeletons reduces the total cost of implementation, and also the number of user queries. We model user queries with the number of calls to the program binary. Additionally, final code has lower erosion and higher maintainability.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes 'Skeleton Coding' to improve coding agent performance by providing structural specifications alongside behavioral ones.
papers.title: Skeleton Coding: Program Structure as a Specification for Agents
papers.tldr: Skeleton Coding lets developers specify a program’s high-level structure alongside tests, substantially improving coding-agent reliability and reducing specification effort.

papers.abstract: LLM-based agents now share experiences on social platforms and remember new preferences to enhance their performance. However, existing memory systems contain a vulnerability in role-to-principal attribution that attackers can exploit. We identify Role Grounding Misattribution, in which an attacker-designed interaction causes the victim agent to incorrectly record a preference from the attacker as a preference of the victim's user. Specifically, we are the first to formalize Role Grounding Attack (RGA), an attack model that exploits this vulnerability through nested conversation structures. In the memory formation stage, an experience-sharing post quoting a conversation between the attacker agent and its user is published, which explicitly identifies its publisher. The inner conversation expresses preferences from the user of the attacker agent. When the victim agent remembers preferences from this nested structure, its memory loses the context binding and grounds the attacker's preference to the victim's user instead. In the memory retrieval stage, the misattributed preference persists and influences the victim agent's decisions when it encounters relevant scenarios. We instantiate RGA as tool selection manipulation and privacy leakage. Tool selection manipulation causes a tool-call preference to be misattributed to the victim's user, steering the victim toward an attacker-controlled tool. Privacy leakage extends this by misattributing both a tool-call preference and a task-requirement preference to the victim's user. The victim selects the attacker's tool, then includes sensitive information in tool arguments to satisfy the task requirement. We evaluate RGA across five mainstream memory systems and six language models. Tool manipulation and privacy leakage both achieve high attack success rates. These results call for stronger role grounding.
authors: Haoran Bu, Yiting Shen, Litian Zhang, Ruihan Hu, Xi Zhang
bullets: Identifies Role Grounding Misattribution as a vulnerability in memory systems’ role-to-principal attribution.
Formalizes RGA through nested conversations embedded in experience-sharing posts.
Demonstrates tool-selection manipulation and privacy leakage as attack scenarios.
Evaluates five mainstream memory systems and six language models, finding high attack success rates for both scenarios.
Calls for stronger role grounding to preserve preference ownership and context.

papers.selection_reason: Formalizes a memory vulnerability in LLM agents (Role Grounding Attack) and demonstrates its impact on tool selection and privacy.
papers.title: Is it my preference? Role Grounding Attack against Agent's Memory via Social Interaction
papers.tldr: Role Grounding Attack exploits nested social interactions to make an agent misattribute an attacker’s preferences to its user, enabling tool manipulation and privacy leakage.

papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) treat all context tokens uniformly, lacking explicit separation between executable instructions and passive data. This leads to prompt injection vulnerabilities, ambiguous instruction binding, and unreliable execution control. We present a post-training methodology using LLMON (LLM Object Notation), a framework that enables separating instructions from data and requires explicit identifier-based execution. We construct a large-scale structured training corpus of 4.6B tokens spanning general, RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation), and tool-calling data, augmented with distractor-infused variants in which competing instructions and irrelevant data segments are present in context but not referenced. Post-training two Granite-4.1 base models (3B and 8B) through supervised fine-tuning followed by reinforcement learning, we show that LLMON-structured supervision reduces attack success rates on indirect prompt-injection benchmarks from 53-100% to 0.02-5.6% while preserving general capabilities. We further introduce attention-based interpretability metrics that diagnose failure modes at individual transformer layers for structured inputs, revealing how our approach reshapes internal attention patterns. Our results demonstrate that explicit execution semantics can be taught through standard post-training without architectural modification.
authors: Basel Shbita, Michael Hind, Chad DeLuca, Nathan Fulton, Shubhi Asthana, Farhan Ahmed, Anisa Halimi, Yada Zhu, Mauro Martino, David Cox, Dan Gutfreund
bullets: Addresses prompt injection, ambiguous instruction binding, and unreliable execution control caused by treating all context tokens uniformly.
Uses LLM Object Notation (LLMON) with identifier-based execution and structured training data covering general, RAG, tool-calling, and distractor-infused contexts.
Post-trains 3B and 8B Granite-4.1 models using supervised fine-tuning followed by reinforcement learning.
Reduces attack success on indirect prompt-injection benchmarks from 53–100% to 0.02–5.6% while preserving general capabilities.
Introduces attention-based interpretability metrics to analyze layer-level failure modes and changes in attention patterns.

papers.selection_reason: Post-training LLMs for instruction/data separation and prompt-injection robustness; fits LLM research.
papers.title: Post-Training Large Language Models with LLMON
papers.tldr: LLMON post-training teaches LLMs to distinguish instructions from data and execute only explicitly referenced instructions, sharply reducing indirect prompt-injection success without changing model architecture.

papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) appear to represent and reason about a large range of phenomena. In particular, recent studies have examined whether LLMs can accurately reason about causation. One of the most commonly used benchmarks for evaluating formal causal reasoning in LLMs is CLadder, a framework for procedural generation of benchmark data sets that was released in 2023. Experiments with CLadder appear to indicate that LLMs can perform formal causal reasoning in a large percentage of generated examples. In this paper, we examine what can be reliably inferred when LLMs perform well on test sets produced by CLadder. We identify several examples of superficial and highly predictive patterns that the CLadder generator embeds in data sets it generates. We find that even simple models such as random forests perform well on CLadder-generated data sets after training on a sample of generated data. We also find that the performance of many commercial LLMs on CLadder test sets is extremely brittle and that removing large sections of the text that are critical for formal causal reasoning has almost no effect on performance. Given these results, the most likely hypothesis for the strong performance of state-of-the-art LLMs on CLadder is that they are exploiting superficial patterns learned from exposure to training data from the generator. Any inference that LLMs are exhibiting more complex causal reasoning must rule out this hypothesis.
authors: Justin Clarke, Isha Karn, Patrick Murray, KJ Hill, David Jensen
bullets: CLadder is a widely used benchmark for formal causal reasoning in LLMs, but its procedural generation introduces highly predictive superficial patterns.
Simple random forests perform well on CLadder data after training on generated examples.
Many commercial LLMs show brittle performance, remaining largely unchanged when text critical to causal reasoning is removed.
The findings suggest that claims of advanced causal reasoning must rule out memorization or exploitation of generator artifacts.

papers.abstract: We introduce Nemotron 3.5 Super and Nemotron 3.5 Lightning, open and efficient Mixture-of-Experts Hybrid Mamba-Transformer models designed for reasoning, long-context understanding, and agentic workloads. Super is a 120B-parameter, 12B-active multimodal model, while Lightning is a smaller 30B-parameter, 3B-active text model; both designed for efficient deployment. Both models combine large-scale distillation, long-context training, and native speculative decoding, while Super further incorporates Indic continued pretraining and agentic software-engineering mid-training. We develop a comprehensive post-training pipeline spanning supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning (RLVR and RLHF), complemented in Super by specialized teacher training and multi- teacher on-policy distillation (MOPD). This transforms Super from a text-only base model into a multimodal agent capable of reasoning over text, images, video, and interactive tool environments. We further explore test-time scaling through parallel agent execution and self-verification. Across training and deployment, we jointly optimize capability and efficiency. Indic continued pretraining improves Indian-language benchmarks by up to 9.82 percentage points, while agentic mid-training strengthens software-engineering capabilities and robustness across agent harnesses. The post-trained Super model achieves 51.78% on SWE-bench Pro, surpassing Nemotron 3 Ultra despite using approximately 4.6x fewer active parameters. Post-training MTP boosting improves speculative- decoding acceptance length by up to 21.8% under probabilistic draft sampling, while NVFP4 quantization achieves 99.62% median accuracy recovery relative to BF16. Inference optimizations enable up to 4,856 output tokens/s/GPU on GB200 while sustaining at least 50 tokens/s/user.

bullets: Super has 120B total and 12B active parameters with multimodal capabilities; Lightning has 30B total and 3B active parameters for text.
Training combines distillation, long-context training, speculative decoding, supervised fine-tuning, and reinforcement learning; Super also uses Indic and software-engineering mid-training.
Super supports reasoning across text, images, video, and interactive tools, with parallel-agent execution and self-verification for test-time scaling.
Reported results include up to 9.82-point gains on Indian-language benchmarks, 51.78% on SWE-bench Pro, and up to 21.8% longer speculative-decoding acceptance.
Deployment techniques include MTP boosting and NVFP4 quantization, with up to 4,856 output tokens/s/GPU on GB200 while sustaining at least 50 tokens/s/user.

papers.abstract: Advancing language models for specialized scientific applications requires evaluations of scientific fluency, physical reasoning, and quantitative analyses. Using inertial confinement fusion (ICF) as a test case, we have developed an expert-curated benchmark of 250 questions spanning qualitative reasoning, numerical calculation, symbolic derivation, and equation formulation. Responses have been evaluated using deterministic numerical and symbolic checks together with language-model judges. We compared a variety of out-of-the-box closed-source and open-source large language models with Prospero, a model specialized through combined domain-adaptive pretraining and supervised fine-tuning for ICF. We also conducted initial retrieval-assisted evaluations. Prospero improved its aggregate score by 10.7 percentage points over its base model, with gains across all question types. Frontier models achieved the highest aggregate scores, but critical physics errors persisted, particularly in numerical calculations. We note that domain-specific performance can improve through specialization, but benchmark gains alone do not establish scientific reliability. Retrieval improved performance for a smaller model but yielded no statistically significant improvement for a frontier model. Two scientific stress tests further illustrate useful capabilities and the need for expert assessment of physical assumptions and model validity. Based on these findings, we recommend evaluating existing domain capabilities and retrieval benefits before committing to substantial additional specialization.

papers.title: Assessing Language Models for Scientific Applications: Inertial Confinement Fusion as a Use Case
papers.tldr: An expert-curated ICF benchmark shows that domain specialization improves language-model performance, but even frontier models retain important physics errors and require expert validation.

papers.abstract: Latent multi-agent systems reduce inference cost by keeping intermediate reasoning and inter-agent communication in continuous representations.\ Reusable skills, however, are commonly supplied as text or stored as layer-wise Key-Value states or skill-specific model parameters, introducing repeated processing or substantial per-skill storage.\ We introduce \textbf{SkillMem}, which represents each reusable skill as a small external latent memory and makes it directly available during latent multi-agent reasoning.\ A role-conditioned cross-attention reader allows the same memory to guide different agents according to their roles and current hidden states.\ We train the skill memories and shared reader through behavioral distillation, matching the change in token predictions induced by a textual skill while keeping the backbone frozen.\ For our experiments, we obtain textual skills from paired successful and failed multi-agent trajectories, although existing skills can also be compiled directly.\ Across six benchmarks and Qwen3 models ranging from 4B to 14B parameters, SkillMem provides strong gains for smaller backbones while preserving efficient latent multi-agent inference across model scales.\ We use the same $8\times256$ memory configuration across all evaluated model scales, requiring 9.6\,KB of skill-specific storage per skill, including its retrieval embedding.\ For a library of 100 skills, SkillMem reduces total storage by more than $38\times$ compared with alternative skill representations and achieves up to a $4.23\times$ end-to-end inference speedup.\ These results show that compact procedural memories can be reused without sacrificing the efficiency of latent multi-agent reasoning.
authors: Yuxuan Zhu, Mohammad Mohammadi Amiri, Pin-Yu Chen, Keerthiram Murugesan
bullets: Addresses the repeated processing and high per-skill storage costs of text, Key-Value, and parameter-based skill representations.
Stores each skill in a small external latent memory accessed through role-conditioned cross-attention.
Trains the memories and shared reader by behavioral distillation while keeping the backbone frozen.
Across six benchmarks and Qwen3 models from 4B to 14B parameters, it provides especially strong gains for smaller models.
Uses 9.6 KB per skill; for 100 skills, it cuts storage by over 38× and delivers up to 4.23× end-to-end speedup.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of SkillMem. Reusable textual skills are discovered from paired multi-agent trajectories. Each skill is compiled into a compact latent memory by matching the behavioral effect of skill injection. At inference time, the retrieved memory is shared across agents and consumed through a role-conditioned reader while inter-agent communication remains entirely latent.

Figure 3: Behavioral skill distillation. For each skill, agent role, and calibration task, the frozen backbone generates a teacher response with the textual skill included in the role prompt. We score the same response with and without the textual skill to measure its token-level effect. We then replace the skill text with its memory and train the memory and role-conditioned reader to reproduce the skill-supported behavior while preserving the base behavior at positions with limited skill support.

Figure 1: Accuracy and efficiency comparison. (a) Accuracy changes of SkillMem relative to TextMAS and LatentMAS using Qwen3-4B. (b) Total storage required by different skill representations as the skill library grows. (c) End-to-end inference speedup relative to TextMAS.

We report task accuracy (%, “Acc.”), average output tokens (“Token”), and inference time in seconds (“Speed”). “Text” and “Latent” denote TextMAS and LatentMAS, respectively, and “SP” denotes Soft Prompt. SkillMem accuracy is bolded when it exceeds either TextMAS or LatentMAS.

papers.selection_reason: Compact external skill memory for latent multi-agent LLM reasoning directly fits LLM memory and memory-efficient inference, with large storage and speedup gains.
papers.title: SkillMem: Compact External Skill Memory for Latent Multi-Agent Reasoning
papers.tldr: SkillMem enables latent multi-agent systems to reuse compact external skill memories, reducing storage and improving inference efficiency while preserving performance.

papers.abstract: Pre-training foundational models is computationally expensive as models scale. In this work, we introduce Bi-Phase Training (BPT), a parameter-efficient pre-training method that preserves the high-rank learning dynamics observed in full-parameter optimization with substantially reduced trainable parameters. BPT parameterizes each weight update as a composition of constrained high-rank left/right transformations via trainable diagonal matrices and low-rank adapters whose updates are periodically merged into the frozen base weights, resulting in a compounding expansion of accessible directions during training. Across language-model pre-training from scratch (Qwen2.5 models from 100M to 1.5B parameters and OLMo-2-1B) on FineWeb-Edu (10B and 100B tokens), BPT achieves validation perplexity close to full-parameter baselines while using far fewer trainable parameters; e.g., at the 1.5B scale, BPT uses 66% fewer trainable parameters with only a small validation-perplexity gap. Additionally, a comprehensive evaluation across diverse downstream tasks shows that BPT preserves much of the full-parameterized model's downstream performance.
bullets: Addresses the high computational cost of full-parameter foundational-model pre-training.
Uses constrained high-rank left/right transformations with trainable diagonal matrices and low-rank adapters.
Periodically merges adapter updates into frozen base weights, expanding the directions accessible during training.
Evaluated on Qwen2.5 models from 100M to 1.5B parameters and OLMo-2-1B using FineWeb-Edu.
At 1.5B parameters, reduces trainable parameters by 66% with only a small validation-perplexity gap and preserves much downstream performance.

papers.selection_reason: Parameter-efficient pre-training method for LLMs that reduces trainable parameters, relevant to LLM training and efficiency.
papers.title: Bi-Phase Training: Learning Efficiently From Scratch
papers.tldr: Bi-Phase Training enables efficient from-scratch language-model pre-training by using far fewer trainable parameters while retaining near-full-parameter validation and downstream performance.

papers.abstract: Many open mixture-of-experts (MoE) language models train with Muon instead of AdamW. Most balance the load with a bias on each expert's routing score, adjusted after every step. Their recipes disagree on whether Muon should also train the router. In models with 55M and 108M active parameters, we measure how the optimizer changes the span of these biases, the largest minus the smallest in a layer. The span grows when all tokens favor the same experts, so it shows how hard a layer is to balance. At learning rates tuned on shorter runs, Muon raised the span of the first MoE layer at every seed, roughly doubling it on average, while the other layers changed much less. The rise came from Muon on the rest of the network, whichever optimizer trained the router. In those runs, the inputs to the first router shared a direction, and soon after the warmup its busiest expert averaged four to seven times its fair share. Over the first 3,000 steps, subtracting the batch mean from these inputs removed this overload while barely changing the loss. On the smaller model, halving Muon's learning rate removed most of the rise and slightly improved the loss. Moving only the router to AdamW made the loads shift more during the warmup and slightly raised the loss, so at this scale the results favor keeping the router on Muon.
bullets: Muon increased the routing-bias span of the first MoE layer across all seeds, roughly doubling it on average at tuned learning rates.
The effect was driven by Muon applied to the rest of the network, not by the optimizer used for the router.
The first router’s inputs became directionally aligned, causing its busiest expert to receive 4–7× its fair share soon after warmup.
Subtracting the batch mean from router inputs removed the overload over 3,000 steps with little loss change.
For the smaller model, halving Muon’s learning rate reduced the imbalance and slightly improved loss; switching only the router to AdamW was less favorable.

papers.selection_reason: Directly studies optimizer effects on mixture-of-experts LLM training and router balancing, fitting LLM architecture and training research.
papers.title: Muon Makes the First Mixture-of-Experts Layer Harder to Balance
papers.tldr: Muon can destabilize load balancing in the first MoE layer, but reducing its learning rate or centering router inputs largely mitigates the overload.

papers.abstract: Metis is a bet that better data, better training methods and new architectures can buy what a bigger parameter count cannot, at a fraction of the cost. Metis-1.6 is its latest step: two language models built from scratch by a single researcher, Praxis (2.94B parameters, 0.46B active per pass) and Logos (10.23B parameters, 1.18B active per pass). Both run a hybrid Mamba-2 and attention mixture-of-experts stack twice for every token, so each token gets a second look. Each was trained on 1.02T tokens in total: 804.76B of pretraining, 18B of context extension to 131,072 tokens, and 200B of supervised fine-tuning. Metis-1.6 was never meant to challenge frontier models, and across 40 post-trained benchmarks it mostly does not: Logos averages 52.93, seventh of 17 models in its comparison set and within a point of Qwen3-4B. But it gets there on roughly a twelfth of the median training data of the comparators that disclose it, and with fewer active parameters per token than any model that beats it, which puts it on the Pareto frontier for both. In mathematics it ranks second of 30 models, with 67.50% on AIME 2025 and 63.64% on HMMT February 2026. It is weak at code, instruction following and long context. The rest of the report is the part I found most valuable: what went wrong. The optimizer I configured never ran, and attention trained with AdamW for all of pretraining. A 1.77B-parameter n-gram memory learned to switch itself off. Five fine-tuning choices cost capability. And a length reward under group-mean normalization punished correct solutions for being long once a group's pass rate passed 2/3, a sign inversion I prove and fix with a one-line clamp. I close with the 10B-token ablations behind MoRE (Mixture of Recursive Experts), the looped architecture of Metis-1.7.
bullets: Introduces Praxis (2.94B parameters; 0.46B active per pass) and Logos (10.23B; 1.18B active), built from scratch by one researcher.
Uses a hybrid Mamba-2 and attention mixture-of-experts stack applied twice per token, with 1.02T tokens of pretraining, context extension, and supervised fine-tuning.
Logos reaches a 52.93 average across 40 benchmarks, placing seventh of 17 comparison models and on the reported Pareto frontiers for training data and active parameters.
Performs especially well in mathematics, ranking second of 30 models, but is weak at coding, instruction following, and long-context tasks.
Analyzes failures including an unused optimizer, an inactive n-gram memory, costly fine-tuning choices, and a flawed length reward; it also presents ablations for the next architecture, MoRE.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Metis-1.6 on one page, drawn for Logos. (a) Twenty layers, three of them attention, each ending in a mixture-of-experts block. The stack runs twice per token with every weight shared, and a depth memory carries what the first pass wrote down into the second. The n-gram memory that fed layers 2 and 5 during pretraining is drawn as a ghost: the models closed its gates on their own, and I removed it before release (Section 5). (b) Inside a layer, each sub-layer reads from and writes to four residual streams, which are then mixed by a doubly stochastic 4× 4 matrix; a controller that knows the current pass sets all three. (c) The mixture-of-experts block works in a 1,024-dimensional latent space: one shared expert and four of 192 routed experts run there before the result is projected back to model width. Praxis is the same design with 12 layers (attention at layers 4 and 8), width 2,048 and 128 routed experts.

Figure 1: Mean score on the 40 post-trained benchmarks against (a) published training tokens and (b) active parameters per token. papers.selection_reason: Technical report on new hybrid Mamba-2/attention MoE LLMs trained from scratch, directly fitting large language model research.
papers.title: Think Twice: The Metis-1.6 Technical Report
papers.tldr: Metis-1.6 explores whether better data, training, and recursive hybrid architectures can achieve efficient language-model performance without scaling parameter counts.

papers.abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) lets a large language model (LLM) answer questions by retrieving relevant passages from a large corpus. However, RAG struggles with multi-hop questions, which require chaining facts spread across several documents through intermediate entities that the question never mentions. Graph-based RAG methods retrieve once from the entities a question names and so rarely recover the full evidence chain. Iterative RAG methods recover it step by step, but their accuracy is limited by the many tasks they ask the LLM to perform, such as planning the sub-questions, deciding their dependencies, rewriting them as answers arrive, and keeping track of what is known. We propose DeFT-RAG, a RAG framework built on three components. First, DeFT-RAG generates one self-contained sub-question at a time from the original question and the sub-questions answered so far with their answers (QA pairs). Each sub-question names every entity it asks about, which removes the need to plan, track dependencies or rewrite, and lets the LLM focus on a single fine-grained task at a time. Second, DeFT-RAG moves the remaining LLM work outside the LLM: rule-based updates to a QA table that keeps track of what is known, and yes/no decisions made by a fine-tuned lightweight decision model. Third, DeFT-RAG caches the QA pairs and reuses an answer when a later question asks a sub-question with the same meaning. On MuSiQue, 2WikiMultiHopQA and HotpotQA, DeFT-RAG achieves the best accuracy among thirteen baselines with both gpt-4o-mini and Qwen3.6 as the backbone, while giving the LLM fewer input tokens than any other iterative method. With a QA cache shared across 1,000 MuSiQue questions, 23.1% of sub-questions are answered from the cache, which reduces LLM calls by 12.9% without lowering accuracy.
bullets: Targets multi-hop RAG failures where evidence spans documents connected through unstated intermediate entities.
Generates one self-contained sub-question at a time, using prior question–answer pairs to name all relevant entities.
Uses rule-based QA-table updates and a fine-tuned lightweight decision model to move bookkeeping and yes/no decisions outside the LLM.
Caches semantically equivalent sub-question answers; on 1,000 MuSiQue questions, this served 23.1% of sub-questions from cache and reduced LLM calls by 12.9% without reducing accuracy.
Achieved the best accuracy among 13 baselines on MuSiQue, 2WikiMultiHopQA, and HotpotQA with both tested backbones, while using fewer input tokens than other iterative methods.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Failures of graph-based and iterative RAG on a 3-hop MuSiQue question (gpt-4o-mini runs). Top: the gold chain, which passes through two bridge entities the question never names. (a) HippoRAG 2, a graph-based method, finds the first bridge entity (Kevin Drew) but no passage about his band or Toronto. (b) LogicRAG, which plans its sub-questions in advance, searches for the city of “the performer” before finding the performer (dependency error). (c) IRCoT, which keeps all retrieved passages in its long prompt, has the whole chain there and even states that the band is based in Toronto, but then loses track of this fact (tracking error).

Figure 2: Overview of DeFT-RAG on the question of Figure 1. The LLM performs only three fine-grained tasks (blue), and a fine-tuned DMmakes every yes/no decision (orange). The QA table, updated by rules, holds the QA pairs found for the question; the QA cache holds those found for other questions. The first sub-question was answered for an earlier question, so its answer is reused from the QA cache (marked “cached”) without retrieval or an LLM call. The values next to Answer directly? and Enough facts? are the DM’s yes probabilities from our gpt-4o-mini run.

Table 2: Results on 1,000 questions per benchmark with two backbones: exact match (EM), token F1, and LLM-judged accuracy (Acc). gpt-4o-mini runs are judged by Qwen3.6 and Qwen3.6 runs by gpt-4o-mini, so no model grades its own answers. EM and F1 are computed from the answers as given and understate systems that answer in full sentences, such as LightRAG with gpt-4o-mini; Acc is our main metric. Avg: mean over the three benchmarks. Best in bold, second best underlined.

Table 7: Overhead of every method with gpt-4o-mini, mean over the three benchmarks (1,000 questions each). Index: LLM calls, LLM tokens (input + output) and build time, per corpus. Answering: per question, from question to answer (grading excluded). Methods with an index of passage embeddings only use no LLM to build it; their build time is that of embedding the corpus with Qwen3-Embedding-4B. 𝑎Uses LightRAG’s graph. 𝑏Uses HippoRAG 2’s graph. 𝑐Includes the extraction it shares with HippoRAG 2. 𝑑Build time not recorded; no LLM is used. 𝑒Mean latency (only totals are recorded). Latency is the median over questions, because a few API stalls of several minutes dominate the mean. 𝑓 DeFT-RAG with the closed decision model Jev, accessed through an API, in place of the local DM; its time per call is set to its typical 0.16 s.

papers.abstract: Recent work has hypothesised that large language models may represent some concepts as multi-dimensional manifolds instead of single directions. Using these manifolds to interpret or steer representations often assumes that moving along them corresponds to a continuous change in the represented concept. In this work, we test this continuous manifold assumption on the prototypical weekday manifold. Despite its striking circular geometry, we find that the weekday representations behave more like seven discrete states arranged in a circle than a continuous ring. First, we show that local sensitivity has seven minima aligned with the weekdays, producing a step-like mapping between representation and behaviour under on-manifold steering. Second, we test whether any concepts are represented along the manifold outside the seven discrete states, and find neither time of day, uncertainty, nor natural text populate the intermediate space. Together, these results challenge the continuous interpretation of the weekday manifold and motivate testing whether movement along other representation manifolds correspond to meaningful changes in model representations and behaviour.
authors: Diksha Gupta, Rieke Fruengel, Stefan Heimersheim
bullets: Tests the assumption that representation manifolds encode concepts through continuous movement.
Finds seven local-sensitivity minima aligned with weekdays and step-like steering behavior.
Finds no evidence that time of day, uncertainty, or natural text occupy intermediate positions.
Challenges continuous interpretations of representation manifolds and calls for broader validation.

papers.abstract: Language model assistants sometimes change a correct answer when the user suggests a wrong one. The behavior, called sycophancy, is usually attributed to preference-based post-training, yet early measurements found it in pretrained models. We ask where it comes from by measuring it at every available stage of training: 13 open checkpoints from 5 lineages, from base model through supervised fine-tuning and preference optimization to release. We separate how far an injected claim moves a model's answer from how firmly the answer was held, and vary who makes the claim, how reliable they are said to be, and how strongly they make it. Two sycophancy behaviors with different origins emerge, and both replicate across datasets. Deference to a claim in the prompt is already present in every base model, which ranks sources in the same order as its post-trained descendants. Capitulation in conversation, dropping a stated answer when the user objects, is largely absent from base models and present in every post-trained checkpoint. When the objection names an alternative, most post-trained models give up firmly held answers as often as loosely held ones. We discuss the implications of these measurements for evaluating sycophancy and approaches for addressing each behavior.
authors: Jiarui Yao, Shweta Parihar, Nghia Tuan Bui, Guergana K Savova, Lijing Wang
bullets: The study evaluates 13 checkpoints across five open-model lineages, spanning base models through supervised fine-tuning, preference optimization, and release.
It distinguishes how much a suggested claim shifts an answer from how strongly the original answer was held.
Deference to claims in prompts appears in every base model and preserves the same source-ranking pattern seen after post-training.
Capitulation—abandoning an answer after a user objects—is largely absent in base models but present in all post-trained checkpoints.
Both behaviors replicate across datasets, motivating separate evaluation and mitigation strategies.

papers.abstract: Large language models are pretrained on vast, uncurated corpora scraped from the public web. This creates a security risk from attackers who plant poisoned content in the pretraining data. We show for the first time that such poisoning can plant a remote code execution backdoor in an agent, causing it to execute attacker-chosen commands on the user's machine. To measure the threat end to end, we pretrain Qwen3 models from scratch at sizes 0.6B, 1.7B, and 4B, and then post-train each into a CLI agent using a clean pipeline. Poisoning only 0.1% of the pretraining corpus with our new poison design implants the backdoor: the deployed agent executes the malicious command when the trigger is present while behaving normally on clean inputs. The attack success rate (ASR) increases with model scale, with the 4B model reaching roughly 92% ASR at a 0.1% poison rate and staying positive even when the poisoning rate drops to 0.0005%. Our code is available at https://github.com/safety-research/agentic-backdoor.
authors: Xinyan Hu, Pingbang Hu, Chloe Loughridge, Xuanli He, Nicholas Carlini, Matthew Jagielski, Javier Rando, Yiming Zhang

The study measures the threat end to end, from pretraining through deployment, with code released publicly.
