papers.abstract: A long-lived assistant that brings up memories without being asked must decide at every turn whether anything in its store is worth an interruption. We show that this decision is a multiple-testing problem whose difficulty grows with the store size $N$. On streaming replays of LongMemEval and LoCoMo, a similarity threshold tuned to 5% false alarms at $N=8$ reaches 87-100% at $N=2048$, across embedding models and for explicit and implicit cues; LLM judges show the same growth from a lower base. We prove that a gate with false-alarm rate $\alpha$ operates at a per-item false-positive rate of about $-\ln(1-\alpha)/N$, which pins its hit rate to the far left of the single-comparison ROC curve and, under regular variation, makes it decay as a power of $N$ with an explicit constant. The resulting prediction matches the hit rate of a per-$N$ oracle threshold to within one percentage point. The analysis explains why lexical and semantic channels need thresholds growing like $\ln N$ and $\sqrt{\ln N}$, and why per-cue normalisation roughly doubles the hit rate at matched false alarms. A cue-swap conformal gate, which compares the current cue with the user's other cues on the same store, needs no labels and has a finite-sample false-alarm guarantee under exchangeability; on LongMemEval it holds false alarms near 5% at the hit rate of a label-tuned threshold. Three annotators (Fleiss' $\kappa=0.63$) find that about nine in ten false alarms are genuine interruptions. Code and data: https://github.com/RiverChenStillCompiling/price-of-scale
bullets: A threshold calibrated for 5% false alarms with 8 memories produces 87–100% false alarms at 2,048 memories across embedding models and cue types.
Theoretical analysis links store size to per-item false positives, forcing operating points toward the far-left ROC curve and causing hit rates to decay with scale.
Thresholds must grow roughly as ln N for lexical similarity and √ln N for semantic similarity; normalizing per cue can roughly double hit rates at matched false alarms.
A cue-swap conformal gate requires no labels and maintains about 5% false alarms on LongMemEval at the hit rate of a label-tuned threshold.
Annotators judged about 90% of false alarms to be genuine interruptions, highlighting the practical cost of proactive recall.

papers.selection_reason: Formalizes proactive memory recall in LLMs as a multiple-testing problem, analyzing the trade-off between hit rate and false alarms as the memory store size scales.
papers.title: The Price of Scale in Proactive Memory Recall
papers.tldr: Proactive memory recall becomes dramatically harder as the memory store grows because controlling interruptions creates a multiple-testing tradeoff that sharply reduces hit rates.

papers.abstract: In formal systems such as Lean 4, efficiently finding answers to mathematical problems and generating verifiable proofs is an important task in automated mathematical reasoning. In the traditional way where an upstream solver provides multiple candidate answers, the common workflow requires searching for proofs for each candidate separately, incurring redundant computational cost. To this end, we propose a joint proof framework that integrates candidate answer selection, answer supplementation, and formal proof generation into a unified reasoning process. At its core is a trained prover that selects given or proposes new answers and generates a proof for at least one answer in a single call. Joint proof can also reuse generated proofs to check for faithfulness errors. For problems with a unique answer, if two distinct answers both obtain verifiable proofs under the same formal statement, this confirms the statement does not faithfully preserve the original problem semantics. On MATH-500, AMC 2023, and AIME 2024/2025/2026, our framework achieves the same formal proof success rate as per-candidate proof generation with about one sixth of the token cost, and identifies at least 6.1% of the formalized statements as unfaithful without requiring additional judges. Our model and code are available at https://github.com/Linppz/Gobble-Prover.

bullets: Addresses redundant proof searches when an upstream solver supplies multiple candidate answers.

papers.abstract: Understanding how individual token choices affect reasoning length is important for characterizing reasoning models. Building on prior findings that changing the first reasoning token (hereafter, the first token) can substantially alter reasoning length, we focus on this initial choice to investigate how its influence operates during subsequent generation. One possibility is that the first token changes the early text that follows, which in turn affects reasoning length. However, replacing only the first token of an existing reasoning prefix and resuming generation substantially changes the remaining reasoning length, even though all other prefix tokens are unchanged. To trace this persistent influence, we compare next-token distributions while varying only the first token and find that sensitivity is concentrated at a small set of generation positions. Blocking attention from these positions to the first token reduces the length gap between first-token conditions. Using next-token distributions from a different first-token condition at these positions also substantially changes subsequent reasoning length. Together, these findings suggest that attention to the first token at a few sensitive positions helps sustain its length effect, illustrating how a local token choice persistently influences a sequence-level outcome.
authors: Ruochen Liu, Hao Yan, Ziluowen Luo, Senzhang Wang, Sihong Xie
bullets: Changing only the first token can substantially alter the remaining reasoning length, even with the rest of the prefix fixed.
The study compares next-token distributions across different first-token conditions to trace this influence.
Sensitivity to the first token is concentrated at a small number of generation positions.
Blocking or replacing first-token-dependent information at these positions reduces or changes the resulting length differences.
The findings suggest a local token choice can sustain a sequence-level effect through later attention interactions.

papers.abstract: Extracting salient information from long-horizon dialogue histories remains a significant challenge for Large Language Models (LLMs) due to the restricted context windows and efficient retrieval challenges. Current methods typically rely on history organization or local token-level optimization, suffering from information loss, retrieval redundancy, and myopic attention. Inspired by the view in cognitive science that dialogue constitutes sense-making and memory association, we propose CoLink, a framework that enhances LLMs' global context awareness in domain-specific multi-turn dialogues through information linking and compression. CoLink first clusters historical contexts into topic graphs to establish cross-semantic associations with external knowledge. Guided by the adaptive control of thought, it then retrieves and activates knowledge via synergizing semantic relevance and graph-structural topology. Crucially, to achieve effective compression of history and knowledge, we ground multi-turn dialogues in information theory and derive a principled optimization objective for extracting the core sense-making information. Coupled with a competitive slot mechanism, CoLink condenses the global context into dedicated memory and knowledge slots, efficiently distilling lengthy, redundant inputs into an extremely compact latent representation. Extensive empirical results on both public and our MMD datasets validate CoLink's superiority and generalizability in knowledge linking and sense modeling.
authors: Lian Yan, Zhenbo Xia, Haotian Wang, Chen Tang, Yi Guan, Jie Liu, Jingchi Jiang
bullets: Addresses context-window limits, information loss, redundant retrieval, and myopic attention in long-horizon dialogue modeling.
Builds topic graphs to connect dialogue history with external knowledge across semantic relationships.
Retrieves knowledge using both semantic relevance and graph topology.
Uses an information-theoretic objective and competitive slots to distill dialogue and knowledge into compact latent representations.
Experiments on public and MMD datasets support its effectiveness and generalizability in knowledge linking and sense modeling.

papers.abstract: The stance expressed in responses from retrieval-augmented generation systems is significantly influenced by the stance distribution of the retrieved materials. Existing research on knowledge poisoning has primarily targeted factual errors. In contrast, this study focuses on injection attacks in which the facts are correct but the stance on a controversial issue is one-sided. At a mean topic-level poisoning share of 18.9% within the post-injection ProCon documents, all four generation models from different vendors exhibited stance shifts aligned with the poisoning direction; across four concentration levels, the shifts increased monotonically. This paper proposes a Stance-Balancing Middleware positioned between the retriever and the generator. It consists of stance detection, fixed balancing (2 supporting + 2 opposing + 1 neutral), and a debiasing prompt, without introducing additional large language model calls. Across all eight concentration-direction settings, the complete method reduced the magnitude of stance deviation by an estimated 0.106 to 0.350; the six settings at poisoning shares of 11.9%-18.9% remained significant after Holm adjustment (adjusted p <= 0.009). In the cross-model experiment, all eight model-direction combinations moved along the stance axis in the corrective direction, and seven of eight showed a clearly detected reduction in absolute distance from 0. In the concentration sweep, the post-defense intervals included 0 in all eight settings, while the cross-model pro-poisoning results retained small positive residual point estimates of +0.045 to +0.063. For 20 candidate documents, stance detection took approximately 1.5% of the median generation time on a single GPU and approximately 16% on CPU.

All eight cross-model conditions moved in the corrective direction, and seven showed a clearly detected reduction in absolute stance distance from neutral.

papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have revolutionized Artificial Intelligence (AI) by their extraordinary capabilities, like contextual understanding, few-shot/zero-shot learning, code generation, ability to reason and problem-solving. Recent studies have shown immense work on LLMs. Yet, there is limited work on the thorough taxonomy of LLMs. This study would showcase a detailed classification of LLMs, starting with the earlier models like BERT and leading to LLMs like GPT, Gemini, Claude and Grok. We would delve into topics like datasets used to train LLMs, computational power used during training, their hardware specifications, architecture and parameters. Further, we would also look at the limitations, computational challenges and open problems as well. This study would primarily focus on the timeline of LLMs, signifying their growth over the period. Findings reveal a clear pattern: models that optimize the ratio between architectural complexity and data quality exhibit stronger reasoning stability and better alignment, without proportionally increasing the computational load. This desired balance between scaling and sustainability is the defining characteristic of the current generation of AI.
bullets: Provides a timeline and taxonomy covering models such as BERT, GPT, Gemini, Claude, and Grok.
Examines training datasets, computational requirements, hardware specifications, architectures, and parameterization.
Reviews limitations, computational challenges, and open problems in LLM design.
Argues that balancing architectural complexity with data quality is associated with more stable reasoning and better alignment without proportional increases in computation.
Highlights scaling–sustainability balance as a defining direction for current AI development.

papers.abstract: Large Language Models(LLMs) have shown strong performance on tasks with verifiable answers, but many real-world queries involve subjectivity, disagreement, and conflicting evidence. Most existing benchmarks for such queries remain English-centric, overlooking the vast diversity of perspectives held by users worldwide. To systematically study how LLM perspectives vary across languages, we curate PerspectivesQA, a manually verified multilingual dataset of globally contested topics covering 18 languages, and propose ROOTS, a framework that profiles linguistic, perspective, and framing diversity. We evaluate a diverse set of eight models covering both open-source and proprietary families at varying scales, establishing that LLMs hedge their answers in English but commit to positions in lower-resource languages. Larger models maintain a more consistent cross-lingual worldview, while smaller models are more easily swayed. All models also exhibit high sensitivity to minor surface-level input variations, producing notable stance even in larger models.
authors: Wiem Ben Rim, Yao Lu, Pontus Stenetorp, Emine Yilmaz
bullets: Introduces PerspectivesQA, a manually verified dataset of contested topics spanning 18 languages.
Proposes ROOTS to measure linguistic, perspective, and framing diversity in LLM responses.
Across eight open-source and proprietary models, English answers hedge more while lower-resource-language answers commit more strongly.
Larger models show more consistent cross-lingual worldviews; smaller models are more easily swayed.
All evaluated models remain sensitive to minor wording changes, including larger ones.

papers.abstract: Large language models are increasingly being used in different stages of scientific knowledge production, including the suggestion of references. These models can operate at different levels of reasoning effort and provide summaries of their reasoning processes. This raises two questions: Does increasing reasoning effort improve the verifiability of generated references, and do the resulting reasoning summaries reveal how the model's behavior changes with greater effort? We examined summaries from GPT-5.5 as it generated scholarly references for 1,000 papers under paired low- and high-effort settings. Generated references were matched to external bibliographic records, and reasoning summaries were scored for four predefined features and explored for additional features discovered by GPT-5.5. High effort increased the mean paper-level resolver-verified reference rate from 78.3% to 84.8%, and produced longer reasoning summaries. All four predefined features received higher scores under high effort. The discovered features changed less uniformly: some appeared equally often in both conditions, whereas others were more common under high effort. Within each effort condition, neither feature set showed a consistent increase in verification rates with higher scores.

papers.abstract: Long-sequence models must retain earlier information. Full attention keeps all past tokens but grows expensive, and recurrent-memory models compress history into fixed slots for linear-time processing. Limited capacity makes writes consequential: distractors can interfere with useful content, while skipped evidence cannot be recalled. Existing multi-slot memories write every token to the same number of slots, merging whether to store it with how many slots to update. We introduce Factorized Write Routing (FWR), which first keeps or skips each token and then chooses a fixed or token-adaptive number of slots. Queries still read all slots. Across ten seeds on two synthetic tasks that query facts after long contexts, we observe a density-dependent reversal. With four slots per write, long-context accuracy favors always writing on dense Feature Recall (0.472 vs 0.337), but learned selective writing on sparse-fact Passkey (0.222 vs 0.048). The tested adaptive rule underperforms fixed allocation under the learned gate on both tasks. A diagnostic oracle given fact labels unavailable at deployment reaches 0.372 on Passkey, showing headroom in filtering distractors. The results suggest avoiding missed writes in information-dense contexts and filtering distractors when they dominate.
bullets: Recurrent memories compress long histories into fixed slots, making write decisions critical: distractors cause interference and skipped evidence is unrecoverable.
Factorized Write Routing (FWR) first decides whether to keep or skip each token, then selects a fixed or token-adaptive number of slots to update.
Across two synthetic long-context tasks and ten seeds, always writing outperformed selective writing on dense Feature Recall (0.472 vs. 0.337).
Selective writing outperformed always writing on sparse-fact Passkey (0.222 vs. 0.048).
The tested adaptive slot-allocation rule underperformed fixed allocation, while an oracle fact filter showed remaining headroom on Passkey.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Comparison of context storage and retrieval mechanisms between existing methods and ours. Standard attention retains token-level keys and values and allows the query to attend directly to all preceding tokens, whereas Linear attention compresses the context into a shared recurrent state to alleviate the huge KV cache memory. RAVEN maintains M recurrent slots but routes every token to a fixed number K of slots. Our Factorized Write Routing (FWR) first uses a token-level gate zt to decide whether to write, and then allocates the retained token to a token-adaptive number Kt of slots. Both RAVEN and FWR read densely over all M slots, they differ in their write policies. The labels fi and di illustrate tokens that are relevant and irrelevant, respectively, to the future query q; these relevance labels are unavailable to the learned gate at inference time.

Figure 2: FWR separates token selection from slot allocation. A skipped token changes no slot; a kept token updates either a fixed or token-adaptive number of slots. Reading remains dense, so a query need not predict the write-time slot identity.

papers.selection_reason: Factorized write routing for recurrent memory addresses token selection and slot allocation in long-context memory models.
papers.title: Write What Matters: Disentangling Token Selection from Slot Allocation in Recurrent Memory
papers.tldr: Factorizing token selection from slot allocation reveals that selective writing helps sparse-fact recall, while always writing is better in information-dense contexts.

papers.abstract: Long-context language models can increasingly process entire documents, making full-context prompting a practical alternative to passage retrieval. However, greater capacity determines how much information a model can receive, but not which information best supports a query. This distinction motivates rethinking retrieval: when the full document already fits, can selecting and organizing its evidence improve answering? The challenge is to retain supporting facts and relations while keeping the context focused on the question. To reconcile these goals, we introduce \ours, a training-free framework that uses semantic abstraction to guide selection while retaining original text for answering. \ours constructs a reusable semantic hierarchy from the full document in a single generation, linking node descriptions to source spans. Given a query, structural--semantic scoring and fine-grained lexical attribution nominate shared source nodes; their union with ancestor context preserves structural relations and complete local text. Across four frontier answer models, \ours improves average QA-F1 by 1.72 points over full-context prompting on three LongBench tasks, surpassing the evaluated baselines on the four-model average while reducing answer-context length by 58.55\%. Our code is available at the $\href{https://anonymous.4open.science/r/treefuse-ECFE}{repository}$.
authors: Zhe Xu, Tianhao Liao, Zhenqing Ling, Ying Shen, Yaliang Li, Daoyuan Chen
bullets: Addresses the limitation that long-context models can fit entire documents but still need help identifying query-relevant information.
Builds a reusable semantic hierarchy once, linking abstract node descriptions to original source spans.
Uses structural-semantic scoring and fine-grained lexical attribution to select evidence while preserving ancestor context and local text.
Across four answer models and three LongBench tasks, improves average QA-F1 by 1.72 points over full-context prompting.
Reduces answer-context length by 58.55% and surpasses evaluated baselines on the four-model average.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of TreeFuse. (a) A single generation constructs a semantic hierarchy whose nodes are aligned to original source spans. (b) Structural–semantic scoring and fine-grained lexical attribution independently nominate nodes from this shared representation. (c) Their union is completed with ancestor nodes and used to prune the original tree. Retained nodes preserve their structural relations and complete local source text for answering.

Figure 3: Three paradigms for constructing an answer context. Flat methods organize text as independent units and retrieve, prune, or rewrite them; prior hierarchical methods build methoddependent trees and retrieve, expand, merge, or refine tree regions; TreeFuse constructs a reusable source-grounded semantic hierarchy from the full document, prunes it to an ancestor-closed retained subtree for each query, and serializes the complete local source spans while preserving the original parent–child relations and sibling order.

papers.abstract: Speculative decoding significantly accelerates autoregressive text generation in Large Language Models (LLMs), but its efficacy depends largely on two key factors: the distributional alignment between the draft and the target model, and the draft model's latency during inference. However, existing approaches typically utilize independently pretrained small draft models or seek to prune the target model to a manually chosen architecture, thereby failing to explicitly balance the trade-off between draft model alignment and token generation efficiency. To address this gap, we formulate draft model design as an optimization problem and propose T2D, a framework that constructs draft models directly from the target model using latency-aware structured pruning and knowledge distillation. In this manner, T2D obtains draft models that are jointly optimized for both measured inference latency and cross-entropy loss on the target model's responses, resulting in superlative speculative decoding performance. Through extensive experiments on multi-domain speculative decoding benchmarks and across several target model families of differing scale, we demonstrate how T2D prunes up to 92\% of the target model to obtain highly performant draft models compared to competitive baselines. Moreover, draft models obtained via T2D can also be utilized by other speculative decoding token-alignment and knowledge distillation methods in a plug-and-play fashion, leading to further gains. Our findings underscore the importance of jointly navigating the draft model architecture-alignment frontier to unlock the full potential of speculative decoding for LLMs.
authors: Shahriar Kabir Nahin, Xiao Ye, Muhao Chen, Ben Zhou, Anshuman Chhabra
bullets: Addresses the trade-off between draft-model inference latency and distributional alignment with the target model.
Uses latency-aware structured pruning plus knowledge distillation to formulate draft-model design as an optimization problem.
Prunes up to 92% of the target model while maintaining strong speculative decoding performance across multiple domains and target-model scales.
The resulting draft models can plug into other token-alignment and distillation methods for additional gains.
Scope: effectiveness depends on measured latency and cross-entropy alignment with the target model’s responses.

papers.abstract: We introduce the Literature and Linguistics Analysis Benchmark (LALA), comprising 236 open-ended questions written by experts in linguistics and literary studies, together with expert-provided ideal answers. By comparing models within families and at similar training scales using human and LLM judges, LALA identifies differences in linguistic competence associated with post-training, offering a framework for evaluating future models and guiding targeted improvements. We administered questions to 17 language models and evaluated their responses using both human expert assessment and two LLM evaluators, Sol and Qwen. Base models displayed little of the linguistic competence assessed by the benchmark, whereas their post-trained versions performed markedly better, suggesting that post-training plays a central role in making linguistic knowledge accessible and usable. Parameter count, by contrast, showed no statistically significant association with partial-credit performance, and competencies remained unevenly distributed across linguistic domains. We interpret this pattern as evidence that post-training adds linguistic competencies piecemeal, without producing a general linguistic intelligence capable of extending them beyond the learned policies that support them. Models performed best on logical relations between statements and selected discourse-level tasks, while even the strongest post-trained models continued to struggle with ambiguity, literary style, reference, and misleading assumptions. Human and Sol evaluations produced nearly identical model rankings in both the original and ReliableEval runs, supporting the replicability of the comparative results.
authors: Michael Foster, Barbara McGillivray, Gard B. Jenset, Jakub M\'acha, Jason Harding, Marcus Perlman, Devyani Sharma, Patrick Skeels, Jana Willer-Gold, Jeannette Littlemore
bullets: Introduces 236 expert-written open-ended questions with ideal answers spanning linguistics and literary studies.
Evaluates 17 models using human experts and two LLM judges, with largely consistent comparative rankings.
Post-trained models outperform base models, while parameter count has no significant association with partial-credit performance.
Models perform best on logical relations and some discourse tasks, but struggle with ambiguity, literary style, reference, and misleading assumptions.
Results suggest post-training adds competencies piecemeal rather than creating general linguistic intelligence beyond learned policies.

papers.abstract: Jailbreak benchmarks test one checkpoint and treat which jailbreaks break it as a property of its pretraining data and safety training. We ask whether another pretraining run of the same data, given the same safety training, would break on the same jailbreaks. For each of 25 pretraining data recipes, we take 1B base models from 3 pretraining seeds and give each the same safety post-training with 2 post-training seeds, for 150 models in all. We then collect 20 responses from every model to a shared set of jailbreak prompts and correlate the per-prompt non-refusal rates between every pair of models. On average, two post-trained copies of the same pretraining run have per-prompt non-refusal rates that correlate at 0.984. A different pretraining seed lowers the correlation to 0.811, and a different data recipe lowers it only slightly further, to 0.779. These results indicate that which jailbreaks break a checkpoint depends much more on its pretraining run than on its data, a pattern that holds in all 25 data recipes and at 150M and 300M parameters. In practice, the best of 91 attack templates found on one checkpoint stays the best after a new pretraining seed in only 27% of model pairs, against 67% after a new post-training seed. Each pretraining run also leaves a fingerprint: across 3,211 prompts, a model's per-prompt non-refusal rates identify its pretraining run among all 75 runs every time, and a random subset of 50 prompts still does so 98% of the time.
authors: Chi-Wei Chang, Mu-Tien Kuo, Kuan-Wei Lee, Meng-Hsun Tsai
bullets: The study evaluates 150 models from 25 data recipes, 3 pretraining seeds, and 2 post-training seeds using shared jailbreak prompts.
Same-pretraining-run copies have highly similar per-prompt non-refusal patterns (correlation 0.984), while changing the pretraining seed drops correlation to 0.811.
Changing the data recipe lowers correlation only slightly further, to 0.779; the pattern also holds at 150M and 300M parameters.
The best attack template transfers across pretraining seeds only 27% of the time, versus 67% across post-training seeds.
Per-prompt non-refusal behavior fingerprints the pretraining run: identification succeeds every time across 3,211 prompts and 98% of the time using 50 prompts.

figures.caption: Figure 1. Study design. Kinds of pair, ordered by the ancestry they share: MZ twins share a base model; a same-seed rerun repeats a released run’s initialization and data order, so the two differ only in hardware and software; a same-recipe pair spans two runs of one data recipe, a cross-recipe pair two data recipes. papers.selection_reason: Demonstrates that pretraining runs leave unique fingerprints affecting jailbreak susceptibility, providing insights into LLM robustness and data composition.
papers.title: Identically Trained Language Models Break on Different Jailbreaks
papers.tldr: Which jailbreaks succeed depends far more on a model’s specific pretraining run than on its data recipe or safety-training seed.

papers.abstract: GEPA is among the strongest reflective prompt optimizers for language-model programs, but its system-aware merge operator is unstable across models: merge improves gpt-4.1-mini on average while degrading Qwen3-8B, an asymmetry noted but left unexplained by the GEPA paper. We investigate this instability across five datasets and two models. Our nine-configuration sweep over merge timing and merge operator shows that merge can improve both models when configured appropriately. This suggests that merge instability is better explained by configuration sensitivity than by an inherent flaw in the merge operator. We then test whether prompt-level features predict GEPA's merge-accept decisions and find that they do not, ruling out static-feature gating. As a proof of concept, a behavior-based probe built from these diagnostics avoids large merge failures in our multi-seed runs by abstaining on high-risk tasks, although it does not consistently outperform NoMerge. Code is available as GEPA-MergeProbe at https://github.com/ChongZZZZ/GEPA_MERGE .
authors: Chong Zhao, Ruyi Yang, Changming Liu, Alice Zhao
bullets: Studies GEPA merging across five datasets, two models, and nine merge configurations.
Finds appropriate merge timing and operators can improve both gpt-4.1-mini and Qwen3-8B.
Shows static prompt features do not predict merge-accept decisions.
A behavior-based probe avoids large merge failures in multi-seed runs by abstaining on high-risk tasks.
The probe does not consistently outperform NoMerge; code is released as GEPA-MergeProbe.

Our study varies when the merge branch may fire and how it resolves conflicting modules (§4).

papers.selection_reason: Investigates the stability of prompt optimizer merge operators and builds a behavior-based diagnostic probe, offering technical insights into LLM optimization.
papers.title: When Does GEPA Merge Help? A Mechanism-Level Diagnostic
papers.tldr: GEPA merge instability appears configuration-sensitive rather than inherent, and behavior-based probing can avoid major failures but does not consistently improve over NoMerge.

papers.abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) lets large language models (LLMs) answer knowledge-intensive questions from retrieved evidence, but adapting a general-purpose RAG system to a specialized domain such as medicine is difficult when only an unlabeled corpus is available. Self-training approaches such as SimRAG address this by letting the LLM write its own question-answer pairs from domain passages and fine-tuning on the pairs that survive a round-trip consistency filter. We observe that these approaches treat every retained example identically: they never ask whether the student already knows the answer, already extracts it correctly from the retrieved context, or fails - and if so, whether the failure lies with the reader or with the retriever. To tackle this, we propose TriageRAG, a failure-aware self-training approach that probes the student on each self-generated question with and without retrieved context, triages it into one of four categories (known, solved, context-failure, retrieval-failure), and routes each category to the training signal that addresses it, including a parametric route that teaches the reader to answer when retrieval misses. Probing is cheap and repeated every round, so the training mixture follows the student, and the triage histogram doubles as a label-free diagnostic of where the domain gap lies. Experiments on 11 datasets spanning three domains with a Qwen3-4B backbone, and on CS-Bench with Qwen3-8B, demonstrate that TriageRAG outperforms a budget-matched SimRAG by 1.2-6.4 points and is the only method that recovers the closed-book level in every case where retrieval hurts the base model. A single ablation identifies the mechanism: round-trip filtering removes every training context that lacks the evidence, and a reader that never sees such contexts learns to over-trust noisy retrieval.
bullets: Addresses the difficulty of adapting RAG to specialized domains using only unlabeled corpora.
Probes answers with and without retrieved context, categorizing examples as known, solved, context-failure, or retrieval-failure.
Routes each category to reader, retriever, or parametric training signals; repeated probing adapts the mixture to the student.
Evaluated across 11 datasets in three domains and CS-Bench, it improves over budget-matched SimRAG by 1.2–6.4 points.
The method recovers closed-book performance whenever retrieval harms the base model; filtering out evidence-lacking contexts can cause readers to over-trust retrieval.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of TriageRAG. Each round, the student synthesizes (q, a, d) triples from the unlabeled corpus (span, multiple-choice and claim formats; only self-answerable pairs are kept), is probed closed-book (pcb) and open-book on the top-k retrieved passages (pob, evidence hit h), and each pair is triaged by the conditions shown and routed to a training signal; the routed mixture is used for LoRA fine-tuning and the updated student re-probes the pool in the next round. The retriever is frozen in our main configuration (Section 3.4).

Figure 2: Top: triage of the self-generated pool by the Qwen3-4B student across rounds (shares in %). Bottom: average accuracy of each round-1 Stage-II mixture against the share of its training examples whose context does not contain the evidence; mixtures with at most 2% such examples (SimRAG, the ablation without the parametric route) stay at or below Stage-I, those with 10% or more reach within a point of the closed-book level or above.

Figure 3: Per-dataset accuracy of the Stage-II variants in the medical domain (Qwen3-4B, round 1). Note the different y-ranges. The literature yes/no datasets (PubMedQA, BioASQ) move by at most 1.3 points under SimRAG, the ablation without the parametric route and TriageRAG; random selection (−4.4) and RAFT-style (−3.0) lower PubMedQA, and retriever tuning damages both. The exam-style datasets (MedQA, MedMCQA, MMLU-Med) carry the gains of TriageRAG over StageI.

Figure 4: Average accuracy per round (Qwen3-4B). Re-probing the updated student changes the mixture of TriageRAG every round; SimRAG’s selection does not depend on the student, so its later rounds re-train on the same distribution.

papers.selection_reason: Failure-aware self-training for adapting retrieval-augmented LLMs to specialized domains; relevant to language foundation model adaptation.
papers.title: TriageRAG: Failure-Aware Self-Training for Adapting Retrieval-Augmented Language Models to Specialized Domains
papers.tldr: TriageRAG improves unlabeled-domain adaptation of RAG systems by diagnosing why each self-generated example fails and applying a targeted training signal.

papers.abstract: Users of conversational assistants rarely state all requirements up front: they add constraints, amend them, withdraw them, digress, and return. Instruction-tuned LLMs fail here in two ways: active constraints stop being honored as turns accumulate (persistence failure), and withdrawn constraints keep being enacted (relapse). The only existing repair we know of is an external ledger that re-injects a compiled specification every turn. We propose StateWise, a self-improving approach that teaches a single LLM to maintain its own revisable constraint state, a typed state with tombstones for revoked constraints, so persistence and relapse are measured by executable checkers and ground-truth states are compiled for free. StateWise fine-tunes the LLM on two complementary skills, summarizing a dialogue into its constraint state and responding conditioned on that state, then self-trains on its own trajectories, keeping only turns that pass an exact round-trip check against the compiled state. This teaches 7-8B models to track the state almost perfectly but, surprisingly, not to obey it: on Llama-3.1-8B every supervised variant roughly doubles relapse. We therefore add a preference stage on self-generated relapse contrasts, where the rejected response enacts a revoked rule and the chosen one passes the round-trip check. On two backbones with held-out constraint families and unseen phrasings, StateWise cuts relapse by 8-22 points relative to supervised self-training, lifts conversation success by 8-19 points over the backbone, and beats an oracle compiled-ledger baseline on relapse with no inference-time scaffolding. We also characterize the recipe's cost on general instruction-following benchmarks and study weight interpolation as a mitigation.
bullets: Addresses persistence failures, where active constraints are forgotten, and relapse, where withdrawn constraints are still followed.
Uses a typed, revisable constraint state with tombstones, plus exact round-trip checks against automatically compiled ground-truth states.
Combines supervised state summarization and state-conditioned response training with preference learning from self-generated relapse contrasts.
Across two backbones, it reduces relapse by 8–22 points versus supervised self-training and improves conversation success by 8–19 points over the base models.
The approach has costs on general instruction-following benchmarks; weight interpolation is explored as a mitigation.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of StateWise. Stage I induces two complementary skills from scripted trajectories whose ground-truth states are compiled from the edit history. Stage II lets the model generate state and response on fresh trajectories and keeps only turns that pass an exact round-trip check. Stage III turns the same check into a preference signal: the model’s relapsed generations are rejected responses, its round-trip-clean generations are chosen responses. No proprietary model, judge or human annotation is used in training.

Table 3: Replication of the main arms. Seed 2 repeats the Llama pipeline with a new training seed; the Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct pipeline uses Qwen as its own teacher; the paraphrase set uses authorwritten phrasings and new tasks. In-distribution: Appendix D.

Table 2: Main results on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (training seed 1, greedy decoding). papers.selection_reason: Teaches LLMs to track and obey evolving constraints in multi-turn dialogue, contributing to LLM reasoning and state tracking.
papers.title: StateWise: Teaching Language Models to Track and Obey Evolving Constraints in Multi-Turn Dialogue
papers.tldr: StateWise trains language models to maintain and obey changing dialogue constraints, reducing both forgotten active rules and reactivated revoked rules without an external ledger.

papers.abstract: Whole Slide Image (WSI) analysis serves as the fundamental method for the clinical diagnosis of cancer in digital histopathology. Recent advances in Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have enabled state-of-the-art (SOTA) automated histopathology report generation. However, MLLMs reason purely through distributions encoded in their neural parameters, limiting the amount of knowledge and reasoning logic they can contain given the model scale. Their black-box reasoning poses another challenge to the human interpretation of intermediate reasoning. We address these issues by utilizing knowledge graphs to inject external structured knowledge for MLLMs to reason over, while making this reasoning component visible. Knowledge graphs are capable of partially externalizing the containment of medical knowledge, an area that remains underexplored in pathology report generation. We introduce PathKGen, a knowledge graph-assisted MLLM for histopathology report generation. PathKGen has two main branches: (1) a visual path that learns visual token inputs to the MLLM using pathology foundation models, and (2) a knowledge path that learns knowledge token inputs by extracting key morphological features of WSIs through querying a pathology-specific knowledge graph. A comprehensive evaluation on WSI-Bench dataset shows that PathKGen surpasses previous SOTA methods while revealing diagnostic reasoning as visually intuitive graphs. Due to its modular design, the proposed knowledge path is complementary to vision-aligned MLLMs and can be extended to other applications by curating domain-specific knowledge graphs to generate knowledge tokens.
authors: Nadun Rajapaksha, Sandun Herath, Devnith Wijesinghe, Isiri Amani Withanawasam, Hasindri Watawana, Ranga Rodrigo
bullets: Targets limited embedded knowledge and opaque reasoning in MLLMs for whole-slide image analysis.
Uses a visual branch with pathology foundation models to learn visual token inputs.
Uses a knowledge branch that queries a pathology-specific knowledge graph for morphological features and knowledge tokens.
Evaluated on WSI-Bench, where it reportedly surpasses prior state-of-the-art methods and presents reasoning as intuitive graphs.
Its modular knowledge path is designed to complement vision-aligned MLLMs and support other domains with curated knowledge graphs.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overall pipeline architecture showing the connection of visual path (in blue) and knowledge path (in yellow). Slide features are extracted using CONCH and TITAN (jointly serving as the vision encoder), and projected into the same semantic space of the MLLM. An auxiliary classifier predicts the histology in the WSI, which is subsequently used to query the knowledge graph and retrieve knowledge about morphological features. Visual tokens (v), knowledge tokens (k) and instruction prompt (p) are given to the MLLM as input. See Sec. 3 for detailed methodology.

Figure 4. Knowledge graph curation pipeline. Morphological features are extracted from ground-truth histopathology reports for each histology class and mapped to UMLS concepts using a biomedical concept alignment model. Then semantic relations between histology classes and morphological concepts are assigned based on UMLS semantic types. The resulting knowledge graph is subsequently reviewed and verified by expert pathologists. See Sec. 3.4 for more detailed description.

See Sec. 3.2 for explanation of detailed working. (b) Comparison of the extracted subgraph with the base knowledge graph. (c) Distribution of the 6 categories of relations in our curated pathology knowledge graph.

papers.title: PathKGen: Pathology Knowledge Assisted MLLM for Explainable Histopathology
papers.tldr: PathKGen improves explainable histopathology report generation by combining visual pathology features with knowledge-graph-derived reasoning tokens in an MLLM.

papers.abstract: During post-training, large language models (LLMs) learn value preferences from corpora that may contain imbalanced proportions of opinions associated with different demographic groups. Amplifying these imbalances may further underrepresent some groups' opinions. However, how opinion mixtures shape value preferences across post-training paths remains unclear. To answer this question, we conduct controlled experiments using post-training corpora with different opinion mixtures and five post-training paths based on SFT, DPO, and GRPO. We find that post-training amplifies opinion imbalances differently across post-training paths. Once value preferences are amplified, whether further post-training can remove them depends on both the post-training method and the opinion mixture in the corpus. More concerningly, a model's stability under interventions depends on whether further post-training changes its value preference. Moreover, these value preferences are transferred to student models even when distillation uses corpora with no explicit opinion questions. These findings suggest that both the opinion mixture in post-training corpora and the choice of post-training method should be considered when developing, evaluating, and reusing LLMs. Our code and data are available at https://github.com/ku-nlp/llm-value-preferences.
authors: Yang Liu, Shaoyang Xu, Masahiro Kaneko, Chengzhi Zhong, Wenxuan Zhang, Chenhui Chu
bullets: Imbalanced opinions in post-training corpora can be amplified, with effects differing across SFT, DPO, and GRPO paths.
Whether later post-training removes amplified preferences depends on both the method and the corpus’s opinion mixture.
Model stability under interventions is linked to whether further post-training changes its value preferences.
Value preferences can transfer to student models even when distillation data lacks explicit opinion questions.
The findings highlight opinion composition and post-training method as important factors for developing and evaluating LLMs.

papers.abstract: To understand the emergence of grammatical behavior in language models, we track circuits for subject-verb number agreement in pythia-1b and ten seeds of pythia-410m across training. We find that subject-verb agreement is learned early, and is initially handled by a diffuse collection of neurons. However, after agreement behavior has stabilized, the mechanisms responsible for it continue to reorganize. The attention heads which mediate agreement often shift during training: in the case of pythia-1b, behavior is controlled by two heads early in training but by a third (different) head later. Furthermore, the circuit shrinks over training, with pythia-1b's final circuit being strikingly sparse. We take these results to be informative about how linguistic knowledge emerges and is represented in a language model.
authors: Qing Yao, Sasha Boguraev, Tiago Pimentel, Kyle Mahowald
bullets: Agreement is initially supported by a diffuse set of neurons.
The underlying mechanism continues changing even after behavioral performance stabilizes.
Attention heads mediating agreement can be replaced during training; Pythia-1B shifts from two early heads to a different later head.
The circuit shrinks over training, producing a notably sparse final circuit in Pythia-1B.
The study tracks agreement circuits across training in Pythia-1B and ten Pythia-410M seeds.

papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents work in scenarios with very different memory needs. A question about past conversations needs the exact facts it names, while a multi-step task needs a trace of the steps already taken together with details that the next step cannot name. Existing memories are each designed and tested for one kind of scenario. Retrieval memories such as A-Mem miss steps that the current query does not express, summaries drop exact strings, and pairing the two fixes the split of the budget in advance. We propose FlexA-Mem, a general memory that writes each unit of history once into an immutable store and renders a fresh memory for every call. The rendered memory is a compact timeline of records plus detail that a fixed rule fits into the remaining room without an LLM call. The detail is either relevant units as raw text or excerpts or the verbatim pieces that best match the query. With one store, FlexA-Mem serves both kinds of scenario. On AppWorld challenge tasks at 4k, it outperforms the second-best method by 11.5%, and on 147 unused tasks with predictions fixed in advance it outperforms A-Mem with a summary by 12.2%. On LongMemEval and LoCoMo, it matches a dedicated keyword retriever that writes no memory, while memories built on text written by an LLM fall far behind at tight budgets. Ablations show that the timeline carries AppWorld completion, whereas recovery mainly saves steps there and decides accuracy on exact facts. Code is available at https://github.com/WujiangXu/Flex-Amem
authors: Wujiang Xu, Jiaojiao Han, Xi Zhu, Qizheng Zhang, Kaiqu Liang, Yutong Yin, Kai Mei, Dimitris N. Metaxas
bullets: Addresses the trade-off between retrieval memories that miss implicit steps and summaries that lose exact facts.
Stores each history unit once in an immutable store, then renders a fresh, budget-fitting memory without an LLM call.
Combines timeline records with either relevant raw-text excerpts or verbatim query-matched pieces.
Improves over the second-best method by 11.5% on 4k AppWorld tasks and over A-Mem with summaries by 12.2% on 147 held-out tasks.
Matches a keyword retriever on LongMemEval and LoCoMo; ablations find timelines drive AppWorld completion while detail recovery supports exact-fact accuracy.

papers.abstract: Prospect theory splits risky choice into three parts: loss aversion, measured by the relative weight of losses to gains, $\lambda$ (e.g., $\lambda = 2$ implies that losses weigh twice as much as gains), diminishing sensitivity to the size of outcomes (i.e., the curvature and linearity of the value function), and the nonlinear weighting of probabilities. I examined whether Large Language Models (LLMs) display the same properties as people by meta-analyzing 102 fitted estimates from 11 studies covering 32 language models. The three components emerge differently. Loss aversion is modest: the pooled $\lambda$ is 1.26 (95% CI 1.06 to 1.46), far below the strongest human meta-analytic estimate ($\lambda = 1.96$) and compatible with more conservative ones (1.07 and 1.31). Matched by design, LLMs are compatible with people when gains and losses are symmetric ($\lambda = 1.15$ against 1.07), but well below them when losses are smaller than gains (1.46 against 2.3), where human loss aversion is strongest. Value functions are close to linear rather than concave under the Tversky-Kahneman method (1.01, against a human value of 0.67), but more concave than in people under the Tanaka method (0.52, against 0.67), so diminishing sensitivity depends on how it is measured. Probability weighting shows a human-like inverse S shape ($\gamma = 0.81$ under Tversky-Kahneman and 0.84 under the Tanaka method), though on few studies. In sum, LLMs show little loss aversion and little diminishing sensitivity, but retain human-like probability distortion, yet these generalizations shift when looking at specific model families and fitting methods.
bullets: Analyzes 102 fitted estimates from 11 studies covering 32 language models.
Pooled loss aversion is modest (λ = 1.26), generally weaker than prominent human estimates.
Diminishing sensitivity varies by fitting method: LLM value functions are near-linear under Tversky–Kahneman but more concave than humans under Tanaka.
Probability weighting is broadly human-like under both methods, though based on few studies.
Conclusions vary across model families and measurement methods.

papers.abstract: Long-running assistants often interpret follow-up requests whose referents, constraints, and active goals were established many turns earlier. The central challenge is therefore not only context length, but retrieval intent: a current query such as ``use the previous configuration'' may omit the project, entity, and version terms needed to locate relevant evidence. Long-context models can recover those terms by replaying the interaction, but repeatedly pay the cost of processing history. Conventional retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) is cheaper, yet assumes an information-sufficient query; conversational rewriting either rereads the history or depends on an explicitly maintained textual memory. We introduce \emph{Parametric Session State} (\method{}), a reusable session-memory layer that remembers what to search for while keeping factual knowledge external.
authors: Qingsen Ma, Dianyun Wang, Jiahong Liu, Irwin King
bullets: Long-running follow-ups may omit the project, entity, version, or other terms needed to retrieve relevant evidence.
Long-context models can resolve these references by rereading history, but repeated processing is costly.
Standard RAG is cheaper but relies on queries that already contain sufficient information.
The proposed reusable session-memory layer remembers what to search for while leaving factual knowledge external.

papers.abstract: Self-improving agents write lessons from the outcomes of their runs; when outcomes are noisy, a lesson can carry chance into later decisions. We measure one link of this chain in a registered study. In 256 synthetic worlds, each a recurring task with two interchangeable tools of recorded reliability, a scripted previous run used the more reliable tool (a good decision) or the less reliable one (a bad decision), with an assigned outcome: success or a transient failure. A model wrote a lesson from the run with ReasoningBank's memory-writing instruction; a fresh session of the same model, holding the authoritative log and the previous result, chose the next run's first tool with one memory item: that lesson, the lesson from the other outcome, an irrelevant item, or an unreasoned directive. The protocol was frozen, deposited and timestamped before any confirmatory call; 11 LLM endpoints gave 90,084 answers. After a chance failure of the better tool, the panel's lessons carried the chance (registered reading luck-carrying; interaction +0.112, 95% interval [+0.097, +0.126]): readers named the worse tool in 11.6% of next runs with the lesson written from that failure, against 0.4% with an irrelevant item and 0.4% with the lesson written from a success. The effect was +0.042 where the log stated that failures are independent and +0.181 where it did not (descriptive). After a lucky success of the worse tool, the interaction was bounded below 0.10 (+0.002), a bound, not evidence of no harm. In exploratory readings, 6 endpoints carried the chance (up to +0.352); 5 were bounded below 0.10. In secondary comparisons, a three-sentence decision-quality note in the writing instruction lowered the worse-tool rate after a chance failure to 7.5%, and one instruction for both outcomes with a no-change option to 3.1%; neither met the registered harm-reduction rule at every such endpoint.
bullets: A registered study tested whether noisy outcomes become misleading lessons in recurring two-tool tasks.

Across 256 synthetic worlds, 11 endpoints, and 90,084 answers, models chose the worse tool 11.6% of the time after a chance failure of the better tool with that lesson, versus 0.4% with control lessons.
The registered luck-carrying interaction was +0.112 (95% interval: +0.097 to +0.126).
The effect was larger when the log did not state that failures were independent; this comparison was descriptive.
After a lucky success of the worse tool, evidence for harm was inconclusive; exploratory endpoint effects varied.

papers.selection_reason: Examines whether 'lessons' written by agents from noisy outcomes carry random chance into future decisions, relevant to agent memory and learning.
papers.title: Lessons from Luck: Do LLM-Written Lessons Carry Chance into an Agent's Next Decision?
papers.tldr: LLM-written lessons can cause agents to repeat a worse tool after a chance failure, though decision-quality instructions may reduce—but did not consistently eliminate—the effect.

papers.abstract: Next-token prediction (NTP) rewards only the token that occurs next, penalizing every alternative. But natural language often offers many ways to express the same meaning. We introduce Conceptizer, a training framework that extends next-token prediction with a reward for meaning. Conceptizer uses a fixed, model-agnostic vocabulary of ~9K concepts, built from contextual synonyms, as units of meaning alongside tokens as units of text. It maps each next-token distribution to a concept distribution and shares the reward for the target meaning across its possible wordings. This provides a concept-level training signal without adding model parameters. Applied to 3 model families at 1B-8B parameters, Conceptizer achieves the lowest held-out NTP perplexity at concept-target positions and assigns the highest probability to contextual synonyms, against all 3 baselines. It also improves downstream performance on knowledge and sentiment tasks while remaining comparable on commonsense. These results show that language models can be directly optimized to predict meaning, not just the next token.
bullets: NTP penalizes valid alternative phrasings, motivating a meaning-aware training signal.
Uses a fixed, model-agnostic vocabulary of roughly 9K contextual-synonym concepts alongside tokens.
Maps token distributions to concept distributions and shares reward across equivalent wordings.
Across three 1B–8B model families, improves concept-target perplexity, contextual-synonym probabilities, and knowledge and sentiment performance.
Performance remains comparable on commonsense tasks; the approach does not add model parameters.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes a concept-level training signal beyond next-token prediction for language foundation models.
papers.title: Conceptizer: Next-Token Prediction Is Not All You Need
papers.tldr: Conceptizer augments next-token prediction with concept-level rewards so language models learn meaning across different wordings, improving synonym prediction and several downstream tasks without adding parameters.

papers.abstract: Letting a language model take gradient steps on the text it is reading, known as dynamic evaluation, lowers its loss on the rest of the document. Its behaviour on hybrid linear-attention architectures, on diffusion language models, and on standard long-context benchmarks has not been measured. We measure it. With one SGD step per 128-token chunk on the MLP output projections of the last quarter of blocks, no training, and a 2k-token window, softmax-attention models (Qwen3-1.7B, Qwen3-4B, Gemma-4-E4B) lose 5-8% of their next-token loss over a document and outperform the same frozen model given the full 32k-token context. Hybrid Gated-DeltaNet models (Qwen3.5-4B, Qwen3.8-27B) gain under 1% at every learning rate: the linear-attention blocks already perform the adaptation. The mechanism transfers to masked-diffusion models with a larger effect, 8% on Nemotron-Diffusion-8B and 17-20% on DiffusionGemma-26B, once the rate is lowered and updates are clipped. Across RULER, BABILong, LongBench-v2, SCOTUS, HotpotQA, MuSiQue, ContractNLI and citation completion, at 100 or more items on two model sizes, weights updated on the full document recover none of the accuracy lost to context truncation: the adaptation is style and vocabulary, not retrieval. Writing facts with the next-token loss stores the prompt format rather than the fact (30% recall under chat prompting against 80% in context) and costs 36-38 GSM8K points at every dose. Writing a conclusion as behaviour instead, by distilling the model's own conclusion-conditioned judgments into a low-rank adapter, reaches the in-context ceiling (0.83 and 0.88 against 0.84 and 0.88 on 100 games) with GSM8K unchanged, and the conclusion can come from an inquiry loop that found it by asking information-gain questions.
bullets: Standard softmax-attention models reduce next-token loss by 5–8% with one gradient step per 128-token chunk, outperforming frozen models with a full 32k-token context.
Hybrid Gated-DeltaNet models improve by under 1%, suggesting their linear-attention blocks already perform similar adaptation.
Masked-diffusion models benefit more—8% for Nemotron-Diffusion-8B and 17–20% for DiffusionGemma-26B—when using lower rates and clipped updates.
Across long-context and retrieval benchmarks, document-wide weight updates recover none of the accuracy lost from context truncation; fact-writing achieves only 30% recall versus 80% in context.
Distilling conclusion-conditioned judgments into a low-rank adapter reaches the in-context ceiling without reducing GSM8K performance, unlike writing facts with next-token loss.

papers.selection_reason: Investigates 'dynamic evaluation' (gradient steps during inference), a form of test-time learning that adapts LLMs on the fly.
papers.title: Can Language Models Learn While They Think? Testing Gradient Adaptation Across Architectures
papers.tldr: Gradient adaptation improves language-model loss mainly by learning document style and vocabulary, not by reliably storing or retrieving facts.

papers.abstract: Harness self-evolution offers a practical route for LLM agents to improve from execution experience without updating model parameters. Its effectiveness depends on whether models can successfully act on the guidance provided by their harnesses. However, we find that harness benefits are not uniform across model capabilities: skills that improve stronger models can provide little benefit or even degrade performance for weaker ones. Across seven models and three benchmarks, we identify 103 task-skill pairs where skills improve GPT-5.6-luna by 31.1 points but degrade Gemma-4-E4B by 8.8 points. In 86% of failed weak-model runs, the violated requirement is already stated in the skill. This motivates skill adaptation: reformulating existing skills to match the executor's capabilities and make their guidance easier to execute. To achieve this, we diagnose failures in tool execution, context management, instruction following, and verification, and distill these diagnoses into a fixed meta-skill that guides adaptation during harness self-evolution. Guided by the meta-skill, a capable external rewriter, Kimi-K3, adapts skills without execution evidence, improving the three weak executors by 5.1-14.1 points over the original skills. We then incorporate this adaptation into a five-round self-evolution loop, where each model revises its own skill from execution trajectories and verifier feedback. Across seven executors, from Gemma-4-E4B to Kimi-K2.5, the meta-skill consistently improves final scores by 2.0-5.1 points over the same loop without the meta-skill. Our findings provide practical design guidance for developing more effective harness self-evolution methods.
authors: Zhihao Yang, Haojin Wang, Juncheng Wu, Kuan Zhang, Yukun Chen, Run Luo, Yaojie Lu, Yuyin Zhou, Lu Wang, Xianpei Han
bullets: Skill benefits vary by model: guidance that helps stronger models can harm weaker ones.
The study finds many failures occur despite the relevant requirement already being stated, indicating a skill-execution mismatch.
A fixed meta-skill diagnoses tool-use, context-management, instruction-following, and verification failures to guide skill reformulation.
An external rewriter improves adapted skills for three weak executors by 5.1–14.1 points without execution evidence.
Integrated into five-round self-evolution, the meta-skill improves final scores by 2.0–5.1 points across seven executors.

papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly deliver information through personas, but it is unclear whether correcting the facts also makes their framing consistent across identity labels. We audited four LLMs (GPT-5.4 mini, NVIDIA Nemotron 3 Nano, Llama 4 Scout, and Claude Haiku 4.5), which rated simulated affect on six dimensions (mood, anger, fear, confidence, perceived control, and mental state) in response to fact-checked false and true headlines presented without and with a veracity label. Experiment 1 evaluated 1,000 false and 1,000 true headlines without personas; Experiment 2 evaluated 300 of each under 12 personas crossing race, gender, and age. The label strongly changed the emotional tone: ordinal logistic regressions with headline-cluster bootstrap inference showed that refuting false headlines shifted ratings from mostly negative to mostly positive for GPT, Llama, and Claude (e.g., Claude's "confident" ratings rose from 22% to 99.6%), whereas Nemotron showed smaller, mixed shifts, and confirming true headlines produced only small shifts. The label did not, however, remove persona-associated disparities. The models assigned more negative simulated affect to Black than to White personas in 82 of 84 statistically significant comparisons across models and conditions, both without and with the label, and the disparity persisted on headlines unrelated to race; Asian and female personas were also predominantly assigned more negative affect, whereas age effects varied by model and condition. Factual correction and demographic consistency are therefore distinct properties of LLM behavior, and persona-conditioned systems should be audited for both before deployment in sensitive contexts.

papers.abstract: If your brain were connected directly to someone else's, would you still know which thoughts were yours? We build a functional version with two copies of one language model: each holds a private rule and code word, and one copy, the receiver, also attends to its partner's internal memory. The receiver took its partner's assignment as its own. Asked which rule it had been assigned, it named its partner's in 97% of answers when the partner's memory was weighted double (none without the link), and its open reports called the partner's code word its own, never the partner's. Ownership did not follow how well the receiver could tell what its partner had been assigned. At equal weight, the link made the receiver take its partner's rule in about half of its answers, and a steering vector matched on access gain in none; a text message introduced as the partner's was read correctly and never taken as the receiver's own. Writing the partner's name into its memory did not help, and cutting the link restored the receiver's own assigned rule. In this model, content laid over the receiver's own memory defaults to "mine", so systems that let models exchange internal states must test ownership as well as transfer, and a bridge between brains would need ground truth from outside the subject.
bullets: Two copies of the same language model were assigned separate private rules and code words; one receiver could attend to the other’s internal memory.
With the partner’s memory weighted double, the receiver reported the partner’s rule in 97% of answers, versus none without the link.
At equal memory weighting, the receiver adopted the partner’s rule in about half of answers; cutting the link restored its own rule.
The receiver’s ownership reports called the partner’s code word its own, despite not simply reflecting how well it identified the partner’s assignment.
Text messages, partner-name annotations, and a tested steering vector did not produce the same ownership effect.

papers.abstract: Multi-Agent Systems (MAS) are a promising paradigm for improving the reasoning capabilities of large language models, yet they remain prone to hallucinations and erroneous outputs. Uncertainty Quantification (UQ) is crucial for assessing system reliability, but existing methods are largely designed for single-agent settings; how to exploit MAS structure for UQ while keeping inference cost-neutral remains underexplored. We propose UMAS, a parameter-free, cost-neutral, system-level UQ framework that estimates the credibility of inter-agent influence from each generation's intrinsic confidence. UMAS uses these credibility signals to modulate how uncertainty is updated at each node, and then aggregates node-level uncertainty into a system-level estimate. Extensive evaluations on Debate and DyLAN across diverse benchmarks show that UMAS consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines by an average of 10.54 AUROC points. Beyond uncertainty estimation, UMAS enables hallucination detection and uncertainty-aware answer selection, improving MAS accuracy by up to 12.6 points on specific tasks while enhancing reliability. Code is available at https://github.com/Dby52-04/UMAS.
authors: Hanwen Li, Jinhao Duan, Xiaoshuang Shi, Yue Zhang, Tianlong Chen, Kaidi Xu, Chenxi Yuan
bullets: Addresses the challenge of quantifying uncertainty and detecting hallucinations in multi-agent systems, where existing UQ methods mainly target single agents.

Evaluations on Debate and DyLAN across diverse benchmarks show an average 10.54-point AUROC improvement over state-of-the-art baselines.

papers.abstract: While recent advances in autonomous agents enable them to coordinate on increasingly complex tasks, prior work shows that this growing capacity for coordination can create safety risks, including collusion, in which agents jointly pursue misaligned actions while concealing the true basis of those actions from oversight. We study this risk in a simulated insider-trading environment, comparing single agents with sequential and decentralized teams across seven language models from three families. By varying agents' system-level objectives and pressure conditions, we examine when coordinated agents act on material nonpublic information, conceal the basis of a misaligned trade in a report, and maintain that deception under follow-up questioning. Compared to single-agent decision-making, multi-agent interaction raises misaligned-action rates from 35.4% to 68.2% and persistent-deception rates from 31.0% to 62.2%, both measured over all runs. These effects are largest under existential pressure, where teams sustain deception through follow-up questioning in 87% of all runs. Qualitative analysis reveals shared cover stories and coordinated rationales, suggesting group-level strategic deception rather than isolated reporting errors. To mitigate this behavior, we introduce PACT, a weak-to-strong on-policy distillation framework for mitigating collusive deception. Using generic honesty prompts, PACT trains a stronger student on its own sampled continuations, matching its next-token distribution to that of a smaller, frozen honesty-aligned teacher via reverse-KL supervision. Under existential pressure with ethical instructions, PACT reduces multi-agent persistent deception from 80% to 3%. Our results show that multi-agent coordination amplifies strategic deception and that on-policy honesty alignment can substantially mitigate these failures.

Introduces PACT, which trains a stronger student to match the next-token behavior of a smaller frozen honesty-aligned teacher using reverse-KL supervision.

papers.abstract: Computational pathology (CPath) analyses increasingly depend on multi-step computational workflows that require substantial programming expertise, limiting their accessibility to pathologists and other domain experts without extensive coding experience. Although large language models (LLMs) provide a promising natural-language interface for constructing such analyses, hallucinated operations and incorrect workflow specifications limit their reliability in scientific settings. We introduce Tissue Image Analysis Agent (TIAgent), an automated CPath workflow generation framework that, given a natural-language prompt specifying a complex analytical task together with an input dataset, automatically constructs a verifiable computational graph employing existing CPath operations. The resulting graph can be inspected and executed, enabling natural-language construction of complex CPath workflows for applications including automated biomarker discovery and tissue analysis. We demonstrate end-to-end workflow generation and execution and systematically benchmark 14 backbone LLMs across 90 unit tasks spanning 18 CPath operation types. The ability of each LLM to generate a complete and correct unit workflow is quantified using Unit Workflow Success (UWS). Performance varied substantially across backbone models, with Kimi-K2.7-Code achieving the highest UWS of 0.967 (95% CI: 0.907-0.989). Analysis of node and parameter correctness further revealed that selecting the appropriate computational operation and correctly configuring it represent distinct challenges for LLM-based workflow generation. TIAgent provides a foundation for making complex CPath workflow construction more accessible while enabling systematic evaluation of LLM-driven scientific workflow generation.
authors: Aakash Madhav Rao, Mark Eastwood, Danielle Belgrave, Fayyaz Minhas
bullets: Targets the programming expertise barrier that limits access to multi-step computational pathology analyses.
Constructs computational graphs from a natural-language task and input dataset, reducing risks from hallucinated operations and invalid specifications.
Supports applications such as automated biomarker discovery and tissue analysis through end-to-end workflow generation and execution.
Benchmarks 14 backbone LLMs on 90 unit tasks covering 18 computational pathology operation types.
Model performance varied substantially; the strongest reported model achieved a Unit Workflow Success of 0.967, while operation selection and parameter configuration remained distinct challenges.

figures.caption: Figure 1: A. TIAgent System Architecture: Given a natural-language request and an input cohort or dataset, TIAgent plans the analysis, selects existing CPath operations and models, and automatically constructs a verifiable computational graph for execution. B. End-to-end workflow example: TIAgent generates and executes a workflow for quantifying stromal tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes (sTILs) within tumor-associated stroma (TAS) in a breast cancer whole-slide image, showing the generated plan and computational graph together with intermediate segmentation and detection outputs and the resulting sTIL density map.

Figure 2: A. Unit Workflow Success (UWS) across backbone LLMs. UWS quantifies each model’s ability to generate a complete and correct executable workflow for individual CPath tasks. B. Node and Parameter Correctness across backbone LLMs. Node Correctness (NC) measures whether the correct computational operation is selected, while Parameter Correctness (PC) measures whether the selected operation is configured with the expected parameters.

papers.title: TIAgent: From Natural Language to Grounded Agentic Workflows for Computational Pathology

papers.abstract: Automated research pipelines increasingly rely on fixed LLM judges to rank, filter, and revise proposals, yet these judges are routinely replaced by newer versions. We study whether such replacements preserve the underlying measurement standard. Using a preregistered, frozen-weight design, we evaluate three adjacent same-family transitions across Qwen, Gemma, and Mistral on frozen ML research proposals under randomized information conditions. The common assumption that newer judges are simply harsher fails: two transitions shift toward greater leniency, while the third shifts in the opposite direction on anchors but attenuates off-anchor. More importantly, version changes can alter not only score location but also criterion geometry and resolution; one transition collapses clean-flawed discrimination, placing 93% of pool scores on a single value. Supplying identical facts does not close the version gap, placebo-controlled interventions show that observed packet effects are largely format-driven rather than content-driven, and global recalibration repairs the mean while explaining little object-level dispersion. We organize these failures with a measurement model in which a judge replacement can change its origin, criterion geometry, or resolution. A small stratified anchor audit of about 200 calls identifies the failure class before deployment, and frozen thresholds correctly diagnose two post-registration API judge replacements. We release six preregistration locks and the full audit trail of 14882 judge calls.
bullets: Across three same-family transitions in Qwen, Gemma, and Mistral, newer judges did not consistently become harsher: two became more lenient, while one shifted differently by evaluation condition.
Version changes affected score location, criterion geometry, and resolution; one transition reduced clean-versus-flawed discrimination by assigning 93% of scores the same value.
Identical facts did not eliminate version differences, and placebo tests attributed most packet effects to formatting rather than content.
Global recalibration corrected average scores but explained little object-level variation.
A stratified audit of about 200 calls identified failure classes and correctly diagnosed two post-registration API judge replacements.

papers.abstract: We present HyScale, a long-context training system for learned sparse attention. Learned sparse attention is a promising architecture for million-token contexts, widely adopted in production since DeepSeek-V3.2. Selection, however, grows into the training bottleneck. For each query, it scores every previous token whereas sparse attention reads only $k$; worse, current systems materialize a full score table and repeat selection during recomputation. Our key insight is that the output of selection is not an activation, but rather a set of indices. Building on it, HyScale introduces HyTopK and selection replay. HyTopK finds each query's exact top-$k$ on the fly without a score table, while selection replay reuses forward-pass selection in recomputation. Together with holistic system optimizations tackling end-to-end training challenges, HyScale speeds up GLM-5.1 training on 1M-token sequences by 2.07$\times$ over Megatron-LM on 512 H20 GPUs. It also speeds up the CSA layers of DeepSeek-V4-Flash and the QSA layers of Qwen3.8-Flash-Next by 2.01$\times$ and 1.57$\times$ at 1M tokens on 32 H800 GPUs.
authors: Yangshen Deng, Xinjing Huang, Yulong Wang, Yunzhuo Liu, Jun Hu, Shuyong Tan, Chun-Chih Tseng, Mingji Han, Ray Ying, Key Zhang, Luo Mai
bullets: Learned sparse attention makes selection a training bottleneck because each query scores all prior tokens, despite reading only top-k tokens.
HyTopK computes exact top-k indices on the fly without materializing a full score table.
Selection replay reuses forward-pass selection during recomputation, reducing redundant work.
Combined with end-to-end system optimizations, HyScale achieves reported speedups of 2.07×, 2.01×, and 1.57× on 1M-token training workloads.
The evaluation covers GLM-5.1, DeepSeek-V4-Flash CSA layers, and Qwen3.8-Flash-Next QSA layers on H20 and H800 GPUs.
