papers.abstract: Building Task-Oriented Dialogue (TOD) systems for high-value scenarios such as financial marketing requires large volumes of domain-specific dialogue data, which privacy regulations, annotation costs, and the need for expert labor make hard to obtain. User simulation offers a remedy, but existing methods target general-domain dialogue and exhibit two key limitations: insufficient modeling of domain-specific business processes and compliance constraints, and inadequate capture of the colloquial, spoken-language character of voice interactions. We propose ProfileSim, a profile-driven user simulation framework for financial marketing outbound calls. It jointly models user profiles---demographics and Big Five personality traits---and business profiles---intents reverse-engineered from real call logs---enabling fine-grained control over simulated behavior. The base model is fine-tuned on real voice dialogue data and refined by Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) with hierarchical rewards at the dialogue and utterance levels. Paired with a customer service agent integrating Standard Operating Procedure (SOP) constraints and Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), ProfileSim achieves the highest colloquial naturalness, the strongest user profile adherence and the lowest agent score on long-tail intents among all evaluated user generators, while producing substantially shorter user utterances at comparable business compliance. The generated dialogue data is designed to support intent recognition training, agent evaluation, and rapid cold-start deployment.
authors: Juan Li, Fangshu Chang, Xinyi Jiang, Ling Huang, Yunzhang Chen
bullets: Addresses the lack of privacy-safe, expert-annotated, domain-specific dialogue data for task-oriented systems.
Models demographics, Big Five personality traits, and business intents reverse-engineered from real call logs.
Fine-tunes on real voice dialogues and applies GRPO with dialogue- and utterance-level rewards.
With an SOP- and RAG-based agent, achieves the strongest reported colloquial naturalness and profile adherence, while handling long-tail intents and shorter utterances at comparable compliance.
Supports intent-recognition training, agent evaluation, and rapid cold-start deployment.

papers.abstract: LLM-based annotation has advanced rapidly, yet existing benchmarks remain misaligned with real-world practice. Actual annotation often involves lengthy, task-specific guidelines, and different annotators may produce divergent but reasonable judgments, especially on boundary cases, where single-labeled dataset fail to reflect this disagreement. This gap also limits existing single-agent and workflow-based annotation systems, which often lack adaptability to complex, evolving guidelines. To bridge this gap, we introduce ANT-A Benchmark, a real-world multi-annotator benchmark spanning 7 datasets across domains and modalities, with task-specific guidelines and 5 independent human labels per instance. ANT-A enables a distribution-aware evaluation, using Fleiss kappa to assess how closely model annotations align with human labeling distributions. We further propose ANT-OR, a multi-agent annotation framework that refines prompts by distilling contrastive decision rules from positive and negative feedback. Experiments show that ANT-OR improves agreement@>=2 accuracy by 4.5 points over the strongest baseline and achieves the highest alignment with human annotator distributions as measured by Fleiss kappa within 2 points. Code and benchmark are available at https://github.com/Krueske/ANT-OR.
authors: Xiaopeng Ke, Zhixin Wang, Xuebo Liu, Xinyu Ma, Xing Zheng, Bowen Song, Weiqiang Wang, Min Zhang
bullets: Introduces a seven-dataset benchmark spanning domains and modalities, with task-specific guidelines and five independent human labels per instance.
Evaluates annotations against human labeling distributions using Fleiss kappa rather than single-label accuracy alone.
Proposes ANT-OR, which refines prompts by distilling contrastive rules from positive and negative feedback.
Improves agreement@≥2 accuracy by 4.5 points over the strongest baseline and achieves near-best distributional alignment, within 2 Fleiss-kappa points of the best result.
Targets complex, evolving guidelines and reasonable annotator disagreement, especially on boundary cases.

papers.abstract: Recursive large language model (LLM) agents solve long-horizon tasks through decomposition, execution, and environmental feedback. Yet after producing an atomic subtask, they often invoke the same large model again to translate a familiar instruction into an executable action. We observe that high-level planning is task-specific, whereas leaf-level action grounding recurs across tasks and can be checked against environment-admitted actions. We introduce LeafSkill, an external reuse layer that retrieves semantically related grounding experience, binds action templates to current objects and admissible actions, and uses a lightweight 1.7B selector to choose a bound action or defer the unchanged subtask to the original agent. Skills remain outside the model parameters, allowing a frozen selector to use post-training additions. Under lexical and syntactic paraphrases, exact matching retrieves none of the reference actions, while semantic retrieval preserves 96.0% and 97.0% candidate coverage; the frozen selector adopts 97.34% of unseen skill types. On an independent confirmation set of 200 Robotouille tasks, LeafSkill completes 137 tasks versus 121 for ReCAP (68.5% vs. 60.5%, exact McNemar p=.0259). On the 106 tasks completed by both, it reduces Qwen3.5-27B tokens by 14.42% and calls by 14.08%. A separate held-out repeat yields a consistent 9.0-point success gain and 18.98% token reduction. Reusable leaf grounding can thus improve task completion while reducing host-model inference without replacing high-level planning.
authors: Shen Liu, Ze Zhou, Zhenguo Xu, Shaopu Wang, Yike Gao, Chunlei Wang
bullets: Targets the repeated translation of atomic subtasks into executable, environment-admitted actions.
Retrieves semantically related experiences, binds templates to current objects/actions, and uses a lightweight 1.7B selector or defers to the original agent.
Skills are stored externally, so a frozen selector can incorporate post-training additions.
On 200 Robotouille tasks, it completed 137 tasks versus 121 for ReCAP (68.5% vs. 60.5%); shared-task usage fell 14.42% in tokens and 14.08% in calls.
A held-out repeat showed a 9.0-point success gain and 18.98% token reduction.

papers.selection_reason: External skill-reuse layer for LLM agents stores and retrieves grounding experience, fitting LLM memory while reducing inference cost.
papers.title: LeafSkill: Efficient Leaf-Level Action Grounding for Recursive LLM Agents
papers.tldr: LeafSkill reuses verified leaf-level action skills to reduce repeated LLM grounding, improving recursive-agent task success while lowering host-model inference.

papers.abstract: Lifelong LLM agents must learn from an expanding history of interactions while making each decision within a bounded context window. Memory makes past experience available, but the agent may still need to infer how to solve each new task from the retrieved records. Skills provide reusable procedures, yet may omit the task-specific facts needed to apply them. Because retrieved memory and skills shape the agent's behavior, they also influence the experience available for future learning. We introduce MemCryst, a framework for lifelong context adaptation through bidirectional learning of memory and skills with a frozen language model. Recurring episodes stored in memory support skill creation and revision, and the interactions guided by those skills supply new memory for subsequent learning. Facts retrieved from memory and learned skills jointly form the agent's context, while task outcomes adjust the future retrieval influence of the records actually served without rewriting their content. Across ten settings spanning embodied control, long-document reading, conversation, mathematics, and code, MemCryst leads seven reported comparisons. On ALFWorld, joint serving achieves 63.17% success, compared with 59.83% for memory-only and 50.50% for skill-only serving. Code is available at https://github.com/tianyi0216/Memcryst.git
bullets: Addresses the challenge of using expanding interaction histories when context capacity is limited.
Uses a frozen language model with bidirectional memory–skill learning: recurring episodes create or revise skills, while skill-guided interactions generate future memories.
Combines retrieved facts and learned procedures in the agent’s context, adapting retrieval influence based on task outcomes without rewriting stored records.
Evaluated across ten settings covering embodied control, long-document reading, conversation, mathematics, and code.
On ALFWorld, joint memory-and-skill serving reached 63.17% success, versus 59.83% for memory-only and 50.50% for skill-only serving.

papers.abstract: Looped language models run each token through the same layers several times, and each run is one iteration. To save compute, an extra layer, the halting head, gives after each iteration the probability that the token stops there, so that easy tokens can stop early. Pretraining models from scratch, up to 1.3B parameters, we find two problems. First, heads trained on a mix of all iterations predict that tokens need under half the iterations, yet under the standard stopping rule tokens run almost every iteration, because this training never scores the single iteration where a token stops. Scoring every iteration instead fixes this, but in our runs it works only with a strong penalty favoring early stops. Second, savings are commonly reported as an average number of iterations per token, but when sequences are generated in batches that run until their slowest token stops, a model without a head is almost as good at that cost. The reported average can therefore overstate the saving. We recommend reporting the iterations tokens actually run, with the stopping threshold and batch size, and give a test, run before training a head, that bounds its gain.
authors: Tsung-Han Wu, Minsuk Heo, Kenny Tan
bullets: Mixed-iteration training can predict early stopping but fail under the standard stopping rule because the actual stopping iteration is not scored.
Scoring every iteration improves halting, but the reported runs required a strong penalty favoring early stops.
Batch generation runs until the slowest token finishes, so average iterations per token can overstate practical savings.
The authors recommend reporting actual iterations run, stopping threshold, and batch size.
They also propose a pretraining test to bound the potential benefit of a halting head.

papers.abstract: Post-training quantization (PTQ) to FP4 has emerged as a key technique for reducing large language model inference cost, especially on Blackwell GPUs, which offer native FP4 tensor core support. Direct PTQ to FP4, however, still leaves a noticeable accuracy gap. Recent work on SVDQuant mitigates the errors introduced through FP4 quantization for diffusion models by adding high-precision low-rank corrections obtained via SVD. However, this high-precision low-rank correction requires many bits per rank, and it runs on the same tensor cores as the main FP4 GEMM. We introduce BiLoCo, a low-rank correction method whose left and right factors are stored as binary ${\{\pm 1\}}$ sign vectors rather than as BF16 numbers. The signed format uses $16{\times}$ less storage per rank-one component, and since the correction now consists of additions/subtractions, this can be run on CUDA cores concurrently with the FP4 tensor-core GEMM. On 4B--72B LLMs, BiLoCo matches or improves memory-matched SVDQuant for PTQ. We implement BiLoCo on B300 as a fused single kernel, where the FP4 GEMM runs on tensor cores, the bit-packed correction on the CUDA cores of the same launch, and the two are combined in the GEMM epilogue. With batch size $1$, the fused kernel is at most $11\%$ slower than the FP4-only GEMM for every rank up to $512$. At rank $128$, it is at most $20\%$ slower up to batch size $8$.
authors: David Jin, Beshr IslamBouli, Tarushii Goel, Han Guo, Yoon Kim
bullets: Addresses the accuracy gap caused by direct FP4 post-training quantization.
Stores low-rank factors as binary ±1 sign vectors, reducing storage per rank-one component by 16× versus high-precision corrections.
Runs the correction through additions/subtractions on CUDA cores concurrently with the FP4 tensor-core GEMM.
On 4B–72B LLMs, matches or improves memory-matched SVDQuant for PTQ.
A fused B300 kernel is at most 11% slower than FP4-only GEMM at batch size 1 for ranks up to 512, and at most 20% slower at rank 128 through batch size 8.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces binary low-rank corrections (BiLoCo) for post-training quantization to reduce memory usage and latency in LLM inference, running efficiently on tensor cores.

papers.tldr: BiLoCo uses binary low-rank corrections to recover FP4-quantized LLM accuracy with far less storage and limited inference overhead.

papers.abstract: Small language models deployed under cost, latency, or privacy constraints cannot simply switch to larger models when reasoning fails. Multi-candidate generate-then-rerank offers a natural test-time scaling route. However, more candidates do not always yield higher accuracy. We identify a previously overlooked bottleneck between generation and selection: a correct answer may appear in the candidate pool yet fail to be selected because it is incomplete, unparseable, or misaligned with the answer mode the fixed selector expects. We term this loss the hidden interface tax and formalize a coverage-conversion decomposition that distinguishes raw oracle coverage from selectable coverage, the subset of problems where a correct candidate can actually be consumed by the selector. We propose Compatibility-Aware Candidate Construction (CACC), an interface layer between the candidate source and the fixed selector that repairs fragments, aligns answer modes, and removes selector-confusing noise without retraining either component. On numeric reasoning (GSM8K, competition_math), CACC raises both oracle coverage and final accuracy. On GPQA Diamond, CACC alone improves final accuracy from 5.6% to 19.2% (+13.6 pp); combined with proposer-side strengthening it reaches 25.8% (+20.2 pp). On MMLU-Pro, CACC exposes a coverage-conversion gap: answer-mode-compatible construction raises oracle coverage, but final accuracy decreases by 0.85 pp under the original selector; adding proposer-side strengthening improves final accuracy.
authors: Qianli Ma, Zhiqing Tang, Fanshuai Meng, Zhi Yao, Hanshuai Cui, Weijia Jia
bullets: Multi-candidate generation can contain a correct answer that is not selected because it is incomplete, unparseable, or in the wrong answer mode.
The paper formalizes a coverage–conversion decomposition separating raw oracle coverage from selectable coverage.
Compatibility-Aware Candidate Construction repairs fragments, aligns answer modes, and removes selector-confusing noise without retraining the generator or selector.
CACC improves GPQA Diamond accuracy from 5.6% to 19.2%; combined with proposer strengthening, accuracy reaches 25.8%.
On MMLU-Pro, improved answer-mode compatibility raises oracle coverage but slightly lowers final accuracy under the original selector, showing the method is selector-dependent.

papers.selection_reason: Identifies and mitigates the 'hidden interface tax' in multi-candidate reasoning for LLMs, proposing Compatibility-Aware Candidate Construction to improve answer selection.
papers.title: Correct but Unselectable: The Hidden Interface Tax in Multi-Candidate Reasoning
papers.tldr: CACC improves multi-candidate reasoning by making correct generated answers compatible with a fixed selector, substantially boosting accuracy in some settings while revealing selector-dependent limits.

papers.abstract: Training large language models (LLMs) in sub-8-bit arithmetic promises substantial gains in memory bandwidth and compute throughput, yet FP4 formats introduce quantization error severe enough to destabilize optimization if left unaddressed. We present ALTO, an open-source training recipe for GPT-OSS-20B, a 20-billion-parameter mixture-of-experts (MoE) model, on the MLPerf Small MoE Training benchmark under the MXFP4 microscaling format. The recipe combines established techniques from Abecassis, Felix et al. [arXiv:2509.25149] (hybrid 1D/2D block quantization, randomized Hadamard transforms, and stochastic rounding) with a simplified weight de-oscillation scheme adapted from TetraJet-v2 [arXiv:2510.27527]. On C4 validation at global batch size 16, MXFP4 + RHT + SR + de-oscillation reaches a validation loss of 3.3350 at 16,128 steps, only 0.007 above the BF16 baseline (3.3283), closing roughly 50% of the gap left by MXFP4 without de-oscillation (3.3418). Measured by steps to reach the MLPerf quality target (validation loss 3.34), de-oscillation cuts the FP4 convergence overhead relative to BF16 from +20.0% to +5.0%. We also report negative end-to-end results from differential gradient estimation, outlier clipping, and macro-block scaling, despite each showing operator-level SNR gains. All experiments use simulated MXFP4 kernels on AMD MI300 hardware and wall-clock speed has not been optimized.
authors: Han Wang, Zhitao Wang, Natalia Frumkin, Xuanwu Yin, Alireza Khodamoradi, Dong Li, Emad Barsoum
bullets: MXFP4 training is challenging because FP4 quantization error can destabilize optimization.
ALTO combines hybrid block quantization, randomized Hadamard transforms, stochastic rounding, and simplified weight de-oscillation.
On C4 validation, the recipe reaches loss 3.3350 versus 3.3283 for BF16, recovering about half the gap from MXFP4 without de-oscillation.
De-oscillation reduces convergence overhead relative to BF16 from +20.0% to +5.0% at the MLPerf quality target.
Differential gradient estimation, outlier clipping, and macro-block scaling did not improve end-to-end results despite operator-level SNR gains.

papers.abstract: Multi-head attention retrieves and combines context representations through query--key interactions and value aggregation, with head dimension constraining the per-head representation space. In long-context processing, it remains unclear whether allocating a fixed parameter budget to fewer, wider heads improves information retrieval. In this paper, we investigate how head dimension affects the performance of long-context retrieval tasks. Our empirical studies reveal that pretraining loss and short-context non-retrieval task performance are not affected much by head dimension, while long-context retrieval performance improves with wider heads at fixed model sizes. We find that models with wider heads have a higher proportion of retrieval heads, associating more parameters with retrieval. Our ablation studies also show that the retrieval performance improves with wider heads even when the projection weights in attention modules are frozen during long-context continual pretraining, suggesting that wider heads not only benefit updates in attention modules but lead to more effective adaptation of components such as embeddings and MLPs.
authors: Seiya Tokui, Shoichiro Yamaguchi, Sosuke Kobayashi
bullets: The study examines whether fewer, wider heads better support retrieval under a fixed parameter budget.
Pretraining loss and short-context, non-retrieval performance change little with head dimension.
Long-context retrieval improves as head dimension increases.
Wider-head models contain a higher proportion of retrieval heads, allocating more capacity to retrieval.
Improvements persist with frozen attention projection weights, indicating benefits beyond attention-module updates.

papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have gained widespread adoption in various natural language processing tasks, but suffer from hallucination issues where they generate unfaithful or inconsistent content. While Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) has shown promising applications in reasoning tasks, its application to span-level hallucination detection is challenged by localization ambiguity, reward sparsity on hard examples, and uncontrolled length inflation. To address these issues, we introduce Socratic Guided Policy Optimization (SOPO), a multi-turn RL framework for robust hallucination detection. The key innovation of SOPO is a Socratic feedback mechanism, where a teacher model guides the reasoning trajectories during rollout by providing indirect hints inferred from the ground truth. This teacher-guided approach enables the model to generate more effective reasoning trajectories for hard examples, thus alleviating reward sparsity. Furthermore, we incorporate Turn-based Advantage Scaling to penalize verbosity bias, encouraging the model to develop efficient and autonomous reasoning capabilities. Empirical results on RAGTruth demonstrate that SOPO (4B) achieves state-of-the-art performance, surpassing leading proprietary models (e.g., GPT-5) and standard RL baselines, while obtaining higher reported mean scores than GRPO on four out-of-domain benchmarks, with mixed evidence against CAPO. We release our training and evaluation code alongside the 1.7B and 4B SOPO models at https://github.com/patsnap/SOPO.
authors: Jiawei Dong, Zilong Bai, Pengtian zhu, Peng Zhou
bullets: Targets localization ambiguity, sparse rewards on difficult examples, and reasoning-length inflation in span-level hallucination detection.
Uses Socratic feedback from a teacher model to guide rollout reasoning with indirect, ground-truth-derived hints.
Introduces Turn-based Advantage Scaling to penalize verbosity and promote efficient, autonomous reasoning.
Achieves state-of-the-art performance on RAGTruth and higher reported mean scores than GRPO across four out-of-domain benchmarks.
Results against CAPO are mixed; released code and 1.7B/4B models are available.

papers.abstract: Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) is often highly sensitive to learning-rate (LR) choices. Recent empirical studies suggest that, once LRs are carefully tuned, vanilla LoRA can remain competitive with many proposed LoRA variants. This shifts the central practical question from designing ever more variants to reducing the cost and brittleness of LR selection. LoRA+ addresses this issue with asymmetric LRs, using a larger LR for the up-projection matrix $B$ than for the down-projection matrix $A$. However, the ratio $\eta_B / \eta_A$ itself becomes an additional hyperparameter: large ratios can improve adaptation, but under the standard LoRA initialization they can also cause unstable training and ratio-dependent performance collapse. We identify the source of this brittleness through a signal--noise decomposition of LoRA dynamics. Under standard \initA, the update contains an initialization-induced noise term whose magnitude can be affected by the LR for $B$, $\eta_B$, the initialization scale $\beta$, and the adapter rank $r$. In practical LLM fine-tuning, this non-vanishing noise can limit the performance gains expected from LoRA+ style asymmetric LRs. To suppress this effect, we propose \initAA, a simple initialization that scales the variance of $A$ as $\sigma_A^2 \propto n^{-2}$ while keeping $B_0=0$. Under matched rank and training time for both initializations, this reduces the initialization-noise energy by an additional factor of $1/n$, stabilizing asymmetric LoRA training while preserving zero initial adapter output. Empirically, \initAA substantially widens the stable LR region across initialization scales, adapter ranks, and LoRA update multipliers. Across tasks and models, \initAA reduces best-ratio drift, prevents the high-ratio collapse observed with standard \initA, and makes the width-based guideline $\eta_B \approx n \eta_A$ a useful starting point for finite pretrained models.
bullets: LoRA+ can improve adaptation with a larger learning rate for the up-projection matrix B, but its LR ratio is brittle under standard initialization.
A signal–noise analysis attributes instability to an initialization-induced noise term affected by the B learning rate, initialization scale, and adapter rank.
The proposed initialization scales A’s variance as proportional to n⁻² while retaining zero-initialized B, preserving zero initial adapter output.
It reduces initialization-noise energy by an additional factor of 1/n and substantially broadens the stable LR region across tested scales, ranks, and update multipliers.
Across tasks and models, it prevents high-ratio collapse and makes ηB ≈ nηA a useful starting point for finite pretrained models.

papers.abstract: One approach to accelerating progress on AI alignment is to automate parts of alignment research itself. Doing so requires systems that can perform reliably on hard-to-supervise research tasks, including identifying flaws in research proposals and evaluating whether a proposed experiment supports its intended claim. To evaluate this capability, we introduce Tampered ML, a benchmark of 1,858 item-pairs, each consisting of an experiment proposal reconstructed from a published machine learning paper and a minimally edited counterfactual that introduces a targeted methodological flaw. Models must identify the more methodologically sound proposal in both presentation orders. A human validation study on a stratified sample estimates that 86% of items are valid (95% CI: 81-91%). Frontier models perform above chance but remain far from reliable (with Opus 5 achieving 77.9% accuracy). They are highly sensitive to the order of presentation and favor flawed designs that appear more specific, transparent, or conventional.
authors: Soroush Ebadian, Parand A. Alamdari, Joe Benton, Hailey Joren
bullets: Introduces 1,858 paired proposals: a reconstruction of a published ML experiment and a minimally edited flawed counterfactual.
Models must select the more methodologically sound proposal under both presentation orders.

papers.abstract: Chain-of-thought (CoT) generation offers an opportunity to intervene before a reasoning model completes its answer. But does the point at which risk is easiest to detect also offer the most effective control? We study this question with REACT, a conditional activation intervention that learns a safety direction from paired safe and unsafe trajectories and applies it once to an early CoT hidden state. The model weights remain frozen, and all subsequent tokens are generated without further edits. To study timing, we train directions separately at each of the first five CoT positions and evaluate ungated edits with full post-edit regeneration. Across three distilled reasoning models and three generation seeds, the strongest gains concentrate in a two- to three-token early window; on DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-8B, the effect falls to approximately zero at the fourth and fifth tokens, even though later states can be more predictive of risk. This separates risk readability from effective control: intervention timing must be evaluated through its effect on subsequent generation. On the same 8B model, REACT raises the rate of fully safe CoT-answer outputs on StrongREJECT-273 from 29.06% to 82.05%, while keeping benign refusal and usefulness near baseline. An anonymized implementation is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/REACT_official2-333B.
authors: Hanwen Zhang, Enyi Jiang, Ruike Zhu, Qinan Yu, Sanmi Koyejo

Learns a safety direction from paired safe and unsafe trajectories, then applies one edit to an early hidden state while freezing model weights.
Evaluates interventions at each of the first five CoT positions with full post-edit regeneration across three distilled reasoning models.
Finds the strongest control effects at roughly two to three tokens; later states may predict risk better but can be ineffective for control.
On DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-8B, fully safe CoT-answer outputs increase from 29.06% to 82.05% on StrongREJECT-273, with benign refusal and usefulness near baseline.

papers.abstract: Language models can answer a question from a supplied document or from their parametric knowledge. When later asked where the answer came from, what determines their source report? We study this by intervening on the model's key-value (KV) cache after the answer is generated and before the source question is asked. On a controlled factual task with four models (7B-32B), changing or removing the document's cache never changes the report. In contrast, transplanting the question-and-answer (Q+A) cache between runs with identical question and answer tokens transfers it: every eligible report follows the donor, while the recipient's document is unchanged. On the two smaller models, steering Q+A values along directions fitted before any source question reverses 98.9-100% of reports across four document conditions at a fixed strength, while norm-matched random directions flip at most 1.1%. The components of keys and values along fitted directions carry the transplant effect: copying them alone nearly reproduces the report change; holding them fixed nearly prevents it. Applied during answer generation, the same value directions also change which source supplies the answer, though more weakly and depending on the prompt. Source reporting in this setting thus depends causally on cached state produced while answering. We do not establish general reporting accuracy or a complete interpretation of this state.
authors: Kirill Afendulev, Alexey Dontsov, Alla Chepurova, Elena Tutubalina, Anton Korznikov
bullets: Across four 7B–32B models, changing or removing the document’s KV cache did not alter source reports.
Transplanting the Q+A cache transferred the donor run’s source report while leaving the recipient document unchanged.
On two smaller models, fitted Q+A value directions reversed 98.9–100% of reports; random directions flipped at most 1.1%.
Key/value components along fitted directions largely reproduced or prevented the transplant effect.
The same directions influenced source selection during answer generation, but more weakly and prompt-dependently.

papers.title: Context or Knowledge: How LLMs Attribute Their Own Answers

papers.abstract: Several formal theories have been developed to characterize the capabilities and limitations of the transformer architecture, each employing different abstractions that capture different features of the architecture. Due to the differences in their underlying assumptions and conceptual frameworks, these theories can disagree in their predictions about what tasks transformers find easy or hard. We map out seven theories of transformer capability (Star-free, $\mathsf{AC}^0$, $\mathsf{TC}^0$, C-RASP, MPC, BAPO, and Sensitivity) and translate their results into a common matrix of predictions across a suite of tasks covering different computational structures. We provide new theoretical results to complete this matrix. We then evaluate theoretical predictions through controlled experiments measuring in-distribution sample complexity, length generalization, and pretrained language model performance. We find that no single theory explains the observed pattern of successes and failures. When a theory does not capture the transformer behaviors relevant to a task, its predictions break down; for instance, we show that the $k$-hop induction task is predicted hard by C-RASP because it does not model content-dependent attention, but we train small transformers on this task that length-generalize. Similarly, theories assuming hard attention like $\mathsf{AC}^0$ and BAPO predict binary majority to be hard, for which we also find success in practice. Together, our results point to several specific features that a theory of transformers must capture: soft rather than hard attention, dynamic content-dependent retrieval, bounded computation at each position, an account of learnability and inductive biases, and a combination of upper and lower bounds.
authors: Awni Altabaa, Tobias Schnabel, Kiran Tomlinson
bullets: Maps seven theoretical frameworks to common predictions across tasks with varied computational structures.
Adds theoretical results to complete the comparison matrix and tests predictions using sample complexity, length generalization, and pretrained-model behavior.
Finds theory–practice mismatches, including transformers length-generalizing on k-hop induction despite C-RASP predicting difficulty.
Finds practical success on binary majority despite hard-attention theories predicting it is hard.
Identifies soft attention, content-dependent retrieval, bounded per-position computation, inductive biases, and both upper and lower bounds as important ingredients.

papers.selection_reason: Empirically tests and compares seven theoretical frameworks characterizing the capabilities and limitations of the transformer architecture.
papers.title: Putting Transformer Theories to the Test

papers.abstract: In drug development, lead optimization must improve competing properties, such as increasing permeability and reducing toxicity, while limiting scaffold changes that could compromise the lead's potency. RL-based post-training, such as C-MORAL, addresses this problem by fine-tuning molecular language models to directly optimize molecular leads for objectives of interest, which relies on expensive task-specific datasets and faces challenges in achieving multi-objective optimization (MOO). We argue a pre-trained model may already contain useful molecular edits that zero-shot generation cannot efficiently reach. Motivated by the limited search capabilities of zero-shot generation, we develop an efficient Metropolis-Hastings search strategy to better explore the proposal distribution. We propose ReMedI, which uses the molecular language model as a base proposer for inference-time alignment. Given a lead and a set of multi-objective tasks, the model proposes edits conditioned on the current molecule, while Metropolis--Hastings refinement guides sequential edits under an objective for property improvement, preservation, and lead similarity. On both C-MuMOInstruct and SMDD benchmarks, refinement improves frozen base models across three backbones, reaching significantly higher multi-objective optimization success rates compared to baselines. These search traces can then distilled into the base model which improves zero-shot generation and subsequent search using approximately 7.8 times less training molecular leads than that of C-MORAL. ReMedI achieves approximately 2.8 times the strict-success coverage of RL baseline C-MORAL, including on out-of-distribution tasks, with matched lead-relative similarity.
authors: Jia Yi Zhang, Shivanshu Shekhar, Allison McLevige, Tong Zhang
bullets: Targets simultaneous property improvement, preservation of lead quality, and minimal scaffold changes without task-specific RL fine-tuning.
Uses a molecular language model to propose edits, while Metropolis–Hastings refinement guides sequential molecule modifications at inference time.
Distills refinement traces into the base model to improve later zero-shot generation and search.
Improves frozen models across three backbones on C-MuMOInstruct and SMDD, with higher multi-objective success than baselines.
Reports approximately 2.8× the strict-success coverage of C-MORAL and uses approximately 7.8× fewer training molecular leads, while matching lead-relative similarity.

papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) exhibit mode collapse, where their output distribution concentrates on familiar semantic modes. When diversity disappears, repeated sampling becomes semantic repetition rather than discovery, making rare but stronger solutions unlikely to surface and leaving self-evolution and continual learning difficult to sustain. Most remedies intervene only at inference time, shaping sam- ples without making diversity a model capability. We propose PRISM, a training-time framework that internalizes diversity within the model. PRISM combines (i) submodular curation that pairs each prompt with diverse-yet-correct multi-teacher solutions, and (ii) stochastic embedding modulation, which turns special-token perturbations into implicit signals for sampling distinct outputs. A theoretical analysis establishes the stability of this mechanism. On WritingPrompts and BookMIA, PRISM moves the quality-diversity frontier outward, achieving the best generation quality in all model-benchmark settings while maintaining the strongest or near-strongest semantic diversity across two open-weight model families. It also improves sampling efficiency on math and code benchmarks. Beyond inference, PRISM yields a stronger foundation for reinforcement learning, sustaining diverse rollouts and mitigating the diversity collapse commonly observed during RL training.
authors: Qixin Xu, Zihan Zhu, Xiaojiang Liu, Bohan Lyu
bullets: Addresses mode collapse, where repeated sampling produces semantically repetitive outputs and misses rare strong solutions.
Uses submodular curation to pair prompts with diverse but correct multi-teacher answers.
Applies stochastic perturbations to special-token embeddings to implicitly condition the model toward distinct outputs.
Improves the quality–diversity frontier on WritingPrompts and BookMIA across two open-weight model families, while also improving sampling efficiency for math and code.
Supports reinforcement learning by sustaining diverse rollouts and mitigating diversity collapse during training.

papers.abstract: Diffusion language models (DLMs) support bidirectional denoising and iterative refinement, but generation remains largely controlled by token-level masking schedules. This leaves draft-level refinement implicit and limits explicit control over when to insert missing content, delete redundant spans, revisit uncertain regions, or stop editing. We introduce Diffusion Editing Language Adapter (DELA), a plug-in framework that enables controllable draft refinement with a frozen DLM. DELA operates on clean, variable-length drafts using four explicit editing actions: Insert, Delete, Remask, and Stop. The controller determines when and where to edit the draft, while the frozen DLM fills masked regions through denoising, separating high-level edit control from token-level generation. A naive single-phase editor would be computationally expensive because arbitrary interior edits can disrupt prefix stability and limit reliable KV-cache reuse. To address this, DELA uses a two-phase decoding procedure: a fast, append-only drafting phase that supports KV-cache reuse, followed by a global refinement phase that enables targeted non-monotonic edits to the full draft. We train the controller using a staged curriculum that begins with learning local edit priors from synthetic recovery tasks and mined actions that improve draft quality. Subsequent stages refine edit selection through rollout-based outcome preferences and alignment with downstream task feedback. Experiments on mathematical reasoning and code generation show that DELA achieves gains of up to 5.5 percentage points over direct diffusion decoding while keeping the backbone frozen. DELA thus provides a modular approach to explicit draft-level control in diffusion language models.
authors: Xinsong Feng, Chenan Wang, Leshu Tang, Johnny Liu, Dong Li, Da Li, Haipeng Chen
bullets: Addresses the limited draft-level control of token-masking schedules in diffusion language models.
Uses a controller to choose when and where to edit, while the frozen backbone denoises masked regions.
Combines fast append-only drafting with global refinement to support efficient KV-cache reuse and non-monotonic edits.
Trains the controller with staged synthetic recovery, mined actions, rollout preferences, and downstream feedback.
Improves mathematical reasoning and code generation by up to 5.5 percentage points over direct diffusion decoding, with the backbone frozen.

papers.abstract: Verifying the provenance of autonomous LLM agents is a critical security challenge. Existing semantic attribution is easily obfuscated by system prompts, while active watermarking conflicts with schema-constrained tool generation. We propose AgentTrace, an active framework that identifies the foundation model behind a black-box agent via observable execution traces. AgentTrace injects structurally ambiguous probes to trigger tokenization-sensitive serialization failures at rigid tool interfaces. While these initial failures provide coarse-grained separation across model families, the temporal sequence of subsequent repair operations reveals fine-grained, model-specific recovery behaviors. By modeling these multi-step trajectories with lightweight Markov chains, AgentTrace achieves 96.0% attribution accuracy under adversarial identity spoofing. Crucially, sequential repair modeling successfully distinguishes the evaluated intra-family variants sharing identical tokenizers (e.g., Llama-3 8B/70B), substantially outperforming unordered behavioral statistics while remaining robust against prompt obfuscation and temperature scaling.
authors: Gejian Zhao, Hanzhou Wu, Xinpeng Zhang
bullets: Addresses provenance verification when prompts can obscure semantic behavior and watermarking conflicts with constrained tool generation.
Injects structurally ambiguous probes that expose tokenization-sensitive serialization failures at tool interfaces.
Models the temporal sequence of subsequent repair operations with lightweight Markov chains.
Sequential repair patterns distinguish intra-family variants with identical tokenizers, including evaluated Llama-3 8B and 70B variants.
Remains robust to prompt obfuscation and temperature scaling in the reported evaluation.

figures.caption: Figure 3: Attribution accuracy under defensive interventions. Figure 1: Conceptual workflow of AgentTrace. A genuine target model may reproduce a structurally ambiguous identifier successfully. A spoofed model with a different tokenization pattern may produce malformed escaping or other serialization anomalies rejected by the parser. AgentTrace combines the tokenization-sensitive failure category with the subsequent sequence of repair operations to identify the underlying model.

Despite identical initial JSON errors, the Llama-3 variants exhibit divergent repair dynamics: the 8B model falls into truncation retry loops, whereas the 70B model employs structured escaping. While both models suffer identical initial tokenization crashes, their repair strategies strictly diverge: (a) Llama-3-8B is trapped in repetitive correction loops, while (b) Llama-3-70B navigates toward success via structured repair.

papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) often exhibit sycophancy, altering their answers to align with user suggestions even on objective factual and reasoning tasks. Yet the quantitative form of this influence--- and whether it is calibrated to source reliability--- remains poorly understood. In this work, we investigate this behavior through hint-induced answer shifts on MMLU questions, evaluating prompts of the form ``[Source] thinks the answer is (X)''. We systematically vary the source to which the hint is attributed (a professor, a friend, or a dog) across three open-source model families, Qwen, Gemma, and SmolLM. We show that the change induced by the hint follows a predictable structure well-characterized by an exponential tilt: the hint induces an approximately constant mean shift in the hinted answer's log-odds, with question--target susceptibility largely shared across sources. To explore how this pattern can arise, we introduce a formal decomposition of the hint response and illustrate in controlled synthetic experiments how KL-regularized reward-based training reshapes both hinted and unhinted answer distributions. Finally, we evaluate whether this shift is calibrated to source reliability, finding that the log-odds shift persists even when the hint-giver is declared inaccurate or accompanied by explicit warnings not to trust the source, highlighting the vulnerability of LLMs to adversarial steering.
authors: Anxin Guo, Chirag Pabbaraju, Sara Ahmadian, Kamesh Munagala, Aravindan Vijayaraghavan
bullets: Studies hint-induced answer changes on MMLU questions across Qwen, Gemma, and SmolLM models.
Hints attributed to a professor, friend, or dog produce approximately constant shifts in the hinted answer’s log-odds.
Question-specific susceptibility is largely shared across different hint sources.
A formal decomposition and synthetic experiments examine how KL-regularized reward training may produce these shifts.
The response is poorly calibrated to source reliability: shifts persist even when sources are labeled inaccurate or untrustworthy.

papers.selection_reason: Quantifies hint-following and sycophancy in reasoning LLMs via log-odds shifts; directly relevant to LLM reasoning behavior and robustness.
papers.title: How Much Do You Trust A Dog? Quantifying Hint-Following in Reasoning Language Models
papers.tldr: LLMs systematically shift their answers toward hinted choices, often ignoring warnings about unreliable sources, revealing a measurable vulnerability to adversarial steering.

papers.abstract: The rapid growth of microdramas has increased demand for high-quality script production. Long-form microdrama script generation with LLMs requires both diverse plot progression and long-range narrative coherence. Our observations reveal that candidate continuations increasingly concentrate on fewer narrative mechanisms as generation progresses, while conventional retrieval may reinforce trope reuse and overlook historical information essential to future plots. To address these challenges, we propose DraMaze, a multi-agent pipeline that explores diverse causal paths through trope memory-guided evolutionary tree search and mutation. It further constructs a Backward Narrative Dependency Tree to organize, retain, and retrieve historical memories based on future narrative goals. We also introduce MiDramaBench, a bilingual benchmark for evaluating script logic and creative quality across different script lengths, together with causal-pattern metrics for narrative repetition and diversity. Experiments show consistent improvements across three backbone LLMs. For 60-episode scripts of up to 60k words, DraMaze reduces causal-pattern repetition by 32.1% and achieves a Logic score of 82.5, outperforming the best-performing baseline by 8.5 points.
authors: Siyang He, Qiqi Wang, Fan Liu, Yuncheng Huang, Pengfei Xu, Xi Chen, Ziwei He, Xipeng Qiu
bullets: Targets the trade-off between diverse plot progression and long-range narrative coherence in LLM-generated microdramas.
Uses trope memory-guided evolutionary tree search and mutation to explore varied causal story paths.
Builds a Backward Narrative Dependency Tree to retrieve historical information relevant to future narrative goals.
Introduces MiDramaBench and causal-pattern metrics for evaluating script logic, creativity, repetition, and diversity.
Across three backbone LLMs, it reduces causal-pattern repetition by 32.1% and reaches a Logic score of 82.5 on 60-episode scripts up to 60k words.

Figure 3 Overview of our multi-agent pipeline for microdrama script generation. (1) Outline Planner creates a four-stage coarse outline. (2) Evolutionary tree search refines event sequences through mutation and trope-guided selection. (3) Develop into episode outlines.(4) Backward Narrative Dependency Tree is constructed from episode outlines to organize subsequent future-aware narrative memory, with episodes attached to goal nodes to guide retrieval. (5) Agents retrieve memories, plan scenes, generate scripts, and update memories after each episode.

Generated events, clues, and foreshadowing are linked to goal nodes, enabling retrieval from the current episode’s goals and their prerequisite subtrees to support subsequent script generation.

papers.abstract: This report introduces Kolibri, an English-German mixture-of-experts transformer with 78.1B total parameters and 3.46B active parameters per token, released as open weights under the Apache 2.0 licence. We built Kolibri for sovereign and specialised deployment, with a particular focus on German and on regulated domains such as public administration, industry, and aerospace. To support these settings, we control the full model-development process, including data, architecture, training infrastructure, post-training, and evaluation. We train Kolibri on 24T tokens across pre-training, mid-training, and long-context extension, with German accounting for more than 20% of the data mix by bytes. To reach this share, we complement German datasets with more than 2T German tokens that we curate from the web with our own pipeline and generate synthetically. Post-training combines supervised fine-tuning on curated German and English data with reinforcement learning on more than 1.2M internally curated tasks, which cover reasoning, tool use, instruction following, code, and retrieval. The model activates 4.4% of its parameters per token, and among the open models evaluated in this report, it lies on the Pareto frontier of quality and serving cost in English and German. Kolibri builds on Kolibri Origin, an earlier iteration that validated our full pipeline at scale. Both models come from our Model Factory, which connects data, experimentation, training, evaluation, and deployment through version-controlled workflows.

At startup, the receive buffers are mapped to the trainer parameters, and each parameter is assigned a trainer rank such that the bytes per rank are balanced. papers.abstract: Looped language models apply one block of layers repeatedly, and the design pays off only if depth is reusable: loop steps beyond the trained budget must remain usable at inference. We ask whether that rests on normalising the state between loop steps, as the released Ouro models do, or on agreement between the loop a model is trained with and the loop it is run with. On released weights this loop-boundary normalisation can be removed without adding parameters and with the readout path bit-identical, and the operation is an identity at one loop step, which serves as an implementation check. Removing it takes Ouro-1.4B and Ouro-2.6B to zero accuracy by the trained budget on a balanced binary task (chance 0.500). State-norm growth, the failure that prior accounts predict, is not the cause: the norm stays within a factor of 2.021 while the head commits to a single wrong token. Yet in 19M-parameter models trained from scratch on two synthetic tasks, 16 seeds per configuration, training without the normalisation is never worse than training with it and extrapolates better: the two are closest at the trained depth and separate on both sides of it (Cliff's delta up to 0.867 beyond the budget). Both results follow if agreement, and not the normalisation itself, is what keeps depth reusable. The damage sits in the readout together with the last layer of the block: in the models trained from scratch, refitting the head over the frozen modified loop recovers a third of the lost accuracy and plateaus, while refitting the last block layer with it recovers all of it. Finally, comparing looped with stacked depth at an equal inference loop count is confounded by unequal overshoot of the trained budget; at matched overshoot the advantage of looping vanishes on one task and shrinks on the other.
authors: Ivan Viakhirev, Kirill Borodin, Maxim Abramov, Grach Mkrtchian
bullets: Removing boundary normalisation from released Ouro models causes performance to collapse by the trained depth, despite limited state-norm growth.
In models trained from scratch, removing normalisation is not worse and often extrapolates better beyond the trained depth.
The failure is localized to the readout and final block layer: refitting both restores the lost accuracy, while refitting only the head gives partial recovery.
Comparisons between looped and stacked models should match overshoot beyond the trained depth; under this control, looping’s advantage disappears on one task and shrinks on another.

papers.selection_reason: Analyzes depth reuse and normalization in looped language models; architectural insight for LLMs.
papers.title: Agreement rather than normalisation keeps depth reusable in looped language models
papers.tldr: Depth reuse in looped language models appears to depend more on agreement between training and inference loops than on loop-boundary normalisation itself.

papers.abstract: As large language models (LLMs) process increasingly long sequences, attention becomes a major computational bottleneck. Sparse attention mostly targets inference, yet many methods still train densely or cannot support sparse training, and their added complexity makes sparsity hard to turn into wall-clock speedups, leaving dense attention widely used in practice. This paper introduces LazyFlash, a forward-dense, backward-sparse attention method built on the observation that attention training is dominated by the backward pass. LazyFlash keeps the forward pass exactly dense, so the trained model remains a standard dense model that existing systems such as vLLM can serve without any change. For the backward pass, LazyFlash proposes a gradient-aware block sparsification design that ranks query blocks by their attention-output gradient norms and skips those contributing negligibly to parameter updates, turning the dense backward into a block-sparse one. A gradient-mass budget adapts the amount of skipped computation to each head and training step, while importance sampling preserves the dense gradient in expectation. These designs are implemented inside the tiled FlashAttention backward kernel, where skipped blocks are never loaded or computed, translating gradient sparsity into real wall-clock acceleration. Experiments on long-context text and speech LLMs show that LazyFlash maintains downstream performance while achieving up to 5.7x attention-backward speedup over FlashAttention and 1.7x end-to-end training speedup.
authors: Keqi Deng, Ruchao Fan, Jinyu Li
bullets: Addresses the training-time bottleneck of dense attention, which limits practical speedups from sparse methods.
Uses gradient-aware block sparsification to rank query blocks by attention-output gradient norms and skip negligible updates.
Adapts sparsity with a per-head, per-step gradient-mass budget while importance sampling preserves dense gradients in expectation.
Integrates skipping into the tiled FlashAttention backward kernel, avoiding loads and computation for skipped blocks.
Maintains downstream performance while delivering up to 5.7× attention-backward and 1.7× end-to-end training speedups.

papers.abstract: Recent Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) decompose the representations of large language models (LLMs) into interpretable features, enabling precise readout and control of encoded knowledge. However, existing SAEs treat each feature as a standalone unit, whereas real-world knowledge is often taxonomically organized. As a result, readout carries no guarantee of taxonomic consistency, and control lacks the granularity to specify the scope of an edit. We propose TaxoSAE, which explicitly encodes taxonomical information, built on is-a (hypernym-hyponym) relations, into the SAE feature space. TaxoSAE mirrors a taxonomy with a stack of SAEs, one per taxonomy level, and introduces a taxonomic alignment loss that trains each concept to be active whenever one of its hyponyms is. On two factual QA taxonomies, one over biographical relations and one over animals, TaxoSAE enables (1) more accurate readout through the taxonomy with concentrated activations, e.g., +31.3 points in reading out the hypernyms of abstract concepts never queried in training; (2) more precise control, with +25.5 points in swap success, while suppressing a concept removes only its own answers (0-2% accuracy vs. 91-100% on other concepts); and, more importantly, (3) readout of unseen concepts through their hypernyms, with up to +37.9 points in hypernym readout accuracy.
authors: Xinyu Guo, Minglai Yang, Clayton T. Morrison, Eduardo Blanco, Mihai Surdeanu
bullets: Addresses the lack of taxonomic consistency and edit-scope control in conventional SAEs.
Uses a stack of SAEs aligned to taxonomy levels and a taxonomic alignment loss linking concepts to their hyponyms.
Evaluated on biographical-relation and animal factual-QA taxonomies.
Improves hypernym readout by up to 31.3 points and swap-control success by 25.5 points.
Supports readout of unseen concepts through hypernyms, improving accuracy by up to 37.9 points; suppression largely affects only the targeted concept.

papers.selection_reason: Taxonomic sparse autoencoders improve LLM representation readout and control, a meaningful method within language foundation model research.
papers.title: TaxoSAE: Rethinking Sparse Autoencoders through Taxonomic Logic
papers.tldr: TaxoSAE organizes sparse autoencoder features according to taxonomies, improving taxonomically consistent knowledge readout and precise concept-level control in LLMs.

papers.abstract: Covariate-aware time series foundation models (TSFMs) accept a future path for a control variable and return a forecast, inviting what-if queries. The query is interventional; the models are trained on observational data. We determine whether their answers are the conditional slope $\partial E[Y|X]$ or the interventional effect $\partial E[Y|do(X)]$, at three levels. Theory: a Bayes-optimal observational predictor answers interventional queries associationally unless the adjustment set is available and used; for in-context least squares we derive the resulting confounding gap -- a model's effect estimate under an observational minus under a randomized context -- in closed form, a parameter-free reference line. Behaviour: on a preregistered grid with exact counterfactual ground truth, Chronos-2, TiRex-2, TabPFN-TS and TimesFM-2.5 all track this line ($R^2$ 0.90-1.00) and respond more confounded than regression itself (slopes 1.3-1.8), on linear and nonlinear structural models. Pairs of models with identical observational laws prove this is not an identifiability limit: when the effect is identifiable, least squares recovers 100% of the true effect difference, Chronos-2 75%, TiRex-2 34%. Representation: linear probes decode the data-generating regime (94-96%) and the true effect ($R^2$ 0.7-0.9) from embeddings that the forecasts ignore. On two physical systems with randomized actuators, pretrained models under-respond by 2-5x and ignore in-window confounding. Minutes of interventional post-training on 3,000 synthetic series cut the gap by up to 83% and transfer outside the training prior. Its forecasting cost is a replay-distribution effect: replaying the model's own pretraining prior cuts it from +47% to +10% MASE, and with low-rank adaptation yields a recipe meeting the preregistered criterion over three seeds (52-61% gap reduction at +1-3% cost) while improving the DoTime benchmark.
bullets: Theory predicts that observationally trained predictors answer what-if queries associationally unless they use an appropriate adjustment set.
Chronos-2, TiRex-2, TabPFN-TS, and TimesFM-2.5 closely follow the predicted confounding pattern across linear and nonlinear systems.
The models’ embeddings contain information about the causal regime and true effects that their forecasts fail to use; randomized physical-system tests show 2–5× under-response.
Minutes of interventional post-training reduce the causal gap by up to 83%; low-rank adaptation achieves 52–61% reduction at 1–3% extra cost and improves DoTime.
Scope: findings concern covariate-aware TSFMs evaluated on synthetic structural models and two physical systems with randomized actuators.

figures.caption: Figure 7. Causal Chambers. An associational predictor has slope 1 (least squares, V1), an adjusting one slope 0 (least squares, V2). Pretrained models have slope ≈ 0 at every visibility and a response one third to one half of the identified effect: they ignore the covariate rather than adjust for it. (b) Response scale on both systems: on the light tunnel the post-trained model overshoots by 1.6–2.1×.

The identity line is in-context least squares; the horizontal line is a causal predictor. The difference at the first intervened step is the confounding gap, derived in closed form for in-context least squares (Proposition 1). papers.abstract: Synthetic rewrites, where a language model rewrites a natural document e.g. into a target style, are now a standard ingredient of pretraining corpora. However, critical aspects of their use remain poorly understood, such as how much compute should be spent rewriting training data and whether a model trained on rewrites can outperform the rewriter. We study these two questions by proposing a rewriting scaling law that predicts loss from model size, training tokens, the fraction of training tokens that are rewrites, and the number of epochs over the natural data, charging the compute spent generating rewrites. We fit this scaling law in two settings. In the compute-limited setting, natural data is plentiful and rewrites come from a third-party rewriter trained with more compute than our largest run. We find that the estimated optimal rewrite fraction increases with compute, from under $10\%$ at $3\times10^{18}$ FLOPs to $32\%$ at $10^{22}$ FLOPs. Our scaling forecast extrapolates $33\times$ in FLOPs to train a 22B-parameter model, whose final loss is within $1.1\%$ of our prediction. This model achieves a better BPB than its rewriter on several web domains at one-tenth the rewriter's training compute. In the data-limited setting, we assume we only have a fixed seed set of natural data and that our rewriter is a model of the same size as the target, pretrained on that seed set. Again, we find the optimal rewrite fraction increases with the compute budget. We also demonstrate that a model trained on rewrites of its own pretraining data, generated by a rewriter of the same size, beats the best run on natural data alone at every model size up to 3B. Our results show that synthetic rewriting can be studied through the scaling law lens: that optimal methodological choices are predictable and scaling does not necessarily break down beyond the rewriter's capabilities.
authors: Nicholas Roberts, Ahmed Ahmed, Suhas Kotha, Percy Liang, Yu Wang, Alex Renda, Nitya Mani

Models trained on synthetic rewrites can outperform their rewriters and natural-data-only baselines, including across sizes up to 3B parameters.

papers.abstract: This article provides an introduction to the mathematical foundations and algorithmic frameworks used to align Large Language Models (LLMs) with human intentions, preferences, and values. We discuss standard alignment techniques, such as fine-tuning (SFT), reinforcement learning with human feedback (RLHF), and direct preference optimization (DPO). We also explore the theoretical underpinnings of learning from human preferences, drawing connections to inverse reinforcement learning (IRL) and discrete choice models. We present state-of-the-art algorithms in a tutorial style, discuss their advantages and limitations, and offer insights into practical implementation. Our exposition is intended to serve as a comprehensive resource for researchers and practitioners, providing both a foundational understanding of alignment methodologies and a framework for developing more robust and scalable alignment techniques.

papers.abstract: Intelligent agents should learn from their mistakes so that experience leads to continuous improvement. Yet today's agents recover from a mistake only temporarily: in-context reflections are easily forgotten across sessions and compete for limited context, while full-parameter fine-tuning is expensive and can interfere with existing capabilities. We introduce Self-Direction, a mechanism for agents to learn from mistakes that combines the benefits of temporary in-context retries and policy updates. When an agent fails a task, it reflects on its own trajectory in order to extract a lesson and immediately distills it into a lightweight low-rank adapter. By keeping the original weights frozen, Self-Direction prevents adapter training from overwriting base-model parameters while training additional parameters equivalent to ~0.02% of the base model's parameter count for each adapter. The agent then saves these adapters in a persistent library of lessons, automatically routing them to solve related problems later. Experiments with agents based on open-weight models from the Qwen family across open-ended research (GAIA), tool-use workflows (Claw-Eval), and terminal tasks (Terminal-Bench 2.1) show that our method improves overall success rates by 8.9 to 17.0 percentage points and performs competitively with frontier systems. We find that Self-Direction reduces repeated mistakes across future encounters of a task, nearly doubling the reliability of an agent's corrections. Learned lessons also transfer: a handful of adapters generalize to dozens of new tasks without additional training. Ultimately, this self-directed repair transforms everyday mistakes into lasting lessons.
authors: Yuval Kansal, Karen Ullrich, Polina Kirichenko, Ilia Kulikov, Niraj K. Jha, Mohammad Pezeshki, Mark Ibrahim
bullets: Addresses the limits of temporary in-context reflection and costly, interference-prone full fine-tuning.
After failure, the agent reflects, extracts a lesson, distills it into a lightweight adapter, and stores it in a retrievable lesson library.
Uses frozen base weights with adapters adding about 0.02% of the base model’s parameters each.
Across GAIA, Claw-Eval, and Terminal-Bench 2.1, success rates improve by 8.9–17.0 percentage points.
Lessons reduce repeated mistakes, nearly double correction reliability, and transfer to new tasks without additional training.

papers.selection_reason: Self-directed distillation of mistakes into lightweight persistent adapters directly fits test-time and continual learning plus LLM agent-memory topics.
papers.title: Don't Forget What You Just Learned: Self-Directed Repair Turns Agent Mistakes Into Lasting Lessons
papers.tldr: Self-Direction lets agents turn mistakes into persistent, reusable low-rank adapters, improving future task performance without modifying base-model weights.

papers.abstract: Tool-calling agents are mostly optimized for accuracy; in deployment, however, their growing cost is latency: every tool call is decoded autoregressively. Speculative decoding accelerates this without changing the output, and retrieved past calls make strong drafts under real use, where each user's behavior tends to repeat. Yet existing systems keep no cross-session memory, or build the draft store once and never update it. We propose SpecMem, a tool-call memory kept alive and managed throughout deployment: verified calls are written back online into bounded per-user stores with LRU eviction, and a side-effect gate defers irreversible calls until verification confirms. On multi-session, multi-user query streams served by three open-weight models, a frozen store steadily loses acceptance while SpecMem holds it: a 27% gap in mean accepted tokens (+11% to +34% across benchmarks, tracking how much novel work arrives after the store is built) and up to 1.74x wall-clock speedup. Ablations attribute the gain almost entirely to keeping the store live; local per-user scoping adds no acceptance but closes a measured cross-user leakage channel, and gating on declared side effects, rather than on retrieval confidence, is what eliminates irreversible mistakes.
authors: Zihe Song, Wenting Zhao, Ye Liu, Yuanjie Zhu, Ke Xu, Shanghao Li, Philip S. Yu
bullets: Addresses latency from autoregressive decoding of repeated tool calls, beyond accuracy optimization.
Maintains bounded, per-user call stores online with verified write-back and LRU eviction.
Uses a side-effect gate to defer irreversible calls until speculative drafts are verified.
Across three open-weight models, it improves mean accepted tokens by 27% over frozen stores and reaches up to 1.74× wall-clock speedup.
Live memory drives nearly all gains; per-user scoping prevents measured cross-user leakage without improving acceptance.

figures.caption: Figure 1: A frozen TOOLSPEC-style datastore vs. SPECMEM on a recurring call: user u checked Google’s stock the day before and now asks for Apple’s. Each arm drafts a candidate call for a draft-then-verify decoder over the fixed served model (acceptance = token longest-common-prefix). SPECMEM retrieves u’s own GOOG call, accepted up to the changed ticker (17 of 28 target tokens) with only the remainder decoded; the frozen TOOLSPEC-style store’s stale build-time entry accepts 9, the schema-only draft 7 (full-run MAT 19.96 vs. 15.70 and 5.92). Only the live store writes the verified target back, so its advantage grows across sessions.

Figure 2: Per-session MAT on the BFCL stream (3 seeds). The frozen store and SPECMEM are nearly tied at session 1; the frozen store then degrades while SPECMEM holds and the no-memory floor stays flat.

Figure 3: Per-session MAT on τ2-bench (3 domains, 3 seeds). At session 1 both stores tie near 31 MAT; the frozen TOOLSPEC/static store then degrades into a 20–25 band while SPECMEM holds at 27–32. Right: the advantage over the frozen store grows from ∼1% (session 1) to a peak of ∼37% (session 10; 34% at the final session 11) as novel per-user calls accumulate, an effect a single-session benchmark cannot expose.

Table 2: Wall-clock decode speedup vs. vanilla autoregressive decoding (p50) on TOOLSPEC’s four benchmarks. Bottom rows: MAT for SPECMEM and for a live token-match store at the same footprint (3 seeds).
Table 3: Ablation: post-warmup MAT as each lifecycle component is toggled (full scale, mean±std over 3 seeds).
Table 1: Post-warmup acceptance (sessions 1–11, 3 seeds; per-arm n: BFCL 6,814, Seal-Tools 7,592). Metrics as defined in §4.1; exact rate = draft identical to target.

papers.selection_reason: Live tool-call memory with online updates, LRU eviction, and side-effect gating directly targets LLM agent inference latency and persistent memory.
papers.title: SPECMEM: Accelerating Agentic Tool Calling via Live Memory Management
papers.tldr: SpecMem accelerates agentic tool calling by continuously updating per-user memories for speculative decoding while gating irreversible actions until verification.

papers.abstract: Speculative decoding is a technique that accelerates the inference speed of autoregressive large language models (LLMs) by sampling from a faster, lower quality draft model. Traditionally, a fundamental characteristic of speculative decoding is that it is lossless with respect to the verifier distribution, guaranteeing speed without sacrificing quality. This differs from recently developed diffusion LLMs (dLLMs), which are notably able to achieve substantial speedups by degrading the quality of their outputs with less diffusion effort. Because diffusion models are able to sample faster than autoregressive models by generating tokens in parallel, they are considered strong candidates for draft models in speculative diffusion. While it is widely understood that diffusion models can sacrifice quality for speed, speculative decoding itself can also be generalized to generate lossy samples faster using more lenient acceptance criteria with respect to the verifier distribution. Presented with the two parameters of diffusion effort and speculative decoding leniency, this paper explores the full achievable Pareto frontier via joint variations of these parameters. Our experiments show that jointly varying diffusion effort and acceptance leniency can extend the speed-quality Pareto frontier over single step diffusion drafting.
authors: Aaron Zorel, Guy Van den Broeck, Aditya Grover, Daniel Israel
bullets: Diffusion language models can serve as fast, parallel-generating draft models for speculative decoding.
Unlike traditional lossless speculative decoding, both diffusion effort and acceptance leniency can deliberately trade quality for speed.
The paper maps the achievable speed–quality Pareto frontier by jointly varying these two parameters.
Experiments show joint tuning extends the frontier beyond using single-step diffusion drafting alone.

figures.caption: Figure 5: Comparison of Pareto frontiers. For a single Qwen3 8B verifier, we benchmark several speculative diffusion methods. Each line corresponds to the achievable speed-quality frontier of a specific draft model. Dashed curves fix one diffusion step and vary leniency, while solid curves are varied over diffusion effort and acceptance lenience. For the SDAR models that support multi-step speculative diffusion, varying over the parameters jointly significantly extends the Pareto frontier.

Figure 1: A conceptual overview. Diffusion has a speed-quality tradeoff parameterized by diffusion effort K, while speculative decoding has a speed-quality tradeoff parameterized by acceptance leniency λ. This work argues that speculative diffusion exposes both tradeoffs and therefore reveals optimal configurations that could not be found by varying only a single parameter.

Figure 4: Examples of the Pareto frontier. We provide examples of speculative diffusion for both masked diffusion (left) and uniform diffusion (right). Each point signifies a configuration of acceptance leniency in verification and diffusion effort (K steps) in drafting. We observe the same qualitative trend that the speedquality Pareto frontier is occupied by many different settings of diffusion effort which require different levels of lenience.

Figure 2: Illustrative examples. Left: Visualization of the proof of Theorem 1 shows that the linear interpolated distribution p̃⋆ is the optimal solution to maximize drafter q and verifier p alignment while staying within a constraint on deviation from the verifier ϵ. The solution to this constrained optimization is p̃. Right: A motivating example shows that the speed-quality frontiers independently induced by diffusion effort and acceptance lenience in speculative decoding can occupy separate regions of the Pareto frontier. We compare diffusion only with AR speculative decoding with leniency.

Figure 12: Complete sweeps for Figure 5. Colors distinguish SDAR’s effort settings within each model size. Hollow markers show measured configurations, including dominated points. Thick curves show the joint and fixed-K = 1 frontiers, using the same definitions as the main figure.
Figure 9: Block-size ablation on GSM8K with Dream–Qwen.

Figure 3: A model of speculative diffusion. Theoretical and measured tradeoffs for Dream-7B drafting for Qwen2.5-32B on GSM8K. (a) The theoretical acceptance rate (speed) and verifier agreement (quality) under linear acceptance for each of K diffusion steps per round. (b) Empirically measured acceptance rate for each K. (c) A transformation from acceptance rate to throughput according to a simple model of throughput. (d) Empirically measured throughput.

Figure 7: Latency and throughput on GSM8K with the Dream-7B drafter and Qwen2.5-32B-Instruct verifier

Figure 6: Per-round latency measurements supporting Figure 3. Left: drafting costs and their linear fit in K. Right: the distribution of verifier costs across configurations, with its mean and one-standard-deviation band.
Figure 10: Latency and throughput on HumanEval with the Dream 7B drafter and Qwen2.5 32B verifier.
Figure 11: Latency and throughput on HumanEval with the DiffusionGemma 26B drafter and Gemma4 31B verifier.

Table 2: Hugging Face checkpoints used in the experiments.

papers.selection_reason: Analyzes the tradeoffs between speculative decoding and diffusion models for inference acceleration, providing insights into efficient generation techniques for LLMs.
papers.title: Speculative Diffusion is a Tale of Two Tradeoffs
papers.tldr: Speculative diffusion accelerates LLM inference by jointly tuning diffusion effort and verification leniency to improve the speed–quality tradeoff.

papers.abstract: Mixture-of-experts (MoE) transformers, the standard backbone for modern large-scale deep learning, employ conditional computation: only a sparse subset of model weights is used in each forward pass. In MoE transformers, this sparsity arises in the MoE operator, which generalizes the multi-layer perceptron in the classical transformer. In this work, we explore an alternative mechanism for conditional computation that analogously generalizes the attention operator. The sparsity induced by this mechanism naturally nests (i.e., hierarchically composes) with the sparsity induced by the MoE operator. We show that a transformer employing this nested sparsity mechanism, which we call Nestor, performs better than a conventional MoE transformer at equal compute and equal sparsity in language model pretraining. We also show that Nestor is well-suited for continual pretraining: it can be adapted to longer contexts more effectively than conventional MoEs, as well as adapt more efficiently to new domains while forgetting less on old domains. Furthermore, we demonstrate that these benefits persist as model size, dataset size, and context length grow. Our results demonstrate the potential of alternative conditional computation mechanisms for deep neural network architectures. Code and checkpoints are available on GitHub at https://github.com/Ma-Lab-Berkeley/Nestor .
authors: Tianzhe Chu, Druv Pai, Yi Ma
bullets: Introduces an alternative conditional-computation mechanism that generalizes attention and naturally nests with MoE sparsity.
Outperforms conventional MoE transformers at equal compute and sparsity during language-model pretraining.
Adapts more effectively to longer contexts and new domains during continual pretraining.
Forgets less about previously learned domains while adapting to new ones.
Benefits persist as model size, dataset size, and context length increase.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Nested sparsity in NESTOR. (a) The NESTOR architecture. In each block, the column router sends the token xj to Kc = 2 of the C = 4 columns. The free parameters are counted below each panel.
