papers.selection_reason: Introduces 'Nestor', a transformer architecture with nested sparsity for scalable pretraining and continual learning, offering a transferable technical contribution to efficient model architectures.
papers.title: Nested Sparsity for Scalable Pretraining and Continual Learning
papers.tldr: Nestor adds hierarchical sparsity to the attention mechanism alongside MoE sparsity, improving scalable pretraining and continual learning.

papers.abstract: A bug report describes what went wrong, but rarely where the code should change. Existing repository-level localization methods often let language models iteratively decide what code to inspect next, requiring repeated model calls and substantial token usage. We investigate whether these inspection decisions can instead be planned before source retrieval. In this research, we introduce CuraLoc, which first selects candidate files and represents their symbols using compact behavioral and structural descriptions. In a single planning decision, the model jointly selects starting symbols, chooses code relationships to inspect from each, and forms hypotheses about likely edits. Deterministic retrieval collects the requested source for a final ranking informed by those hypotheses, concentrating model reasoning on choosing and comparing code rather than directing each retrieval step. We demonstrate the efficacy of our proposed approach on the SWE-Bench Lite and Verified datasets. On SWE Bench Verified with GPT-5.2, CuraLoc raises Func@1 from LocAgent's 53.8% to 59.3% while using 90.3% fewer recorded tokens, and also outperforms RepoSearcher (56.2%) and Agentless (39.6%) on Func@1. On SWE-bench Lite, CuraLoc achieves a high 83.8% Func@5 accuracy improving on Agentless by more than 15% in relative accuracy. Additionally, CuraLoc supports different model backbones, with strong localization accuracy demonstrated using both GPT-5.2 and GPT-6 Astra. These results provide evidence that repository-level code inspection can be planned effectively without iterative model-controlled navigation.
authors: Sangeeta Warrier, Anush Sankaran, Ryen White
bullets: Targets the high cost and repeated model calls of language-model-driven repository navigation.
Selects candidate files, summarizes symbols behaviorally and structurally, and makes one joint plan for symbols, code relationships, and likely edits.
Uses deterministic retrieval to gather requested source, then ranks locations using the planned hypotheses.
On SWE-bench Verified with GPT-5.2, improves Func@1 from LocAgent’s 53.8% to 59.3% while reducing recorded tokens by 90.3%.
Achieves 83.8% Func@5 on SWE-bench Lite and supports multiple model backbones, including GPT-5.2 and GPT-6 Astra.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes a method for planning code inspection to reduce token usage in LLMs, a transferable technical idea for improving efficiency in LLM-based agents.
papers.title: CuraLoc: Repository-Level Fault Localization via Planned Code Inspection
papers.tldr: CuraLoc plans repository code inspection upfront, achieving stronger fault localization with far fewer recorded tokens than iterative approaches.

papers.abstract: Scientific computing increasingly relies on large language model-based agents for performance engineering tasks such as instrumentation, analysis, and workflow porting. However, agent effectiveness depends heavily on the surrounding harness, which typically relies on manually written skills and curated memory. This limits autonomous learning, forcing agents to repeatedly rediscover solutions rather than retain and reuse knowledge from prior executions. We introduce Phronix, a capability-centric learning paradigm that enables agentic harnesses to acquire, validate, and refine reusable capabilities from their own executions. Phronix operates through a predictor-validator-corrector loop: MCP tools and associated skills propose solutions, tool executions validate them, and observed outcomes refine the stored capabilities. It distills every observed interaction into a capability store and researches a failing task rather than abandoning it. First, such learned capabilities solve a recurring task on the first attempt in 93-95% of cases across every model, significantly reducing solution non-determinism and improving reliability. Second, Phronix turns an agent's own execution into 7.6-30.8 durable capabilities per task without user instruction, and creation falls below two once the needed capability exists. Third, warm-start runs consume only 0.38-0.40 million tokens per task, which is three to four times less than a single baseline attempt, while a cold-start costs no more than the baseline. On the 1000 Genome Pegasus workflow, instrumenting a production application for I/O performance analysis, Phronix passes all 11 correctness checks against six for the baseline harness, and also lifts the task solving rates of two cheaper models from 29% and 27% of SWE-bench tasks solved to 91% and 87%, respectively, matching the performance of the most expensive evaluated model.
authors: Hariharan Devarajan, Neeraj Rajesh, Aniruddha Marathe, Nikoli Dryden, Kin Ng, Michela Taufer
bullets: Addresses the reliance on manually authored skills and curated memory, which causes agents to repeatedly rediscover solutions.
Uses a predictor–validator–corrector loop: tools and skills propose solutions, executions validate them, and outcomes refine a persistent capability store.
Learned capabilities solve recurring tasks on the first attempt in 93–95% of cases across evaluated models.
Each task produces 7.6–30.8 durable capabilities without user instruction; once capabilities exist, creation drops below two per task.
Warm-start execution uses 0.38–0.40 million tokens per task, and Phronix improves correctness and task-solving rates on evaluated workflows and models.

papers.selection_reason: Agent harness that learns, validates, and stores reusable capabilities from executions directly matches continual agent learning and persistent agent-memory topics.
papers.title: Phronix: The Capability-Centric Learning Paradigm for Agents
papers.tldr: Phronix lets agents learn reusable capabilities from their own executions, substantially improving reliability, efficiency, and performance across recurring tasks.

papers.abstract: Long horizon agentic tasks are now pushing LLM agents past their context window. To continue the task, the agent scaffold has to free up the context window, a process known as context compaction. Compaction is generally lossy by design: agents can silently lose task constraints, instructions, or their reasoning behind earlier decisions. Although compaction is a standard component of coding agent scaffolds, it has not been studied systematically with frontier models on realistic, long horizon agentic tasks. Previous work evaluate smaller open weight models on toy or synthetic trajectories. We fix the agent scaffold (OpenCode), implement five compaction strategies inside it, and evaluate three frontier models on three long horizon benchmarks (PaperBench, ProgramBench, PostTrainBench). For the two 1M context models, the compaction threshold does not measurably affect the task performance, whereas GPT-5.3-Codex, the model with the smallest context window, performs worse at lower thresholds on PaperBench and, less clearly, on PostTrainBench. No compaction method outperforms default self-summarization, and methods that discard more content cost some models up to 20 points while leaving other models the same. Compaction can, however, silently remove task constraints: on ProgramBench, the first compaction summary already drops about one third of the task's anticheating rules on average, and this rises monotonically with the number of compactions. On real user-agent sessions from SWE-chat, instructions about how the agent should work and what it should not do are dropped around 6 times more than specifications of what to build. We argue that current benchmarks are compaction-friendly: i.e., the objective is fixed and the agent's progress stays on disk, so most of what compaction discards can be recovered, except constraints that don't exist anywhere else.
authors: Jeanne Salle, Hardik Bhatnagar, Matthias Bethge, Sahar Abdelnabi, Maksym Andriushchenko
bullets: Context compaction is evaluated systematically in a fixed OpenCode scaffold across five strategies, three frontier models, and three long-horizon benchmarks.
For models with 1M-token contexts, changing the compaction threshold does not measurably affect performance; the smallest-context model degrades at lower thresholds on some tasks.
Default self-summarization performs best overall; more aggressive content removal can reduce some models’ performance substantially while leaving others unchanged.

Compaction summaries increasingly omit constraints: the first summary drops roughly one-third of ProgramBench anticheating rules on average, and procedural instructions are lost far more often than build specifications in real sessions.
The benchmarks are described as “compaction-friendly” because objectives and progress remain recoverable on disk; unrepeated constraints are most vulnerable.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Compaction keeps what the agent can re-read from disk and drops some of the rules it cannot. Left: overview of a ProgramBench run. The task prompt states the goal and anti-cheating rules: no copying or vendoring the reference, no internet access, and an original implementation that does not derive from or wrap the reference. At each compaction the agent replaces its context with a summary. The goal and the agent’s progress survive, because the agent can re-read its files, the rules exist only in the context, so a rule the summary discards is lost. On average, around one of the three rules is missing after the first compaction and around two after the tenth. Right: (1) for the 1M context models, task scores barely change when compaction is forced at thresholds from 160K to 380K tokens; (2) rules are dropped more often as compactions accumulate on ProgramBench, and on real user sessions from SWE-chat, compaction drops process instructions (“how to work”) and scope exclusions (“don’t touch X”) far more often than feature requirements (“what to build”).
Figure 3: Accuracy conditional on producing a valid submission by compaction method, for each benchmark (rows) and model (columns), at a fixed compaction threshold (160K).

Figure 2: The compaction threshold does not affect 1M context models; GPT-5.3-Codex performs worse at lower thresholds on PaperBench. Accuracy conditional on producing a valid submission as a function of the number of tokens before compaction, for each benchmark (columns) and model. All models are run at the same absolute compaction thresholds. Error bars are bootstrap 95% confidence intervals over runs.

Figure 4: Compaction preferentially drops constraints about how the agent should work and what it should not do. (a) On ProgramBench, the task’s anti-cheating rules disappear from the summaries progressively over a run. (b) On real user-agent sessions, process instructions and scope exclusions are dropped much more than feature requirements.

Figure 7: Failure rate by compaction strategy. Fraction of runs in which the agent failed to produce a valid result, for ProgramBench and PostTrainBench, per model. For each task, the failure rate is the number of failures divided by the number of attempts; bars corresponds to the mean over tasks, so every task has equal weight (ProgramBench: Canop/broot and jarun/nnn; PostTrainBench: GPQA, GSM8K and BFCL, each on two base models). Error bars are bootstrap 95% confidence intervals. Runs were launched until enough succeeded, so the number of attempts per task differs across tasks and conditions. Pooling all attempts would weight each task by how often it was retried, and since harder tasks fail more and are rerun more, this would inflate the weight of exactly the tasks that fail most. We therefore compute each rate per task and average, so that every task contributes equally and strategies are compared on the same task mix. Tasks with few attempts will thus have noisier rates, which the bootstrap intervals reflect. All runs were obtained at a fixed compaction thresholds (160K tokens before triggering compaction).

Figure 8: Number of compactions as a function of the compaction threshold. Average number of compactions per run for each model, in the baseline condition (self-summarization).

Figure 11: Per-category drop rate under two LLM judges (Claude Sonnet 5 and GPT-5.6 Sol), using each judge’s majority verdict over three runs. The categorization is fixed. Error bars are Wilsonscore 95% confidence intervals. Dashed lines correspond to each judge’s overall drop rate. Hatched bars indicate categories containing fewer than 10 samples. However, Gemini 3.1 Pro Preview rarely compacts (see Appendix 6.8). Figure 8 shows that on average it compacts once per run at the 160K threshold. So the above results are not informative about the effects of compaction.

papers.selection_reason: Studies context compaction for LLM agents and constraint loss; relevant to agent memory and long-horizon context management.
papers.title: Benchmarks Are Surprisingly Compaction-Friendly
papers.tldr: Current long-horizon agent benchmarks often tolerate lossy context compaction, but compaction can silently discard unrecoverable task constraints.

papers.abstract: Muon has become a popular optimizer for large language model training, yet its theoretical foundations remain poorly understood. In this work, we study how gradient noise geometry shapes Muon's preconditioning benefits. We first show, theoretically and empirically, that under the classical isotropic noise assumption, Muon offers no acceleration beyond a rescaling of the learning rate. This motivates us to investigate structured noise arising from mini-batch sampling in associative memory with heterogeneous task frequencies. We establish an exact balancing threshold for two tasks and extend the analysis to multiple tasks, revealing how task coverage and gradient reliability jointly shape learning. Our analysis shows that Muon can soften the dependence on task frequency from linear to square-root, helping balance the learning of frequent and rare tasks. We further identify rotation-induced negative transfer in SignSGD that Muon avoids, and explain how momentum reduces sampling noise while tracking changing gradients. Controlled numerical experiments validate these mechanisms, and a preliminary LLM pretraining study illustrates the practical promise of fast-slow momentum.
authors: Xiaoran Chen, Binghui Li, Liwei Wang, Pinyan Lu
bullets: Under isotropic gradient noise, Muon provides no acceleration beyond learning-rate rescaling.
For heterogeneous task frequencies, Muon changes task-frequency dependence from linear to square-root scaling.
The analysis derives an exact two-task balancing threshold and extends to multiple tasks based on coverage and gradient reliability.
Muon avoids rotation-induced negative transfer identified in SignSGD, while momentum reduces sampling noise and tracks changing gradients.
Controlled experiments support the theory, and a preliminary LLM pretraining study suggests promise for fast-slow momentum.

Right: the full conditional-mean matrix remains within a few percent of the scalar-response prediction over the tested low-SNR amplitudes.

Left: Muon preserves support, so the rare-task margin remains nonnegative and grows on its occurrence clock. (b) Late-time stationary standard deviation of the gap versus B; the fitted exponent is −0.531, compared with the B−1/2 diffusion prediction.

(b) RMS contrast-to-average coupling versus expected task count Bp̃µ/C; the fitted log–log slope is −0.512, matching the predicted −1/2. papers.selection_reason: Provides a theoretical analysis of the Muon optimizer's preconditioning benefits in the context of large language model training, addressing a key architectural and training question.
papers.title: When and How Does Muon Precondition? The Role of Structured Gradient Noise
papers.tldr: Muon’s preconditioning benefits arise from structured, rather than isotropic, gradient noise and can improve balance between frequent and rare tasks.

papers.abstract: This article introduces Latin Modern BERT (LAMB), an encoder for the Latin language based on the ModernBERT architecture, pretrained in two phases on more than 74B Latin tokens using a novel morphologically informed masking regimen. We also present two corpora for the Latin language. Acervus contains 24B BERT WordPiece tokens, including over 760K samples from heavily damaged OCR transcriptions, repaired by a ByT5 model trained for Latin text repair. The second dataset, Corpus Trinum, contains a mixture of over 100M strong and weak Latin language semantic triplets. Corpus Trinum is the first Latin semantic triplet dataset, opening the door for Latin language models to be adapted to general sentence semantic similarity tasks. We construct an experimental grid using five tasks and seventeen subtasks, applying a variety of finetuning configurations and subword aggregation techniques for 15 pretrained encoders, 6 LAMB training checkpoints, and an ablation model designed to quantify the impact of different masking regimens. Using this benchmark, we rank Latin encoders and find that LAMB outperforms all other evaluated models on 16 of 17 subtasks, coming within 0.8 percentage points of state of the art on the seventeenth. We provide additional analyses relating Latin encoder performance to tokenizer behavior, syntactic structure, finetuning configuration, pretraining state, subword aggregation, and variation in source texts and domains. In these, we identify unique acquisition dynamics for Latin open class words during terminal decay phases, and establish that for some task categories, finetuning configuration selection can have a greater effect on downstream scores than additional pretraining tokens.
bullets: Pretrained in two phases on more than 74B Latin tokens using a morphologically informed masking strategy.
Introduces Acervus, a 24B-token corpus incorporating repaired OCR text, and Corpus Trinum, a 100M+ semantic-triplet dataset.
Evaluated across five tasks and 17 subtasks, with varied checkpoints, finetuning settings, and subword aggregation methods.
Outperforms all other evaluated encoders on 16 of 17 subtasks and approaches state of the art on the remaining task.
Analyses examine tokenizer behavior, syntax, pretraining, finetuning, subword aggregation, and domain variation.

papers.abstract: Mobile GUI agents frequently perform repetitive tasks with similar interaction procedures. Reusing previous executions can reduce redundant LLM inference and execution overhead, but variations in user instructions and execution environments may invalidate previously successful actions. We systematically characterize these variations into six representative categories and observe that such changes do not necessarily invalidate entire procedures: individual transitions can remain reusable when validated against the current task context and interface state. Based on this insight, we propose graph-text templates for selective execution-trace reuse. The graph captures UI states and action transitions, while the text encodes task intent, procedural structure, and typed slots for variable content. A record-template-replay framework constructs templates from verified executions and leverages the current instruction and live UI state to reuse, adapt, or discard individual transitions. Given an execution trace, our framework reduces LLM inference token consumption by approximately 80% on average across five base agents on AndroidWorld, with most agents achieving at least 1.5-fold execution speedup over LLM-only execution. In real-device evaluations on Android and HarmonyOS, our framework achieves action reuse ratios of 70.7-79.8% while maintaining over 2-fold execution speedup in most evaluated configurations.
authors: Bingyu Bai, Cheng Zhang, Erhu Feng
bullets: Addresses how instruction and environment changes can invalidate previously successful GUI execution traces.
Represents reusable traces with UI-state/action graphs plus text for task intent, procedure structure, and variable slots.
Uses a record-template-replay process to validate each transition against the current instruction and live UI state.
Reduces LLM inference token consumption by about 80% on average across five agents on AndroidWorld, with most achieving at least 1.5× speedup.
Real-device tests on Android and HarmonyOS reuse 70.7–79.8% of actions while delivering over 2× speedup in most configurations.

papers.abstract: Machine learning (ML) is increasingly used in astronomy, but choosing a suitable method for a scientific problem often requires expertise in both astronomy and ML. Large language models (LLMs) could help astronomers make such choices, yet this ability remains underexplored in existing benchmarks. We introduce Astro2Method, a benchmark of 500 expert-reviewed binary questions from 346 astronomy papers (2024/01-2026/06), based on clear performance differences and complete (Easy) or partial (Hard) explanations from the authors. Across five LLMs, direct prompting achieves 87.50-92.55% accuracy on Easy questions but only 58.87-64.52% on Hard. Using historical papers, neither retrieval-augmented generation nor most agent methods with additional reasoning or retrieval (including ReAct, Self-Ask, and CRITIC) bring consistent improvement. Agents required to search the web improve accuracy mainly when they find the papers the questions are based on, with no consistent improvement otherwise. Providing the source paper's pipeline description with method names masked improves Hard accuracy, matching or exceeding web search. Together, these results suggest that relevant experimental information helps distinguish ML methods, but inferring it from related studies and domain knowledge remains challenging for LLMs in astronomy.
authors: Xingzhong Fan, Hangfeng He, Fatemeh Nargesian
bullets: Benchmarks ML-method selection with 500 expert-reviewed binary questions from 346 astronomy papers.
Direct prompting reaches 87.50–92.55% accuracy on Easy questions versus 58.87–64.52% on Hard questions.
Retrieval-augmented generation and most agent approaches do not consistently improve performance.
Web-search agents help mainly when they locate the source papers; masked pipeline descriptions can match or exceed web search on Hard questions.
Relevant experimental information is important, but inferring it from related work and domain knowledge remains difficult.

papers.abstract: Long chain-of-thought decoding is memory-bound: the KV cache of the generated tokens grows linearly with the test-time compute being spent. Evicting cache entries does not fix this, because a model never trained on a cache with entries removed generates longer, often up to the length limit. We instead train the model to compress its own output. AbridgeKV compresses each completed block of generated text into the KV entries of a few learned pause tokens. These are extra input tokens with trained embeddings that produce no output. Once the pause tokens have encoded the block, AbridgeKV frees the block's original cache; subsequent tokens attend to the pause tokens' KV entries in its place. Three novel choices make this work: the pause tokens' KV entries take positions inside the block they replace, the cache budget is allocated across layers according to the measured value of each layer's entries, and compression operates on relatively large blocks. On 446 competition problems from AIME, HMMT, AMC, BRUMO, CMIMC and SMT with 32K-token generations, keeping a quarter of the generated cache matches an identically trained full-KV model in accuracy and output length; the strongest published evictor at a matched budget writes far longer, and the closest trained compressor, retrained on the same data, loses 10 points. Served in vLLM, the cache is 3.5x smaller per sequence and a saturated H100 finishes a problem 3.2x faster than with full KV.
bullets: Addresses the linear KV-cache growth caused by long chain-of-thought decoding.
Compresses completed text blocks into a few learned pause tokens, then frees the blocks’ original cache entries.
Uses in-block pause-token positions, layer-wise cache allocation based on entry value, and relatively large compression blocks.
On 446 competition problems with 32K-token generations, one-quarter of the generated cache matched an identically trained full-KV model in accuracy and output length.
In vLLM, it reduced cache size 3.5× per sequence and improved saturated-H100 problem completion speed 3.2× versus full KV.

papers.selection_reason: Training learned pause tokens to compress long reasoning into a much smaller KV cache is a direct contribution to memory-efficient LLM inference and persistent memory.
papers.title: AbridgeKV: Compressing Long Reasoning into the KV Cache of Learned Pause Tokens
papers.tldr: AbridgeKV compresses long reasoning into learned pause-token KV entries, reducing cache use while preserving performance and speeding inference.

papers.abstract: Looped LMs are parameter efficient and promise dynamic computation (saving memory and FLOPs on easy tokens). However, state-of-the-art open Looped LMs trained with this dynamic computation capability (Ouro models) do not realize it in practice as each loop iteration (depth) requires its own level of KV-cache, necessitating all loop computations. Moreover, Ouro's early-exit prior is enforced on each token equally, which results in static lower-depth like processing of all tokens regardless of difficulty. In this work, we propose a simple "best-available" KV caching strategy that works out-of-the-box, creating a new frontier in the performance vs depth space. Our approach enables up to 30% reduction in FLOPs and KV memory while retaining full-depth performance, showing the true flexibility of Looped LMs. Furthermore, training looped LMs with awareness about this KV caching strategy improves performance and efficiency. Finally, we apply a small but effective fix to the early-exit prior enforcement objective that makes tokens exit at truly heterogeneous depths based on effort. Our findings are validated on Ouro models as well as smaller looped LMs pre-trained from scratch.
bullets: Existing Ouro Looped LMs require KV-cache storage for every loop depth, forcing all loop computations despite supporting dynamic computation.
The proposed “best-available” KV caching strategy enables up to 30% lower FLOPs and KV memory without losing full-depth performance.
Training with awareness of this caching strategy further improves efficiency and performance.
A revised early-exit objective produces heterogeneous token depths based on token difficulty rather than uniform shallow processing.
Results are validated on Ouro models and smaller looped LMs pretrained from scratch.

figures.caption: Figure 2: (First row) Exit depth distribution of pre-trained Ouro models: predominantly depth 2/3 depending on the threshold τ , illustrating the lack of true dynamic exits due to local prior enforcement. Noticeably, depth 1 exits are non-existent. (Second row) Jump rate fractions. A high majority of tokens do not jump around and exit at similar depths as their neighbors. Even when they do, they typically only jump one depth up or down. Large jumps (|ei − ei−1| ≥ 2) rarely happen. These numbers undermine the claims of dynamic computation based on difficulty in Ouro models.

Figure 3: To enable early-exit, Ouro models are trained with a KL divergence term (w.r.t a uniform prior) over all tokens equally. This causes the same local pressure on all tokens regardless of difficulty, and makes the policy learn similar high entropy distributions. Our fix: enforce the KL to prior w.r.t the global expected exit distribution across tokens. On the right, we show that this simple fix creates confident (low-entropy), difficulty-aware exits per token while maintaining low KL with the prior (P: Poisson, G: Geometric, U: Uniform) overall. The exits are truly heterogeneous as evident by the large jump rates (|ei − ei−1| ≥ 2).

Figure 1: Ouro forces full-depth computation even after a token exits, as future tokens may need it. This makes early-exit practically useless. Ragged KV enables true early-exit by aliasing deeper blocks to the best-available cache. It avoids forced computation and saves memory+FLOPs during inference. Surprisingly, it works out-of-the-box for Ouro models! On the right, we compare fixeddepth (1-4 loops) with Ragged KV at different exit thresholds on BigBenchHard (details in §E.1). Ragged KV unlocks significantly higher performance at low average decode depths.

Figure 12: global prior enforcement produces visibly heterogeneous hard exits. True RaggedKV prefill at τ = 0.5 for the final 20B models (Poisson prior). Each column shows the first of five matched held-out 2,048-token sequences for one prior; the local and global rows within a column receive exactly the same tokens. Colored points are individual hard exit depths and the black curve is their 128-token rolling mean. A large jump is an adjacent pair with an absolute harddepth change of at least two, |ei − ei−1| ≥ 2]: 3→ 2 is not a large jump, while 3→ 1 and 1→ 4 are. global traces have large-jump rates of 19.2%, 20.9%, and 13.2% for Poisson, Geometric, and Uniform priors, respectively, versus 0.2%, 2.5%, and 1.9% for the paired local traces. And we can see that the low depth tokens in global are actually placed meaningfully according to difficulty (commas, spaces, semicolons, simple words that follow obviously, etc).
Figure 7: With a simple β-schedule, looped model pre-training collapses to a fixed-depth-1 like behavior. The model processes inputs in the first loop and then acts like identity in the next 3 loops.

papers.title: Enabling Dynamic Computation in Looped LMs
papers.tldr: A practical KV-cache strategy and improved early-exit training make Looped LMs dynamically allocate computation, reducing costs while preserving full-depth performance.

papers.abstract: Test-time language models adapt a compact memory while processing the input sequence. This perspective encompasses nonlinear fast-weight learning in LaCT, associative delta-rule updates in DeltaNet, and generalized delta-rule state updates in RWKV-7. Training these models to predict the next token does not explicitly require a fact to remain accessible after many subsequent memory updates. We study delayed supervision for this test-time memory: during post-training, ask a simulator-grounded question only after a long interval of unrelated events, and supervise its answer alongside ordinary next-token prediction. Questions are evaluated on disposable branches, so their answers never enter the continuing event stream. The construction distinguishes retention from revision: a retained fact must remain valid throughout the delay, whereas a revised fact must be answered with its latest value. We evaluate this approach on LaCT-760M and plain DeltaNet-1.3B using TextWorld training trajectories and shared BABILong and RULER evaluation panels, and include a separately reported RWKV-7 comparison. Relative to event-only training, delayed QA improves BABILong by 5.48 percentage points for LaCT and 1.32 points for DeltaNet, and single-needle RULER by 1.45 and 3.27 points, respectively. The RWKV-7 comparison reports gains of 4.60 and 7.00 points on its own panels. These results support delayed semantic supervision as a practical outer training objective for usable test-time memory, while leaving open how much of the benefit derives specifically from delay rather than general question-answering and answer-termination supervision.
bullets: Targets a gap in next-token training: facts need not remain accessible after many memory updates.
Supervises simulator-grounded QA after long delays, using disposable branches so answers do not alter the event stream.
Separately tests retention of unchanged facts and revision to a fact’s latest value.
Improves BABILong and single-needle RULER performance for LaCT and DeltaNet; a separately reported RWKV-7 comparison also shows gains.
The study does not isolate how much improvement comes from delay versus general QA and answer-termination supervision.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Original, event-NTP, and delayed-QA scores. The gain over NTP is positive on both reported benchmarks for each backbone. RWKV-7 (*) is a separately reported comparison on different length panels; its original-model result is unavailable.

Figure 3: BABILong by context length on the shared panel, with 500 examples per point. LaCT improves consistently over event NTP; DeltaNet’s gains are concentrated at the longer evaluated lengths. Curves show one trained checkpoint per condition, not averages over seeds.

Only the branch’s answer and EOS receive auxiliary cross-entropy targets. The main trajectory continues without seeing that answer. papers.selection_reason: Delayed supervision for test-time memory in language models directly addresses inference-time adaptation and persistent LLM memory mechanisms.
papers.title: Delayed Supervision for Test-Time Language Models
papers.tldr: Delayed question-answer supervision improves test-time language models’ ability to retain and revise facts across long sequences of unrelated events.

papers.abstract: Interpretability research on large language models has produced accounts of factual recall in feed-forward layers and of token relationships in self-attention, but little work offers a unified way to compare the causal contribution of different architecture components to a model's output. We introduce MechaTerp (the Mechanistic Interpretability suite) -TRACE (subset for Teacher-forced Registry of Ablated Component Effects), an architecture and study that measures how much each registered component of a language model supports the production of a named entity. TRACE ablates one component at a time and measures the resulting change in the output distribution at a fixed answer token, so component types from whole transformer blocks down to individual neurons and output logits can be compared on a common scale. We apply it to thirteen instruction-tuned dense decoder models spanning five families and one to thirty billion parameters, ablating 49,656 components across 48 medical and 42 general-knowledge prompts. We find that the components carrying the most effect are the same few, positionally fixed components in every model, regardless of which entity a prompt asks about, and that once these are removed, the remaining support is close to evenly spread in eleven of the thirteen models. Apparent localisation of entity knowledge is therefore largely attributable to generic generation machinery, which has direct consequences for methods that assume entity knowledge sits in a findable place, including targeted knowledge editing.
bullets: Addresses the lack of a common method for comparing causal contributions across language-model components.
Ablates one registered component at a time and measures changes in the output distribution at a fixed answer token.
Enables comparison from whole transformer blocks to individual neurons and output logits on a shared scale.
Applied across 13 instruction-tuned dense decoder models, covering five families and 1–30 billion parameters, with medical and general-knowledge prompts.

The most influential components are positionally fixed across models and entities; after removing them, support is nearly evenly distributed in 11 of 13 models, challenging assumptions behind targeted knowledge editing.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Median block/lane LLI (Eq. 4) by model and component lane, before floor removal (raw), split by domain. Shown as a cross-lane diagnostic: floor removal is validated and applied only at the block lane (Fig. 2 and Table 1), so the raw values here illustrate where effect concentrates architecturally prior to correction and should not be read as the corrected localization result. Blank cells denote lanes absent from that model’s architecture. Sub-figure A shows results for medical prompt subset and sub-figure B shows results for general-knowledge prompt subset.

Figure 2: Block-lane effective support (Neff/B ′, Eq. 4) after hard removal of generation-floor components (Eq. 10), ranked across the 13-model cohort. Lower values indicate more localized entity support (few components carry the effect); higher values indicate distributed support. Once structurallyfixed always-on components are removed, all models but MediPhi-Clinical and Qwen3-1.7B fall toward the distributed pole, indicating that raw concentration is largely attributable to generic generation machinery rather than entity-specific processing. papers.selection_reason: Component-level causal ablation across LLM families, relevant to understanding architecture components and knowledge localization.
papers.title: MechaTerp-TRACE: A Novel Approach for Component Ablation Analysis in Language Models
papers.tldr: MechaTerp-TRACE provides a unified causal framework for comparing how model components affect named-entity generation, finding that apparent entity-knowledge localization often reflects generic generation machinery.

papers.abstract: Standard tokenizers used in large language models produce malformed text when applied to Brahmic scripts. They are a family of abugidas, writing systems whose consonants carry an inherent vowel that dependent marks can modify. They include Devanagari, Telugu, Tamil, Kannada, and others. The underlying issue is that these tokenizers violate orthographic constraints that do not arise in alphabetic scripts like English. We observe that while English orthography forms a \emph{semigroup} (any two valid tokens can be freely concatenated), Brahmic orthography forms a \emph{partial semigroup}: not every concatenation yields a valid string. We formalise this distinction in Agda, model valid Brahmic tokens as chains in a transition system, and derive a provably correct \texttt{fixToken} function that extends any candidate token to respect orthographic boundaries. We then show how this formal derivation translates into a practical patch for SentencePiece as well as a standalone Rust-based pre-tokenizer library, eliminating the observed errors across Indic scripts.
bullets: Standard LLM tokenizers can produce malformed text for Brahmic abugidas because they ignore script-specific orthographic constraints.
Brahmic token concatenation is modeled as a partial semigroup, unlike the freely composable tokens assumed for English.
The authors formalize valid tokens as chains in a transition system using Agda.
They derive a provably correct `fixToken` function and implement it in SentencePiece and a standalone Rust pre-tokenizer.
The approach eliminates the observed tokenization errors across the Indic scripts studied; the abstract does not report quantitative results.

figures.caption: Figure 1. Valid transitions between Brahmic character classes. Edges represent the constructor names in the Agda formalisation (e.g., the edge Consonant → Virama corresponds to DeadConsonant).
Table 1. Decomposition of the Telugu syllable cluster (vijñā). Characters marked No are dependent, they cannot begin a valid token.

papers.selection_reason: Formal analysis and correction of tokenization for Brahmic scripts, relevant to LLM tokenizer and architecture design.
papers.title: Type-Driven Tokenization for Brahmic Scripts
papers.tldr: A formally verified tokenizer design enforces valid orthographic boundaries in Brahmic scripts and removes malformed-token errors across Indic scripts.

papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) depend fundamentally on the diversity, depth, and factual rigor of their pre-training corpora. However, contemporary foundational pre-training datasets (such as The Pile, S2ORC, and Dolma) exhibit a severe structural omission: African scientific, medical, legal, and agricultural scholarship constitutes less than 0.5% of global pre-training tokens. Consequently, state-of-the-art models suffer from systematic failure modes when reasoning about tropical epidemiology, localized smallholder agro-ecologies, regional economic governance, and indigenous linguistic structures. To resolve this representation deficit and advance African intellectual sovereignty in artificial intelligence, we introduce Africa-Papers, the largest curated multi-domain Pan-African academic pre-training corpus to date. Comprising over 844,807 full-text papers spanning 10.15 billion tokens across 879 Parquet shards, Africa-Papers unifies four primary scientific streams: (1) continental peer-reviewed journals indexed in DOAJ across 31 African nations, (2) the CGIAR CGSpace agricultural repository, (3) African-authored and African-focused STEM/AI preprints on arXiv, and (4) open-access international publications by scholars affiliated with African institutions indexed via OpenAlex. The entire corpus is processed into layout-aware, clean Markdown preserving section hierarchies, mathematical equations, and tabular data, accompanied by exact BPE token counts and a standardized 8-domain taxonomy. We release Africa-Papers openly on the Hugging Face Hub under the AfriSpeech organization to accelerate continual pre-training and domain evaluation for foundation models globally.
bullets: Addresses the underrepresentation of African scholarship in major pre-training datasets, especially for region-specific knowledge.
Aggregates 844,807 full-text papers from African journals, agricultural repositories, preprints, and publications by scholars at African institutions.
Covers scientific, medical, legal, agricultural, STEM/AI, and related domains across 31 African nations.
Provides layout-aware Markdown that preserves document structure, equations, and tables, with exact BPE token counts and an 8-domain taxonomy.
Released on Hugging Face to support continual pre-training and domain evaluation of foundation models.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Representative Markdown sample in AfricaPapers. Each sample contains structured metadata frontmatter, followed by clean, linear section bodies ready for autoregressive modeling.
Table 1: Domain taxonomy and volume distribution in Africa-Papers. Audited across all 879 Parquet shards currently live on the Hugging Face Hub.

papers.selection_reason: Pan-African academic pretraining corpus is a language foundation-model resource.
papers.title: Africa-Papers: A 10-Billion-Token Multi-Domain Academic Corpus for African Foundation Language Models
papers.tldr: Africa-Papers is an openly released 10.15-billion-token corpus designed to improve African representation in foundation-model pre-training across scientific and societal domains.

papers.abstract: Data selection plays a central role in modern large language model training, as the quality of training data strongly influences downstream performance. A common approach is to curate a development set that encodes the desired skills (e.g., reasoning or multilinguality) and select data that are similar to them. Existing methods compute similarity using cosine distance over either the model's hidden states or gradients. However, we observe that this max-similarity strategy induces a mode-seeking bias: the selected data clusters tightly around the development samples. To address this, we propose ICLHerd, a data selection framework that leverages the von Mises-Fisher kernel to balance mode-seeking with mode-averaging. We further introduce in-context learning as a validation proxy, enabling efficient hyperparameter search over the balance trade-off. Results show that ICLHerd outperforms existing LLM data selection algorithms, highlighting the importance of balancing mode-seeking and mode-averaging.
bullets: Existing cosine-similarity selection over hidden states or gradients tends to select data tightly clustered around development examples.
ICLHerd uses a von Mises–Fisher kernel to balance selecting representative modes with averaging across broader data regions.
It uses in-context learning as an efficient proxy for tuning this trade-off during hyperparameter search.
Experiments report that ICLHerd outperforms existing LLM data-selection algorithms.
The approach focuses on selecting data aligned with targeted skills such as reasoning or multilinguality.

figures.caption: Table 7. Comparison of kernels within our herding framework, all using fused hidden-state and gradient features.

Table 1. Main results on five tasks with 10K selected samples per task. Training data are selected using Qwen3-1.7B representations and used to finetune Qwen3-1.7B, 4B, and 8B. Due to resource constraints, Top-PPL and Mid-PPL are only evaluated at 1.7B as their performance is relatively low. The best and second-best results within each model size are bold and underlined, respectively. ICLHerd significantly outperforms RDS+, the strongest baseline, under a two-sided binomial test across tasks and model sizes (𝑝 ≈ 0.007).

Table 6. Efficiency comparison. Times are in minutes, with inference measured on 1K samples. papers.selection_reason: LLM data-selection method with in-context learning as a proxy is relevant to language foundation-model development.
papers.title: ICLHerd: Herding-Based Data Selection for LLMs with In-Context Learning as a Proxy
papers.tldr: ICLHerd improves LLM training-data selection by reducing the clustering bias of similarity-based methods through balanced mode-seeking and mode-averaging.

papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable capabilities in solving complex tasks in coding, mathematical logic, and iterative reasoning, especially by coordinating effectively within multi-agent systems (MAS). However, language agents traditionally communicate via text exchange, which introduces a bottleneck in information transfer and adds prefill latency for downstream agents. Recent work proposes that directly sharing the key-value (KV) cache between language models can enable efficient latent collaboration, entirely bypassing standard text-based communication. To enable latent communication between heterogeneous models of different sizes, prior work introduces trained fusion adapters for each model pair, which limits practical deployment. We introduce CacheFuse, a training-free method which demonstrates that augmenting a downstream model with an upstream model's KV cache using linear interpolation consistently enables superior performance than the standalone downstream model can achieve. We systematically analyze CacheFuse across four reasoning and knowledge benchmarks and demonstrate up to 8.6 percentage points higher accuracy compared to single-model baselines and up to 12.2x TTFT speedup compared to text-based communication in multi-model inference.
bullets: Addresses text-based communication bottlenecks and downstream prefill latency in multi-agent systems.
Combines an upstream model’s KV cache with a downstream model through linear interpolation, without fusion-adapter training.
Evaluated across four reasoning and knowledge benchmarks.
Reports up to 8.6 percentage-point accuracy gains over single-model baselines.
Achieves up to 12.2× faster time to first token than text-based multi-model communication.

figures.caption: Figure 1: CacheFuse pipeline. The sharer and receiver each prefill the same prompt independently, producing per-layer KV caches of identical geometry (nkv, dhead, L). Every layer’s key and value tensors are linearly interpolated with a single scalar θ to form a fused cache, which the downstream receiver model then decodes from directly to produce the response.

Figure 2: MMLU-R accuracy sweep for Qwen3-8B → Qwen3-4B. Receiver (θ = 0) and Replace (θ = 1) are included as endpoints. Fusion peaks at θ = 0.5, exceeding the receiver model individually (Qwen3-4B), direct KV cache replacement, and even the larger sharer model individually (Qwen3-8B).

Figure 3: TTFT speedup over T2T for Qwen3-8B → Qwen3-4B on ARC-C. Linearly interpolating the sharer and reciever caches (CacheFuse) achieves 12.2× faster TTFT than dense prefill of text-to-text communication (T2T). Single-model baselines are ∼18× faster.
Figure 5: Calibration vs. test θ sweeps on ARC-C. Left: Qwen3-8B → Qwen3-4B (calibration peaks at θ = 0.7 while test peaks at θ = 0.6). Right: Qwen3-1.7B → Qwen3-0.6B (both peak at θ = 0.2).

Figure 4: TTFT–accuracy Pareto plot for Qwen3-8B → Qwen3-4B on ARC-C. Lower TTFT and higher accuracy (top left) is better. The gray line traces the Pareto frontier. CacheFuse achieves the highest accuracy at significantly lower TTFT than T2T.
Table 3: Latency in milliseconds (ms) across model pairs and transfer methods. TTFT denotes time-to-first-token. TTEoA denotes time-to-end-of-answer.

Table 1: Full θ sweep across benchmarks on Qwen3 model pairs. Receiver corresponds to θ = 0 (pure receiver cache). Columns 0.1–0.9 are θ values for the CacheFuse linear interpolation. Replace corresponds to θ = 1 (pure sharer cache). Sharer denotes the standalone sharer model (reference). T2T denotes the text-to-text transfer baseline (reference). Bold underlined marks the best score in the θ sweep (across the Receiver to Replace endpoints).

Table 2: Accuracy across all four benchmarks for the best-performing θ per pair (exact θ per benchmark given in Table 1). Bold underlined marks where CacheFuse exceeds Receiver (otherwise Receiver is marked).

Table 4: Accuracy of offline θ calibration sweep on the first 1000 examples of each train split (ARC-C and OBQA), averaged over seeds. Column conventions match Table 1: Receiver corresponds to θ = 0. Columns 0.1–0.9 are linear interpolation between the sharer and receiver. Replace corresponds to θ = 1. Sharer denotes the standalone sharer. Bold underlined marks the best score in the θ sweep (across Receiver to Replace endpoints).

Table 5: Top-k offline calibration for reducing the test-time θ search. Test peak is the best accuracy (%) over the full test θ sweep (Table 1). Top-k selects the k highest-accuracy θ values from the averaged 1000-example train calibration sweep (Table 4), then reports the best test accuracy among only those k candidates (selected θ in parentheses). Bold underlined denotes where the top-k sweep exactly recovers the oracle score found on the test time search.

papers.selection_reason: Training-free KV-cache sharing between language models reduces latency and enables efficient latent LLM communication.
papers.title: Think Before You Speak: Enabling Training-Free Latent Communication Between Language Models
papers.tldr: CacheFuse enables training-free latent communication between heterogeneous language models by linearly interpolating their KV caches, improving accuracy while reducing communication latency.

papers.abstract: Multi-agent systems built from frozen language models communicate through text, which discards the internal state the sender already computed and makes the receiver pay to rebuild it. Work on internal channels avoids that cost, framing the problem as transfer: agent A sends information to agent B. Every agent pair that must communicate needs its own transfer bridge, and every agent added to a system needs a new bridge fitted against each previous agent. We reframe this problem as sharing: an agent publishes its internal state once into a pool, and every peer reads that pool through a single mechanism fitted to no sender in particular, so adding an agent adds a publisher and no new bridge. Whereas the carrier of the internal state and the fusion mechanism are usually chosen independently in the literature, our main finding is that these two choices are coupled; the deciding factor is where the carrier enters the receiver's computation. Consumability is a property of the receiving computation rather than of the representation. We find that the key-value (KV) cache must be augmented rather than swapped in: the receiver cross-attends over a peer's cache while keeping its own, and with only a small query-side adapter trained, matches the accuracy it gets from reading the source document. Activations invert this. They are best written straight into the receiver, with no bridge, no adapter and no training, which beats exposing them alongside the receiver's own, though that advantage rests on knowing where in the receiver the state belongs. The rule is augment the KV cache, replace the activation, established under one protocol with a shared control ladder. One adapter, trained once, also serves publishers it never trained on, and a pool of several at once, but only those whose internal state lies close to the receiver's own.
bullets: Reframes multi-agent internal communication as shared publishing to a common pool, avoiding pair-specific transfer bridges.
Shows that carrier and fusion mechanism are coupled through where peer state enters the receiver’s computation.
KV-cache sharing works by cross-attending to peer keys and values while preserving the receiver’s own cache, using only a small query-side adapter.
Activation sharing works best by directly writing into the receiver, without a bridge, adapter, or training.
A single adapter generalizes to unseen publishers and multiple pooled agents when their states are sufficiently close to the receiver’s.

figures.caption: Figure 1: The two carriers take opposite mechanisms. (a) The KV cache cannot be substituted, even at the fidelity annotated on the bar, and must be augmented instead. (b) Activations invert this: direct replacement works, training-free. Floors and native references are per carrier.

Figure 2: Carrier ordering across injection depth: activations dominate values, which dominate keys, and keys never leave the floor band. The clean operating band is shallower than the peak (Section 4.3).

Figure 6: The boundaries. (a) Cross-family KV augmentation collapses at every rung of the adaptation ladder, while the same ladder within one model reaches the native ceiling. (b) On the activation carrier, the apparently strongest trained arm fails a mis-source control (0.300 against a floor of 0.19); the additive arm passes it (0.069) at a lower but genuine 0.454.

Figure 3: Multi-source KV augmentation over a pool of 𝑁 holders, one of which read the answer-bearing passage. (a) Raw cross-attention collapses below the floor by 𝑁=4; the trained query-side bridge decays gracefully and remains above floor at 𝑁=8. Dotted lines are the corresponding controls, which themselves lift above floor at large 𝑁 . (b) Lift over the strongest control at each pool size: positive throughout, eroding with 𝑁 .

Figure 4: Held-out senders. (a) The bridge, trained on the receiver’s own pools only, reaches the same accuracy on the nearest held-out sender as on the sender it trained on, and falls to its control on the two more distant senders. (b) Control-subtracted lift against the cosine between the sender’s cache and the receiver’s own. The effect is present at 0.9994 and absent by 0.9933, which measures where the effect falls on the sender axis. Three checkpoints locate a transition, not a radius.

Figure 5: Why the two carriers differ. (a) The measured readout Jacobian gain is 𝑂 (1) both on and off manifold, with a ratio of only 1.47×: the wall is not built by amplification, so no single layer and no stacking of layers blows up a tolerable perturbation. (b) Tolerable displacement by carrier: activations remain usable to cosine 0.90, keys only to ≈ 0.995, about 20× less headroom. Same receiver, same depth; the difference is the consumption point.

Table 6: The substitution bound across architectures. Each receiver is probed with its own bank of genuine keys and its own anchors. Identity hands the receiver its own exact keys and recovers that receiver’s ceiling in every case, which verifies the harness on each architecture. Nearest genuine substitutes the closest key the receiver itself produced elsewhere. Depth spans 𝐿=6 to 𝐿=36 and the grouped-query factor spans 𝐺=1 (multi-head) to 𝐺=8. 𝑛=120.

Table 2: KV augmentation. The receiver keeps its own cache and cross-attends over the holder’s verbatim cache; only the receiver’s projections adapt. The control feeds a holder cache built on the answer-masked passage. Same-model, 𝑛=200.

Table 1: Oracle substitution: the receiver’s key is interpolated toward the 𝑘-th nearest key the receiver itself produced elsewhere, so every candidate is on its own manifold. No neighbor rank recovers a graded tolerance. Qwen2.5-1.5B, 𝑛=200, floor 0.18, ceiling 0.665.

Table 4: The asymmetry. Best result per (carrier, mechanism) cell, each against its own probe’s anchors. Cache numbers are shared-fact accuracy at 𝑛=200 (floor 0.18, ceiling 0.665); activation numbers are conditional accuracy at 𝑛=120 (floor 0.20, ceiling 0.742). Cells are not comparable across columns in absolute terms, only relative to their anchors.

Table 3: Activation replacement, training-free. The receiver’s hidden states at the fact region are overwritten with the holder’s. Qwen2.5-1.5B, 𝑛=120 (cond 𝑛=89), floor 0.20, ceiling 0.742. The mismatch control is clean at 𝐿 ≤ 12 but not at 𝐿 ≥ 16 (shaded reading in the text).

Table 5: Held-out senders. One rank-16 query-side bridge, trained on pools built from the receiver’s own weights only, evaluated against senders it never saw. Senders are Qwen2.5-1.5B checkpoints with the receiver’s geometry and a bit-identical tokeniser, ordered by the cosine between their cache and the receiver’s. We report relative Frobenius difference alongside cosine: the two rank the senders identically, so the ordering is not an artifact of one metric, though two metrics over three checkpoints cannot settle which is the right notion of compatibility. Lift is shared accuracy minus the stronger of the two controls; intervals are 95% normal-approximation intervals on that difference. Pool size 𝑁=4, 𝑛=200, floor 0.18, native ceiling 0.665. The self row reproduces the 𝑁=4 point of Figure 3 exactly.

papers.selection_reason: Internal-state sharing through KV caches and activations in frozen LLM agents is relevant to language-model mechanisms and multi-agent inference.
papers.title: Augment the Cache, Replace the Activation: A 2x2 Study of Internal-State Sharing
papers.tldr: A shared internal-state protocol works best when KV caches are augmented with peer states, while activations directly replace the receiver’s corresponding state.

papers.abstract: Activation steering adds a vector to a model's hidden states to control a named behaviour. A gain on that behaviour, however, does not show that the vector controls it directly: it may act through a component shared with neighbouring behaviours, which unsteered and random baselines cannot separate. We introduce the competing-target test: a vector is compared with the vector built the same way for a competing target, and an equivalence test states when their difference is below a useful margin. We apply it in open-weight models to vectors for Kantian deontology, which judges an act by the rule it follows, and act utilitarianism, which judges it by the welfare it produces. On held-out situations, prompting a framework raises its score and lowers the other's, whereas vectors for either framework move both scores alike, and none reaches the margin. The two vectors share most of their direction, a request to apply some framework; the same construction separates an optimistic from a pessimistic tone, whose vectors share much less. What a vector shares with its competitors therefore sets what it controls: steering a perspective can deliver a mixture, and measuring a disposition can measure its neighbours, unless tested against the competing target.
bullets: A gain on the intended behaviour may reflect components shared with competing behaviours.
The competing-target test compares a steering vector with one constructed for its competing target and checks whether their difference exceeds a useful margin.
On held-out situations, prompting one ethical framework raises its score and lowers the other, but either framework’s steering vector moves both scores similarly.
The ethical vectors share most of their direction, unlike optimistic and pessimistic tone vectors, which are more distinct.
Steering vectors may therefore produce mixtures of perspectives and require competing-target evaluation to establish specificity.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Prompting separates the frameworks; every steering configuration stays below the margin. Held-out situations of Section 3. (a) Score planes. An arrow joins the two members of a matched pair, from the utilitarian to the Kantian one; for prompting, thin arrows are single situations under either instruction and the bold arrow the mean under the defined instruction; the inset enlarges the origin, where each arrow is the mean pair of one recipe at one positive dose (bold: persona at dose 3) and grey points are random vectors. (b) Equivalence test. Averaged specificity of each configuration, with prompting right of the broken axis: estimate (circle), one-sided 95% upper bound (bar) and situation values (grey dots); filled circles are classed below 1/12 and confirmed by the sign-flip test.

Figure 4: Single-site edits recover no more than a random direction at the natural norm and at most four tenths of prompting within the quality limits. papers.selection_reason: Activation steering in open-weight LLMs is a transferable technical method for controlling hidden-state behaviour in language foundation models.
papers.title: Steering Vectors for Competing Ethical Frameworks Are Interchangeable: A Competing-Target Test for Activation Steering
papers.tldr: Activation-steering vectors for Kantian and utilitarian ethics appear to control a shared “apply a framework” disposition rather than distinct ethical frameworks.

papers.abstract: We investigate the problem of role-capability leakage (RCL), in which a role-prompted reasoning model generates convincing in-role text while continuing to exhibit capabilities on benchmarks that exceed those implied by the assigned role. For example, when a model is prompted to assume the role of a kindergarten student, one might expect its performance on a mathematics benchmark to reflect kindergarten-level ability rather than expert-level proficiency in solving calculus problems. We introduce RoleCapBench, a curriculum-grounded benchmark for evaluating RCL across six educational roles and four assessment levels spanning elementary school through A-level, and use it to evaluate three open-weight reasoning models. We find that although the models can generate stylistically convincing in-role responses, they consistently fail to align their underlying capabilities with their assigned roles. Naive role prompting yields strong role-voice scores of 1.218--1.389 while retaining above-role accuracy of 0.811--0.898. RCL persists across a range of prompting conditions, including prompts that explicitly instruct the model to match the role's capability level. To mitigate this problem, we propose Injection, an inference-time intervention that combines explicit, role-specific capability guidelines with a guiding prefilled response prefix. Injection improves role-capability alignment across models, reducing above-role accuracy by up to 0.562 while preserving in-role accuracy with a marginal drop of less than 0.058 across most models. All artifacts, including scripts and evaluation data, will be released upon acceptance.
bullets: Defines role-capability leakage (RCL): models sound like assigned roles while retaining capabilities beyond those roles.
Introduces RoleCapBench, covering six educational roles and four assessment levels from elementary school through A-level.
Evaluates three open-weight reasoning models and finds persistent above-role performance across prompting conditions.
Proposes Injection, combining role-specific capability guidelines with a prefilled response prefix.
Injection reduces above-role accuracy by up to 0.562 while generally preserving in-role accuracy, with drops below 0.058 in most models.

papers.selection_reason: Studies capability leakage and inference-time intervention in role-prompted reasoning models, contributing to LLM behavior and reasoning research.
papers.title: When a Kindergartener Solves Calculus: Measuring Capability Leakage in Role-Prompted Reasoning Models
papers.tldr: Role prompting changes a reasoning model’s style more reliably than its underlying expertise, but a targeted inference-time intervention improves capability alignment.

papers.abstract: Deepresearch (DR) agents interact with real-world web environments through multi-turn search and visit, causing their contexts to grow rapidly over time. We observe that, even after DR Agentic Reinforcement Learning (DR-RL), 61.6% of the model's remaining prediction errors can still be attributed to insufficient long-context understanding, including longcontext hallucination and failures in cross-document evidence integration. It motivates us to further break the bottleneck of DR-RL by strengthening the model's long-context ability. However, effective LongContext training requires more than simply increasing context length. To bridge the data gap, we propose `DR Rollouts to LongContext-QA (DR-to-Long)'. The method repurposes DR-RL trajectories, which naturally contain search histories, visited webpages, evidence snippets, and final-answer supervision. It then replaces the compact snippets and webpage summaries in each trajectory with the full contents of their corresponding URLs, producing substantially longer multi-document contexts while preserving the original evidence relationships. Building on DR-to-Long, we introduce DLD (DR -> LongQA -> DR)-RL. DLD-RL first performs a short DR-RL stage to collect rollout trajectories, which are then converted into LongQA instances at zero annotation cost. The model is subsequently optimized with LongQA-RL to strengthen LongContext ability, followed by full DR-RL to continue improving its DR capability. Experiments show that DLD-RL outperforms standard DR-RL by 7.3% on three Deepresearch benchmarks and improves performance by 13.5% on three long-context benchmarks.
bullets: Deep-research agents still face substantial errors from long-context failures, including hallucination and poor cross-document evidence integration.
DR-to-Long expands existing DR-RL trajectories by replacing snippets and webpage summaries with the full contents of their source URLs.
DLD-RL alternates short DR-RL, zero-cost conversion to LongQA, LongQA-RL, and subsequent DR-RL.
The method improves over standard DR-RL by 7.3% across three Deepresearch benchmarks and 13.5% across three long-context benchmarks.

papers.abstract: Wrong automatic routing of an IT support ticket can cost more than human triage. We evaluate cost-aware abstention as an offline, cost-conditional readiness assessment: select a routing policy on calibration data under explicit costs, then evaluate that frozen policy once on held-out test data. On a public 47,837-ticket, eight-class corpus, we compare four trained non-LLM classifiers with four large language models under zero- and few-shot prompting. Under the illustrative cost model (c_ok, c_triage, c_wrong) = (0, 1, 5), TF-IDF with logistic regression and a threshold of 0.60 selected on calibration reduces test cost from 0.763 to 0.472, a 38.1% relative reduction (paired ratio-bootstrap 95% CI [35.7%, 40.4%]), while lowering wrong routes from 15.3% to 3.5%. Frozen calibration-selected policies also beat both always-route and always-defer on held-out test data in 14 of 16 settings in a post-hoc cost-parameter analysis. The strongest prompted configuration reaches 0.477 accuracy on a stratified 1,000-ticket test subset, versus 0.879 for fine-tuned DistilBERT on the same tickets. Isotonic lowers expected calibration error without reliably improving discrimination: GPT-4o-mini few-shot has one confidence value before and after recalibration and correctness AUROC 0.500. We therefore report correctness AUROC and tie-aware risk-coverage area alongside ECE. At the analytically derived break-even probability 0.80, seven prompted configurations defer all tickets; Haiku few-shot routes only 19/1,000. An LLM-only agreement control and margin/entropy rejection baselines further separate calibration from discrimination. The findings are scoped to this dataset, prompt design, model endpoints, and illustrative costs; the work is an evaluation framework, not a new abstention algorithm or universal deployment certification.
bullets: Wrong routing is modeled as five times more costly than human triage, motivating selective deferral.
TF-IDF with logistic regression and a calibration-selected 0.60 threshold lowers test cost by 38.1% and wrong routes from 15.3% to 3.5%.
Calibration-selected policies outperform always-route and always-defer in 14 of 16 post-hoc cost settings.
Fine-tuned DistilBERT reaches 0.879 accuracy on the reported subset, versus 0.477 for the strongest prompted LLM configuration.
Recalibration can improve ECE without improving correctness discrimination; at the derived break-even probability, most prompted systems defer nearly everything.

papers.selection_reason: Evaluates cost-aware abstention strategies for LLM-based classification tasks, focusing on calibration and risk coverage. This is relevant to the application and reliability of LLMs in decision-making.
papers.title: Cost-Aware Abstention for LLM-Based IT Ticket Classification
papers.tldr: Cost-aware abstention substantially reduces costly IT-ticket misrouting in this evaluation, but traditional classifiers outperform prompted LLMs and results remain scoped to the tested costs and setup.

papers.abstract: Many recent open-weight language models use n-gram embedding tables to improve performance. These tables store learned representations of short token sequences, such as pairs or triples of consecutive tokens, which the model retrieves during processing. However, they can require substantial memory: DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, for example, allocates 196 billion parameters to its Engram n-gram memory. We therefore investigate whether this memory cost can be reduced while preserving the performance improvement that the tables provide. We propose storing n-gram embeddings at low precision and systematically investigate different quantization methods and bit allocations across tables. Across nanochat-, Llama-, and GPT-2-family models trained from scratch, four-bit tables save approximately 75% of table memory while preserving more than 99% of the validation-loss improvement from adding the tables. Using fewer bits leads to a larger drop in performance, although we find that a short fine-tuning phase recovers a significant part of this loss. In addition, reinvesting the saved memory in larger tables can improve performance beyond that of the original full-precision tables while still using less memory. These table memory savings also extend to large existing models: on DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash and Qwen3.8-Flash-Next, low-bit tables save 47-55% of table memory, with perplexity increases of less than 1.2% and largely preserved downstream task performance. These findings establish low-bit precision as a practical way to reduce the memory requirements of n-gram embeddings and use the saved capacity to improve model performance.
bullets: N-gram embedding tables improve language models but can consume substantial memory.
Four-bit tables reduce table memory by about 75% while retaining over 99% of the validation-loss improvement from full-precision tables in models trained from scratch.
Using fewer bits causes larger performance losses, but brief fine-tuning recovers a significant portion of them.
Reinvesting saved memory into larger tables can outperform the original full-precision tables while using less memory.
On large existing models, low-bit tables save 47–55% of table memory with perplexity increases below 1.2% and largely preserved downstream performance.

papers.selection_reason: Investigates quantization methods for n-gram embedding tables in LLMs to reduce memory footprint. This is a significant technical contribution to LLM architecture and efficiency.

papers.abstract: Chain-of-thought (CoT) prompting elicits step-by-step rationales that appear to explain model predictions, but there is no guarantee these steps causally drive the final answer. In standard autoregressive generation, dense attention allows each reasoning step to attend to the full context, enabling the model to derive answers through direct lookup while generating plausible-sounding but post-hoc justifications. We introduce CausalCoT, an inference framework that enforces causal transparency by decomposing problems into a directed acyclic graph of atomic sub-questions, evaluating each node in an isolated context containing only its direct causal parents. This Markovian structure removes attention pathways to non-parent content, making downstream predictions sensitive to local reasoning rather than global context leakage. Across a diverse suite of reasoning benchmarks, CausalCoT preserves competitive predictive performance while improving explanation faithfulness, increasing causal sensitivity of intermediate reasoning steps by an average of 12 and up to 21 percentage points over the strongest baseline. The structured dependency graph additionally enables test-time interventions in which local corrections propagate predictably through downstream reasoning.
authors: Gabriele Dominici, Teague McMillan, Fazl Barez, Marc Langheinrich, Martin Gjoreski
bullets: Standard chain-of-thought can produce plausible rationales that do not causally determine the answer because attention can leak across the full context.
CausalCoT decomposes problems into atomic sub-questions organized as a directed acyclic graph.
Each node is evaluated using only its direct causal parents, blocking access to unrelated reasoning content.
Across diverse reasoning benchmarks, it improves intermediate-step causal sensitivity by an average of 12 percentage points and up to 21 points over the strongest baseline.
Its dependency graph supports test-time interventions, allowing local corrections to propagate predictably downstream.

figures.caption: Figure 1: CoT vs. CausalCoT. (Left) In standard CoT, the model generates a continuous, autoregressive stream of reasoning. (Right) Our proposed CausalCoT framework structurally isolates reasoning into a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG). Each sub-question is evaluated in a restricted context containing only its explicitly routed parental dependencies. This enforces a procedural Markovian property, making the final prediction depend on explicitly routed intermediate outputs rather than unrestricted access to the full reasoning trace as done in CoT.(Completions shortened for illustration).

Figure 2: Attention Leakage: Standard Chainof-Thought suffers from causal opacity: dense attention creates “leakage” pathways (red dashed arrows) that bypass intermediate logic. CausalCoT enforces a strict DAG. By evaluating intermediate steps in isolated contexts, each answer is causally derived only from its direct parent nodes.

CausalCoT enforces absolute procedural faithfulness across all difficulty scales, whereas standard CoT frequently makes unfaithful corrections on simpler problems.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes CausalCoT, a framework to enforce causal transparency in Chain-of-Thought reasoning by isolating context. This addresses reasoning and attention mechanisms in LLMs.
papers.title: Causal Chain of Thought: Mitigating Attention Leakage via Context Isolation
papers.tldr: CausalCoT improves the causal faithfulness of chain-of-thought reasoning by isolating each sub-question to its direct causal context while maintaining competitive accuracy.

papers.abstract: Instrumental convergence is often invoked as a general reason to expect capable agents to acquire or express power-seeking subgoals: self-preservation, resource acquisition, deception, or resistance to oversight which poses an important threat to the society. For LLMs, reinforcement learning is the first stage of post-training that directly optimizes behavior against an objective; therefore, it is the stage where convergent instrumental behavior, on IC grounds, likely to appear. Does reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) make a model more likely to express instrumental-convergence behavior, or does this depend on the training regime, evaluation frame, and stage of post-training? We study this question as a checkpoint-conditioned behavioral trajectory rather than as a single before/after safety score. Using InstrumentalEval, we evaluate OLMo-3-7B-Think across SFT, DPO, 13 intermediate RLVR checkpoints, and the final RLVR model. The trajectory is nonmonotonic: instrumental rate rises from 25.0% at SFT to 46.1% near RLVR step 200, then falls to 11.8% at the final checkpoint. Paired item-level tests and step-wise regression support the final SFT-to-RLVR reduction. Prompt framing does not explain this pattern: a harmful-prompt indicator combined with other framing effects explains only 15% of within-checkpoint score variance on average, and Iterative Null-space Projection (INLP) removes a detectable framing direction without changing the SFT-to-final-RLVR gap. Together with preliminary 32B endpoint results (35.53% SFT to 22.37% RLVR final), these findings indicate that RLVR does not monotonically increase instrumental behavior in this setting: the rate rises early, then falls below the SFT baseline. The result is specific to this model family and benchmark, and judge agreement is moderate, so absolute rates should be read cautiously.

bullets: Instrumental behavior is evaluated across SFT, DPO, 13 intermediate RLVR checkpoints, and the final RLVR model.

Paired tests and step-wise regression support a final SFT-to-RLVR reduction.
Prompt framing explains little of the within-checkpoint variation, and INLP does not change the SFT-to-final-RLVR gap.
Preliminary 32B endpoint results show the same direction, but findings are limited to this model family and benchmark; judge agreement is moderate.
