papers.selection_reason: Proposes LM2LM for LLM self-improvement using a Research World Model (RWM) to predict gains from experimental records.
papers.title: Language Models Learn to Improve Language Models
papers.tldr: LM2LM trains language models to propose effective language-model improvements using a learned research world model as scalable feedback, with periodic real experiments to keep that feedback reliable.

papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can generate fluent outputs that lack source support or conflict with local operational constraints. We introduce Self-Reflective Chain-of-Thought (SRCoT), a modular architecture that organizes generation as a closed Retrieve--Reflect--Revise loop. SRCoT separates environment state, persistent knowledge, accumulated experience, and short-term memory into provenance-labeled stores. BM25 retrieval supplies local context; subsequent passes expose intermediate drafts, missing-information markers, follow-up queries, and optional claim--evidence mappings. These artifacts inform retrieval, revision, clarification, or abstention decisions. We examine the architecture through qualitative, trace-based case studies in two fully synthetic settings: emergency medical services and Munich-Sim, an emergency-operations simulation. Local prototype runs on an Apple M4-family laptop with 128 GB memory illustrate source-labeled documentation, explicit gap marking, and structured dispatch-style outputs. The traces also reveal provenance-assignment errors, incomplete evidence coverage, and unsafe assumptions that remain possible despite prompting constraints. These cases demonstrate report-level inspectability and local execution, not comparative superiority, hallucination reduction, clinical validity, or operational safety. The architecture separates retrieval and control from the model interface, but behavior across different models remains to be evaluated. SRCoT is a research proof of concept requiring human review, with its principal contribution lying in an inspectable control procedure rather than a new model.
authors: Fabian Broszio, Michael Hoffmann, Adrian Paschke
bullets: Addresses unsupported or operationally conflicting LLM outputs.
Separates environment state, persistent knowledge, experience, and short-term memory into provenance-labeled stores.
Uses BM25 retrieval and reflective passes to identify gaps, generate follow-up queries, map claims to evidence, and choose revision, clarification, or abstention.
Qualitative trace-based case studies in synthetic emergency-services settings show inspectable source labeling, gap marking, and structured outputs.
Traces still reveal provenance errors, incomplete evidence, and unsafe assumptions; comparative effectiveness and safety remain unevaluated.

papers.tldr: SRCoT is a local, inspectable Retrieve–Reflect–Revise pipeline that uses provenance-labeled evidence to guide LLM generation, while still requiring human review.

papers.abstract: Native language identification (NLI) infers a non-native speaker's first language (L1) from their second language (L2) production. We investigate a token probability approach that scores each text sample as a continuation of a prompt prefix specifying a candidate L1, then predicts the candidate with the highest score. We evaluate our approach using Llama 3.1 8B and 70B on three datasets: TOEFL9, Write and Improve 2024, and BULATS-L1. We compare its performance with previous prompting-based classification approaches. Token-probability scoring substantially improves on direct classification, particularly with the 8B model, while the 70B model achieves state-of-the-art performance across all datasets. Our results indicate that pretrained LLMs' token probabilities contain information useful for distinguishing L1 backgrounds from L2 English production.
authors: Ahmet Yavuz Uluslu, Mark Gales, Kate Knill, Gerold Schneider
bullets: Frames NLI as choosing the candidate L1 with the highest token-probability score.
Evaluates Llama 3.1 8B and 70B on TOEFL9, Write and Improve 2024, and BULATS-L1.
Token-probability scoring substantially outperforms direct prompting-based classification, especially with the 8B model.
The 70B model achieves state-of-the-art performance across all three datasets.
Findings suggest LLM token probabilities encode information about L1 backgrounds in L2 English.

papers.abstract: Current Chain-of-Thought (CoT) verification methods detect reasoning faithfulness from model outputs or static activations, but are limited in explaining how unfaithfulness develops during generation. We introduce VERITAS to verbalise the model's computation: how different reasoning anchors emerge, transfer across layers, and surface in the output. VERITAS adopts the layer-wise Jacobian projection to produce a verbalised account of the model's internal reasoning evolution at each generated CoT token. By training a classifier on the extracted features along the traces, we show that these structured features provide insightful perspectives on how and where reasoning diverges toward unfaithfulness. Experiments on four datasets from FaithCoT-Bench and BonaFide show that VERITAS achieves a significant performance gain over LLM-as-Judge, with a 28.4% gain in balanced accuracy, and an average improvement of 16.0% over activation probing. Further analysis shows VERITAS can be generalised to different datasets and model architectures. Our work shows that verbalising model computation provides a richer and more interpretable lens on CoT faithfulness, moving beyond detection toward a mechanistic understanding of how reasoning fails.
authors: Yujing Wang, Yulan He, Wenya Wang, Hanqi Yan
bullets: Addresses the limited interpretability of CoT faithfulness methods based on outputs or static activations.
Uses layer-wise Jacobian projections to trace reasoning anchors, their layer-to-layer transfer, and their emergence in generated tokens.
Trains a classifier on structured features extracted from these computation traces.
Across four FaithCoT-Bench and BonaFide datasets, improves balanced accuracy by 28.4% over LLM-as-Judge and 16.0% on average over activation probing.
Generalises across datasets and model architectures, supporting mechanistic analysis of reasoning failures.

papers.abstract: LLM-agent memory selection often uses retrieval rankings based on record relevance or individual influence. Such rankings cannot identify sufficient subsets under redundant or jointly necessary evidence. We study per-decision memory sufficiency: selecting a small subset that preserves full-memory behavior. To separate search error from model error, we introduce JointCoreBench, a benchmark with nine interaction families, six workflow domains, natural-language decisions, and exact sufficient-set oracles, and JointCore, a relevance cost-ordered group-deletion baseline that tests blocks before individual records. On 6,912 exact conditions, cost-ordered JointCore recovers a minimum-cost sufficient set in 100.0% of cases, reduces subset evaluations from 30.00 to 11.13 (62.9%), and achieves 87.8% active-memory savings. Across four 12B-70B model families and 432 tasks per model, its unweighted mean is 10.28 versus 16.00 model queries and 50.6% versus 43.1% minimum-cost recovery relative to cost aware singleton deletion. Both methods preserve full-memory behavior under the deterministic primary interface. Tests with physical deletion, UNKNOWN masks, PENDING sentinels, counterfactual values, and alternative labels identify interface dependent behavior. JointCore is an efficient benchmark baseline; the study does not establish deployment-ready memory compression.
bullets: Marginal relevance and individual influence miss redundant or jointly necessary evidence needed for per-decision memory sufficiency.
JointCoreBench provides exact sufficient-set oracles across nine interaction families, six workflow domains, and 6,912 exact conditions.
JointCore tests relevance-ordered blocks before individual records, recovering minimum-cost sufficient sets in 100.0% of benchmark cases.
It reduces subset evaluations by 62.9% and achieves 87.8% active-memory savings on the benchmark.
Across four model families, JointCore averages 10.28 queries and 50.6% minimum-cost recovery, but results depend on the memory interface and do not establish deployment readiness.

papers.selection_reason: Interaction-aware memory selection for LLM agents directly addresses persistent LLM memory beyond current context.
papers.title: Beyond Marginal Influence: Interaction-Aware Memory Selection for LLM Agents
papers.tldr: JointCore efficiently selects small, interaction-aware memory subsets that preserve an LLM agent’s full-memory decisions, while revealing interface-dependent behavior and deployment limitations.

papers.abstract: Small differences between internal representations can shrink or grow as they pass through a Transformer layer, affecting how information is preserved and how sensitive the model is to perturbations. Yet it remains unclear when changes in attention weights can turn a representation difference that would otherwise shrink into one that grows. We develop a \textbf{Mixture-Gated Theory of Anisotropic Representation Dynamics} that separates self-attention into value transport, query gating, and key gating. Our analysis reveals how the geometry of attended representations constrains gating and how interactions between these mechanisms can reverse contraction induced by value transport. We formalize this phenomenon as gating-induced regime switching, where a representation difference contracts under fixed attention routing but expands under full attention. We derive a necessary and sufficient spectral criterion that certifies the existence or absence of switching and identifies switching directions without exhaustive search. Beyond existence, our theory characterizes maximum relative switching strength, certifies the severity of contraction that gating can overcome, and determines the largest dimension of a subspace in which every nonzero direction switches. Experiments across four Transformer architectures validate these predictions through analytical and finite-forward comparisons, revealing distinct and joint query--key gating mechanisms and nontrivial switching subspaces. Our results provide a mechanistic and spectral understanding of how attention routing can alter local representation dynamics.
bullets: Decomposes self-attention into value transport, query gating, and key gating to analyze anisotropic representation dynamics.
Defines gating-induced regime switching: differences that contract under fixed attention routing can expand under full attention.
Derives a necessary-and-sufficient spectral criterion for detecting switching and identifying switching directions without exhaustive search.
Also characterizes switching strength, the contraction gating can overcome, and subspaces where all nonzero directions switch.
Experiments across four Transformer architectures support the theory and reveal distinct, combined query–key gating effects.

figures.caption: Figure 6: Switching across architectures and depths. (a) Median normalized effective switching dimension across seven normalized depths and four Transformer architectures. Normalization uses the projected transport-contractive subspace. (b) Mechanism composition among sampled switching directions. Measurements use two WikiText-2 validation prompts per model and 64-dimensional random orthonormal probe subspaces.

Figure 7: Cross-architecture regime geometry and spatial adjacency. (a) Analytic regime spheres: Two orthographic views (View A and B) of selected spherical slices across four Transformer architectures, colored by their predicted growth regimes. (b) Spatial adjacency graphs: Node sizes indicate regime proportions, and edges represent shared regime boundaries. NC: transport non-contractive; NS: contraction without switching; Q/K: query-/key-driven switching; E: either pathway sufficient; J: joint query–key required. Percentages are computed over all sampled sphere directions, rather than only switching directions as in Figure 6(b). Results characterize the selected slices, not the full representation space.

Figure 15: Projected spectra across architecture and depth. (a) Median leading switching eigenvalue and the λ = 1 threshold. Figure 2: Geometric support and null directions of query gating. Centered attended representations span a subspace Ur, whose dimension may be substantially smaller than the ambient representation dimension. The transformed subspace WQKUr determines which query perturbation directions can influence the attention output through query gating. Perturbations orthogonal to this subspace produce no first-order query-gating change. Consequently, query gating is insensitive to at least d− dim(Ur) independent input directions. The three-dimensional projections provide a schematic visualization of the higher-dimensional geometry.

Figure 3: From self-attention decomposition to gating-induced regime switching. Self-attention induces three local mechanisms: value transport, query gating, and key gating, represented by their corresponding Jacobian components. These components jointly determine directional representation growth through the induced growth operator GM = J⊤MJ −M . The three-dimensional illustration shows how different perturbation directions can exhibit contraction or expansion. Interactions between value transport and attention gating can reverse transport contraction, causing a representation difference to grow under full attention.

(b) Spectral preprocessing incurs a one-time setup cost but becomes advantageous for sufficiently many directional evaluations. Total-cost curves are projected from measured setup and throughput timings.

Figure 1: Conceptual illustration of gating-induced regime switching. Two nearby representations initially differ by a small perturbation δzℓ. Under fixed attention weights, value transport contracts this difference. However, a small change in the query can redistribute attention among token representations, introducing an additional gating contribution. When this contribution is sufficiently strong, the full attention computation amplifies the same representation difference rather than suppressing it. The illustration motivates our analysis of how attention routing can reverse transport contraction.

papers.selection_reason: Develops a Mixture-Gated Theory of Anisotropic Representation Dynamics in Transformers, providing mechanistic understanding of attention routing.
papers.title: Anisotropic Representation Dynamics in Transformers
papers.tldr: A spectral theory explains when query–key attention gating can reverse contraction and amplify small representation differences in Transformer layers.

papers.abstract: Multi-turn LLM routing selects a model at every turn before its response is available, yet task success is revealed only when the interaction ends, leaving each intermediate choice without a label of its own. Logged trajectories, however, retain the response each call produced, which exposes what each turn required and how well the chosen model served it, evidence that outcomes alone hide. We introduce RIVET (Response-Informed Value Estimation for Turn-Level Routing), which exploits this post-call evidence during training while keeping routing strictly pre-call at deployment. RIVET jointly trains two value estimators over a shared state-model representation: a deployable Routing Value Estimator that scores candidate models from pre-call information, and a training-only Response-Informed Value Estimator that additionally observes the realized response. Conditioning on the response turns response-induced return variation from residual noise into an observed covariate, and we show that this reduces the leading asymptotic estimation error of the shared representation. On the MINT benchmark, RIVET solves more held-out tasks than the strongest multi-turn baseline while using 74.7% less total call cost.
authors: Haotian Yan, Jiaqi Liu, Bingyi Jing, Tianjun Yao
bullets: Multi-turn routing lacks turn-level labels because task success is known only after the interaction ends.
RIVET uses logged responses as training-only evidence while keeping deployment routing strictly pre-call.
It jointly trains a deployable Routing Value Estimator and a response-informed training estimator over shared representations.
Response conditioning reduces estimation error by explaining return variation otherwise treated as noise.
On MINT, RIVET solves more held-out tasks than the strongest multi-turn baseline while reducing total call cost by 74.7%.

figures.caption: Figure 2: RIVET separates pre-call deployment from post-call training. Both estimators read the same trainable state–model representation zθ(st,m). The Routing Value Estimator (RVE, deployed) scores every candidate model from pre-call information and makes the routing decision; the Response-Informed Value Estimator (RIVE, training only) additionally conditions on the executed response and shapes the shared representation through its own regression loss. Both estimators regress to the same scalar return target; deployment uses RVE alone.

Each turn demands a different ability (bottom labels), and the response exposes whether the model met it: check and cross mark acceptable and unacceptable responses, and the remaining icons mark responses that are vague, over-deliberated, or needlessly verbose. The green path is the cost-efficient route and switches models across turns. Illustrative; each logged turn observes only the selected model’s response.

papers.abstract: Drifting Models generate a sample with a single function evaluation, making them attractive for fast parallel language generation, but their one-step formulation does not support iterative refinement. We propose Recurrent Language Generation via Drifting (ReLaDrift), which uses a shared Drifting Model to generate an initial draft from noise and iteratively refine it in a continuous latent space. We train this recurrence by sampling the number of rounds and applying the drifting loss only at the final round, stopping gradients through preceding rounds so that only one round requires backpropagation. Unlike the one-step Drifting Model, whose accuracy does not improve when iterated, ReLaDrift enables a trade-off between test-time computation and generation quality, as diffusion and flow language models do. On Sudoku Hard and GSM8K, it achieves competitive or superior performance compared with these iterative-generation approaches across a range of inference budgets. Our code is available at https://github.com/Yuki-Ots/ReLaDrift
authors: Yuki Otsuka, Daisuke Oba, Naoaki Okazaki
bullets: Drifting Models generate samples in one function evaluation but cannot benefit from iterative refinement.
ReLaDrift first creates a draft from noise, then repeatedly refines it using a shared model in continuous latent space.
Training samples different recurrence lengths and applies the drifting loss only at the final round, avoiding backpropagation through earlier rounds.
On Sudoku Hard and GSM8K, it performs competitively or better than iterative diffusion and flow language models across inference budgets.
The approach supports adjustable test-time computation while retaining the parallel-generation advantages of drifting models.

papers.abstract: Process Reward Models (PRMs) play a central role in test-time scaling for large language model (LLM) reasoning. However, PRMs may provide inaccurate process rewards for test-time scaling, which we identify as arising from two sources of uncertainty: (1) \textit{PRM uncertainty} that arises from insufficient supervision data and imperfect PRM training; and (2) \textit{policy uncertainty} that results from the mismatch between the policy to collect supervision data and the policy for test-time scaling, leading to systematic reward overestimation. Previous studies fail to jointly consider both uncertainties. To bridge this gap, we propose BayesianPRM, which treats the process reward as a random variable within a reward hypothesis space and maintains a Bayesian belief over it. Since exact Bayesian inference over the continuous hypothesis space is generally intractable, we discretize the reward hypothesis space with a reward ensemble and introduce two complementary belief updates, each targeting one source of uncertainty: (1) to address PRM uncertainty, we introduce \textit{reliability-aware belief updating} that measures how well each ensemble member explains the supervision data and updates the belief with an amortized belief network optimized by the evidence lower bound (ELBO); and (2) to tackle policy uncertainty, we propose \textit{conservatism-aware belief calibration} which further reweights the belief toward lower rewards to suppress overestimation. These two updates yield a reliability- and conservatism-aware Bayesian belief, whose expectation determines the process reward. Experiments on multimodal reasoning benchmarks indicate that BayesianPRM consistently yields more accurate process reward estimates while enhancing test-time scaling performance.
authors: Zhongjian Qiao, Zhixiang Zhou, Jiafei Lyu, Peisong Wang, Qiaosheng Zhang, Siyang Gao, Shuang Qiu
bullets: Identifies two PRM error sources: PRM uncertainty from limited or imperfect training and policy uncertainty causing systematic reward overestimation.
Represents process rewards with a Bayesian belief over a discretized reward hypothesis space using an ensemble.
Uses reliability-aware belief updating to assess ensemble members against supervision data via an ELBO-trained belief network.
Applies conservatism-aware calibration to shift belief toward lower rewards and reduce overestimation.
Experiments on multimodal reasoning benchmarks show more accurate process rewards and improved test-time scaling.

papers.abstract: Neural combinatorial optimization (NCO) rapidly produces high-quality solutions for problem structures encountered during training, but operational requirements may change after deployment and be communicated in natural language. We propose LangNCO, a framework that compiles instance-specific requirements into structured inference-time interventions for a frozen NCO solver, without changing the pretrained policy's architecture, learned input representation, or parameters. A pretrained LLM serves as a replaceable semantic front end, translating each requirement into a schema-validated domain-specific language (DSL) rule set. A deterministic Rule Executor applies the rules as nonexpansive hard action masks. Because local masking prevents immediate violations but does not ensure that a complete feasible continuation remains reachable, Critical-Offset Decoding extracts rule-referenced critical nodes and reallocates part of a fixed rollout budget to multi-strength biased rollouts. Using controlled task-specific language to isolate solver adaptation from open-ended language robustness, we evaluate a CVRP policy on road closures, time windows, vehicle assignments, visit-order requirements, all pairwise combinations, and twelve additional constraint types. LangNCO achieves 100% feasibility on the four primary datasets with mean reference gaps of 1.63--3.26%, 97.33--100% feasibility when separately generated rules are composed for pairwise constraints, and 98.67% feasibility across the additional constraints. These results demonstrate modular post-training adaptation of a frozen NCO solver through inspectable language-derived rules, without retraining.
bullets: A pretrained LLM converts requirements into schema-validated domain-specific rules.
A deterministic executor enforces rules through hard action masks, while Critical-Offset Decoding preserves feasible continuations via targeted biased rollouts.
Evaluated on CVRP tasks including road closures, time windows, vehicle assignments, visit-order constraints, combinations, and additional constraint types.
The method reaches 100% feasibility on four primary datasets, 97.33–100% for composed pairwise constraints, and 98.67% across additional constraints.
Results use controlled task-specific language, so open-ended language robustness is not directly assessed.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) has substantially improved Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) LLMs, but its outcome-level rewards provide only sparse supervision. On-Policy Distillation offers dense token-level feedback, yet requires a stronger compatible teacher, while on-policy self-distillation relies on hand-designed privileged information. We observe that the MoE architecture itself offers a way to resolve this dilemma, as increasing the activation budget per token exposes latent expert capacity and yields a potentially stronger teacher within the model. However, naive expansion degrades performance because newly co-activated experts are not optimized to work together. We therefore propose MoEvolve, a bidirectional distillation framework following a recovery-then-improvement strategy: we first restore the activation-expanded high-$k$ model and further strengthen it by exploiting its additional active capacity, then reverse the direction of distillation to transfer the enhanced capabilities back into the original low-$k$ configuration, retaining its inference-time activation budget. Across diverse MoE models and benchmarks, MoEvolve improves the initial models by up to $22.2$ domain-average points and outperforms same-budget RLVR baselines by up to $6.5$ points. Notably, the final low-$k$ models often surpass their activation-expanded teachers.
authors: Haoyu Chen, Jun Bai, Yang Liu, Jianfei Zhang, Wenge Rong
bullets: RLVR provides sparse outcome-level supervision, while on-policy distillation offers denser token-level feedback but typically needs a stronger compatible teacher.
Activating more experts per token exposes additional capacity, yet naive expansion harms performance because the experts are not jointly optimized.
MoEvolve first recovers and improves the high-k expanded model, then reverses distillation to strengthen the original low-k model without increasing inference cost.
Across diverse MoE models and benchmarks, it improves domain-average performance by up to 22.2 points and exceeds same-budget RLVR baselines by up to 6.5 points.
Final low-k models often outperform their activation-expanded teachers.

papers.abstract: Detecting faithfulness hallucinations in large language models (LLMs) is crucial for their safe deployment in high-stakes domains. Recent approaches address this by contrasting contextual against parametric knowledge utilization, yet measuring context reliance typically demands noticeable overhead, such as materializing attention maps, running additional forward passes, or training auxiliary probes. In this work, we show that context reliance can be estimated by projecting hidden states onto the dark space - directions that compose weakly with the unembedding matrix. Beyond its recognized function as an initial-token attention sink, we show that this subspace actively mediates context processing, and that its share of hidden-state norm - termed the Dark Matter Ratio (DMR) - provides a direct score of context utilization. Pairing DMR with a parametric knowledge score yields DarkLens, a lightweight faithfulness detector operating strictly within a single forward pass. Evaluated across three QA and summarization benchmarks on six open-weight LLMs (4B-13B parameters), DarkLens matches or outperforms a wide range of baselines without requiring extra forward passes or probe training.
authors: Alexandra Kuleshova, Andrey Volodichev, Daria Kotova, Alexey Zaytsev
bullets: Context reliance is estimated from the hidden-state norm in weakly unembedded directions, called the Dark Matter Ratio (DMR).
The dark space is shown to mediate context processing, beyond its known role as an initial-token attention sink.
Combining DMR with a parametric knowledge score yields the lightweight DarkLens detector.
Across three QA and summarization benchmarks and six open-weight LLMs, DarkLens matches or outperforms many baselines without extra passes or probe training.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards has become a scalable post-training paradigm for large language models. However, training agents over long-horizon interactions presents two challenges: using only terminal rewards makes turn-level credit assignment sparse and high-variance, while sequential mini-batch updates on a fixed rollout batch introduce policy staleness as the current policy drifts from the behavior policy. Existing approaches obtain denser credit via learned critics, process reward models, or on-policy distillation, but they rely on a value network, step-level annotations, or a stronger external teacher that increase training complexity. Meanwhile, importance sampling and clipping mitigate policy drift, but they do not specify a finite target that stops sequential updates from overshooting. In this work, we introduce TreeOPSD, a critic-free, tree-aware posterior self-distillation framework for long-horizon agentic reinforcement learning. Treating each interaction turn as a tree node, TreeOPSD branches alternative continuations from shared prefixes and recursively backs up terminal rewards into implicit turn-level credit. It then maps each credit to a closed-form, bounded teacher distribution parameterized by the likelihood ratio relative to the frozen behavior policy. Minimizing the divergence between this teacher and the student policy recovers the policy-gradient direction as the tangent at the behavior policy while bounding updates toward a finite target across sequential mini-batches. Empirically, TreeOPSD improves agentic capabilities across several competitive benchmarks and model scales, especially for long-horizon tasks, e.g., raising the average accuracy of Qwen3-30B-A3B-Thinking-2507 by 4.97 points over GRPO on the Deep Research setting.
authors: Heming Zou, Qi Wang, Yixiu Mao, Yun Qu, Yuyi Guo, Zeyuan Liu, Chenglin Li, Weijie Liu, Saiyong Yang, Xiangyang Ji
bullets: Addresses sparse, high-variance credit assignment from terminal-only rewards and policy drift during sequential updates.
Builds a tree of alternative continuations from shared interaction prefixes and recursively backs up terminal rewards into implicit turn-level credit.
Converts credit into a closed-form, bounded teacher distribution based on likelihood ratios to the frozen behavior policy.
Distillation matches policy-gradient behavior near the behavior policy while limiting overshooting toward a finite target.
Improves agentic performance across benchmarks and model scales, including a 4.97-point average accuracy gain over GRPO for Qwen3-30B-A3B-Thinking-2507 on Deep Research.

papers.abstract: Outcome-reward reinforcement learning such as GRPO gives every token of a search-agent rollout the same advantage, although the rollout exercises two capabilities: finding evidence and using it. We show that accuracy improves without grounding: Search-R1 raises accuracy on all seven QA benchmarks, yet on Bamboogle the evidence-supported share of correct answers falls from 84.0% to 42.9%. We attribute this to GRPO's credit assignment: rollouts that retrieve answer-bearing evidence are favoured in aggregate only in proportion to their accuracy gain over the rest, a grounding gap that answering from memory or misusing evidence shrinks or reverses. To address this, we propose Grounded Credit Assignment (GCA), which uses verifiable sub-outcomes (evidence retrieval and answer correctness) to correct search and answer credit separately: a wrong answer is blamed more than the search that found the evidence, and a correct answer that bypasses retrievable evidence is credited less. Never negative on evidence-finding search, the correction does not shrink with the grounding gap; capped at 10% of each token's advantage, it never overrides the outcome signal. Without extra models, rollouts, or training stages, GCA improves average EM over Search-R1 by 5.7 (Qwen2.5-3B) and 6.3 points (Qwen3-30B-A3B) and raises this share from 76.9% to 93.4%.
authors: Qirui Liu, Hao Chen, Yi Wen, Weijie Shi, Yao Zhao, Xianhe Chen, Hao Zhao, Xing Tang, Weihong Luo, Yuyu Luo
bullets: Outcome-only GRPO can improve QA accuracy while encouraging answers based on memory or misused evidence.
The proposed GCA separately credits evidence retrieval and answer correctness using verifiable sub-outcomes.
GCA penalizes unsupported correct answers and assigns more blame to incorrect answering than to successful evidence-finding search.
It requires no extra models, rollouts, or training stages, and its correction is capped so it cannot override the outcome signal.
Across two model settings, GCA improves average exact match by 5.7–6.3 points and raises evidence-supported correct answers from 76.9% to 93.4%.

papers.abstract: Alignment is known to change the output characteristics of large language models (LLMs). Base models tend to generate more diverse outputs, whereas aligned models tend to produce higher-quality outputs. The appropriate balance between the two depends on the task. Existing methods either require costly fine-tuning or, like temperature sampling, mainly improve lexical diversity rather than semantic diversity. We introduce a depth-aware FrankenMerging approach for controlling the diversity--quality trade-off between an aligned model and its base model without additional training. This approach combines the lower layers of an aligned model with the higher layers of its base model based on the hypothesis that lexical diversity is more closely associated with lower layers and semantic diversity with higher layers. Experiments showed that varying the number of layers taken from each model adjusts both diversity and quality. In most cases, the merged models exhibited higher semantic diversity than the aligned model, and at some split positions, they showed higher lexical diversity than both original models. They also demonstrated a better diversity--quality trade-off than temperature sampling in most settings. A supporting ablation, in which we reversed the merging order, yielded results largely consistent with the hypothesis.
authors: Yasuaki Sumita, Tomoharu Iwata, Toshiyuki Tanaka
bullets: Aligned LLMs generally favor quality, while base models favor diversity; the desired balance depends on the task.
The method merges lower layers from an aligned model with higher layers from its base model, motivated by links between lower layers and lexical diversity and higher layers and semantic diversity.
Changing the layer split controls both diversity and output quality.
Merged models usually achieved higher semantic diversity than the aligned model and sometimes higher lexical diversity than both source models.
Results generally showed a better diversity–quality trade-off than temperature sampling; reversed-order ablations supported the depth-based hypothesis.

papers.abstract: Computer-use agents (CUAs) are commonly evaluated against fixed task specifications, but users may omit requirements, add constraints, or require approval before consequential actions. Completing the benchmark instruction does not guarantee serving the person who asked. We introduce PersonaCUABench, which holds 74 tasks across 11 domains fixed and varies only who asks. A persona agent, playing one of 44 personas in four groups, rewrites each instruction in that user's own words and answers the CUA's questions, while the CUA sees only the dialogue, never the profile or the original instruction. Across nine backbones (3,330 runs), mean task completion falls by 36% relative to the original requests. The losses have two sources: in 59.9% of cells that lose points, the agent engages with what the user asked for and still gets it wrong, and 11.2% are stops the user requested that the checker scores as failures. Even when a persona request is fully completed, the user gives the top satisfaction rating in only 62.7% of cells, against 84.1% for the original requests. CUAs should therefore be evaluated not only on task completion but also on whether they meet the requirements and constraints users express. Code: https://github.com/MatrAIx-ai/PersonaCUABench. papers.abstract: Brain alignment of large language models (LLMs) offers a way to investigate representational similarities between LLMs and the human brain during language processing. While previous studies have mainly focused on passive language comprehension, little is known about such alignment during dialogue, in which speakers engage in both language production and comprehension. In this study, using fMRI data collected during dialogue, we examine brain alignment during language production and comprehension across LLM layers and brain regions. We assess its association with the intrinsic dimension (ID) of LLM representations and the contributions of several interpretable linguistic and communicative features. Our results reveal distinct patterns of brain alignment between production and comprehension, as well as strong associations with ID in brain regions associated with each processing mode. Furthermore, we show that the contributions of linguistic and communicative features also vary across processing modes, LLM layers, and brain regions.
authors: Yuko Nakagi, Yuya Chiba, Yasue Kishino
bullets: Uses fMRI collected during dialogue to examine LLM alignment with the brain.
Compares alignment during language production versus comprehension across LLM layers and brain regions.
Finds distinct alignment patterns for the two processing modes.
Reports strong associations between alignment and the intrinsic dimension of LLM representations in mode-relevant brain regions.
Shows that linguistic and communicative features contribute differently across processing modes, layers, and regions.

papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents increasingly rely on persistent memory to support long-term reasoning and personalized interactions. However, information collected from external sources can introduce security risks when untrusted claims (i.e., atomic statements) are later treated as authorized preferences, policies, or permissions. Existing defenses typically rely on content-based filtering or coarse-grained provenance tracking, which either fail to prevent unauthorized memory use or block legitimate information, sacrificing memory utility. To address these limitations, we propose SAFE-Mem, a fine-grained memory governance framework that improves security while preserving legitimate memory use. First, SAFE-Mem annotates each claim with three governance labels (i.e., kind, authority, and scope) to capture its provenance and permitted use. Second, governance-aware retrieval matches query requirements with claim permissions to block unauthorized influence while retaining legitimate information. Third, a governance-enabled memory graph connects source sentences, claims, and entities to support provenance tracking and efficient retrieval. Across four LLM backbones on MPBench and LoCoMo, SAFE-Mem attains the lowest attack success among defenses that retain legitimate memory, at least 77% below the strongest of them, and the highest answer accuracy of all evaluated defenses, improving it by up to 15%. The code is available at https://github.com/LVenum/SAFE-Mem.
authors: Haoming Li, Dingyi Kang, Xu Hu, Jinxin Yang, Zhu Xu, Chenru Wang, Yi Ge, Miao Yin, Guanpeng Li, Feng Chen, Bingzhe Li

Annotates claims with kind, authority, and scope governance labels.

Builds a memory graph linking source sentences, claims, and entities for provenance tracking and efficient retrieval.
Across four LLM backbones on MPBench and LoCoMo, it reports the lowest attack success among defenses retaining legitimate memory and the highest answer accuracy, improving accuracy by up to 15%.

papers.abstract: Small variations in prompt characteristics can meaningfully alter the semantics, tone, and contextual assumptions of large language model outputs. Such characteristics can involve group variables such as demographics or other sensitive latent attributes. Sensitivity to such input variables is undesirable when demographic information is causally irrelevant to the task, but might still be relevant for generation of semantically coherent responses. This makes the task of enforcing counterfactual invariance while preserving model utility difficult. To study this problem, we first show that standard model alignment recipes (such as reinforcement learning) increase differences in response quality across demographics, while improving overall response quality, ultimately amplifying what is known as counterfactual bias. To address this, we develop a policy gradient technique involving a group-level reward function that operates on matched pairs of counterfactual prompts. For completeness, we build a dataset of controlled counterfactual prompt pairs and design an evaluation that separately measures cases where demographic information is causally relevant to the answer. Finally, we validate our findings on several fairness benchmarks. We demonstrate that our methods reduce counterfactual differences while preserving overall response quality and that the models continue to adapt appropriately when such sensitive information is relevant.
authors: Basar Demir, Emily Shen, Ksheeraj Sai Vepuri, Sourabh Kulkarni, Harihar Subramanyam, Ankit Jain, Nan Jiang, Chirag Nagpal
bullets: Standard alignment methods can improve overall quality while increasing response-quality disparities across demographic counterfactuals.
The proposed approach trains on matched counterfactual prompt pairs using a group-level reward function.
The authors create controlled counterfactual prompt-pair data and an evaluation that distinguishes relevant from irrelevant demographic information.
Experiments on several fairness benchmarks show reduced counterfactual differences without sacrificing overall response quality.
Models still adapt appropriately when demographic information is causally relevant to the answer.

papers.abstract: Language models often abandon a correct answer when the prompt contains a cue, a hint toward a wrong option such as "I think the answer is B." Sycophancy and related biases show this failure. They are often studied separately and blamed on alignment. We test this view causally, tracing the attention heads behind these biases through the stages of two post-training pipelines. In multiple-choice tests on most models, four cue types rely largely on the same few heads, a shared circuit already present in pretrained models. Most base models follow cues in plain text. Fine-tuning a base model on about 200 generic assistant examples without cues activates these heads in chat format, so cue-following can be a side effect of assistant tuning. The final reinforcement learning (RL) stage strengthens the effect of cues in almost every comparison. In Tulu-3-8B and OLMo-2-7B, we swap the attention patterns of six middle layers between the RL checkpoint and its predecessor. For suggested-answer cues, this shifts each checkpoint's cue effect most of the way to the other's level. Post-training thus seems to change when and how strongly models use this circuit. Mitigation for these multiple-choice biases could target this circuit.
authors: Prakhar Gupta, Terry Jingchen Zhang, Zhijing Jin
bullets: Several cue-driven biases, including sycophancy-like behavior, rely on largely the same small set of attention heads.

papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable success in complex reasoning through explicit Chain-of-Thought (CoT), but the associated computational overhead and token verbosity remain significant barriers to efficiency. While implicit reasoning in continuous latent spaces offers a promising alternative, existing methods like Coconut and CODI often rely on fixed-length latent sequences and suffer from representational collapse. In this paper, we propose Sep-Latent, an adaptive implicit reasoning framework that utilizes separator tokens as structural semantic anchors. By introducing an Attention-Decay mechanism, we force the model to aggregate and compress reasoning logic into these anchors during training. We then align explicit and implicit pathways through multi-level distillation across all layers to ensure logical consistency. Crucially, Sep-Latent enables dynamic reasoning depth by adaptively terminating the latent thinking phase based on query complexity. Experimental results on the GSM8k-Aug benchmark show that Sep-Latent achieves an accuracy of 56.8\% with an average of only 5.4 tokens, significantly outperforming prior fixed-length implicit models in efficiency while narrowing the performance gap with explicit CoT. Further analysis via PCA and symbolic variant testing confirms that our method ensures semantic grounding and exhibits superior robustness to perturbations.
authors: Yinlong Xu, Jianfeng Huang, Zhengdong Zhou, Mingjie Lin, Fuyu Lv, Dan Ou, Hongxia Xu, Jian Wu
bullets: Targets the verbosity and computational cost of explicit Chain-of-Thought reasoning, while addressing collapse and fixed-length limitations in prior implicit methods.
Uses separator tokens as semantic anchors, with Attention-Decay to aggregate reasoning and multi-level distillation to align explicit and implicit pathways.
Adaptively terminates latent reasoning according to query complexity rather than using a fixed latent sequence length.
On GSM8k-Aug, reaches 56.8% accuracy using an average of 5.4 tokens, outperforming prior fixed-length implicit models in efficiency.
PCA and symbolic-variant analyses support semantic grounding and robustness to perturbations; scope is primarily demonstrated on GSM8k-Aug.

papers.abstract: Language models generalize beyond their training corpus to learn linguistic phenomena (Patil et al., 2024; Misra and Mahowald, 2024), showing that there exists indirect evidence driving learning. Prior work has inferred that indirect evidence exists without identifying its character or considered specific hypotheses about what it might be. We explore an alternative bottom-up method for identifying indirect evidence. We use influence functions (Koh and Liang, 2017) to measure how individual training sentences affect model predictions in 15 grammatical phenomena from BLiMP (Warstadt et al., 2020). We filter out a phenomenon's direct evidence using hand-constructed rules and take the 60,000 most influential remaining sentences as indirect evidence. This indirect evidence substantially affects learning: retraining without it lowers held-out accuracy more than removing a matched random group for every phenomenon across five models (by a median of 12 points). We characterize the indirect evidence by its similarity to our direct evidence filters: it (partially) meets the filters' structural conditions at a median of 4.7 times the rate of a matched random group. Finally, clustering phenomena by indirect-evidence overlap recovers three of the five BLiMP categories that include multiple phenomena, suggesting that this method can reveal linguistic relationships.
authors: William Dai, Zhenghao Herbert Zhou, Maya Viswanathan, Robert Frank
bullets: Studies indirect evidence for 15 grammatical phenomena from BLiMP across five language models.

Clustering phenomena by shared indirect evidence recovers three of five multi-phenomenon BLiMP categories.

papers.abstract: Federated Learning (FL) is a powerful machine learning framework that allows building a global model from the contributions of multiple, distributed clients, while ensuring the privacy of their local data. However, its heavy computational and communication overheads challenge its use for contemporary AI workloads such as natural language processing (NLP) and multimodal analysis. For this reason, this paper presents a novel small language model that leverages byte-level text and multimodal data processing, enhanced by a linear attention mechanism, to enable manageable Federated Learning of NLP and multimodal analysis tasks. The proposed model, nicknamed FederatedBytes, manages to process text and any other data types, including images, by treating its input as a mere sequence of bytes, while its lean linear attention mechanism allows abating the overall memory and computational footprint. To prove the effectiveness of the proposed model we have carried out an extensive performance evaluation on sentiment analysis tasks in multilingual and multimodal settings over the Multilingual Amazon Reviews and ScienceQA datasets. The experimental results show that FederatedBytes has been able to outperform comparable models such as ByT5 and LSTM, achieving higher accuracy while significantly reducing memory and communication overheads.
authors: Ali Sarabadani, Massimo Piccardi, Mehran Abolhasan, Farzad Tofigh, Ian Zhou, Justin Lipman
bullets: Targets the computational and communication costs that hinder federated NLP and multimodal learning.
Processes text, images, and other modalities uniformly as byte sequences, without tokenization.
Uses lean linear attention to reduce memory and computational requirements.
Evaluated on multilingual and multimodal sentiment analysis using Multilingual Amazon Reviews and ScienceQA.
The abstract reports higher accuracy than ByT5 and LSTM, alongside substantially lower memory and communication overheads.

figures.caption: Figure 2: The FederatedBytes Inference Pipeline. An illustrative walkthrough of the running example (“This product is amazing...”) as it passes through the three stages of the model architecture. Stage 1: Input text is patched and processed by the Hierarchical Encoder (Conv1d) to reduce sequence length. Stage 2: Patches are contextualized via Performer linear attention. Stage 3: Features are pooled for final classification.

Figure 1: End-to-end FederatedBytes Architecture. The pipeline operates in three sequential stages tailored for efficient federated learning: Stage 1 (Input Processing): Raw multilingual text is encoded into UTF-8 bytes. These bytes are compressed into patch embeddings using a Hierarchical Patch Encoder (1D Convolution→ ReLU→Adaptive Pooling) to reduce sequence length. Stage 2 (Memory-Efficient Processing): The patch sequence is processed by a Transformer Encoder utilizing the Performer mechanism. This approximates the full attention matrix using Orthogonal Random Features (ORFs) Yu et al. (2016), achieving linear O(L) time and space complexity. Stage 3 (Prediction & Classification): The encoded representations are aggregated via global mean pooling, normalized via BatchNorm, and passed through a linear classification head to generate final class logits.

papers.abstract: Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) have brought impressive performance across diverse tasks; however, shortcomings remain in logical reasoning, including inconsistencies under linguistic variation. To improve the reasoning capacity of LLMs, we must be able to accurately measure their reasoning capacity. Current benchmarks primarily report single accuracy numbers on selected reasoning tasks. Such a performance-based evaluation methodology says little about a model's generalization capacity in reasoning. To address this limitation, we argue for a different evaluation paradigm, called competence-based evaluation (CBE), which tests whether models reliably apply the same competence across a family of problems. A parameterized generator scales complexity while keeping the required competence fixed, and matched answer-preserving presentations test correctness beyond one formulation. We instantiate CBE on elementary ordering tasks, scaling input size while varying presentations of the same ordering rule. Across six GPT and Qwen models, performance is reasonably good over bounded complexity ranges, but even strong models fail the competence condition across the tested family. Chain-of-thought and GRPO extend strong performance without resolving all tested failures; supervised LoRA shows little held-out transfer. CBE provides diagnostic profiles and an evaluation protocol that can grow with future models.
bullets: Standard benchmarks may overstate reasoning ability because they measure performance on selected tasks rather than generalization across a problem family.
CBE uses parameterized generators to increase complexity while preserving the required competence, plus answer-preserving reformulations to test robustness.
Applied to elementary ordering tasks across six GPT and Qwen models, the evaluation found good performance within bounded ranges but failures of consistent competence across the tested family.
Chain-of-thought and GRPO improved or extended strong performance but did not eliminate all failures; supervised LoRA showed limited held-out transfer.
The protocol produces diagnostic competence profiles and is designed to scale with future models.

Accuracy can decline less than robust correctness, while shared errors can keep invariance high. Chance-corrected profiles for both vocabularies appear in Appendix E.

papers.title: Competence-Based Evaluation of Logical Reasoning in Large Language Models
papers.tldr: Competence-based evaluation tests whether LLMs consistently apply the same reasoning skill across increasingly complex and differently phrased problems, revealing failures hidden by single accuracy scores.

papers.abstract: Tree search enhances multi-step reasoning in large language models (LLMs), yet prevailing methods expand every step with a fixed budget, irrespective of the marginal utility of expansion. We first show, across existing search algorithms, that continuations sampled from a shared intermediate state are largely duplicates and collapse to a few distinct answers. Critically, we find that the semantic dispersion of sibling actions predicts the redundancy of their downstream continuations, permitting a subtree's budget to be fixed before expansion. An information-theoretic analysis motivates this: treating the per-step budget as the Monte Carlo sample size for estimating a step's residual answer entropy, we derive a sufficient budget that shrinks with sibling dispersion. We accordingly propose $\textbf{Uncertainty-Aware Allocation}$ (UAA), a training-free framework that decouples value from uncertainty: values determine which candidates are promising, while uncertainty, estimated from sibling dispersion at no additional model cost, determines how many merit expansion, via uncertainty-aware pruning and uncertainty-aware budgeting. Across mathematical reasoning, logical reasoning, and planning benchmarks, UAA reduces token usage by up to $90\%$ and latency by up to $9\times$ at comparable accuracy, generalizing across four tree search algorithms and both open- and closed-source LLMs.
authors: Jianguo Huang, Zhiyi Lyu, Fuxiang Zhang, Yanchen Deng, Deheng Ye, Bo An
bullets: Sibling continuations from the same intermediate state are often redundant and collapse to a few distinct answers.
Semantic dispersion among sibling actions predicts downstream redundancy and can estimate uncertainty before subtree expansion.
UAA is training-free and separates candidate value from uncertainty: value selects promising candidates, while uncertainty controls pruning and expansion budgets.
Across reasoning and planning benchmarks, UAA reduces token use by up to 90% and latency by up to 9× at comparable accuracy.
The framework generalizes across four tree-search algorithms and both open- and closed-source LLMs.

papers.abstract: Chain-of-Thought (CoT) faithfulness matters for monitoring, explaining and safely deploying large language models, yet it has been studied mostly in English. Languages differ in level, the amount of text available to learn from, so models know less in lower-resource languages, which may change how much they rely on their reasoning. To our knowledge, we are the first to relate CoT faithfulness to both resource level and task type (knowledge- or reasoning-intensive). On parallel multiple-choice questions from Multilingual Massive Multitask Language Understanding (MMMLU) in eight languages, faithfulness rises as resource level falls on knowledge-intensive tasks but not on reasoning-intensive ones, a gap that points the same way across four models and several faithfulness measures. We propose, and find support for, the Reliance Hypothesis: models rely more on their reasoning when they cannot recall the answer, as in lower-resource languages on knowledge-intensive tasks. Model confidence partly explains the effect of resource level, but not the knowledge-reasoning gap. Languages in which models are less confident rely more on reasoning, yet less confident answers within a language do not, a Simpson's paradox. In lower-resource languages, models rely on their reasoning for more answers, not more strongly for each. CoT monitoring may therefore be most informative in lower-resource languages, where it is least often validated.
authors: Lucas Resck, Jingyi Sun, Qianli Wang, Isabelle Augenstein, Anna Korhonen
bullets: Studies CoT faithfulness across eight languages, four models, and multiple measures using parallel MMMLU questions.
Faithfulness rises as language resource level falls on knowledge-intensive tasks, but not on reasoning-intensive tasks.
Findings support the Reliance Hypothesis: limited knowledge access increases reliance on stated reasoning.
Model confidence partly explains the resource-level effect, but not the gap between knowledge- and reasoning-intensive tasks.
Lower-resource languages may be especially valuable for CoT monitoring, despite receiving less validation.

papers.abstract: Standard autoregressive language models generate text sequentially, but revision requires referring back to tokens in the input context or those already generated. Causal Edit Serialization (CES) is introduced as a framework for expressing such revisions within the same causal token stream. Special pointer tokens are paired with predicted source addresses, allowing insertion, deletion, replacement, copying and movement to be localized explicitly. A lightweight localization head and dual-index rotary position encoding support both address prediction and conditioning on previously emitted pointers, while retaining a standard causal attention mask. A pretraining procedure combines ordinary language modeling with serialized repairs derived from random corruptions, model-generated edits and repeated text. Across model scales and editing baselines, CES models demonstrate complete applied edits with modestly higher clean-text bits per byte than clean autoregressive models. Supervised and reinforcement-learning post-training provide a grammatical-error-correction proof of concept, producing more beneficial than harmful changes under reference-blind model judging. Correct repair programs also improve subsequent text prediction while the original context and its cached states are retained. CES provides a common interface for generation and localized revision, with potential extensions to iterative refinement and additional pointer-addressed transformations.
bullets: Supports insertion, deletion, replacement, copying, and movement through explicit source-address pointers.
Uses a localization head and dual-index rotary position encoding while preserving standard causal attention.
Pretraining combines language modeling with repairs from random corruptions, generated edits, and repeated text.
Across scales and baselines, models complete edits with only modestly worse clean-text bits per byte than standard models.
A grammatical-error-correction proof of concept shows more beneficial than harmful edits, and correct repairs improve later prediction while cached context is retained.

papers.abstract: Recent studies have shown that position bias remains a critical vulnerability in large language models (LLMs), undermining both the integrity of multiple-choice evaluations and the reliability of retrieval-augmented generation. However, existing understanding of this phenomenon is largely derived from studies with limited model coverage and English-centric benchmarks, leaving the behavior of frontier models and diverse languages underexplored. In this work, we conduct a comprehensive investigation of position bias across model scales ranging from billion-level to trillion-level parameters, covering both multiple-choice and multi-document tasks in five languages. Our experiments reveal that while position bias remains noticeable in small-scale models and Non-English languages, increasing model scale and employing standard Chain-of-Thought prompting significantly mitigate this issue. Moreover, we demonstrate that emerging \emph{thinking models} with extended reasoning capabilities are nearly immune to position bias, suggesting a costly but general approach toward resolving this vulnerability.
authors: Yining Li, Huayang Li, Lemao Liu, Taro Watanabe

papers.abstract: Reusing a Transformer block across depth increases computation without replicating its parameters, but successive passes have no dedicated state through which positions can exchange compact summaries of their causal prefix. We introduce the causal latent workspace Transformer: an anchored, four-round shared-depth architecture in which each position writes gated vectors into prefix-specific latent slots and retrieves a content-addressed summary before the next shared block application. This path complements causal self-attention while the original input embedding remains accessible at every round. Across three byte-level corpora, three seeds, and two matched parameter budgets, the proposed model achieves the best mean held-out perplexity in five of six settings against five Transformer controls. At 101.71M parameters it leads on WikiText-103 raw, enwik8, and TinyStories, reaching perplexities 2.7820, 2.7843, and 1.6823; these improve upon the strongest non-workspace control on each corpus by 1.06%, 0.73%, and 1.01%. All nine seed-labelled comparisons at this budget favor the workspace. At 0.918M parameters it leads on WikiText-103 and TinyStories, whereas a conditioned loop is stronger on enwik8. Architectural ablations show that adding the workspace improves upon the anchored loop in all six settings and support refreshing its causal summaries at each round. Together, these results identify a causal, content-addressable prefix workspace as an effective structural augmentation of looped Transformers.
bullets: Addresses the lack of dedicated state for causal prefix information in parameter-shared Transformer loops.
Uses an anchored four-round architecture with gated writes to causal latent slots and content-addressed retrieval before each shared block pass.
The workspace achieves the best mean held-out perplexity in five of six settings across three byte-level corpora and two parameter budgets.
At 101.71M parameters, it leads on WikiText-103 raw, enwik8, and TinyStories; at 0.918M, it leads on WikiText-103 and TinyStories.
Ablations show consistent gains over the anchored loop and support refreshing causal summaries each round; a conditioned loop remains stronger on small-budget enwik8.

papers.abstract: Fine-tuning large language models (LLMs) on proprietary records enables domain adaptation but introduces two challenges: (i) privacy leakage of memorized private data, such as personally identifiable information (PII), and (ii) balancing private data removal with utility preservation. Existing defenses, including data sanitization and differential privacy, often degrade performance, while privacy-neuron editing lacks a PII-free reference to distinguish identity-specific neurons from those supporting useful text. We propose JEPA-Prune, a post-hoc neuron pruning framework guided by a model trained exclusively on PII-free views. Alongside the fine-tuned private model, JEPA-Prune, trains a public model on surrogate and masked views of the same records using a joint-embedding predictive architecture (JEPA), capturing domain knowledge without identifiers. A cross-model representation probe quantifies deviations between private representations of leaked records and this PII-free reference. Integrated gradients and a scale-invariant specificity score then identify PII-responsive neurons, which are pruned without retraining. Experiments show that pruning just 1.6% of neurons reduces PII inference accuracy by up to 7.4x and PII extraction recall by up to 13.9x, while keeping unseen-text perplexity within 16% of that of the unpruned model for most LLMs. In contrast, privacy-neuron editing increases perplexity by at least 26x.
bullets: Fine-tuning on proprietary records can memorize PII, creating a privacy–utility trade-off.
JEPA-Prune trains a PII-free public reference model on surrogate and masked views of the same records.
Cross-model representation probing, integrated gradients, and a scale-invariant specificity score identify neurons associated with PII.
Pruning 1.6% of neurons reduces PII inference accuracy by up to 7.4× and extraction recall by up to 13.9×.
Unseen-text perplexity generally remains within 16% of the unpruned model, outperforming privacy-neuron editing in utility preservation.

papers.title: Prune the Leaky Neurons: Mitigating Private Data Leakage in Fine-Tuned LLMs via Joint-Embedding-Guided Pruning

papers.abstract: Split language models keep input text on a client but send intermediate representations to a server. Attacks can reconstruct text from these messages. Comparing privacy evaluations is difficult when attackers see different messages, know different model weights or use different datasets and recovery measures. We present LLM-Attacker, a framework that records these choices and lets researchers check, compare and extend an evaluation. Compatible attacks reuse recorded messages, and their predictions are saved for independent scoring. The scoring rule requires a linked undefended reference before a defence can pass. Reports also identify attacks that remain untested. In a controlled GPT-2 experiment, adding gradients returned during training increased token recovery from 94.20% to 97.38% and exact-document recovery from 13.71% to 37.77%. The 95% interval for the token gain lay above the two-percentage-point threshold fixed before testing. This experiment is shared with a companion study; here, it tests how the evaluation responds to a change in attacker access. Further studies measure how corpus choice and compression defences affect recovery, compare an adapted published attack with its reference implementation, and test the measurement code. The framework reports implementation checks separately from measured attack effectiveness. Each privacy claim should state the attacker, dataset and scoring rule, report its controls and identify untested attacks.
bullets: Addresses inconsistent evaluations caused by differing attacker access, model knowledge, datasets, and recovery metrics.
Records messages and attack settings so compatible attacks can be reused, independently scored, and compared.
Requires a linked undefended reference before a defence can pass and separates implementation checks from attack effectiveness.
In a controlled GPT-2 experiment, adding training-time gradients increased token recovery from 94.20% to 97.38% and exact-document recovery from 13.71% to 37.77%.
Supports further analysis of corpus choice, compression defences, attack implementations, and measurement code; claims should state controls and untested attacks.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces LLM-Attacker, a framework for evaluating privacy in split and distributed LLM systems. It provides a unified approach to red-teaming LLM architectures.
papers.title: The LLM-Attacker: A Unified Red-Team Framework for Privacy Evaluation of Split and Distributed LLM Systems
papers.tldr: LLM-Attacker standardizes and audits privacy evaluations for split and distributed LLMs by tracking attacker assumptions, enabling reproducible comparisons, and exposing untested attacks.

papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) unlearning aims to forget certain information while preserving others, without retraining from scratch. SoTA methods such as NPO, SimNPO, and SatImp balance forgetting and retain through whole model fine-tuning, while FOM-UL explores selective layer updates. Prior works show that suppressing target information can damage retained knowledge. This trade-off can vary across layers even under the same unlearning loss. In this work, we propose Confidence-Weighted Layerwise Unlearning (CoLU), which combines a novel confidence-weighted forgetting and retain regularization while updating a single selected transformer layer, rather than the whole model for unlearning. To reduce CoLU compute cost, we further propose Brief Layer Screening (BLS), which uses a newly defined normalized forgetting-retention (NFR) score to first rank layers through a brief unlearning trials using a subset of forgetting dataset and fewer epochs. BLS pre-selects top-k ranked layer candidates, which will then be fully profiled using full data analysis. BLS is proven to reduce the runtime of CoLU by 60.2-79.7% with almost the same performance. On TOFU dataset, CoLU improves both forgetting and retention over NPO, SatImp, and GA-based FOM-UL in all six TOFU settings, and over SimNPO in five of the six settings. On MUSE Books and News datasets, CoLU achieves the highest retained KnowMem and the PrivLeak closest to zero among the compared SOTA unlearning methods. CoLU presents a new record performance in both unlearning and retain in most settings up to date. Moreover, across the measured settings, average CoLU GPU memory usage is 77.4% to 79.5% lower than full-model unlearning.
authors: Jingkai Guo, Ziyi Zhao, Chaitali Chakrabarti, Deliang Fan
bullets: Addresses the risk that suppressing target information damages retained knowledge, with trade-offs varying across layers.
Uses confidence-weighted forgetting and retain regularization while updating only a selected layer.
Brief Layer Screening (BLS) ranks candidate layers using a normalized forgetting-retention score before full profiling.
BLS reduces CoLU runtime by 60.2–79.7% with nearly unchanged performance.
Across TOFU, MUSE Books, and News, CoLU generally improves forgetting and retention while using 77.4–79.5% less GPU memory than full-model unlearning.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes CoLU, a layerwise unlearning method for LLMs. It balances forgetting and retention by updating specific layers, contributing to the understanding of LLM memory and adaptation.
papers.title: CoLU: Confidence-Weighted Layerwise Unlearning for Large Language Models

papers.abstract: As assistants move from reactive answering toward proactive intervention, memory changes role: it no longer only supplies the answer to a query, it determines whether and when to speak at all. Prior work in this setting hands the system the relevant fact in context; we study the regime that makes the problem hard, where the evidence justifying an intervention must be mined from a long-horizon personal memory. We introduce ProPerMem, a benchmark for memory-driven proactive assistance (MPA), pairing egocentric video with year-long, distractor-rich user memories (~618K tokens on average), human-verified trigger windows, and a protocol that scores content and timing jointly. Every baseline we evaluate performs poorly (at most 15%), including frontier models given summarized or retrieval-augmented memory. A controlled study explains why: with oracle evidence delivered inside the trigger window GPT-5.3-Chat reaches 96%; letting it choose the timing drops it to 38%, and replacing oracle evidence with retrieval drops it to 15%. Content and timing are separately necessary, and missing either is catastrophic. Guided by this, we build ProPerAgent (Proactive Personalized Agent) with a plug-and-play harness that surfaces memory from a graph-organized store and gates it down to what is worth interrupting for, plus a lightweight RL stage that curbs early and repeated firing. Without any training, ProPerAgent lifts strict accuracy from below 10% to 37.5% on Qwen3.8-27B and 38% on GPT-5.3-Chat; RL post-training reaches 42.4%.
authors: Shenglai Zeng, Xiao Yang, Tiffany Ma, Xinyuan Zhang, Nanshu Wang, Deren Lei, Kai Sun, Xilun Chen, Tammy Stark, Xianhui Zhu, Yuetai Li, Rulin Shao, Tianxin Wei, Rakesh Wanga, Anuj Kumar, Jiliang Tang, Wen-tau Yih, Xin Luna Dong
bullets: Introduces ProPerMem, a benchmark combining egocentric video, year-long distractor-rich memories, verified trigger windows, and joint content-timing evaluation.
Shows that both evidence retrieval and intervention timing are essential: performance collapses when either is not provided by an oracle.
Presents ProPerAgent, which uses graph-organized memory retrieval and interruption gating, followed by lightweight reinforcement learning to reduce premature and repeated interventions.
Improves strict accuracy from below 10% to 37.5–38% without training, and to 42.4% after RL post-training.
Scope: evaluated results remain substantially below oracle-evidence performance, highlighting the difficulty of long-horizon memory retrieval and timing.

papers.abstract: Methods for training language models on sensitive data differ in how they balance capability gains against the risk of leaking private information. In this paper, we present a controlled comparison of data-level and training-level interventions for navigating the capability-privacy tradeoff on synthetic medical records with canaries to probe for leakage. Direct finetuning performs best on capability metrics but leads to the most privacy leakage, while DP-SGD reduces leakage at substantial cost to capabilities. Generating synthetic data from these records offers a more favorable balance, particularly when guided by a uniqueness-aware instruction to replace private details. Relative to naive paraphrasing, privacy-aware rewriting improves privacy protection across a variety of different rewriting models. We also find that more capable rewriting models generally reduce the risks of downstream privacy leakage, although held-out fit does not improve monotonically and increased test-time compute yields inconsistent gains. Overall, these results highlight privacy-aware rewriting as a promising direction for achieving a more favorable trade-off between capabilities and empirical privacy compared to other training-level methods, and our evaluation framework supports comparisons of future models and methods.
authors: Zihao Zhao, Avi Schwarzschild, Casey Meehan, Katherine Lee, Zhili Feng, Dylan Sam
bullets: Direct finetuning achieves the strongest capabilities but causes the most privacy leakage.
DP-SGD reduces leakage substantially, but with significant capability costs.
Synthetic-data generation, especially uniqueness-aware rewriting, provides a more favorable balance.
Privacy-aware rewriting outperforms naive paraphrasing for privacy protection across rewriting models.
More capable rewriting models generally lower downstream leakage, but held-out fit and extra test-time compute show inconsistent trends.

papers.abstract: Recent work suggests that switching optimizers between pretraining and subsequent training stages incurs a performance cost, but systematic investigation of this phenomenon is lacking. We study the mismatch between AdamW and Muon optimizers by pretraining 1.2B Llama-3 models from scratch while varying the proportion of updates taken with each optimizer, and similarly interpolating between the two optimizers during continued pretraining and supervised fine-tuning (SFT). Surprisingly, we find little evidence of a meaningful optimizer mismatch penalty: final performance is largely explained by the independent effects of the pretraining and post-training optimizers, with downstream performance generally improving as the proportion of Muon updates during SFT increases. Although matching the pretraining optimizer can reduce forgetting during SFT, this does not translate into improved final benchmark performance. We further evaluate AdamW and Muon for task-general SFT of open-weight models, across the Llama and Qwen families up to 14B parameters, where Muon remains competitive with AdamW, despite these models having been pretrained with AdamW. Together, our results suggest that the choice of optimizer for post-training can be made largely independently of the optimizer used during pretraining.
authors: Xinyu Zhao, Davis Wertheimer, Ashutosh Sharma, Rameswar Panda, Paul Pu Liang
bullets: Studies optimizer mixtures across pretraining, continued pretraining, and supervised fine-tuning.
Finds final performance is mostly explained by the separate effects of the pretraining and post-training optimizers.
Increasing Muon updates during SFT generally improves downstream performance.
Matching the pretraining optimizer may reduce SFT forgetting but does not improve final benchmark results.
Muon remains competitive with AdamW for task-general SFT of Llama and Qwen models up to 14B parameters, despite AdamW pretraining.

papers.abstract: Recent advances in AI make Recursive Self-Improvement (RSI) increasingly plausible. Large Language Models (LLMs) can already propose, select, and run Machine Learning (ML) experiments. However, the space of possible design choices in ML is vast. An LLM that proposes an experiment needs a reliable intuition of whether it is worth running given the timing constraints of long training runs. In this work, we measure such intuition in current frontier LLMs by evaluating how accurately they predict the impact of self-generated ML experiment ideas before these are put into training runs. To this end, we construct a dataset of 288 LLM-proposed ideas on eight MLE-bench tasks. We then prompt five frontier LLMs (GPT-6 Astra, Claude Opus 5.5, Claude Fable 5.1, Kimi K3, and GLM-5.3) to predict the impact of each idea and compare their predictions with the actual outcomes after training. We report four main findings. First, LLM predictions are substantially better than random chance but far from accurate: even the best model, Claude Opus 5.5, explains only half of the variance in outcomes (R^2 = 0.49). Second, we notice that all tested models systematically underestimate the magnitude of the changes. Third, prediction quality varies widely across tasks. Finally, the choice of the coding harness that actually implements the ideas has little effect on outcomes, and we find no evidence of self-preference. Higher reasoning settings and additional context lead to modest gains. Overall, our results show that current LLMs have useful but limited intuition about which ML ideas will work. We release our dataset to support further study.
authors: Ayush Bansal, Aldo Pareja, Sean Klein, Serge Didenko, Artem Lukoianov
bullets: Evaluates predictions for 288 LLM-generated ideas across eight MLE-bench tasks using five frontier LLMs.
The best model explains 49% of outcome variance, indicating useful but imperfect predictive ability.
All tested models systematically underestimate the magnitude of experimental effects.
Prediction quality varies substantially by task; more reasoning and context provide modest improvements.
Coding-harness choice has little impact on outcomes, with no evidence of self-preference; the dataset is released.
