papers.abstract: Modern Transformers rely on many scale-control mechanisms, including normalization, residual scaling, attention temperatures, loss weighting, and adaptive updates. To explain how these mechanisms maintain scale consistency, we introduce Neural Dimensional Analysis (NDA), a unified framework based on dimensional consistency. We define neural units that specify how tensors rescale and which quantities can be added, just as physical units do in physics. Our rules match residual units, nondimensionalize attention and gate inputs, combine losses across units, and convert gradient units into parameter units. We implement NDA through dimensionless Unit Violation Indices (UVI) for diagnosing scale mismatches within Transformers, a unit-consistent multi-loss objective, and the Gauge-Canonical Transformer (GCT) with normalized coordinates and orthogonalized residual additions. In language-model experiments spanning 51M to 1B parameters, GCT remains stable during training across a broad sixteenfold learning-rate range, outperforming Pre-LN, LLaMA-style, and QK-Norm in 124M validation loss at tuned learning rates. GCT's normalized residual stream also shows improved robustness to quantization. At 1B parameters, calibrated per-tensor int8 quantization increases GCT's validation loss by only 0.009 nats, compared with up to 5.51 nats for the baselines. Vision and physics-informed neural network experiments further confirm NDA's benefits beyond language modeling. These results establish dimensional consistency as a neural network design principle.
authors: Bum Jun Kim, Makoto Kawano, Yusuke Iwasawa, Yutaka Matsuo
bullets: Motivated by the many scale-control mechanisms required in modern Transformers, including normalization, residual scaling, attention temperatures, and loss weighting.
Defines neural units and dimensional-consistency rules for tensor rescaling, valid additions, attention and gate inputs, multi-loss objectives, and gradient-to-parameter conversion.
Introduces Unit Violation Indices for diagnosing scale mismatches and the Gauge-Canonical Transformer with normalized coordinates and orthogonalized residual additions.
Across language, vision, and physics-informed experiments, the approach supports stable training over a broad learning-rate range and improved quantization robustness.
In the reported 1B-parameter experiment, calibrated per-tensor int8 quantization increased validation loss by 0.009 nats for GCT versus up to 5.51 nats for baselines.

papers.abstract: Long-context inference makes the key-value (KV) cache a major memory bottleneck for large language models. We propose BELT, a low-rank KV cache compression framework. Its key-side objective targets attention distributions rather than raw keys or pre-softmax logits, yielding a quadratic surrogate with a closed-form low-rank solution. A learned global rank allocator uses differentiable soft selection during training and hard selection at deployment to meet a user-specified component budget. Experiments demonstrate improved model quality under aggressive compression and increased decoding throughput at comparable accuracy. Evaluated across three LLMs and multiple benchmarks, BELT achieves up to 70% low-rank KV cache compression while outperforming the strongest baseline by up to 23.3 points on LongBench, and up to 17.8x overall KV cache reduction when combined with quantization. With Triton-based GPU kernels and a quantized cache, BELT delivers up to 2.7x speedup for the attention module and 3.3x end-to-end decoding throughput.
authors: Yaoyang Liu, Shuwei Shen, Jincheng Tang, Jinguang Liu, Jinbao Xue, Hailong Yang, Ke Zhang, Yinjun Wu

papers.title: BELT : BEhavior-Aligned Low-Rank KV Cache Compression with Learned Top-k Rank Allocation

papers.abstract: The design of attention mechanisms in long-context large language models faces an ``impossible triangle'' among KV cache size, training and prefill FLOPs, and model quality. GQA achieves strong quality but incurs high KV cache overhead; alternative approaches such as MLA and MFA can compress the cache, but MLA suffers from quality loss while MFA substantially increases training and prefill compute. We propose Virtual Head Attention (VHA), which simultaneously improves all three vertices through two lightweight linear operations: Q Premix applies a near-identity transformation to queries within each KV group to recover virtual head diversity from halved physical query heads, and Linear Postmix fuses inter-head features via a low-rank $I + AB^\top$ residual structure. Since VHA introduces no nonlinear operations, Premix can be folded into the query projection and Postmix into the output projection at inference time, reducing the model to a standard GQA-2 architecture that directly reuses all existing GQA inference optimizations. With only two KV heads, the group size in large models readily reaches 64, fully exploiting Tensor Core parallelism during decoding. Across four scales with 4K-context 50B-token pretraining, VHA consistently surpasses the standard GQA baseline at every scale ($+$0.05\% to $+$0.81\%), while reducing KV cache by $4\times$ vs.\ GQA-8 at dense scales and $2\times$ vs.\ GQA-4 at the MoE scale, and lowering training and prefill FLOPs by 7.9\% (1.7B, $S{=}4096$). On an industrial 30B-A3B MoE model trained on 500B tokens at 8K context, VHA outperforms both MLA and GQA-4 by $+$0.70\,/\,$+$2.60\,\% on a 12-benchmark base-model evaluation suite; in a separate matched 10B-A1B MoE comparison after long-context mid-training, VHA attains an average RULER score of 84.4 over 8K--128K versus 73.0 for GQA, while using two rather than four KV heads in the full-attention layers.
authors: Xibo Ding, Guoxia Wang, Jinle Zeng, Jiabin Yang, Sirui Tao, Chao Yang, Dianhai Yu
bullets: Targets the trade-off among KV-cache size, training/prefill compute, and model quality in long-context LLMs.
Uses two lightweight linear operations: Q Premix restores virtual query-head diversity, while Linear Postmix fuses inter-head features with a low-rank residual structure.
The operations can be folded into existing projections at inference, yielding a standard GQA-2 model compatible with GQA optimizations and Tensor Core decoding.
Across four model scales, VHA improves over GQA while reducing KV cache by 2–4× and training/prefill FLOPs by 7.9% in one reported setting.
On industrial MoE evaluations, VHA outperforms MLA and GQA and achieves higher long-context RULER scores than GQA while using fewer KV heads.

papers.abstract: Diffusion large language models (dLLMs) have attracted increasing research attention due to their bidirectional attention and arbitrary order decoding. However, there are two issues in dLLMs inference: the decoding difficulty is dominated by the tokens on the right side of the block, and the block-wise decoding inherently suffers from boundary contextual discontinuity. To tackle these limitations, we propose HaloBlock, a difficulty-aware adaptive halo mechanism for dLLM inference. We first leverage bidirectional cumulative entropy to characterize block decoding difficulty. Then, based on the bidirectional decoding difficulty, we adaptively allocate bidirectional halo regions on both sides of each block to mitigate boundary contextual discontinuity. The difficulty-aware design of HaloBlock smooths cross-block context propagation and lowers decoding difficulty for hard tokens, yielding better generation quality and faster convergence. Evaluated on LLaDA-8B-Instruct, Dream-7B-Instruct and LLaDA-1.5 across mathematical reasoning and code generation benchmarks, HaloBlock demonstrates consistent accuracy improvements and higher inference efficiency. Source codes are publicly available at https://github.com/PolyU-VCLab/HaloBlock.
authors: Zhaohui Zheng, Chenhang He, Jinrui Zhang, Ming-Ming Cheng, Lei Zhang
bullets: dLLM block-wise decoding is challenged by difficult right-side tokens and discontinuous context across block boundaries.
It estimates block difficulty using bidirectional cumulative entropy.
It adaptively allocates halo regions on both sides of each block to improve cross-block context propagation.
Experiments on LLaDA-8B-Instruct, Dream-7B-Instruct, and LLaDA-1.5 show consistent accuracy gains and higher inference efficiency on math and code-generation benchmarks.
Source code is publicly available.

papers.tldr: HaloBlock improves diffusion LLM decoding by adaptively adding context around block boundaries based on token difficulty, achieving better quality and faster inference.

papers.abstract: Recent advances in vision-language models (VLMs) have substantially improved the capabilities of GUI agents, while memory augmentation has emerged as a promising approach for reusing knowledge from past interactions. However, existing memory augmented GUI agents typically adopt a fixed representation strategy, providing retrieved experience as a static modality. It remains unclear whether a single memory modality is consistently optimal, or how modality preference changes across interaction steps. In this work, we conduct a systematic study of memory modality in VLM based GUI agents. Across GUI benchmarks, we find that the preferred memory representation is strongly step dependent. Motivated by the finding, we introduce \textbf{SwitchMem}, a routing framework that dynamically selects between textual and visual memory representations at each step. Across three GUI benchmarks, SwitchMem outperforms memory augmented baselines that rely on static memory representations. Our findings validate our claim that memory modality is a step dependent decision rather than a fixed design choice. Code and project resources are available at https://txxnrd.github.io/switchmem
authors: Taeyun Roh, Suhyeong Park, Gijin Kim, Wonjune Jang, Jaewoo Kang
bullets: Existing memory-augmented GUI agents typically use one fixed memory representation.
A study across GUI benchmarks finds that the best memory modality varies substantially by interaction step.
SwitchMem routes each step to either textual or visual memory.
Across three GUI benchmarks, it outperforms baselines using static memory representations.
The results support treating memory modality as a dynamic, step-dependent choice.

A pairwise router scores both memory candidates and is trained to match their score difference to this target. At inference, the router selects one memory modality for the frozen actor to generate the next action.

papers.abstract: Long-context training of large language and multimodal models couples structured attention masks (document, prefix-LM, share-question, sliding-window, block-sparse) with multi-node context parallelism, making the mask a dominant bottleneck. FlashMask's column-wise sparse mask compresses them from $O(n^2)$ to $O(n)$ via four query-axis boundary vectors, covering broad structured patterns. Implemented for Ampere GPUs, it neither exploits FlashAttention-3's TMA/WGMMA warp-specialized pipeline on Hopper nor supports distribution. The column-wise sparse mask is indexed by key positions but stores query-axis interval boundaries. Under any multi-chunk context-parallel assignment, it reduces per-rank mask localization to a provably zero-communication \emph{clip--shift--max} on the boundary vectors, compatible with the single-GPU kernel. FlashMask-3 introduces a mask-aware Hopper kernel with three-role warp specialization atop FlashAttention-3's TMA/WGMMA pipeline, plus a mask-aware distributed extension: zero-communication mask localization, a sparsity-aware load balancer (HCC-IPO), and a mask-aware compute-communication overlap with mask-driven communication pruning, whose forward all-gather uses topology-aware hierarchical routing. On a single H100 across 12 masks at 4K--128K context, it improves achieved TFLOPs over FlashMask, FlexAttention, and MagiAttention by 45--141%, 34--71%, and 2--44%. At context-parallel degrees 4--32 with 8K sequence per device, it attains 31--75% compute-communication overlap efficiency and improves throughput over Megatron-Core CP ring, Megatron-Core CP all-gather, and MagiAttention by $1.80\times$--$3.71\times$, $1.71\times$--$2.92\times$, and $1.09\times$--$1.46\times$. In end-to-end training of a 118B-A14B MoE at 128K on 128 H100 GPUs, it raises throughput by 7.3--11.0% over a Dual Chunk all-gather baseline, with attention forward+backward 24.5--44.9% faster.
authors: Guoxia Wang, Qianyue He, Siming Wu, Haoyang Xie, Qiwen Bao, Jinle Zeng, Jiabin Yang, Tian Wu, Dianhai Yu
bullets: Targets the bottleneck of structured attention masks in long-context, multi-node training.
Uses a Hopper-optimized FlashAttention-3 kernel with TMA/WGMMA and three-role warp specialization.
Provides zero-communication mask localization via a clip–shift–max operation, plus load balancing and mask-aware communication overlap with pruning.
On a single H100, improves achieved TFLOPs by 2–141% over prior mask-aware attention systems across 12 masks and 4K–128K contexts.
Across 4–32 context-parallel degrees, improves throughput by up to 3.71×; in 128K end-to-end MoE training, raises throughput by 7.3–11.0%.

papers.title: FlashMask-3: Efficient and Expressive Mask-Aware Distributed Attention
papers.tldr: FlashMask-3 makes structured, mask-aware attention efficient on Hopper GPUs and across distributed context parallelism, delivering substantial kernel and end-to-end training speedups.

papers.abstract: Extended chain-of-thought reasoning improves problem-solving performance but increases inference cost and latency, motivating more accurate answers with shorter reasoning. We introduce PaceReasoner, a label-free test-time reinforcement learning framework that uses a model's LONG responses to improve its SHORT-mode accuracy. Both modes share a trainable policy, creating a need for reliable supervision, sufficient SHORT training samples, and continued LONG responses to guide learning. PaceReasoner combines all-response and LONG-only answer consensus through progressive, confidence-weighted supervision. A behavior reward gradually shifts from encouraging SHORT exploration to rewarding agreement with LONG answers, while a ratio controller regulates the balance between modes. Across three model backbones and four benchmarks, PaceReasoner improves average SHORT accuracy over the baselines by 7.4--13.5 percentage points, with fewer than 25 reasoning tokens per response on average. Ablations support the key components, and cross-dataset results demonstrate transfer beyond the adaptation set.
authors: Changguo Jia, Zhiyou Xiao, Xinbei Ma, Geng Chen, Weiming Zhang, Yiming Xu, Tianqi Zhao, Minghui Zhou
bullets: Addresses the inference cost and latency of extended chain-of-thought reasoning.
Uses a shared policy with label-free test-time reinforcement learning to train SHORT responses from LONG responses.
Combines all-response and LONG-only consensus with progressive, confidence-weighted supervision.
Gradually shifts rewards from encouraging SHORT exploration to matching LONG-answer guidance, while regulating the mode balance.
Across three backbones and four benchmarks, improves average SHORT accuracy by 7.4–13.5 percentage points; results transfer beyond the adaptation set.

papers.selection_reason: Label-free test-time RL to shorten LLM reasoning while preserving accuracy, directly targeting reasoning efficiency and LLM inference cost.
papers.title: PaceReasoner: Label-Free Learning to Answer Briefly from Long Reasoning
papers.tldr: PaceReasoner uses long responses as label-free guidance to improve short-answer accuracy while keeping reasoning under 25 tokens on average.

papers.abstract: Effective collaboration among large language model (LLM) agents in multi-agent systems requires sharing relevant evidence, requesting missing information, and incorporating teammates' contributions into decisions. Training these behaviors is challenging because final task outcomes provide limited feedback on the value of individual messages. We introduce CoSIR (Collaboration via Surprisal-based Information Rewards), a post-training approach that uses a simple, verifiable environment to teach collaboration behaviors that generalize to more complex, unseen tasks. We propose a Bayesian evaluator that scores shared information by its reduction in team surprisal, defined as the sum of the negative log probabilities assigned to the correct option given each agent's available evidence. Requests are scored by the potential reduction in the same quantity if the requested information were truthfully provided. Separate rewards encourage agents to use the received information in their private choices and calculations. We post-train Qwen3-4B, Qwen3-8B, and Gemma-3-4B-it through self-play and evaluate transfer to seven unseen natural-language collaboration tasks. CoSIR achieves the highest aggregate score, while its performance in general tasks remains competitive. Behavioral analyses show increased disclosure of private evidence and fewer judged failures to use teammates' input.
authors: Keru Chen, Sen Lin, Yingbin Liang, Nathaniel D. Bastian, Shaofeng Zou
bullets: Addresses the difficulty of crediting individual messages when only final task outcomes are available.
Uses Bayesian surprisal reduction to score shared information and the potential value of requests.
Adds rewards for incorporating received information into agents’ choices and calculations.
Post-trains several LLMs via self-play and evaluates transfer across seven unseen collaboration tasks.
Achieves the highest aggregate score, with more evidence disclosure and fewer failures to use teammates’ input.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of CoSIR. Agents receive different parts of a rating table and exchange messages before choosing an option. Self-play updates a policy shared by all agents, which is then evaluated on seven unseen collaboration tasks. The table and briefings illustrate one training instance.

papers.selection_reason: Post-trains LLMs for multi-agent information sharing and collaboration with verifiable rewards, directly relevant to LLM reasoning and agent behavior.
papers.title: Training LLMs for Multi-Agent Collaboration with Verifiable Information Rewards
papers.tldr: CoSIR trains LLM agents to collaborate by rewarding verifiable information sharing, requests, and use of teammates’ input.

papers.abstract: Multi-agent Large Language Model (LLM) systems typically commit to a deliberation protocol before inference. A fixed protocol cannot allocate computation differently to resolved and unresolved instances, and it may mistake repeated support for independent confirmation. We study this failure as semantic false consensus: a confident group answer supported by narrow, duplicated, or correlated rationales. We introduce ECMR, an evidence-aware controller over frozen role-conditioned LLMs. At each step, ECMR summarizes answer concentration, support diversity and independence, contradictions, role behavior, verification history, and remaining budget, then selects whether to propose, challenge, verify, arbitrate, diversify, correct a role, or stop. We formulate this decision as finite-horizon budgeted control and derive sufficient conditions under which state conditioning, risk-triggered verification, and role correction improve cost-adjusted utility. Across a declared held-out evaluation of 9,000 records from MedQA, CaseHOLD, and FinQA, ECMR-Full increases pooled accuracy from 62.1% to 84.9%, reduces false-consensus rate from 40.7% to 17.0%, and raises evidence-support rate from 58.0% to 88.7%. State shuffling loses 11.7 accuracy points with only 0.7 fewer rounds, while harder traces shift from early stopping toward arbitration. ECMR-Full uses the largest token budget, yielding the strongest absolute reliability rather than uniformly superior token efficiency.
authors: Yuan Liu, Haoyue Peng, Fanliang Hu, Lei Huang, Wenli Cai
bullets: Targets fixed deliberation protocols that waste computation and can mistake duplicated or correlated support for independent confirmation.
Controls frozen, role-conditioned agents by choosing among proposing, challenging, verifying, arbitrating, diversifying, correcting roles, or stopping.
Tracks answer concentration, evidence diversity and independence, contradictions, role behavior, verification history, and remaining budget.
On 9,000 held-out records across MedQA, CaseHOLD, and FinQA, pooled accuracy rose from 62.1% to 84.9%, while false-consensus rate fell from 40.7% to 17.0%.
The full controller uses the largest token budget, achieving stronger absolute reliability but not uniformly better token efficiency.

figures.caption: Figure 1: ECMR separates trainable deliberation control from frozen LLM execution. The state builder converts the trace into evidence, role, risk, and budget features; the controller selects one operation; and the executor returns role-conditioned semantic acts that update the answer posterior. Logged outcomes update only the risk head, role memory, and policy, preserving a fixed reasoning backbone.

Figure 4: Three-domain held-out reliability. Panel (a) traces domain accuracy and uncertainty for every method; panel (b) shows ECMR-Full accuracy gain, FCR reduction, and ESR gain over Direct with independently propagated uncertainty.

Figure 2: Inference budget and marginal return. Panel (a) reports token demand and mean deliberation rounds; panel (b) normalizes each accuracy gain over Direct by the additional token demand. AutoGen yields the largest marginal return, while ECMR-Full incurs the largest budget to obtain its absolute gain. Whiskers propagate the registered uncertainty.

Figure 3: Where evidence-aware control pays. Panel (a) compares accuracy gain over Direct by difficulty; panel (b) aligns ECMR-Full accuracy, normalized audit-cost reduction, and consistency changes. Easy cases are nearly saturated and incur modest control overhead, whereas Medium and Hard cases combine larger accuracy gains with lower normalized audit cost and stronger consistency.

Figure 5: Ordered compliance ablation over 9,000 records per variant. Panel (a) compares role-violation and false-consensus incidence as controls are added; panel (b) relates the derived role-compliance score to evidence-support rate. The full loop matches the ECMR-Full macro endpoint; whiskers are binomial standard errors.

Figure 6: Difficulty-conditioned controller actions. Panel (a) reports the explicit-verification trigger rate for every policy and difficulty stratum. Panel (b) shows ECMR-Full reallocating complementary terminal routes from early stopping on Easy cases to arbitration on Hard cases; whiskers mark routing uncertainty.

papers.abstract: Diffusion language models apply bidirectional attention over the whole context at every denoising step, so a longer context makes each step substantially more expensive. Sparsifying only at inference leaves the pretrained weights unchanged, so the model is never trained under the sparse pattern it runs with. We propose Prefilling-dLLM v2, which continues training a diffusion language model so that it routes with its native mask token. One mask is appended at the end of each chunk, and a learned role offset marks it as a routing slot. On every fourth layer, a query keeps a bidirectional local window and the top-K chunks scored from that mask; the other layers use a bidirectional sliding window. Starting from Dream-v0-Base-7B extended to 16K with YaRN, we compare Prefilling-dLLM v2 with bidirectional NSA, DSA, and SWA under the same layout, key budget, and dense initialization, using the same Fast-dLLM decoder. With the YaRN factor scaled to the evaluation length, Prefilling-dLLM v2 leads the other sparse methods on all three RULER tasks from 16K to 128K. Its mean accuracy at 128K is 7.4 points above NSA, the next sparse model, while DSA and SWA remain near zero. At the same length, decoding is 172x faster than with full dense attention.
authors: Qi Han, Jing Xiong, Ziyuan Zhang, Ngai Wong
bullets: Addresses the high per-step cost of bidirectional full-context attention in diffusion language models.
Adds one learned routing mask per chunk; every fourth layer selects the top-K chunks while other layers use local sliding-window attention.
Continued training aligns the model with the sparse attention pattern used at inference.
Outperforms bidirectional NSA, DSA, and SWA across three RULER tasks from 16K to 128K; at 128K, it is 7.4 accuracy points above NSA.
Achieves 172× faster decoding than dense attention at 128K, within the evaluated setup and context range.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Mean accuracy of the four sparse methods on the three RULER tasks. The YaRN factor scales with the evaluation length.

Figure 2: What query q can see. Each chunk is three cells, and q sits in the middle so the local window extends both ways. Teal cells are the local window and orange cells are selected. The bar above each NSA chunk is its summary. DSA reads scattered tokens, and Prefilling-dLLM v2 marks the last cell of every chunk as a mask.

Figure 3: Computation on a route layer. A chunk is S − 1 content tokens followed by one routing mask. The role offset r is added to that mask at the input. Its query pools the content keys with an intra-chunk softmax, and the weighted sum is the summary key sc. A content query adds a lowrank residual and scores these summaries. Inside a GQA group (Ainslie et al., 2023) the scores are reduced by a maximum, and the top K chunks are shared by every head in the group. Attention mass puts the selected chunk scores and the local-window log-sum-exp in one partition, then a second softmax distributes each chunk’s mass over its content tokens.

papers.abstract: Multi-agent deliberation can improve recognition by criticizing and revising candidate answers, but fixed controls cannot respond to changes in disagreement or reasoning quality. We present an adaptive multi-agent controller (ADMA) that learns continuous policies for proposal, challenge, arbitration, and coordination while keeping the task model frozen. Shared trace features describe quality, agreement, and progress, while role-specific features support decentralized control during inference. One controller trained on legal and financial reasoning is transferred without policy updates to four textual and multimodal benchmarks and two successive task-model versions. With Qwen3.5 held fixed, ADMA-Full improves accuracy by 6.2-14.2 percentage points over Direct and by 2.8-3.0 points over ADMA-Fixed. Paired bootstrap ranges for the Full-Fixed comparison are positive on three tasks. Outcome decompositions show that recoveries exceed introduced errors, while process assessment records fewer false-consensus events and more supported correct outcomes. Transfer to Qwen3.6 remains task dependent, which bounds the generality of the learned policy. Median token and latency ratios are 14.3-18.7 and 7.8-16.5 relative to Direct. These results show that adaptive deliberation can improve fixed-model recognition when its task-dependent gains justify the additional computation.
authors: Yuan Liu, Haoyue Peng, Fanliang Hu, Lei Huang, Wenli Cai
bullets: Fixed deliberation controls may fail when disagreement or reasoning quality changes.
ADMA learns continuous proposal, challenge, arbitration, and coordination policies from shared and role-specific trace features.
A controller trained on legal and financial reasoning transfers without policy updates across four textual/multimodal benchmarks and two model versions.
With Qwen3.5, ADMA-Full improves accuracy by 6.2–14.2 points over Direct and 2.8–3.0 points over ADMA-Fixed; recoveries exceed introduced errors.
Transfer to Qwen3.6 is task dependent, while token and latency costs are substantially higher than Direct.

papers.abstract: Existing approaches to training and evaluating search agents focus heavily on final-answer quality, largely neglecting how generated answers map back to retrieved evidence. Recent methods track citations to enforce grounding, but citation support alone does not establish source independence or whether an answer appropriately handles conflicting evidence. We argue that credibility in open-web retrieval depends on principled cross-source evidence grounding that accounts for source independence and systematically attributes and adjudicates conflicting evidence, while hierarchical judgments of these grounding decisions provide a unified signal for training and evaluation. To this end, we propose an evaluation framework, Cross-Source Evidence Grounding (CSEG), that employs a fine-grained, six-layer decision tree over the complete search trajectory. We introduce CSEG-Bench and trainable reward models to provide targeted supervision following this framework. Our approach helps eliminating the severe data skew of natural trajectories by providing targeted coverage over complex, deep-layer decision paths, such as cross-source conflict resolution and nuanced attribution, that standard rollouts fail to capture. Specifically, (1) we define the hierarchy at label, node, and path levels; (2) we construct 1,160 verified trajectories over nine canonical paths by rewriting answers on real retrieved document pools, with independent frontier judges reproducing the entire gold path and human experts deciding inclusion; (3) we train CSEG-RM, which reaches 83.9% exact accuracy on our benchmark while lying on the performance-token efficiency Pareto frontier. Experiments that use this reward alone to supervise a frozen-retrieval answer policy raise the independently judged mean label from 2.83 to 4.19, and show that learning the hierarchy generalizes across layers at a fraction of frontier-judge cost.
authors: Haochen Zhao, Minsheng Hao, Zheng Li, Yifan Li, Zikang Liu, Bowen Qin, Yuhao Cheng, Chuang Fan, Haosheng Zou, Jeff Chen, Sujian Li
bullets: Targets shortcomings of answer-quality and citation-only evaluation, especially source dependence and conflict handling.
Uses a six-layer decision tree over complete search trajectories, with labels, nodes, and paths.

CSEG-RM achieves 83.9% exact benchmark accuracy and improves independently judged mean labels from 2.83 to 4.19 when supervising a frozen-retrieval policy.
Shows hierarchical supervision can generalize across layers while reducing reliance on costly frontier judges.

papers.abstract: Theory of mind (ToM), the ability to reason about others' mental states, underlies effective communication and coordination. Its higher-order form enables reasoning over nested perspectives in strategic interactions. However, existing evaluations often equate belief-nesting depth with reasoning order, allowing nominally higher-order questions to admit lower-order shortcuts. We formalize effective order through the distinct events supporting successive belief prefixes, revealing widespread order inflation across existing benchmarks. We introduce HopToM, with certified full-order questions and controls for lower-order alternatives. Under direct prompting, mean accuracy across four frontier LLMs falls from 73.5% at first order to 20.0% at fourth order, and human participants also struggle. Causal interventions link a recurring class of errors to evidence for shallower belief prefixes. We introduce HopTrace, a plug-and-play inference-time method that encodes each interaction once into perspective records and resolves nested queries deterministically. On certified narrative questions, it improves fourth- and fifth-order accuracy by 22.0 and 38.5 percentage points over strong prompting baselines, while using 20-39 times fewer tokens than multi-call methods. These results sharpen how higher-order ToM is evaluated and offer a practical way to improve perspective reasoning in interactive agents.
authors: Shanshan You, Zhengqi Wang, Hao Liu, Yuqin Liu, Ya He, Xin Hao, Liyuan Wang
bullets: Existing benchmarks can mistake belief-nesting depth for genuine reasoning order because lower-order shortcuts remain possible.

HopTrace improves fourth- and fifth-order accuracy by 22.0 and 38.5 percentage points over strong prompting baselines while using 20–39× fewer tokens than multi-call methods.

papers.abstract: Large reasoning models (LRMs) achieve strong performance by externalizing explicit reasoning traces before producing the answer, yet suffer from overthinking challenge that allocates uniformly heavy computation to queries of varying difficulty. While proprietary models mitigate this via opaque routing, open-source LRMs still lack an efficient mechanism to internalize adaptive reasoning due to both expensive training cost and limited disclosure of training recipes. In response, we introduce RPO (Root-token Policy Optimization), a framework that enables LRMs to self-determine when to reason by training only the initial root token (e.g., whether to invoke the tag) via group relative reward and group-wise advantages. By focusing on this pivotal branching point, RPO drastically reduces training overhead and VRAM usage. Across multiple model families and scales, RPO learns difficulty-aware adaptive thinking at just ~2% of the training compute of prior adaptive-reasoning methods.
authors: Taehyeon Kim, Hyunsoo Lee, Youngsoo Jang, Moontae Lee
bullets: Addresses overthinking caused by applying equally heavy reasoning to queries of different difficulty.
Optimizes only the initial root token that decides whether to invoke explicit reasoning.
Uses group-relative rewards and group-wise advantages to learn difficulty-aware routing.
Reported across multiple model families and scales, with substantially lower training overhead and VRAM use.
The abstract does not specify detailed datasets, baselines, or inference-time gains.

papers.abstract: Long-term memory supports agents across sessions. Repeated retrieval and write-back can let one historical claim occupy multiple retrieval positions and influence current answers without independent evidence. Existing work examines retrieval, updating, and question answering, leaving same-source record accumulation and post-correction persistence underexplored. Motivated by research in social cognition and memory psychology on repeated exposure, retrieval, and revision, we define \emph{Memory Echo} as the excess retrieval exposure gained by historical information from the same source without additional independent evidence, and introduce MEchoBench to evaluate its emergence, correction resistance, persistence, and effect on answers. To address this phenomenon, we introduce the Family--Provenance--Authority framework (FPA). Specifically, FPA selects one representative per source family, conditions the eligibility of old records for the answer context on verified corrections, and constrains final answers with authoritative evidence. In paired replay on 190 fixed questions across four memory frameworks, FPA raises accuracy from 0.825 to 0.920 with DeepSeek V4 Flash and from 0.782 to 0.916 with Kimi K2.6; mean Decision Contamination Effect falls from 0.106 to 0.030 and from 0.109 to 0.038, respectively. These results show that agent memory can preserve traceable history without allowing repeated historical information to govern current decisions. The code is available at https://github.com/OrcasSam/memory-echo-benchmark.
authors: Yufeng Li, Sheng Yao, Peng Zeng, Dezhang Kong, Shi Lin, Changting Lin, Xun Wang, Meng Han
bullets: Defines Memory Echo as excess retrieval exposure for historical information repeated from the same source without new independent evidence.
Introduces MEchoBench to evaluate emergence, correction resistance, persistence, and answer impact across memory lifecycles.
FPA selects one representative per source family, filters outdated records after verified corrections, and prioritizes authoritative evidence.
In paired replay on 190 fixed questions across four memory frameworks, FPA improves reported accuracy and lowers Decision Contamination Effect for both evaluated models.
Scope: the evaluation focuses on same-source accumulation, post-correction persistence, and provenance-guided mitigation.

papers.abstract: Exploration bounds learning efficiency in reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR). Current methods explore mostly through independent sampling, without fully using the information gathered along the way, such as known wrong answers and environment feedback. We propose LEAF, which injects a dynamic, problem-specific memory into the context before every rollout. The memory contains the most recent response, its reward, and other environment feedback. It is updated after every verifier call. We decouple policy updates from rollouts and update the policy through self-distillation. On four benchmarks and two open models, LEAF accelerates exploration by about 4x compared with a random sampling baseline. On unseen test sets, it improves accuracy over the strongest baseline by 1.59 and 1.83 percentage points on the two models, while using less compute than any RL baseline. These results highlight the potential of LEAF in improving both exploration and learning efficiency. Code is available at: https://github.com/on1262/LEAF
authors: Yutong Chen, Zhichao Xu, Rui Liu, Kunpeng Liu
bullets: Targets inefficient independent sampling in reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards.
Stores recent responses, rewards, and verifier feedback in an evolving per-problem context memory.
Separates rollouts from policy updates and uses self-distillation for learning.
Across four benchmarks and two open models, it accelerates exploration by about 4× versus random sampling.
Improves unseen-test accuracy by 1.59 and 1.83 percentage points while using less compute than RL baselines.

papers.selection_reason: In-context memory for exploration in LLM reasoning; fits LLM memory mechanisms.
papers.title: Explore with Memory, Learn without It: In-Context Exploration and Self-Distillation for LLM Reasoning
papers.tldr: LEAF improves RLVR exploration by giving each rollout dynamic problem-specific memory and training the policy via self-distillation.

papers.abstract: Agents build knowledge graphs as memory, and building them has become easy. Maintaining them has not. When a source is retracted, overruled, or erased, everything built on top of it (entity merges, entailed edges, community summaries) must be re-examined, and the maintainer must choose between deleting too much and too little. Deployed pipelines delete only the directly extracted facts: on our corpus that reduces contaminated queries from 32.2% to 28.0% under a real retraction and changes nothing under predicate revocation. Rebuilding is no repair for a constructor that samples: two builds of the same 300-document corpus differ in 29,475 artifacts, five times the 6,248 that removing the 61 retracted documents changes. PolyGraph instead asks the constructor for receipts: for every artifact, alternative bundles of source evidence, each claimed sufficient on its own, emitted in the call that creates it. Cleanup is then set arithmetic over the receipts, with no model calls. Because receipts are the model's own self-report, a re-derivation audit checks them by deleting the cited evidence and testing whether the constructor still produces the artifact. The audit finds that a receipt is trustworthy when it is shaped like the claim it backs. Merge receipts, each backing one narrow claim, agree with re-derivation 68% and 85% of the time. Summary receipts, elicited per sentence but stored as one flat list for the whole text, are wrong about two thirds of the time, almost always by keeping dead content. One receipt per sentence instead is 100% and 88% faithful and lets cleanup keep 33 of 35 touched summaries. The result holds under a second oracle model, a claim-blind prompt, ten further deletions, a second domain and a second constructor. Distrusting the summary layer cuts contaminated queries to 0.4% and 0.8% at 99.8 to 100% of the recall a perfect maintainer would return.
bullets: Retractions or predicate revocations can invalidate merges, inferred edges, and summaries, while deleting only directly extracted facts leaves substantial contamination.
PolyGraph captures alternative sufficient evidence bundles when each artifact is created, enabling cleanup through set arithmetic without additional model calls.
A re-derivation audit tests whether receipts actually support their artifacts; narrow merge receipts were faithful 68%–85% of the time.
Per-sentence summary receipts were substantially more reliable than one flat receipt list, achieving 100% and 88% faithfulness across reported settings.
Distrusting unreliable summary evidence reduced contaminated queries to 0.4%–0.8% while retaining 99.8%–100% of perfect-maintainer recall across robustness tests.

papers.abstract: Longer contexts allow large language models (LLMs) to condition their predictions on more information, but inference costs grow prohibitively with context length. An emerging alternative uses test-time updates to encode context as temporary changes to model weights. However, encoding this information into weights that already represent general knowledge obscures its role as context, so the LLM may fail to use it properly to condition subsequent inference. To restore this contextual role, we first associate each context with an identifier during encoding, thereby distinguishing the newly encoded information from pre-existing knowledge. Invoking the identifier at inference then enables the LLM to recite the encoded context. Nevertheless, successful recitation does not ensure that the LLM will use the recalled information as context. We therefore further introduce a prompting framework that explicitly guides the LLM to use this information as context. Across diverse controlled tasks and practical benchmarks, our method outperformed the baseline using only off-the-shelf LLMs, showing its advances in context encoding.
authors: Yue Wang, Qizhou Wang, Feng Liu, Gang Niu, Masashi Sugiyama, Bo Han
bullets: Long-context inference is costly, motivating test-time encoding of context into model weights.
Weight-encoded information can be confused with the model’s pre-existing knowledge and ignored as context.
The method associates each encoded context with an identifier, enabling the LLM to recite it later.
A prompting framework further guides the model to use the recalled information for subsequent inference.
It outperformed a baseline across controlled tasks and practical benchmarks using off-the-shelf LLMs.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Comparison of (a) full-context inference, (b) encoded-context inference with meta-trained TCE, and (c) encoded-context inference with ACE. Full-context inference jointly processes c1:T and x, becoming infeasible when their combined length exceeds the input context window. TCE and ACE instead encode the chunks c1:T into LLM weights, illustrated here as FFN weights. Prior TCE methods often rely on additional meta-training-based fine-tuning, whereas ACE operates directly on off-the-shelf LLMs without such fine-tuning.

papers.abstract: Long-horizon coding requires agents to maintain an evolving view of the project they are changing: what problem is currently being solved, what has already been learned or modified, which other artifacts may be affected, and what work remains unresolved. When this information is scattered across a growing interaction history, local edits can become disconnected from their later consequences and progress can be difficult to carry forward. We introduce StateHarness, a runtime framework that maintains evolving project state without updating model parameters. The working agent records its current problem and hypothesis, important findings and decisions, discovered repository relationships, and unfinished work. Runtime support prompts record updates, searches for callers, tests, and documentation that may be affected by a change, and maintains a compact working brief for subsequent decisions. When behavioral signals accumulate, a separate diagnostic session revisits the recorded history and surfaces overlooked evidence. Across three repository-level evaluations, StateHarness improves task completion and several measures of change consistency. On RefactorBench, full-chain completion increases from 29.4% to 35.3% and cleanup-check accuracy from 87.0% to 95.4%. On five LHTB software-engineering tasks, mean reward improves from 0.427 to 0.576, exceeding LongHorizon-Harness at substantially lower recorded execution cost. On ChainSWE, bug-fix rate increases from 35.1% to 39.5% and residual debt decreases from 60 to 43 items, although pass-to-pass regressions increase. These results show that maintaining project state can improve long-horizon coding while introducing measurable execution and regression trade-offs.
authors: Chuan Zou, Yujun Zhou, Xiaonan Luo, Xiangliang Zhang
bullets: Addresses project knowledge scattered across long interaction histories and disconnected local edits.
Maintains hypotheses, findings, decisions, repository relationships, and unresolved work without changing model parameters.
Uses runtime prompts for updates, impact searches, tests, documentation checks, and a compact working brief; diagnostic sessions revisit history for overlooked evidence.
Across three repository-level evaluations, it improves completion, change consistency, and bug-fix outcomes, while reducing residual debt in one evaluation.
Scope limitation: pass-to-pass regressions increase, showing a trade-off between stronger state maintenance and execution consistency.

papers.abstract: Diffusion language models (DLMs) have attracted wide attention for their fast, parallel decoding, but they are believed to be far less efficient to train than autoregressive language models (ARMs): a widely cited study reports that a DLM needs roughly 16x the training compute of an ARM to match its likelihood, a figure that has made pretraining DLMs from scratch look prohibitive at scale. We find that the methodology behind this figure has fallen out of step with current DLM practice: it scores the model with its evidence lower bound (ELBO) and trains a full-sequence, decoder-only model. We therefore revisit the scaling laws of DLMs, adopting the exact likelihood under the model's own decoding order, block diffusion training, an encoder-decoder architecture, and a sweep over the block sizes used in practice. Under this new protocol, we study across ten model variants, about 1,700 models in total, and find that pretraining DLMs is far cheaper than previously thought. Concretely, scoring with the exact likelihood reduces the compute multiple to 12.8x; block diffusion training and an encoder-decoder architecture further reduce it to 7.8x at block size 32, and smaller block sizes narrow it to 4.6x at block size 8 and 3.0x at block size 4. We complement these scaling analyses with an empirical rule for the optimal decoder depth of encoder-decoder block diffusion, a held-out compute budget beyond the fitting range at which the gap between variants persists, and downstream benchmark results where likelihood improvements carry over to accuracy. Overall, the 16x figure substantially overstates the pretraining cost gap between DLMs and ARMs, and pretraining DLMs from scratch is far more viable than previously assumed.
authors: Guanghan Wang, Bing He, Zhan Shi, Benoit Dumoulin, Hanqing Lu, Volodymyr Kuleshov
bullets: The prior estimate used ELBO scoring and full-sequence decoder-only training, which do not reflect current DLM practice.
Using exact likelihood, block diffusion training, encoder-decoder models, and practical block sizes reduces the compute gap from 16× to 3.0×–12.8×.
The study evaluates about 1,700 models across ten variants and tests scaling behavior beyond the fitting range.
Likelihood gains also transfer to downstream accuracy, supporting the practical relevance of the revised scaling results.
Overall, training DLMs from scratch appears substantially more viable than previously assumed.

papers.title: Revisiting the 16x Pretraining Compute Gap between Diffusion and Autoregressive Language Models
papers.tldr: A revised evaluation and training protocol shows that diffusion language models require far less extra pretraining compute than the previously reported 16× gap suggests.

papers.abstract: Thought templates, skill libraries, agent memories and caches turn many reasoning steps into one. We call this reasoning contraction. A contracted memory saves reasoning steps and errors until its facts change, then quietly answers wrong. Most systems trust memories by counting successes and failures. We prove that such counters are badly tuned change detectors: a symmetric counter notices a partial change only after a power of its false-alarm horizon, and an unclipped one may never notice it. On five LLMs answering multi-hop questions over edited facts, ExpeL- and ACE-style counters serve 7.0-13.5x more stale answers than certified memories given the same information, and on code tasks with an exact verifier 35-73x more. Safety also has a price. When facts change and each memory is judged only by its own verified outcomes, one number, the certification load, sets how much reasoning any safe memory can skip, and under Zipf demand it yields a scaling law. Our recipe weighs each memory's failures by its own likelihood ratio, certifies its utility against live reasoning, and restarts the certificate when facts change, with the likelihood-ratio detector as the safety net for unannounced changes; for large edits it also invalidates the memory.
authors: Jianghong Zhou, Hao Rong, Chen Lin, Daoan Zhang
bullets: Reasoning contraction compresses many reasoning steps into reusable templates, skills, memories, or caches, but becomes unsafe when underlying facts change.
The paper shows symmetric and unclipped counters can detect partial changes extremely slowly or not at all.
Across five LLMs, ExpeL- and ACE-style counters produced 7.0–13.5× more stale answers than certified memories; on verified code tasks, the gap was 35–73×.
The proposed approach weights failures by likelihood ratios, certifies memory utility against live reasoning, restarts certification after changes, and invalidates memories after large edits.
Certification load determines how much reasoning a safe memory can skip; under Zipf demand, the paper derives a corresponding scaling law.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Trusting a contracted memory is a sequential test. (a) Top: the lifecycle of a contracted memory (a macro). In shadow mode a betting certificate scores the macro’s verified answers and folds it (one-step answers) once its wealth reaches 1/δ; a likelihood-ratio CUSUM (LR-CUSUM) alarm or an edit notice retires it, and the next candidate restarts the test. Middle: both tests on one real macro (Qwen3-8B, KQA-STREAM; per candidate, no notices). Its log-wealth reaches ln 20 (δ = 0.05) after 33 labels; an edit then drops its reliability from 1.00 to 0.37, below break-even (r⋆ = 0.49), and the LR-CUSUM crosses h = 7 on the fourth label. Bottom: its timeline (hatched: certification); ExpeL- and ACE-style counters have not retired it by stream end (2,427 stale answers, against 29). (b) Exact detection delay D against uses to a false retirement A for three clipped counters (score per failure/success), failure rate 0.05→ 0.25: the symmetric ±1 rule is slow by a power of A; likelihood-ratio weights (+7/−1) track the optimum. q̃: the failure rate a rule implicitly tests (Remark 1). (c) The exact coverage gap M (share not answered in one step) of a restarted test for 2,520 settings (dots) lies on the limit Fπ(Θ) (lines).

papers.selection_reason: Addresses safe memory reuse, certification, and change detection for LLM agents, fitting LLM memory.
papers.title: Many Steps into One: Reasoning Contraction and the Limits of Safe Memory Reuse for LLM Agents
papers.tldr: Safe reuse of compressed reasoning memories requires principled change detection and certification, because common success/failure counters can silently preserve stale answers after facts change.

papers.abstract: In humans, proprioception corresponds to the sense of self-movement or position, e.g. understanding the position of one's arm. This sense is often less well-understood and in popular understanding sometimes conflated with introspection. But, notably, proprioception is a separate sense, with dedicated receptors and verifiable outcomes. On the other hand though, language models cannot observe their own internal states during training (and for example answer the question which experts activated in a certain layer of an MoE) and so cannot accurately report on them. Yet, such information is, by virtue of being internal to the model, both accessible, and readily constructed into verifiable signals. We argue that this provides the basis for a digital analog of proprioception. As such, we train models through SFT and on-policy training to equip them with this ability. We show that modern models can be trained to understand a range of subtypes of proprioception, such as routing decision awareness, token entropy, decision depth or logit lens information, without affecting model capabilities. We then run these models through a broad evaluation of situational awareness, legibility, and epiphenomenality, to evaluate in what ways access to proprioception changes model behavior.
bullets: Defines model proprioception as awareness of internal signals, distinct from introspection.
Trains models using supervised fine-tuning and on-policy training.
Covers routing decisions, token entropy, decision depth, and logit-lens information.
Evaluates effects on situational awareness, legibility, and epiphenomenality.
Reports that this internal-state awareness can be added without affecting model capabilities.

figures.caption: Figure 3: Training for proprioception does not break model capabilities, if done correctly. Figure 1: Schematic of proprioception analogs for a generative language model. Top: We are interested in analogs of proprioception (which is the sense of body positioning in humans) in language models, as proprioception is a question about internal states adjacent to introspection, but compared to introspection (which is classically understood not to be a sense and not objectively verifiable) proprioception is tractable. Bottom: We train models with various forms of proprioception and observe whether this sense is learned and whether this affects model behavior.

Figure 2: Learning proprioception capabilities across domains. This figure shows prefill readout accuracy for the SFT stage and free-form conversational accuracy for the on-policy SFT stage, for trained LFM models. In almost all domains, the trained model is capable of learning to verbalize its internal state report, although how well this works is modulated by domain hardness.

Figure 6: Routing Proprioception across model families. We show that routing proprioception also works in other model families. Interestingly the success at predicting routing decisions from the assistant turn (i.e. the model’s own prior turn in conversation) varies highly between model families. We also note that success is not directly correlated to how many experts the model has per layer.

Figure 7: Routing Proprioception in Tie Situations. In tie situations caused by inference engine differences in batched and single sequence generation, the model is still accurately predicting one of either options (left), but, on the subset of decisions that change between both modes, is effectively guessing, showing that this level of awareness of floating point differences is not (yet) present (right).

Figure 5: Left: Overall rates of model reconfiguration across domains, showing that labels become stale after training in most domains. Right: However, our models are trained on-policy and reports track the model’s on-policy state after training and, in cases where the label is changing after training, predominantly predict the live label, showing that on-policy training did lead to models tracking their expressed behavior.

Figure 4: Access to Routing Proprioception generalizes across novel settings. We show that routing proprioception generalizes across roles, with varying turn distances (in-distribution is 1 model turn for SFT and 2 for on-policy SFT), and placement at the start or end of the message. We also show generalization to recursive queries, i.e. queries about the routing decisions taken during a previous answer turn about a routing decision. Accuracy is averaged over all routing domain questions.

Figure 8: Routing Proprioception under Non-normal Ablations. We experiment with externally injected changes to MoE routing, to observe whether the model can predict the injected routing change, noting that this is not observed in training, and not a normal state of the model (given that injected routing change does change the forward pass of the model). We find that accuracy remains significantly above chance for the on-policy-SFT models, especially when trained in higher precision, except for the case where the top-1 expert is replaced by a fully random other expert.

papers.selection_reason: Training language models to report internal states, relevant to LLM capabilities and behavior.
papers.title: A Sense of Proprioception in Language Models
papers.tldr: The paper develops a digital analog of proprioception that lets language models report verifiable information about their internal states without reducing their capabilities.

papers.abstract: Language models are often evaluated alone but increasingly deployed together, routed between, made to debate, ensembled, or collaboratively trained. For a model inside a system, what matters most is not how well it performs on its own, but how much the system gains from its presence. We call this a model's compositional strength and formalize it using the Shapley value of a cooperative game over coalitions of a model pool, and use a model's leave-one-out contribution to the full coalition as a tractable proxy, requiring n+1 rather than 2^n system evaluations. Evaluating individual vs. compositional strengths across five model pools, twelve collaboration methods, and twelve datasets, we find them largely uncorrelated: in 12 of 15 (pool, method-family) settings, individual strength does not translate into compositional advantages, and the coupling is weakest among general-purpose models that practitioners are most likely to deploy. Standalone benchmarks are therefore often poor proxies for models' value in collaborative systems. We then propose compositional reinforcement learning (C-RL), which trains a policy inside a live multi-model system and rewards the outcome produced by the system as a whole, rather than the policy's correctness in isolation. The leave-one-out baseline in Shapley values cancels under a group policy gradient, so this needs no additional rollout cost beyond RL on the collaborative system's outcome and never requires running a coalition without the policy. Across three collaboration protocols and eight tasks spanning reasoning, coding, and scientific discovery, C-RL produces the strongest collaborator in 21 of 24 settings, lifting collaborative performance by +4.0 to +5.4 pts on average (~3x the gain of baselines), up to +13.1 pts.
authors: Shangbin Feng, Yulia Tsvetkov, Jan Kautz, David Acuna
bullets: Compositional strength is defined through a coalition game’s Shapley value, with leave-one-out contribution as an efficient n+1-evaluation proxy.
Across five model pools, twelve collaboration methods, and twelve datasets, individual and compositional strength are largely uncorrelated.
The proposed compositional reinforcement learning (C-RL) optimizes the outcome of a live multi-model system rather than isolated model correctness.
C-RL was the strongest collaborator in 21 of 24 settings across reasoning, coding, and scientific discovery tasks, improving performance by 4.0–5.4 points on average and up to 13.1 points.
The findings suggest standalone benchmarks are often poor proxies for a model’s usefulness in collaborative deployments.

Individual and compositional strength are largely uncorrelated: in 12 of 15 (pool, method) panels the two show no significant relationship, visible from each panel’s near-flat fitted line and its printed ρ (|ρ| ≤ 0.29 throughout) and p-value (marked n.s. when p > 0.05); the decoupling is sharpest among pools of general-purpose models, namely >100B Open Models and Proprietary Models (rows 3-4), where all six panels are n.s.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces compositional strength and reinforcement learning for LLMs in collaborative systems; relevant to language foundation model training and evaluation.
papers.title: Compositional RL: Evaluating and Training LLMs for Collaborative Reasoning
papers.tldr: A model’s standalone ability poorly predicts its value in collaborative LLM systems, while compositional RL trains models to improve the whole system and substantially boosts collaboration.

papers.abstract: Training large language models is constrained by both wall-clock time and memory footprint, and recent matrix-aware optimizers sharpen this tradeoff: Muon can improve optimization but its dense polar update remains expensive. We propose Monarch-Muon, a structured matrix-aware optimizer for weights parameterized by Monarch factors. The resulting structure reduces weights, gradients, and optimizer state, and exposes small independent update subproblems in place of a single dense orthogonalization; we formalize this through a blockwise trust-region interpretation. In quality runs, Monarch-Muon improves over Monarch-AdamW at fixed structure: 3.06 vs. 3.09 in the dense 257M model and 2.68 vs. 2.77 in the 1B MoE model; the two-block MoE variant also matches dense AdamW while using 15% fewer active and 25.4% fewer total parameters. In 6.89B-parameter systems measurements, Monarch-Muon reduces peak memory from 68.9 to 52.9 GB, Muon optimizer state from 14.60 to 6.77 GB, and the Muon optimizer step from 1288 to 304 ms.
authors: Alexander Miasnikov, Ruslan Kabirov, Gleb Molodtsov, Dmitrii Vlashchuk, Vladimir Aletov, Nail Bashirov, Daniil Tikhonov, Maxim Krutikov, Aleksandr Shestakov, Aleksandr Beznosikov
bullets: Targets the compute and memory costs of dense Muon updates for large language models.
Parameterizes weights with Monarch factors, reducing weights, gradients, and optimizer state.
Replaces dense orthogonalization with independent blockwise update problems, formalized via a trust-region view.
Improves over Monarch-AdamW in reported dense and MoE quality runs, and matches dense AdamW with fewer parameters in a two-block MoE.
For 6.89B-parameter systems, reduces peak memory from 68.9 to 52.9 GB and the Muon optimizer step from 1288 to 304 ms.

papers.selection_reason: Memory-efficient structured optimizer for LLM pretraining, relevant to both efficient AI and language foundation models.
papers.title: Monarch-Muon: Structure-Aware Muon for Fast and Memory-Efficient Pretraining
papers.tldr: Monarch-Muon makes Muon-style pretraining more memory- and time-efficient by exploiting structured Monarch factorization while maintaining or improving model quality.

papers.abstract: On-policy distillation (OPD) is a post-training approach for large language models (LLMs) that enables a student model to learn a teacher model's distribution from sequences sampled from the student's own policy. Despite its promising capability, OPD for diffusion language models (DLMs) remains underexplored and existing studies primarily focuses on DLM-to-DLM distillation. The limited availability of strong teacher DLMs and the flexible generation order of DLMs impose additional technical challenges as well. However, it remains unclear how to effectively distill knowledge from a strong autoregressive language model (ARM) into a weaker DLM, given the mismatch between the left-to-right decoding of ARMs and the flexible decoding order of DLMs. Inspired by Ni et al. (2026), we propose JustOPD, an ARM-to-DLM on-policy distillation method that uses autoregressive rollouts during training to align the student's generation process with the ARM teacher's left-to-right decoding. This alignment enables effective distillation from ARM teachers while preserving the DLM's flexible generation-order capability at inference time. Experiments using Qwen3-14B as the teacher and Dream-7B as the student demonstrate that JustOPD consistently improves mathematical reasoning performance over the base DLM across multiple divergence choices.

bullets: Addresses the challenge of ARM-to-DLM distillation caused by mismatched decoding orders.
Uses autoregressive rollouts to align the DLM student’s training process with the teacher’s left-to-right generation.
Retains the DLM’s flexible generation-order capability during inference.
Experiments with Qwen3-14B as teacher and Dream-7B as student show consistent mathematical-reasoning gains across multiple divergence choices.

papers.abstract: As LLM agents take on more autonomous roles, they may interact with multiple clients and counterparties whose goals and incentives conflict. If an agent maintains shared inference state across these interactions, information associated with one relationship may influence decisions made for another. We test OLMo-3-7B-Instruct in a controlled two-client environment with 20 market scenarios, where each client is assigned an opposing objective. With shared conversational memory, the model deviates from the current client's objective in 22% of eligible decisions. We then investigate how these goals are represented in the KV cache. Linear probes show that client-goal ownership becomes highly recoverable in middle layers and is concentrated in particular attention heads. We use these results to identify where to intervene in the cache and test whether these representations affect the model's decisions. Ablating the competitor's cached goal representations at these locations shifts the model toward the current client. The effect is larger for heads identified by probing than for randomly selected heads, and larger when ablating goal tokens than matched non-goal tokens from the same client. Our results show that client-specific goal representations persist in the KV cache and can causally influence decisions made for other clients, highlighting the importance of relationship-specific state isolation in persistent LLM agents.
authors: Saloni Gupta, S\'ebastien Krier, Glenn Matlin
bullets: In a controlled two-client setting with opposing objectives, shared conversational memory led to deviations from the current client’s goal in 22% of eligible decisions.
Client-goal ownership was highly recoverable from middle-layer KV-cache representations and concentrated in specific attention heads.
Ablating a competing client’s cached goal representations shifted decisions toward the current client.
Interventions were stronger for probe-identified heads and goal tokens than for random heads or matched non-goal tokens.
The findings motivate relationship-specific state isolation for persistent multi-client agents.

papers.abstract: Formal verification proves that a program satisfies its specification, but says nothing about whether the specification captures what the author meant. As LLMs increasingly write both code and specifications, a gap between the author's natural-language requirement and the specification becomes a live risk. A machine-checked proof of a property narrower than the one requested is worthless but passes every check. Closing this gap is solving the spec formalization problem: given a natural-language requirement, produce a formal artifact whose meaning matches it. To measure the gap, we curate an end-to-end benchmark for spec formalization spanning four formal languages: Dafny contracts and Lean 4, Isabelle and Rocq theorem statements. Each of its 3,234 rows pairs a natural-language requirement with a formal artifact and a label established by execution, by proof, or by the benchmark it is drawn from. A third of the rows are meaning-preserving rewrites of the artifact that keep the faithful label, so a judge cannot score by detecting that a row was edited. We introduce claimcheck, a tool that detects incorrect formalizations: the formal artifact is translated back into plain English by a model that never sees the requirement, and a separate model, the judge, decides whether the informalization and the requirement express the same guarantee. On all four languages it gains 8.2 to 9.8 points of macro recall over a single call shown the requirement and the artifact, and 4.2 to 6.0 over that call handed the same list of meaning-preserving rewrites. Showing the judge the artifact as well costs 1.4 to 4.5 points. Across four judges that also see the artifact, the gain shrinks as the judge gets stronger, to within a point of the informed single call for the strongest.
authors: Martin Amster, One An, Holly Baker, Fernanda Graciolli, Simon Henniger, Nada Amin
bullets: Addresses the risk that verified code satisfies a formal specification narrower than the author’s intent.
Introduces a 3,234-row benchmark covering Dafny, Lean 4, Isabelle, and Rocq formalizations.
Uses a two-model pipeline: one translates the formal artifact into plain English, and another judges semantic agreement with the requirement.
Improves macro recall by 8.2–9.8 points over a single informed call, and by 4.2–6.0 points against meaning-preserving rewrites.
Benefits diminish for stronger judges, approaching informed single-call performance within one point.

papers.abstract: We revisit the statistical mechanics of Transformer attention via modern Hopfield models. We present a free-energy formalism to characterize parameter regimes and critical thresholds for robust attention inference. The resulting free-energy landscape incorporates randomness in query states and attention weights. Attention then emerges as the equation of motion of the corresponding statistical-mechanical system (i.e., modern Hopfield model) through the standard free-energy minimization principle. This allows us to identify first-order phase transitions in attention between glassy and robust-inference phases. We further extend to attentions with stochastic queries and keys. Together, our results provide a rigorous statistical-mechanics framework for characterizing phase structure and inference reliability across a family of Transformer attention mechanisms.
authors: Jerry Yao-Chieh Hu, Yu-An Chen, Maojiang Su, Han Liu
bullets: Formulates attention through a free-energy landscape with random queries and attention weights.
Derives attention as the system’s equation of motion via free-energy minimization.
Characterizes parameter regimes and critical thresholds for robust attention inference.
Identifies first-order transitions between glassy and robust-inference phases.
Extends the analysis to stochastic queries and keys across multiple attention mechanisms.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Illustration of the procedure from the microscopic to macroscopic energy landscapes. Left. “(Microscopic) Fluctuations” means x is random, has nonzero variance, and follows Gibbs distribution pJ(x). Built from microscopic x, the local stable point xJ exhibits randomness. Middle. W [J ] = log (∫ X exp{−βH[x] + Jx} ) encodes macroscopic responses, i.e., φ = Ex∼pJ [x] = ∇JW [J ]. Hence, the slope of W [J ] gives a deterministic average. Right. Γ[φ] = supJ{Jφ−W [J ]} is the Fenchel conjugate of W [J ]. Its response is J = ∇φΓ[φ], so local stable macroscopic points occurs at J = 0. Γ[φ] describes the energy landscape built from macroscopic φ after integrating out microscopic fluctuations.

papers.abstract: We introduce StartLux-Decision, decision models from 0.8B to 27B parameters that combine efficient single-pass prediction with adaptive, confidence-guided reasoning. The Instant models use bidirectional attention in full-attention layers to improve decision accuracy while keeping single-pass inference. The AutoThink models invoke explicit reasoning for uncertain decisions and answer confident cases directly. A three-stage training pipeline establishes shared decision capabilities, specializes the two variants, and equips AutoThink with reasoning through reasoning supervision and reinforcement learning. We introduce Reinforcement Learning for Calibrated Deliberative Decisions (RLCD$^2$), which uses a frozen model and proper scoring rules to reward improvements in decision probability quality and applies a soft penalty to overlong reasoning traces. RLCD$^2$ raises the share of reasoning traces that terminate within the generation limit by up to 48 percentage points and cuts average reasoning length by up to 65%, while largely preserving decision accuracy. On the public subset of Decision Index 0.3, the Instant models outperform the strongest evaluated comparable-scale open-weight decision models by 7.4-16.9 points, and the 27B AutoThink model reaches 73.4. We also introduce DecisionPivot, a programmatically verifiable benchmark of computational decisions built from contrast pairs that differ in a single answer-changing detail. On DecisionPivot, AutoThink outperforms its Instant counterparts by 11.5-18.4 points in pair accuracy and leads among evaluated systems. The models run on vLLM, llama.cpp and MLX, with quantized variants for lower memory use.
authors: Xialie Zhuang, Zunhai Su, Jia Pan, Ngai Wong, Guanhua Chen, Chuan-Wei Kuo
bullets: Offers Instant models for efficient single-pass decisions and AutoThink models that reason only when uncertainty warrants it.
Trains the models in three stages, adding reasoning supervision and reinforcement learning to AutoThink.

RLCD² uses proper scoring rules and a soft length penalty, reducing average reasoning length by up to 65% and increasing within-limit termination by up to 48 percentage points while largely preserving accuracy.
Instant models outperform comparable open-weight models by 7.4–16.9 points on the public Decision Index 0.3 subset; the 27B AutoThink model scores 73.4.
Introduces DecisionPivot, where AutoThink exceeds Instant models by 11.5–18.4 points in pair accuracy; models support common inference runtimes and quantization.

papers.selection_reason: LLM-based decision models with reinforcement learning for calibrated deliberative reasoning.
papers.title: StartLux-Decision: AutoThink Decision Models with Reinforcement Learning for Calibrated Deliberative Decisions

papers.abstract: The success of autoregressive language models trained with Chain-of-Thought~(CoT) supervision raises a fundamental question: How simple can a next-token predictor be while still enabling the efficient simulation of general computation through its autoregressively generated CoT? Surprisingly, we show that a single neuron suffices. For a broad family of activations, including threshold and ReLU, a single autoregressive neuron can simulate any feedforward circuit with the same activation. Specifically, a size-$s$ circuit on $n$ inputs can be simulated by a neuron of dimension $O(ns+s^2)$ using $O(s^2)$ generation steps, with both bounds independent of circuit depth and tight under natural assumptions. For threshold activations, this improves upon the simulation of Joshi et al. (COLT 2025), whose bounds scale exponentially with circuit depth. Consequently, autoregressive threshold neurons can simulate polynomial-time Turing machines, while remaining efficiently learnable from CoT supervision. Our main expressivity result relies on a novel connection to Sidon sets from additive combinatorics. As an experimental illustration, we efficiently train a single autoregressive ReLU neuron to mimic a neural network teacher with nontrivial test accuracy on CIFAR-10.
authors: Roey Magen, Nirmit Joshi, Gal Vardi
bullets: Shows that one autoregressive neuron with threshold or ReLU activation can simulate any same-activation feedforward circuit.
A size-s circuit on n inputs is simulated in dimension O(ns+s²) and O(s²) generation steps, independently of circuit depth.
For threshold activations, the result improves prior bounds that grew exponentially with circuit depth.
The construction uses a novel connection to Sidon sets from additive combinatorics.
Experiments train a single autoregressive ReLU neuron to imitate a neural-network teacher with nontrivial CIFAR-10 test accuracy.

papers.title: The Surprising Expressivity of a Single Neuron with Autoregressive Chain-of-Thought
papers.tldr: A single autoregressive neuron, when guided by Chain-of-Thought, can efficiently simulate broad classes of neural circuits and even polynomial-time computation.

papers.abstract: Diffusion language models are a promising and more efficient alternative to autoregressive models. However, most RL post-training techniques are not easily adapted to these models. One issue is that diffusion language models generate answers through many intermediate states, deciding at each step which masked positions to reveal and which tokens to place in them. Many existing RL methods used in this setting approximate intractable sequence likelihoods or weight every denoising step by the same advantage, without explicitly distinguishing how these intermediate states of the denoising trajectory affect the expected reward. To address this issue of trajectory blindness, we introduce PACT (Potential-Anchored Consistency of Transitions). Motivated by a reward-tilted reference distribution, PACT jointly learns the policy and a scalar potential that scores each intermediate state, anchored by terminal reward. For each sampled denoising transition, a consistency loss matches the policy-to-reference log-probability ratio of revealed tokens to the change in this potential. This formulation requires neither sequence-likelihood estimation nor importance-ratio clipping. On four tasks, PACT improves LLaDA-8B-Instruct by +9.9 points on GSM8K, +12.0 on MATH500, +55.7 on Countdown, and +72.6 on Sudoku, and reaches the best average accuracy across the four tasks reported for this model, +3.7 points over the next best method. Further compared to AGRPO, it reaches that baseline's best accuracy in about half the training compute on GSM8K.
bullets: Diffusion language models generate through multi-step denoising trajectories, making standard RL methods difficult to apply.
PACT addresses trajectory blindness with a learned scalar potential over intermediate states, anchored by terminal reward.
A consistency loss matches revealed-token policy/reference log-ratio changes to potential changes, avoiding sequence-likelihood estimation and importance-ratio clipping.
On four tasks, PACT improves LLaDA-8B-Instruct by 9.9–72.6 points and achieves the best reported average accuracy for this model.
On GSM8K, PACT reaches AGRPO’s best accuracy with about half the training compute.
