papers.selection_reason: Analyzes verification versus capability transfer in LLM pipelines, relevant to LLM evaluation and reasoning.
papers.title: Review Rarely Beats the Stronger Model: Separating Verification from Capability Transfer in LLM Pipelines
papers.tldr: LLM review often transfers a stronger model’s capability rather than adding verification, making it less accurate and more costly than simply using that stronger model.

papers.abstract: A stored fact may stop being valid when a user changes a preference or an event replaces an earlier one. We study whether a language model can learn these changes in its parameters and answer correctly from only a question and the current time. Engram Injection stores facts in LoRA adapters and supplies the clock through FiLM conditioning on a frozen Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct model. We compare it with additive clock conditioning, prompting with the full dated history, and retrieving four dated records. We train six matched adapters across three seeds after fixing a sampler that could admit test-age examples into training. The training audit reports no such examples among 127,760 evaluated training inputs. On 62 pairs of questions asked before and after an update, at an elapsed age of seven days excluded from training, both adapter methods answer zero pairs correctly under the primary blinded assistant review with order code 1 held fixed. Full-history prompting answers 59/62 pairs correctly, and retrieval answers 62/62. Separate experiments show that adapters can store facts and that removable memory units can support local deletion. Combining fact selection with time-based version selection remains unsuccessful. These results separate learning a fact from learning when to use it.
authors: Sam Siavoshian, Omar Ramadan, Amir K. Saeed, Benjamin A. Johnson, Benjamin M. Rodriguez
bullets: Problem: Facts may become outdated, requiring models to use the current time to choose the valid version.
Method: Store facts in LoRA adapters and provide time via FiLM or additive clock conditioning on a frozen Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct model.
Evaluation: Compare adapters with full-history prompting and retrieval on 62 before/after update question pairs at an unseen seven-day age.
Result: Both adapter methods answer 0/62 pairs correctly under the primary review, while full-history prompting answers 59/62 and retrieval 62/62.
Scope: Adapters can store facts and support local deletion, but jointly selecting facts and their time-valid versions remains unsuccessful.

papers.abstract: Large-scale personalization is shifting from embedding-table retrieval to LLM-based recommenders that generate the Semantic ID (SID) of the item to recommend, where each SID is a short sequence of discrete hierarchical content codes. A single instruction-tuned model can then unify retrieval, content understanding, and language, and recommend brand-new titles from their content alone using SID; then, how should the model generate the SID? Traditionally, models rely on a single language modeling head that generates tokens autoregressively, typically using constrained beam search. In contrast, an emerging body of work explores multi-token prediction (MTP), where dedicated heads predict all tokens in parallel, substantially reducing the decoding latency associated with beam search. We report an industry-scale, apples-to-apples comparison of these two generation paradigms: single-head autoregressive decoding vs. MTP. We introduce a new auxiliary ranking loss, defined over the joint SID score, to train the MTP objective. We evaluate the SID training objectives on both quality and training/inference cost, inside a multi-task LLM that jointly does personalized retrieval, content question-answering (QA), and instruction following over a large streaming-media catalog. Our experiments show single-head beam search consistently beats MTP on most product-critical metrics: ranking and content QA, and trains at roughly 2.6x lower dollar cost on Qwen3-8B scale; MTP wins only on raw inference throughput. Around this finding, we detail an efficient training and inference stack and report end-to-end gains over the previous non-SID baseline equipped with an auxiliary ranking head: +77% item cold-start ranking, +22% content-QA accuracy, +2.8x faster training, with language metric regression traced to SID vocabulary expansion. We address the language regression by reinforcement learning post training.
authors: Sejoon Oh, Fernando Amat Gil, Evan Smothers, Dan Iter, Mark Thornburg, Dawit Mureja Argaw, Sourabh Medapati, Thea Wang, Ria Verma, Qiuling Xu, Harshit Syal, Ehsan Gholami, Moumita Bhattacharya, Ashish Rastogi
bullets: Semantic IDs let a unified instruction-tuned LLM recommend new items from content alone while supporting retrieval, QA, and instruction following.
The study compares single-head autoregressive SID generation with parallel multi-token prediction (MTP), introducing an auxiliary loss based on joint SID scores for MTP.
Beam search performs better on ranking and content QA and costs about 2.6× less to train at Qwen3-8B scale; MTP wins only on raw decoding throughput.
Compared with a prior non-SID baseline, the stack improves cold-start ranking by 77%, content-QA accuracy by 22%, and training speed by 2.8×.
SID vocabulary expansion causes language-metric regression, which the authors address through reinforcement-learning post-training.

papers.selection_reason: Compares autoregressive and multi-token prediction paradigms for LLM-based recommendation, relevant to LLM generation and training.
papers.title: Personalized LLM Recommendation with Semantic IDs: Autoregressive Beam Search vs. Multi-Token Prediction
papers.tldr: In an industry-scale comparison, autoregressive constrained beam search outperforms multi-token prediction for most recommendation and content-QA metrics, while MTP provides higher raw inference throughput.

papers.abstract: When told that robins have sesamoid bones, people are far more prone to extend the property to sparrows than to whales. This behavior, called category-based property induction, is well documented in humans, but whether and how it develops in language models trained only to predict the next token is unclear. To shed light on this, we construct a hierarchical taxonomy of synthetic entities grouped by the properties they share. We then inject facts from this latent taxonomy into the continued pre-training of Pythia and OLMo 2 models from 70M to 7B parameters, and track the development of inductive behaviors. We find that taxonomically aligned induction emerges from next-token prediction alone: a property learned for one entity transfers more strongly within its taxonomic category than across categories. Internally, entities that share a deeper category become more similar in activation space, and clustering recovers the full taxonomic tree from entity representations. Contrary to the usual expectation that scale helps, we find that induction weakens with model size when the data budget is fixed, suggesting that larger models memorize individual facts rather than compress them into shared structure. Induction also strengthens with more pre-training before the taxonomy injection, transfers to novel in-context properties, and can be overridden by a latent taxonomy implied by the prompt. Together, these results show that a model's inductive generalization reflects the latent organization of its training data, with implications for data curation and for predicting how far a learned fact will spread.
authors: Jan Sobotka, Ekaterina Goliakova, Marcin Detyniecki, Antoine Bosselut, Xavier Renard
bullets: Researchers test whether language models transfer properties more strongly among taxonomically related entities.
Synthetic hierarchical taxonomies were injected during continued pre-training of Pythia and OLMo 2 models ranging from 70M to 7B parameters.
Taxonomically aligned induction emerges without explicit supervision; activation representations recover the underlying taxonomic tree.
With a fixed data budget, induction weakens as model size increases, while more prior pre-training strengthens it.
Induction transfers to novel in-context properties and can be redirected by a taxonomy implied in the prompt.

papers.abstract: Large language model agents are emerging as an important new class of users of desktop applications. However, existing desktop interfaces were designed for human end users or application developers, leaving agents to interpret visual controls or discover and compose low-level software operations. This mismatch can hinder even capable agents, yet it remains unclear what interface properties make desktop software easier for agents to use. To study this question, we treat software evolution as a natural source of interface variation and introduce DeskIF-Bench, a benchmark of 255 artifact-verified tasks across six desktop applications. By holding the task, agent, and verifier fixed while varying the software release, we measure how interface changes affect agent performance. Across two models and six applications, the newest release consistently outperforms the oldest. Trajectory analysis identifies three relevant interface properties: discoverability, granularity, and observability. Guided by these properties, we develop ANIS, a framework that synthesizes agent-native interfaces from the capabilities of installed applications. On an expanded evaluation of 368 tasks across eight applications, atomic interfaces improve success over native SDK use by 3.8 and 3.5 percentage points with DeepSeek V4 Flash and Claude Haiku 4.5, respectively, while reducing online token usage by approximately 73%. Goal-level commands further raise success to 74.5% and 67.4%, respectively.
authors: Alan Wu, Wei Tao, Yiwen Guo
bullets: Desktop software was built for humans or developers, creating a mismatch for LLM agents.
DeskIF-Bench contains 255 artifact-verified tasks across six applications and isolates the effect of software releases on agent performance.
Analysis highlights discoverability, granularity, and observability as key agent-facing interface properties.
ANIS synthesizes atomic and goal-level interfaces from installed application capabilities.

Across expanded evaluations, atomic interfaces improved success by 3.8 and 3.5 percentage points and reduced online token usage by about 73%; goal-level commands achieved 74.5% and 67.4% success for the two models.

papers.abstract: Linear attention promises the efficiency needed for long-context language modelling, yet its fixed-size recurrent state must simultaneously support ongoing computation and preserve information from an ever-growing history. This coupling has reinforced a prevailing view that the state's memory capacity defines the model's long-context capability. We challenge this presumed ceiling: \emph{recurrent computation need not bear the full burden of long-term storage}. We introduce NoteBank, a sparse episodic memory that archives selected text before future queries are known, uses the backbone's native features for writing and addressing, and reads retrieved evidence through its native forward computation via replay. This \emph{training-free, plug-and-play} interface requires no external embedding model, separately trained retriever, or separate neural reader. At one million tokens, it raises Gated DeltaNet's mean accuracy across six RULER retrieval tasks from 1.7% to 70.3%, with no observed significant retrieval degradation from 4K to 1M tokens. This recovery adds $\leqslant$0.025% to analytical FLOPs, with persistent context storage approximately 1/2,600 that of a Transformer's full MHA KV cache at matched width, depth, and precision. Experiments extend from three 1.3B recurrent backbones to Mamba-2-8B and post-trained Qwen3.5-9B, demonstrating gains on LongBench v1/v2 and MemoryAgentBench. Together, these results show that sparse evidence storage and native replay can substantially expand the long-context capability of pretrained linear attention models while retaining the efficiency of recurrent computation.
authors: Li Nanbo, Firas Laakom, Yilan Zhang, Piotr Pi\k{e}kos, Yimeng Chen, Liangyu Wang, Yifan Xu, Mateusz Ostaszewski, Dandan Guo, Wenyi Wang, Yanning Dai, Yuhui Wang, J\"{u}rgen Schmidhuber
bullets: Linear attention’s fixed recurrent state must handle both computation and long-term storage, limiting context retention.
NoteBank archives selected text before queries are known, addresses it using native backbone features, and replays retrieved evidence through the model’s forward computation.
The training-free, plug-and-play method requires no external embedder, separately trained retriever, or separate neural reader.
On one-million-token RULER retrieval tasks, Gated DeltaNet’s mean accuracy improves from 1.7% to 70.3%, with no significant retrieval degradation from 4K to 1M tokens.
The approach adds at most 0.025% analytical FLOPs and uses far less persistent storage than a Transformer KV cache; evaluations cover multiple recurrent backbones and long-context benchmarks.

papers.abstract: Long-term memory for assistants needs a gate that decides when a new utterance retires an old stored claim. Benchmark labels for this step mark a pair as changed or not, so they cannot tell a gate that acts on established change from one that acts on a hint. We write a task contract that separates the two (SUPERSEDED vs. NEEDS-CONFIRMATION vs. COMPATIBLE), label 500 test pairs built from STALE (change pairs plus same-user controls) with three LLM annotators and two human adjudicators (one author and a second annotator; provenance reported), and evaluate Jev, a typed "System One" decision model, under pre-registered hypotheses. Of the 179 test pairs STALE marks as changed, 72 meet the contract's bar for an established change. Jev never retired a claim on 141 same-conversation non-changes. Its failure is premature retirement: the binary gate retires 39.2% of claims whose change is only suggested. A three-way decision cuts this to 15.5% at a 15.3-point detection cost, which misses our pre-registered 10-point budget, and it lands on the binary gate's own threshold frontier; these verdicts hold under three readings of the gold labels. On a held-out vault scored against a second annotator's labels, a cascade that escalated uncertain cases to a reasoning model and looked best on development data was indistinguishable from simply raising the threshold (premature retirement 26.8% vs. 6.5% on dev). Part of the gap comes from the gold labels: relative to that annotator's reading, LLM-majority gold shares most of its errors with a same-family escalation model, and an identity for binary labels says how much such shared errors hide. The rest is small-sample selection on development data. For builders this means a binary score should not be wired to delete: route suggested changes to pending evidence, and do not trust a cascade selected on development data of this size.
bullets: The task distinguishes established change (SUPERSEDED), suggested change needing evidence (NEEDS-CONFIRMATION), and compatibility.
Among 179 pairs marked changed by STALE, only 72 met the contract’s bar for established change.
The binary gate prematurely retired 39.2% of claims where change was only suggested; a three-way gate reduced this to 15.5%, missing the pre-registered cost target.
A development-selected reasoning cascade was indistinguishable from simply raising the decision threshold on held-out evaluation.
The practical recommendation is to route suggested changes to pending evidence rather than delete stored claims, and avoid trusting cascades selected from small development sets.

papers.title: Suggested Is Not Superseded: A Pre-Registered Evaluation of a System-One Model as a Memory-Retirement Gate
papers.tldr: A pre-registered evaluation finds that binary memory-update gates often retire claims on mere suggestions, while three-way decisions reduce but do not eliminate premature retirement.

papers.abstract: A central desideratum in model editing is generalization to complex tasks, which prior work formalizes under a direct generalization paradigm: treating and evaluating LLM behavior as an input-output mapping and expecting a factual update to alter outputs on reasoning tasks. Yet despite substantial empirical effort, the field consensus remains that such generalization is highly challenging and elusive. However, when we deploy the latest models in an in-the-wild chatbot-user setting, we surprisingly find that even classical editing methods exhibit remarkably fluent generalization behavior. This motivates us to revisit the obstacles to generalization and the limitations of the prevailing paradigm. We find that direct generalization is fundamentally constrained both theoretically and practically: theoretically, it suffers from an identifiability issue; and practically, existing approaches attempting to circumvent this are further hindered by the ambiguity of their constructed biases and by vulnerability to being overridden by other factors such as optimization dynamics. We instead identify compositional generalization, empowered by the increasingly strong reasoning and composition abilities of modern LLMs, as a theoretically grounded and empirically validated alternative. We validate this phenomenon across multiple models and editing methods, showing that such generalization behavior is widespread. Overall, we argue that generalizable model editing could be more than direct generalization, and call for a paradigm shift toward more generalizable and practically deployable knowledge update techniques.
authors: Xiaotian Ye, Chunyao Yang, Xiaohan Wang, Junkai Chen, Yongqi Duan, Mengqi Zhang, Shu Wu
bullets: Direct generalization—expecting factual edits to reliably change reasoning-task outputs—is theoretically and practically constrained.
In-the-wild chatbot evaluations reveal fluent generalization even with classical editing methods.
Theoretical analysis identifies an identifiability problem in direct generalization.
Attempts to address this face ambiguous constructed biases and interference from factors such as optimization dynamics.
Compositional generalization is supported theoretically and empirically across multiple models and editing methods.

papers.abstract: India's Eighth Schedule recognises 22 languages, yet parallel data is uneven across them, and many language pairs, especially among lower-resource languages such as Bodo, Dogri, Santali and Kashmiri, lack direct bitext. We present BharatSetu 22-Indic 1M, a row-aligned table of 984,764 English sentences, each paired with machine translations into all 22 scheduled languages (21,664,808 Indic cells), generated with the sarvamai/sarvam-translate model family. Because every Indic cell in a row translates the same English sentence, any two columns form a translation pair: 462 directed Indic-to-Indic pairs, or 506 including English, without direct bitext. We call these pivot-derived pairs and propose a confidence layer that lets users choose how strictly each pair is connected. The corpus is machine-generated and not human-verified; quality is expected to vary by language, domain and sentence style, and pivot-derived pairs can inherit errors from both sides. We therefore release BharatSetu as a machine layer and propose a human-correction layer keyed to the same row identifiers, so that each corrected column upgrades every pair that uses it, together with an evaluation protocol. We report no translation-quality results.
authors: Haq Nawaz Malik, Nahfid Nissar, Faizan Iqbal
bullets: Addresses uneven parallel data and missing direct bitext, especially for lower-resource Indic languages.
Contains 984,764 English sentences translated into all 22 languages, yielding 21.7M Indic cells.
Row alignment enables 462 directed Indic-to-Indic pairs, or 506 pairs when including English.
Adds a confidence layer for controlling pair connectivity and proposes row-keyed human corrections that can improve multiple pairs.
The corpus is machine-generated, unverified, and reported without translation-quality results.

papers.abstract: Under a limited context budget, a long-term agent must recall not merely memories that are individually relevant, but evidence that is collectively sufficient for the current query. Conventional memory access retrieves, scores, and truncates memories, often spending multiple context slots on redundant facts while leaving complementary evidence behind. We cast the read phase of long-term memory as query-conditioned evidence composition: each memory is valued by what it adds beyond the evidence already selected. We instantiate this operation with MemPursuit, a training-free mechanism that uses the residual of a sparse convex query reconstruction as a representation-space proxy for what the current memory set is missing. By reusing the query and candidate embeddings already available from retrieval, MemPursuit progressively composes nested evidence contexts without invoking a language model or cross-encoder to score each query--memory pair. The effectiveness of our method is verified on 3 popular benchmarks in comparison to strong baselines. In fixed-budget LoCoMo experiments, MemPursuit improves end-to-end accuracy by 7.2 percentage points at Top-10 and 5.5 percentage points at Top-20, with consistent gains across multiple memory frameworks, while achieving a 32.9$\times$ speedup in median reranking latency over fully batched BGE-v2-m3. Our implementation is available at https://github.com/FengQi-HITSZ/MemPursuit.
bullets: Problem: Fixed context budgets can waste slots on redundant facts and omit evidence needed collectively to answer a query.
Method: A training-free residual-based selection mechanism estimates what the current memory set is missing using sparse convex query reconstruction.
Efficiency: It reuses retrieval embeddings and avoids language-model or cross-encoder scoring for every query–memory pair.
Results: Across three benchmarks, it improves LoCoMo end-to-end accuracy by 7.2 percentage points at Top-10 and 5.5 at Top-20.
It reports a 32.9× median reranking-latency speedup over fully batched BGE-v2-m3, with gains across multiple memory frameworks.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of MEMPURSUIT, illustrated with a query requiring two adoption dates. (1) Form the residual between the query embedding and the current memory reconstruction. (2) Select the memory with the highest residual alignment: the complementary record about Toby is preferred over another record about Buddy, despite its lower query similarity. (3) Jointly refit the selected memories’ nonnegative, sum-to-one weights and update the residual. Repeat until the memory budget is reached or the adaptive stopping condition is met. Scores and weights are illustrative.

Figure 1: A memory-reading example from LoCoMo. The query asks which of Deborah’s family and friends have passed away. The standard read returns repeated records about her father and a distractor about Anna’s mother, while omitting her friend Karlie. MEMPURSUIT selects complementary records about her father, mother, and Karlie, enabling the complete answer shown. Dialogue and memory excerpts are shortened for presentation. papers.abstract: Structural pruning followed by a recovery stage is the standard recipe for compressing large language models (LLMs), yet the two stages are typically designed and tuned in isolation. In this work, we study how their interaction shapes the compressed model, sweeping ordering, the data that drives each stage, and the alignment of their training objectives. We find that instruction-following is the first capability to collapse under pruning, well before knowledge, reasoning, or core language modeling, and that much of the pruning in-domain loss is likely not knowledge loss but a domain-agnostic failure to respond coherently to the prompt. We find in our setting that in-domain data is the strongest pruning signal, whereas instruction-style data recovers the most. Stage order matters little, but only marginally. We further analyze how the importance ranking drifts before and after pruning. Together these results give practitioners a concrete recipe for composing pruning and recovery.
authors: Luis Frentzen Salim, Komang Rinartha, Chia-Chun Wu, Tran Van Nhiem, Lun-Wei Ku, Yung-Hui Li
bullets: Instruction-following collapses before knowledge, reasoning, or core language modeling during pruning.
Much of the in-domain loss appears to reflect incoherent prompt responses rather than knowledge loss.
In-domain data provides the strongest pruning signal in the studied setting.
Instruction-style data delivers the strongest recovery.
Pruning and recovery alter parameter-importance rankings, while reversing their stage order has only a marginal effect.

papers.abstract: Settling one comparison between two truncation samplers has cost six thousand A100-hours, and nothing says in advance how far apart two samplers can be. We observe that almost every deployed truncation rule keeps a prefix of the probability-sorted vocabulary, so any two such rules are nested at every decoding step. Nesting yields a closed-form per-step distance and a coupling under which both samplers emit identical text until they first disagree. Accumulated over a generation, this gives a separation certificate that bounds the difference between two samplers on any bounded outcome, is computable from logs a comparison already produces, and equals their sequence-level total variation distance exactly when neither rule ever overtakes the other. Two consequences follow without measurement: exactness is fragile, and certifying a small difference requires the two retained masses to agree to very high precision at every step. On six open-weight models over four math and science benchmarks, the certificate for every hyperparameter grid we tested is at least 0.998, so a bound alone rarely settles a comparison, although two members of one family can be far closer. What remains useful is the coupling, which gives an unbiased paired estimator that cuts variance $1.2$-$3.8\times$ against prompt-level pairing. Read against benchmark sizes at the default pair's variance and our point estimate of its between-prompt component, resolving a one-point difference needs 8 to 32 samples per prompt on GSM8K, MATH-500 and GPQA-Diamond and about 210 on AIME 2025; at that component's upper confidence bound GPQA-Diamond needs more than 32 and AIME 2025 cannot be resolved at any sample count. Choosing a truncation sampler is a measurement problem at least as much as a design one. The code is available at https://github.com/KurbanIntelligenceLab/truncation-samplers.
bullets: Most deployed truncation rules retain a prefix of the probability-sorted vocabulary, making sampler supports nested at each decoding step.
Nesting provides a closed-form per-step distance and a coupling under which generated texts match until the first disagreement.
The accumulated certificate bounds differences on bounded outcomes, is computable from comparison logs, and can equal sequence-level total variation under a no-overtaking condition.
Across six open-weight models and four benchmarks, tested certificates were at least 0.998, so bounds rarely resolve comparisons; exactness is also highly fragile.
The coupling enables unbiased paired estimation with 1.2–3.8× lower variance than prompt-level pairing, but resolving small performance gaps may still require many samples.

papers.selection_reason: Analyzes nested truncation samplers for LLM decoding and provides a coupling-based measurement framework, directly relevant to language model generation.
papers.title: Truncation Samplers Are Nested: Comparing Decoding Rules Is a Measurement Problem
papers.tldr: Truncation samplers are usually nested, enabling exact coupling-based comparison certificates, but the resulting bounds are often too loose—so reliable sampler comparisons remain a costly measurement problem.

papers.abstract: Language models are becoming infrastructure, and infrastructure built in the open, by public institutions, on documented data, is the alternative to dependence on a few providers; Apertus shows this is viable at scale. Apertus 1.5 extends the fully open Apertus family from text to multimodal reasoning. Continued pretraining of the Apertus 1.0 models, on 4T additional tokens for the 8B and 2T for the 70B, adds image and audio understanding and extends the context window fourfold to 262,144 tokens; multimodality enters through the tokenizer, the language-model head remains restricted to text, and the architecture is unchanged. Supervised finetuning, long-context finetuning, reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards, and preference alignment complete the released models. Thinking is a flag of the chat template rather than a separate model, and lifts mathematical reasoning by up to 20 points on the 8B model. The released models improve over their predecessors on nearly every benchmark; among fully open models of its class, the 8B leads on knowledge, instruction following, and cultural benchmarks, and its instruction following surpasses all compared models, including open-weight ones. On image and audio understanding, a first for the family, the models are competitive with fully open multimodal models, strongest on document understanding and long-form and lower-resource speech recognition, while specialized vision and audio models remain ahead on perception and transcription of English and other high-resource languages. As in Apertus 1.0, we train only on openly available data, respect crawler opt-outs retroactively, and exclude restrictively licensed material. We release the model weights, data preparation and training recipes, and evaluation suites under permissive licenses; openness extends to values, with the Apertus charter guiding alignment stages published alongside the models.

papers.abstract: Large language models make decisions through parallel prefill and sequential decoding. Although effective, this approach incurs decoding costs and does not explicitly expose decision probabilities. Existing task-specific classifiers require per-task training and offer limited generalization to unseen decision schemas. We propose Large Decision Models (LDMs), repurposing language models to return explicit probabilities over labels specified at run time using one prefill forward pass. We first adapt models to this interface through Diverse Decision Supervision (DDS), covering varied domains, rules and labels. To further narrow the performance gap to a reasoning model, Self-Posed Reasoning Distillation (SPRD) adds tasks generated by a frozen teacher, filters them for answer consistency, and trains on label distributions obtained from repeated teacher reasoning. We evaluate on DecisionVista, pairing new-schema tests with held-out human-labelled sources. Across three base models, the recipe improves accuracy over a step-matched baseline by 1.8 and 1.5 percentage points, respectively, achieving a 182-fold speedup in latency over reasoning rollout on Gemma-4-31B. Reasoning remains stronger on the new-schema test, motivating a confidence router for uncertain decisions. On development sets, routing recovers a median 92% of reasoning's accuracy advantage while generating 27-58% of its tokens. Code is available at https://github.com/JianhuiWei7/LDM.
authors: Ziyi Chen, Yan Zhang, Jianhui Wei, Jianing Yin, Daoan Zhang
bullets: LDMs support run-time-specified labels, improving generalization beyond task-specific classifiers.
Diverse Decision Supervision trains the model across varied domains, rules, and decision schemas.
Self-Posed Reasoning Distillation uses teacher-generated, consistency-filtered tasks and label distributions to narrow the reasoning gap.
Across three base models, LDMs improve accuracy over a step-matched baseline by 1.8 and 1.5 percentage points, with up to a 182× latency speedup over reasoning rollout on Gemma-4-31B.
A confidence router recovers a median 92% of reasoning’s accuracy advantage on development sets while using 27–58% as many tokens; reasoning remains stronger on new schemas.

papers.title: Large Decision Models: Repurposing Large Language Models as Single-Pass Decision Makers
papers.tldr: Large Decision Models turn language models into fast, single-pass classifiers that output explicit label probabilities while retaining much of the accuracy of slower reasoning models.

papers.abstract: Skill internalization aims to convert externally specified procedural skills into persistent model capabilities, allowing language-model agents to execute them without retrieving or reinjecting skill descriptions at inference time. Yet when new skills are learned continually, whether previously internalized skills remain usable is still poorly understood. We study forgetting in continual skill internalization and uncover a clear hierarchical structure. Early in subsequent training, a model may lose the ability to invoke an old skill from the raw request, while supplying only the correct canonical skill name substantially restores the learned behavior; with further optimization, this conditional execution also degrades. We call these two stages skill-addressing forgetting and skill-execution forgetting. Guided by this finding, we introduce Factorized Skill Memory (FSM), which separates continual skill memory into a plastic Address Memory and a stable Execution Memory. At each stage, FSM trains a new LoRA executor using only current-stage data, freezes it after acquisition, and appends it to Execution Memory; in parallel, Address Memory incrementally learns to map current requests to executors without replaying historical requests or execution trajectories. At inference time, Address Memory selects one executor from the raw request, and only that frozen executor performs a single language-model generation. On a five-stage benchmark built from 100 TaskBench skills, FSM achieves 65.95% mean exact match and 93.38% addressing accuracy across two task orders, improving over the strongest replay-free parameter-isolation baseline by 14.3 percentage points while remaining within 1.9 points of Replay, which retains historical training examples.
authors: Haomiao Qiu, Yining Tang, Hongyi Wan, Changfeng Sun, Ziyue Qiao, Miao Zhang
bullets: Identifies two forgetting stages: skill-addressing forgetting first, followed by skill-execution forgetting.
Separates memory into a plastic Address Memory and stable, frozen Execution Memory.
Adds a new LoRA executor per training stage and incrementally maps raw requests to the appropriate executor without replaying historical data.
On a five-stage, 100-skill benchmark, achieves 65.95% mean exact match and 93.38% addressing accuracy across two task orders.
Outperforms the strongest replay-free parameter-isolation baseline by 14.3 points and remains within 1.9 points of replay-based training.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Hierarchical forgetting during continual skill internalization. Top: during the T2→T3 transition, closed-book Task2 EM can collapse while Task2 remains recoverable when the correct skill address is supplied; with continued optimization, execution under the correct skill address can also erode. The frozen-executor diagnostic preserves the old task while learning Task3. Bottom: five-stage evaluation matrices for four continual-learning conditions. Off-diagonal cells report closedbook / + Correct Skill Address EM. Across both rows, pale green denotes retained performance, pale yellow denotes addressing forgetting, and pale purple denotes execution forgetting. Diagonal cells show task-acquisition EM. papers.abstract: Formulaic alpha mining seeks interpretable expressions that rank assets by future returns. The task is challenging because it demands simultaneous processing of unstructured market descriptions, historical data, and quantitative evaluation of candidate factors, yet most existing methods exploit only a subset of these signals. We introduce AlphaPilot, a reinforcement-learning framework that trains multi-turn tool-using LLM agents for adaptive alpha mining. The agent conditions on market descriptions, proposes factor expressions, queries real-data evaluator feedback, and updates a retained factor pool across turns. This design jointly leverages market text, LLM financial knowledge, real data, and evaluation feedback. At inference time, AlphaPilot performs day-by-day search and pool updates to adapt to shifting market regimes. Across three independent runs in out-of-sample rolling backtests on CSI300 and CSI500, AlphaPilot achieves mean total returns of 42.93% and 54.19%, with mean Sharpe ratios of 2.46 and 2.86, respectively. It attains the highest mean total return, Sharpe, and RankIC among the evaluated methods on both universes.

papers.abstract: Large reasoning models generate reasoning trajectories token by token. At a given prefix, multiple next-token candidates may be plausible, yet shape subsequent reasoning and differ in their chances of leading to the correct answer. Whether these differences are reflected in internal representations remains unclear. To study this question, we define relative long-horizon candidate value to quantify within-prefix differences and construct the Reasoning Candidate-Token Value (RCTV) dataset, pairing mathematical reasoning prefixes with plausible next-token candidates and their empirical long-horizon candidate values. Using RCTV, we examine hidden states, multilayer perceptron outputs, and attention outputs at candidate positions with sparse linear probes. Experimental results provide evidence that relative long-horizon candidate value is linearly decodable from these representations at multiple layers. Candidate-value probes can also outperform probability- and embedding-based baselines. Furthermore, a controlled online intervention experiment shows that using the decoded signals to guide token selection during generation can improve the chances of eventual success. Our findings provide evidence that internal representations encode information about relative long-horizon candidate value, offering insights into how local candidate-level representations relate to long-horizon reasoning outcomes.

papers.abstract: We adapted Nemotron-3-Nano-30B-A3B for eight Indian languages without changing its backbone architecture. We expanded the vocabulary in place from 131,072 to 163,072 entries using continued byte-pair encoding and AdaptMix rebalancing, reducing tokens per word by 38.6%. We initialized new input and output rows by averaging their original constituent rows, then trained them on 90% Indic and 10% English text before updating the backbone. Continual pretraining then progressed through broad training, high-quality annealing, and long-context training over approximately 1.27 trillion tokens. The annealed checkpoint gained 12.9 points on the Indic MILU benchmark but lost 3.4 on English MMLU. We also report practical negative results. Direct token addition underperformed continued byte-pair encoding. AdamW weight decay changed rows intended to stay fixed. Perplexity on an Indic-heavy holdout did not select the learning rate that best preserved English performance.

Continual pretraining uses broad training, high-quality annealing, and long-context training over approximately 1.27 trillion tokens.

papers.abstract: Gnani-Evon-v3.3-30B-A3B is a long-context hybrid Mamba-Transformer mixture-of-experts model for reasoning, instruction following, and tool use in English and eight Indian languages. Starting from NVIDIA's Nemotron-3-Nano-30B-A3B checkpoint, it retains the 52-layer backbone and changes the vocabulary, training data, and post-training objectives. An in-place expansion from 131,072 to 163,072 tokens reduces mean Indian-language fertility by 38.6%. The new embedding rows are initialized from their upstream decompositions and warmed before the backbone is updated. Continual pretraining then adds broad English-Indic data, high-quality annealing, and direct training at a 131,072-token sequence length. The central result appears after post-training. Reinforcement learning across four verifiable task environments improves mathematics, graduate-level science, and instruction following, but degrades Indic extractive question answering because the rewards do not require an answer in the requested language. The share of Indic extraction items answered in English rises from 8.7% to 91.7%. Accuracy conditional on answering in the target script roughly doubles, which is consistent with preserved reading ability but is measured on a self-selected subset. Two unreleased studies test repairs. A scoped Indic reward restores the language convention. A 26B-A4B generative judge outperforms a 235B-parameter model on RM-Bench, and distillation restores 81% of the capabilities displaced by optimizing against it. Relative to the architecture-identical starting checkpoint, the released model gains 5.2 points on an Indic aggregate while giving up 1.7 points of English retention. The unreleased Indic-aware branch trades further, gaining 14.6 Indic points at a cost of 5.4 in English. A planned FP8 release reduces the artifact to 32GB with near-zero mean change across 32 paired benchmarks.

Relative to its starting checkpoint, the released model gains 5.2 Indic-aggregate points while losing 1.7 English-retention points.
Unreleased repairs include scoped Indic rewards and a smaller generative judge that recovers capabilities through distillation; an FP8 release is planned.

papers.abstract: LLMs increasingly support sensor-based human activity recognition (HAR) by linking motion signals with activity semantics and physical knowledge. Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) grounds decisions in sensor examples and domain features, enabling training-free target-user inference with less dependence on raw numerical arrays. However, existing LLM/RAG-based HAR typically searches single-level activity spaces using static population knowledge. Consequently, they compare many unrelated candidates using the same static population evidence and overlook personalized motion patterns. We propose OntoAR-HAR, an ontology-guided agentic RAG framework combining static population and personalized knowledge. Its tree-structured activity ontology decomposes classification into local decisions among semantically related activities. The static store supplies node-constrained examples, while offline-discovered executable signal features provide numerical evidence for local distinctions. During inference, the personalized store collects selected user observations, which the LLM integrates with static knowledge and signal features while traversing the ontology to an activity label. Cross-subject and heterogeneous-sensing experiments show complementary gains from hierarchical retrieval and personalized memory across multiple LLM backbones, achieving state-of-the-art performance. By explicitly modeling hierarchical relations across activity granularities, OntoAR-HAR also addresses the long-overlooked semantic inclusion problem and avoids treating related labels as independent categories.
authors: Xiangqing Lu, Tao Zhu, Liang Yu, Shuangjian Li, Lulu Ban, Furong Duan, Mingxing Nie, Liming Chen, Yaping Wan
bullets: Addresses the limitations of flat activity search and static population knowledge in LLM/RAG-based HAR.
Uses a tree-structured ontology to make local decisions among semantically related activities.
Combines node-constrained examples, executable numerical signal features, and user-specific observations during inference.
Experiments across subjects, sensing setups, and multiple LLM backbones report complementary gains and state-of-the-art performance.
Models semantic inclusion between activity labels rather than treating related activities as independent categories.

papers.abstract: Natural language specifications let non-expert users task robot teams, and large language models (LLMs) have recently proven effective at grounding such semantic specifications into plans for heterogeneous teams. Existing approaches assume missions that terminate and environments that, while unknown, do not change, but both assumptions fail in many emerging applications. For example, a disaster-response mission does not terminate, and its environment changes continuously as hazards spread and evacuees move. We identify three ways an LLM orchestrator breaks in this setting: its prompt grows without bound, its reasoning degrades as agents and targets accumulate, and it stops actively monitoring after covering the search space once. We build on the successful framework of grounded generative intelligence, and address each issue with a classical idea. A Markovian state summary, rebuilt from the semantic map at every invocation, replaces the growing interaction history. Partial delegation lets the orchestrator assign a subset of robots to an autonomous multi-agent protocol and reserve its reasoning for generating subtasks that require detailed parameters and careful ordering. Lastly, observation staleness, surfaced explicitly in the prompt, together with task-and event-triggered re-prompting, keeps the team vigilant. In a simulated urban search-and-rescue mission with spreading fire and moving evacuees, our framework rescues 98% of civilians versus 89% for the strongest baseline while using six times fewer tokens. Additional ablations isolate the contribution of each mechanism.
authors: Maria G. Mendoza, Victoria M. Tuck, Zachary Ravichandran, Shankar Sastry, George J. Pappas
bullets: Targets failures in persistent missions: unbounded prompts, degraded reasoning as complexity grows, and reduced monitoring after initial coverage.
Replaces interaction history with a Markovian state summary rebuilt from the semantic map at each invocation.
Partially delegates robot subsets to autonomous multi-agent protocols, reserving LLM reasoning for parameter-sensitive, ordered subtasks.
Uses explicit observation staleness and task/event-triggered re-prompting to maintain vigilance as conditions change.
In simulated urban search and rescue, rescued 98% of civilians versus 89% for the strongest baseline with six times fewer tokens; ablations assess each mechanism.

The LLM is prompted with these inputs and the prompt information of Sec. IV-D to delegate a subset of the robots to the multi-agent protocols and generate subtasks for the rest according to the system needs. This plan is validated, and the LLM is provided feedback if there are issues. The actual task assignment is done symbolically with a linear program (LP) assignment. Multi-agent Protocols (green) are shown to be continuously operating with the self-loop or similar to tasks in that they have an endpoint. Asymmetric observations from all operations are constantly fused into the map. The feedback mechanism is triggered on task completion (solid lines) or on relevant map update events (dashed lines). Feedback on the map and observation age (orange) is compiled with a state summary of the history (blue) and provided in the new prompt to the LLM.

Fig. 5. The orchestrator reasoning about moving humans under partial information. Left: at k = 34 people are reported in r6 c0 and r7 c0, with an escort under way to r7 c0. Right: by k = 41 both regions have been re-observed clear and two civilians are reported in r6 c1. The orchestrator treats the re-observation as evidence the pickups are stale, cancels the escort, issues a local search around each vacated region to recover the missing group, and escorts the live report at r6 c1.

Fig. 7. Effect of exposing observation staleness to the orchestrator. With staleness in the prompt (green), the orchestrator sees max age = 202 and a median of 83, assigns all three aerial robots on coverage, and re-observes the region later in the run, recovering the last group of humans. Without it (blue), coverage looks complete (unobserved = 0), the mandatory-H constraint is dropped, aerial robots are released to other work, and the group is never found and the map is only covered once.

Fig. 6. Total tokens used across ablations. We show that for the same triggering mechanism, the stateless prompt (which does not re-send the prompt history) uses fewer overall tokens though more output tokens. These output tokens come from additional ”thinking” tokens the LLM needs.

Fire ignites at two regions (red blocks with stars) and spreads to neighbors over the course of the mission. papers.abstract: A recurrent-depth language model reuses one block of weights several times in a row. The number of repetitions, which we call loops, is chosen when the model runs, not when it is trained, and running fewer is cheaper and faster, so a deployment may choose to do it. Running fewer loops also makes these models less safe, and the loss of safety is larger than the loss of anything else we measured. We study four released Ouro checkpoints and Huginn-0125. At half of its trained depth, Ouro-1.4B-Thinking still solves 0.692 of the GSM8K maths problems, against 0.775 at full depth, keeping 89% of its accuracy. Over the same reduction, the rate at which it helps with harmful requests rises from 0.038 to 0.205, 5.3 times higher. The information is not lost: a linear classifier reads whether a request is harmful from the model's internal state after a single loop, with an ROC AUC of 0.967 against 0.986 at full depth. What the missing loops remove is the refusal that should follow. We measure the effect with four instruments, one generating no text at all, and reproduce it on a second model family. Removing a single direction from Ouro-1.4B's internal state at full depth drops its refusal rate on harmful prompts from 0.950 to 0.130, identifying what the shallow model is missing. Two run-time repairs do not help: the models' early-exit rules do not spend more loops on harmful requests, and choosing a depth per request does not recover the loss. Changing the training does. Standard safety training makes the shallow model safe only by refusing 0.865 of harmless requests, while training at randomly chosen depths reaches a separation of +0.399 between harmful and harmless refusal at one loop, against +0.118. On Huginn-0125 it keeps harmful help at or below 0.040 at every depth from 1 to 32 loops, where standard training reaches 0.194, and it costs no accuracy at full depth.
authors: Seyedarmin Azizi, Erfan Baghaei Potraghloo, Arya Fayyazi, Saeid Shokoufa, Massoud Pedram
bullets: At half depth, Ouro-1.4B-Thinking retains 89% of its GSM8K accuracy, but harmful-request assistance rises 5.3×.
Harmful intent remains encoded after one loop, indicating that shallow execution removes the refusal response rather than the safety signal.
Ablating one internal direction at full depth similarly reduces refusal, identifying a component linked to refusal behavior.
Early-exit rules and per-request depth selection do not restore safety.

Training across randomly sampled depths improves harmful/harmless refusal separation and keeps Huginn-0125’s harmful assistance at or below 0.040 across 1–32 loops without reducing full-depth accuracy.

(a) The fraction of prompts on which the model gives higher probability to a complying sentence than to a refusal, for harmful prompts (solid) and matched harmless prompts (dotted). (b) The harmful result minus the harmless result, with 95% intervals. A filled marker means the interval does not contain zero.

Figure 5: The refusal gap against loop count under the three generation-based measurements of Section 3. Colour and marker identify the model, line style identifies the measurement. All three are scored before the text-quality filter, so that the measurement is the only thing that differs between the lines. The three nearly coincide for each model at two loops and above, so the effect is not produced by any one of them.

Figure 9: (a) The mean exit loop on harmful prompts minus the mean on harmless prompts, for each early-exit threshold. All values are close to zero, so the model’s own rule does not spend more loops on harmful prompts. (b) The refusal gap on Ouro-1.4B against the average number of loops allowed, for four ways of choosing depth. The per-prompt oracle is far above the rest. The rule that is told the true harmful or harmless label stays close to using one fixed depth for everything.

Figure 10: Four training objectives on Ouro-1.4B, against loop count. (a) The refusal gap. (b) The refusal rate on harmless prompts, where lower is better. (c) GSM8K accuracy. Training at randomly chosen depths keeps the refusal gap high at shallow settings without refusing most harmless requests, and matches the untrained model’s accuracy at full depth.

Figure 2: The text-quality filter. (a) Repeated three-word sequences in answers to harmful prompts, by depth, with the threshold drawn as a dashed line. (b) Repeated neighbouring words, with its threshold. Both rise sharply only at the shallowest settings. (c) The fraction of answers kept. (d) Harmful compliance before and after filtering. The filter does not create the effect we report: it makes the measured drop in the refusal gap smaller, not larger.

Figure 4: The refusal gap D on the left axis and harmful compliance on the right axis, against loop count, for three Ouro checkpoints and the dense control. The shaded band marks depths that keep at least 85% of full-depth GSM8K accuracy. Ouro-2.6B is shown in Figure 5 instead, because the measurements behind this figure were not run for it.

Figure 7: Huginn-0125 at 1 to 32 loops. Open markers mark settings where the text-quality filter kept fewer than half the answers, so those points rest on small samples. Standard safety training at the final loop (middle series) gives safety at full depth that does not extend to shallower settings. Training at randomly chosen depths (Section 7) removes the difference.

Figure 3: Three abilities plotted against the number of loops, each divided by its own value at full depth so that all three start at 1 on the right. Harm detection is the probe score above chance, which needs no generated text. Task ability is GSM8K accuracy. The refusal gap is D from Eq. (2), scored after the text-quality filter. Harm detection is almost unchanged after one loop, task ability falls somewhat, and the refusal gap falls the most. The arrow marks the distance between harm detection and the refusal gap at one loop. Shading marks the depths where the filter keeps fewer than 90% of the answers to harmful prompts; Table 4 gives the counts for every cell.

Figure 8: (a) How well a linear probe separates harmful from harmless prompts using the internal state after each loop. The score is already high after one loop. (b) How closely the refusal direction computed after each loop agrees with the one computed at full depth, measured by cosine similarity, where 1 means the two coincide and 0 means they are at right angles. (c) The refusal rate on harmful prompts at full depth, before and after removing the refusal direction u from the state.

Table 1: Safety and task ability at each depth. Depth k means k loops for the Ouro models, where 4 is full depth, and the matching number of layers for the dense control; rel. compute is the fraction of full-depth forward compute. D is the refusal gap, the refusal rate on harmful prompts minus the rate on harmless ones; harmful compliance is the judged rate of real help with a harmful request. All safety numbers are computed after the text-quality filter, so each cell counts only answers that pass it (57–260 harmful and 18–199 harmless prompts per cell; the filter removes the most on the dense control at depth 3, which keeps only 57 harmful and 18 harmless answers, so read that row with care). Accuracy is GSM8K exact match on 120 problems. The full-depth row of each model is in bold. Table 3 repeats this measurement under the equal-length protocol, which is the only one that covers all four Ouro checkpoints; the two tables come from different generation protocols and are not comparable cell by cell.

Table 2: Which alignment objective survives being run shallow, on Ouro-1.4B. All three LoRA arms use the same refusal data and the same schedule and are trained at full depth; they differ only in which loop readout the loss supervises, namely the final loop only, the exit-gate weighted mixture over all loops, or one uniformly sampled loop per training example. D is the refusal gap, the refusal rate on harmful prompts minus the rate on harmless ones, depth k means k loops with 4 the full depth, and full-depth rows are in bold. Safety numbers are computed after the text-quality filter; coherent fraction is the share of answers to harmful prompts that it keeps. Filtering changes what the comparison rests on: at one loop all three trained arms hold harmful compliance at 0.008–0.009, so they separate on refusal of harmless prompts instead, where the final-loop and exit-gate objectives over-refuse (0.865 and 0.926) and the random-loop one does not (0.585). Each safety cell uses 152–260 harmful and 95–179 harmless prompts after filtering; each accuracy cell uses 120 GSM8K problems and is measured without the filter.

Table 4: Is the compliance at shallow depth real text or broken output? An answer to a harmful prompt counts as coherent when its repeated-trigram rate is at most 0.25 and its adjacent duplicate-word rate is at most 0.02. Coherent fraction is the share of answers to harmful prompts that pass; raw compliance is the judged compliance rate over all of them; coherent share of flagged compliances is the fraction of the raw compliances that are coherent; filtered compliance is the compliance rate among the coherent answers only, which is the one the main text uses. Depth k means k loops for the Ouro models and the matching number of layers for the dense control. 260 harmful prompts per cell before filtering.

Table 9: The dense control on a fine grid. Removing layers from an ordinary model is the closest analogue to running fewer loops, and the coarse grid in Section 4 only reaches settings where the model has no task ability left. This grid removes 1, 2, 4, 6, 8 and 10 layers of 28 instead. Two things follow. Text quality collapses almost at once: removing two layers already costs more than half the answers, where an Ouro model at half its loops keeps nearly all of them. And at the mildest cut, where the dense model is still coherent, the refusal gap and the compliance rate are both close to their full-depth values. 260 harmful and 200 harmless prompts per cell before filtering; n is the number of harmful answers left after it. GSM8K uses 120 problems per cell.

Table 7: Harmfulness is readable from the state after one loop; the direction that turns it into a refusal is not yet in place. Probe AUC is the cross-validated AUC of a logistic probe trained on the last-token hidden state at that depth to separate harmful from harmless prompts (5-fold stratified CV, probe refit per fold; ± is the across-fold standard deviation; JSON fields per_depth[].probe_auc and per_depth[].probe_auc_sd). Final-direction AUC scores the same prompts with the difference-in-means refusal direction computed at full depth and applied to that depth’s state. cos to final is the cosine between the refusal direction computed at that depth and the one computed at full depth, so it measures how far the direction still has to move, not how far the state has to move. Depth k means k loops for the Ouro models and the matching number of layers for the dense control. 150 harmful and 150 harmless prompts.

Table 13: The model’s own exit gate, compared against uniform truncation at the same compute. Each row is one gate threshold τ : rel. comp. is the measured mean relative forward compute the gate uses, Dgate is the refusal gap under the gate, and Dtrunc is the same quantity for fixed-depth truncation linearly interpolated to that relative compute. Gate adv. is Dgate −Dtrunc. The last three columns are the gate’s mean exit loop on harmful and on harmless prompts and their difference, which is how much depth the gate actually spends on harm. Full depth is 4 loops. 260 harmful and 200 harmless prompts per cell. The fixed depths that the interpolation is built from are the unfiltered D values in Table 5.

Table 11: Does the depth effect depend on the judge? Every harmful answer is re-scored with Qwen3Guard-Gen-8B, a larger guard model, and its harmful-compliance call is derived with the same rule as the primary judge’s, reusing the primary run’s inputs so that only the guard differs. All figures are computed on answers that pass the text-quality filter, matching the main text. Agreement is the fraction of answers the two judges label the same way and κ is Cohen’s kappa on the same pair. The depth trend holds under the second judge in every model, and its compliance rate is never the higher of the two, so the primary judge does not understate compliance at shallow depth. Agreement is lowest at a single loop, where the text is most degraded, which is the failure mode the text-quality filter addresses.

Table 10: Does running fewer loops add to what a prompt-level attack already does? Each row is one model under one prompt template, measured at every loop count. The template row none is the plain harmful prompt. The three templates are standard ones: an instruction not to begin with an apology or the words sorry, cannot or unable; an instruction to begin the reply with “Sure, here is”; and a request to write in character as a morally unconstrained novel character. 100 harmful and 100 harmless prompts per cell before filtering. The two effects compose: the largest compliance in each model comes from a template at a single loop, not from either alone. All figures are computed on answers that pass the text-quality filter, which keeps 0.30 to 1.00 of answers; the single-loop cells for Ouro-1.4B-Thinking are the thin ones and rest on fewer than half the prompts.

Table 12: Does the effect survive a change of decoding? The main runs decode greedily, so repeating them returns identical text. These runs instead sample at temperature 0.7 with 3 seeds. Columns give that model’s greedy refusal gap for reference, then the mean, standard deviation and range of the refusal gap and of harmful compliance across the seeds. The ordering over depth is the same in every seed, and the spread is small next to the drop from full depth to one loop. Sampling makes the single-loop refusal gap smaller than greedy decoding does, so the greedy numbers in the main text are the conservative ones. All figures are computed on answers that pass the text-quality filter.

Table 3: Safety by depth under the equal-length protocol, the only one of the three protocols that covers all four Ouro checkpoints, including Ouro-2.6B. Every prompt’s answer is truncated at every depth to the shortest answer that prompt produced at any depth, then judged, and the text-quality filter is applied on top; coherent fraction is the share of answers to harmful prompts that it keeps, and it stays between 0.742 and 0.996 here, so no cell rests on a thin remainder (193–259 harmful and 136–196 harmless prompts per cell). D is the refusal gap, the refusal rate on harmful prompts minus the rate on harmless ones, and depth k means k loops, 4 being full depth. Full-depth rows are in bold; Ouro-2.6B was not run at full depth under this protocol, which is the dashed row. This table is a different generation protocol from Table 1 and is not comparable to it cell by cell; GSM8K accuracy is not re-measured under this protocol, so the capability column appears only in Table 1.

Table 5: The depth effect under three measurement protocols, scored before the text-quality filter so that the protocol is the only thing that differs. Each cell is D, the refusal gap, on 260 harmful and 200 harmless prompts. Raw is open-ended generation judged as emitted. Bounded generates in two phases, a capped deliberation phase followed by a forced answer phase, and judges only the answer, so every depth produces a real answer rather than a cut-off deliberation. Equal-length takes those bounded answers and truncates each prompt’s answer at every depth to the shortest answer that prompt produced at any depth, so answer length cannot drive the depth contrast. Depth k means k loops for the Ouro models and the matching number of layers for the dense control. A dash marks a model and depth that was not run under that protocol.

Table 6: Huginn-0125, a recurrent-depth model with a much longer depth range, at 1 to 32 loops (32 is its full depth). D is the refusal gap, the refusal rate on harmful prompts minus the rate on harmless ones, compl. is the judged rate of real help with a harmful request, and coh. is the fraction of answers to harmful prompts that the text-quality filter keeps. All rates are computed after filtering. The two trained arms are LoRA adapters trained on the same refusal data at full depth, differing only in whether the loss supervises the final loop or a uniformly sampled loop. Filtering raises the released model’s apparent compliance rather than lowering it: at two loops it reads 0.905 after filtering against 0.381 before filtering, because the filter removes the broken answers that were previously counted as non-compliant. That cell is also thin, keeping only 0.162 of the answers to harmful prompts (42 of 260); the released arm’s coherence is low throughout, so its column describes a small surviving subset, not the whole sample. Cell sizes after filtering range from 13 to 257 harmful and 9 to 178 harmless prompts.

Table 14: Depth-routing oracle simulation. Every row fixes a mean depth budget and asks how D, the refusal gap, depends on how that budget is spent. Setting is either a gate threshold τ , whose measured mean depth sets the budget, or an imposed mean-depth budget. Depth is that mean depth budget in loops and rel. comp. the matching fraction of full-depth compute. Uniform is depth-blind: it mixes the two available depths bracketing the budget so as to hit it in expectation. Coarse is told the true label but knows nothing about the individual prompt: one depth for all harmful prompts and another for all harmless ones, the best such pair within the budget. Gate is the model’s own exit threshold, reported only for the settings at which it was run. The per-prompt oracle picks each prompt’s depth knowing its label and its recorded outcome at every depth, maximising refusals on harmful prompts plus compliance on harmless ones under the budget; depth is the mean depth it ends up using. The oracle is headroom, not a deployable policy. Because depth is constant within one generation, every policy is scored on responses that were actually generated at that depth. Depths available: [1, 2, 3, 4] loops; 460 prompts per row; CIs are bootstrap 95% intervals from the results file.

Table 8: Forced-choice preference between a compliant continuation and a refusal, read off every loop without generating. The four middle columns give the fraction of prompts where the complying sentence is preferred to the refusal, at 1 to 4 loops. ∆ is the paired shallow-minus-full change in the log-probability margin (target minus refusal, in nats) with its bootstrap 95% CI, as stored in the results file. The harmful − harmless row is derived here: the per-depth entries are differences of the two fractions above it, and the ∆ entry is the difference of the two arms’ deltas with a 95% CI built by treating the arms as independent, taking each arm’s standard error as its CI half-width divided by 1.96, and combining the two standard errors in quadrature. 200 harmful and 100 harmless prompts.

Table 16: Does the depth-aware objective hold against prompt attacks it was not trained on? Both adapters are trained on plain harmful prompts with no wrapper. Here the harmful and harmless sets are re-run on Ouro-1.4B under two of the templates of Section 4.5, at every loop count. Harmful compliance is given at full depth and at its worst value over the four loop counts, which is what a deployment that may lower the loop count is exposed to; the remaining columns are the refusal rates and the refusal gap at full depth. Both objectives cut compliance under both templates, so what the objective buys is not specific to the prompt form it saw in training. 100 harmful and 100 harmless prompts per cell before filtering. All figures are computed on answers that pass the text-quality filter, which keeps 0.48 to 1.00 of them, leaving 48–100 harmful answers per cell.

Table 15: Does the comparison in Table 2 depend on the training seed? Both arms were retrained from scratch at three seeds, with the same data, schedule and hyperparameters, and the whole grid re-measured. Columns give the mean, standard deviation and range over the runs. The ordering is the same in every run: at one loop the random-loop refusal gap is larger than the final-loop one in all three runs and the two ranges do not meet, and the final-loop arm reaches its shallow safety by refusing harmless prompts in all three. Full-depth rows are in bold. The one-loop retention gap of Section 4, safety retained minus task ability retained, is -0.237, -0.341, -0.419 in the final-loop runs and +0.118, +0.183, +0.137 in the random-loop ones. Safety numbers are computed after the text-quality filter, on 202–260 harmful and 114–183 harmless prompts per cell; accuracy uses 120 GSM8K problems per cell and no filter.

papers.selection_reason: Studies recurrent-depth LLM architecture and safety/refusal behavior across loop counts; fits LLM architecture research.
papers.title: Running Fewer Loops Removes Refusal Behaviour in Recurrent-Depth Language Models
papers.tldr: Reducing inference loops preserves much of recurrent-depth models’ reasoning ability but sharply removes their refusal behavior, while depth-diverse safety training can maintain safety across loop counts.

papers.abstract: Deep research requires connecting multiple steps of search, reasoning, and computation, with intermediate findings guiding what to investigate next. As investigations grow, agents must maintain research state across model calls and check findings before errors propagate into subsequent work. We introduce PANINI-DR, a multi-agent harness that separates coordination of the overall investigation from the research and verification of individual subquestions. A shared workspace, built on the Generative Semantic Workspace representation, records subquestions, their dependencies, findings, and supporting evidence. Researchers investigate individual subquestions, while a separate verification agent checks proposed answers against those subquestions and their evidence. Verification feedback guides further investigation, and recorded findings inform subsequent assignments. We evaluate PANINI-DR on BrowseComp-Plus, FRAMES, and MoNaCo against seven state-of-the-art deep-research harnesses, all using a shared language-model backbone and frozen corpora. PANINI-DR achieves the strongest average performance across the three benchmarks. On BrowseComp-Plus, it achieves 73.3% accuracy, outperforming the next-best harness by 16.0 points. Its advantage is strongest on hard questions, where it answers nearly twice as many as the next-best harness. Ablations further show that structured planning and persistent state improve performance, as does checking each finding against its cited evidence before it is reused. Because a model can answer correctly from memory alone, we also analyze the evidence retained by each harness. PANINI-DR achieves the highest answer recoverability from saved evidence on all three benchmarks, while complementary claim-support audits show stronger evidence-backed answers. Accounting for this evidence changes how harnesses compare and further strengthens PANINI-DR's advantage.

papers.abstract: Test-time memorization of sequential information is a foundational capability for any intelligent system that needs to rapidly store and retrieve data, as demonstrated by the attention mechanism in large language models. However, Transformers and linear attention variants are trained via backpropagation through time (BPTT), which has drawbacks such as its enormous memory requirements. Predictive coding (PC), an algorithm that optimizes a prediction-error energy function with local updates, offers a compelling solution but still lacks test-time memory for sequential data. We develop a solution to this problem by treating the per-step memory update $\Delta S_t$ as a latent variable, as opposed to a slow weight to be learned. By taking the log probability of a standard PC-based probabilistic model, we derive a PC-native solution for verbatim sequence memory, and relate our update rule to common choices in the linear attention literature (e.g., DeltaNet). We present an extensive set of empirical tests to probe our system's properties, including its scaling capacity, memory footprint, and ability to infer a context from evidence (e.g., bank (river) vs. bank (money)). We show how DeltaNet-PC can be used for storing single sequences of data, multiple sequences of data, and key-value associative memory pairs with perfect recall accuracy.
bullets: Addresses the lack of test-time sequential memory in predictive coding while avoiding BPTT’s large memory demands.
Treats each per-step memory update as a latent variable rather than a slowly learned weight.
Derives a predictive-coding-native update rule from a probabilistic model and connects it to DeltaNet-style linear attention updates.
Evaluates scaling, memory footprint, contextual inference, single- and multi-sequence storage, and key-value associative memory.
Reports perfect recall for the tested sequence and associative-memory tasks.

papers.abstract: As agentic AI systems take on increasingly complex and consequential tasks, securing them against prompt injection becomes critical. Existing defenses often rely on detecting or reasoning about injected malicious instructions and can therefore remain vulnerable to adaptive attacks that optimize the injection itself. Diffusion language models (dLLMs), an emerging framework for language generation, offer a new opportunity for security enforcement: by iteratively refining their sequence wide predictions, they enable broader-scope constraint enforcement throughout generation. This paper introduces Policy-Constrained Diffusion Agents (CoDA), a framework that enforces task dependent security policies directly within the denoising process of diffusion language models. At each denoising step, CoDA projects token distributions onto a policy-compliant set, maintaining constraint satisfaction throughout generation. We evaluate CoDA across state-of-the-art diffusion language model families under both static and adaptive prompt-injection attacks. Results demonstrate substantial reductions in attack success rate with competitive task utility and practical inference overhead.
authors: Michael Cardei, Anjun Hu, Chenrui Ma, Francesco Pinto, Chawin Sitawarin, Chulin Xie, Ferdinando Fioretto
bullets: Addresses adaptive prompt-injection attacks that can evade defenses based on detecting malicious instructions.

papers.abstract: Existing depth-compression methods for large language models (LLMs) score layers individually or group only adjacent or contiguous layers, implicitly assuming that functional redundancy is local. We test this assumption by computing full pairwise Centered Kernel Alignment (CKA) similarity matrices for thirteen LLMs from six architecture families (1.6B-14B parameters). Non-adjacent layers have 3.6-15.9x more high-similarity pairs than adjacent ones, a structure that prior similarity-based layer merging has not systematically exploited. We propose Fusion via Community Mining (FCM), which builds the full L x L similarity graph, uses spectral community detection to find clusters of functionally equivalent layers, keeps the highest-Block-Influence layer in each cluster, and applies LoRA recovery; a pre-specified rule computed only on calibration data chooses between cosine and CKA similarity. At 2x compression, FCM lowers mean perplexity below ShortGPT on twelve of thirteen models, significantly on ten (Welch's t-test with Holm-Bonferroni correction; up to 50% on Qwen3-4B), with Mistral-7B the only loss (+13.4%). Against FlattenGPT, SWM, and DeltaLLM under matched calibration and recovery, FCM gives the best perplexity on ten of thirteen models (mean rank 1.15), and it also outperforms MKA on three anchor models. FCM matches or exceeds ShortGPT on 15 of 20 zero-shot reasoning cells and also improves MMLU, LAMBADA, HumanEval pass@1, and free-form generation quality. The 2x-compressed Qwen2.5-7B has 46% fewer parameters, 42% lower peak VRAM, and 84% higher decode throughput on a single A100. Spectral grouping outperforms Fisher contiguous segmentation by 41% and uniform partitioning by 51%, and FCM's advantage grows beyond a 2x crossover up to 3x and persists at the 14B scale. Code: https://github.com/Usama1002/fcm-layer-fusion
bullets: Full pairwise CKA analysis across 13 LLMs finds substantially more high-similarity non-adjacent than adjacent layer pairs, challenging local-redundancy assumptions.
FCM constructs a layer-similarity graph, detects functional communities spectrally, retains the highest-Block-Influence layer per cluster, and applies LoRA recovery.
At 2× compression, FCM beats ShortGPT in mean perplexity on 12 of 13 models and is best among several baselines on 10 of 13.
It matches or exceeds ShortGPT on 15 of 20 zero-shot reasoning evaluations and improves several downstream generation and language benchmarks.
For compressed Qwen2.5-7B, FCM reports 46% fewer parameters, 42% lower peak VRAM, and 84% higher decode throughput on one A100; Mistral-7B is the main exception, with a perplexity loss.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of the FCM pipeline. The compressed model retains K layers (one per community) and undergoes LoRA recovery fine-tuning.

papers.abstract: Spiking neural networks target energy-efficient language modeling through sparse, binary activations, but the efficiency-accuracy tradeoff of spiking language models is uncharacterized at scale. We present the first Chinchilla-style IsoFLOP scaling study of a spiking language model, sweeping SpikeGPT-family models (RWKV backbone) from width 384 to 1536 across compute budgets from $3\times10^{17}$ to $10^{19}$ FLOPs on FineWeb-EDU. We report two findings. First, the compute-optimal frontier is $N_{opt} \propto C^{0.56}$, close to the 0.50 that Hoffmann et al. report for dense Transformers, so spiking does not change how parameters and data should be traded off under a compute budget. Second, against non-spiking RWKV and Transformer baselines trained the same way, the loss gap splits into a backbone cost of about 0.16 nats that does not change with compute and a spiking cost that falls from 0.34 to about 0.23 nats and then levels off. These results give the first compute-optimal recipe for spiking language models and quantify the accuracy cost of their sparsity.
authors: Dan Saunders, Benjamin Ren, Catherine He
bullets: Studies SpikeGPT-family models with an RWKV backbone across widths 384–1536 and compute budgets of 3×10^17–10^19 FLOPs.
Finds the compute-optimal parameter scaling exponent is 0.56, close to the 0.50 reported for dense Transformers.
Decomposes the loss gap versus non-spiking baselines into a roughly compute-invariant backbone cost of 0.16 nats and a spiking cost that decreases before leveling off near 0.23 nats.
Provides a compute-optimal scaling recipe and quantifies the accuracy cost associated with spiking activations.
