papers.abstract: Agentic large language models now tackle complex tasks, yet strategic reasoning over long horizons is under-studied: most agentic benchmarks are short and episodic, and performance on long tasks is hard to dissect into stored knowledge, reasoning and luck. We introduce SpireBench, in which models play the complete commercial deck-builder Slay the Spire (StS), where early decisions decide long-term success. Across 20 large language models (LLMs) at the game's highest difficulty, frontier models beat heuristic baselines and match the average human player but remain far behind experts. This gap widens as the run lengthens: the strongest models win the first act as often as experts, then fall behind. What separates strong models from weak is how well they play each fight; all of them misjudge risk over a run, preserving health rather than spending it to grow stronger. A comprehensive, self-consistent renaming of every game term shows that part of their performance rests on prior knowledge of the game, and models do not improve from the memories they write across runs, which are often wrong and overly cautious. Our harness is the first to give a model the complete original game, and we compare it with existing harnesses. Overall, SpireBench offers an unsaturated long-horizon benchmark with tools to locate where and why agents fail.
authors: Scott C. Lowe, Sander W. Keemink
bullets: Tests 20 LLMs at Slay the Spire’s highest difficulty against heuristic baselines and human performance.
Models win the first act about as often as experts, but their performance declines as runs become longer.
Stronger models distinguish themselves mainly through better fight-by-fight play, while all models misjudge long-term risk.
Agents tend to preserve health instead of spending it to become stronger, and written memories across runs are often incorrect, overly cautious, and unhelpful.
Renaming game terms shows that performance partly depends on prior game knowledge; the benchmark is designed to diagnose long-horizon failure modes.

figures.caption: Figure 6: The harness as a sequence of messages, with time running downwards. In combat the model returns a whole turn as several tool calls in one reply; the harness sends them to the game one command at a time, diffs the state after each, and returns each call’s own effect as that call’s result, followed by each enemy’s action and the next turn’s state. At the end of each floor the model forecasts its chances and may update its run notes; at the end of the run it consolidates them into the memory bank that the next run’s system prompt carries. Code on the right is the shape of what the model sends and receives, with names as it sees them under the reskin.

Figure 1: Multiple time horizons at play in Slay the Spire. Cohort: the model plays a series of runs on different seeds, carrying memories it writes between them. Run: four acts of escalating difficulty, each ending in a boss; the player must grow stronger fast enough to keep up. Act: about 17 floors (Act 3 ends in two bosses at this difficulty; Act 4 has 4) through which the player plans a route, trading safer floors against riskier ones with larger rewards. Floor/Combat: most floors are fights of several turns, each followed by a deck choice that persists for the run; a card weak now may matter later, and a generally good one may be wrong for what lies ahead. Turn: the player draws part of the deck; the model plans the turn and plays it in one response of several tool calls (purple). Sometimes the best play takes more damage now to end the fight sooner. Magenta: choices made during the example Turn, and the part zoomed into for the other rows.

Figure 2: Mean acts cleared per run for the LLM agents of Table 1. (a) Against mean dollar cost per run (log scale), across reasoning-effort levels. Only points on the Pareto front (blue step line) are named; see Fig. 20 for other names. Dashed lines: the non-LLM baselines (no cost). (b) Against the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, at their highest effort and at low effort (low). Dashed line: least-squares fit. Only models on the cost Pareto front of (a) are named. For correlations with each Artificial Analysis evaluation, see Table 18.

Figure 3: Do models use HP as a resource? (a) Rest sites can be used to heal or upgrade a card; both top (blue) and other (grey) tier LLMs nearly always rest if they are missing any HP, whereas Twitch streamers (magenta) favour upgrading much more heavily. Bars are labelled with their number of visits. (b) Relative HP left at the end of each floor. Each act is drawn over the runs that reached the act boss (runs that die to the boss count as 0 HP for the boss floor); run counts are above each act. Lines: medians; bands: interquartile range. Streamers spend their HP in Act 1 to get stronger, reducing the amount of damage they take in future floors as a result.

Figure 4: Survival over a run. The share of each agent’s runs that reached each floor. Every LLM agent in Table 1 with all 10 seeds is shown; models on the cost Pareto front (Fig. 2a) are shown. Floor 57 indicates a win of the full game (defeating the Heart at the end of Act 4); a win at the Act 3 boss without the keys to unlock Act 4 stops at floor 52. Dark grey dash-dot: the random-choice policy. Purple: the mean of four Twitch streamers (band spans the four, weighted equally). Black: the 3,641 A20 Ironclad telemetry runs that follow an earlier A20 Heart kill in the same session chain (Appx. D). Shading marks the acts.

Figure 19: How the memory bank grows over a 10-run chain. For each model, top: the number of xml memories held after each run (line), with the memories added (blue, up) and deleted (grey, down) in that run’s consolidation. Bottom: the size of the bank carried into the next run, in thousands of characters, for xml consolidation, the single compact summary, and notes kept verbatim. Size is measured exactly, from the system prompt of the following run, relative to the first run’s empty bank; the bank after run 10 is never read, so that curve ends at run 9.

Figure 5: Our harness. Game states become text, each action’s effect attributed to its tool call; a router sends each part of the game to the model or a symbolic player; in-game names are (optionally) reskinned; tool calls are mapped back and validated. The prompt runs from cached layers to turn messages. Bottom: when the model plans, forecasts and writes notes.

Figure 10: Act 1 choices and combat against mean acts cleared, one point per LLM agent of Table 1 with at least three runs reaching the Act 1 boss (16 models), over those runs; lines are the telemetry population (dashed) and the four Twitch streamers. 𝜌 is Spearman's correlation across the models and 𝑝 a two-sided permutation test. HP change per hallway fight is the net HP change over a hallway-fight floor, including the relic heal after it, computed the same way for humans. Last panel: each model's rate of beating the Act 1 boss against the rate expected from its runs' states on reaching it, by a logistic model fitted on the 143,071 telemetry runs that reached it with a complete state record; the dotted line is equality.

Figure 15: Prediction error against distance from the outcome, for the runs of Table 1. Left: Brier score of the act-survival prediction against the number of floors before the act resolves (at its end if the run cleared it, otherwise where the run died). Middle: the same for the run-win prediction, against floors before the run ends. Right: mean absolute error, in HP, of the predicted HP at the end of the fight against the number of turns still to be played in it. Darker is worse, on a scale per panel; blank cells have fewer than 5 predictions. The bottom row pools all models, and its mix of distances is the one each model is scored over in Table 15. Fight-end predictions sharpen steeply as the fight ends; act-survival predictions barely sharpen before the act resolves.

Figure 16: As Fig. 14, for the forecasts made within a floor: the HP a model expects at the start of its next turn and at the end of the fight, both optional when ending a turn. Each is scored by its mean absolute error in HP, divided by that forecast's mean error over the predictions of every model in Table 1 (so 1 is average), and the two are averaged for each run. The division matters: fight-end errors are about ten times next-turn ones, so without it a run that made only next-turn predictions would look excellent. A run with no HP predictions has no score. Within-floor error tracks play more closely than end-of-floor calibration (Table 16).

Figure 17: Each ablation, model by model. Each grey line is one LLM agent: its mean over the 10 seeds in each condition, shown only where it has all 10 seeds in both that condition and the condition’s baseline, so every comparison is paired. Bars are the mean over those agents, and 𝑛 beneath each bar is how many there are. Baselines are the first bar of each panel, except that the compact summary is read against no memory bank with compact notes. Panels show mean acts cleared per run; the pooled tables are Tables 2, 27 and 29. Brackets test each condition against its baseline with a paired sign-flip permutation test over agents (* 𝑝 < 0.05; n.s. not significant). Orak is shown for the four models with all 10 of its seeds scored; its full paired comparison is in Table 2.

Figure 11: Do models learn from their memories? Mean acts cleared per run over the first five runs of each chain (open circle) against the last five (arrowhead), by memory mechanism; a circle alone means no change. The two halves are different seeds, so the no-memory cohort on the same seeds (grey) is the control for how hard each half is: learning shows as an arrow further right than the grey one. Only cohorts with all 10 seeds are shown. For reference, the top row is one of the authors (a non-professional player) over their first ten A20 Ironclad runs, playing the unmodified game without a harness or memory bank; with five runs per half, a single win moves a half’s mean by 0.8 acts.

Figure 12: Effect of difficulty on performance. Final floor reached against the pinned ascension level, for every agent in Table 1 with runs at more than one level, on the held-out seeds under the same configuration as the table. Each level is a separate cohort (its own memory chain). The solid line is the median floor at each level, the blue band the interquartile range, and the dotted lines the lowest and highest floor reached. Background shading marks the floors of each act. Levels with fewer than 10 completed seeds are annotated with their seed count. The last panel is every Ironclad run in Mega Crit’s released telemetry (October–November 2020, final content build; abandoned runs excluded), with the dotted lines at the 5th and 95th percentiles instead, since over tens of thousands of runs per level the extremes are always the first and last floors reachable. papers.selection_reason: Benchmark evaluating long-horizon agentic LLM play and memory written across runs; directly relevant to agent memory.
papers.title: SpireBench: Evaluating Long-Horizon Strategic Play of Agentic Models with Slay the Spire
papers.tldr: SpireBench evaluates long-horizon strategic reasoning by having LLM agents play the complete game Slay the Spire, revealing that frontier models match average humans early but remain well below experts over full runs.

papers.abstract: A latent recurrent language model applies a shared block of layers repeatedly, so one checkpoint can trade inference compute for accuracy by changing the loop count. At one loop, however, such models typically fall well short of a non-recurrent model of the same size, a one-loop tax that makes a separate non-recurrent model the better choice whenever latency matters. We present Elastic Latent Recurrence (ELR), a recipe for training looped language models without this tax. At one loop, an ELR model costs the same to serve as a non-recurrent model of the same size and, trained on the same data, reaches similar accuracy. Each additional loop then buys more accuracy for more inference compute. Three choices make this work: a gated state update with a learned step size, loop counts mixed within each optimizer update, and conditioning each pass on its loop index and budget. The first two preserve one-loop accuracy, and the third lowers loss at every additional loop. Mixed depths can be introduced late in pretraining to limit the added training cost, and with zero-initialized conditioning added at the switch, this late schedule reaches lower loss than mixed-depth training from scratch. In MoE models, reusing first-loop expert routes on later loops cuts mixed-depth update time by 11.7% with no measurable change in accuracy. At inference, keeping only the last loop's attention KV cache holds attention KV memory at its one-loop level while retaining most of the gain from additional loops. On 4B dense and 30B-A3B MoE hybrid models, ELR at one loop is 0.52 points below and 1.04 points above its matched baseline on a ten-task average, and four loops add 7.25 and 4.75 points. Carried through post-training, the recipe yields Koi-4B, a single checkpoint that scores an estimated 18 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index at one loop, matching Qwen3.5-4B, and 29 at four loops.
authors: Faisal Ladhak, Shantanu Acharya, Santiago Akle Serano, Simeng Sun, Boris Ginsburg, Krishna C Puvvada
bullets: Addresses the one-loop accuracy tax that often makes recurrent models unattractive under latency constraints.
Uses gated state updates with learned step sizes, mixed loop counts during training, and loop-index/budget conditioning.
Late mixed-depth training can reduce added training cost; reusing MoE expert routes cuts update time by 11.7% without measurable accuracy loss.
Retaining only the final loop’s attention KV cache keeps KV memory at the one-loop level while preserving most multi-loop gains.

On 4B dense and 30B-A3B MoE models, four loops improve ten-task averages by 7.25 and 4.75 points, respectively; the post-trained Koi-4B reaches estimated Intelligence Index scores of 18 at one loop and 29 at four.

papers.abstract: Zeroth-order (ZO) optimization offers a memory-efficient alternative to backpropagation for fine-tuning large language models. However, existing ZO methods typically sample training examples uniformly, overlooking their evolving importance and leaving avoidable estimation variance. To address this limitation, we propose Sample-Adaptive Zeroth-Order Optimization (SAZO), which learns sample importance online and adaptively allocates queries to accelerate convergence. SAZO extracts gradient-norm information from existing directional differences to estimate sample importance without access to true gradients. Furthermore, to track evolving importance from sparse minibatch feedback, SAZO maintains per-example exponential moving averages that aggregate observations across updates. The method requires no additional model evaluations and only $O(N)$ additional scalar state compared with MeZO. We prove that SAZO asymptotically matches the leading convergence term of the minimum-variance sampling oracle, and achieves a strictly faster convergence rate than standard methods. Extensive experiments across four model families demonstrate improved average downstream performance and up to $6\times$ faster convergence to the same training loss in terms of query count.
authors: Haiyuan Wan, Yanyi Li, Weicheng Lin, Cong Fang
bullets: Uniform sampling in existing zeroth-order methods can waste queries and increase estimation variance as sample importance changes.
SAZO estimates sample importance from directional differences, without requiring true gradients.
Per-example exponential moving averages track importance under sparse minibatch feedback.
It adds only O(N) scalar state over MeZO and theoretically approaches minimum-variance sampling convergence.
Experiments across four model families show improved average downstream performance and up to 6× faster convergence by query count.

figures.caption: Figure 2: SAZO substantially accelerates convergence across model scales. At 24K forward passes, SAZO reaches MeZO’s endpoint loss 6×, 4×, and 4× faster in (a)–(c), respectively; HiZOO achieves 2.29×, 2.66×, and 4×.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces Sample-Adaptive Zeroth-Order optimization for fine-tuning large language models, relevant to efficient LLM training and adaptation methods.
papers.title: Sample-Adaptive Zeroth-Order Post-Training
papers.tldr: SAZO improves zeroth-order fine-tuning by adaptively prioritizing important training examples without extra model evaluations.

papers.abstract: Autoregressive decoding is less suited to non-causally ordered data, e.g., cross-references or future dependencies, since their outputs cannot be revised post hoc, unlike iterative human reasoning. Diffusion LLMs partially mitigate this limitation but still cannot flexibly insert or remove arbitrary numbers of tokens from a pre-generated context. We design AutoIndexer as a generative model with a novel training and decoding mechanism that simulates a Chain of Edits, allowing the model to flexibly modify its prior outputs in hindsight via token insertions, substitutions, and deletions. The model learns to predict marker tokens for opening and closing edits, simultaneously moving a cursor to positions in the existing token sequence, analogous to a text editor. Training sequences are obtained by perturbing ground-truth labels with inverse chained edit operations, and the model learns to edit by undoing those inverses. The perturbation training allows AutoIndexer to be robust to erroneous context and adaptable to editing tasks such as code correction. We demonstrate that our method exhibits post-generation context-editing capabilities that most autoregressive and diffusion models lack without compromising performance on standard LLM benchmarks. The code is available at https://github.com/AutodeskAILab/autoindexer.
authors: Shu Ishida, Aliasghar Khani, Tianyu Zhang, The Cong Luong, James Seale Smith, Adam Gaier
bullets: Addresses causal decoding’s difficulty with non-causal dependencies and outputs that require hindsight revision.
Trains models on perturbed sequences created through inverse chained edits, teaching them to undo errors.
Predicts edit markers while moving a cursor through the existing token sequence, like a text editor.
Supports flexible post-generation context editing and potential applications such as code correction.
The abstract reports retained performance on standard LLM benchmarks, but gives no quantitative results or detailed scope limits.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of the AutoIndexer method. Analogous to using a text editor, AutoIndexer can edit its prior outputs by predicting edit-start/-end cursor positions. The positional encodings of the tokens are modified after each edit and efficiently computed by our specialized attention kernel.

Figure 3: A simulated edit sequence for training. The ground-truth clean sequence (top) in display order is randomly perturbed to obtain a target sequence (bottom) with edit/return markers, which the model learns to generate. A sequence parser recovers the intended display order of the tokens.

The edit start head attends to all tokens in the previous context to identify the beginning of a potential erroneous content. papers.title: AutoIndexer: Flexible-Order Decoding by Training Causal Models on Chains of Edits
papers.tldr: AutoIndexer augments causal language models with chain-of-edit decoding so they can revise generated text through insertions, substitutions, and deletions.

papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used in molecular discovery and structure elucidation, where decisions depend on physical observations. Existing evaluations primarily focus on end-to-end molecular reconstruction, where correct predictions do not necessarily indicate reliance on the supplied properties. We introduce MolP2SBench, a benchmark for molecular property-to-structure (P2S) reasoning in LLMs. Each task presents a masked molecular scaffold with given properties and asks the model to select the missing structure from plausible candidates. We shuffle or replace properties to test reliance on correct property-structure pairing and responsiveness to counterfactual property changes. A channel-wise leaderboard uses Property-Grounded Recovery (PGR), giving equal weight to source and counterfactual recovery. Evaluating seven models, we find that LLMs can use physical properties for structure prediction, but performance varies substantially across property types. Higher accuracy with a property does not necessarily imply greater responsiveness to it: a model may benefit more from $^1$H NMR than from $^{13}$C NMR, yet be less likely to change its prediction when the $^1$H data is replaced. LLM performance also need not reflect the relative difficulty of these properties for human chemists. Although UV-Vis spectra provide less direct structural information than NMR spectra, Astra achieves higher accuracy with UV-Vis data than with NMR peaks. MolP2SBench supports studying how LLMs extract and use physical-property information, revealing patterns that may differ from conventional chemical intuition and providing a foundation for more reliably property-grounded models for molecular and quantum-chemical inference. Code and dataset: https://github.com/DUAL-Xiao/MolP2SBench.
authors: Yuhang Xie, Zhiyi Shi, Zeyi Zhang, Zhisheng Qi, Yushun Dong, Yu Wang, Xiongye Xiao
bullets: Benchmarks property-to-structure reasoning using masked scaffolds and plausible candidate structures.
Shuffled and counterfactual properties test whether predictions depend on correct property–structure pairings.
Introduces Property-Grounded Recovery (PGR), weighting source and counterfactual recovery equally.
Across seven models, property use varies substantially by property type and does not consistently match human chemical intuition.
A model may achieve higher accuracy with one property yet be less responsive when that property is changed.

papers.selection_reason: Benchmark probing LLM reasoning from molecular properties to structure; relevant to language foundation model reasoning.
papers.title: MolP2SBench: Do LLMs Really Reason from Molecular Properties to Structure?
papers.tldr: MolP2SBench evaluates whether LLMs genuinely use molecular properties—not just scaffold patterns—to select the correct molecular structure.

papers.abstract: Sequence models with a fixed-size state avoid the quadratic cost of attention, but face a design choice. An input-dependent state transition gives content-dependent memory at the cost of FFT-based training, while a fixed transition keeps the O(T log T) convolutional path but reads memory the same way for every input. ResonatorLM, a recent model of the second kind, reads a bank of damped complex oscillators through a fixed learned phase per head. We make that readout phase a function of the current token, which adds input dependence to the read only, keeps the convolution exact, and costs 0.2 percent more parameters. An analysis of the untrained bank shows that phase does encode elapsed time, but an ordinary token falls below the background within 2-8 steps and no choice of damping extends linear reconstruction beyond about 16 tokens. In 6M-parameter character-level models on WikiText-2, the input-dependent phase matches the original at the training length and removes its failure beyond it: trained on 256 tokens and tested on 1024, perplexity falls from 12.81 to 3.76. We trace the failure to long-memory heads that accumulate more history than training exposed them to. The learned phase tracks the current character rather than distance and does not improve retrieval.
bullets: Fixed-state sequence models retain efficient O(T log T) convolution but normally read memory identically for every input.
The proposed input-dependent readout changes only the phase, preserving exact convolution and adding 0.2% parameters.
Untrained oscillators lose ordinary-token information after 2–8 steps, with linear reconstruction limited to about 16 tokens regardless of damping.
In 6M-parameter WikiText-2 character models trained on 256 tokens and tested on 1024, perplexity drops from 12.81 to 3.76 versus the original model.
The learned phase follows the current character rather than elapsed distance and does not improve retrieval; long-memory heads explain the baseline’s extrapolation failure.

papers.selection_reason: Improves the long-context capabilities of ResonatorLM sequence models by making the readout phase input-dependent, relevant to LLM architecture and context handling.
papers.title: An Input-Dependent Readout Phase for Resonant Sequence Models
papers.tldr: Making ResonatorLM’s oscillator readout phase depend on the current token preserves efficient convolution while substantially improving extrapolation to longer sequences.

papers.abstract: Persistent memory allows an LLM agent to carry experience across conversations, but it also turns a local reasoning mistake into a durable one. During deliberation, an agent may consider a plan, simulate a tool result, report another speaker's belief, and then reject all of them. If memory retains only the resulting sentences, those once-useful possibilities can later return as facts. The record is neither fabricated nor irrelevant; it has simply been detached from the context in which it was valid. We identify this missing context as \emph{discourse ownership}: the world, branch, or speaker that licenses a proposition. Our first finding is counterintuitive. Language models already carry a causally active signal for ownership, yet conventional memory interfaces discard it when they convert reasoning into records. We introduce CASK (Causally Anchored Scoping Keys), a commit rule that preserves this signal so that shared-world facts enter durable memory while provisional content remains available only within its original scope. Our second finding is that the most obvious way to preserve the signal---storing the discovered internal coordinates---is unreliable because equivalent representations need not keep the same coordinates. CASK instead preserves the stable relations that express ownership. Controlled long-conversation conflicts and tool-agent traces show that this design improves memory admission and prevents provisional content from contaminating later answers while complementing runtime provenance. The resulting commit boundary lets agents explore more possibilities without granting every intermediate sentence authority over future behavior.
bullets: Persistent memory can turn discarded plans, simulated tool results, or reported beliefs into misleading future facts when their context is lost.
The paper identifies this missing context as discourse ownership: which world, branch, or speaker licenses a proposition.
CASK preserves stable ownership relations rather than unreliable internal representation coordinates.
Controlled conflict and tool-agent traces show improved memory admission and reduced contamination from provisional content.
The approach complements runtime provenance and enables broader reasoning without granting every intermediate sentence durable authority.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Reasoning creates propositions that belong to different worlds. The agent considers Paris but rejects that branch, while committing to Sydney. CASK converts the model’s ownership-sensitive relational geometry into an explicit commit edge: Sydney enters actual-world memory, whereas Paris remains available only inside its scoped world. A later query may use committed evidence without turning the discarded branch into a fact.

Figure 2: Controlled evidence for scope-sensitive memory. (a) The CASK advantage is concentrated in scope-only, not payload-only, attachment. Error bars on the random row denote one standard deviation across 20 decompositions. (b) At τ = 0.5, CASK moves toward higher recall and lower contamination relative to full-Gram. Under a development-calibrated 95% actual-admission constraint, output logits define the stronger high-recall boundary. (c) The safety gain reduces adoption of the injected answer, while ordinary reader utility remains a separate trade-off.

Table 2: Complete source-isolated attachment comparison (%). All models use the same conversation folds and fold-local alternative sources. CASK uses its default symmetric threshold τ = 0.5 and is best across every evaluated representation family on both frozen backbones.

papers.selection_reason: Scope-aware commit rules for persistent LLM memory; directly fits LLM memory.
papers.title: Whose Memory Is It? Scope-Aware Commit Rules for Long-Term LLM Memory
papers.tldr: CASK makes LLM long-term memory scope-aware, preserving only facts licensed by the correct world, reasoning branch, or speaker while keeping provisional content local.

papers.abstract: We introduce a post-training method for diffusion language models (DLMs) that minimizes Maximum Mean Discrepancy (MMD) between generated and reference distributions in the feature space of a frozen pretrained DLM. To estimate MMD, we retain contextual features at individual token positions, obtaining multiple observations per sequence from a single extractor pass. We optimize this objective using policy gradients for discrete models and direct differentiation through generated latents for continuous models. In both cases, computing the loss directly from these features enables efficient post-training without full sampling trajectories or jointly trained auxiliary models. Experiments show lower generative perplexity at comparable entropy on OpenWebText and better accuracy-computation trade-offs on GSM8K. On 16B DMax-LLaDA2.0 models with hybrid masked-uniform diffusion, we increase decoding parallelism with similar or higher accuracy on math and code benchmarks.
bullets: Matches generated and reference distributions using contextual token features from a frozen pretrained DLM.
Uses policy gradients for discrete diffusion models and latent differentiation for continuous models.
Avoids full sampling trajectories and jointly trained auxiliary models during optimization.
Reports lower generative perplexity at comparable entropy, improved GSM8K accuracy–compute trade-offs, and higher decoding parallelism with similar or better math/code accuracy.
Demonstrated on OpenWebText, GSM8K, and 16B DMax-LLaDA2.0 models with hybrid masked-uniform diffusion.

For continuous DLMs (bottom left), K bootstrap passes provide self-conditioning without gradients, followed by a differentiable generation pass. In both cases, token-level RBF MMD compares contextual features extracted by a frozen pretrained DLM (right).

papers.selection_reason: Presents a post-training method for diffusion language models, a language foundation model architecture, with accuracy and decoding improvements.
papers.title: Representation-Space MMD for Diffusion Language Models
papers.tldr: A feature-space MMD objective enables efficient post-training of diffusion language models, improving generation quality and decoding efficiency without auxiliary models or full sampling trajectories.

papers.abstract: LLM agents rely on long-term memory to retain and reuse information when performing tasks over long horizons. Existing methods provide limited support for handling memories that become outdated as new observations or domain evidence arrive. Such outdated memories may remain semantically relevant, continue to affect dependent records, and retain value as historical evidence. This calls for two capabilities: dependency tracking to identify downstream effects and historical preservation to retain useful past records. We propose Provenance-Aware Cascading Memory Invalidation (PACMI), a framework that represents memories and new evidence in a provenance graph with typed dependency edges. PACMI assigns records to a four-state validity lattice, propagates validity changes to dependent memories, and uses the resulting states for retrieval and stale-premise detection. We also introduce a diagnostic benchmark with 100 cases and 300 queries across five domains. The evaluation separates node, context-, and answer-level performance. PACMI achieves the highest final-answer accuracy on this benchmark, and its paired difference from the strongest baseline is significant under an exact McNemar test. The premise checker achieves perfect precision, recall, and F 1 on the controlled query distribution. Cascading propagation primarily improves memorystate correctness: removing it increases final-answer errors from 3 to 11, but the paired difference does not reach the 0.05 significance threshold. Code and data will be made publicly available.
bullets: Addresses stale memories that remain relevant, influence dependent records, and may retain historical value.
Represents memories and new evidence in a provenance graph with typed dependencies and a four-state validity lattice.
Uses propagated validity for retrieval and detecting answers based on stale premises.
On a 100-case, 300-query benchmark across five domains, PACMI achieved the highest final-answer accuracy; its advantage over the strongest baseline was statistically significant.
Cascading propagation reduced final-answer errors from 11 to 3, though this difference was not statistically significant; the premise checker achieved perfect metrics on the controlled queries.

papers.abstract: Three recent results describe what look like unrelated LLM reliability problems. Yin et al. (2026) show reasoning RL collapses tool-reliability representations. Suleymanov et al. (2026) show that under safety-constrained generation, large models rewrite flagged spans while small models truncate. Bastounis et al. (2024) prove any consistent-reasoning system without an implicit "I don't know" function must hallucinate infinitely often on broad problem classes. We argue these findings converge on a single intervention: calibrated abstention is what each independently identifies as the missing capability, even though the unavailability they document, a capability gap, a policy gap, and a recursion-theoretic gap, has a different source in each case. Honesty post-training has narrowed the gap in deployed models, but principled closure of the class Bastounis identifies requires a calibrated abstention function whose training signal at the leaderboard level is absent: dominant benchmarks assign zero reward to decline, so the leaderboard gradient that would select for the function does not exist. We propose four changes to evaluation: triple-scoring, abstention-rate reporting, capability-stratified evaluation, and mandatory calibration metrics. Benchmark reform is necessary, not sufficient, for closing the gap the theorem identifies.
bullets: Reasoning RL, safety-constrained generation, and a recursion-theoretic result identify different sources of missing uncertainty handling.
The authors argue calibrated abstention unifies these capability, policy, and theoretical gaps.
Current benchmarks provide no leaderboard reward for declining, weakening training signals for abstention.
Proposed evaluation changes include triple-scoring, abstention-rate reporting, capability-stratified tests, and mandatory calibration metrics.
Benchmark reform is necessary but may not fully resolve the theoretical gap identified by Bastounis et al.

papers.selection_reason: Addresses LLM reasoning reliability and calibrated abstention, relevant to language foundation models.
papers.title: The Missing "I Don't Know": Why Three Reasoning-Reliability Findings Converge on Calibrated Abstention
papers.tldr: Three distinct LLM reliability failures point to the same missing capability: calibrated abstention—knowing when to say “I don’t know.”

papers.abstract: Unlearning benchmarks such as TOFU and MUSE certify forgetting by reading the model's final answer, where a model that refuses to answer already counts as having forgotten. We show that this model-level certificate does not transfer once the model is deployed as an agent. We introduce K-Bench, a benchmark that scores LLM unlearning under agentic deployment. K-Bench inspects all six channels a ReAct agent exposes, including its chain-of-thought (CoT), tool calls and tool observations, and elicited summary. A query counts as leaked if the secret appears in any of them. Each experiment places the secret in exactly one of the agent's three sources (the weights, the prompt, or the retrieval store). The K-Score is computed separately for each source and credits forgetting only when the agent remains usable. Clearing the answer channel does not make the secret unrecoverable. On structured retrieval, the secret stays verbatim in the tool-observation channel and the aggregate leak rate is unchanged. When the secret lives in the prompt or the retrieval store, TOFU and MUSE report no leakage, while the deployed agent still leaks it on 22--86\% of queries. When the secret is in the weights, none of the twenty evaluated published methods demonstrably removes it, and only an input-corruption intervention reaches selective forgetting under the evaluated observer. The top-ranked method changes across base models. A refusal-tuning method resists the evaluated extraction without verified knowledge removal.
bullets: Evaluates leakage across six ReAct channels, including chain-of-thought, tool interactions, observations, and summaries.
Tests secrets stored separately in model weights, prompts, or retrieval stores, and credits forgetting only when the agent remains usable.
Secrets in prompts or retrieval stores leaked in 22–86% of agent queries despite TOFU and MUSE reporting no leakage.
For weight-stored secrets, none of 20 evaluated published methods demonstrably removed the knowledge; only input corruption achieved selective forgetting under the evaluated observer.
Refusal tuning resisted extraction but did not verify knowledge removal, and the top-ranked method varied by base model.

papers.title: K-Bench: A Benchmark for LLM Unlearning in Agentic Deployments
papers.tldr: K-Bench shows that LLM unlearning verified at the answer level often fails when models are deployed as agents with multiple leakage channels.

papers.abstract: Agentic pipelines for structured-query generation are rapidly expanding, but it is unclear which part of the loop produces the gain. We use LAST-CQ -- a five-agent, training-free, execution-grounded Text-to-Cypher framework -- as an instrumented testbed, running three counterfactuals over 2,471 live-database queries and six backbones spanning three vendor scale tiers. Removing correction is worth between 3.1% aggregate execution-BLEU against the single-pass system and 12.3% against a no-refinement counterfactual (up to 80.7% for the weakest backbone). Replacing schema-grounded, LLM-synthesised feedback with raw database error strings costs almost nothing (20.9% vs. 19.9% naive exact match; <0.2% end-to-end; equivalent within $\pm 0.075$ set-F1 by two one-sided tests). Spending the same call budget on parallel sampling degrades quality by 10-11%. What works is detecting failure and routing it to a retry, not the feedback sophistication or number of samples. LAST-CQ itself recovers 91.7% of queries that fail under single-pass generation, while a query that succeeds first time still costs exactly one LLM call. We also show that n-gram overlap on serialised results is not a bound in either direction: it over-scores against set equivalence on 65.9% of results while under-scoring against judged semantics. Finally, we calibrate our LLM judge against blind human labels and find it optimistic by 9 points.
bullets: Evaluates five-agent, training-free, execution-grounded Text-to-Cypher refinement using 2,471 live-database queries and six backbones.
Removing correction reduces execution-BLEU by 3.1% versus single-pass generation and 12.3% versus no refinement, with larger effects for weaker backbones.
Raw database error messages perform nearly as well as schema-grounded synthesized feedback, while allocating calls to parallel sampling lowers quality by 10–11%.
LAST-CQ recovers 91.7% of queries that fail under single-pass generation, while successful first-pass queries use one LLM call.
Serialized-result n-gram overlap poorly reflects set equivalence and judged semantics; the LLM judge is 9 points more optimistic than blind human labels.

papers.selection_reason: Focuses on LLM agent self-refinement for Text-to-Cypher generation, analyzing the agent loop and recovery mechanisms.
papers.title: What Drives Recovery in Agentic Text-to-Cypher? LAST-CQ: An LLM Agent Self-Refinement Framework
papers.tldr: LAST-CQ’s recovery gains mainly come from detecting failed queries and retrying them, rather than sophisticated feedback or parallel sampling.

papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) process long contexts, including long documents and lengthy conversations, but face token-level memory usage that increases proportionally to input length. Although model optimization and lossy prompt compression are widely used, these methods still fail to solve the long-context recall problem beyond pretrained and size-constrained context windows. This paper proposes a long-context recall method that maintains near-constant GPU memory usage as context length increases, without additional training. The main idea is to reconstruct facts using parameter activations in the LLM's feed-forward layers, which store residual vectors representing facts from the source document. Utilizing residual vectors allows the LLM to deterministically reconstruct query relevant facts without referencing the original document, preserving high fidelity and reducing memory usage without fine-tuning weights. Experimental results show that the proposed method enables answering single-fact questions in two-million-token story contexts where previous methods fail.
bullets: Targets long-context recall while avoiding memory growth proportional to input length.
Stores source-document facts in residual vectors from the LLM’s feed-forward layers.
Reconstructs query-relevant facts deterministically without rereading the original context or fine-tuning weights.
Answers single-fact questions in two-million-token story contexts, where prior methods fail.
Scope: demonstrated for single-fact question answering in long story contexts.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of the proposed method in the two-phase flow. Memorization reads the source in bounded windows, extracts anchor key and value entries, encodes each value as a residual 𝛿 indexed by a model activation, and stores the indexed residual vector outside the frozen model before the source is discarded. At response time the question routes to stored entries, gated injection adds each selected 𝛿 at its assigned feed-forward layer, and the frozen model generates the answer from the reconstructed facts.

papers.selection_reason: Training-free long-context recall via residual vectors with near-constant memory; fits long-context and memory-efficient inference.
papers.title: Residual Vector-based Reconstruction as Long-Context Recall Regardless of Context Window Size
papers.tldr: A training-free method uses feed-forward residual vectors to recall facts from contexts far beyond standard context-window limits with near-constant GPU memory.

papers.abstract: Advanced large language models (LLMs) with long context windows can substantially reduce input truncation in document-level machine translation (DocMT). However, direct Doc2Doc translation remains prone to n-gram repetition and progressive quality degradation. A common remedy is to segment the document into finer-grained chunks. Nonetheless, conventional rule-based chunking approaches fail to handle the length distribution mismatch between training and inference. To address this, we introduce Fixed-Range Chunking (FRC), utilizing dynamic programming to partition documents into chunks within a predefined length interval. By consistently applying FRC during training and inference, the input documents of any length are mapped to the same length distribution, substantially reducing train-test length mismatch. Centered on FRC, we propose a lightweight dual-boundary matching algorithm for chunk alignment, alongside four distinct training strategies. Experimental results show that FRC-based fine-tuning substantially improves 7B LLMs over direct Doc2Doc fine-tuning and outperforms existing DocMT methods on IWSLT2017. We further construct GlobVDoc, a 10-language test set independent of mainstream DocMT training sources, and show that FRC improves out-of-distribution document translation.
bullets: Direct long-document translation can suffer from n-gram repetition and progressive quality loss.
Fixed-Range Chunking (FRC) uses dynamic programming to partition documents within a predefined length interval.
The same chunking distribution is applied during training and inference to reduce train–test mismatch.
The approach includes a lightweight dual-boundary chunk-alignment algorithm and four training strategies.
Experiments report gains for 7B LLMs on IWSLT2017 and improved out-of-distribution translation on the 10-language GlobVDoc test set.

papers.abstract: Multivariate ordinal data along with covariates are commonly collected in problems ranging from alignment of language models with human preferences, as well as in recommender systems. For example, data sets such as MovieLens contain several movies rated on a scale 1--5 by human users, along with their demographic information such as age or gender. Similarly, data sets such as HelpSteer collect human feedback on several attributes such as "helpfulness" or "verbosity" of LLM response on an ordinal scale, with covariates depending on the LLM prompt--response pairs. Unfortunately, the standard approaches for modeling these data (a) look at the attributes individually rather than jointly, and (b) often convert the data into pairwise or list-wise win--loss comparisons for fitting models such as Bradley--Terry and Plackett--Luce. Both of these lead to a coarsening of what is actually observed, which we address via a joint covariate-dependent consecutive ratio Markov random field model. We also show pairwise or listwise comparison models are obtained under restrictions of our joint model, and that joint modeling improves comparisons. We also develop a maximum likelihood inference procedure even in the presence of an intractable normalizer.
bullets: Addresses the loss of information from modeling ordinal attributes separately or reducing them to win–loss comparisons.
Introduces a joint covariate-dependent consecutive ratio Markov random field for multivariate ordinal data.
Shows Bradley–Terry- and Plackett–Luce-type comparison models arise under restrictions of the joint model.
Develops maximum-likelihood inference despite an intractable normalizing constant.
Reports that joint modeling improves comparisons, without specifying quantitative results in the abstract.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes a joint model for multivariate ordinal preferences with covariates, providing a statistically rigorous approach relevant to LLM alignment and human feedback.
papers.title: Covariate-dependent Joint Modeling of Multivariate Ordinal Preferences and Its Connections with Comparison Models
papers.tldr: A joint covariate-dependent model preserves multivariate ordinal preference information while encompassing common pairwise and listwise comparison models as special cases.

papers.abstract: As small language models (SLMs) are increasingly deployed on resource-constrained and on-device platforms, including as components of agentic systems, the integrity of locally stored model parameters becomes an important safety concern. We investigate whether safety-sensitive behavior in LLaMA-2-7B-Chat is concentrated within a sparse subset of parameters, creating a reduced fault surface for targeted analysis. We study two complementary localization methods: low-rank safety-associated subspace analysis and parameter-level safety--utility importance filtering. Both approaches reveal highly non-uniform safety sensitivity across the network, with the MLP down_proj consistently emerging as a prominent safety-sensitive component and o_proj providing a smaller contribution. Using parameter-level localization, modifying only 0.19% of model weights in down_proj yields 53% Basic ASR and 56% GCG ASR, while tinyBenchmarks accuracy remains at 51.6% compared with a 52.2% unmodified baseline. These results motivate targeted fault analysis and selective integrity protection for language models deployed in resource-constrained, on-device, and agentic settings.
bullets: Safety sensitivity is highly uneven across the network, with the MLP down_proj most prominent and o_proj contributing less.
The study uses low-rank safety-subspace analysis and parameter-level safety–utility importance filtering.
Changing only 0.19% of down_proj weights produces 53% Basic ASR and 56% GCG ASR.
tinyBenchmarks accuracy remains nearly unchanged: 51.6% versus 52.2% for the unmodified model.
The findings support selective integrity protection for on-device and agentic deployments.

papers.selection_reason: Investigates safety in on-device LLMs and localizes safety-critical parameters, addressing a key concern for resource-constrained deployment.
papers.title: How Fragile Is On-Device Language Model Safety? Localizing Safety-Critical Parameters for Sparse Fault Analysis
papers.tldr: Safety behavior in LLaMA-2-7B-Chat is concentrated in a tiny subset of parameters, enabling targeted fault analysis with minimal utility loss.

papers.abstract: Multi-agent LLM systems are expected to be more reliable because agents can catch each other's mistakes. But peer pressure cuts both ways: the same correction that fixes a wrong answer can overturn a right one. The tempting safeguard is a brake that keeps the beneficial revisions and blocks the harmful ones. We show this brake is hard to build, for a simple reason: a revision is harmful exactly when the original answer was right, so deciding whether to block it is the same as knowing whether the model was already correct. This turns the open-ended hunt for a brake into one measurable quantity, the model's self-knowledge: any brake built from a deploy-time signal is a correctness probe in disguise, and self-knowledge is far from perfect (AUROC $\approx 0.64$--$0.89$ across six model families). We call this ceiling the wall. Even white-box steering of the model's own correctness direction does not breach it: it changes how often the model revises, but harmful and beneficial revisions move together. At population scale the wall becomes the cliff: when most agents start wrong, debate amplifies the shared mistake into a confident, wrong consensus. In our multiple-choice societies, more agents, more model diversity, and a stronger member do not fix it. What helps is adding information before the revision, not filtering after it. Local agreement is not global correctness.
bullets: Peer correction can help fix wrong answers but can also overturn correct ones.
Any deploy-time filter for harmful revisions effectively probes whether the original answer was correct.
Self-knowledge is imperfect, with AUROC around 0.64–0.89 across six model families.
White-box steering changes revision frequency but does not separate harmful from beneficial revisions.
When most agents are initially wrong, debate can amplify shared errors into confident consensus; adding information before revision helps more than filtering afterward.

Dotted lines (Llama) use an SAE-feature direction (Goodfire L19) with the same null; grey triangles mark α beyond the plotted range (full values in Appendix C).

papers.selection_reason: Studies LLM self-knowledge and revision filtering in multi-agent systems, directly relevant to LLM reasoning and reliability.
papers.title: One Axis, No Brake: Self-Knowledge Limits the Filtering of Harmful Peer Conformity in LLMs
papers.tldr: Filtering harmful peer conformity in LLM societies is fundamentally limited by imperfect self-knowledge: models cannot reliably tell when their original answer was already correct.

papers.abstract: Large language models can produce engineering descriptions and structured process representations, but standards-level serialization can substantially increase the generation burden. This diagnostic study examines whether separating engineering reasoning from Data Exchange in the Process Industry (DEXPI) serialization changes where representation and engineering failures occur in constrained greenfield surface-process design for underground gas storage. We compare Direct DEXPI generation with generation of a lightweight Engineering Intermediate Representation (IR) on three cases: single-pressure injection, withdrawal and export, and dual-pressure injection. All six conditions use one fixed model snapshot, qwen3.8-max-0902, with one completed hosted generation per condition. Direct outputs are XSD-valid in 2 of 3 cases, while all 3 Engineering IR outputs are structurally valid under a minimal validator. Direct prompt inputs contain approximately 121.8k-121.9k tokens, compared with 617-699 tokens for the Engineering IR prompts. Engineering feasibility does not uniformly favor the IR: one IR output is rejected for an explicit cooling-state contradiction. The cases also reveal two distinct Direct DEXPI failure modes: engineering inconsistency and standards-level serialization failure. The observed comparison shows that, in these evaluated method bundles, deferring DEXPI serialization substantially reduces representation burden and helps isolate serialization failure, but reducing representation burden alone does not eliminate engineering inconsistencies.
bullets: The study compares direct DEXPI generation with a lightweight Engineering Intermediate Representation (IR) for three greenfield underground-gas-storage surface-process cases.
Direct DEXPI outputs were XSD-valid in 2 of 3 cases, while all three IR outputs were structurally valid under a minimal validator.
Engineering IR prompts were approximately 617–699 tokens versus about 121.8k–121.9k tokens for direct DEXPI prompts.
Direct generation showed both engineering inconsistency and standards-level serialization failures.
One IR output still failed engineering review because of an explicit cooling-state contradiction.
papers.selection_reason: Investigates the application of LLMs in engineering process design, relevant to the general application of language foundation models.
papers.title: Separating Engineering Reasoning from DEXPI Serialization in LLM-Based Greenfield Surface-Process Design: A Three-Case Study for Underground Gas Storage
papers.tldr: Separating engineering reasoning from DEXPI serialization reduced representation burden and isolated serialization failures, but did not prevent engineering inconsistencies.

papers.abstract: Russian state propaganda spreads across many languages and online spaces. Yet, most computational work examines only one such space, usually social media, in one or two languages, and analyses sources rather than content. We introduce SWARM (Search-Web documents Annotated for Russian propaganda, Multilingual), a dataset of 2,183 search engine results across nine languages and diverse web domains (e.g., news, blogs, government sites), each annotated by trained coders for whether it supports a recurring Russian propaganda narrative. We benchmark a source-based blocklist, supervised classifiers, and zero-shot LLMs against these labels. The blocklist misses most propaganda-supporting documents, because such content is not confined to flagged "propaganda" outlets but also appears on mainstream ones. Content-level analysis helps, though how much depends on the model: the strongest LLM reaches a positive-class F1 of 0.73, whereas the supervised classifiers reach only about 0.5, with the smaller LLMs over-predicting support, mistaking topical relevance for endorsement. Detecting search-borne propaganda thus requires per-language, content-level evaluation, which we hope SWARM and our evaluation code enable.
bullets: Covers 2,183 search results in nine languages and diverse web domains.
Documents are labeled for support of recurring Russian propaganda narratives.
Benchmarks source blocklists, supervised classifiers, and zero-shot LLMs.
Blocklists miss propaganda on mainstream outlets; content-level models perform better.
The strongest LLM achieves 0.73 positive-class F1, while supervised models reach about 0.5; performance varies by language and model.

papers.abstract: Instruction-tuning datasets for large language models (LLMs) are often large, redundant, and imbalanced, limiting efficient adaptation. Naive large-batch fine-tuning repeatedly includes overrepresented sample groups while weakly covering underrepresented but informative ones, especially under data parallelism (DP) across multiple GPUs. We propose CluSTER, a Cluster-aware balanced Sampling framework for Training Efficient data Reduction in DP instruction tuning. CluSTER curates a representative reduced dataset through gradient-space clustering and DP-aware balanced allocation, ensuring dual-level coverage across clusters and workers, while preserving the original data distribution by weighted update. As a result, CluSTER reduces redundant computation and improves training stability without compromising model quality. Across multiple instruction-tuning datasets, CluSTER reduces training time by up to 69.6% with almost no accuracy loss compared to prior sampling and data reduction methods. Code is available at https://github.com/kaist-dmlab/CluSTER.
bullets: Targets redundancy and imbalance in large instruction-tuning datasets under data parallelism.
Uses gradient-space clustering and DP-aware allocation to balance coverage across clusters and workers.
Preserves the original data distribution through weighted updates.
Reduces training time by up to 69.6% with almost no accuracy loss across multiple datasets.
Scope: focuses on efficient data reduction for data-parallel instruction tuning.

papers.abstract: On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) scores student-generated prefixes with a solution-conditioned self-teacher, yet transfers supervision only through next-token probabilities. We ask whether the aligned final-layer discrepancy offers a useful second channel, and how to test that channel without confusing its geometry with auxiliary strength. SCOPE-OPSD projects the privileged teacher-student residual onto a frozen rank-64 factor estimated from residual covariance and language-model-head Fisher sensitivity. It reuses the forwards already required by OPSD and adds neither rollouts nor inference-time modules. A matched Random control preserves the structured factor's rank and nonzero spectrum and uses per-arm gradient-RMS calibration, isolating the effect of the data-dependent orientation. Across the complete 25/50/75/100-step trajectories for Qwen3-1.7B, 4B, and 8B, Structured is never below Pure OPSD, with strict gains in 11 of the 12 model-checkpoint combinations and an exact tie at 4B step 25. Structured also exceeds matched Random in 10 of the 12 combinations. At step 75 on Qwen3-1.7B, Structured exceeds matched Random by 1.39 Macro Avg@12 points in each of two independent training reruns. A cross-fitted diagnostic also shows 4.40 times greater held-out privileged-gap capture than the matched random orientation. The results support a compact, Fisher-conditioned privileged subspace for short-budget OPSD.
bullets: Addresses whether final-layer teacher–student discrepancies can provide a useful supervision channel beyond next-token probabilities.
Uses a frozen rank-64 factor derived from residual covariance and language-model-head Fisher sensitivity, reusing existing OPSD forwards without extra rollouts or inference modules.
A matched Random control preserves rank, spectrum, and gradient-RMS calibration to isolate the effect of the learned orientation.
Across 12 model-checkpoint combinations, Structured never underperforms Pure OPSD, improves in 11, and exceeds matched Random in 10.
The method is supported by a 4.40× higher held-out privileged-gap capture in a cross-fitted diagnostic and is presented for short-budget OPSD.

papers.abstract: Existing model marketplaces typically trade and select individual models as indivisible units, limiting their ability to exploit complementarities among heterogeneous experts. This paper proposes an MoE-based model market framework that lifts Mixture-of-Experts from a model-level learning architecture to a market-level coordination mechanism. In this framework, brokers use gating networks to coordinate multiple heterogeneous experts and deliver a composite model service. We formalize the market participants, service workflow, expert cost structure, and a welfare objective that combines predictive utility with heterogeneous execution costs. We then derive a cost-aware gating mechanism and market-aware training objective, and introduce a cost-adjusted revenue allocation rule that distributes residual revenue according to realized expert participation and execution cost. We also establish basic theoretical properties of the allocation rule, including budget balance, participation monotonicity, and cost sensitivity. Experiments over five random seeds on fifteen tabular and image benchmarks use independently trained and frozen neural and tree-based experts together with latency-derived execution costs. MoE Market achieves the highest mean welfare on all fifteen datasets and a lower mean expected cost than Standard MoE in every case, while maintaining competitive predictive performance. The allocation experiments further demonstrate systematic sensitivity to expert participation and cost, together with substantially lower computational overhead than exact Shapley allocation. These results suggest that MoE can serve as a market-level coordination principle for collaborative, cost-aware, and economically grounded model marketplaces.
bullets: Addresses the limitation of marketplaces that select individual models without exploiting complementarities among experts.
Uses broker gating networks, a welfare objective combining predictive utility and execution cost, and cost-aware training.
Introduces a cost-adjusted revenue allocation rule with budget balance, participation monotonicity, and cost sensitivity.
Across 15 tabular and image benchmarks, it achieves the highest mean welfare and lower mean expected cost than Standard MoE, while retaining competitive predictive performance.
Allocation is more computationally efficient than exact Shapley allocation; results are based on independently trained, frozen experts and latency-derived costs.

papers.abstract: Scaling laws describe power-law improvements in model performance with dataset size and parameter count, yet their underlying mechanisms are not fully understood. To explain the parameter count scaling, existing theory posits power-law scaling with model depth. In linear-attention models, this scaling is tied to a power-law data spectrum: unable to selectively attend to relevant tokens, these models learn according to global spectral strength, with stronger directions learned before weaker ones. Large language models, however, can be strongly nonlinear. Here, we show that nonlinear attention yields inverse-depth decay of loss across all tested data spectra. Nonlinearity enables attention to focus selectively on relevant tokens, allowing strong and weak spectral directions to be learned in parallel. Similar focusing across layers motivates a connection to the central limit theorem: shared error across layers sets the loss plateau, while aggregation turns layer-specific differences into continued gains with depth. Our findings suggest that depth scaling may arise from nonlinearity in attention, which allows large language models to focus locally and may make the global covariance structure less relevant.
authors: Zirui Peng, Yizhou Liu, Ziming Liu, Jeff Gore
bullets: Existing linear-attention theories link depth scaling to power-law data spectra and sequential learning of spectral directions.
Theoretical analysis finds inverse-depth loss decay for nonlinear attention across all tested data spectra.
Selective attention lets strong and weak spectral directions be learned in parallel rather than according to global spectral strength.
A central-limit-theorem perspective attributes the loss plateau to shared error and continued gains to aggregation of layer-specific differences.
The findings suggest attention nonlinearity may explain depth scaling in large language models, though the scope is limited to the tested spectra and setting.

papers.abstract: Uncertainty quantification (UQ) for large language models (LLMs) aims to provide reliable measures of predictive confidence, yet current methods are often unstable under meaning-preserving perturbations. Semantically equivalent paraphrases can induce substantial variability in predictive confidence, even for methods with formal guarantees, such as conformal prediction. To address this issue, we propose a paraphrase-aware UQ framework robust to semantic rewordings. Our approach trains a lightweight proxy model on LLM hidden states and aggregates its predictions across paraphrases to construct label-wise nonconformity scores. Under score exchangeability, conformal calibration retains marginal coverage. This guarantee can also hold under test-only rewording, provided that the paraphrase pipeline satisfies an additional distributional alignment condition. We evaluate three settings (normal, fully reworded, and semi-reworded) which apply rewording to neither dataset, both calibration and test datasets, or only the test dataset, respectively. Across seven multiple-choice QA benchmarks and multiple model families, our method produces compact prediction sets with empirical coverage generally near the nominal target, even in the semi-reworded setting. Ablation studies show that the learned proxy accounts for most of the reduction in set size, while paraphrase-augmented training and inference-time aggregation improve stability under rewording. Code is available at https://github.com/Raina-Xin/PA_Score.
bullets: Targets confidence variability caused by semantically equivalent paraphrases, including in conformal prediction.
Trains a lightweight proxy on LLM hidden states and aggregates predictions across paraphrases to form label-wise nonconformity scores.
Retains marginal coverage under score exchangeability; test-only rewording additionally requires distributional alignment.

Across seven multiple-choice QA benchmarks and multiple model families, produces compact prediction sets with coverage generally near the nominal target in normal, fully reworded, and semi-reworded settings.
Ablations identify the learned proxy as the main source of smaller sets, while paraphrase augmentation and aggregation improve rewording stability.

papers.abstract: We connect the spurious-reward paradox to a model's reachability and propose random-reward reinforcement learning (RL) as a useful tool for the probing enterprise, addressing a decade-long debate over what probing performance actually reveals about a model. There are two prevailing explanations for the surprising finding that even random rewards can improve the performance of large language models (LLMs): one attributes the gains to particular mechanisms within RL training; the other to data contamination. Our results motivate a different view: spurious-reward RL can probe a model's reachability, or what further training can attain from its current state under specified constraints, beyond what is reflected in its current performance. Two OLMo checkpoints with the same accuracy on synthetic arithmetic (3.5%), for example, reach 8.5% and 55% in their best runs under the same correctness-rewarded RL. Examining OLMo checkpoints across pre-training and mid-training reveals three distinct regimes of training response: early on, RL produces little improvement even when correct answers are rewarded; later in pre-training, rewarding correct answers becomes effective while random rewards remain weak; and, upon entering mid-training, even random rewards can produce large gains. A similar ordering appears in a number-masked supervised fine-tuning (SFT) analysis of these checkpoints, suggesting that the pattern is not specific to a particular RL mechanism. Moreover, RL with random rewards offers a distinctive perspective on what training can make an LLM do, since its reward signal supplies no information about which answers are correct. By asking what training can attain without correctness feedback, it addresses the label-leakage side of a central problem in decodability-based probing: whether a successful probe reveals the model's capabilities or learns the task itself.
bullets: The paper reframes gains from spurious or random rewards as evidence about training reachability, not necessarily RL-specific mechanisms or data contamination.
Two OLMo checkpoints with identical 3.5% synthetic-arithmetic accuracy reached 8.5% and 55% under the same correctness-rewarded RL, showing current accuracy can hide different trainability.

Across training, responses fall into three regimes: little early improvement; effective correctness-rewarded RL with weak random-reward gains later in pre-training; and strong gains from even random rewards during mid-training.
A number-masked supervised fine-tuning analysis shows a similar ordering, suggesting the pattern is not unique to RL.
Because random rewards provide no correctness information, this approach helps distinguish a model’s capability from a probe that learns the task or leaks labels.

papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents that reason over clinical records must track changes in a patient's state while preserving the history needed to understand them. Simply accumulating memories leaves it unclear which information still applies, whereas overwriting earlier memories can erase evidence needed to reconstruct treatment history and clinical trajectories. We introduce STAM, a state-transition-aware memory framework that records state changes as new clinical entries arrive. STAM combines semantic retrieval with typed clinical relations to identify affected memories, maintaining current information in Active and superseded or resolved information in History. At read time, a query-dependent gate selectively serves historical memory. Across four longitudinal clinical benchmarks, we evaluate STAM with downstream question answering, direct state-maintenance diagnostics, and comparisons at approximately matched context lengths.
bullets: Addresses the tension between accumulating memories and overwriting outdated clinical information.
Uses semantic retrieval and typed clinical relations to detect which memories are affected by new entries.
Separates current information into Active memory from superseded or resolved information in History.
Applies a query-dependent gate to selectively retrieve historical memory.
Evaluated on four longitudinal clinical benchmarks using question answering, state-maintenance diagnostics, and matched-context comparisons.

papers.abstract: Electronic health record (EHR) foundation models trained on longitudinal patient trajectories have demonstrated strong performance across diverse clinical prediction tasks. However, their clinical reasoning capabilities remain constrained by next-token prediction on limited and incomplete EHR data. To address this, we propose a reinforcement learning (RL) fine-tuning framework that treats EHR foundation models as generative policies over patient trajectories. We formulate common clinical prediction problems (e.g., hospital readmission) as event-conditioned, time-windowed reasoning tasks. We then design time-aware, rollout-sensitive rewards to account for finite rollout lengths and temporally inconclusive outcomes. We find that RL fine-tuning consistently improves over pre-trained backbones and strong baselines. Notably, it enables smaller models to surpass larger pre-trained models in data-limited regimes and induces positive transfer across tasks. Further analysis shows that RL fine-tuned models generate trajectories with stronger structural and semantic alignment to ground truth and greater downstream utility.
bullets: Recasts clinical prediction as event-conditioned, time-windowed reasoning over patient trajectories.
Uses time-aware, rollout-sensitive rewards to handle finite rollouts and temporally inconclusive outcomes.
RL fine-tuning consistently outperforms pretrained backbones and strong baselines.
Smaller RL-tuned models can surpass larger pretrained models in data-limited regimes and transfer positively across tasks.
Generated trajectories show stronger structural and semantic alignment with ground truth and greater downstream utility.

papers.tldr: Reinforcement learning fine-tuning improves EHR foundation models’ clinical reasoning over longitudinal patient trajectories, especially in data-limited settings.

papers.abstract: Meeting continuation requires tracking the agenda, speaker roles, participant intentions, and disagreement across long multi-party discussions. We introduce the Meeting Dynamic Forecasting Benchmark (MDFB), constructed from 2,207 real-world meetings and 24,794 future-facing queries. Given a transcript prefix and an active question, a model generates a plausible multi-turn continuation in one call. We evaluate utility---progress toward the question---and human-likeness---plausible conversational flow and role consistency---without requiring exact reproduction of the observed future. We further present GLARE, an adaptation of adversarial imitation learning to conditional language generation. A discriminator ranks the observed continuation above samples from the current actor, and its score supplies a KL-regularized policy reward; retraining on current-policy negatives allows the reward landscape to evolve with the actor. GLARE attains average human-evaluated win rates of 0.66 on utility and 0.70 on human-likeness, outperforming SFT and SPIN while remaining below the observed human continuation. We also demonstrate MDFB as a social reasoning arena for comparing general-purpose models, including closed-source systems, through reference-assisted judgments. Together, these studies illustrate the benchmark's use for both task-specific learning and output-based evaluation of meeting behavior.
bullets: Introduces MDFB, a benchmark with 2,207 real meetings and 24,794 future-facing continuation queries.
Evaluates generated continuations for progress toward the active question, conversational plausibility, and role consistency rather than exact future matching.
Adapts adversarial imitation learning: a discriminator scores observed versus generated continuations, producing a KL-regularized policy reward that evolves with the model.
GLARE achieves human-evaluated win rates of 0.66 for utility and 0.70 for human-likeness, outperforming SFT and SPIN but trailing human continuations.
MDFB also supports reference-assisted comparisons of general-purpose models, including closed-source systems.
