papers.abstract: AI agents based on foundation models (FMs) have demonstrated strong capabilities to perform complex open-ended tasks. However, they face some common challenges in practice: (a) agent behavior can deviate drastically even for semantically similar tasks, leading to catastrophically propagated errors; (b) high cost and latency due to FM calls, repeated in full whenever a task recurs with different inputs; (c) FMs' limited context and instruction following capability confine how well agents manage the ever-growing execution context and follow complex plans. We introduce $\textbf{A}$gent $\textbf{B}$ehavior as $\textbf{C}$ode $\textbf{Agent}$ (ABCAgent), which uses a symbolic program (e.g., Python code with potential neural functions) to fully specify the agent's behavior at runtime, with a powerful FM agent editing that program for flexibility. Behavior is thus specified without premature variable binding, and its execution is deterministic. We evaluate ABCAgent on six agent benchmarks, two of which we construct to test how well a derived program generalizes to variants of the task it was written for. ABCAgent matches a model-matched neural agent on GAIA and augmented GAIA, and surpasses it where robustness and long control flows matter: 98.3% against 97.3% on GSM-Symbolic ($p = 0.001$), 71.9% against 47.4% $\mathrm{Pass}^4$ on the telecom domain of $\tau^2$-bench ($p = 0.0001$), and more records written correctly at every loop length on our control-flow-augmented WorkArena benchmark. For more parametric task families, ABCAgent is also significantly superior in efficiency. Without authoring a new program, ABCAgent solves 92.6% of GSM-Symbolic instances and 20.1% of augmented GAIA variants, which yields $5.2\times$ lower latency and $7.0\times$ lower cost on GSM-Symbolic, 19% lower cost on augmented GAIA, and $9.5\times$ lower agent latency on $\tau^2$-telecom.
authors: Peng Qi, Chunliang Lyu, Gang Li, Fabian Chan, Cheng Chang, Ignacio Cases, Will Lu
bullets: Addresses behavior drift, repeated FM-call costs, and difficulty managing long contexts and complex plans.
Uses an FM agent to edit a runtime program, while program execution remains deterministic and avoids premature variable binding.
Matches a model-matched neural agent on GAIA and augmented GAIA, while outperforming it on robustness- and control-flow-focused benchmarks.
Reports stronger GSM-Symbolic, telecom $tau^2$-bench, and WorkArena performance, including 98.3% vs. 97.3% on GSM-Symbolic.
Reusing programs improves efficiency, including 5.2× lower latency and 7.0× lower cost on GSM-Symbolic; generalization is evaluated on task variants.

figures.caption: Figure 1: How ABCAGENT improves over traditional FM agents. Left: Traditional FM agents (e.g., ReAct (Yao et al., 2023)) re-invoke the FM at every action step, making reruns costly when task inputs change. Center: ABCAGENT separates design (task → program) from execution (program → result). The program can contain neural functions (e.g., papers() in this example) for flexibility. On any new input, only the program is re-run, eliminating redundant FM calls, especially orchestration calls. Right: Error reduction against cost efficiency on six benchmarks relative to the neural agent.

Figure 3: Cost efficiency of ABCAGENT relative to the neural agent under three forms of amortization: (a) reusing a program across the tasks of a family, (b) reusing a loop body, and (c) evaluating a policy repeatedly. The open squares in (a) are ABCAGENT on GSM-Symbolic without rebinding.

Figure 2: ABCAGENT processes new tasks by authoring programs from scratch, or reusing them from previously solved similar tasks. In the latter case, ABCAGENT attempts to substitute parameter values into the existing program (with a lightweight FM call for parsing only when necessary), before resorting to editing the program if substitution fails.

Figure 4: Accuracy and token consumption on WorkArena-CF as a function of loop length N , with the legend in (a) applying to both panels. In (a), circles give the fraction of records written correctly and squares the task success rate, with the non-loop tasks at N = 1; in (b), the dotted lines are least-squares power-law fits, both sublinear in N , labeled with 95% confidence intervals on their exponents.

Figure 6: Programs authored by ABCAGENT, taken verbatim from run artifacts. In (a), all instances of a GSM-Symbolic family share one derivation, so a sibling is solved by rebinding the highlighted constants; in (b), rebinding fails on an augmented GAIA family, because a new Boggle board requires a new search rather than a new constant.

Figure 5: Instances of a GSM-Symbolic family that a program frozen after seeing k of its 50 instances solves among the other 49, split into instances it has already seen and instances it has not. Each bar’s total is shown above it, and the dashed line marks all 49.

Table 1: Task success rate (%) and efficiency of ABCAGENT relative to model- and harness-matched neural agent on six agent benchmarks. Bold marks a statistically significant difference (p < 0.01) and italics the stronger system otherwise; cost efficiency and speedup are the neural agent’s cost and time divided by those of ABCAGENT on the tasks where both systems produced a result, highlighted when the deviation is ≥ 20%. The reference row is the strongest published result we are aware of, with — where none exists (see Appendix B for details).

Table 3: Fraction of task pairs within a family on which a program stored for one task (indexed by i) solves the other (indexed by j), for unseen (forward) and earlier (backward) tasks, with and without program reuse. On GSM-Symbolic, parameters are rebound with one FM call (Appendix B); bold marks p < 0.01 and italics the stronger result otherwise.

Table 2: Ablation of ABCAGENT’s components. We use the L1 subset of Augmented GAIA and 20% of GSM-Symbolic for this experiment. Free is the share of tasks solved without authoring a program, and Records is the percentage of records written correctly on the loop tasks (N = 30). §On WorkArena-CF, cheap rebinding never took effect, so this setting behaves as family reuse with the variant check alone. ‡Without the variant check, the replayed programs commit records with wrong field values, including one program that ignores its per-record input entirely (details in Appendix H).

Table 7: Performance on the two τ2-bench domains, with the benchmark’s own stock agent as the model-matched neural baseline. The paired row gives the mean per-task difference, ABCAGENT minus stock, with win, loss and tie counts; the reference row is the strongest model evaluated by Barres et al. (2025) under the same stock agent.

Table 8: Transfer of a stored program to other tasks of the same family, to tasks it has not seen (forward) and to tasks it was authored on earlier (backward). Bold marks differences from the no-reuse control that are significant at p < 0.01, by McNemar’s test on augmented GAIA and by a sign test over the 20 families on GSM-Symbolic, where a program whose parameters cannot be bound to the target counts as a failure. The frozen-parent rows bind a child task either with one FM call (FM-assisted) or with the parameter values from the child’s own program, and the last block binds every pair with one FM call, on GSM-Symbolic over 100 families with the full configuration’s programs, tested with the Wilcoxon test over families (Appendix B), and on augmented GAIA from each family’s first child solved in both arms to its siblings.

Table 5: Task success rate (%) on GAIA and augmented GAIA by difficulty level, with the number of tasks in parentheses. The reference row is the strongest generalist agent on the HAL leaderboard (Kapoor et al., 2025), p is the exact McNemar test, and italics mark the strongest system in each column; no level differs significantly.
Table 4: Prompt-based neural agents and ABCAGENT adapting in a continual learning setting on τ2-telecom. Revealing the reward at authoring is an oracle ceiling.

Table 9: Component ablation on GSM-Symbolic over 1000 tasks from 20 templates, adding components cumulatively. Cheap rebinding is the only component that reduces cost, and accuracy is near ceiling for every setting.
Table 6: Complex Task types and corresponding task names

Table 10: Records written correctly (%) on WorkArena-CF at N=30, crossing the variant check with the executor loop, without family reuse. ⋆ is the configuration reported as ABCAGENT; ‡without the variant check, the replayed programs commit records with wrong field values, including one program that ignores its per-record input entirely and submits the same values on every record.

papers.selection_reason: Programmatic specifications for robust and efficient LLM agents; relevant to LLM-based agent design and efficiency.
papers.title: Agent Behavior as Code: Efficient and Robust LLM Agents with Programmatic Specifications
papers.tldr: ABCAgent specifies LLM agent behavior as editable symbolic programs, improving determinism, robustness, and efficiency across diverse tasks.

papers.abstract: An agent with long-term memory can answer from a record it should no longer use, such as a plan the user later cancelled. We ask what a memory store must expose for an agent to know this before retrieving anything, and we score that judgment on its own, as metamemory monitoring. Readers see only a value-free summary: record counts by lifecycle state and a list of attribute names. Each of 148 questions is asked against three versions of one store that differ in one attribute, so wording cannot give the answer away. What a model adds depends on the length of that list. On the short lists the benchmark's ground truth produces (2.6 names on average), none of five language models reliably beats a cosine-similarity lookup over the names, and the three stronger ones are equivalent to it within 0.05. Under a control that fixes counts and list length, none is reliably above it and none is shown equivalent. On lists longer than the stores we tested write, padded to 60 names, the lookup loses 0.18; GPT-5.6 Luna and Sol lose 0.06 to 0.07 and lead it by 0.13 to 0.14, while the other three fall with it. The lead holds for Sol against a sibling padded to the same length and counts. Reworded to share no word with the names, the lookup loses 0.02 and one stronger reader edges 0.04 ahead. On the short lists the three stronger readers lead only where the summary counts a state without naming it, and one count feature closes that lead within a question, though not when items are pooled. The backends we tested omit or misstate this information: under FR-Bank's own metadata, GPT-4.1 mini, Haiku 4.5 and the lookup fall from 0.73, 0.82 and 0.75 to 0.60, 0.71 and 0.59. In these tests, what the store wrote down limited every reader we gave it to. All stores are synthetic; control, whether a better judgment yields a better answer, is left to a later study.
bullets: The study evaluates metamemory: whether an agent can judge a record’s usability before retrieving its contents.
Readers receive only lifecycle-state counts and attribute names across 148 controlled questions and three minimally different store versions.
On short, realistic lists, five language models generally do no better than cosine-similarity lookup over attribute names.
Longer attribute lists reveal some stronger models outperforming lookup, but backend metadata omissions still substantially reduce performance.
The experiments use synthetic stores and do not test whether better pre-retrieval judgments improve downstream answers.

Figure 5: Reliability diagram for the pooled hard tier (bins with n ≥ 10). The indexed conditions rank well (Spearman ρ = 0.9000 intact, 1.0000 names-only) and scale badly (mean predicted 0.217 against observed 0.056, about 3.9× over-confident), while the blind condition neither ranks (ρ = 0.1026) nor calibrates: the elicited number behaves as a ranker rather than a probability.

Table 7: The exact capability table records the cross-model set on FR-Bank with n = 84; luna, sol, and the three new models use k = 5, while mini is the original primary elicitation; h marks the rows elicited through the vendor’s agent harness (the paragraph above). The clustered column reports the persona-clustered sensitivity uniformly for the whole set; the item-level interval remains the preregistered primary endpoint.

Table 57: The main-study record separates frozen design choices from measured checks in pipeline order. It shows how the labels, presence control, leakage screen, and querying apparatus constrain the reported estimates.

Table 1: Counterfactual obligation AUROC: 88 supersession, 30 retraction and 30 expiry positives. Brackets: persona intervals. The matched column is the within-triple comparison of PN against PRESENT, (W +T/2)/148; it and W/T/L are post hoc; persona intervals keep triples intact. Questiononly AUROC is 0.50. Differences at four decimals. (Appendix C.2)

Table 13: The authorship-matched set (n = 36; 12 PN, 29 non-ABSENT; one generator voice for every label; label transfer 36/36). Blind NOK includes chance on all three models. The paired NOK gain is positive on all three and excludes zero on Opus 5 only, the resolution an n = 36 set affords. FOK rows are descriptive; their blind intervals are not reported. The probe block is the recorded supervised probe of Table 12, run unchanged on these same 36 questions.

Table 17: The moved-count control: each model under the moved text against its recorded supersededonly row, whole set and per state, with the paired difference and both intervals, beside the reference readers on the same text. Descriptive; no prediction was registered on the first three readers’ rows. Opus 5’s five-draw row was registered before its four added draws (Amendment 1), which predicted that the one-draw movement on retraction and expiry would replicate at five draws with both intervals excluding zero; it did. GPT-5.6 Luna and GPT-5.6 Sol ran at five draws under the second amendment, whose one prediction, that each falls reliably on both counted states, failed on retraction for both.

Table 41: Supersession only (post hoc): each model minus the name lookup under the same summary on the 76 supersession pairs (228 items), on the paraphrases and on the original questions of the same pairs; upper panel the pooled AUROC with the item-level and the persona-clustered paired intervals, lower panel the matched metric with the triple-level and the persona-grouped intervals. ∗: both intervals clear of zero.

Table 46: The long-list check on the whole counterfactual set, 444 items and 148 triples (descriptive; the registered comparisons are the supersession slice): every reader’s padded and unpadded scores as in Table 44 (the first two panels), then each model minus the name lookup as in Table 45 (the last two). ∗: both intervals exclude zero; bold: reliable.

Table 6: Run coverage, model by question set, in the words of the run records. Two runs stopped at the budget on the full populations, so their complete rows are on the cross-model set; five models ran on the counterfactual set, and five ran its paraphrase set (Table 5): GPT-4.1 mini one call, Haiku 4.5 five, Opus 5 one, GPT-5.6 Luna and GPT-5.6 Sol five through the raw interface under the default summary only; the same five ran it again with the superseded-names list padded to 60 names, GPT-4.1 mini, Haiku 4.5, GPT-5.6 Luna and GPT-5.6 Sol at five calls and Opus 5 at one. h: elicited through the vendor’s agent harness rather than the raw API (Appendix A).

Table 9: Blind and indexed judgments with the paired gain and both intervals: coverage by backend for GPT-4.1 mini (positives non-ABSENT) and the obligation judgment on FR-Bank by model (positives PN). On the hard tier every coverage positive is an obligation, so that FOK row scores the same positives as the NOK row.

Table 92: The registration record lists each frozen monitoring artifact, commit, freeze day (day 0 is the first freeze), scope, and outcome. It distinguishes held or failed predictions from N-A method freezes.

Table 96: The registration record, continued: the sibling-name control and the names-against-counts amendment on the three stronger models, both registered after the matched metric had been read, the long-list check on the counterfactual set, registered after the paraphrase check had been read, and the sibling-name control at 60 names, registered after the long-list check had been read; the Outcome column lists each prediction’s outcome. Every row was committed before its first call.

Table 37: The list-length check and its amendment. Upper block: the superseded-names list of each of the 661 main-study summaries padded with correct attribute names that no scored question of the persona targets, to 15, 30 and 60 names, and for the two lookups to 100 and 200 names under the registered draw order, which continues into other personas’ names once the store’s own pool is exhausted (79 of the 242 summaries at 100, every summary at 200); obligation AUROC of each reader against its recorded 1.75-name row, with the paired difference and both intervals. Lower block: the counterfactual set’s 444 superseded-only summaries with wrong names injected into the negatives’ lists at FR-Bank’s measured rate (0.232) and at 0.40; AUROC against the recorded list, the paired difference and both intervals, and for the models the difference from the embedding lookup on the same lists (the weaker of the two intervals). Descriptive; no prediction was registered, and every branch prints as it came out.

Table 35: A hybrid reader with no generative-model call on the counterfactual set (registered; ADDENDUM_CF2_HYBRID_READER): a logistic regression of the label on the name lookup’s cosine, the category-guessing reader’s share and an indicator that a category was assigned, fitted under leave-persona-out over the 40 personas and scored out of fold, under the superseded-only summary. Upper panel: whole set and per state with the persona interval, and the paired differences against the name lookup and the category-guessing reader with both intervals. Lower panels: each model’s recorded row minus the hybrid, and GPT-4.1 mini’s five-draw row (Table 1) beside its one-draw row; then the same reader under the matched metric (post hoc), whole set and per state, minus the lookup and against each model. Predicted before the run: that the hybrid exceeds the name lookup reliably (it does not: the item-level interval includes zero, a failed prediction) and that GPT-5.6 Sol stays reliably above it (as predicted). The fitted coefficients on the standardized features range over the folds from +1.13 to +1.29 on the lookup and +0.39 to +0.53 on the share.

Table 81: The downstream experiment. Seven registered policies assemble a view from the five retrieved entries and, where a rule fires, the store’s non-active records for the attributes the summary names (the oracle: the item’s own attribute; the gold labels decide abstention). Table 88 carries each policy’s fires, reach, view size, tagged reach and coverage; the first block here adds the abstention counts and the reach by the state the obligation arises from. Stage 2 is one GPT-4.1 mini answer per distinct view, scored by the ground-truth token detector at its high-precision threshold (0.80) and at the ground-truth join’s threshold (0.50), split by whether the forbidding record carried its tag. The literal-threshold lookup row is descriptive; its answer stage was registered after the first draft (Amendment 2) and prints in the second block, whose lower rows give the same counts under the answer stage run once more with an added instruction to treat tagged records as not to be used (Amendment 3; the Amendment 1 policy’s views were not answered again). The last row of each block is the descriptive policy of the amendment registered after the study: the model rule with its obligation score elicited under the summary that names all three states, and the all-states fetch set, so that the counted-state gate can fire. Scored with the store’s tags as joined, one retraction tag inverted (the negation paragraph).

Table 26: The intent crossover on the counterfactual set (registered; ADDENDUM_CF2_INTENT_CROSSOVER and its Amendment 1). Each supersession pair of the set is asked its recorded present-tense question and a second question about how the attribute has changed, of the same two store versions (PN and PRESENT) under the default summary (population A, 87 of the 88 pairs); each expiry pair is asked its recorded upcoming-intent question and a question about the past event under the all-states summary (population B, 26 of the 30 pairs); our read of the crossed questions dropped five pairs before any call. The crossed question makes the same stale record licensed, so a reader that conditions on intent scores the PN version of the original question above the same version under the crossed question. This table: that same-store AUROC, chance 0.50, with the persona-grouped and the pair-clustered interval and the within-pair W/T/L. Table 27: the interaction, the mean of the two-by-two contrast, with both intervals, and the pooled AUROC of the original question’s PN version against the other three cells. Each reader ran under the main-study rubric and under a rubric that states the intent rule. GPT-5.6 Luna and Haiku 4.5 ran five draws; their draw-1 rows are the column comparable with the one-draw readers, and the body reads that column. GPT-5.6 Sol was added after an interim read of three models’ rows, and its prediction is labelled so in Appendix F; under the intent-explicit rubric it counts 76/0/11 within pairs on population A, and in 9 of its 11 losses both questions score 0.96 or higher, so the rule was not applied on those pairs. Under the intent-explicit rubric no model’s discrimination on its original questions falls by more than 0.05 (the largest fall −0.0458, Haiku 4.5 on population A; the largest rise +0.1716, GPT-4.1 mini on population B).

Table 85: The composite per policy over the full obligation set (661 questions) with its three components (DS Amendment 7, descriptive; no prediction was registered; no generative-model call). A licensed item counts when its answer is correct at 0.50. An obligation counts when it is reached, answered and reported: the answer names the lifecycle state from a closed word list (superseded, retracted, expired, no longer, not current, outdated, cancelled, replaced, withdrawn, discontinued, past, and previous or former in a sentence that also carries one of those) without giving the stale value by the committed detector at 0.50, or, on a supersession item, gives the successor value; the count by the successor alone is printed beside it. An absent item counts when the policy’s coverage rule abstained on it or, where the rule let it through, the answerer abstained on its recorded five-line view (the Amendment 6 answers under the header; the absent items a gated rule answers on a longer view, ten under the model rule, seventeen under the lookup rule and seventy-two under the literal rule, are read on that longer view, answered under the same header prompt after the registration, 99 distinct views per answerer; read on the five-line view as a proxy instead, every composite is within one of the value printed). The last column is the rule-only reading, in which an absent item counts only when the coverage rule abstained. The oracle’s rule is the label itself, so its absent component is 383 of 383; the row is printed and enters no comparison. Rows: retrieval alone and the literal rule (no coverage rule), the gated rules under the header prompt, the same rules with the store’s untagged duplicates tagged (tagged), then the oracle; the denominators are 174 licensed items, 104 obligations, 383 absent items and 661 in all. Scored with the store’s tags as joined, one retraction tag inverted (the negation paragraph).

Table 36: The sibling-name control (registered; ADDENDUM_R125_SIBLING): a fourth version of each of the 88 supersession pairs, rendered from the PN version’s text with the target’s name in the superseded-names list replaced by a same-category sibling under HV-B’s pool and neighbourhood rule (no content token shared with the question or the target; 88 of 88 pairs kept; the leak screen 0 of 30), so counts, list length and every other line are identical to the PN version’s. Upper panel: W/T/L and the matched AUROC of the PN version against the sibling version with both intervals; the PN-against-PRESENT value on the same pairs; and the sibling version against the PRESENT version (how far an unrelated name in the list raises the score, the list-length component; descriptive). Lower panels: the sibling-minus-PRESENT mean score with both intervals, and each reader minus the name lookup on the primary comparison, ∗ where both intervals exclude zero. Four predictions, all as written: P-SB1, the lookup at or above 0.90 (0.9489); P-SB2, every model at or above 0.80 with the persona interval above 0.50 (lower bounds 0.8409, 0.8351, 0.8681, 0.8274, 0.9387); P-SB3, the random-token lookup and the count reader within 0.05 of 0.50 (0.4716, 0.5000); P-SB4, no model reliably above the lookup. Disclosure: the scorer was dry-run once before the freeze to check its code path and computed the three no-model readers on the sibling texts, so P-SB1 and P-SB3 are recorded values rather than predictions and are not counted in Appendix F; no model row existed at the dry run. GPT-4.1 mini, Haiku 4.5 and GPT-5.6 Luna are five-draw means as in Table 1; Opus 5 and GPT-5.6 Sol one draw.

Table 90: What the gate buys, reach only (registered; ADDENDUM_R122_GATE_REACH): three policies assembled from the recorded ranking and the store’s records with no reader (monitor) call and no answer call, against the recorded model rule. The always-open fetch keys the lifecycle fetch on the name the lookup matches best and never abstains; the similarity view is the recorded top-k retrieval; the recency-aware view keeps the newest record of each attribute and fills to k. Each is read at its named depth and budget-matched to the model rule’s mean view over the 661 questions (5.43 lines) by interpolating between the two bracketing depths (the always-open fetch between k = 3 and 4 with weight 0.91 on the deeper, the similarity and recency-aware views between k = 5 and 6 with weight 0.43). Upper panel: the forbidding record in view over the 104 obligations with the Wilson interval and the per-state census, and the difference from the model rule with both intervals. Lower panel: the licensed record in view over the 174 licensed items with its difference from the model rule, and the mean lines per question over the 661 and over the 104. The fetch keyed on the best-matched name at four similarity lines reaches 85 of 104 at 5.53 lines; the matched always-open row loses licensed records reliably because the truncated fill drops them; the recency-aware view reaches no retraction obligation because the retracted record is never the newest of its attribute. All three predictions came out as written: the ungated fetch within 0.05 of the model rule at the matched budget, its unmatched form spending more lines, and the recency-aware view below the rule by more than 0.05.

Table 44: The long-list check, supersession (registered): the 264 items of the 88 supersession triples with the superseded-names list padded to 60 names, every reader’s pooled AUROC (upper panel) and matched score (lower panel, with W/T/L) beside its recorded unpadded value on the same items, and the paired difference padded minus unpadded with the item-level and the persona-grouped interval (pooled) or the triple-level and the persona-grouped interval (matched). The three lookups read the padded lists as printed; the models ran the padded summaries at the settings of their Table 1 rows. ∗: both intervals exclude zero.

Table 45: The long-list check, supersession (registered): each model minus the name lookup on the same lists, pooled (item-level and persona-grouped intervals) and matched (triple-level and personagrouped), on the padded lists (upper panel) and on the unpadded lists (lower panel: the recorded model minus the recorded lookup). A difference in bold is reliable (both intervals exclude zero, ∗).

Table 54: The expiry state of the counterfactual set extended by a third descriptive draw: the 444’s 30 expiry pairs (90 items), the 14 eligible pairs the first draw left undrawn (42 items, built by the same construction with questions written before any store version existed), and the two pooled (44 pairs, 132 items). Obligation AUROC per reader and summary; question only (blind) is 0.5000 by construction on every set, so each value is also a gain. Intervals are the weaker of the item-level and persona-grouped paired intervals for the models and the persona interval of the AUROC for the lookups. The pooled row joins two cells scored on different dates under two registrations with the same prompts, models and construction; Opus 5’s rows are five-call averages on the 444 and single calls on the extension, so its pooled row mixes the two; the rows below them read Opus 5 at its first draw on every pair, so the pooled value there mixes nothing. Descriptive; no prediction was registered.

Table 53: The sibling-name control at 60 names (registered; ADDENDUM_R141_SB60): the PN version with its list padded to 60 names against a fourth version with one name swapped for a same-category sibling, identical pad and counts, on the 88 supersession pairs. Upper panel: each reader’s matched score (W + T/2)/88 with the triple-level and persona-grouped intervals, the pooled AUROC over the 176 items, and the sibling against the padded PRESENT version (descriptive). The no-model rows were recorded before the freeze. Lower panel: each model minus the name lookup, paired; ∗: both 95% intervals exclude zero; equivalent: both 90% intervals inside [−0.05,+0.05]. Haiku 4.5 and Opus 5 were not run on this control.

Table 97: Obligation AUROC on the counterfactual set by whether the question names the plan or value its attribute is about (89 flagged questions, n = 267; 59 unflagged, n = 177), whole and by lifecycle state (supersession / retraction / expiry), for the two lookups on their own summaries and the three models under each summary. Every reader scores higher on the unflagged half. Exploratory: post hoc, no prediction, no interval.

Table 12: Question-only probes measure how much PN label signal is available without a store. Labelsupervised term-frequency–inverse-document-frequency (TF–IDF) features expose generator-specific template signal rather than monitor cue use, whereas the zero-shot mini probe on the cross-model set remains at chance.

Table 4: Reach on the full obligation set: forbidding records among the 104 obligations, mean lines over the 661 questions, and licensed records among the 174 items. Matched rows interpolate between depths (Table 90, Appendix E.10). No answer is scored here.

Table 14: Label structure by item-construction category on the cross-model set (n = 84, 40 PN). Ranking by category alone attains AUROC 0.9736, above the supervised probe’s 0.7972 on the same set. This is a deterministic census on recorded labels (no model is fit and nothing is resampled), so no interval is defined, the same reporting convention as the one-bit is-FR-Bank rule in Appendix E.8. Six of the eight categories carry a single class, and only expired logistics carries both at usable size.

Table 95: The registration record, continued: the fourth backend’s frozen readings, the five registrations of the counterfactual and downstream follow-ups, the intent crossover, the four registrations of the encoder, draw, rubric and reach checks, and the hybrid reader; the Outcome column lists each prediction’s outcome, and a prediction registered after an interim read of other models’ rows is labelled so. Every row was committed before its first call.

Table 24: The ablations under the matched metric (post hoc). Upper panel: the names-only, countsonly, totals-randomized and moved-count rows, W/T/L against the PRESENT version and the matched AUROC, whole set and per state (Tables 18 and 17 carry the pooled rows). Middle panels: the paired contrasts, one row per scope, with both intervals, ∗ where both exclude zero; the counted states are the 60 retraction and expiry triples. Names alone leave both smaller models where the intact summary left them and counts alone cost each about 0.14, all of it on supersession; the moved count moves the three stronger models reliably on the counted states and neither smaller model. Lower panel: Opus 5 under the all-states summary minus the all-states lookup, five draws and its first draw alone.

Table 19: Names against counts on the three stronger models (E2, Amendment 1; registered, ADDENDUM_R125_E2_AMENDMENT_1). E2’s two renderings, byte-identical to Table 18’s, on Opus 5 (one draw, Batch), GPT-5.6 Luna (five draws through the raw API; its one-draw reading beside) and GPT-5.6 Sol (one draw; not run, see below): the pooled AUROC (its persona interval is in the ledger), the paired difference from the recorded intact row with both intervals (∗ both exclude zero), counts only minus names only, and the renderings under the matched metric, the whole set and the two counted states (ret., exp.; their persona intervals are in the ledger, P-N5’s two failing lower bounds below). Three predictions: P-N3, names only within tolerance of the intact row at the point, failed (on the models run) (GPT-5.6 Luna −0.0598; Opus 5 −0.0426, within the band); P-N4, counts only reliably below names only, held (on the models run); P-N5, counts only above 0.50 on both counted states under the matched metric with the persona interval excluding 0.50, failed (on the models run) (Opus 5 reads 0.4833 on retraction; GPT-5.6 Luna’s expiry lower bound is 0.4615). GPT-5.6 Sol’s lane was dropped by the registration’s own rule when the vendor’s projection for this task and the sibling-name control together exceeded the cap, so its rows print as not run.

Table 10: Five capability items were registered before the cross-model run. The first four held, while the sol threshold failed, revising the earlier one-call account. The first, third, and fourth items are scored on the 84-item cross-model set; the second and fifth on the original per-model populations, the shared 150-item stratified set, with mini’s value from its recorded one-call main-study elicitation and luna’s and sol’s from the five-call average.

papers.title: Knowing the Store: What a Memory Backend Must Write Down Before an Agent Can Read It
papers.tldr: Memory backends must record lifecycle-relevant metadata explicitly, because missing or ambiguous information limits an agent’s ability to avoid using obsolete records.

papers.abstract: At the core of modern prompting techniques is contextual sensitivity, the ability of large language models to adapt their predictions based on inference-time context. Despite its central role, inference behavior under strong contextual influence remains poorly understood, particularly at the level of internal inference dynamics. We introduce a theoretical framework for analyzing contextual influence through inference dynamics, enabling quantitative characterization of inference behavior beyond output-level answer changes. Our analysis shows that inference dynamics do not exhibit unbounded drift under repeated contextual assertions. Instead, predictive representations converge to stable, query-dependent regimes that fundamentally constrain whether contextual signals can alter a model's prediction. This leads to a surprising finding: Repeated contextual assertions do not act as accumulating evidence during inference and may therefore fail to alter a model's prediction even under unbounded repetition, while in other cases a prediction change becomes inevitable. We empirically validate our theoretical predictions, demonstrating strong alignment between theory and observed inference behavior. These contributions offer a principled pathway toward characterizing the limits of contextual influence during inference, providing practical implications for model development.
authors: Zongye Hu, Weiqing Luo, Yanjie Fu, Yu Gan, Haofeng Zhang, Ziyi Huang
bullets: Contextual sensitivity is central to prompting, but its internal inference dynamics remain poorly understood.
The paper introduces a theoretical framework that quantitatively analyzes contextual influence beyond output changes.
Predictive representations converge to stable, query-dependent regimes rather than drifting without bound.
Repeated contextual assertions do not accumulate as evidence during inference and may have no effect in some cases.
Empirical results align strongly with the theoretical predictions, helping characterize limits on contextual influence.

papers.selection_reason: Theoretical analysis of inference dynamics and contextual influence in LLMs; relevant to LLM behavior and inference understanding.
papers.title: Not All Answers Are Contextually Persuadable: Inference Dynamics in Large Language Models under Contextual Influence
papers.tldr: Large language models’ responses to repeated contextual influence converge to query-dependent limits, so repetition may fail to change some predictions while inevitably changing others.

papers.abstract: Self-evolving large language model (LLM) systems repeatedly propose, evaluate, and incorporate updates to prompts, skills, or other persistent artifacts. Despite their growing effectiveness, these systems typically operate under a predetermined iteration or compute budget, without a principled criterion to determine when further evolution is no longer worthwhile. This can lead to two undesirable consequences: unnecessary computation after performance has saturated and the risk of returning late updates that overfit or exploit the evaluation signal. These issues motivate us to study two fundamental questions: when should a self-evolving system stop, and what should it output once it stops? We address the first by formulating an online sequential testing problem and constructing an anytime-valid restart detector using the per-item paired evaluation outcomes already produced by self-evolving LLM systems. We address the second by formulating a change-point estimation problem and using the estimated transition to select an earlier artifact for output. The resulting procedure is plug-and-play and requires no modification of the underlying self-evolving algorithms. Across two self-evolving frameworks, three LLM model families, and five benchmarks, our method substantially reduces computation costs while maintaining comparable unseen-test performance. For example, on SearchQA with SkillOpt and DeepSeek V4 Flash, our method stops at round 4 rather than the full budget of 40, reducing token usage by 91.6% while achieving 82.43% unseen-test accuracy versus 82.00% under the full-budget run.
authors: Enoch Yin, Bin Liu, Zhengling Qi
bullets: Addresses when self-evolving LLM systems should stop and which artifact they should return.
Uses anytime-valid online sequential testing on paired evaluation outcomes to detect when further updates are no longer worthwhile.
Estimates a change point and selects an earlier artifact to reduce the risk of late-update overfitting or evaluation-signal exploitation.
Evaluated across two frameworks, three LLM families, and five benchmarks, with comparable unseen-test performance and lower computation.
On SearchQA with SkillOpt and DeepSeek V4 Flash, it stopped at round 4 instead of 40, reduced token usage by 91.6%, and achieved 82.43% versus 82.00% unseen-test accuracy.

papers.title: When Is Enough Enough in Self-Evolving LLM Systems?
papers.tldr: A plug-and-play stopping and artifact-selection method lets self-evolving LLM systems stop near performance saturation, reducing computation while preserving unseen-test performance.

papers.abstract: utoregressive generation in Large Language Models (LLMs) is constrained by the memory and computational demands of attention mechanisms. Sparse attention methods mitigate this cost by selecting only high-probability entries of the attention matrix. We observe that in many such methods, this renders the probability-value multiplication negligible, shifting the bottleneck to the query-key step. Key heads can therefore be reduced to accelerate inference, while retaining more value heads preserves capacity with limited additional decoding cost. We introduce Sparse Asymmetric Group-Query Attention (SAGA), which decouples key and value head counts to exploit this principle, and pair it with approximate top-N (Atop-N) attention, a simple sparse attention method designed to study the interaction between sparsity and head-count asymmetry. We formalize the benefits of this asymmetry theoretically and validate them empirically through latency measurements and quality evaluations on models up to 1.5B parameters. Together, SAGA and Atop-N achieve end-to-end decoding speedups exceeding $2\times$ over our full-attention GQA baseline at long contexts. Models trained from scratch with SAGA nearly match the quality of comparable GQA variants on the evaluated benchmarks. To facilitate adoption, we introduce an efficient fine-tuning method that converts pretrained models to the SAGA architecture, enabling practitioners to benefit from our approach without costly retraining.
authors: Noam Elata, Itay Lamprecht, Mikey Shechter, Daniel Ohayon, Itay Hubara, Daniel Soudry
bullets: Attention sparsity shifts the decoding bottleneck from probability-value multiplication to query-key computation.
SAGA decouples key and value head counts, retaining more value heads while reducing key heads.
The method is paired with approximate top-N attention (Atop-N) to investigate sparse, asymmetric attention.
Experiments on models up to 1.5B parameters report over 2× end-to-end decoding speedups at long contexts versus a full-attention GQA baseline.
Scratch-trained SAGA models nearly match comparable GQA quality, and an efficient conversion fine-tuning method supports pretrained models.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces asymmetric sparse attention with decoupled key/value heads for faster LLM decoding, an architectural and efficiency contribution.
papers.title: More Value per Key: Asymmetric Sparse Attention for Faster LLM Decoding
papers.tldr: SAGA accelerates long-context LLM decoding by using fewer key heads than value heads, while preserving quality with sparse attention.

papers.abstract: Beyond scaling their parameters and data, large language models currently gain versatility on new problems along a single axis: the tokens they spend on chain-of-thought (CoT). We investigate whether dynamic routing programs, which execute a subset of the model's layers or iterate some of them, can open a second axis of test-time adaptation, complementary to CoT and free of any gradient update. Prior work showed that such programs exist and bring accuracy and efficiency gains on problems similar to those they were trained on; we ask whether they can also be identified rapidly, from a handful of demonstrations (3 or 10), by a strategy that transfers across models and tasks without training. First, we find that strategies that select programs by the probability they assign to the demonstrations' labels, arbitrated by the model's own confidence, bring consistent gains: on average over the 49 tasks of MMLU and substantially on four of seven models, and most of all on far out-of-distribution tasks such as ARC-AGI, where programs double the accuracy of a 7B model whose CoT fails. Second, on MMLU across the seven post-trained models, routing complements CoT in practice: the two succeed on different queries, and their composition exceeds CoT alone. Despite these gains, our analyses show that confidence-based selection leaves much of the potential untapped, in two places in particular: (1) in surfacing the routing potential that is already present early in pre-training but becomes harder to select after post-training, and (2) in making models robust to the refinements routing introduces, since unsuccessful routes tend to drive the residual stream out of the distribution that the following layers expect. Together, our results point to dynamic routing as a paradigm for extending the plasticity of existing and future LLMs in rapid test-time adaptation.
authors: Michal \v{S}tef\'anik, Marek Kadl\v{c}\'ik, Josef Kucha\v{r}, Michal Spiegel
bullets: Selects routing programs from only 3 or 10 demonstrations using label likelihood and the model’s confidence, without gradient updates or task-specific training.
Produces consistent gains across 49 MMLU tasks and seven models, with especially large benefits on far-out-of-distribution ARC-AGI tasks.
Routing and chain-of-thought succeed on different queries; combining them outperforms chain-of-thought alone on MMLU.
Selection remains limited: post-training can obscure routing potential, and unsuccessful routes may push representations outside the distribution expected by later layers.
Scope: results focus on rapid, confidence-based program selection across benchmark tasks and models.

papers.selection_reason: Dynamic routing as gradient-free test-time adaptation for LLMs, directly relevant to test-time learning and LLM research.
papers.title: Dynamic Routing as a New Dimension for Test-time Versatility of LLMs
papers.tldr: Dynamic routing lets LLMs adapt at test time by selecting or repeating layers, providing a training-free complement to chain-of-thought that can substantially improve performance on new tasks.

papers.abstract: When a team of robots delegates planning and mutual trust to LLM agents, a single compromised robot can corrupt the shared outcome. We study this threat in a grounded task: a multi-robot survey in which measurements can be verified against the physical world, but every verification costs budget that would otherwise advance the mission. We treat the compromised robot as a stealthy adversary in the system-theoretic sense: it is limited not by an energy bound but by the team's own detectors. We then derive two bounds. First, the probability that the adversary's reports are verified is bounded below in terms of the degrees in the communication graph and the verification budget. Second, the map error caused by any stealthy adversary is bounded above by the value of a linear program over the adversary's bias distributions; its solution is an exchange rate between stealth budget and damage: below a critical verification level the worst stealthy attack tells rare, full-magnitude lies on the records least likely to be verified, and above it the better purchase is small biases hidden in the noise. In experiments where the honest robots are LLM agents, both bounds hold at the budget the attack actually spent. The experiments also show that which records an LLM robot re-checks is unbiased, but how much it re-checks is unpredictable.
authors: Sribalaji C. Anand, George J. Pappas
bullets: Studies stealthy insider attacks in multi-robot LLM teams performing physically verifiable surveys.
Derives a lower bound on how often adversarial reports are verified using communication-graph degrees and verification budget.
Bounds worst-case map error via a linear program over adversarial bias distributions.
Finds a tradeoff: rare, full-scale lies are optimal below a critical verification level, while small noise-hidden biases are preferable above it.
LLM-agent experiments support both bounds; re-check choices appear unbiased, but re-check magnitudes are unpredictable.

papers.selection_reason: Investigates stealthy insider attacks on LLM-based robot teams, analyzing the interaction between LLM agents and verification budgets in a grounded task.
papers.title: Lie Rarely, Lie Big: Stealthy Insider Attacks on LLM Robot Teams
papers.tldr: A single compromised LLM-controlled robot can stealthily distort a robot team’s survey map by exploiting limited verification budgets, with attack strategies changing sharply at a critical verification level.

papers.abstract: Numerical Linear Algebra (NLA) has consistently played a vital role in advancing science by providing tools to solve fundamental problems encountered in scientific and engineering applications. Over the decades, it has continually evolved to meet the demands driven by successive waves of scientific discovery. For instance, during the 1950s and 1960s, substantial efforts were devoted to developing methods for solving eigenvalue problems that emerged from the rapidly growing field of aerodynamics. This led to the discovery of the LR and QR algorithms. Later the attention turned to the solution of sparse linear systems that were common in applications like computational aerodynamics. Today we are experiencing yet another wave of major scientific advancement and NLA is once more at the heart of its development. This Machine Learning (ML) wave is proving to be utterly disruptive in science and engineering. Many tools in ML particularly Large Language Models (LLMs) are grounded in matrix and tensor methods. As we are approaching Artificial General Intelligence (AGI), it is clear that matrix methods will be called to play an even more significant role. For the numerical linear practitioner the speed of the current change makes it particularly challenging to adapt. This is a survey article that centers on machine learning techniques, with a particular focus on large language models. It has two main objectives. The first is to clarify the core concepts behind Large Language Models in a manner accessible to specialists in numerical methods. The second is to examine the key Numerical Linear Algebra concepts employed by LLM techniques, while also highlighting several significant recent contributions of NLA to the field.
bullets: Motivates NLA’s renewed importance during the current machine-learning-driven wave of scientific advancement.
Introduces core LLM concepts for readers specializing in numerical methods.
Examines matrix and tensor methods central to LLM techniques.
Highlights significant recent contributions from NLA to machine learning.
Provides context for the growing role of matrix methods as research approaches AGI.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Major milestones in the evolution of artificial intelligence. The timeline highlights selected developments that shaped the field, from early perceptrons and expert systems to deep neural networks, Transformers, and the current era of large language models and generative AI. It is intended as a schematic historical overview rather than an exhaustive chronology.

Figure 5: Components of artificial intelligence: the big picture. The schematic situates large language models within the broader AI landscape and highlights the interplay among core ingredients such as data, optimization, numerical linear algebra, hardware, and software frameworks. Its purpose is to emphasize that modern AI systems emerge from the interaction of several mathematical, algorithmic, and computational components rather than from a single isolated idea.

Figure 2: Growth of parameter sizes in large language models. The plot shows the rapid increase in parameter counts across representative models over time, from early Transformer-era systems to recent frontier models. The horizontal reference lines and the indicated “data wall” emphasize that simple parameter scaling cannot continue indefinitely and may eventually be constrained by data availability and practical training considerations.

Figure 4: Main ingredients of the recent AI wave. The schematic emphasizes the interaction among three mutually reinforcing factors: improved hardware, the availability of large amounts of data, and advances in methods and algorithms. Together, these ingredients explain much of the rapid progress of modern deep learning and large language models.

Figure 3: Order-of-magnitude argument for recent AI progress, adapted from [13]. The figure illustrates the claim that advances in effective compute, algorithmic efficiency, and related “unhobbling” factors may combine multiplicatively, leading to rapid capability gains over relatively short time scales. It is included as a schematic argument about scaling trends, not as a precise predictive model.

Figure 20: Decoder-only Transformer architecture. Repeated masked self-attention and feedforward updates act along a shared residual stream, producing contextual representations used for autoregressive prediction.

Figure 16: Schematic pipeline of a decoder-only large language model. Tokens are mapped to embeddings with positional structure, propagated through repeated Transformer blocks, and finally projected to logits for next-token prediction.

Figure 19: Encoder-decoder Transformer architecture. The encoder computes source-side contextual representations, while the decoder combines masked self-attention and encoder-decoder attention to generate target-side outputs.

Figure 6: A simple multilayer perceptron with three hidden layers. The input vector x is propagated through successive affine transformations and nonlinear activation functions to produce the final output ϕ(x). The figure is intended to illustrate the layered composition that underlies feed-forward neural networks and serves here mainly to establish notation.

Figure 26: Empirical power-law scaling in large language models. Test loss decreases L(N, D) predictably as model size N , dataset size D, and compute budget C increase, following approximate power-law relationships. The schematic summarizes the scaling-law perspective that performance improves smoothly with scale, with diminishing returns captured by the exponents in L(N, D) defined in (3.16.1)

Figure 17: Sinusoidal positional encoding coordinates across dimensions. Each subplot shows the two coordinates P (i, 2j) = sin ( i/100002j/dmodel ) and P (i, 2j + 1) = cos ( i/100002j/dmodel ) as functions of token position i for a representative pair of dimensions. Low-index dimensions vary rapidly with position, while higher-index dimensions vary more slowly, so the encoding provides a multiscale representation of sequence order.

Figure 30: Gradient descent versus natural gradient descent on a two-dimensional Gaussian model with direction-dependent geometry. The left panel shows the decay of the objective L(w) over the iterations, while the right panel displays the corresponding trajectories on the loss surface. Standard gradient descent is slowed by the distorted geometry of the parametrization, whereas natural gradient descent accounts for this geometry through the Fisher metric and converges much more rapidly. Standard (Cauchy) steepest descent is shown by blue plus markers, while natural gradient descent is shown by red circles.

Figure 23: Training and inference in a decoder-only Transformer. During training, the model processes an entire token sequence in parallel and adjusts its weights so that the output probabilities match the target next tokens at all positions. During inference, by contrast, generation is autoregressive: the predicted next token is fed back as input, and the process is repeated sequentially.

Figure 27: Teacher–student knowledge distillation. A pretrained teacher model produces logits and softened output probabilities for the training data, and a smaller student model is trained to match these outputs while also fitting the original targets. The distillation loss transfers information from the teacher’s predictive distribution to the student, allowing the student to imitate the teacher’s behavior with a more compact model.

Figure 18: Pre-LayerNorm Transformer block at layer ℓ. The block applies layer normalization before the attention and MLP sublayers, and writes both outputs additively into the same residual stream. This makes the block an identity-plus-correction map composed of token mixing through attention and channel mixing through the MLP.

Figure 25: Pre-LN Transformer layer as residual-stream accumulation. The input residual stream xℓ−1 is updated by adding the attention-block contribution aℓ and the MLP-block contribution mℓ, giving xℓ = xℓ−1 + aℓ + mℓ. Across layers, the residual stream can be expanded as xℓ = x0 +∑ℓ i=1 ai +∑ℓ i=1 mi, showing how attention and MLP updates accumulate additively through the network.

Figure 12: Recovering an underlying function from noisy data. The figure illustrates the basic problem used to motivate attention: given a cloud of noisy training points (xi, yi), estimate the value of an unknown function at a new query point. In the numerical-analysis viewpoint this suggests interpolation or least-squares approximation, whereas in the machine-learning viewpoint it motivates weighted averaging based on relevance, i.e., attention.

Figure 14: Nadaraya–Watson kernel regression on periodic data. The figure compares an attentionbased kernel-regression estimate with a classical low-degree approximation for an oscillatory target function. In this setting, the similarity-based weighted average captures the periodic behavior more accurately than a simple cubic approximation, illustrating how attention can recover useful structure directly from data when the functional form is not known in advance.

Figure 24: Concentration of pairwise angles in high dimension. The figure shows the distribution of angles between 10,000 random vectors in a 12,288-dimensional embedding space. The sharp concentration around 90◦, together with the narrow 88◦–92◦ band, illustrates the near-orthogonality phenomenon that characterizes random directions in high-dimensional spaces.

Figure 28: Forward step in LoRa. A frozen pretrained weight matrix W0 is augmented by a trainable low-rank update AB, where A ∈ Rd×r, B ∈ Rr×dv , and r ≪ min(d, dv). Instead of updating the full weight matrix, LoRa keeps W0 fixed and learns only the small-rank factors A, and B, thereby reducing the number of trainable parameters while preserving the original forward structure.

Figure 13: Illustration of Nadaraya–Watson kernel regression. Given a query point q, the prediction is formed as a weighted average of the observed values vi, with weights that depend on the similarity between q and the keys ki. This provides a useful bridge to attention, where output representations are likewise obtained by similarity-based weighted averaging.
Figure 29: Illustration of linearized attention. If the softmax is temporarily omitted, the attention map takes the form A (lin)

Figure 7: A simple multilayer perceptron with two hidden layers. The figure illustrates the layer structure used in the classification example and, together with Table 1, helps explain the dimensions of the weight matrices and the total number of trainable parameters.

Figure 8: A simple computational graph for composite-function evaluation. The leaf nodes x, y, and z are primary variables; the intermediate nodes a(x, y, z), b(x, y, z) and c(x, y, z) are derived quantities; and the root node is the target function. The figure illustrates how forward evaluation computes intermediate quantities first, while reverse-mode differentiation (back-propagation) propagates derivatives backward from f to the leaves via the chain rule.

Figure 21: Post-LayerNorm and Pre-LayerNorm Transformer blocks. In the Post-LayerNorm form, normalization is applied after each residual addition, whereas in the Pre-LayerNorm form, it is applied before each sublayer. The comparison highlights that Pre-LayerNorm preserves an exact identity path along the residual stream, which is one reason it is favored in modern LLMs.

Figure 10: A local computational-graph view of one neural-network layer. The figure shows how the pre-activation sℓ = W T ℓ zℓ−1 + bℓ is formed from the previous-layer representation zℓ−1, the weight matrix Wℓ, and the bias bℓ and is then mapped by the activation function σ to produce zℓ. It illustrates how each layer of a neural network can be interpreted as a small computational subgraph whose variables participate in forward evaluation and back-propagation. The circled nodes represent input or parameter variables, whereas the rectangular nodes represent computational operations or derived quantities.

Figure 11: Backward propagation in a multilayer perceptron. The figure schematically illustrates the reverse flow of derivatives through the layered computational graph associated with equations (2.6.9)– (2.6.12). Starting from the loss η, sensitivities are propagated backward through the intermediate states s3, s2, s1 in order to compute gradients with respect to the parameters (W3, b3), (W2, b2), and (W1, b1).

Figure 15: High-level view of autoregressive language modeling. Given a context u < t = (u1, . . . , ut−1), the model assigns a probability distribution to the next token ut, and text generation proceeds by repeating this prediction step sequentially.

Figure 9: Local back-propagation step at an intermediate node in a computational graph. Assuming the partial derivatives of the objective f with respect to the downstream nodes aj, aℓ, and am are already known, the derivative with respect to the current node ak is obtained by applying the chain rule and summing the contributions along all outgoing paths. The figure illustrates the recursive local structure that underlies reverse-mode automatic differentiation.

Figure 22: Generic residual unit in Post-LayerNorm and Pre-LayerNorm form. In both cases the sublayer contributes a learned correction F to the incoming state, but the location of normalization differs: Post-LayerNorm applies normalization after the residual sum, whereas Pre-LayerNorm applies it before the sublayer.

Table 1: Dimensions and parameter counts for a simple multilayer perceptron. The table lists the sizes of the weight matrices and bias vectors for each layer in the digit-classification example, together with the corresponding number of trainable parameters. It illustrates how the total parameter count is determined directly by the layer widths. The total number of parameters is 51,210

Table 2: Comparison of key architectural hyperparameters for GPT-3 175B and Llama-3 405B. The table shows that, although both models follow the decoder-only Transformer template, they differ substantially in vocabulary size, depth, model width, feed-forward dimension, head configuration, and activation design.

Table 6: Illustrative low-rank concentration of gradient energy. The table shows a normalized singular-value distribution ∑i σi = 1, for which the cumulative energy exceeds 90% within roughly 10 components. Despite the ambient parameter dimension D = 110× 106, most of the gradient energy is concentrated in a very low-dimensional subspace, illustrating the motivation behind low-rank gradient methods.

Table 4: Parameter breakdown of Llama-3 405B by major architectural component. The table decomposes the total parameter count into attention, MLP, embedding/unembedding, and normalization contributions, illustrating that the gated MLP blocks account for the dominant share of parameters in this model.

Table 5: Representative model dimensions illustrating the scale of modern embedding spaces. The table lists the model dimension dmodel for GPT-2, GPT-3, GPT-4, and Llama-3 405B, showing that contemporary large language models operate in ambient spaces of dimension on the order of 104. Such dimensions help explain why many randomly chosen directions are nearly orthogonal, as illustrated in Figure 24.

Table 3: Parameter breakdown of GPT-3 175B by major architectural component. The table decomposes the total parameter count into attention, MLP, embedding/unembedding, and normalization contributions, illustrating that the dense MLP blocks dominate the parameter budget.

papers.abstract: On-policy distillation (OPD) has emerged as a widely used paradigm for post-training large language models, reducing the train--test mismatch of conventional distillation by supervising the student on its own generated trajectories. However, existing OPD objectives remain largely token-local and outcome-agnostic, optimizing teacher--student agreement at each prefix despite reasoning quality being determined at the trajectory level. Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR), particularly Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), provides complementary outcome-level supervision but suffers from sparse rewards and coarse credit assignment. We show that OPD and RLVR exhibit complementary blind spots: teacher signals provide dense local guidance but are weakly aligned with rollout correctness, whereas group-relative rewards capture task success but provide coarse token-level credit and vanish on all-failure groups. We introduce DiffGate, an outcome-gated objective that combines GRPO with selective, bounded teacher guidance. Teacher supervision is applied only to failed trajectories, scaled by group difficulty, and smoothly bounded to prevent extreme teacher--student discrepancies from dominating optimization. The verifier therefore determines \emph{which trajectories} receive teacher guidance, while the teacher provides dense token-level update directions within those trajectories. Across Qwen3-0.6B and Qwen3-1.7B students, DiffGate improves code avg@8 over matched GRPO by $+1.7$ and $+1.8$ points and pass@8 by $+1.6$ and $+5.7$ points, respectively. On mathematics, avg@8 remains within $0.5$ points of GRPO while pass@8 improves by $+1.1$ and $+3.9$ points. Overall, DiffGate improves pass@8 across all four model--domain settings, demonstrating improved solution coverage under our evaluation protocol.
authors: Karn Tiwari, Varnith Chordia, Prathosh A P
bullets: Addresses the mismatch between token-level teacher agreement and trajectory-level reasoning correctness.
Applies bounded teacher supervision only to failed trajectories, with guidance scaled by group difficulty.
Uses verifier outcomes to select trajectories and the teacher to provide dense token-level updates.
Improves pass@8 across all evaluated model–domain settings, with reported gains in code and mathematics.
Evaluation covers Qwen3-0.6B and Qwen3-1.7B on code and mathematics under the stated protocol.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of DiffGate. The student generates on-policy trajectories that receive sequence-level correctness feedback from a verifier and token-level guidance from a frozen teacher. DiffGate bounds the sampled-token teacher–student log-probability gap, applies teacher guidance only to failed trajectories, and scales its strength according to the group solve rate. The resulting token-level advantage combines local teacher guidance with the global GRPO outcome signal to update the student policy. See Algorithm 1 for details.

Figure 4: Performance over training. avg@8 (top) and pass@8 (bottom) across training checkpoints for the 1.7B student on the code benchmarks in Table 2. Step 0 denotes the base model (dotted line), enabling comparison of how each method improves accuracy and solution coverage.

Figure 3: Why DiffGate helps. Maths, 1.7B student; all methods use the same data, teacher, and step budget. (a) Student gradient norm over training: the bar denotes the median and the whisker spans minimum to maximum, shown on a log scale. (b) Policy entropy, shown as a five-step rolling mean; the dotted line marks 0.1. (c) The two components of DiffGate’s update on failed rollouts: the applied teacher term per token (dark blue) and the magnitude of the GRPO advantage per token (light blue). The GRPO advantage is zero for an all-failure group and, with n = 16, is approximately 0.25 or larger for groups with 1–8 successes and approximately 1.10 or larger for groups with 9 or more successes, ignoring the small ε term; values are weighted by the measured frequency of each group type. The grey region indicates this approximate lower-bound contribution. (d) Applied teacher term per response token under difficulty-gated and additive weighting on the same rollouts.

Figure 7: Teacher-side training dynamics: GRPO, OPD and DiffGate. Columns are the four model–domain settings. GRPO and DiffGate use n=16 rollouts and the outcome reward, DiffGate adding the gated teacher term; the two OPD baselines use one rollout per prompt and no reward. All four share data, teacher, and step budget. Faint traces are per-step values, bold lines are a five-step rolling mean. Rows: mean ∆ over all response tokens, and the teacher’s log-likelihood of the student’s own samples.

Figure 10: Performance over training. avg@8 (top) and pass@8 (bottom) on the benchmark sets of Tables 1 and 2; step 0 is the base model (dotted line). GRPO and DiffGate were evaluated at steps 50 and 62 on code, and GRPO at steps 50, 100, 150 and 171 on mathematics; their other points are filled in as described in the text.

Figure 9: Training reward, response length and policy entropy. Rows: verifier pass rate of the n=16 rollouts on each step’s training prompts; mean response length in tokens; mean token entropy of the student. Faint traces are per-step values, bold lines a five-step rolling mean. DiffGate is a dense retrain; the remaining arms are the original runs. The reverse-KL arm’s solve rate is a single-sample diagnostic, not the quantity it optimises.

Figure 5: Hyperparameter sweep, 1.7B student. Teacher strength λ (left) and difficulty sharpness γ (right), for mathematics (top) and code (bottom); avg@8 on the left axis, pass@8 on the right. Every point is DiffGate at a different setting, so this figure varies one constant rather than comparing arms. Hollow markers are the reported configuration λ = γ = 1.

Figure 1: Teacher disagreement alone does not reliably identify incorrect rollouts. For a distillation-only Qwen3-1.7B student evaluated with a frozen Qwen3-8B teacher: (a) average token-level teacher–student disagreement distinguishes correct from incorrect rollouts only at chance level on mathematics (AUROC 0.50 and 0.49) and weakly on code (AUROC 0.60); (b) aggregate disagreement becomes more predictive mainly when it also reflects response length; and (c) within an incorrect rollout, large disagreement can occur on ordinary tokens rather than on the token associated with the decisive error. These observations motivate DiffGate to use the verifier to determine which trajectories receive teacher guidance, while the teacher provides the local token-level update direction. Further analysis is provided in Appendix Section B.

Figure 8: Reward-based routing of teacher guidance. the rows show: (1) the ratio of the all-token mean of −∆ to the failed-rollout mean of |∆|, with the dotted line marking a ratio of 1; (2) the fraction of the applied teacher contribution assigned to all-failure groups, together with the fraction of prompts belonging to such groups (dashed); (3) the effective gate factor, defined by the fraction of trajectories on which the gate fires multiplied by their mean difficulty weight; and (4) for DiffGate, the fraction of failed-rollout tokens on which the teacher signal opposes the outcome advantage.
Figure 6: Student gradient norm over training. Bars: median. Whiskers: minimum to maximum step, with the maximum printed above. Log scale.

Table 4: Training and evaluation configuration. Shared across methods unless otherwise specified. Training uses 128 prompts per step. The mathematics and code training sets contain 21,928 and 4,082 prompts, respectively; the reported budgets correspond to approximately 1.00 and 1.94 dataset passes. GRPO-based methods differ only in their teacher-guidance configuration.
Table 2: Code generation results. We report avg@8 and pass@8 on MBPP+, HumanEval+, and LiveCodeBench. Bold and underlined values indicate the best and second-best student results, respectively.

Table 1: Mathematical reasoning results. We report avg@8 and pass@8, with GRPO serving as the outcome-only baseline. Bold and underlined values indicate the best and second-best student results, respectively. The science (OOD) columns report average performance on GPQA, MMLU-STEM, and OlympiadBench-Physics (Table 6), evaluated using the mathematics-trained students without additional science training.
Table 3: Summary of notation. Symbols used for the policy setup, outcome supervision, teacher guidance, and DiffGate optimization.

Table 6: Out-of-distribution transfer to Science. avg@8 / pass@8 of mathematics-trained students on GPQA, MMLU-STEM and OlympiadBench-Physics, with no science training; the final columns average the three and are the science columns of Table 1. Bold / underline: best / second-best per student.

Table 9: Effect of rollout group size. GRPO and DiffGate trained with n=16 and n=4 rollouts per prompt, holding data, teacher, optimizer, and budget fixed; averages over the benchmark sets of Tables 1 and 2. The n=16 rows are the runs of Tables 1 and 2. Bold marks the better of the two arms within each group size.

Table 14: Teacher-side diagnostics over training. Each entry reports start → end, where start” averages the first five training steps and end” averages the final ten. For GRPO, teacher-derived quantities are computed only for diagnostic purposes and are never used for optimization; rows that require an applied teacher update are therefore left blank. The disagreement block reports the raw teacher–student log-probability difference ∆ before bounding, evaluated on teacher-scored tokens. The gradient row instead reports the median/maximum gradient norm over the full training run.

Table 13: Advantage and teacher-signal statistics over training. “Start” is the mean of the two arms at step 1; GRPO and DiffGate report averages over the final ten steps. Reward-uniform groups (all-fail or all-pass) have zero group-relative advantage. We measure teacher-signal statistics only on failed rollouts, and we average over the final block of all generated response tokens.
Table 10: Bounded versus unbounded teacher term. Top: held-out avg@8 / pass@8 of the two DiffGate variants. Bottom: median and maximum student gradient norm over training.

Table 15: Performance across base-student difficulty bands. Problems are grouped by the number of successful responses produced by the base student out of 16. “Teacher pass@16” denotes the fraction of problems in each band for which the Qwen3-8B teacher produces at least one correct response under the same sampling protocol. Base, GRPO, and DiffGate report the mean number of successful generations out of 16, and ∆ denotes DiffGate minus GRPO. “Wins” counts problems favoring DiffGate versus GRPO for which a two-proportion z-test comparing their 16 sampled outcomes satisfies |z| ≥ 2, with DiffGate listed first.
Table 5: Training cost. Wall-clock hours on 4× A100-80GB for the runs behind main Tables 1 and 2.

Table 8: Code generation with a Qwen3-4B student and Qwen3-8B teacher. Avg@8 and pass@8 on MBPP+, HumanEval+, and LiveCodeBench. Bold and underline denote the best and second-best student results, respectively.

Table 7: Mathematical reasoning with a Qwen3-4B student and Qwen3-14B teacher. Avg@8 and pass@8 across five mathematics benchmarks. Bold and underline denote the best and second-best student results, respectively.
Table 12: Selector and additive controls. All rows add the teacher term to GRPO; the first three apply it to every rollout. Bold and underlined: best and second-best per column.

Table 11: Difficulty gating against the additive baseline. Both arms are GRPO plus the same bounded teacher term on failed trajectories, matched on data, teacher, n=16 rollouts, and step budget. They differ only in that term’s weight: constant (additive, γ=0) against the failed fraction of the group (DiffGate, γ=1).
